en: Chapter 2, Pāda 1 // Now begins the section on Smṛti in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā // 5.1 // That state which is perceivable through the Veda, even to be seen by a mere glance—
Those of wavering minds cannot endure him; we worship that Lord of Śrī.

Desiring to state the subject matter of the second chapter in its logical connection with the subject matter of the first chapter for the sake of establishing their syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), [the author] first restates the subject matter of the first chapter— since a connection cannot be demonstrated with something not present to the mind— with the words:
"It has been stated."
The direct concordance has been stated... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.1a]

In Nārāyaṇa— the Supreme Brahman, who is the instrumental cause of the birth and so forth of the entire world, who is replete with infinite qualities such as omniscience and omnipotence, and who is entirely free from even a trace of defects such as ignorance— in Him, the entirety of the scripture, consisting of vowels, consonants, words, sentences, and great sentences, functions by its direct, primary, and most eminent sense, and not by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The meaning is that in the first chapter, the *samanvaya* (harmonization) was established by means of the primary purport (*mahātātparya*), and not by way of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*).
Although the sense of "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is already obtained by the word *samanvaya* itself,
there is no fault in providing this explanation in order to indicate that one must be attentive to the refutation of the interpretation of the prefix *sam* offered by others.
Alternatively, by the word "samanvaya" (concordance), "anvaya" (connection) is understood in its primary sense;
however, the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is used to show that connection in its most primary sense.

Or rather, he explains by this [word] that it is not through an indirect succession—by means of the refutation of [theories such as] Pradhāna or atoms, nor by the demonstration of [Brahman's] being the material cause—but indeed directly.
Having thus stated the subject matter of the first chapter, he states the subject matter of the second chapter as being connected to it: "Non-contradiction" (avirodha).
...non-contradiction is established here. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.1.1b)

Regarding this stated matter, the absence of contradiction— that is, the lack of conflict— is established here in the second chapter (*adhyāya*), which is present to the intellect because it is intended to be explained.
By this, the connection between this chapter and the preceding one, characterized by the relationship of cause and effect, is indicated.

Indeed, it is precisely through the synthesis of all the scriptures that the Supreme Brahman is declared to be the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe, to be entirely full of all excellences, and to be devoid of every defect; for otherwise, a contradiction would manifest there,
as [the attributes] would lack a substratum.
The opportunity for establishing the absence of that [contradiction] arises only when there is the manifestation of contradiction, and not otherwise;
for a negation is impossible regarding what has not been reached.
Therefore, it is determined that the subject matter of the preceding chapter is the cause and the subject matter of this chapter is the effect.

Alternatively, even an object established through the systematic interpretation of the scriptures does not become firmly rooted for the listeners as long as the absence of contradiction regarding that comprehension is not proven;
for there arises a suspicion of the very lack of authority of the scriptures due to perceived contradiction.
And thus, it results in a mere unestablished conceptualization;
however, when establishing the absence of contradiction, it indeed becomes firmly established,
as it has been said:
"Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is the determination of the object through the consideration of the thesis and the counter-thesis.
Therefore, the connection between these two is characterized by a reversed relationship of cause and effect. [Objection:
But surely, the contradiction regarding the stated meaning has already been resolved in various places.
What remains here [to be explained] such that another chapter must be commenced for its sake?
True.
The Teacher will respond to this:

"But if, in this way, the entire chapter constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) because it has a single purpose characterized by non-contradiction (*avirodha-lakṣaṇa*), then what is the basis for the division into sections (*pāda-bheda*)? Furthermore, in that case, what is the basis for this particular section being first? To address this expectation, he says: "Of the fourfold... (*caturvidhasya*).
Of that fourfold [dharma], at the beginning, the one consistent with reason... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.1.1c //
The genitive case in *tasya* (of that) is used for specification;
it refers to the beginning, namely the first quarter-verse (*pāda*).
The phrase "non-contradiction is established" is understood to carry over [from the previous context].

Because of the reference to "that which is fourfold," it is understood that "it is fourfold. This is the meaning: *5,17* This is the sense: [the non-contradiction] is established; by the restatement of "of that which is fourfold," it is obtained that "it is fourfold.
*5,17* This is the meaning.
Although one sense is that there is no contradiction regarding the stated meaning,

nevertheless, by way of its internal subdivisions— consisting in the absence of contradiction with reasoning (*yukti*), established convention (*samaya*), sacred tradition (*śruti*), and logic (*nyāya*)— it becomes fourfold. By demonstrating those [subdivisions], the distinction between the four quarters (*pāda*) is justified.
Among these four kinds of absence of contradiction, the absence of contradiction with reasoning (*yukti-virodhābhāva*) is established in the first chapter (*pāda*).
This is because all other contradictions depend upon reasoning; since contradiction with reasoning is the most powerful, it is logical that its absence be established first.
Because it is based on reasoning and depends upon reasoning, contradiction with reasoning is the most forceful, and thus it is appropriate that its absence be proven at the outset.
And because this treatise of investigation proceeds by means of employing reasoning (*yukti*).
Now, one might ask: how can non-existence (*abhāva*) be of four kinds?
It is said: for there are four kinds of contradictories,
namely reasoning (*yukti*) and so forth.
Because it is based upon that [non-existence], contradiction (*virodha*) is also said to be fourfold;
consequently, the absence (*abhāva*) which is its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is likewise so designated.
For this very reason, it is logically established that it is "proper" (*yukta*).
Because even non-existence (*abhāva*) is indirectly connected to reasoning (*yukti*);
or else, it refers back to "contradiction" (*virodha*) as being brought to mind by the proximity of the word "non-contradiction.
And thus, since contradiction is fourfold through its association with reasoning and so forth, a division of chapters is appropriate for the purpose of establishing that [non-existence].

Among those four types of contradiction, since the contradiction that is logical is the most powerful—according to the manner stated at the outset—it should be understood that its absence is established here first.
Alternatively, the word "tasya" (of that) refers back to the contradictory;
for that too is present in the mind by virtue of being associated with the term "non-contradiction."
For non-opposition is defined in dependence upon the definition of opposition;
and opposition is not possible without that which opposes.

Furthermore, since the opposites are fourfold according to the distinctions of reasoning (*yukti*) and so forth, the division of the chapters is justified by the establishment of the absence of contradiction with respect to each of them.

Among those four types of opposites, because reasoning is the most powerful, it should be understood that first the absence of contradiction pertaining to reasoning—that which is connected to reasoning—is established. (5.20)
Regarding this, he states a specific distinction in the first section: "tatrāpi" (even there).
And in that case as well, it is because of memory. (Manu 2.1d)
This is for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the phrase "at the beginning of a quarter" (*pādādau*).
Alternatively, it is intended to indicate a suspicion of impropriety (*anaucitya*) even in that which establishes the absence of contradiction with reason, by means of the word "quarter" (*pāda*).
By the word "and" (*ca*), the fact that there is no contradiction is established; this [phrase] is what is carried over.
Regarding the Smṛti of the Pāśupatas and others:

although the connection of the word "smṛteḥ" with the meaning of the negative particle is not logically possible, and because contradiction is subordinate within a compound, nevertheless, a connection with that [Smṛti] is possible when it is mentally distinguished [from the other term]. (5.22)

In this section (pāda), which has the characteristic of resolving contradictions with reasoning (*yukti*), a resolution of contradictions with Smṛti should not be undertaken because it would be irrelevant; or, even if it were to be undertaken, why should it come first? To this he says: "Of that" (*tasyāḥ*).
Because it possesses four aspects... // MAnu 2.1.2a //
This is because that *smṛti* of the Pāśupatas and others possesses a fourfold nature consisting of contradictions with reasoning (*yukti*), established tenets (*samaya*), and so forth.
What is meant is this:

for although the *smṛtis* of the Pāśupatas and others are of the nature of established tenets (*samaya*) by virtue of being the words of those whom they themselves regard as authoritative, they nevertheless possess a fourfold nature consisting of contradictions with reasoning, established tenets, and so forth, as they attempt to corroborate their own intended meanings with reasonings and *śruti* [scriptures].
Consequently, once the subject matter has been stated, the resolution of contradictions with that [subject] is indeed included within the chapter;
however, although it is connected to the meaning of all four quarters (pādas),
it is not extracted and included in any single quarter alone.
Therefore, it should be stated either at the beginning or at the end of the chapter;

furthermore, since there is no reason whatsoever for skipping the first [case], this is established in the initial section (*ādyādhikaraṇa*). And thus, even though the phrase "and there too, because of tradition" (*tatrāpi ca smṛteḥ*) serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to what was previously stated, it is understood that this does not apply in every respect.

Furthermore, because contradictions regarding the *samaya* (traditional tenets) and so forth can also be resolved, and because contradictions with reasoning (*yukti*) can be included by virtue of the absence of distinct categories (*pādārtha*), it is possible for them to be subsumed [within the fourfold structure].

By describing how a single *adhikaraṇa* (section) possesses a fourfold nature through its connection to the meanings of the four quarters (*pāda*), [the author] speaks of another fourfold classification as well—in order to generate great respect for the treatise among the students by means of this incidental discussion—saying: "Each one... (*pratyekam*).
Each of these consists of four parts;
all the quarters and their respective portions are thus.
Each of the four quarters should be understood as having a fourfold nature, possessing the meaning of all four quarters.
For example,

this quarter, while characterized by the avoidance of contradiction with reasoning, also consists of the avoidance of contradiction with the three [points] beginning with the formal agreement (samaya).

Likewise, the second [section], characterized by the avoidance of contradictions with the *samaya*, also consists of the avoidance of contradictions regarding the triad beginning with reasoning (*yukti*), and so forth.
When only "the feet" (*pādāḥ*) are mentioned, it is understood that they belong specifically to this chapter because of their immediate proximity;
for that reason, the word "all" (*sarve*) is stated.
The meaning is that this applies even to those belonging to all chapters.
Whatever quarter (pāda) occurs within a particular chapter should be understood as conveying the meaning of the four quarters contained within that chapter.
It is not only the chapters that are thus, but also their parts; "tadaṃśāḥ" means those which have those [chapters] as their parts, namely the sections (adhyāyas).
This implies that the first chapter establishes not only the concordance (*samanvaya*), but also the other three topics, such as non-contradiction (*avirodha*) and so forth.
Since the fourfold nature of the quarters is established, the same applies to the topics (*adhikaraṇas*).
Nor should it be argued that this results in an inconsistency regarding the division of chapters and so forth, or the fault of redundancy;
for there is consistency due to the difference in intended meaning (*vivakṣābheda*).
When the first meaning of "concordance" (samanvaya) is intended to be expressed, then the others do not have that as their meaning, and so forth.
[The verse] beginning with "anyat" shows the fourfold nature of the treatise: "of the forms," etc. (*5,24*) //1//
...the color of the images according to the traditional scriptures. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.2d)
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: one should understand that He possesses a fourfold nature also by virtue of being the proponent of the four forms beginning with Vāsudeva.
To the objection, "But this has already been stated;
why is it said again?", he says: "the color," etc.
In this context, the connection of two factors should be understood as being derived from traditional authority (āgama).
Therein, the first [factor] has the sense of "starting from," while the second is used in the sense of "inclusive limit" (abhividhi).
"Āgama" refers to the treatise consisting of four chapters.
Consequently, this is the meaning:
not only with respect to each syllable, each word, each sūtra, or each topical section, but rather starting from a single phoneme contained within this treatise up to the entire treatise.
The meaning is that four forms (mūrtis) are propounded in each section (adhikaraṇa), each quarter (pāda), each chapter (adhyāya), and by the entire scripture (śāstra).
From what is this to be understood? To this he says: "From scripture" (āgamāt).
The meaning is "from the *Bṛhattantra* and other such works.

He states the arguments for the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of this section of the chapter in brief, beginning with the words "authoritativeness" (*āptatā*).
Trustworthiness arises from the power of impartiality, vision, learning, and equanimity;
it consists in following all [duties], lightness [of conduct], and being free from the fruit of perceiving distinctions.
The accomplishment of one's desires and the restrictive rules regarding the prima facie views (pūrvapakṣas) are the logical arguments;
these very factors, when exceedingly powerful, are the determinants of the final conclusion (siddhānta).

Having raised an objection against the stated meaning on the grounds of its contradiction with other Smṛtis, the Sūtra provides a resolution: "If it be argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for Smṛti, we say no, because that would entail the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis. Om.
Thus [ends the objection]. Its meaning is as follows:

that which was stated—that the Supreme Brahman Viṣṇu is the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire world, that He is complete in all qualities such as omniscience, and that He is remote from all defects—is untenable.
Because it contradicts the Smṛtis of the Pāśupatas, Sāṅkhyas, Buddhists, Ārhatas, and others;
for those [Smṛtis] establish that Śiva and the rest alone are the cause of the world's birth and so forth.
And there is no other scope for them by which we might perceive an absence of intent (tātparya) regarding the meaning already established [by the Veda].
Otherwise, those Smṛtis would face the fault of invalidity due to having no scope [for application].
That is not so;
for it is the Supreme Person alone who is declared by the Pañcarātra and other Smṛtis to be the cause of the entire universe and so forth.
Otherwise, because there would be no room for other Smṛtis such as the Pañcarātra and so forth— distinct from those such as the Pāśupata— the fault of their lack of authority would follow.
In this regard, the objection raised is indeed improper.
Because this meaning has been established through the systematic concordance of the Vedas (śruti-samanvaya),
and because it is accepted that those Smṛtis which contradict the Vedas lack authority.

Furthermore, because even the Smṛtis such as the Pāśupata and others possess scope— either through their concordance with the Supreme Brahman according to the logic of the concordance of Śruti, or by being devoted to the worship of Śiva and so forth—
this rebuttal is also untenable.
Having stated that the aforementioned matter is established by the authority of all the Śāstras, there is now no reason for citing Smṛti alone.
Having understood the fault intended by the opponent, it is improper to abandon the scripture;
rather, that fault must be refuted.
Otherwise, even previously, the scripture would have been unacceptable.

Furthermore, the opponent himself must admit that the *Smṛtis* such as the *Pañcarātra* lack authority; moreover, because they are devoted to the worship of Vāsudeva and so forth, their validity could be considered to have a limited scope (*sāvakāśatā*). Even if one were to attempt to establish parity [between the Vedas and these texts], victory would belong to the opponent alone, as it would obstruct the certainty [of the Vedas' authority]. Therefore, he revives the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), which is otherwise baseless, with the words: "By the authoritative ones... (*āptaiḥ*). (5.27)
If it is argued that this leads to the fault of leaving no room for the *smṛti* tradition, we say no; for that would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other *smṛtis*.

How could the *Śruti*, which was proclaimed by authoritative persons after perceiving the matter directly, be set aside by a *smṛti* that resembles the scribblings of ants? For those [authorities] are all-pervading.
This is the underlying intention of the opponent here:
one who desires the invalidity of the Smṛtis on account of their contradiction with Śruti must, in every respect, establish their relative strength and weakness;
otherwise, there would be an over-extension of the principle.
The relative strength or weakness [of a cognition] does not depend on the presence or absence of causes for its validity,
because validity is accepted as being intrinsic (svataḥ),
and because the opposite would also follow.
For the authority of a statement depends on the reliability of the speaker; and the authors of the Smṛtis are reliable,
whereas the author of the Śruti is not.
Because it is accepted as being of non-human origin;
for this very reason, [the Veda] possesses a foundation while the Smṛtis lack one, since the Smṛtis are rooted in authoritative tradition.
Because that [distinction] is not heard [in scripture];
nor is it established by being produced or unproduced,
since the essential nature [of these properties] is irrelevant to the matter.
This is because it is the opposite of the manner described above.

This very point has been stated by authoritative teachers such as Rudra, Kapila, and Kamalāsana: "The meaning declared regarding Śiva and others being the cause of the world and so forth is devoid of prior intention, resembling the scribbling of ants."
The Śruti asks: "How could it [the Smṛti] set aside [the Śruti]?"—meaning, "Not at all.

Now, one might object: "In cases such as 'One should chant the Udgītha while touching the Audumbarī post,' we have observed that Smṛtis which contradict such Śrutis—for instance, the Smṛti stating 'The entire Audumbarī post must be covered'—lack authority; the same would apply here."
It would not be so, because of the disparity.
For those Smṛtis are held to be rooted in Śruti; therefore, their authority is desired on the grounds that they lead to the inference of the underlying Śruti.
Furthermore, since it is impossible for a Smṛti that contradicts Śruti to imply a foundational Śruti, its lack of authority is indeed appropriate.
As Jaimini has stated: "In case of contradiction, however, it should be disregarded; for [the inference of a Vedic text] occurs only when [no contradiction] exists.
But this is not the case here.
Because the Smṛtis such as the Pāśupata and others are based on the direct perception of Śiva and others, they lack a basis in the Śruti.
This is what he expresses by saying, "having seen it through direct perception."
[Objection: In that case, since the Smṛtis have scope according to the manner stated, let them lack authority due to their contradiction with the Śruti, which has no other scope.
[Reply: Not so;
for the opposite is true.
For the *smṛtis* speak with clarity and thus do not deserve to deviate from their intended meaning;

the *śrutis*, however, speak in an indistinct and scattered manner, concern subjects characterized by unstable and non-worldly linguistic conventions, consist of infinite and incomplete sentences that are impossible to master through study, and are observed not to be fixed upon any specific meaning.
For this very reason, you have undergone the exertion of investigation (*mīmāṃsā*).
This too has been "spoken with excellence" (*prakarṣeṇoktam*);
that is to say, it has been stated quite clearly.
And "fearing the script of ants" means that it is unclear (*asphuṭa*).
Furthermore, the Vedic scriptures (*śruti*) themselves have meanings that are not clearly defined.
Devoid of the tradition of the author’s own commentary, independent [treatises] are not capable of establishing any meaning whatsoever; rather,
they must be interpreted by following the words of authoritative persons (āpta) who perceive all objects through direct perception— whether innate, or attained through the power of yoga—
as it has been said:
"One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas"—
here, the mention of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa).
Thus, how could [the Itihāsas and Purāṇas] be capable of refuting the meanings stated in Smṛtis such as the Pāśupata?

This has been stated: since the Veda resembles the writing of ants and is incapable of establishing any meaning without corroboration, how could it—being dependent on the corroboration of their words—contradict that very object which those same authoritative persons (āpta) have seen directly and proclaimed? [For] its independence (*svātantrya*)...

Because it does not establish [the meaning] during the state [of the suffix], whereas in the case of dependence (*pāratantrya*), there is no contradiction at all; however, it must be interpreted solely in accordance with that [dependence]. *5,34*
This might be so if the authors of the Pāśupata and other Smṛtis were authoritative;
but why should they be so? To this he says: "For [they] are all-pervading," and so forth.
They are called "all-pervading" (sarvagāḥ) because they go to and understand everything;
this is an indication of their authoritative nature.
They are Rudra and the others.
The word "hi" indicates that [omniscience] is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that context;
or rather, it is omniscience itself that is being proven here through its establishment by valid cognition,
because the proof of anything else follows from that very [proof].
For instance:
Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Brahmā are well known in the Vedas, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas as being omniscient;
among them, it is Viṣṇu alone whose incarnations are Buddha, Ṛṣabha, and Kapila, the authors of the Buddhist and other Smṛtis.
And thus, due to the absence of delusion in them, there is also an absence of attachment and aversion, and consequently, the desire to deceive is eliminated.
Furthermore, their knowledge, intention, effort, the proficiency of the vocal organs (sthāna), and the articulatory organs (karaṇa) are ascertained by the mere fact of their instruction.
Moreover, their knowledge, intention, effort, the proficiency of the vocal organs, and the articulatory organs are ascertained by the mere fact of their instruction.
However, knowledge may be either true or false;
likewise, the desire [to speak] may be a wish to explain or a wish to deceive. Thus, a doubt remains.
In that regard, when there is a general certainty that "this person possesses this object" because they have reached a state of proficiency, that knowledge indeed occurs.

The ascertainment of truth—as in the case where travelers determine that "this forest has become familiar to these barbarians, and therefore they are experts in its paths"—is a certainty belonging solely to those travelers.
Furthermore, the desire to deceive is pervaded by the observation of a cause; it would exist only when such a cause is present.
And that [harm] is of two kinds:
either benefit to oneself or harm to others.
Now, when travelers are setting out on a wrong path, there is no benefit to the barbarians for themselves whatsoever.
Because one's own [body] has already been grasped;
because the body has other duties to perform; or, even if it did have such duties, it would be impossible to abandon it.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for those who are not insane do not inflict harm upon one who has done them no wrong,
nor is the mere harming of another the goal of human endeavor.
If that were the case, everyone would be able to deceive everyone else;
thus, even the intent to deceive is ruled out.

However, regarding objects concerning which one has not yet attained proficiency, the cessation of both delusion and the intent to deceive occurs through corroboration by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or through the efficacy of successful action (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*); for this reason, even barbarians (*mleñcha*) can be authoritative persons (*āpta*).
"How much more so, then, [beings] of great majesty such as Rudra and others?
Having thus stated the intention of the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra, he states the purport of the *siddhānta* (conclusive) sūtra with the words "iti cet" (if it be argued).
If this is so, then why are Rudra and the others, headed by Hari, not all-knowing? ... MAnu 2.1.6a-c.
The word "not" is to be supplied [to the previous statement].
Why?

Because if the authority of the Pāśupata and other Smṛtis were established as certain, then that which contradicts them—such as Viṣṇu being the cause of the entire universe and so forth—would be non-existent.
But it is not so,
because there is a counter-argument;
let us set aside for now the question of capacity.
For the Smṛtis such as the Pañcarātra are indeed observed to declare that Viṣṇu alone is the cause of the entire world and so forth.
Now, one might object: "If two contradictory means of valid cognition were equal in strength, there would be a 'counter-balanced' (satpratipakṣa) state;
but this is not the case here."

Because the *Smṛtis* such as the Pāśupata are composed by authoritative persons (*āpta*) and, due to their explicit declarations, leave no room for alternative interpretations, whereas the *Smṛtis* such as the Pañcarātra lack these qualities, [the author] says: "If... (*yadīti*).
"Omniscient" and "all-knowing" are indicators of being an authoritative person (*āpta*).
Viṣṇu and others, such as Nārada, are the authorities for the *Pañcarātra* and other scriptures as well;
the sense is that there is no specific reason [to prefer one over the other].
And this is an elliptical indication;
it should also be understood that [the Buddha] is without any opportunity for contradiction because he speaks with perfect clarity. *5,40*
To the question, "What follows from this if it is so?", he says: "Pride."
For pride would indeed be equal in both cases. (Manu 2.1.6cd)
The word "hi" indicates the reason.
Since it is so, therefore, in both cases—namely, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—the two traditional authorities (*smṛti*) would be equal.
And thus, the implication is that the *smṛtis* such as those of the Pāśupatas and others remain subject to counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*).
Is it not the case that those two which are contradictory do not possess equality,
since we observe the absence of such equality in the cognitions of mother-of-pearl and silver;
and those two which are equal do not possess contradiction?
Since [the qualities of] "white" and "long" do not exist in the cloth [itself],
how could there be the possibility of the Smṛti texts of the Pāśupatas and others being counter-evident (satpratipakṣatva)? Even if such a possibility existed, the opponent would have won.
Because it would be impossible to determine the final conclusion [of the system], he says: "The means of valid cognition" (māna).
In both cases, between two recollections, that which exists equally along with me as the original authority is alone valid; the other is invalid.
This is what is meant.
Only when there is no determination of a specific distinction does the state of being counterbalanced (satpratipakṣatva) exist;
in reality, however, one means of knowledge (māna) is accompanied by its root [justification], while the other is not.
[Objection: But if validity is determined by the presence of a root, does this not result in the fallacy that validity is extrinsic (paratastva)?
Not so;
for when a doubt regarding invalidity arises due to mutual contradiction, that doubt is removed by the fact that [the Smṛti] possesses a root.
Likewise, in the case of both [Smṛtis], that Smṛti such as the Pañcarātra which is equally rooted in a valid source and endowed with corroboration from other means of knowledge—
That alone should be the authority, and not the Pāśupata and other systems,
because they lack a root source and so forth;
therefore, it should be understood that the aforementioned fault does not apply.
For it will be stated that the Pañcarātra and other systems possess the status of being rooted in Śruti and being in agreement with it.
[Objection: But how can the Pāśupata and other Smṛtis be considered rootless? For surely the authority of Paśupati and others is declared to be their root. To this, he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
And no certainty regarding attainment is possible there, because of the possibility of deviation.
In this context, the ellipsis is to be supplied as "because there is no means of certain knowledge regarding Śiva and the others.
Now, it might be argued: "But was it not stated here that 'they are indeed omnipresent'?
Not so.
Because it has been stated— in the passage beginning with "always possessed of increase and decrease"— that all others besides the Supreme Person lack omniscience,
and because the Śrutis and other authorities are used here in a figurative sense.
Indeed, Viṣṇu possesses non-figurative omniscience;
Śiva and others likewise possess it regarding the means and the goal.
What is the use of knowing the number of insects in the sands of the Gaṅgā?
True;
however, the knowledge of reality itself is not yet attainment, because it would over-extend to a deceiver. Thus he says: "because it deviates."

Now, it might be argued that because all omniscient beings lack delusion (*moha*), and because attachment (*rāga*) and aversion (*dveṣa*)—which are rooted in that [delusion]—are absent, even the desire to deceive (*vipralipsā*) ceases; thus, there is certainty regarding their being authoritative (*āpti*).

In this regard, is it assumed that all the founders of various schools (*tīrthakara*) are authoritative, and based on that, such an inference is made? Or is it only one specific individual, as favored by each person, who is so inferred?
He refutes the first [position] with the words: "Because of deviation" (vyabhicārataḥ).
The meaning is that this acceptance [of the doctrine] is refuted in the case of Nārāyaṇa, the author of the *Smṛtis* such as the *Pañcarātra*;
or, if it were not refuted, our desired conclusion would be established.
Alternatively, "inconsistency" refers to mutual contradiction;
for it is not appropriate to accept that all those who propound mutually contradictory views are authoritative,
as that would lead to the absurdity of the reality of things being subject to conceptual alternatives.
He states the second [reason] as "due to deviation" (vyabhicārataḥ).
The meaning is that in the case of that very Tīrthakara whose status as an authoritative person (āpta) is not accepted, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding omniscience;
nor is it reasonable to claim that omniscience is not accepted in his case.
This is because the same logic applies.
If, however, one were to qualify the reason, then it would be subject to fallacies such as being "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*).

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that knowledge, desire, effort, the articulatory places (*sthāna*), the producing organs (*karaṇa*), and their proficiency are ascertained merely by means of instruction—[that too is problematic].
That is not so;
for he says "it is fallacious" because there is deviation [from the rule], since we observe instruction even for those whose faculties are not sharp.
Furthermore, the fault has already been stated regarding the qualification of the instruction.
Let it be granted that there is knowledge; but from what source does its correspondence with reality (yāthārthya) arise?

He says "no" to the claim that its establishment occurs when there is a general certainty that "this object belongs to this person who has reached the stage of practice," because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicārataḥ*).

The meaning is as follows: there is deviation and remoteness; for people such as ourselves, the proximity of those [sages] is difficult to attain, and far more so is the ascertainment of their practice.
If it is argued that this ascertainment occurs through a succession of words from those to be trained (*vineya*), [we say] no.
He says "due to deviation" because of the occurrence of deviation among other Tīrthakaras.
For in their respective traditions, all those [teachers] are indeed declared to have been practitioners of that particular teaching in that particular matter;
yet it is impossible to accept their knowledge as being in accordance with reality, because it contradicts your own tenets.
Otherwise, however, it would follow that your own tenet is unreal; thus he says: "Because of deviation."
Inconsistency is contradiction.
One must state why even the desire [to deceive] does not exist here.
If it is argued that this is because there is no observation of a motive consisting of self-benefit or the harming of others, then does it follow that all the authors of the Smṛtis are not deceivers?
If one objects:
"Because this rule is violated in the case of the Buddhas and others," he replies: "because it is subject to deviation."
Furthermore, there is self-contradiction in the restriction;
for if anyone at all were a deceiver,
the absence of a perceived reason would itself be an instance of deviation (vyabhicāra) in that very case.
With the intention that those various specific purposes associated with particular individuals cannot be ascertained by people like us who possess only eyes of flesh, he says: "Because of deviation."
If it is argued that the absence of apprehension of a reason by any means of valid cognition is the cause for non-deception, we say no,
because this is doubtful. Rather,
the absence of a motive is the cause for non-deception.
If it is argued that the absence of purpose is determined because deceiving others is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*) and is not a means to achieve it, we say no;
for there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) with those who are acknowledged to be deceivers. Thus he says: "because of inconsistency."
If it is argued that this [Prakṛti] deceives by deluding even that which is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha) into appearing as a human goal (puruṣārtha),
what of it? If you say, "But the subject under discussion, being discriminative (vivekin), does not act thus," we say no.
Because it is illogical to determine that this [person] possesses a discernment (*viveka*) that does not exist among other *tīrthakaras*.
If it is argued that the absence of deception is inferred from his engagement in teaching for the welfare of the world, we say no;
because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the presence of such [engagement] in similar cases like the Buddha and others. Thus he says: "Because of deviation."
If it is argued that this is not so, but rather for the purpose of deluding unworthy persons,
then how is it determined that the subject under discussion is also not so?

Because the means for establishing certainty is the same in other cases as well. Furthermore, as for the claim that delusion and the desire to deceive are excluded through corroboration by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is incorrect;
for a further means of valid cognition is not, first of all, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Because the object in question is beyond the reach of the senses, there is disagreement regarding it.
If you argue that there is inference [of such objects], then there is deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the Buddhas and others.
If you say, "That is merely a fallacious appearance, whereas my own is indeed a valid inference," we say no.
With the intention of saying, "Do not hasten; we shall ward off the wonder of your statement," he says: "Because of deviation" (vyabhicārataḥ).
Now, as for that scripture (*āgama*), is it the Vedas and so forth, or another Smṛti text contradicting them, or perhaps another work composed by one of our own school?
It cannot be the first or the second, because there can be no agreement with what is contradictory; thus he says: "because of deviation" (*vyabhicārataḥ*).
Nor is the third [alternative] tenable;

for even the Smṛtis composed by the Buddha and others are subject to deviation, since they are corroborated by the words of other persons belonging to their own school. Thus he says: "because of deviation" (vyabhicārataḥ).
If it is argued that they too are of doubtful reliability, we say no; for there is likewise no means to ascertain that [reliability] in the cases under discussion.
As for what was said—that through the efficacy of their activity, delusion and the desire to deceive are excluded—[that remains to be proven].
That is incorrect;
for the capacity for successful action consists in the attainment of a result by one who has acted after having understood the object through that [cognition].
And the result of a memory regarding a disputed matter—characterized as heaven or liberation—is not perceived by direct perception.
He says "because of deviation" (vyabhicārataḥ), meaning that the sense faculties do not have such objects as their domain.

Nor can it be established by means of inference, because [reasons] such as "being a memory" are inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*). Inference proceeds through the absence of deviation (*avyabhicāra*), whereas deviation consists in the occurrence of a phenomenon contrary to what is intended. Furthermore, [the reason] is inconclusive because [memory] possesses the nature of being a recollection and so forth.
And because of the absence of anything else, he says: "due to deviation" (vyabhicārataḥ).
Now, as for [establishing it] through scripture,
that too is not yet accepted;
nor can it be established by means of what is rejected.
He says "due to deviation" (*vyabhicārataḥ*) because that [Smṛti] exists even with respect to subjects such as Buddhism, which would thus constitute a deviation [from the rule].
This might be so:
indeed, Smṛti composed by Śiva and others is of two kinds.
One [type of activity] proceeds with an unseen fruit in view, while the other proceeds with a seen result such as prosperity and the like.
Among these, the capacity for action in that which has a seen purpose is perceived through direct perception.
"Therefore, the author of that [Smṛti] must be authoritative.
This is not so;
for even then, there is a lack of evidence to establish that a Smṛti held in disagreement is rooted in an authoritative source.
If it is argued that its establishment [as valid] follows from that very same [source], we say no;
because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
For there is no rule that what has been established as authoritative in one instance must necessarily be so in all instances.

And this being the case, it would follow that all Smṛtis are based on valid cognition (āpti), since even among them, those whose objects are perceptible are observed to have the capacity for effective action; thus he says: "because of deviation" (vyabhicārataḥ).
This has been stated even while granting [the opponent's point];
however, even for those [actions] whose results are visible, a great deal of deviation from their [expected] fruit is observed.
And so, how can there be an inference—based on that example—that the others have their root in non-attainment? To this he says: "Because of deviation" (vyabhicārataḥ).

Furthermore, since it is established that a portion [of a tradition] lacks a foundation in authoritative testimony due to the deviation of its results, how could there be any inference based on such factors as "being composed by Paśupati," given that these too deviate? Thus he says: "due to deviation.

Consequently, because it cannot be determined that the Pāśupata and other Smṛtis are rooted in authoritative testimony, it is logical that they lack authority precisely because they are rootless and contradict the Pañcarātra and other Smṛtis.
By this, [the Sūtra] "and because others are not perceived... [is explained].
By this, the two sūtras beginning with "by this, Yoga is refuted" are explained;
as is the explanation that the Smṛti of the Sāṅkhyas lacks authority because their other principles, such as Mahat and Ahaṅkāra, are not perceived.
That [argument] is incorrect because it is subject to deviation even within the Vedānta scriptures, and because it has already been stated that non-perception in every respect is unproven.
[Objection: But do not the Smṛtis such as the Pañcarātra also deviate regarding their results?
For in some cases, even when one performs what is prescribed therein, the observed result is not perceived.
Therefore, since those [Smṛtis] lack authority, the Pāśupata and other Smṛtis do not lose their authority due to contradiction with them.
Otherwise, the deviation regarding the result would be inconclusive; hence he says: "And not... (na ca).
And even if there is an exception to this rule, its status as a valid means of knowledge is never lost.
The connection is that even though there may be some deviation in this Smṛti, such as the Pañcarātra and others, [it does not lose its authority].
If it is asked, "Why does it not lose [its authority]?"—
is it being asserted that there is an absence of validity for that which has an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha)?
Or is it only for that which has a visible purpose?
Not the first,

because when there is a deviation from the result in a cause that has a visible purpose in some instances, [the same would apply] to this [inference] which has an invisible purpose, even when there is a deviation from the result.
Therefore, even though it lacks authority in that regard, the validity of this [Veda], which has unseen results as its object, is not thereby lost;
for there is no cause for such invalidation.
And it is precisely because of contradiction with that [Veda] that the lack of authority of the Pāśupata and other systems has been stated.
The intention [of the author] is that the statement regarding the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of [scripture] whose purpose is perceived (*dṛṣṭārtha*) is irrelevant to the present context.

Now, if it is argued: "If that which has a perceived purpose lacks authority due to the deviation of its results, then for that very reason, that which has an unperceived purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) will also lack authority," we say:
no. For what does "for that very reason" mean—is it because of that [logical] reason (*hetu*), or because of that [empirical] example (*dṛṣṭānta*)?
Not the first [alternative]:
it is not tenable to claim that its status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) is lost merely because of an occasional deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Nor is it the second [alternative], because if there were deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in some cases, there would be a lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*).
It is not tenable to claim that its status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) is lost,
because there is no supporting reason;
furthermore, [the reasons such as] "because it is the word of Nārāyaṇa" are inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*).

It should not be argued that "let the entire word of Nārāyaṇa not be authoritative," or that "since there is deviation from the result and lack of authority in cases where the object is perceptible, the status of this [Veda] as a means of knowledge is also lost because it becomes a subject of doubt. He states the reason for this: "Because it is faultless" (*nirdoṣa*).

"Because it is rooted in faultless speech, it is not rooted in reasoning. Faultless speech is the Veda; "rooted in reasoning" refers to its capacity to produce effective activity, which is the basis for determining its authority—this is the implied sense.
This is the underlying intention.
Is this an inference of the lack of authority for the *Smṛti* texts such as the *Pañcarātra*, which have perceptible objects, based on the deviation of their results;
and is the suspicion of the lack of authority for the other [Vedic] texts likewise made independently on that very basis, or is it an employment of a *pratibandi* (counter-example)?
We shall refute the first alternative in the subsequent section (*adhikaraṇa*).
Not the second [alternative],
for the employment of a *pratibandī* occurs when the object of proof (*prameya*) is yet to be established; but such is not the case here.

Indeed, by means of another instance such as the correspondence with results (*phalasaṃvāda*), we have inferred that the *Smṛti* texts of the Pāśupatas and others possess a foundation in authoritative revelation (*āptamūla*) and are thus valid; it was against this very principle that we pointed out their defect by demonstrating their lack of correspondence with results.

If the determination of the validity of the *Smṛti* texts such as the Pañcarātra were to be desired through the reasoning of correspondence with results, then this [pointing out of a defect] would constitute a "taking up of the counter-example" (*pratibandīgrahaṇa*).
Nor do we maintain that the determination of the authority of the *Pañcarātra* and similar texts is based on reasoning;
nor should it be said that such a determination of their authority would thereby be groundless,
for it is self-evident by virtue of its capacity to produce knowledge (*bodhakatva*).
If it is asked, "From what does the removal of the doubt regarding invalidity arise?", it has been stated: "By virtue of its being rooted in authority.
If it is objected that such ascertainment is itself rootless, we say no;
for it is based upon its correspondence with the Śruti.
Now, it might be argued that scripture (*śruti*) lacks authority if it is devoid of the excellence of a speaker; therefore, it is stated that it must be "a faultless sentence.
For authority is established solely by virtue of being informative, and since it possesses the nature of a sentence, this is accepted by both parties.
Faults, however, are what subvert that authority.
The meaning is that since such [authorship] is impossible for what is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), we shall demonstrate that the authority of the Veda (*śruti*) is indeed unshakable.
In this state, even by way of contradiction with the Veda, it is possible to establish the lack of authority of the *smṛtis* such as the Pāśupata and others.
As for what was also stated: "One should augment the Veda with the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*."
Thus, that is indeed so; however, only those [means] that are not contradictory possess the status of being means, and not those that are contradictory.

Nor does this result in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), because the determination of the meaning of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) does not depend solely upon corroboration by traditional scripture (*smṛti*). *5,62*
Now, surely those who accept the authority of the *Smṛtis* such as the *Pañcarātra* must in every way accept the efficacy of their performance;
and they must admit that any deviation [from the expected result] is caused by defects in the agent, the instruments, and so forth.
Otherwise, there would arise the contradiction of something being both a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and yet failing to produce its result.

And since it is thus possible to establish validity and so forth even through correspondence with the results [of action], why is it said that [this] is not rooted in reasoning? To one who asks this out of a friendly disposition, he replies: "Of what is declared in the Veda... and so on.
Since the eligibility prescribed in the Vedas is always difficult to determine,
it is indeed impossible to know whether there is a rule or a transgression.

It is stated "of that which is declared in the Veda" because, regarding the performance of practices taught in the Vedic texts, only those sacraments (saṃskāras) such as *niṣeka* and so forth mentioned in the Veda constitute the requisite qualification (*adhikāra*).

Alternatively, by the word "Veda," the *Pañcarātra* and other such scriptures are also included. Furthermore, the term "of the qualification" (*adhikārasya*) is used as an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).
It should also be understood that this refers to the performance of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
"Difficult to ascertain" means being imperceptible to those such as ourselves.
"Always" means by its very nature, and not due to spatial or other types of obstruction.
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "there is either a necessity or a deviation regarding the result.
The word *hi* means "because";
therefore, the remainder is: "validity and so forth are not inferred by means of correspondence with the result."
This is what is meant:
indeed, it is the cognized mark (*liṅga*) that is the instrument of inference,
not its mere existence.
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument].
In this regard, one should employ the following formal argument:
the *Pañcarātra* and other such texts are authoritative.
"Because it generates an efficacious activity, like that which is commonly accepted.
And this is its meaning:
because for those who perform the practice of the means prescribed by this [scripture], the result is necessarily attained.
Nor can this logical mark (liṅga) be definitively ascertained;

for since deviation is frequently observed, it is impossible to apprehend a necessary rule (niyama). Furthermore, even if such an ascertainment were made, there would be grounds for suspecting that it was merely a coincidence (kākatālīyatā).
In this regard, the following must be said:
an effect is to be produced by the complete assemblage of causes, and not by a mere portion thereof; for if it were otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension.

In the present context, however, ritual action that has been properly performed by one possessing pure intention and so forth— preceded by the eligibility for Vedic sacraments such as *niṣeka* and the like, which require purity of both lineages—
is sufficient to produce results such as prosperity, provided there is no obstacle and the will of the Lord (*īśvara*) and other auxiliary factors are present.

And thus, it is argued that where a result is not obtained, there is a deficiency in the qualification (*adhikāra*) and so forth, whereas elsewhere there is its excellence; from this, a certainty regarding the rule [of cause and effect] is established.
But this is not tenable, because it is impossible for persons such as ourselves to ascertain the presence or absence of qualifications and the like residing in another person.

Indeed, it is certainly not the case that the mental purity of another's father, grandfather, and so forth, nor the propriety of the *niṣeka* and other rites, nor the non-decayed nature of the mantras, nor the purity of the substances and such, [are the causes of efficacy].
It can be understood by those belonging to more recent times.
Thus, let it be that there is indeed a fixed rule regarding its fruit, while any deviation is caused by defects [in the performance];
or rather, let there simply be such deviation in this case.
In some cases, the perception of a result may be purely accidental—like the "crow and the palm fruit"—or it may indeed have another cause; thus, doubt does not cease.
Furthermore, it is not logical to infer validity based on what is still doubtful.

Moreover, if one were to postulate that the deviation [from the rule] is caused by a deficiency in the causal factors only after validity has been established, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
Once its authority has been established through corroboration with the Veda, it is possible to postulate another explanation for any deviation regarding the results.

Therefore, the authority of the Pañcarātra and other such texts is established solely by their corroboration with the Veda, and not by the efficacy of their practical application. Thus, the counter-argument (*pratibandī*) is refuted due to the lack of parity in reasoning.

As for the intended point of one who employs a counter-argument—that just as one desiring the authority of the *Pañcarātra* and other such texts must postulate that the failure to obtain the result is due to a deficiency in qualifications (*adhikāra*) and so forth, so too shall I postulate it regarding the *Smṛtis* of the Pāśupatas and others—that is incorrect because of the disparity; thus he says: "For the qualification... and so on.
For it is said that eligibility is easily obtained in other scriptures;
however, the eligibility declared in the Veda is difficult for all human beings to attain.
The mention of "attaining authority" (adhikāragrahaṇa) is also an indication for the means (sādhana).
In other scriptures such as the Pāśupata and others, the authority described is sufficient, easily accessible, and achievable without effort.
Why is this so?
For it is stated thus in other scriptures;
likewise, the assumption that such [qualifications] are lacking is obstructed by a lack of credibility.
Moreover, it is well known that the entitlement prescribed in the Veda—consisting of birth from a pure lineage and so forth—is difficult for all ordinary humans to attain.

Therefore, the assumption that those [auxiliaries] are deficient is indeed possible. Now, one might ask: "How is it that in other scriptures (āgamas) the qualification and the means of proof are said to be easily obtained? To this, he shows [the answer] briefly with the words: "In other scriptures... (*anyāgameṣu*).
Even for those born as Caṇḍālas, the status of a Brahmin is gradually established in other scriptures through entry into the inner circle of the mandala.
The meaning is that even that which is otherwise unattainable without great austerity (tapas) is attainable; or, it means that even [virtues] such as striving (yatitva) and so forth are attained.
Or [it may mean]: "How much more so for those born as Kṣatriyas and others?

Or, since even those who are Brāhmaṇas by birth but have become Caṇḍālas through their actions are somehow accepted as capable of restoration by followers of the Veda, it is said "even for those born as Caṇḍālas.
Alternatively, it means "those whose birth is among the Caṇḍālas."
Alternatively, they are so called because their birth is that of a *caṇḍāla*, due to their connection with a *caṇḍāla*.
By the phrase "gradually by entering into the mandala," this is expressed:
for one who is separated from [the goal] by as many births, that many mandalas are to be worshipped (or prepared).
In this regard, the connection is as follows: whatever [caste] one enters into that maṇḍala, one becomes of that same caste;
however, it is established in other āgamas that upon entering the final maṇḍala, one becomes a brahmin.
And so it has been said:
“Merely by entering the initiation, one becomes a Brahmin in an instant;
by undertaking the Kāpāla vow, a human being becomes an ascetic.”
Thus ends the illustration regarding the ease of access to this [teaching].
In the same way, the ease of obtaining the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) should also be understood.
As the Kāpālikas have said:
"One who knows the reality of the six mudrās and is proficient in the supreme mudrā,
having meditated upon himself as seated upon the vulva-throne (bhagāsana), attains nirvāṇa."
"The *karṇikā*, the *rucaka*, the *kuṇḍala*, the crest-jewel (*śikhāmaṇi*), the ashes,
and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*)— these are declared to be the six seals (*mudrā*).
One whose body is sealed by these is not born again here [in this world] as a possessor of a body," and so forth.
Likewise, the Kālāmukhas also [bear these marks]:
a rudrākṣa bracelet on the hand, a single lock of matted hair on the head,
a skull, bathing with ashes, and a staff.
"the worship of the jar," and so forth.

[Objection: But if it is argued that just as the ease of attaining both qualification (*adhikāra*) and the means (*sādhana*) has been stated there, the difficulty of attaining them has likewise been stated in that very same place; [Response: Then the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the Pāśupata and other systems is not established merely by the discrepancy regarding their results, but indeed also by their mutual contradictions. Thus he says: "qualification... (5.70).

Having declared that authority is difficult to attain yet again very easy to obtain, and having stated that the means of accomplishment are impossible yet easily achievable for the sake of attaining that fruit, it is therefore said:
"For what has been so stated is indeed subject to deviation even regarding its result. (Manu 2.11)
How may it attain the status of a valid means of knowledge? ... // MAnu 2.1.12a //

Because, after stating in some places that qualification is difficult to attain, he speaks again of it as being easily obtained; and because, for the sake of attaining that fruit— and for the sake of attaining fruits such as prosperity— he speaks of a means that is impossible and then declares it to be easy to perform.

And since that stated means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is also fallible with respect to its result (*phala*), how then could that which was stated—the teaching of the Pāśupatas and others—attain the status of valid authority? The meaning is: it cannot do so in any way. If it is argued: "Let the statement regarding ease of attainment (*saulabhya*) be explained as being for the purpose of persuasion (*prarocanā*), in accordance with the description of [the result] being difficult to obtain;
and likewise, the discrepancy regarding the result may be caused by defects in the qualification (*adhikāra*) and so forth, just as in the case of the Pañcarātra and other systems," we say: no.
Because of the disparity.
For such a construction is appropriate in the case of the *Pañcarātra* and other such texts,
since their authority is established by being rooted in the *Śruti*, and thus a basis for such a construction exists.

In the case of the Pāśupata and other such systems, however, since that [correspondence] is absent, it is logical that their lack of correspondence constitutes the basis for their invalidity, as there is no evidence to the contrary.
Any occasional correspondence, moreover, must be either accidental—like the "crow and the palm fruit"—or motivated by mere deception, like "sweetness on the tongue.
This is precisely what is expressed by the word "tu" (however).
The connection is with the phrase "it has been stated by him.

Thus, it is established that since the Pāśupata and other such systems are considered *apasmṛtis* (spurious smṛtis), one should not suspect the impossibility of the stated meaning on account of contradiction with them.
This concludes the section on Smṛti in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
[======= JNys_2,1.II: The Section on Non-Dissimilarity =======] *5,71* // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section concerning non-dissimilarity (navilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇa).
Oṃ. [The world] is not [identical to Brahman] because it has different characteristics; and its being so [as Brahman] is known from scripture. Oṃ.
The contradiction with scripture has been resolved;
now, the contradiction with reasoning is being resolved. For instance:
Indeed, through the systematic concordance of scripture and other means of knowledge, the status of Brahman as the cause of the origin and so forth of the world has been established.
In that regard, the very authority of scripture is difficult to maintain;
for whatever is observed to deviate from its result is seen to be non-authoritative.
For example, there is the speech of a deceiver,
and there is scriptural revelation (*śruti*) that fails to yield its fruit;
for even when one performs the rites for those desiring a son, such as the *putrakāmeṣṭi*, the birth of a son or similar results is sometimes not observed.
Otherwise, the lack of authority attributed to the Pāśupata and other systems on account of the non-perception of their results would not hold.
Furthermore, if a portion of a text lacks authority, it is easy to infer the lack of authority of other portions as well by that same logic.
Moreover, whatever is not preceded by conscious intelligence is not authoritative, just like the tracks of ants.
Furthermore, the Veda is not preceded by conscious intention, because its non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) is accepted;
and if it were of human origin, it would be entirely without authority due to the absence of any foundational means of valid cognition,
like the speech of a deceiver.

Moreover, because it consists of words not uttered by a reliable person (*āpta*), the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the Veda is to be inferred, just like the speech of a madman. When the Veda is in such a state,
what then can be said regarding the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas, given their defects such as the failure of their promised results?
[This refers to] the validity of the arguments of the Kharkharas.

And so, since the status of Brahman as the cause of the origin and so forth of the world is not established through the concordance of the Vedas and other sources, when this [objection] has been reached, the author states the purport of the sūtra "na vilakṣaṇatvāt" (not because of being of a different character), which serves as a refutation of that, by saying:
"because of eternality."

[The Veda is not authoritative] because it is dissimilar [to other means of knowledge], and its suchness is derived from words. ... Since it is eternal and free from all defects produced by human beings, how could it not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.12cd)
The word "Vedic statement" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
This is the meaning:
the validity of instruments of knowledge indeed consists in their capacity to produce cognition, whereas [invalidity] arises from defects.
At times [the Veda] is set aside;
however, the Vedic statement is accepted by both proponent and opponent as being informative.
Otherwise, there would be no deviation from the result even in that case.

Furthermore, all defects that subvert the validity of a sentence—such as its failure to produce cognition or its producing a contrary cognition—are invariably rooted in the defects of the speaker, as this is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Since the Vedic sentence is eternal and authorless (*apauruṣeya*), it is devoid of all defects rooted in human agency; thus, it attains validity by its own nature (*svataḥ*).

Once validity has been ascertained, one will postulate either a deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) or the presence of an obstructing factor (*pratibandhaka*) as the cause for the deviation from the result;
otherwise, between that which is established and that which is not otherwise established, the latter is stronger. In this regard, the following formal arguments (*prayoga*) occur:
The Veda is authoritative because, while being a source of knowledge, it does not produce contrary knowledge, just like [any other] accepted [source].
That which is under dispute does not produce contrary knowledge, because it is a statement not composed by an unreliable person, just like an accepted statement.
That which is under dispute was not composed by an unreliable person, because it is not of human origin, like space.
The disputed deviation from the result must be based on deficiencies [in the causal factors] and so forth,
because it is a deviation from a result established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like the deviation from results mentioned by Caraka and others.
It might be argued as follows:
From what source does the eternity of the Veda derive?
We reply: from the previously mentioned establishment of its general nature and through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

To those of our own school who, while accepting the authority of the Veda, do not admit its eternity, he establishes that [eternity] by means of scriptural citations indicated in the Sūtra—beginning with the word "virūpa."
...with speech that is always improper. // MAnu 2.161a //
By this [verse], he cites the Śruti passage: "O Virūpa, urge forth with an eternal word a beautiful hymn for that bull who is directed toward heaven."

Here, the eternity of speech is being asserted, not that of the Veda; for even that [speech] will be something existing over a long period of time. Therefore, [the verse says]: "With the eternal and the non-eternal, I praise that supreme state, Brahman."
Thus, he cites the Śruti: "The Śruti alone is eternal; the Smṛtis are indeed non-eternal, as are all other words," by means of the phrase "by the eternal."
"...always by means of the eternal and the non-eternal," and so forth; from such scriptural passages, it is understood that the Veda is eternal.
To refute other interpretations, the term "nityayā" (by the eternal) has been explained as "sadā vidyamānayā" (by that which is always present).
For in the remainder of the passage, even though Smṛtis belonging to long periods of time are included within the category of the non-eternal, [the author] declares that only Śruti is eternal.
If it is argued that even Śrutis express their own human origin, we say no.

Since it was previously stated that the status of being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*) is difficult to ascertain, and because there would otherwise follow the undesirable consequence that validity could not be established if [the Veda] were of human origin;
and since the objection—that even if the Veda is not of human origin, its validity would not exist due to the absence of a cause for validity because validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*)—is fallacious;
therefore, in accordance with the more powerful Śruti, the meaning of those [Vedic passages] must be understood as simply being set in motion by various individuals.
And thus, such passages as “The Ṛks and Sāmans were born” and “From Agni, the Ṛgveda itself was produced” become logically consistent;
for indeed, it is impossible for a single sentence to have multiple authors.
"But it is possible that [the Veda] was produced by many [authors].
(*5,81*) As for the claim that the Veda lacks authority because it is not preceded by conscious intention— like the lines of ants—
he refutes that with the verse beginning "pipīlikā."
And the Pipīlikā script is also authoritative, as it is not in contradiction [with other sources].
The word *ca* is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*), or else it serves to conjoin [the reason] with the capacity to produce cognition (*bodhakatva*).
Therefore, the ellipsis is: "Consequently, because the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), it is an invalid inference."
The meaning of "also" (*api*) is that it is not only the Veda (*śruti*), but even the "ant-script" (*pipīlikālipi*).

Indeed, the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the ant-script would have to be due either to its being non-informative (*abodhakatva*) or to its being informative of the contrary (*viparītabodhakatva*).
It is not the first [alternative].
Because it contradicts experience;
otherwise, even the script of a human being would be non-informative,
and thus it would fall into futility.
Moreover, this being the case, space and so forth would be cited as examples; why then search for the tracks of ants?
It is not the second [alternative], for that must be postulated because it contradicts powerful means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), otherwise there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with any means of valid cognition regarding the meaning conveyed by the script of the ants;
therefore, how could this [script] be invalid?
It might be argued as follows:

Scripture (lipi) is not a separate means of valid cognition, because it is accepted as being included within the three [other] means of valid cognition; nor does it fall within the scope of perception (pratyakṣa) or scripture (āgama).
Because it lacks the characteristics [of direct perception],
it must be stated that this is indeed inference (*anumāna*).
And that [inference] would have as its object either the word residing in the mind of the scribe, or the meaning understood from that [word].

And this [kind of cognition] is not possible regarding the scribbling of ants, because it is sublated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); so how can that [scribbling] be a valid means of knowledge?
Do not say so.
For if that were so, it would follow that even the writing of a mute sheep would lack authority.
If you argue, "Let that [writing] be non-authoritative, but the other is inference," we say no;
for even the writing of a mute sheep is seen to possess conventional validity (*sāṃvyāvahārikatva*).

Furthermore, regarding this other inference as well, it must be stated: should some qualification be employed for the purpose of excluding the "mute and dumb" (those incapable of verbal expression), or not? Not the first [alternative], because it would result in the fallacy of the unestablished reason (*asiddha*) due to doubt.
If it is argued that inference is like a script whose author is determined, we say no;
for even a script whose author is not determined is still used in worldly practice.
Nor is the second [alternative] correct.
Because of the absolute lack of connection to the writing of a mute sheep.
Now, if it is thought that there is no fault whatsoever in inferring the word and its meaning as they existed in the mind of the original scribe,
that too is not correct.
Because the alphabet of ants is exclusively [used] for that [purpose],
and because it is doubtful and unestablished when one attempts to exclude it;
for there is no distinction between the alphabet of ants and the alphabet of humans by which one could determine that "this is not the alphabet of ants."
Therefore, even human writing must be accepted as the cause for the recollection of phonemes, just as a word is the cause for the recollection of its meaning;
this is the same as in the case of the writing of ants. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that such recollection is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). (5.85)
Now, even though memory is a valid cognition (*pramā*), it is not the case that everything which is its cause possesses validity;
for if it were, then the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and other such factors would also follow as being valid.
Rather, validity belongs only to that which is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*).
And the established conclusion is that this [cognition] is indeed the mind alone.

As for the observation of written characters and so forth, its purpose is fulfilled solely by bringing about the auxiliary conditions known as the two types of *saṃskāra* (latent impressions); how then could it possess authority?
Not so.
For the sense organ is perception when accompanied by the intermediate operation characterized by contact with the object, not the sense organ alone.
And in the arising of memory, the mind’s contact with the object is precisely the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

Thus, just as the eye possesses validity only when accompanied by the object’s approach and its conjunction [with it], so too the mind possesses validity only when accompanied by the sight of a script and the awakening of the latent impression produced thereby; how then can the script not possess validity?
If it is argued that [the status of being a means of knowledge] does not exist for the isolated [Veda],
then it is certainly not accepted even for the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
Now, in this context, the word *pramāṇa* (means of knowledge) must be either a term denoting the state (*bhāvasādhana*) or a term denoting the cause (*kāraṇasādhana*).

In the first case, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the anthill-script is the means of valid cognition" (*pipīlikālipiḥ pramāṇam*). In the second case, however, it ought to be "the anthill-script is a means of valid cognition" (*pipīlikālipiḥ pramāṇī*); how then could one say "the Vedas are the means of valid cognition" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*) or "the Smṛti is the means of valid cognition" (*smṛtiḥ pramāṇam*)?
This is because, having generally indicated "valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*), it prescribes [the Vedas] as its source;
otherwise, there would be an insurmountable difficulty even in that regard.
Do not say so.
This is because it is accepted as having the nature of an action (*bhāvasādhana*).
As for its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), however, it is figurative.
[Objection: But surely, the authority of scripture is desired on the basis of its being a means for correct experience (*samyaganubhava*), and not by way of its being a mere reminder (*smāraka*).

And so, lest it be inferred that the Śruti is not authoritative because it is preceded by an intellect that employs a means for correct experience—just like the scribbling of ants—he says: "Just as... (yathā).
Just as that which was done by Ulūka served as a warning to the son of Droṇa.
... which is not contradictory. // MAnu 2.15a //

Just as even a single owl, acting without prior intention, became the means for the correct experience that realizes the destruction of many crows, so too did Aśvatthāman think, "I alone shall slay many," and this became the means for the correct experience of that fact;
likewise, the Śruti, though not preceded by conscious intent, is the means for the correct experience [of Brahman].
This is what is meant:

Is "not being preceded by intelligence" intended to mean beginninglessness? Or, even if there is a beginning, is it the absence of being produced by intelligence that is to be established? Or is it the absence of being preceded by intelligence in the sense of the lack of the intention, "I shall establish this matter in such-and-such a way"? Or is it the deficiency of the prior intention [to act]?
Not the first, because there is an absence of even the word "pipīlikā" (ant).
If it is argued that the sky itself will serve as the example, [we reply: no.
Nevertheless, the first [position] is untenable because the opponent does not accept that the Veda is beginningless, and thus its eternity remains unproven.
Nor is the second [position] tenable,
because I accept that whatever is produced is necessarily generated by the intellect.
The third and fourth [alternatives] are not [viable],
because there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the activity performed by an owl;
for although it might be possible here to state a deviation in the case of perception (pratyakṣa).
Nevertheless, because it belongs to the same class as those whose causes are known, it was stated that this [inference] is capable of being refuted.

Although it is easy to state in the case of mere inference, it was not demonstrated here because it is more appropriate to demonstrate in the context of augury (śākuna) an object of conscious activity that is of such a nature.
[Objection: But is it not observed that augury sometimes fails to correspond with the actual fact?
True;

however, with the intention that whatever is not contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) will serve as an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it was stated: "not contradicted" (*aviruddham*).
Although it is possible to demonstrate deviation even in the case of mere augury (*śākuna*), this example was cited because, as a matter of scripture (*āgamika*), it is incapable of contradiction.
Now, how can it be said "he sat" (*āsa*)? For the substitution of *bhū* for the root *as* is obligatory (*nitya*).
There is no fault, for by the rule stating that "that which resembles an inflected case-ending is an indeclinable (*avyaya*)," this word is an indeclinable.
It is said to resemble an inflected case-ending, yet such a case-ending does not actually exist here.
It is not that it does not exist,
because there exists the application of the affirmative particle (*āmantānuprayoga*).
If that is so, then it is indeed employed.
"Scripture is not a means for correct experience because, while being verbal in nature, it is not preceded by [human] cognition.
Alternatively: "Scripture is not an authoritative testimony (āgama) because it is not preceded by cognition.
And "not being preceded by cognition" means the absence of being preceded by the knowledge of the true nature of the intended object.

Even for the first [type of person], when entering the path of the ants' letters, the words of a madman will serve as an example; yet even the words of a madman are not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because they contradict valid means of knowledge. Therefore, he says: "But that which is contradictory... (*viruddhaṃ tu*).
But that which is contradictory is sublated precisely because of its contradiction.

Whatever statement contradicts valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, the speech of a madman—is sublated precisely because of that contradiction with valid cognition; that is to say, it is non-correspondent with reality (*ayathārtha*).
It is not, however, [sublated] by the two reasons previously mentioned.
By this, he indicates the presence of a limiting condition (*sopādhikatā*).
For this very reason, the reason "being a statement not composed by a reliable person" (*āptāpraṇītavākyatva*) is also refuted.
This is the underlying intention:
