first of all, the absence of being a means for correct experience does not follow from the absence of being a means for knowledge.
This is because the status of being a means to knowledge is established for both parties;
nor can it be [a means] to memory,
since it is accepted that its object has not been previously experienced.
Therefore, it must be stated that [the reason] functions solely as a cause for contrary cognition.
Likewise, in the second formulation as well, there is no lack of scriptural authority (*anāgamatva*) on the grounds of being non-verbal (*aśabdatvena*),
because its status as speech (*śabdatva*) is admitted by both parties.
Therefore, it should be stated as "by way of being non-conformable to reality.
Likewise, in the third application as well, the extraction of the probandum (sādhya) must be performed;
and thus, in that case, "being sublated by a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇabādhitatva) is the limiting condition (upādhi).

Alternatively, this is an *upādhi* (limiting condition) with respect to the first probandum as delimited by being a means of experience, the second probandum as delimited by being a sentence, and the third probandum as delimited by being a cause of cognition.

Now, one might ask: even though this *upādhi* pervades the probandum—since whatever is non-correspondent to reality is contradicted by valid cognition—how is it that it does not pervade the probans? To this, he says: "Because of contradiction... (*virodha*).
Because no contradiction is observed... MAnu 2.1.15c.
Even though the stated probans (*sādhana*) exists in the Veda which has been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛtāyām*), no contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*) is observed;
the remainder of the sense is that [the probans] does not pervade the locus of the probandum (*sādhanāvyāpakatvam*).

Here, although it should have been said "because there is no contradiction," it is stated as "because it is not observed" for the purpose of establishing the absence of contradiction; this is how it should be understood. *5,100*
If it is asked, "What follows from this if being contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is thus a limiting condition (*upādhi*)?"—

the author says "Therefore," with the intention that since it will be explained later that a limiting condition functions as a counter-inference (*pratipakṣonnāyaka*), the inferences [in question] are subject to a counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatva*).
... therefore, the authority of the Veda is accepted.

Since being contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) pervades being non-conformable to reality (*ayathārthatva*), and this pervader is excluded from the Veda which is the subject of the proposition;
and since the exclusion of the pervader necessarily entails the exclusion of the pervaded,
therefore the authority of the Veda must be accepted.
The formal argument here is as follows:
The Veda is not non-conformable to reality, because it is not contradicted by valid means of cognition, just like perception;
or alternatively, the Veda is conformable to reality, because, while being informative, it is not contradicted by valid means of cognition, just like perception.
Thus, the Veda is a means of valid direct experience because, while being a means of direct experience, it is not contradicted by other means of knowledge, just like perception.
Or: the Veda is authoritative scripture because, while being a sentence, it is not contradicted by other means of knowledge, just like that which is commonly accepted.

In this way, when "being a sentence" is the delimited probans (*sādhana*), "being composed by an unreliable person" (*anāptapraṇītatva*) is the extraneous condition (*upādhi*); and by its opposite, the counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*) must be stated.
Let it be so that the Veda possesses authority; but how is it with the Smṛtis such as the Pañcarātra?
For they, too, are not of non-human (apauruṣeya) origin.
Thinking that we shall determine validity by means of this [scripture] so as not to otherwise admit a deviation from the result, he says: "Because it is rooted in that."
And because the Smṛtis have that [the Veda] as their source...
The connection is that "validity is desired.

Even though there is no "being rooted in the Veda" (vedamūlatva) in the sense of having been composed after perceiving the meaning of the Vedas as spoken by the Blessed One, [the Smṛtis are still valid].
He is omniscient by his very nature;
nevertheless, the intended meaning here is that being composed in accordance with him constitutes its being rooted in him, and thus the aforementioned fault does not apply.
The formal argument (prayoga) in this case is as follows:

The Smṛti texts such as the Pañcarātra are authoritative because they are rooted in authoritative sources and are consistent with authoritative means of knowledge, like that which is already accepted [as authoritative].
Alternatively: "That which is under dispute is authoritative because it is consistent with the Veda, like the sentences concerning non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth admitted by the opponent.
If it is argued that "the state of being the word of a trustworthy person" (*āptavākyatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*), [we reply] no.
Because [the probans] does not pervade the probandum in the case of perception and so forth.
If it is argued that there is no fault because it is a pervader of the probandum as delimited by "being a sentence" (*vākyatva*), we say no;

for even so, since the condition (*upādhi*) is easily established in the subject (*pakṣa*) by means of the probans as delimited by "being a sentence other than the Veda," [the condition remains a flaw].
This being the case, since the Smṛtis possess authority, even the apparent deviation from the results [of Vedic injunctions] must be explained away by their force.

Now, it may be objected that Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas are also found which speak in contradiction to the stated meaning; and if one were to establish their authority, there would be much confusion. To this, he says: "In case of conflict... (virodhe).
...where there is no contradiction anywhere. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.16b)
The logical connection is exactly as before.

The intention is that there is no fault whatsoever, because only those Smṛtis for which there is no contradiction with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in any way are being made the subject of the argument.
[Objection: But if this is so, then the presentation of their being rooted in the Veda (*vedamūlatva*) is redundant.
If it is argued that the validity [of a cognition] is established simply by the absence of contradiction—which must necessarily be accepted for those things that produce knowledge—we say no;
for this would lead to the consequence of non-establishment, since a contradiction characterized by the deviation of the result is observed.
And if one were to remove that [deviation] by means of validity, there would result the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
"But once their authority is established on the basis of being rooted in the Veda, no fault whatsoever remains.
It has been stated that there is no lack of authority for the Śruti and Smṛti because there is no contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is the cause of non-authority;
however, that is incorrect.
The omniscience of God and other attributes stated in the Vedas and other sources [are challenged by the following]: God is not omniscient because He is a person,
just like Yajñadatta.
Because it is contradicted by such inferences as these, he says: "There is also contradiction."
A contradiction is said to exist only when it occurs with respect to perception or scripture.
The word "api" (even/also) has the sense of connecting to the subject at hand.
The word "yat" (which) is to be supplied [as the correlative].

Since it is sublated precisely because of contradiction, that very contradiction which serves as the ground for invalidity is said to be that which exists either through perception or through scripture.
Nor, however, by means of inference.
This is the intended meaning:
this effort of the opponent is indeed aimed at establishing, even within our own position, that which we have stated as being the cause for invalidity.
Furthermore, we intended only to point out a contradiction with perception and scripture (*pratyakṣāgama*), not a contradiction with inference (*anumāna*).

Thus, to demonstrate that [contradiction] regarding the subject (*pakṣa*) would be entirely irrelevant to the present context. As for the contradiction with an independent inference (*svatantrānumāna*), the author of the Sūtras will refute it later.
[Objection: Let it be that contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone is the cause for invalidity; what is the use of the qualification "by perception or by scripture"?
For it has been stated that the Veda and so forth lack validity due to contradiction with inference.
[Reply: Not so.
For we shall explain here that regarding entities such as Brahman and the like, the Veda alone is the sole authority; thus, there is no scope for inference concerning a Vedic matter.
And where something has no access, it cannot invalidate that [subject];
for the sense of sight is not held to be a sublater of the perception of touch.
And thus, how could inference serve as the cause for the invalidity of the Veda and so forth by means of contradicting their meaning?
For it is the Veda and so forth themselves that are the subject under consideration. (5.109)

[Objection: "If this were so, then the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedas (*vedārthamīmāṃsā*) would not need to be undertaken, because inquiry consists essentially in the investigation of reasoning. To this, he says: "By means of scripture" (*āgamena*).
When there is a contradiction between two scriptural authorities, reasoning is required.
The word *eva* (indeed) is to be understood as following the word *virodha* (contradiction);
the phrase "for the sake of determination" is the ellipsis.
This is what is meant:

For inference depends upon the cognition of the locus (*dharmin*) and other such factors; yet, since the nature of the locus and so forth—such as Brahman and the like—is not established apart from the Veda, if inference were independent of it, there would be fallacies such as the unestablished basis (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

However, if it does depend on it, there is a contradiction with that which apprehends the locus and its properties. Thus, it is asserted that there is no scope for inference regarding a subject matter that is based on the Veda.
In Mīmāṃsā, however, in certain instances where there is a contradiction between one scripture and another, reasoning is employed for the sake of determining the meaning;
that reasoning indeed serves to reinforce the authority of one of the scriptures.
One [of the two scriptures] is capable of determining the meaning by way of not contradicting the other,
because by relying on the subject (dharmin) and other factors established by one scripture, there is no room for fallacies such as the unestablished nature of the locus (āśrayāsiddhi).
Because one scripture, lacking the capacity to apprehend the nature of reality and so forth, is not authoritative; and because reasoning indicated by that scripture is even weaker than it,
being ineffective.
Thus, because such reasoning (*upapatti*) is applicable even to matters based on scripture (*āgamika*), Mīmāṃsā is established as valid.

Furthermore, a contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa*) or scripture does not, by its very nature, entail invalidity. Rather, this is because when those two [perception and scripture] possess greater force due to being foundational (*upajīvyatva*) and so forth, the weaker [inference] cannot result in a determination of invalidity simply by being sublated; and when they are of equal strength, it serves merely as a cause for mutual obstruction. Thus, the ascertainment of invalidity is untenable.
Furthermore, the invalidity of the Veda resulting from its contradiction with sources of livelihood and the like does not consist in being entirely non-conformable to reality;
rather, it is merely a deviation from the meaning as it is perceived.
This is because, being authorless and thus free from defects, it is impossible for it to be entirely invalid.

With the intention that, in such a case, one must necessarily assume another meaning [for the Veda], he says: "But when there is a conflict with what is to be relied upon, one must assume another meaning for the Veda. (Manu 2.13cd)
This is an elliptical indication; other factors such as "leaving no room" (niravakāśatva) and so forth are also to be understood.
Let it be so; what follows from that?
Furthermore, qualities such as being the basis of the Vedas are generally possible only in the case of perception and scripture;
they occur in the case of reasoning only occasionally,
while they do not exist at all in the case of reasoning based on [the opponent's] being a human being and so forth.

And for this reason, one should not consider the Veda to be invalid on account of its contradiction [by perception]; with this intention, he says: "Perception... (Manusmṛti 2.1.18). "Perception should be the basis of reliance; reasoning also generally [serves as such], though in some cases [it is not]. For among those for whom scripture alone is the means of valid knowledge, that [scripture] itself is indeed the basis of reliance. *5,111* Perception should be that which is relied upon; reasoning also generally [serves as such], though in some cases [it does not].
For among those for whom scripture is the sole means of valid knowledge, that [scripture] alone possesses the status of being the basis of reliance.

The term "of the Veda" (vedasya) is understood from the previous context. After the word "syāt" (it may be), the word "iti" (thus) is to be supplied. The connection is as follows: for the Veda in such passages as "That thou art," direct perception (pratyakṣa) is the basis upon which it depends;
furthermore, in some cases, reasoning (yukti) is also that upon which the Veda depends.

Just as in the case of such [scriptural statements] as "The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed subtle (*aṇavas*)," when one proceeds toward objects such as Viṣṇu, which have scripture alone as their means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), regarding the Veda that says "He was born from Viṣṇu," [the opponent might argue] against that Veda [by citing passages] such as "He is without origin, he is blameless."
The meaning is "that which provides sustenance.

In this way, qualities such as being without scope (*niravakāśatva*) generally apply only to perception and scripture, whereas they apply to reasoning only in rare instances; furthermore, it should be understood that this does not apply to the reasoning under discussion here. *5,115*

It has been stated that when there is a mutual contradiction between two scriptures (*āgama*), it is appropriate to engage in critical inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*) because it is possible for reasoning (*yukti*) to enter by relying on one of those scriptures;
however, that is untenable,
because such a rule does not apply universally.
For it is not the case that Mīmāṃsā is introduced solely because of mutual contradiction between two scriptures in every instance; therefore, he says: "It is appropriate."
If the meaning of a scripture is understood as being both reasonable and unreasonable, then in that case, only the reasonable meaning should be accepted. Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.19a-c.
In that case, this is the intended meaning:
it is true that this principle applies only in certain instances.

Nevertheless, where it does not apply, one adopts the meaning that accords with reason from among the multiple meanings perceived in a single scripture, thereby discarding those meanings that are inconsistent with it; thus, there is no violation of the aforementioned rule.
This is because it is not accepted that pure reasoning can enter into a Vedic matter;
nor is there any inconsistency with Mīmāṃsā, since reasoning that conforms to one or the other Vedic meaning is indeed accepted. (5.116)
It was previously stated that the lack of authority of scripture cannot be asserted on the grounds of its contradiction by reasoning such as [the argument for] "being a person" (*puruṣatva*).

Now, however, it is this very reasoning that is unauthoritative due to its contradiction with perception and scripture; for, since that [reasoning] is dependent upon them, it is weaker than they. With this intention, he says: "And reasoning... (*yuktiśca*).
And reasoning is considered to be threefold. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.19d)

Alternatively, he says "And the reasoning" (*yuktiśca*) in order to demonstrate now that which was previously set aside as an established fact, on account of which the impossibility of commencing the inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*) had been resolved.
The word "ca" (and) serves to connect with the subject under discussion.
To the question "In what way is there a threefold nature?", he says: "Pervasion."
Its pervasion is perceptible, and it likewise rests upon both reasoning and scripture.

That reasoning for which the pervasion with the probandum is perceived by direct perception—that is the first. That reasoning for which the pervasion is understood through reasoning—that is the second. Likewise, that reasoning for which the pervasion is understood through scripture—that is the third.
Thus, it should be applied as being threefold.
Furthermore, this is an illustration;
one should also understand that there is a threefold division based on the distinction between the grasper of the dharma, the grasper of the dharmī, and so forth.

And we shall clarify this point. If that is so, then a reasoning (*yukti*) that is rooted in reasoning itself does not depend upon scripture (*āgama*) and the like; therefore, it should be the sublater of that [scripture]. And let it be such that it is not sublated by it. To this, he says: "Perception" (*pratyakṣa*), etc. (5.118).
But in that matter, reasoning rooted in direct perception and scripture is more powerful.
In that regard, among those three types of reasoning,
"having perception and scripture as its basis" means having perception as its basis and scripture as its basis.
For even reasoning that is rooted in reasoning must ultimately be accepted as being rooted in perception and scripture;
otherwise, the reasoning based upon it would be groundless or lead to an infinite regress.

Thus, although they are equal in their dependence on perception and so forth, those reasonings rooted in perception and scripture are stronger because they do not depend on a long series of intermediate steps, whereas reasoning rooted in reasoning is weaker due to its dependence on such a series.
This is indeed appropriate; and if such is the state of two powerful arguments, then what need is there to speak further?

Because a weak argument is invalidated by scripture (*āgama*) and so forth (5.119), it follows that when there is a lack of authority, the contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone is the determining factor. Since there is no contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa*) or scripture regarding [the validity of] words and the like,
and since contradiction with inference (*anumāna*) is not a determining factor, there is no lack of authority.

It has been established that validity (*prāmāṇya*) belongs to a cognition by its very nature as an awakener [of certainty]. However, this distinction between valid and invalid cognition is difficult for those who do not know it to discern; therefore, the subsequent portion of the text is intended to define it through enumeration, definition, classification, and critical examination.
Nor should it be argued that since validity and so forth are merely conventional (*sāṃvyāvahārika*), there is no need to define them.
Nevertheless, because there exist disputes among scholars regarding its essential nature, number, object, and result, it is worthy of investigation.
Although this subject matter is the domain of the science of logic (*tarka-śāstra*) and not that of the science of Mīmāṃsā,
it is nevertheless investigated by the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣya-kṛt*), who desires the welfare of his students, as it arises in the course of the discussion.
There is no fault here, as was previously stated by the author of the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya.

For this very reason, the re-examination of a matter already established in the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and elsewhere does not constitute a defect; for even such a unified treatment is for the benefit of the students. (5.121)
In that regard, the desire to know [the specific qualities] such as number belongs only to one whose essential nature has already been determined;
and the definition is the means for determining that [nature].

And since there is no occasion for a specific definition without a general definition, he first states the general definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa): "It is simply correspondence with reality (yāthārthya)."
"Validity consists precisely in accordance with reality...
Regarding this, someone asks:
for what purpose is the definition stated?

Is this for the purpose of cognizing the object of definition as distinguished from similar and dissimilar things? Or is it for the purpose of cognizing its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, by pointing out its defining characteristic?
Or is it for the purpose of determining the basis for the application of terms such as "means of valid cognition"?
Or for some other purpose whatsoever?
Not the first,
because that [purpose] itself is difficult to ascertain.
For instance:
is "homogeneity" intended here in the sense of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or in some other form?

Not the first [alternative], because it would be non-pervasive; for if one accepts exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)— since it would otherwise be impossible for something to function as an excluder (*vyavacchedaka*) without being excluded from its own delimiting boundary (*svavyavacchedāvadhi*), which is of the same class— it would fail to encompass all instances.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
because it would render the mention of a term denoting a different class (vijātīya) redundant;
for [the property of being] an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) and so forth [already exists].
[This refers to] similarity with everything.

Now, if this is stated with the intention of expressing similarity through the specific property of being cognition (*jñānatva*), then since the definiendum (*lakṣya*) would also possess similarity [with everything] by virtue of its being cognition and so forth, it would fall within the category of things to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*); consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence that nothing remains to be included (*saṅgrāhya*).
If it is argued: "That which is of the same class (*sajātīya*) as the definiendum (*lakṣya*) by virtue of being a cognition and so forth is what is to be excluded;
however, the definiendum is not of the same class as itself, because the relation denoted by the genitive case is established as residing in difference."

If that is the case, then let it simply be said that there is an exclusion of others distinct from the object of definition (*lakṣya*); what is the use of describing a commonality such as "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*), which is irrelevant to the subject at hand?

Furthermore, when others understand the object of definition to be different from themselves, they necessarily understand that the object of definition is also different from them; thus, since the purpose of the definition is already established beforehand, the statement of the definition would be entirely redundant. (5.125)
Moreover, an exclusionary cognition cannot possibly arise through this characteristic while it remains unapprehended,
for that would lead to an over-extension;
nor can it arise when it is already apprehended.
Because it is difficult to ascertain: perception is not [defined] by its characteristic [alone],
for such qualities as "arising from faultless sense organs" are not themselves perceptible qualifiers.
Nor can there be an understanding of that [cause] through the effect as a logical mark (*liṅga*) or through its impossibility otherwise (*tadanupapatti*);
for by those two, only a cause in general is implied, and since a uniform nature residing in the cause is not established, a single defining characteristic is not proven.
If it is argued that the establishment of a cause of a single kind follows from the effect being of a single genus (*ekajāti*), [we reply:]...

In that case, since one must necessarily admit that the single universal residing in the effect is cognized beforehand, let the same fault [of infinite regress] arise from that very fact regarding the exclusion of homogeneous and heterogeneous instances.
This has been done by her through a series of devious maneuvers.
But even with this much, the refutation of the definition under discussion is not possible,
if it is argued that neither the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) nor over-extension (*atibyāpti*) has been pointed out.
Not so;

for when the accomplishment of the goal is possible through a simpler means that must necessarily be accepted because it occurs first, this [criticism] applies only to you, who proceed toward a more complex means that is not necessarily to be practiced because it occurs later.
Pointing out a fault:
for example, when a person, seeking to dispel darkness, lights one lamp within another lamp,
there is no defect whatsoever in that lamp.
However, it is precisely the person who acts in such a manner who should be questioned;
or rather, this fault is common to all means of proof,
namely that the possibility of such an easy method constitutes a failure of essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) for all instruments of knowledge.
Therefore, let there be no fault such as over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and so forth;
for a definition is indeed flawed by virtue of general defects.
By this, the second [position] is also refuted.

Since the comprehension of that [object] is impossible without the comprehension of its being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) in the cognition of it for the sake of comprehending that [means of valid cognition].
Or, let there be some other mark (*liṅga*) in the definition;
even so, that very [mark] should be presented as the definition because it is inseparable from the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) and is thus more readily understood.

If it is argued that this need not necessarily be stated as a pervader (*vyāpaka*), because its status as a logical mark (*liṅgatva*) is established by its being the pervaded (*vyāpya*) itself—[we reply:

no, for in a case where the logical mark is absent due to non-pervasion, the definition cannot be cognized there because of a lack of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); how, then, could validity and so forth be understood from that?

And when, in some cases, because there is an absence of means of valid cognition regarding the very class of things to be defined (*lakṣyajātīya*), the definition cannot be ascertained and thus its pervasion of the objects to be defined (*lakṣyavyāpakatā*) is not apprehended, even then it remains a definition.
In that case, what wrong has been committed by another mark (*liṅga*) that is non-pervasive?
Now, where that characteristic mark (liṅga) is not present, it must be understood there from another mark;
nevertheless,
let those two themselves remain as the marks in the object to be characterized (lakṣya).
Is it preceded by an inference based on a definition? Or rather,
is it that those two types of logical marks (liṅga), being individually non-pervasive, do not constitute a definition?
If it is argued that the definition is rather that which is inferred from that [object], because it conforms to its nature, we say no;

for since the object to be defined and the purpose of the definition are both established by those two alone, what is the use of such an all-encompassing [definition]? Nor is the third [alternative] possible.
For it is argued that such a thing, being in accordance with reality, should be designated as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is untenable,
because it is impossible to know the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) in all cases.
If that [object] is understood through its being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) and so forth, let that alone be the cause for the regulation of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-niyama*);
for it has already been explained that this involves an unmediated comprehension.
Precisely for this reason, the fourth [alternative] is not tenable.
Furthermore, there is the additional fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava-doṣa*).
Nor is it the fifth [alternative],
because such a thing cannot be demonstrated.
To this it is replied:
Let us first grant the position that a definition exists for the purpose of cognizing the definiendum as distinguished from both similar and dissimilar things.

For when one who knows the connection with the definition sees a particular individual possessing a dewlap and so forth, it is established that "this is not a horse or the like, nor is it a jar or the like."
Now, is it not the case that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), and difference (*bheda*) are synonymous?
And difference is simply the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the thing itself.
Thus, since the cognition of that [difference] is nothing other than the cognition of the nature of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), there is no need for a definition.
Now, if it is held that exclusion is understood by means of a definition independently of the cognition of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*),
that is not so; for there can be no understanding (or perception) of that [exclusion] without a substratum.
"Because it is impossible to separate them.
This is true; for the very cognition of the essential nature (or the thing-in-itself) is itself the cognition of difference.
Nevertheless, the definition is useful for the cognition of that [object] as qualified by its specific counter-correlate.
For even one who perceives a cow-individual in its unmixed state does not cognize "this is not a horse" or "this is not a jar" so long as he has not understood the definition.
If it is argued that "possessing a dewlap and so forth" is what is cognized at that time, we say no.
This is because what is intended to be understood is the cognition that "a cow is that which possesses a dewlap and so forth.
For this very reason, the qualifiers such as "of the same class" (*sajātīya*) and so on are employed.
Regarding what was stated here concerning "of the same class" and so forth:
That is incorrect;
for human speech, being dependent upon the speaker's intention, cannot be restricted [to a fixed meaning],
since that which is indicated (lakṣya) is indeed distinct from [the literal sense].
It is intended to be presented as two groups by way of being of the same class or of a different class:
for example, with respect to valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is knowledge of an object as it truly is and its means, that which is knowledge or its means is of the same class;
that which is neither knowledge nor its means is of a different class.
And just as inference and the like are of the same class as perception,
whereas objects such as a jar are of a different class,
so too should it be distinguished in other cases as well.
If it is argued that, in that case, it would be said that the exclusion of the non-dual is distinct from the perspective of the object to be characterized (*lakṣya*), who says "no"?
For no person of sound mind declares that the purpose of a definition is an exclusion from oneself alone. (5.140)
As for what was stated here, beginning with "And when," etc., that is irrelevant. In reality,

since a definition (*lakṣaṇa*)— which is the means of communication— is intended for the purpose of understanding the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) from that which is different from the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), although the cognition of its difference from the object to be defined [is necessary] regarding the non-object to be defined...
Even if it is not required by the subject,
there is no fault because the subject does not require it.

Since the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the knowledge of the meanings of its constituent words, some maintain that without the knowledge of the difference between the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) and other things— both similar and dissimilar— as conveyed by the words, the purpose of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), which is the knowledge of the difference of the indicated from the non-indicated (*alakṣya*), cannot be established. That is untenable.
The exclusion of others from the objects to be defined is not what is to be conveyed by the sentence stating the definition;
rather, it is the knowledge of that [exclusion] which is stated as the purpose of the definition.
Only the meaning of the sentence stating the definition itself is to be understood by the learner as that which is to be conveyed. *5,141*
As for what was asked with the words "And yet...
and so forth, we reply that it is precisely the already understood definition that produces the cognition of the defined object as excluded [from others].
Nor is its determination difficult.

[Objection: Since that [definition] is ascertained by means such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) according to the case, where it is understood through an inferential mark (*liṅga*), the purpose of the definition is accomplished by that very mark; therefore, mutual interconnection is useless. [Response:
This is not so, because when a purpose exists, even if there is complexity (*gaurava*), it is possible—and indeed appropriate—to disregard it.

Just as, by inferring that [cognition] arises from the sense organs because it conforms to their presence and absence through positive and negative concomitance, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is defined by that [inference],
so too is the purpose [of the definition] to make known the etymological designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*);
the same should be understood in other cases as well.
If it is argued that one should disregard the purpose in order to comply with respect, we say no;
for the intentions of individuals cannot be constrained.
Moreover, in terms of comprehension, the gain of an abundance of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) outweighs mere respect.
If it is argued that there is a redundant proliferation [of definitions] due to the absence of a purpose, we say no;
for when a purpose exists, even complexity (gaurava) may be disregarded.
This is just as, by inferring that a cognition arises from the sense organs because it follows their presence and absence, one defines perception (*pratyakṣa*) by means of that inference.
In this case, the purpose is to make known the designation according to its etymological meaning;
it should be understood in the same way elsewhere as well.
If it is argued that the purpose should be disregarded in favor of showing respect [for the tradition], we say no.
Because it is impossible to restrain the intentions of individuals,
and because in practice there is a gain of greater weight through the abundance of objects of knowledge;
whereas in the absence of a purpose, a succession of artificial fabrications is simply not to be respected— therefore, it is not our intention to demonstrate the faults inherent in such [traditions].
By this, the second, third, and fourth [types] should also be understood as being resolved,
because the means for determining their characteristics has been stated and because respect is concentrated. *5,144*
But even so, what is reality?
It is all fourfold according to their respective natures;
for instance:
In some cases, the definition is distinct from the definiendum, as in "earth is that which possesses odor. In other cases, it is not distinct from the definiendum.
For example: "Earth is that which possesses earth-ness," or "valid cognition is that which accords with the object," and so forth.

In these cases, the first [type of definition], by serving as the cause for the comprehension of the essential nature of the definiendum (*lakṣya*), establishes its positive concomitance (*anvaya*), its exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), and its status as the referent of that specific term.
The second, however, is the ground for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*), which serves merely as the cause for worldly convention.

In that regard, one should infer for oneself that the status of being the subject (*pakṣa*) belongs to the established portion, while the status of being the probandum (*sādhya*) belongs to the unestablished portion.
Now, does a definition exclude what is already excluded, or what is not yet excluded?
Regarding the first [alternative], does its own exclusion depend on another definition or not?
Not the first;
for if that too requires a definition, there would be the fallacy of infinite regress.
Not the second [alternative], because that same consequence would apply to the object characterized as well; furthermore,
if one were to accept an effect without a cause, its occasional occurrence would be inexplicable.
Not the latter, because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). To this,
it is said:
A characteristic also excludes only that which is excluded;
and that too is by means of a characteristic itself.
Nor does this lead to an infinite regress.
Because [the relationship between word and meaning] is established among objects already previously known.

However, one who is like a piece of wood or a clod of earth—who does not know some object or that a certain thing is denotable by a certain word—is not qualified for the science of grammar (*lakṣaṇa-śāstra*).

For what person, having already understood the connection between words and their meanings through instruction and so forth, would require a grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) for the sake of independent linguistic usage and the like? (5.149)
Furthermore, it might be argued:
is the understood characteristic the cause of the fruit, or is it the ununderstood?
The last [alternative] is not tenable,
because it would entail the futility of that designation;
for a designation serves as a means for the production of knowledge.
And because it is accepted that this [means] is a means to the fruit precisely when it is not yet understood:
in the first case, does its understanding come from something else, or from your own defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*)?
If it comes from something else, [then what need is there for your statement?]
This effort of defining the denotative function is superfluous;
for there is no purpose for the denotative function other than the production of cognition,
and that [cognition] is established through other means alone.

Regarding the latter [alternative], does this statement of yours indicate the definition by way of being a reliable instruction (*āptopadeśa*), or by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth?
It cannot be the latter,
because it is impossible to demonstrate an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) and the like between your words and the definition.

Nor is the first [alternative] tenable, because the status of being a reliable authority (*āpta*) with respect to another person has not been established; for if it were established, the probandum would be proven by the mere statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) alone, rendering the reason (*hetu*) and so forth superfluous.
The statement of the definition would be purposeless;
for indeed, the statement of a definition is not meaningful with respect to the opponent,
since he does not accept the existence of the property belonging to the proponent.
However, the definition is stated in the treatise for the sake of the student;
for he regards the author of the entire treatise as an authoritative person (āpta).
Therefore, with respect to the student, the sentence containing the definition will convey the meaning solely by virtue of being the word of an authoritative person.
Not so;

for if the treatise is not intended for the opponent but for the student, then since the student’s ascertainment of the object is established by the mere statement of the proposition (pratijñā) as the word of a reliable authority (āpta), the formulation of the reason (hetu) and other members would result in pointlessness within the treatise.

Now, suppose you think that while that scriptural statement— wherein the reason (*hetu*) and other members are included— is intended for the opponent as well, the definition-statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*), however, is effective only for the student, because the author of the treatise has been recognized as an authoritative person (*āpta*).
That too is untenable,
because this matter is established by other treatises;
for there exist treatises composed by the sages that record conventions, such as the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana*, grammar, and so forth.
To this we reply:
for it has already been stated that the very definition [of a means of knowledge] is that it is the cause of valid cognition;
and that such cognition occurs through the appropriate means of valid cognition, such as perception and so forth.

Nor do we accept that "a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that which corresponds to reality" is the definition of the sentence "an ox is that which possesses a dewlap and so forth," such that this [definition] would be redundant because it is already established from another source. Rather, it is for one who knows the definition from another source...
And because he does not know [the nature of things] by way of being the basis for conventional usage and so forth,
this statement is intended for his understanding;
for it is as follows:

When, through instruction such as "this is a cow," a single individual has been understood as the referent of the word "cow," one who desires to know whether this very individual alone is so, or whether others are as well, is addressed by the following statement concerning pervasion (*vyāpti*): "Whatever possesses a dewlap and so forth, that is the referent of the word 'cow'. This is because it would be impossible for a person to teach the status of the word "cow" with respect to every other instance due to their infinity and so on. Thus, he speaks this sentence which has pervasion as its object.
And this [statement] does not indicate pervasion (*vyāpti*) solely by virtue of being the instruction of a reliable person;
rather, it functions as a reminder of a pervasion already perceived, just like other formal applications (*prayoga*).
However, in the case of a pervasion not yet perceived, it is useful for producing valid cognition by way of generating a desire to know it.

Furthermore, what is the fault in [the view that] one who has remembered the pervasion (vyāpti) infers each individual object possessing a dewlap and so forth— which he perceives— to be the referent of the word "cow"? Alternatively,
when one understands the word "earth" or a particular individual as having that [earth] as its referent, [one understands] its basis for application (pravṛttinimitta).
When one desires to know it, [one asks] "Is earth that which possesses earth-ness? and thus earth-ness is stated to be the basis for the application of the word "earth.
In that regard, one who perceives the speaker to be authoritative is satisfied by that much;
however, for another person, the remainder of the sentence proceeds on the grounds that [the speaker] is free from non-pervasion and other such defects.

Alternatively, for one who has understood that there exists an object named "cow," when the cognition of "cow" might apply indiscriminately to any cow, or even to a jar, a horse, or other things, the following statement is employed:

by means of ascertaining the specific nature of the cow, it effects an exclusion of others, stating, "Only that which possesses a dewlap and so forth is a cow, but not a jar or the like which lacks those features, nor a horse or the like."
This too, as before, relies on two possible courses—either the ascertainment or the non-ascertainment of its being authoritative; so what is there that is illogical here?
But surely, in this case, the argument should be formulated thus:
"This [animal] must be treated as a cow, because it possesses a dewlap and other such characteristics."
In that regard, is it the cow that is the qualifier of the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), or is it the word "cow"?
In the first case, if he did not know the linguistic usage as qualified by the cow, then how could he—through inference—know its necessity with respect to the individual present before him?
For one who has not known fire cannot be made to understand the connection with fire through inference.
Then, since it would merely be making known what is already known, inference would be useless.
Nor is the second case [viable];
for in that case, the inference would be: "This is denotable by the word 'cow' because it possesses a dewlap and so forth."
In that case, there would be an over-extension of the principle;
for then even the state of being denotable by words such as *ja-ba-ḍa-da-śa* would have to be established as the probandum (*sādhya*) in that very same instance.
These [words] are not even generally recognized as being meaningful.
If it is argued that there is a distinction because the word "cow" is not like this [i.e.,
non-existent], even so, let the state of being denotable by words such as "hare's horn" be established as the probandum;
for those too are well-known precisely as having non-existent objects.

If it is argued that the word "cow" is not like this because of usages such as "the cow exists," even so, there would be an inference of being denotable by words such as "Svastimatī" for any cow whatsoever. If it is further argued that this is not the case because, although "cowness" (gotva) exists [in all cows], that word is not applied elsewhere [than to specific individuals], [we reply: ...
In that case, for one who knows that where the possession of a dewlap and so forth is absent, the application of the word "cow" is also absent,
and where the possession of a dewlap and so forth exists, it exists everywhere— that person is the one for whom the formulation of a definition is intended.

And since such a person has already ascertained the relationship between the signifier and the signified through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) just as in other linguistic conventions, inference would be redundant.
Not so;
for there is no fault in either case. Indeed, it would be appropriate to state this only in the case of a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) inference.

For one who has understood that a linguistic usage is qualified by a cow through [means such as] instruction and so forth, what contradiction would there be in accepting that the necessity to perform it elsewhere is to be established by inference?
It must be stated whether the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) occurs in proving the necessity of performing a usage qualified by a word for the person being informed or for the informer.
It is not the first case.
Because that pervasion has not been apprehended by him,
whereas the pervasion of being denotable by the word "cow" has been apprehended;
thus, the second [alternative] is not [tenable].
For by him as well, pervasion was previously understood in that very same way through the words of elders and so forth;
moreover, sublation (*bādha*) has been determined by the presence or absence of the formal application (*prayoga*).

Indeed, merely because the person to be informed (*bodhya*) lacks familiarity with sublation, the informer (*bodhaka*), even though already familiar with sublation, should not cause them to understand something contrary to reality.
This is because it would result in the fallacy of deception,
and because a treatise follows the method of debate (vādakathā) for the purpose of determining the truth.
In this same manner, the method of formulating an inference should be understood in other positions as well.
As for what was said— that this matter need not be stated because it is established by other treatises—
that is incorrect. For we have not asserted that whatever is established by other treatises in every respect must not be stated.
Nor should one suspect a confusion of treatises in this way, because their subject matter and purpose differ.

If it is argued: "If the subject matter of your treatise includes even that which is to be accomplished by other treatises, then why is that which is to be accomplished by grammar and the like not also mentioned?"—the answer is no.
This is because there is a disparity [between the two cases] due to the presence or absence of doubtfulness and lack of purpose (*aprayojanatva*).

Even if doubtfulness and so forth were present, the fact that [the opponent] does not state [the reason] is because it can be understood by the students themselves in the manner already described; therefore, this objection is trivial.
Otherwise, even the opponent would be destroyed by the very arguments put forward by his own offspring, like a crab [devoured by its young].
For he too has set forth definitions such as "superimposition (adhyāsa) is the appearance, in the form of memory, of something previously perceived upon another" in his own treatise;
and the author of the Sūtras [has stated], "from which [proceeds] the birth and so forth of this [universe].
It must now be stated whether these defects affect those definitions or not.
The second [alternative] is not tenable,
because it is subject to the same logical reasoning as the [refutation of the] universal (*sāmānya*).
Nor is the first [alternative] tenable.
Because the inclusion of defects is a cause of defeat [in a legal proceeding].
If it is argued that even those [statements] overwhelmed by defects carry through the legal process, we say no;
for if defective statements were to possess that quality even at the very outset, why would the same not apply to the utterances of the insane?
For there is no other reason for their non-establishment than this [lack of coherence].

Furthermore, by speaking thus, you would have to abandon even the view that what is sublated prior to the direct realization of Brahman is "empirical" (vyāvahārika), while that which is sublated by the direct realization of Brahman is [also] empirical.
For this is neither a direct realization of Brahman nor a sublation.
Furthermore, why should our own definition not likewise accomplish practical usage?
Nor do we desire anything to be accomplished by it other than the fulfillment of such usage.
If it is argued that the ultimate reality (pāramārthikatā) desired by you is thereby sublated, [we reply: no.
Is it of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or of the characterized (*lakṣya*)? Not the first; for as follows:

It might be argued that "the object of doubt is not ultimate reality because it is a statement devoid of purpose," and so forth; however, a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this [reason] cannot be established against us. Furthermore, under this position, you would not be able to avoid the untenability of the definition of superimposition (*adhyāsa*).
Because that [conventional reality] does not conflict with the maintenance of worldly transactional practice (*vyavahāra*),
and because it is accepted as a means for negating ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), it does not constitute a proof of what is desired;
by this, defects such as over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and so forth do not apply to the non-ultimate (or ultimate).
Therefore, that [first position] would be a proof;
however, it would be a proof of the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇatā*),
not the second.
Because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of Brahman when proving the falsity of the object of definition by means of the characteristic of being impossible;
for the aforementioned impossibility of the definition applies equally to that [Brahman] which is its own definition.
Furthermore, is the definition of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) tenable or not?
In the first case, the probans would not enter into the similar instances (*sapakṣa*);

in the second case, the effort to refute its impossibility would be futile. Let this suffice for the detailed discussion. "It does not overstep the object" means it is "in accordance with the object" (*yathārtha*).
Its state is "conformity with reality" (*yāthārthya*);

that itself is "the nature of being a means of valid cognition" (*mānatva*), meaning it is the basis for the application of the term *pramāṇa* and, in short, the definition of a means of valid cognition. Although the relationship between the definiendum and the definition is indeed understood even when it is stated that "a means of valid cognition is that which conforms to reality"—just as in the case of "an ox is that which possesses a dewlap and so forth"—nevertheless, one might still suspect, as in that same example, that the definiendum is something distinct from the definition.

Furthermore, lest one should suspect that it might be something to be determined separately [from the object], it has been stated that being a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) is simply the state of corresponding to reality (*yāthārthya*), and not something distinct from it—unlike "cowness" (*gotva*), which is distinct from the possession of a dewlap and so forth.
Now, what is this so-called "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*)?
It is the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of the thing to be defined (*lakṣya*).
As many as are the things intended to be designated by a single word,
and as many as are the things to be excluded from it, those are called the "objects of definition" (*lakṣyāṇi*). Is it not [the case that] the uncommon...?
If non-pervasion were also considered a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), then even that which is non-pervasive would incur the status of being a defining characteristic;
for, like over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and impossibility (*asambhava*), non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) is indeed a defect of a defining characteristic.
To this it is replied:
For a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is employed as a mark (liṅga);
and pervasiveness (vyāpakatā) is not useful for being a mark,
since that is established solely through being the pervaded (vyāpyatva).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that smoke and the like could not function as valid logical marks (*liṅga*). Indeed, [the mark] must depend upon its pervasion being observed both in the subject (*pakṣa*) and in the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*).
For if that which is presented as the means were absent, the attainment of its goal would be impossible.
Because pervasion, which consists of both properties, cannot be demonstrated in the absence of either one;
and thus, at that time, the definition requires the state of being pervaded by that which is intended to be defined.
And it has already been stated that this is a property of the definiendum.

The claim that non-pervasion (*avyāpakatva*) constitutes a fault in a definition (*lakṣaṇadoṣa*) should be understood as applying to every case where [the subject] is intended to be defined; or else, that statement is made because it is certain that no other definition exists elsewhere.
In reality, however, even that which is manifold, like a single entity, certainly functions as a definition when it effects exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and so forth within its own respective substrata.

For this very reason, Kaṇāda stated that "possessing action" (*kriyāvat*) is also a definition of substance, in his formulation: "Substance is that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause.
If it is argued that the inclusion of the term "possessing action" is for another purpose, [we reply:]...
In this regard, is there an alternative explanation because it is impossible for that which is non-pervasive to function as a definition, or is it due to some other cause?
It cannot be the latter,
because no such [other] cause is observed.
Not the first [alternative], because its impossibility has already been refuted.
But surely, in this case, one should employ the argument by taking all nine substances, beginning with earth, as the subject (*pakṣa*), stating: "These are substances because they possess action."
Or [the reason] might be "possessing activity" or "being corporeal.
Not the first, because of the fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*).
Nor the second.
Because it is not definitively established;
how then could there not be an inconsistency?
Do not say so.
This is because some do not accept that non-determination (*anadhyavasita*) constitutes a logical fallacy (*doṣa*).

Furthermore, even for those who do accept it as a fallacy, once the substantiality (*dravyatva*) of a jar or similar object has been ascertained through instruction and other means, what kind of fault could there be in employing something other than that [ascertained object] as the subject (*pakṣa*) when proving its substantiality? Enough of this!
Some disputants have maintained that consciousness (*vijñāna*) possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*).
Others, however, [hold it to be] the cause of that.
What, then, is the truth in this matter?
We say: both.
Valid cognition (*pramiti*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),

because the word *pramāṇa* has the capacity to denote both the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*), as in the definition "that by which something is cognized is the means of valid cognition" (*pramīyate 'nena iti pramāṇam*).
Although the suffix *-lyuṭ* is traditionally taught to denote the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as well as the abstract action and the instrument, [here it is understood in the sense of instrument].
Nevertheless, because the word *pramāṇa* lacks [the required] denotation (*abhidhāna*), it does not function there;
for *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compound formations depend upon denotation.
But is there not also usage in the locative case, such as "the Brahmins are the authority" (*viprāḥ pramāṇam*)?
Not so;
for Brahmins, who are independent agents with respect to valid cognition (*pramā*), cannot be the locus [of such an action].
For a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is not the substratum of an action;
rather, that *kāraka* which is the substratum for the act of supporting the agent and the object—which are themselves the substrata of the action—is [the locus].
Therefore, because of the authority of their cognition or of their speech, Brahmins are metaphorically designated as "authority" (*pramāṇa*).
If, then, both the cognition and its cause are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
does validity— which is synonymous with "conformity to reality" (*yāthārthya*)— operate in a single mode in both cases, or in multiple modes?

In the first case, there would arise a contradiction with the established doctrine that cognition alone is the primary means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), while its causes—characterized as perception, inference, and scripture—are secondary means of valid knowledge (*anupramāṇa*).

In the second case, the definition is untenable; because the two modes do not exist within one another, the definition suffers from the fallacy of being too narrow (*avyāpti*). Therefore, he says: "That" (*tad*).
... that is the primary [meaning] of the words "knowledge" (jñāna) and "word" (śabda). // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.1.21b //
The implication is that perception and inference, being the instruments [of knowledge], are secondary;
this will be made clear later. *5,185*
This might be so:
if being in accordance with reality were the definition of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*),
it would not be possible, because it is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*).
For instance:
fitness, distributive repetition,
and non-transgression of the word-meaning.
"Similarity" (*sādṛśya*) is also among the meanings of the word *yathā*.
Furthermore, the word *artha* is used in the senses of "denotable object," "wealth," "thing," "purpose," and "cessation.
Among these, the word *yathā* in the sense of "similarity" is not accepted here.
Because of the specific qualification in the rule for forming an *avyayībhāva* compound— namely, "in the sense of 'as' or 'resemblance'" (*yathāsādṛśye*)—
and because other types of compounds are precluded by a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) and other such factors.

For this very reason, it is untenable for someone to raise the question: "In the definition that valid cognition (*pramā*) is an experience that accords with reality (*yathārtha*), what constitutes this 'accordance with reality'?"—such as whether it means similarity to the object, and so forth.
Nor is there room for such a question regarding the meaning of the terms *yogyatā* (fitness) or *vīpsā* (repetition), because of the [absence of] deficiencies in the remainder of the sentence.
Because, by virtue of the existence [of the object], there would result the validity of either the fitness of the objects or the repetition of the meaning;
therefore, this inclusion is for the purpose of excluding the non-cessation of the word-meanings.

If the word *artha* were taken in the sense of "denotable object," there would be the consequence of under-extension (*avyāpti*); therefore, it must be understood as referring specifically to that which is synonymous with "object" (*viṣaya*).
Thus, it would be stated that "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is that which does not transcend—that is, does not deviate from—the object (*artha*), i.e., the object (*viṣaya*).
And this [definition] applies to every action that possesses an object (*sakarmaka-kriyā*).
For motion does not transcend that which is to be traversed,
nor does cutting transcend that which is to be cut;
for that very thing which is to be reached by means of motion and so forth is itself the object to be traversed and so on.
Therefore, because this is not the definition, he says: "the state of being an object" (arthatva).
"Being an object (arthatva) would indeed be being an object... (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.1.21c).

The intended meaning is that for us, "being an object" (*arthatva*)—that is, "being knowable" (*jñeyatva*)—is what is meant by the basis for the application of the word "object" (*artha-śabda-pravṛtti-nimitta*), and not "being an objective domain" (*viṣayatva*). This is the sense.
This is what is meant:
it is indeed accepted that the word *yathā* expresses the sense of not exceeding the meaning of a term;
however, the word *artha* is not taken here as a synonym for "object" (*viṣaya*).

However, it denotes the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Although it has no conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) in that sense, it certainly possesses the capacity to denote it through its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), namely, "that which is to be known" (*arthyate*).
This is because the suffix *than* belonging to the *uṇādi* class is well-known [in this sense],
and because verbal roots meaning "to go" (*gati*) also carry the sense of "to know" (*jñāna*). But how is it that [the word] *arthatā* [is used]?
“Because of the qualification ‘an Ārya [is the officiant] for a master or a Vaiśya,’ it is not so.
No, that is not correct.
This is due to the metaphorical designation of ownership (*svāmitva*).

For an object (*artha*) is intended to be primary in relation to knowledge and so forth. [Objection: What follows if this is so? If being an object (*jñeyatā*) is itself the state of being an object (*arthatva*), [the author] says: "No. (*na*) [Vibhūticandra’s commentary on the verse].
... that [speech] is not considered appropriate for matters concerning ritual action.
In the case of actions—that is, regarding objects of action—there is that "accordance with reality" (yathārthatā);

however, due to the absence of such [an object], there is no accordance with reality. The implication is that the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) when applied to actions.
But even by this much, the over-extension [of the definition] has not been avoided;
for even movements such as going do not transcend the category of the knowable.
Indeed, it cannot be said that the village or other objects which are their objects are not knowable in every respect.
"Because that would entail the consequence of its absolute non-existence"—

do not say so; for just as the statement "one who is virtuous toward his father is virtuous toward his mother" does not terminate in [the sense of] being virtuous toward some mere father or the like, [so too is the case here].
But [it applies] to one's own father and so forth.
For what reason?
Because words such as "father" and the like are relative terms.
For this is the inherent power of words denoting relations;
otherwise, there would be great confusion in cases such as "one should take the father's wealth.
And since this is so, one who objects while disregarding the power of words would be defeated for being a caviller (*chala-vādin*).

Likewise, in the present case as well, since the word "knowable" (*jñeya*) is a relative term, it would mean that whatever does not exceed its own object of knowledge is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, a village is not "knowable" by means of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of going, nor is it knowable by the act of going itself as the cause.
Since it exists without overstepping that [object], its movement would be consistent with reality;
however, it is indeed something to be traversed.
So how could there be an over-extension [of the definition]?
And a jar or the like becomes an object of knowledge through cognition and its cause, which serve as limiting conditions (*upādhi*) and instrumental causes (*nimitta*).
This is what was stated by those who know the true nature of the meaning of words: "That [cognition] is not considered [to be the meaning] in the case of things that are objects of action.
Now, even so, there would still be either mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) or self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatva*).

If it is argued that this is not so because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is denoted by its own specific term, we say no; for the definition has already been explained by employing only "cognition" and its "causes. [This applies to] one's own quality (the grasper).
Regarding the statement "the sense organ is the ear, [which is] grasping," as in that case:
now, what is this so-called non-deviation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) from the object of knowledge (*jñeya*)?
Is it being pervaded by the object of cognition (*prameya*), or is it having as its scope all objects of cognition?
Even regarding the first [alternative], is the pervasion spatial or temporal?
Not the first,
because there would be no pervasion in the case of those means of valid cognition whose objects are entities located in a space different from that of the means of valid cognition themselves.
Not the second,
because it does not extend to valid cognition regarding objects such as the past;
nor the last.
"Because it would follow that the cognitions of those who are not omniscient, or their causes, would lack validity"— this is not so;
for even by the opponent, who accepts the validity— characterized by its capacity to reveal reality— of the non-dual scripture (*advaitāgama*) and so forth...
If it is argued that this matter must also be explained,
[and that] we employ [the term] based on what is accepted by others, but do not establish any definition at all— this is not so.
This is because the establishment [of truth] must necessarily rely upon one's own realization;
for it cannot be admitted that the reality is realized merely by the fact that it is self-luminous without the comprehension provided by the Vedāntas.
Furthermore, if one were to define it as "the state of being real" consisting in "making known the reality," then there would be over-extension to the case of error.
Even in that case, this is because the form (ākāra) that has been communicated exists.

Now, if you were to say that "truthfulness" (*tattvāvedakatva*) consists in the existence of whatever has been communicated—that is, the state of having a single object (*ekagocaratva*)—then we too would say that such [correspondence] is precisely what constitutes "accordance with reality" (*yāthārthya*). *5,202*
But even so, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of error;

for is it not the case that neither the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*), nor the universal of "silver-ness" (*rajatatva*), nor its relation—whether inherence (*samavāya*) or identity (*tādātmya*)—is unreal?
If you argue that although it exists elsewhere, it is non-existent here, [we reply: no.
For Devadatta, when not present in the house, is not simply non-existent;
nor does this undesirable consequence apply to us,
because we accept that everything other than the substratum is indeterminable (anirvacanīya).
Do not say so; for we also accept its absolute non-existence.

Now, it may be thought: is the existence of that object intended at that very time, or previously, or later, or always, or at some time or other, or whatever [existence] it has in whatever place and time as it is perceived?
[The definition] applies because of the suchness of that place and time.
Not the first [alternative],
because it does not encompass the means of valid cognition regarding past and future objects.
The second [alternative] is not tenable,
because it does not encompass objects that are present or future;

and because it would result in over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the cognition of "blue" even in a jar that has been baked red, or to the cognition of "conjunction" at a time subsequent to disjunction.
Not the third [alternative],
because it does not extend to objects such as the past,
and because it would result in over-extension to the case where a jar that is black due to a future ripening of passion appears red to one suffering from jaundice.
Nor is it the fourth,
because it does not pervade impermanent objects.
Nor is it the fifth.
Because it would over-extend to the previously mentioned error;
nor is it the sixth,
because it does not pervade [the cases of] place, time, and means of valid cognition.
"It is not the case that for space and time there exists another space and time.
Do not say so;
for it will be explained later that even space and time are defined by their own relations.

Alternatively, it has already been stated that the existence of a thing is its being as it is perceived; thus, there is no over-extension [of the definition]. This is because space and time, like any other qualifier, are already subsumed by the phrase "as it is" (*yathābhūtam*). Since no specific distinction [regarding space and time] has been mentioned, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
And because of the consequence [of over-extension]:
likewise, in this case, this definition is impossible due to the absence of any determinative factor. To explain:

Is the truthfulness of knowledge to be determined by its being produced by a non-defective instrument, or by its not being produced by a defective instrument, or else by the efficacy of purposeful action?
Or [is it] by corroboration with another cognition,
or by the absence of non-corroboration?
Not the first.
Because that [validity] itself is difficult to ascertain;
for if it were inferred through the truthfulness of the cognition, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya),
and because such validity is absent in the case of eternal cognitions.
Not the second,
because it is impossible to determine [the object];
not the third.
It is not the first [alternative], because that [nature] is absent everywhere;
nor is it the fourth,
because that is absent in the cognition of pleasure and so forth.

Furthermore, if one accepts that correspondence consists merely in the cognition itself, then it would follow that even in a continuous stream of error (*dhārāvāhika-vibhrama*), there would be the apprehension of that [object]. However, if one maintains that correspondence is with a cognition that is in accordance with reality (*yathārtha-jñāna-saṃvāda*), then because one must ascertain the reality of each respective cognition, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) results.

Nor is it the fifth [alternative], because that would apply even to those who have not yet experienced the error of sublation; furthermore, the conceptual distinctions of person, place, and time would be untenable.
Not so;
for if that were the case, it would follow that even the cognition produced by the Vedānta texts could not be determined to be in accordance with reality.
If you argue that its determination as such follows from the truth of its object, then how is that very truth established?
If it is argued that this is due to the power of cognition (*jñāna-sāmarthya*), is this the power of mere cognition, or of cognition ascertained as being in accordance with reality?
In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that even the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like would possess reality.
In the second case as well, does this refer to that very same cognition or to another cognition?
It cannot be the first,
because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence.
The second [alternative] is not [tenable], because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and other such fallacies.
Now, one might think: "The apprehension of the validity of cognitions occurs through themselves alone; it is only in some cases that this is set aside by sublation (*bādha*)."
Furthermore, the sublation of the knowledge of Brahman is not possible,
because such sublation is not observed even when an investigation is conducted according to one's capacity,
and because a groundless doubt does not arise.
Because no sublation (bādha) is observed that is without limit or without a witness;
and because, if limits and so forth were admitted, it would be impossible to sublate that very [limit] since it would be Brahman itself.
This same point applies equally in our own system as well.
And since this meaning has been explained here and there, it is established that being in accordance with reality (*yāthārthya*) is the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, it is not tenable to say that this [definition] applies primarily to both knowledge (*jñāna*) and words (*śabda*);
for if that were the case, the word would also result in being a [valid means of cognition] in its own right, just like knowledge.
He dispels this doubt with a supporting argument: "For the sake of knowledge."
The state of being knowable is primary with respect to the object of knowledge, and immediately thereafter [it is primary] with respect to the object of words.

Since knowability is primary in the case of cognition— meaning in the object of cognition— and subsequently knowability is primary in the case of words— meaning in the object of words— it follows that validity, characterized by correspondence with reality, is primary in cognition alone,
whereas it is secondary in the case of words.

And thus, the meaning is that it does not follow that [the Self] becomes isolated (kevalatva). Since "being the object of desire" (aryatā) is the primary [meaning] in the context of objects of knowledge, one might raise the objection: "If it must be stated that 'being the object' exists even among actions whose goal is movement (gatikarma), then the over-extension (ativyāpti) of the definition to 'movement' remains as it was. To dispel this doubt, "being the object of knowledge" (jñeyatā) is provided as the explanation of "being the object" (aryatā).
This is what is meant:
the correspondence with reality in the case of a word is not primary by virtue of being on an equal footing with knowledge;
rather, it is merely instrumental (*karaṇa*).

With respect to the triad [of agent, instrument, and object], primary correctness (*yāthārthya*) resides primarily in cognition (*jñāna*), while among instruments (*karaṇa*), it resides primarily in the word (*śabda*).
Thus, having unified these two—the most primary and the primary—it was stated that "that primary [correctness] belongs to cognition and the word. (5.215)
Alternatively, this meaning should be explained right here in the context of the words "jñāna" (knowledge) and "śabda" (word):
namely,
that [the word] is primary with respect to knowledge when it refers to its correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*), but secondary with respect to the instruments [of knowledge].

When the inquiry arises as to whether the means of knowledge (*karaṇa*) are of one kind or many kinds, it was stated that with respect to verbal testimony (*śabda*), [the former] is primary, while for perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), it is secondary. And here,
by the term "verbal testimony," the venerable Sage intends specifically the Veda,
because the discussion of its primacy is precisely what is useful for Mīmāṃsā.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the inquiry being purposeless and its resolution being irrelevant.

Although the words *jñāna* and *śabda* are presented as a copulative compound (*dvandva*), nevertheless, since [the word *śabda*] is not primary when referring to the instruments of knowledge, he says: "for the sake of knowledge" (*jñānārtha*).
The mention of "sound" is illustrative;
it should be understood that this applies to perception and inference as well.
The explanation, however, is as before.

The explicit mention of "word" (*śabda*) by its own name [in the definition] is intended to preclude the notion that it is perceived as being on the same footing as cognition in the preceding [definition].
In cognition, truthfulness is primary; in instruments [of knowledge], it is secondary.
In that regard as well, it was stated that [the word] is primary.

Therein, in order to establish the primacy and non-primacy of the correspondence between the cognition and its instrument, the primacy and non-primacy of the knowability of their respective objects were stated as the reason.
To establish that point, he says: "yathārtha... (MAnu 2.1.22cd):
"Reasonings that produce knowledge in accordance with reality are considered to be valid."
Sentences are accompanied by their contextual supplements (*sopaskara*).
Therefore, [the phrase] "knowledge is directly in accordance with reality" (*jñānaṃ sākṣādyathārtham*) and so forth should be supplied.
The plural number is used in the sense of "and so on" (*ādi*).
The meaning is "reasoning and so forth. By this, it is established that they are "producers" (*janaka*).
Without relying on the neuter indeclinability of the *avyayībhāva* compound by treating it as equivalent to Vedic usage, it was stated that they are "according to the object" (*yathārtha*).

Alternatively, by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound in some way, or else, taking the word *yathārtha* as primarily denoting a state (*bhāvapradhāna*), the suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*) because it belongs to the *arśa-ādi* group; thus the meaning is "endowed with truthfulness" (*yāthārthyopeta*). This is the sense.
For knowledge alone is the direct limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for an object—that is, for that which is to be known—in its status as being known;
this is because "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) will be refuted later.
