Therefore, it is [knowledge] that belongs to that very object.
Since "knowability" (*jñeyatva*) is primary, it is knowledge alone that possesses primacy in terms of correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*).

However, instruments such as reasoning (*yukti*) produce a cognition that serves as a limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the knowability of an object; therefore, the knowability of their respective objects is secondary. For that very reason, their correspondence with reality is also secondary. (5.224)
In this context, the statement "those which produce knowledge of things as they are are themselves [known] as they are" is intended to indicate the ultimate probandum (*paramasādhya*) as well.
The inclusion of the reason (*yukti*) first among the three [reasons] is for the purpose of indicating its relative inferiority.
The superiority and inferiority of scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*) have been established in their respective places, so they are not discussed here.

What follows from this, if such is the case—that the correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*) of cognition is primary, while that of the instruments of perception and so forth is secondary? To this he says: "It is a means of valid knowledge" (*anupramāṇam*).
For these words, therefore, are authoritative because they are consistent with reason and scripture.
Here too, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) should be read first as the sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for the connection is that "because it is thus, therefore [it is so]. The singular form "subsequent means of cognition" (*anupramāṇa*) is used in the sense of the plural.

This is because of the grammatical rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). Alternatively, the connection is that even those words presented as a *dvandva* compound—namely, "the senses" (*akṣa*) and "statements" (*vacas*)—are to be understood individually through mental discernment as being each a means of valid cognition (*anumāna*). Or rather, there is no fault here in stating that these [words] possess the nature of "senses" and so forth by way of restating them as means of valid cognition.
Without intending to express the intermediate operation, it is stated as "perception" (*kṣam*) with the intention of expressing only that which possesses the nature of an instrument;
otherwise, one would have to say "direct perception" (*pratyakṣam*).
The term "word" (*vaca*) is an illustration for scripture (*āgama*).
Nor should it be said that even so there is an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) of the definition;

for that [over-narrowness] would only occur if one were to accept that cognition alone is the "true" [means of knowledge], while the instruments [of knowledge] are merely metaphorically designated as such because they produce that [cognition].
But this is not the case,
because in both instances there is equality regarding the fact that they have as their object an entity as it actually exists;
for the object of the instruments of cognition is precisely the object of knowledge itself.
For those [senses] do not produce cognition without making anything their object,
nor do they have other things as their objects,
for that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

The distinction between direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) as independent means of valid cognition is established by relying on this much difference: that knowledge brings about the knowability of the object solely by way of being its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), whereas the instruments of cognition bring it about by way of being its producers.

If, however, there were a flaw of under-extension (*avyāpti*) based on this alone, then there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since one could point out some slight distinction in every case.
This is the collective meaning here.
Valid cognition is that which corresponds to reality.
It is of two kinds:
direct perception and inference.
In that regard, knowledge of things as they truly are is *kevala* (direct perception);
the means of achieving that is *anupramāṇa* (inference).
*Kevala* is also of two kinds.
And consciousness is of the nature of a modification (*vṛtti*).
Consciousness, moreover, is threefold,
distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior.
In that regard, the superior is indeed according to reality;
the middling is mixed;
the inferior is indeed not according to reality.
The second [type of valid cognition] is also exclusively threefold, based on the distinction between that which arises from perception, inference, and scripture.
Likewise, subsequent valid cognition (anupramāṇa) is also exclusively threefold, based on the distinction between perception, inference, and scripture.
[Objection: Even so, the over-extension [of the definition] to the "crow-and-palmyra" (kākatālīya) coincidence remains unavoidable.
For instance, someone having hidden five cowries in his hand asks another, "How many cowries are in my hand?
And being thus questioned, he replies, "Five," according to the maxim of the she-goat and the sword.
It follows that this knowledge of both the questioner and the speaker would be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it corresponds to reality.
Furthermore, since that [knowledge] does not arise without a cause, it follows that its cause must also be a valid means of cognition.
Moreover, such an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would be difficult to avoid even in the case of accidental coincidences, deceptive signs, or errors.
Not so;
for it does not follow that the speaker's cognition is of the nature of doubt.
Furthermore, any occasional usage [of such terms] in that context is based merely on audacity.
It is not based on one's own cognition;
otherwise, even a deceiver would incur such a certainty, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction between him and those who are actually mistaken.
By this, the postulation of an induced certainty is also refuted.
For the questioner, however, knowledge that occurs both prior to and after [the inquiry] is indeed valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [as it accords with reality],
and perception is its basis.
The cognition produced by a statement from someone standing nearby is exactly like this;
however, the statement itself may be coincidentally concordant.

Even though that which is produced by a fallacious statement or a deceptive mark—which are coincidentally concordant—may possess the status of a mere means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), those two [the fallacious statement and the deceptive mark] do not possess validity (*prāmāṇya*).
For instance,
it is not possible to claim that there, either the vapor itself or that which is cognized as vapor functions as a means for knowledge in accordance with reality.
Nor can it be smoke, because that which is non-existent cannot function as a means of proof; nor can it be smoke even if it exists, because it is not perceived as such.
Therefore, it must be stated that [the object] is either steam known as smoke, or a delusion of smoke regarding steam.
And that is not possible, because for everything of that same class, there is [only] the operation of the cause upon the effect.
If it is argued that [the definition] results in over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), we say no;
for although the confusion of gender may have a worldly cause, it has already been stated that it lacks the status of being a technical means (*sādhana*) according to our definition.
By this, the undesirable consequence that even a fallacious statement might possess validity is refuted. Even if such a consequence were to arise, it would cause us no harm;
for unlike the logicians (*tārkika*), we do not rely on an inference of validity based on the fact of being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*). (5.238)
Alternatively, the means of cognition (*sādhana*) is distinguished by its faultlessness (*nirdoṣatā*).

And this faultlessness should be explained as being characterized by the correspondence with reality (*yathārthatva*) and so forth of the cognition of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and other factors.
If that is the case, let it simply be said that a faultless means of cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*anupramāṇa*).
If it is argued that [the term] "yathārtha" (corresponding to reality) is used as a qualification of cognition (*jñāna*), [we reply:
no, because the very meaning resulting from that [qualification] has already been described by the inclusion of the term "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*).
Or rather, it is a statement of the essential nature [of cognition], namely that cognition produced by faultless instruments does not deviate from correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*). *5,240*
Now, one might object: "If the definition stated by other systems already exists, what is the purpose of this new construction? To this he says: "Validity...
[Verse 2.1.23cd]: "The validity of a restatement is not forfeited even in the case of a traditional scripture (smṛti)."
The intended meaning of the word "validity" (prāmāṇya) is precisely "conformity with reality" (yāthārthya).

Whenever the intended meaning of the term "validity" (*prāmāṇya*) is precisely "conformity with reality" (*yāthārthya*), only then is the validity of memory and restatement—which are both conformable to reality—not lost. However, if one accepts the definitions stated by other schools, since they admit that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is all-pervasive, it would follow that validity is entirely absent in memory and the like due to the absence of that [particular characteristic] therein; thus, it is logical to formulate a different definition while disregarding those [other views].

For instance, it is clear that the definition stated by the Mīmāṃsakas— that "valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which cognizes an object not previously apprehended"— is absent in the case of memory and the like,
because those have as their domain objects already apprehended.
[Furthermore,] the Prābhākara (or Bhāskara) [holds that] "valid cognition is experience (*anubhūti*)."
Furthermore, even the definition [of perception] does not apply there,
because of the etymological explanation that "perception" (anubhūti) is knowledge distinct from memory.

Likewise, the definition stated by the Naiyāyikas— that a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that which is pervaded by valid cognition (pramā), or that a means of valid cognition is the instrument of valid cognition— also does not apply.
For they too have explained that valid cognition (*pramā*) is an experience that accords with reality;
for this very reason, the view that the causal complex of valid cognition (*pramāsāmagrī*) is valid cognition is refuted.
This also applies to the Buddhist claim that non-discrepant cognition (*avisaṃvādivijñāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Because the non-contradiction intended by that [definition], such as being produced from an object (*arthaja*), is absent in memory and the like, it is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). Furthermore,

the definition stated by the Jains— that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is knowledge consisting of a determinative ascertainment (*vyavasāyātmaka*) of its own novel object (*apūrvārtha*)— does not apply to memory and the like,
because those lack the quality of having a novel object as their domain.

If it is argued that memory has as its object something not previously [perceived], because it is characterized by the mental projection "that," and because that [object] was not made an object of experience through direct perception— [we reply: no.
For if that were so, it would follow that there is nothing to be excluded by the inclusion of the term "previously unapprehended" (*apūrvagrahaṇa*).
If it is argued that a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhika*) is what is to be excluded by it, we say no; because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*).

Since the momentariness of all things is accepted in debate, it is easy to admit that even in the case of a continuous stream of cognitions (dhārāvāhika-vibhrama), each possesses the quality of apprehending a new object.
Alternatively, let there be no fault here in the loss of the validity of memory.
In the case of a continuous stream [of cognition], however, the loss of that [validity] is unavoidable;
yet even that is indicated by the two terms "recollection" (*smṛti*) and "restatement" (*anuvāda*).
[Objection: But even in your own position, the validity of recollection is indeed lost.
Because that [memory] lacks correspondence with reality;
for when an object is remembered in a certain way, it is not necessarily exactly like that at that time.
Because the prior state has ceased in the present;
for if it had not ceased, it would no longer be "prior.
Nor does memory take that object as its support by means of the very fact that the prior state has ceased.
Because, when the prior state has ceased, experience (anubhava) does not occur.
Now, even though memory and experience have the same object, why is it that experience is accurate while memory is not? Because at the time of experience, that object remains in its original state;
whereas at the time of memory, it no longer remains in that state.
[Objection: Surely, since that [object] was already in that very state previously, it would perish; let knowledge be considered "in accordance with reality" (yathārtha) by this much alone. [Reply:
No, because it would follow that even the cognition of blackness in something turned red by baking would be "in accordance with reality.
[Objection: But the cognition of past blackness in that case is indeed "in accordance with reality."
True;
at that time, the object itself is in that state,
but the state being remembered is not in that state at that time.
Therefore, memory is indeed non-correspondent with reality.
Not so;
for that would entail the fallacy of contradicting one's own established tenets (apasiddhānta).
For instance,

regarding the definition "valid cognition is the cause of apprehension" (*upalabdhi-hetu*), Vācaspati, having raised the objection that this definition over-extends (*ativyāpti*) to doubt and other such states, qualified "apprehension" by its contextually relevant quality of being "true-to-reality" (*yāthārthya*). Furthermore, fearing that this would still over-extend to the cause of memory, he stated that the word "apprehension" here signifies direct experience (*anubhava*) and not cognition in general.
By this it is known that he accepts the correspondence of memory with reality;
otherwise, if memory were excluded from being correspondent with reality, he would not have suspected it again.

Or, if he were so suspecting, he would not have extended that very same solution [to memory], nor would he have explained the word "perception" (*upalabdhi*) as referring specifically to "experience" (*anubhūti*).

The statements of the masters of Nyāya, such as "valid cognition (pramā) is experience corresponding to reality" and "the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that which brings about correct experience," also lead one to understand this very same point; otherwise, because it lacks two of its constituent factors, memory would not be excluded by the term "experience. Even the followers of Kaṇāda, who accept a fourfold division of knowledge into perception, inference, memory, and prophetic vision, have admitted that memory possesses correspondence with reality (*yathārthatva*).
As for the statement, “For [when] one [is] such-and-such,” and so forth— what is expressed by this?

Alternatively, it may be argued that memory is not in accordance with reality (ayāthārthya) because at the time of recollection the object no longer exists in that state; or because it does not take as its object the cessation of the previous state;
or because it takes as its object the object as if its previous state had not ceased.
In the first case, there would be a loss of the validity of inference and scripture regarding past and future objects,
because those objects do not exist at that time.
In the second case, it follows that all means of valid cognition would be invalid.
Because nothing whatsoever can be made an object in its entirety;
as for the third [alternative], it is unproven,
for memory does not take as its objective support that which remains in its undestroyed state.
But at that time, it is of such a nature;
thus, [the cognition] remains indifferent regarding whether that state has ceased or not ceased.
Now, by means of experience, "at that time..."
If it is asked, "How can those [cognitions] which make such a thing an object—[a thing] that was not previously made an object—attain correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*)?", we reply:
this would be so if we were to say that correspondence with reality consists in following the [prior] experience;
however, it has been stated that it consists rather in following the [actual] object.
If it is asked, "When the experience has one form, from where does this other form of memory arise?",
is this a misconception that [the other form] does not exist, or is it without cause?
Or, [it may be] merely a question. It is not the first case,
because it is established by direct perception (*sākṣisiddha*).
Not the second, because it involves a contradiction.
As for the third, from what source would even the experience itself arise?
If it is argued that [the memory] is produced by its own cause, the same [objection] applies.
Furthermore, if memory were produced solely from mental formations (*saṃskāra*),
then some degree of dissimilarity [between the object and the memory] would be impossible.
For it will be stated that "that [cognition] is indeed mental consciousness (*mānasa-vijñāna*).
Therefore, the rejection of the validity of memory based on its correspondence with reality is motivated merely by audacity.
Thus, it is well said that another definition was formulated in order to include the validity of memory as a restatement (*anuvāda*). *5,255*
But surely, inclusion is a merit for that which is included, not for that which is not included;
why then is over-extension considered a fault?
If it is argued that memory and the like are not included within the definition [of valid cognition] because they lack validity,
then why should the validity of memory and the like not be accepted simply because of the absence of a proving means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?
Nor [is it so] because of the existence of a sublater (*bādhaka*).
First, [the first alternative] is not [correct],
because worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*) exists.
For it is precisely with respect to that which possesses knowledge of an object as it truly is, and its means of accomplishment, that the world employs the term "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).
Indeed, there exists no other means of establishing the validity of perception and the rest than worldly convention.
Now, one might object: for those who are experts in valid cognition, such as the followers of Kaṇāda...
If it is argued that there is no conventional usage of the term "valid cognition" (*prāmāṇya*) regarding the Kṣapaṇakas and others in that context, we say no;
for [the definition] states: "Valid cognition consists of memory, perception, and tradition."

This is because for those who do not accept the meaning established by such Śruti and Smṛti, the status of being an authoritative source (āptatva) is unestablished. If it is argued that Smṛti is merely a human-authored work (pauruṣeya-grantha), [the response follows].
In this regard, is this word [brahman] a term with an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍavṛtti*), or is it etymological (*yaugika*)?
It cannot be the first,
because its status as a derivative formed with a *kṛt* suffix is clearly manifest.
Not the second [alternative],
because it is untenable due to the faults of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Therefore, one must accept that "Smṛti" is a metaphorical designation based on its having the recollection of Manu and others as its source.

For they, having remembered an object experienced through scripture and other means, compose a text that explains it; the application [of the term "author"] to those composed by Vyāsa and others occurs because of their similarity to that.
And a metaphorical usage is not permissible without an obstacle to the primary sense.
Let it be granted that even Akṣapāda and others are indeed authoritative (āpta).
Nevertheless, it is improper to deny the validity of memory and other such cognitions merely because of the absence of those specific conventional usages;
for by them, individual objects have not been defined.
If it is argued that they are nonetheless subsumed under the aforementioned definitions, [we reply:]...
The same applies to recollection (*smṛti*) and the rest,
since it is easy to state that they are included within perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [means of valid cognition].
Furthermore, recollection and so forth are denotable by the term "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) because they correspond to reality (*yathārthatva*), just like perception.

Nor is "being an experience" (anubhavatva) a limiting adjunct (upādhi); for in the case of equal pervasion (samavyāpti), the pervasion is broken in instances such as doubt, whereas in the case of unequal pervasion (viṣamavyāpti)— [The argument continues: ...the probans would be over-pervasive (vyabhicāra). Furthermore, since the nature of being an experience is not established in the case of memory, it cannot serve as a counter-example (vipakṣa). Therefore, because there is no instance where the probandum is absent while the probans is present, the status of being an experience is not a limiting adjunct. Thus, the definition is faultless. Consequently, the cognition of silver in the shell is indeed an error, and it is sublated by the subsequent cognition of the shell. This concludes the section on the definition of error. Now follows the section on the nature of error. Regarding this, some hold that error consists in the manifestation of an object as something other than what it is (anyathākhyāti). Others hold that it consists in the non-apprehension of the distinction between two things (akhyāti). Still others hold that it consists in the apprehension of a non-existent object (asatkhyāti). And yet others hold that it consists in the manifestation of a mental construction (vikalpākhyāti). Among these, the first view—that it is the manifestation of an object as something other than what it is—is held by the followers of Prabhākara. They argue as follows: "In the case of the cognition 'this is silver,' the word 'this' refers to the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) which is the shell, and the word 'silver' refers to silver itself. Since both are real entities, there is no contradiction in their co-occurrence. However, the relation between them is not real; rather, it is a false relation. That is to say, the relation between the substrate and the superimposed object is a relation of identity (tādātmya), and this identity is unreal. Therefore, the manifestation of an object as something other than what it is is simply the manifestation of an unreal identity. This is the position of the Prābhākaras. However, this view is untenable. For if the identity were unreal, how could it be manifested? Manifestation is possible only for that which exists. If you say that it is manifested through its own form (svarūpeṇa), then even the identity with a jar or a cloth would be manifested. If you say that it is manifested as the identity with the substrate, then since that identity is unreal, it would follow that the substrate itself is unreal. Furthermore, if the identity is unreal, it must be either a non-entity (avastu) or a mere absence (abhāva). If it were a non-entity, it could not be manifested, just like a rabbit's horn. If it were an absence, it would be perceived as a negation, and thus the cognition would take the form "this is not silver," which contradicts the actual experience. Moreover, if the identity is unreal, it cannot be related to anything else, just as a sky-flower cannot be related to anything. Therefore, the theory of manifestation as something other than what it is (anyathākhyāti) is untenable. As for the second view—that it is the non-apprehension of the distinction between two things—it is held by the followers of Kumārila. They argue as follows: "In the case of the cognition 'this is silver,' two cognitions arise: one is the recollection of silver, and the other is the perception of the substrate. Because the recollection of silver is similar to the perception of the substrate, the distinction between the two is not apprehended. Due to this non-apprehension of the distinction, the two cognitions are erroneously unified, resulting in the single cognition 'this is silver. Thus, error is merely the non-apprehension of the distinction between two things. This is the position of the Bhaṭṭas. However, this too is untenable. For if the distinction were not apprehended, the cognition would have to take the form "I do not know whether this is silver or not," or "I do not know whether this is a shell or not. But such a cognition does not occur. Furthermore, if the distinction were not apprehended, the desire to act toward the substrate would not arise, just as it does not arise toward a piece of wood. If you say that the desire arises due to the similarity between the two, then why does the desire not arise toward a piece of wood as well? If you say that it does not arise because the wood lacks the quality of "silverness," then we reply that since the quality of "silverness" is absent in the wood, the cognition "this is silver" would not occur there either. If you say that the cognition occurs because the silverness is remembered, then we ask: why is that silverness not remembered in the case of the wood as well? If you say that it is not remembered because the wood lacks the specific causal factors (sāmagrī) for such remembrance, then we reply that those causal factors are equally absent in the case of the shell. Therefore, the theory of non-apprehension of distinction is also untenable. As for the third view—that it is the apprehension of a non-existent object—it is held by the followers of the Yogācāra school. They argue as follows: "In the case of the cognition 'this is silver,' the silver is not external; rather, it is a mental construction. Just as in a dream, various objects appear within the mind, so too in the waking state, due to the force of latent impressions (vāsanā), silver appears as if it were external. Therefore, error is the apprehension of a non-existent object. This is the position of the Vijñānavādins. However, this too is untenable. For if the silver were non-existent, it could not be manifested, just as a rabbit's horn cannot be manifested. Furthermore, if the silver were non-existent, the cognition "this is silver" would be false, and the subsequent sublating cognition "this is not silver" would be true; however, this contradicts the fact that the former is sublated by the latter. Moreover, if the silver were non-existent, it would be impossible to explain the practical activity (pravṛtti) directed toward it. If you say that activity occurs due to the similarity between the mental image and the external object, then we ask: why does activity not occur toward a piece of wood as well? If you say that it does not occur because the wood lacks the quality of "silverness," then we reply that since that quality is absent, the cognition "this is silver" would not occur there either. If you say that the cognition occurs because the silverness is remembered, then we ask: why is that silverness not remembered in the case of the wood as well? If you say that it is not remembered because the wood lacks the specific causal factors, then we reply that those causal factors are equally absent in the case of the shell. Therefore, the theory of the apprehension of a non-existent object is also untenable. As for the fourth view—that it is the manifestation of a mental construction—it is held by the followers of the Mādhyamika school. They argue as follows: "In the case of the cognition 'this is silver,' the silver is neither external nor internal; rather, it is a mere mental construction. Just as in a dream, various objects appear within the mind, so too in the waking state, due to the force of latent impressions, silver appears as if it were external. Therefore, error is the manifestation of a mental construction. This is the position of the Mādhyamikas. However, this too is untenable. For if the silver were a mere mental construction, it could not be manifested, just as a rabbit's horn cannot be manifested. Furthermore, if the silver were a mere mental construction, the cognition "this is silver" would be false, and the subsequent sublating cognition "this is not silver" would be true; however, this contradicts the fact that the former is sublated by the latter. Moreover, if the silver were a mere mental construction, it would be impossible to explain the practical activity directed toward it. If you say that activity occurs due to the similarity between the mental image and the external object, then we ask: why does activity not occur toward a piece of wood as well? If you say that it does not occur because the wood lacks the quality of "silverness," then we reply that since that quality is absent, the cognition "this is silver" would not occur there either. If you say that the cognition occurs because the silverness is remembered, then we ask: why is that silverness not remembered in the case of the wood as well? If you say that it is not remembered because the wood lacks the specific causal factors, then we reply that those causal factors are equally absent in the case of the shell. Therefore, the theory of the manifestation of a mental construction is also untenable. Thus, all these views are refuted. What then is the correct view? It is the theory of the manifestation of a non-existent object (asatkhyāti). We argue as follows: "In the case of the cognition 'this is silver,' the silver is not real; rather, it is a non-existent object. Just as in a dream, various objects appear within the mind, so too in the waking state, due to the force of latent
Furthermore, even in the case of perception in the form of an instrument (*karaṇa*), [the definition] fails to pervade the probandum (*sādhya*).
Moreover, if it is argued that this "nature of experience" (*anubhavatva*) means "being a cognition distinct from memory," for what purpose is this qualification?

If it is argued that [the definition] is for the purpose of excluding the subject (*pakṣa*), then there would be no such thing as a non-qualifier (*anupādhi*) by virtue of being other than the subject;
otherwise, even in the inference for God (*īśvara-anumāna*), it would be impossible to eliminate a qualifier.
By this, the claim that [the object] is either the experience itself or its instrument is also refuted.
If it is argued that the second alternative holds because there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), he says: "If it is accepted... and so forth.
If the authority of tradition and the like is accepted, what contradiction could there be?
The connection is that "the authority belongs to mindfulness and so forth.
[The word] "what" is used in the sense of an objection; the word "then" is to be supplied as the remainder.
Memory (*smṛti*) and restatement (*anuvāda*) are not means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) because they are fruitless.

If it is asked, "How can this be so, given that whatever is a means of valid cognition is seen to be fruitful, as in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest, since there exists a sublation [of your claim]?"—
is it the case here that every memory and every restatement [is fruitless]?

Is the whole [subject] being made the locus of the argument (*pakṣīkriyate*), or is it a part thereof? Regarding the first case, he states "not so," because there would be the fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*).
Nor should it be said that both the Smṛtis and the restatements (of Vedic texts) are fruitless.
The meaning is also that the fruitfulness of certain Smṛtis and certain restatements (anuvādas) is observed; and this will be established later.
Furthermore, he states that this reason is inconclusive (aprayojaka): "phalavattvam" (the state of having a fruit).
For we do not intend to define validity as the possession of a fruit.

For if we, the investigators, had intended that "possessing a result" (*phalavattva*) were the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of validity (*prāmāṇya*), then indeed, by the cessation of that pervader, there would be a cessation of the validity of memory and so forth. But this is not the case; such is the meaning.
This is the intended meaning:
in the conventional usage of "validity" (prāmāṇya), the sole determinant is simply the absence of non-conformity with reality (ayathārthya).
"But in the case of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), the defect in the instrument (*karaṇadoṣa*) and the sublating cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*) [are the causes], not fruitlessness (*niṣphalatva*).

By this, the second position—that only the fruitless portion is made the subject (*pakṣīkaraṇa*)—is also refuted. To the objection—"Why should fruitlessness itself not be a cause of invalidity, just like the defect in the instrument and the sublating cognition?"—he says: "grass, etc. (*tṛṇādi*).
Furthermore, what fruitfulness can be predicated of the perception of grass and such other things?

The locative case [in the term *dharmi-adhikaraṇa*] signifies "the locus of the property" (*dharma*). This refers, for example, to the sight of grass and so forth scattered along the path of one going to a village;
and this is merely an illustration.
It should also be understood that this follows from the inference derived through the capacity of its own causes. [The word] "kim" (what) is used in the sense of an objection:
if being fruitless were the cause of invalidity, then the perception of grass and such things would also be invalid, as they are likewise fruitless.
But it is not so;
the intention is that [it would] contradict worldly convention.
Alternatively, he indicates by this that the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntika).

Regarding that which is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) but is actually its opposite—the perception of grass and such—is it said to possess a result? Not at all; thus, it is understood to be resultless (*aphala*) in that regard.
Now, it is indeed beyond dispute that the multitude of effects for living beings arises from merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).

Furthermore, if the perception of grass and such things— which is not itself of the nature of pleasure or pain— were not produced by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), and were neither pleasure nor pain nor a means to them, then merit and demerit would be rendered useless, or else the authority of the Vedas and other scriptures would be undermined.
Therefore, even through the perception of grass and such, some form of pleasure, pain, or the like must necessarily be produced.
Therefore, as to how that [practice] could be fruitless, he says: "Sukha... (happiness).
For even in memory, some degree of pleasure, pain, and so forth is observed.

By this reasoning, since every recollection and every restatement possesses fruitfulness, the reason (hetu) would indeed be unestablished in its own nature (svarūpāsiddha). However, the point is that "partial unestablishment" (bhāgāsiddhatā) was stated with the intention of referring to cases where no clearly perceived result is obtained.
However, this is the distinction:
the fruit of seeing grass and such is in every way unmanifest, whereas that of memory and so forth is not so; as it has been said, "for it is also seen," etc.
In this context, even a restatement (anuvāda) should be accepted; for instance, there is happiness when recollecting a desired object.
Attachment to that which belongs to the same class,
proficiency in formative predispositions,
and suffering when there is no mindfulness of the purposeful object.
Hatred toward that which is of a similar kind,
proficiency in mental formations, and merit in the recollection of praiseworthy objects.
However, in the case of recollecting an unwholesome object, there is demerit;
this should be understood to apply to mere repetition as well,
otherwise it would follow that practices such as formal vows (*praṇidhāna*) would be rendered useless.
"Repetition of word and meaning is 'redundancy' (punarukta), except in the case of restatement (anuvāda)";
by stating this, Akṣapāda himself admitted the utility of restatement.
Furthermore, the purposes of the conclusion (nigamana) have been established by those learned in the Nyāya system. (5.268)
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) produces a state of being known (*jñātatā*), which is synonymous with manifestation (*prākaṭya*), residing in the object—
just as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [means of knowledge] do."
Furthermore, it is not possible for the state of being known (*jñātatā*) to arise in an object through recollection and so forth,
because that state is produced by experience alone;
for once a cutting has been performed, the act of cutting does not occur again.
"How then could it possess validity? To this, he says: "No."
And the authoritative cognition is that which is not merely the act of delimitation. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.1.27ab)
"Determination" (*pariccheda*) means "the state of being known" (*jñātatā*).
The phrase "it is thus" (*evam iti*) is a restatement of what has been asserted by the opponent.
Only that which performs the function of determination is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
The meaning is that it is not the case that memory and so forth are invalid because of the absence of that [perception].
Why is it not so? To this he says: "And thus... (iti ca).

By the word "iti," he refers to the "cognizedness" (jñātatā) residing in the object. The particle "ca" (and) serves to draw forward the word "na" (not). The meaning is that there is no valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) for the existence of cognizedness.

The point is this: the property of being a generator of "cognizedness" (jñātatā) exists not only in similar instances (sapakṣa), but also in dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) such as perceptual error and so forth—just as it does in cases like delusion—and is therefore a common inconclusive reason (sādhāraṇānaikāntika).
Furthermore, since successive cognitions (dhārāvāhika-vijñāna) do not produce cognizedness, just as memory and the like do not, how can there not be an inconclusiveness?
Moreover, you must admit that even doubt and error produce cognizedness.

Because the logic is the same; consequently, since it would be excluded from the similar instances (sapakṣa) just as it is from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) such as direct perception, your reason would become an "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) one.

Alternatively, since the very determination characterized by "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) lacks any basis in valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), there is no proof for the pervasion that "only that which performs the function of determining is a means of valid cognition" (*paricchedakāryeva pramāṇam*). This should be construed as part of the same continuous argument. Thus, the meaning is that inference based on the mark of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi-liṅgaka-anumāna*) is cast far aside.
Now, [the opponent objects]: "But surely, a means of valid cognition is precisely that which makes known what was previously unknown."
Or rather, it is simply the knowledge of what was previously unknown;
and since this [quality] does not exist in memory and the like, that [memory] is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). For this reason, he says "no."
"Determination" (*pariccheda*) means the knowledge of what was previously unknown; that which has the habit of performing this is "that which effects determination" (*paricchedakārī*).
Alternatively, "determination itself is the act" (*kāra*); thus, "the act of determination" (*paricchedakāra*), and that which possesses this is "that which effects determination" (*paricchedakārī*).

Is the state of being a determiner (*paricchedakāritva*) the definition of validity (*prāmāṇya*) in the sense of a pervaded-pervader (*vyāpyavyāpaka*) relationship, such that memory and the like are said to lack validity due to its absence;
or is it [the definition] as the pervader alone?

In the first case, the definition—that only that which performs the function of determination is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is untenable, as it would not apply to valid cognition itself. This is the construction of the argument.
Because of under-extension and over-extension;
for it is thus:
is "the cognition of an object not previously apprehended" stated with reference to the subject (*dharmin*) or to the mode (*prakāra*)?

In the first case, there would follow the consequence that cognitions of eternal objects lack validity; furthermore, it would entail the invalidity of inference—which takes as its object a subject already known to possess a pervaded property by way of making it possess the pervading property—as well as the invalidity of verbal testimony, which has as its domain things previously known separately by presenting them in a state of connection. In the second case, however, there would be the invalidity of successive cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-vijñāna*).

For we do not perceive the jar as being something entirely different [from its constituent parts], as the Mīmāṃsakas maintain along with the Nihilists (Vaināśikas); nor do we see it as undergoing transformation, as the Sāṅkhyas hold; nor do we observe it as possessing even a mode that is subject to arising and passing away.

Now, even if the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or the mode (*prakāra*) remains in the same state, nevertheless, in a stream of perceptual cognitions such as "this is a jar, this is a jar," it is only the object existing at that very time which appears clearly. Furthermore,
there cannot be only one object for cognitions occurring sequentially at a single moment, because that would entail the absurdity of simultaneous cognitions, as if there were multiple perceivers.
And because recognition of that [object] would be impossible;
for even if there were multiple cognitions, one could not perceive them as existing at the same time.

Therefore, since the present object, which was not apprehended by the preceding cognitions, is determined by each subsequent one, it follows that [each cognition] indeed possesses an object not previously attained.
If that is the case, then even memory and the like would have as their object only what has not been previously apprehended.
For memory also grasps an object experienced at its present time as having belonged to a past time;
otherwise, it would not take the form "that."
If even a restatement (*anuvāda*) were the subject matter of a formal argument (*vāda*), then it would clearly lack the quality of having an unapprehended object.
Furthermore, if its scope were an object distinguished from a prior cognition, the same logic would apply as in the case of a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika*).
This remains true even if there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) through the addition of further information.
Since doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyāsa*) also have objects not yet apprehended, they too would possess validity (*prāmāṇya*).
If it is argued that what is intended is "the state of making known an object as it truly is, which has not been previously apprehended," we say no.
Because the qualification [of "not previously apprehended"] would be useless;
if it is argued that it is for the purpose of excluding memory and so forth, [we reply] no—
for why should memory and the like be excluded?

If it is argued that [the definition does not apply] because of the absence of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), then this results in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Therefore, let the second position be accepted: that there is the exclusion of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) through the exclusion of the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
It might be so;

however, if only that which performs the function of delimitation were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then valid cognition (*pramā*) would be the means of valid cognition, but that is not the case. For instance:

Is the pervasion of validity by the property of having an unapprehended object established merely through the observation of concomitance, or by that [observation] assisted by the observation of deviation, or by that which is accompanied by a subverting argument against the counter-example?
Not the first,
because it would lead to an over-extension;
not the second.
The third [alternative] is not [tenable], because deviation is observed in a continuous stream [of cognitions] and because the [resulting] over-extension cannot be avoided.
If it is argued that [the means of knowledge] would be merely grinding what has already been ground— since it would be making known an object already attained because that [object] is not absent—
what indeed is this so-called "grinding what has already been ground"?
Is it that when an object has been apprehended, the culmination of apprehension does not arise;
or is it that it is fruitless; or rather, that its fruit is indistinguishable [from what has already been attained]?
Now, as for the claim that the result is not required:
it is not the first case;
for this might be so only if the absence of knowledge were itself a constituent part of the causal complex for knowledge.
Or perhaps that [past object] would be an obstacle to cognition;
but this is not the case, for if it were so, it would follow that memory itself could never arise.
Not the second,
because it has already been answered;
not the third.
Because it would follow [absurdly] even in the first case;
nor is the fourth [alternative] valid,
since [one still perceives] grass and so forth.
And because it follows as a consequence that there would be ten means of knowledge (*heyadaśarna*).
Now, is it not the case that a specific instrument is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and that an instrument is that which is most effective in accomplishing an action?

If it is argued that once the probandum has been established, there is no longer the status of being the "most effective means" (*sādhakatama*) even for something of the same class— as with an axe after the wood has been cut—
this is not so.
The status of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*) does not consist in being superior in relation to another more effective instrument;
rather, it consists in being superior in relation to other factors (*kāraka*) involved in the primary action.
Otherwise, in cases where there is a combination of instruments, they would lack the status of being instruments altogether, because they would not be superior in relation to one another.
"But when the axe is broken, there is the state of non-acting because of the non-arising of the result;
and it has been stated that such is not the case here. [Verse 5.291] Now, independence is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of validity.
However, cognitions that proceed in a continuous stream (dhārāvāhika-buddhi) are mutually independent;
therefore, they attain the status of valid cognition (prāmāṇya).

If it is argued that memory and so forth are not like this [i.e., not like perception] and thus are simply invalid, we say no; for this pervasion (*vyāpti*) itself lacks any basis in valid cognition (*aprāmāṇika*). Thus he says: "No."
Ascertainment is cognition that is independent.
Furthermore, if independence means being so in every respect, it does not exist in the case of impermanent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it means independence from other cognitions, then it is absent in inference and the like.

If it is argued that inference and the like depend upon a mark (*liṅga*) and so forth at the very moment of their arising, and not for the sake of determining the object (*arthapariccheda*), [we reply:
no, because there is no such thing as the determination of an object apart from cognition itself;
and because this can be said with equal ease regarding memory and other such states.
If [the definition] is "not depending on a cognition having the same object," then that [property] is absent even in inference and so forth when taking the locus (*dharmin*) as the object;
furthermore, since it exists in memory and the like even with respect to the mode (*prakāra*), [the definition] is unestablished (*asiddhi*).
"Memory is not a valid means of knowledge because it lacks direct experience,
since validity belongs only to direct experience and its instruments"— this too is incorrect.
He says "No," because, as before, the pervasion (vyāpti) is unestablished.
"Ascertainment is experience.

(*5,294*) Having thus stated the general definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and desiring to define its specific types, [the author] first states the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*), since it was mentioned first: "faultless," etc. (*nirdoṣa*, etc.).
For in this context, perception is said to be that which arises from faultless sense organs.
In these means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
or rather, in both worldly and Vedic usage—
how indeed is this to be understood?
Does this mean that its arising is from faultless sense-faculties (*akṣa*),
or that it is both faultless and arisen from sense-faculties?
It is not the first case.
Because [the definition] is both under-extended and over-extended.
To explain: the direct perception of Īśvara and others does not arise from the sense organs, because it is eternal.
Even the effect of the sense organ, such as the act of seeing and so forth, would have to be considered perception;
yet this is not the second [alternative],
because a compound is untenable when both members function as qualifiers.
And because the previously stated lack of pervasion has not been resolved;
to this it is replied: let us first grant the first point.

That which has its arising (*udbhava*) by means of those sense-faculties (*akṣa*, *indriya*) that are free from defects such as cataracts or jaundice— which are the causes of ignorance and distorted cognition— [is the definition].
Nor is there a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*),
because the word "arising" (*udbhava*) signifies either production (*utpatti*) or manifestation (*abhivyakti*).
As it has been said: "Everything is considered to have the sense-faculties as its essence. Nor is there the fault of over-extension, because knowledge is established by the context of the discussion.
Even so, if it is argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to inference based on the senses (*akṣaliṅgaka*), we say no;
for that [inference], being produced by sensory cognition, lacks the quality of being produced by the sense-organ alone.
Furthermore, even a cognition arising from a faultless sense-organ may arise as non-correspondent (*ayathārtha*) due to defects in the object.

As it has been said: "Due to excessive distance, excessive proximity, defects of the sense organs, instability of the mind, subtlety, lack of attention, being overwhelmed, and collision with similar objects."
Nevertheless, there is no fault because of the qualification "in proximity to an object that is free from defects.
Regarding this, some maintain that the inclusion of the term "cognition" (*jñāna*) is for the purpose of excluding pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth;
that is incorrect.
Since the direct perception of the object itself is the cause of pleasure and so forth,
the contact between the sense organ and the object is sought for that purpose.
If it is argued that, this being the case, it would follow that the Supreme Lord—who possesses direct perception of all objects—would experience the arising of pleasure and so forth;
[we reply: why would that consequence not apply to Him when He assumes a *līlā*-body and possesses the contact of sense-faculties with their objects?
Or, if you say that those factors alone are not the cause of pleasure and so forth; [then we ask: what else could be the cause?
If it is argued that even factors such as the mental object (*dharma*) and so forth do not exist [there],
and therefore, due to their absence, pleasure and the like do not arise for him, then the same logic applies.
For this very reason, there is no over-extension of the argument even to the case of yogis.
Thus they have said: "Because of the connection with cold, heat, and so forth in the body, the self experiences cold, heat, and the like; and from that, pleasure and pain arise."
Here, by the word "body" (*deha*), the sense faculties (*indriya*) residing therein are indicated. Thus, the meaning of the definition is this:
perception (*pratyakṣa*) is cognition produced by faultless sense faculties that are in contact with a faultless object. *5,300*
Alternatively, the meaning is simply that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is knowledge arising from the contact of a faultless sense-organ with its object;
this [definition] has been explained as referring specifically to the objects of produced perception (*janyapratyakṣa*).
Thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply;
however, for the sake of establishing a definition that applies universally, we adopt the second position:
"That which is produced by the sense organs is faultless and in accordance with reality."
There is no fault whatsoever in the fact that direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) is indicated by the term "arising from the sense organs" (*akṣodbhava*);
moreover, the nature of being a direct perception is a specific quality residing solely in the cognition itself, and is not a property derived from the instrument (*karaṇa*).
By this, only perception (*pratyakṣa*) has been defined.

In this very context, by supplying the two words "since" (*yatas*) and "that" (*tat*), the definition of valid perception as an instrument of knowledge (*anupramāṇa*)—namely, "the means for attaining non-erroneous, immediate cognition"—should also be explained.

And that [means], according to a difference in intended meaning, is either "the faultless contact between the sense organ and the object," or "the sense organ which is not defective and is in contact with the object."

But surely, since it is stated that "the unimpaired sense-organ is the *akṣa*," the word *akṣa* itself expresses the state of being unimpaired. Why, then, is the qualification "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*) applied to the *akṣa*?
Not so;
for it is explained that "indriya" means "akṣa," and what is intended here is that which is unimpaired (*aduṣṭa*).

[Objection: But surely this definition—namely, that "pratyakṣa" is that which has gone toward (*prati*) the sense-organ (*akṣa*)—is understood from the very etymology of the word itself, and thus it does not differ from the definiendum, "pratyakṣa."

If it is argued that the relationship of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) cannot belong to one and the same thing because the states of being known and being unknown are impossible [in a single entity], we say no;
for the intention here is that what is intended to be proven is the status of being denotable by the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*). With this in mind, it is said: "Thus it is proclaimed."
Now, how is it to be understood that the sense-faculties are faultless?
If you say it is from the correspondence of cognition with reality (*jñānayāthārthya*), then what is the basis for that [correspondence] as well?
It should be known as faultless either because it is free from defects or because there is an absence of contradictory means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It is not the former.
Because it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence;
nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
because it would follow even in the case of an error where no contradiction has yet arisen.
Not so;

for it is admitted that the correspondence of knowledge with its object is established by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin). However, if an examination were required, there would be a powerful contradiction.
The positive state (bhāva) acts as an auxiliary;
as it has been said: "Defects are to be known through a powerful means of valid cognition, and not otherwise.
But since that which has not yet encountered a contradiction is merely an error, how [can it be considered a valid cognition]?
If it is argued that [the cognition] is due to a contrary means of valid cognition (pramā) related to another place, time, or person,
then how can there be the state of having no contradiction yet arisen?
In that case, one would have to admit the total absence of any contrary means of valid cognition.
Indeed, that too is ascertained through various specific investigations; however,
it is not suspected to be without foundation.
Otherwise, because there would be no confidence in anything at all, even what is desired would not be established.
[Objection: If sensory perception consists in the contact between a sense faculty and its object, then knowledge should also arise from the contact between the eye and the sky.
[Reply: Not so.
This is because by the word "object" (artha), only that which is capable of being grasped by each respective sense faculty is intended;
and in the case of space and so forth, the absence of such capacity is established precisely from the absence of the effect [of perception].
By this, the undesirable consequence that the eye and other senses would grasp odor and other qualities is also refuted.
Now, it might be thought:
if capacity is inherent [in the sense-faculties], what is the use of the "contact" (*sannikarṣa*) which is like an internal goiter?
The respective object of each sense-faculty is apprehended by that very sense-faculty.
Otherwise, how could there be the perception of something obstructed by glass, a film of clouds, or similar media?
Furthermore, the apprehension of an object as being at a distance would not be possible on the view that the sense-faculty must physically reach its object (*prāptipakṣa*).
Because that [property of reaching the object] is absent in the case of the skin and other [senses] which function by reaching their objects;
furthermore, if the eye were to function by reaching its object, it would grasp only that which is in direct contact with itself,
as is observed in the case of axes and similar tools.
Furthermore, it would grasp [the object] more extensively;
and there would be no doubt regarding the specific direction,
because that certainty would have been attained through contact.
Furthermore, because the branch and the moon— though one is near and the other distant— are perceived simultaneously,
this could not be the case if the sense organ acted only by reaching its object. Moreover, the eye reveals objects without reaching them, because it does not reveal what is too close.
By way of exclusion, like the ear and other [senses], the eye does not reach out and connect with the object because it is a sense organ, just like the sense of touch and others;
nor is there any coming of the object, because that would contradict direct perception.
Thus, its status as a manifestor without reaching [the object] is established. *5,310*
To this it is replied:
having taken up merely the capacity of the object and the sense-organ, one must state whether the exclusion of contact applies everywhere or only in the case of the eye.
It is not the first [alternative].
For it would follow that cutting and other such actions could occur in wood and the like even by axes and other tools without reaching them;
and it would also entail the occurrence of the perception of odors and so forth by the nose, tongue, and body-sense even without reaching their objects.
Thus, just as suitability (*yogyatā*) is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), so too is reaching (*prāpti*) a necessary factor for the production of action.
The second [alternative] is not tenable, because there is no specific cause [for such a distinction].

If it is argued that this is so because the capacity [of the sense organs] is known through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and because contact is never perceived, we say no; for even in the case of the eye, contact is perceived by virtue of its being both an instrument (*karaṇa*) and a sense organ (*indriya*). (5.311)
Now, one might object: "In this case, is the eyeball (golaka) being made the subject of the proposition, or is it the eye as distinct from that?
In the first case, there is sublation by valid cognition;
in the second case, however, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi). If this is said, we reply: no.
Even for you, if the eyeball (*golaka*) is made the subject of the proposition, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*),
because it can be argued that in other cases there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
Now, if you say that, setting aside the specific [eyeball], the mere instrument inferred from the perception of color is made the subject;
It is the same for me as well;
therefore, that [object] will be established even as something distinct from the eyeball (*golaka*).
Furthermore, "proximity" (*sannikarṣa*) is intended here merely in the sense of nearness.
It is not [the case that] "conjunction and so forth" [are the cause], for there is no deviation [in the rule] regarding sound and the like.
What is this "capacity" (*yogyatā*) by virtue of which the eye could illuminate even that which is not in contact?
If it consists in a particular nature of form (*rūpa-viśeṣa*) and so forth, then since that [nature] exists even in the past and the future, it would follow that those too are visible to the eye.
Indeed, the postulation of "presentness" is for the sake of establishing sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*).
Since sensory contact is established otherwise— given that in recognition the aspect of "that-ness" (*tattā*) appears to the eye— if that [aspect] is not required,
what then is the use of "presentness"?
Alternatively, if presentness (*vartamānatā*) were also included within the capacity [of the object] such as form (*rūpa*),
then recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) would not be established; furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving objects obstructed by walls and the like.
For since an obstruction such as a wall is what prevents attainment, its absence would have to be sought for the sake of attainment.
If that [absence] is not accepted, then what harm could a wall or the like do?
If it is argued that the absence of an obstruction is itself the capacity, we say no.
Because it would follow that [an object] situated on the far side of a wall could not be perceived.
If it is argued that what is intended is the absence of a substance with dense parts between the eye and its object;
Because it would follow that there would be no perception of objects separated by crystal and the like.

If it is argued that what is intended is the absence of non-transparent substances, even so, it results in the very same consequence: the impossibility of seeing distant objects that are not obstructed.
Now, if you consider that "capacity" and "incapacity" are simply the arising and non-arising of such a thing based on momentary destruction and transformation,
then that object would sometimes be perceived by everyone and sometimes not perceived by anyone at all.
If you argue that there is a distinction [in perception] dependent upon the perceivers, we say no.
Because it is improper to abandon a perceived sense-object contact and instead postulate numerous unperceived factors;
furthermore, in the case of a cognition of something not in contact, there would be no distinction between clarity and lack of clarity for objects that are near, in contact, or distant.

For us, however, the rays of the eye are properly in contact with what is near, but with what is distant they are imperfectly so—just like the rays of a lamp—and thus the clarity and lack of clarity of the cognition are logically accounted for.

Do we postulate that [the eye] illuminates without reaching its object because it perceives things screened by glass and the like, or because glass and such do not act as obstacles to its reaching [the object]?
The first alternative contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and is refuted by numerous over-extended consequences (*atiprasaṅga*); therefore, only the second should be accepted.
If it is argued that, in that case, glass and so forth would necessarily undergo a transformation into a different configuration (*vyūhāntara*), [we reply: no.
[This is] not [the case], because even when there is a separation by water or fire, jars and the like do not cease to exist;
and even if one were to admit a subtler [separation] in those cases, let it be so here as well.
Furthermore, if you claim that the perception of something with an interval is actually the perception of something unconnected, that is unproven.
If it is argued that the perception [of objects] as being "at a distance" (sāntara) is [the reason], this is inconclusive with respect to a lamp.

For just as a lamp, although in contact with an object by means of its rays, is nevertheless perceived as being "at a distance" in relation to its own form, so too why should it be untenable for the eye to be [perceived as such] in relation to its physical locus?
Furthermore, the perception of [objects] as being larger [than the eye] will be explained by the fact that the visual rays have extremely fine tips, like the blossoms of the *unmattaka* plant.
If there were no contact, there would be no apprehension even of something minute.

If it is argued that if there were contact, there would be no doubt regarding the specific direction [of the object], we say no; for if there were no contact, one would simply imagine [the object] to be everywhere.
The conceit of simultaneous perception, however, is merely an illusion based on the rapid movement of light,
since its actual arrival [at the object] is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Another says:
The claim that the rays of the eyes, having become unified with the solar rays joined to the moon on the branch, simultaneously cause one to perceive both the branch and the moon—
that is incorrect, because it would entail the consequence of perceiving all objects.
If it is argued that the determination of that [effect] arises from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), [we reply:
no, because nowhere is it observed that when external means are complete, the non-arising of an effect occurs due to a deficiency in the unseen force;
for if there were a deficiency in the unseen force, the external causal complex (*bāhyasāmagrī*) would itself be incomplete.

Otherwise, even a jar situated in the midst of abundant light and in contact with the sense-faculties accompanied by the mind might sometimes not be perceived. Furthermore, the qualification "that which reveals an object without reaching it" is unestablished;
for the quality of not revealing what is too close exists even in the olfactory and other senses, which do reveal objects upon reaching them.
Because one's own odor and so forth are not perceived;
it is illogical that another's [odor] alone should not be perceived when extremely close due to glass or similar media, since its capacity [to be perceived] has not been lost. (5.325)
Regarding the statement "having gone, [the object] is not proximate through purpose," is the negation of going the point to be proven,
or is it the negation of proximity, or rather the negation of both?
Not the first,
because it is subject to the fallacy of missing the proper time (*kālātīta*) and because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Not the second.
Precisely because it is inconclusive;
for this very reason, even the third [alternative] is not [valid].
If it is argued that "this is a negation of a specific [case]," we say no.
For that [argument] also fails to escape the refutation of the alternatives, such as "due to the absence of a qualifier" and so forth.

If it is argued that the thesis is that "that which possesses motion does not exist for the sake of contact," this is not so, because it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntya*) in the case of touch and the like;
for indeed, bodily movement occurs for the sake of the tactile sense organ's contact with the water of moral conduct (*śīla*).
Now, if the intention is that [the visual organ] does not go outside its substrate,

then, even though the status as a sense organ (*indriya*) is the same, the olfactory and other organs— which are not composed of fire (*taijasa*)— do not possess such a nature; whereas the eye, being composed of fire (*taijasa*), does.
If it is accepted that it is so, there is no subverting proof (bādhaka), and thus [the opponent's reason] is non-conclusive (aprayojaka).
If it is argued that this would entail the perception of the visual rays, we say no.
Because its being beyond the senses is logically established.

If it is argued that a substance of the nature of fire is perceived as possessing sensory qualities when it is large, then [we reply] that visual form is also perceived; thus, [fire] situated in water would likewise be so.
If it is argued that by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), its visible form is unmanifested in that case, [then we reply: ...
Why is it not also postulated that this [eye] possesses non-manifest color and touch?
For a means of valid cognition has already been stated for the hypothesis that [the sense organ] functions by reaching its object.
Furthermore, if the eye were to go out and grasp the object, then there would be the perception of the object even while the eyes are opening and closing.

Furthermore, if the visual [faculty] were something distinct from its physical basis, then medical treatments for injuries to that basis would be useless; thus, its status is equivalent to that of a lamp.
Moreover:

Sitting in the shade while looking at the sunlight, the lack of coolness in the eye is indicated by the sight of the sun; likewise, sitting in the sunlight while looking at a cool object, the state of coolness is indicated by that very same fact.
For this would not be possible if [the sense organ] had not reached its object.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that all of this is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so what more need be said here?
Thus ends the determination of the general definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Regarding the faultlessness mentioned as a qualification of the sense-faculties (*akṣa*), [the author] first states the different types of sense-faculties in order to show what is to be excluded [by that qualification], beginning with the words "prākṛtam" (the ordinary).
Prakṛti and pure consciousness are considered to be the two kinds of indriya (the senses).

By the word *prakṛti*, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and the five elements (*pañcabhūta*) are expressed. Although [the Self] is eternal, it is called *prākṛta* because it is augmented by the portions of the ego and the elements in their subtle form. The term "pure" (*śuddha*) is further explained as being "consciousness" (*caitanya*).
The words "and" (*ca*) and "iti" are to be supplied [in the text].
By the word "but" (*tu*), [the author] indicates those such as the Sāṅkhyas who assert that the sense organ is indeed insentient and that it is composed solely of the *ahaṅkāra*,
as well as those such as the Vaiśeṣikas who maintain that it is composed solely of material elements (*bhautika*).

This [verse] excludes the opinion of the Jains, who assert that [the sense-faculty] is twofold— consisting of the material faculty (*dravyendriya*) and the functional faculty (*bhāvendriya*)— due to the distinction between the faculties.
By using the word "opinion" (*mata*), he indicates that the matter he has stated is established by valid cognition (*pramita*).
In this regard, he will demonstrate immediately below the distinction between the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*caitanya*).

Furthermore, the insentient consists of both the eternal ego-principle (*ahaṅkārika*) and the material (*bhautika*): "The subtle senses certainly exist; they may also become gross through the ego-principle.
Their development by means of the elements is brought about at the time of creation."
This is established by such Smṛti texts;
furthermore, there is no proof for [the mind] being composed solely of ego (ahaṅkārika) or being material (bhautika),
because the authority of Kapila and others is not established.
The nose is composed of earth, because while it does not manifest taste, it manifests odor, like clarified butter which manifests the odor of saffron.
The tongue is composed of water, because while it does not manifest form, it manifests taste, like saliva.
The eye is composed of light (*taijasa*), because while it does not manifest touch, it manifests color-form (*rūpa*), like a lamp.
Alternatively, the tactile organ (*sparśana*) is composed of air (*vāyavīya*), because while it does not manifest sound, it manifests touch, like the wind from a fan.
Herein lies [the proof of its] being composed of earth and so forth.

If one proves merely that [the body] consists of these [elements], it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*). If one proves that it consists of those elements alone, the examples lack the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*),
because it is universally accepted that [all things] are composed of the five elements.
Furthermore, because there is deviation due to the unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*) everywhere,

if it is argued that "it [the universal] is the manifester of everything," is this stated with reference to the act of manifestation (*vyakti*), or with reference to the delimitation by adjuncts (*upādhi*)?
Not the first [alternative],
because there is no way to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding that which is unperceived as a single manifestor;
if it is argued that "it is not certain," [we reply:]...
Nevertheless, there is the fallacy of doubtful deviation (*sandigdhavyabhicāritā*).
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*) with respect to the delimitation of being a sense-faculty (*indriyatva*). *5,337*
Furthermore, if the terms "earth" and so forth are used to denote "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so on, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) due to those respective types of contact.

If the reason is qualified by the property of being a sense organ (*indriyatva*), the examples lack the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*). If the term "only" (*mātra*) is employed to avoid the previously mentioned fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) when proving that [the sense organs] are effects of earth and so forth, the defect of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) remains as it was in the case of contacts that manifest the color and other qualities of earth and so forth. (5.343)
Moreover,
water and the like manifest the odor of leather and other such things,
while salt and the like manifest taste.
Since collyrium and the like possess the quality of manifesting color (*rūpa*),
and camphor and the like possess the quality of manifesting touch (*sparśa*), there is indeed a logical fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Thus, it has been stated that the twofold nature of the sense organs is established by valid cognition (*pramita*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "Pure."
It is pure in the case of the Lord and those who are liberated; elsewhere, it is joined with material elements.
It should be understood that even in the enumeration (uddeśa), the demonstration is made with respect to the gradation of predominance, having first considered the gradation of established renown;
this applies elsewhere among transmigrating beings.
The meaning is that [the Self] exists as pure, though joined with the natural senses (prākṛtair akṣaiḥ).
This is the underlying intention:
for it will be established that the senses of those liberated from the Lord possess the nature of sense-faculties (*akṣavat*),
and it is not tenable to claim that such a sense-faculty is of a material nature.
Because it would contradict scriptural and traditional texts stating that [the Self] is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and so forth,
it must therefore be pure consciousness alone. Furthermore, the possession of eyes is well-established among transmigrating beings.
Nor is it correct to argue that, by the force of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) establishing liberation, that [consciousness] must be exclusively pure;
for if that were so, it would follow that even in saṃsāra there would be the necessity of perfect knowledge and so forth.
Therefore, one must accept that in that state both the ordinary and the pure exist as two distinct types.
Thus, the two-fold nature of the sense-faculties as established and liberated has been shown.
By others who accept that Īśvara and Lakṣmī assume playful bodies (līlā-vigraha), it is admitted that those faculties are material (prākṛta).

Regarding them, what need is there for further discussion? Thus, the term "liberated" (mukta) is employed; for in our own system, it is accepted that liberated beings assume playful bodies (līlā-vigraha).
What else remains? There is no need for the exertion of establishing [the existence of] sense faculties (*indriya*) even at other times. Thus ends the section on Īśvara. *5,349*
What follows from this, if there is such a twofold nature of the sense organs? To this he says: "It is indeed faultless."
Consciousness alone is indeed faultless; elsewhere, both are held to be so.
In this context, the meaning is that the consciousness associated with the highest class of living beings (*uttama-jīva*) is indeed faultless (*nirdoṣa*).
It has been stated elsewhere as well that this is precisely because of the presence of faultlessness;
"elsewhere" refers to the consciousness associated with the middle class of living beings (*madhyama-jīva*).

In all cases regarding the natural sense organ (*akṣa*), both faultlessness and the presence of faults are accepted according to the distinction of time and other factors. However, it remains a point of consensus among authoritative scholars that in the case of consciousness associated with an inferior [agent], there is only the presence of faults. This is the implied conclusion. It is accepted by those who follow valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).
By this, he demonstrates both scripture (*āgama*) and inference based on an effect as signs (*kāryaliṅgaka-anumāna*) regarding this matter;
the intention is that whatever has been stated here as being faulty is to be excluded by the inclusion of the faultless.
Now, one might object: for the sake of establishing the activity of those in cyclic existence (*saṃsārin*), the sense-faculties (*indriya*) must necessarily be admitted.
And that [soul] is not pure,
because of the aforementioned logical inconsistency;
therefore, since it is established as being accompanied by its own nature (prakṛti), the assumption of pure faculties among transmigrating beings is entirely baseless.

Nor can it be accepted that [the senses] exist even prior to liberation simply because they exist in their pure state during liberation; for, just as with liberation, it is possible for the pure senses to be acquired later as well. To this, he says: "sukha... (beginning with "pleasure").
