It is pure even among those in the cycle of existence, having pleasure, pain, and so forth as its objects.
Not only among those liberated from the Lord, but even among those in the cycle of existence, a pure sense organ must be admitted;
why? Because it has pleasure, pain, and so forth as its objects.
This is the meaning:
there indeed exists for transmigrating beings a direct manifestation regarding objects such as pleasure, pain, desire, and so forth.
For we observe the clear manifestation of "I am happy" and so forth even without any investigation of a logical mark (liṅga) and the like;
nor is it logical for pleasure and the like to have immediate manifestation without being objects of the senses,
as that would entail the same [immediate manifestation] for dharma and other such things.
Therefore, one must admit that there is a sense-faculty whose objects are pleasure, pain, and so forth; that very faculty is the pure [self].
Let it be that among transmigrating beings there is a sense-faculty whose objects are pleasure, pain, and so forth.
How is it that this [knowledge] is pure?
Since even through ordinary means such an immediate manifestation is possible, he says: "Because of its faultlessness."
Because it is faultless and possesses absolute certainty, that [cognition] is considered the most powerful. To this extent,
the sense organ whose object is pleasure and so forth is considered by everyone to be the most powerful and, in every respect, incapable of being sublated.
For never, when pleasure is absent, is there the cognition "I am happy"; nor, when it is present, is there the cognition "I am not happy.
For if that were so, the sense faculty would be subject to contradiction.

The state of being the most powerful faculty is established only through the restrictive rule of its being free from defects (*nirdoṣatva*), and not otherwise; for in the case of those [faculties] that possess defects, sublation (*bādhadarśana*) is observed as a matter of course.

Furthermore, since the restrictive rule of being free from defects is a property belonging solely to the pure (*śuddha*) and not to the ordinary (*prākṛta*), the purity of the faculty whose object is pleasure and so forth is thereby established.
This is what is meant:
pleasure and so forth are objects of the sense faculties because they appear directly, like a jar.
The sense faculty whose object is pleasure and so forth is pure, because it possesses the certainty of being free from defects, like the sense faculties of Īśvara and others.
The subject under dispute is necessarily free from defects because it is in every respect uncontradicted, just like that [liberated state];

for although the possession of pure faculties by those in saṃsāra can be established through the possession of such faculties by the liberated, since that [purity] is understood to be their very nature.
Furthermore, because one's own nature (*svarūpa*) is not adventitious,
nevertheless, this presentation of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is intended to clarify that which was stated regarding the direct perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*) of the witness (*sākṣin*).
For the witness is said to be the faculty of consciousness (*caitanya-indriya*) which constitutes one's own nature and has pleasure and so forth as its object.
And that knowledge manifested by it. [Objection:
Is it not the case that the statement "the sense organ is of two kinds, due to the distinction between the primordial (prākṛta) and the pure (śuddha)" is incorrect? [For it is said:
"The ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose..."

Because this would contradict the traditional teaching on the sixfold nature of the sense organs—based on the distinction between the five sense organs and the mind—as in the statement, "and having presided over the mind," he says: "five."
The ordinary [mind] is traditionally held to be sixfold, due to the distinction between the five sense organs and the mind.

Since it is traditionally taught that the sense organ (*indriya*) is of six kinds due to the distinction between the five [physical] faculties and the mind, this refers only to the primordial (*prākṛta*) ones and not to all of them; therefore, there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, because only the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*) are intended to be mentioned here, there is no inconsistency regarding the number eleven.
There is no contradiction with the [traditional] enumeration.
Since the intellect (*buddhi*) is also included within the mind (*manas*), there is no contradiction regarding the number seven.
[Objection: But how can the auditory organ, which consists of space (*ākāśa*), be considered a product of primordial matter (*prākṛta*)?
Not so;
for it is admitted that [space] is a transformation of elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*).
If it were of the nature of unmanifest space (*avyākṛtākāśa*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of perceiving sound everywhere.
Even if one accepts that [the auditory organ] is delimited by the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), it would follow that deafness could never occur.
If you argue that this is not so because of the influence of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), we say no;

for if that were the case, it would be sufficient to hold that space itself—when delimited by various [cavities] and influenced by *adṛṣṭa*—functions as the olfactory organ and the others, making the assumption that they are composed of earth and so forth redundant.

If it is argued that its existence is established because [the sense organs] possess qualities such as odor, we say no, because that reason is unproven (*asiddhi*). There is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that "whatever sense organ perceives a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*), it must possess that [quality]"; for this would fail in the case of the mind, which perceives pleasure and so forth, and in the case of the eye, which perceives natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatva*) and viscidity (*sneha*).

If it is argued that the ear is understood from scripture to be elemental in nature— consisting of earth and so forth— because its faculty of touch, which perceives cold and hot sensations, has been destroyed [in the case of the other senses], then one must likewise accept, for that very same reason, that the ear is an effect of space derived from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). *5,360*
[Objection: But how can the mind and the *nādi* be material (*prākṛta*), given that they are eternal?
[Reply: Not so;
because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that [the probans] does not [apply] because of the existence of "substance-ness" (dravyatva) and so forth which are devoid of tangibility (sparśa), we say no; for [that reason] is inconclusive (anaikāntika) for us.
Furthermore, if one were to prove merely [its] eternality and so forth, it would be a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatva).
"But in establishing immutability, there is a contradiction with scripture.
Thus ends the examination of perception.
Having reached its turn in the sequence, he defines inference, which is the sole means of valid cognition based on subsequent knowledge (anumāna), as follows: "Inference... [is defined].
Inference is said to be nothing other than reasoning... // MAnu 2.1.31a //
Here, "inference" (anumā) is the definiendum (lakṣya),
and "reasoning" (yukti) is the definition (lakṣaṇa).
Furthermore, since reasoning alone has been the subject of discussion many times, this [treatise] has been composed for the purpose of investigating its true nature.
In that case, the relationship between the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) would be reversed.
Now, are not "inference" (*anumā*) and "reasoning" (*yukti*) synonyms?
For it is as follows:

In the view that the result [of inference] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the word *anumā*—derived in the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*) as "that which is inferred"—denotes a correct cognition (*yathārthajñāna*) called "inference" (*anumiti*), which arises from the observation of a mark (*liṅga*) and has the inferential object (*laiṅgika*) as its domain.

The word *yukti* is likewise used for that very same thing, in the sense of "joining" (*yojana*). In the alternative view that the means of proof (*sādhana*) is the means of valid cognition, the word *anumā*—derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*) as "that by which something is inferred"—denotes the object itself; and the word *yukti* is also used for that same object, in the sense of "that by which one is joined [to the truth]."
Therefore, as to how there can be the relationship between the characterized and the characteristic, it was said: "It has already been stated."

The point here is that in this case as well, it is merely conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that is to be established, and not the state of being an inference (*anumānatva*) or the state of being a logical argument (*yuktitva*),
by which the aforementioned fault would arise.

Is it not the case that the words *yukti* and *upapatti* have the same meaning? Thus, in other contexts such as "faultless *upapatti* is inference" (*nirdoṣopapattiranumā*), if there is something to be excluded by the inclusion of the term "faultless," then it should also be included here;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
If [you say] it does not exist [there], then [it should not be included here either].
It must be done; thus it is said:
indeed, words have a twofold function, distinguished as primary (mukhya) and secondary (amukhya).

And so, since a cognition may arise from the word "upapatti" (justification) regarding both actual justification and its semblance, the term "faultless" (nirdoṣa) was employed therein to exclude the latter and to indicate the primary meaning.
Furthermore, in this context, it is stated that "reasoning" (yukti) refers precisely to the primary meaning of being internally faultless;
for example, [the statements] "a correct reason" and "an inconclusive reason.
Thus, this too is said to be simply reasoning.
But it is not [valid] when qualified by faultlessness;
for, in the case of intending the primary meaning of the word "reasoning" (*yukti*), there is no dependence on that [faultlessness], such is the remainder [of the sense].
Alternatively, this is not a definition of a synonym (*paryāya*).
"What is it that is called *yukti*? It should be understood as that which is joined or connected; thus, *yukti* is said to be inference (*anumāna*). [Objection:

If this were the case, then even an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason—provided it excludes what is contradictory and what is not established—would constitute an inference. To this, it is said: 'It is precisely *yukti*'; for it is indeed joined (*yujyate*), but not..."
The meaning is that it is also logically possible.
For instance, properties such as being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) are both logically connected with and not logically connected with properties such as impermanence (*anityatva*).
But it is indeed logical;
therefore, by this [reasoning], the pervaded (vyāpya) is like the rule of concomitance (sāhityaniyama),
[and thus] the logical mark (liṅga).
It has been stated that this is called "inference" (*anumāna*).
However, the followers of the Sugata (Buddhists) maintain that identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) alone are the two relations that constitute the basis of inference.

The Vaiśeṣikas, however, enumerate the grounds for inferential knowledge as follows: "the effect, the cause, the related, that which inheres in the same object, and the contradictory. Thus it is said: "For the Sāṅkhyas, inference is sevenfold by means of the measure, the cause, the conjoined, the contradictory, the concomitant, and [the relations of] master and servant, killer and killed, and so forth."
Thus the Sāṅkhyas have enumerated [their views].
To refute all of that, the restriction is made that it is "reasoning alone" (yukti);
the meaning is that inference possesses a necessary connection (niyata-sambandha) but does not possess a specific connection (sambandha-viśeṣa).
We shall establish this point later.
Some say that the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is also a constituent part of inference.
Refuting that as well, he explains what was already stated: "It is simply pervasion (vyāpti)."
...but that alone is traditionally known as pervasion (vyāpti).
Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is that which is obtained specifically [through the relationship between the probans and the probandum].

That inferential mark (*liṅga*) which is endowed with an invariable concomitance (*avyabhicarita-sāhitya*) is inference (*anumā*); it does not necessarily require the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
The meaning is "that which leads to the conclusion" (*vinīti*).

Alternatively, it is a formation denoting the state (*bhāvasādhana*), meaning "pervasion" (*vyāpti*). In that case, the term "inference" (*anumā*) is used figuratively to refer to the pervasion itself.

The meaning is that pervasion alone (*vyāpti*) is the constituent factor of inference, not the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). And this will be demonstrated by the Teacher himself when he establishes that even a [reason] residing in a different locus can be a prover. By this [it is refuted], as in: "From the perception of one part [of the reason] whose relation and rule are known..."
The claim that "inference is knowledge [arising] from one part [of the object] when it is uncontradicted" is also refuted,
because the restriction to "one part" is not a necessary condition. *5,372*

As it has been stated: "Inference is that which is endowed with five characteristics—presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), existence in the similar class (*sapakṣe sattva*), exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣād vyāvṛtti*), the state of having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), and the state of having no counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*).
As he [Dignāga] said: "That which is connected with the object of inference, well-known, and included by the word 'ca' (and)."
That is incorrect;

for the purely positive (kevalānvayin) lacks exclusion from the counter-example (vipakṣa), while the purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) lacks presence in the similar example (sapakṣa), and thus neither is all-pervasive.
If it is argued that in some cases it possesses four characteristics and in others five, [we reply: no.

If it is argued that these [three] are mentioned because they are useful for establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*) and being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), since no single motivating factor [for mentioning all three together] exists,
and that in reality only those two are the actual members of inference— [we reply: no.

Since the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is also not the effective factor, one must state that pervasion (*vyāpti*) alone is the effective factor. To the question, "What is the use of this prattle? he says: "Pervasion alone... [and so forth].
Inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is pervasion (*vyāpti*).
It is of two kinds,
based on the distinction between positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Some declare that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is the pervasion of the probans by the probandum, while negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is the pervasion of the absence of the probandum by the absence of the probans;
[the author] excludes this twofold classification by means of the word "but" (*tu*).

For instance: does the negative pervasion—that "whatever is not possessed of fire is not possessed of smoke"—contribute to proving fire by means of smoke, or does it contribute to proving the absence of smoke by means of the absence of fire?
It is not the first.
This is because that [conclusion] is established solely through positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*), namely: "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that a reason possessing only positive concomitance (*kevalānvayin*) would be incapable of proving its point.
Furthermore, in this case, the relationship of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva*) exists between two absences (*abhāva*).

The well-said maxim that "an entity is established by means of an entity" [is correct], because if one thing were to establish another through a pervasion residing elsewhere, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that there is no such over-extension provided one accepts that the relationship of probandum and probans exists only between those two things that stand in the relation of pervaded and pervader when they are both non-existent, we say: no.
Nevertheless, this would entail the consequence that the definition "the probans is that which is pervaded" lacks universal applicability (*avyāpti*).

If it is argued that there is no such over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because one accepts that the relationship of probandum and probans exists only between those two absences that stand in a relationship of the pervaded and the pervader, we say no;
for even so, the definition "the probans is that which is pervaded" would still result in being unapplicable.
If it is argued that there is no fault because of the rule that "the absence of which is the pervader of the absence of another, that [latter] is the pervaded of the former," [we reply:

no; in that case, negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) would not be useful for establishing the probandum under discussion, but rather would be useful for establishing the pervasion of the probans under discussion.
In that case, its nature is indeed positive (anvayi);

however, the second [type of pervasion] is certainly accepted. But if one asks whether that too is exclusively of a positive nature, then a twofold division of pervasion is not possible in every respect. *5,377*
By this, even the threefold division of inference— into *kevalānvayi*, *kevalavyatireki*, and *anvayavyatireki*— is refuted;
for negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is not a constituent factor of inference,
and because establishing it by its mere existence would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is asked, "In that case, how is it that the purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) [reason] functions as a means of proof?"— then what is this so-called "purely negative" reason?
If you say it is that which possesses "purely negative concomitance" (vyatireka) alone;
In that case, how could there be the relationship of probandum and probans between two things that are absolutely non-existent?
If it is argued that this is nevertheless observed, we say no; for its explanation is something else entirely.
The pervasion of the possession of breath and so forth by the state of having a self was apprehended only in a living body;
therefore, since there is disagreement regarding that very instance, it could not be demonstrated there.

Since the mere pervasion alone is a constituent of inference, and not the demonstration of it in a similar instance (sapakṣa), its establishment is carried out through the pervasion of the two negative concomitances (vyatireka).
This is the sequence of the formal argument (*prayoga*) here:

"The living body possesses a self (*sātmaka*), because it possesses breath and so forth; whatever possesses breath and so forth possesses a self, and this [living body] possesses breath and so forth; therefore, it possesses a self. When this is formulated, its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not perceived, just as [the pervasion] of smoke [is not perceived] by fire.
In response to the inquiry "How is that so?", another formulation proceeds.
The possession of breath and so forth is pervaded by having a self, because it is the absence of that which pervades its absence;
for whatever is the absence of that which pervades the absence of something is itself pervaded by that thing, just as smoke is pervaded by fire.

When this much ought to have been said, the fact that it is formulated otherwise is due either to the desire for clarity of comprehension by those who possess discernment, or to a preference for conciseness.
It might be argued:
if inference were the pervaded (vyāpya), then smoke would also be an inference with respect to the impermanence of sound.
"For that too is pervaded by fire"—
do not say so; for the term "the pervaded" (vyāpya) is a relative term.
And thus, it would be stated that whatever is pervaded by something [serves as] an inference with respect to that [pervader].
Nor is there any such over-extension (atiprasaṅga) here;
for properties (dharmas) are of two kinds.
Some exist solely through mutual exclusion,
such as producedness and impermanence,
independence and dependence, and so forth.
Some are mixed;
they too are of three kinds;
some are intermingled.
Commixture (*saṅkara*) is the coexistence in a single locus of two properties that exist by way of mutual exclusion,
such as being an element (*bhūtatva*) and being corporeal (*mūrtatva*), or being a person (*puruṣatva*) and being a cook (*pācakatva*), and so forth.
Some exist in a state of being both the higher and the lower,
such as the existence of a sentient being and substantiality, or the possession of smoke and the possession of fire, and so forth.
Some possess equal modes of occurrence,
such as producedness and impermanence, or heaviness and possession of taste, and so forth.
In that regard, for the first [types], there is no mutual relationship at all; thus, there is no state of being an inference (*anumāna*) and an object of inference (*anumeya*).
They are designated by the name "contradictory" (*viruddha*).

As for the second [types], even though a relationship exists, because they mutually deviate from one another, the relation of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is absent; therefore, they do not possess the status of inference and the object of inference.
However, it is stated that [the relationship] is not mutually certain;

for among the third [category of things], there is the status of being the object of inference and the status of being the means of inference, respectively, by virtue of one being the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the other being the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
But others, by virtue of not being the pervaded, do not attain the status of being the means of inference with respect to the others.
Are not the [first] three exclusively inconclusive?

As for the fourth, however, because they stand in a relationship of mutual pervasion (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*), they are fit to be inferences for one another; yet they are distinguished by being established or unestablished—this is the summary.
[Objection: Even so, would not the knowledge of fire from smoke belong to everyone? To this it is said: "by memory" (*smṛti*).
This is an illustration of the state of being cognized (*pramitatva*).
The meaning is that it is the very cognition of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the very cognition of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) that constitutes inference;
it is not a means of valid cognition by its mere existence, as is the case with the sense organs.
[Objection: Even so, does it not follow that for an inhabitant of Nārikela Island, there would be the undesirable consequence of an inference of fire from the sight of smoke?
[Reply: Not so;
for just as the cognition of the nature of the pervaded (vyāpya) is required, so too is the cognition of the pervasion (vyāpti) required.
Nevertheless, since the same undesirable consequence remains because the pervasion might have been grasped but forgotten or not yet recollected, it is said "recollected" (*smṛta*).
The meaning is that only the recollected pervasion is useful for inference.
And thus it is stated that inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of the probandum (*vyāpya*) which is dependent upon the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Some maintain that inference is the "consideration of the mark" (*liṅgaparāmarśa*), and that this consideration is a third cognition consisting of a synthesis (*anusandhāna*).
For instance:
The first [cognition] is that which occurs at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke by fire in a kitchen or similar location.

The second is the cognition of smoke on a mountain or similar place by one who has already grasped the pervasion. Following that, there is [the third], caused by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) awakened by the perception of the related term (*sambandhidarśana*).

Some do not accept that the third [cognition]— the knowledge of smoke consisting of a synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) in the form "this [mountain], which possesses smoke pervaded by fire, is itself possessed of fire," occurring immediately after the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire"— is inference.
For they hold that the capacity for inference consists solely in the recollection of the pervasion and the knowledge of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatājñāna*).
In that regard, the first cognition is accepted because it is impossible to remember a pervasion that has not been previously experienced;
the second cognition is also accepted because its object is the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā).
Therefore, once the recollection of pervasion has occurred, what else remains for which a third cognition must be sought? [The opponent replies:
"It is that [object] which is seen as coarse," and so forth. [The author answers:
Certainly not, because the status of being a cooperative cause is untenable.
But since it is synthesized,
and since that synthesis does not occur without a third cognition, how can that [synthesis] be avoided?
If you say that the self synthesizes it, [we reply:]...
True;
for it would aggregate [the objects] through its function (*vṛtti*), but not by its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Nor should it be said that, in this case, let it be that very [nature].
"Because that [inference] is impossible without the former.
But we say:
let the aforementioned method apply in those cases where the recollection of the pervasion occurs solely from the perception of the mark (liṅga).

However, when for one who has grasped the pervasion (vyāpti), the recollection of that pervasion arises through mere verbal testimony and the like even without the perception of the logical mark (liṅga), and when a second perception of the mark— consisting of a synthesis (pratisandhāna)— is about to arise, this process is not necessarily required. For just as recognition in the form "this is that" arises from sensory contact alone when accompanied by mental impressions (saṃskāra), so it is here as well.
"In accepting this, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
[Objection: "By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is pervasion (*vyāpti*) itself to be apprehended?
[Reply: "It has been stated that it is by means of perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*), according to the specific case."
We shall explain how this is so.
Inference is of two kinds: for one's own sake (*svārtha*) and for the sake of others (*parārtha*). Among these, that which [proceeds] without depending on the instruction of another...
Inference for oneself (*svārtha-anumāna*) consists of the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the perception of the sign (*liṅga*) that is pervaded.
Inference for others (*parārtha-anumāna*), however, depends upon instruction for another.
Instruction for another is a statement that generates the cognition of a sign possessing the capacity [to prove the probandum].

And some maintain that this [inference] is endowed with five members: the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). Not accepting this restriction, [the author] says: "It has been stated... (*uktā*) and so forth.
That very pervasion (vyāpti) which has been described is inference;
that is to say, the statement of pervasion itself is the instruction for others.
The word "eva" (only/very) is intended to exclude other [possible] restrictions, and not for the purpose of excluding any alternative position.
Since the other alternative will be stated by [the author] himself, one might ask:

"How is the statement of the pervasion—that whatever possesses smoke possesses fire—a factor for communication, given that there is no mutual trust between the proponent and the opponent? To this, it is said: "[It is] remembered."
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "ca" (and); it conjoins [the two cases] as "jijñāsitā" (sought to be known).

It is stated that for one who has grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the mention [of the reason] is a cause of recollection, whereas for one who has not grasped the pervasion, it generates the desire to know (*jijñāsā*). The intention is that it is not employed as a source of valid knowledge (*āgama*). *5,389*
Now, one might object that it is incorrect to say that the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*) itself constitutes instruction for another,

because stating the pervasion at the very outset is irrelevant. Anticipating this doubt, the author refutes it by establishing his initial proposition, “That very pervasion has been stated,” with the words beginning with *pratijñātā*.
When the pervasion itself is stated for the sake of establishing the meaning of the proposition, [that is the *udāharaṇa*]. (MAnu 2.1.31cd)
What remains here? ... // MAnu 2.1.32a //

The phrase "for the sake of establishing the meaning of the proposition" is the refutation of the [charge of] lack of connection (*asaṅgati*). The word "then" (*tadā*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. The word "what" (*kim*) is used in the sense of an objection (*ākṣepa*).
Regarding what is to be said here,
this is what is meant:
for when someone who perceives a mountain as possessing fire is questioned by another who considers it to be without fire, asking "What is the proof for the mountain's possession of fire?"—

If he were to state, for the sake of establishing a matter already understood by himself, merely the pervasion— that "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire"— to another person, what inconsistency would there be?
For it is being presented as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in response to what has been asked by the other.
Or rather, what else remains to be said, for the sake of which another word would need to be stated?
Therefore, the statement of pervasion alone constitutes the instruction for another.
It might be argued:
"Inference is indeed the consideration of the logical mark (liṅga) as being endowed with both pervasion and presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatā)."

Even by those who consider the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) not to be a necessary factor [of a valid reason], the existence of the mark (liṅga) must nevertheless be admitted;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the admission of pervasion (vyāpti).
And that [locus] is not one where [the property] is not intended to be expressed;
for if that were the case, it would follow that every mountain, by virtue of possessing smoke and so forth, would necessarily possess fire and so forth.
Therefore, in accordance with pervasion (vyāpti), it must indeed be admitted that [the probans] possesses the property of being restricted to a specific location.
For even when they are in different loci, the rising of Kṛttikā alone indicates the proximity of the rising of Rohiṇī,
but not its occurrence at any random place.

Therefore, first of all, that much must be stated by which there would be a consideration of the logical mark (*liṅga*) as being endowed with both pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) in the intended locus; and since it is established that this too must be expressed according to the sequence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), the thesis-statement (*pratijñā*) "the mountain possesses fire" must be uttered. This is because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be stated without a substratum, and thus the thesis-statement, in the form of an introduction to the object, serves to arouse the desire to know the means of valid cognition. Then, when the expectancy arises—"From what means of valid cognition is this to be understood?"—there follows the statement of the reason (*hetu*), "because of possessing smoke," which merely establishes the nature of the logical mark as it functions as an auxiliary to the [thesis].
Then, when there is a desire to know its capacity and for the purpose of demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is the example statement: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire.
For the purpose of demonstrating the property of being present in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) in the intended location, there is the application (*upanaya*): "And this [mountain] possesses smoke.
Then, so that everything may ascend into the intellect and be brought into a single syntactical unity, there is the conclusion (*nigamana*): "Therefore, it possesses fire indeed."

For this very reason, those who believe that the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*) are redundant because their meaning is already conveyed by the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) are refuted.
Thus, when so much must be stated, how could one be satisfied by merely stating the pervasion (*vyāpti*)? To this it is replied:
As for the reason stated for the necessity of the thesis (*pratijñā*), that is incorrect;

for the requirement [of the thesis] is established by the very fact that the presentation of the subject (*viṣaya*) occurs through the dispute itself, thereby accounting for the arising of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

If it is argued that, nevertheless, because there is still such expectancy, the statement of the reason (*hetu*) and the application (*upanaya*) must be made in order to demonstrate the nature of the logical mark (*liṅga*) and its property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), we say no.
Because conceptual construction is untenable;
for instance, should the statement of the reason and the application be addressed to one who has already understood that the mountain possesses smoke?
Or [it may refer] to the opposite case.
He refutes the first [position] with the words: "The mark (liṅga)."
...the characteristic mark of that [sin] for one who recognizes it. (Manu 2.1.32b)
In that context, at the point intended [for discussion], the connection with what precedes is: "What remains?

For the purpose of making known the nature of the logical mark (*liṅga*), its subsistence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), and its knowledge, there is the employment of the statement of the reason (*hetūpanyāsa*).
The sense is: if that cognition were established for the other party by itself (*svataḥsiddha*), then what would be the use of the reason (*hetu*) and the application (*upanaya*)?
He refutes the second alternative by restating it with "yadi" (if).
If the indicative mark (liṅga) were unestablished, how indeed could it possess the status of a means of valid cognition?
The word "therein" (tatra) is understood [from the previous context]. "Unestablished" (asiddha) means not established for the opponent.
In that case, how can there even be the status of a means of valid cognition (māna) for this mark (liṅga) which is unestablished in its own nature?
"It does not exist" is the meaning;
"it must be stated at a distance" is the sense of the word *eva*.
[Objection: If this is so, then even pervasion (*vyāpti*) need not be stated.
If that [reason] is also stated as having its pervasion known, then the statement is redundant;

however, if it is contrary [to the fact], then because its pervasion is unestablished, it is not a means of valid cognition at all—so how could there be a statement of pervasion? For this can be said in that case as well.
And thus, it would follow that silence alone would result for both the proponent and the opponent.
This is not so;
for there is no fault in either case.
For pervasion (vyāpti) is not useful by its own nature,
nor merely by being known; rather,
it is useful when being remembered.

And thus, it has already been stated that the statement of the pervasion (vyāpti) is useful as a reminder for one who has already grasped the pervasion, whereas for one who has not grasped the pervasion, it is useful precisely at that time by generating the desire to know it.
If that is the case, then the statement of the reason (*hetu*) and the application (*upanaya*) are likewise not useful.
For the mark (*liṅga*), though endowed with the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), is not useful by its own nature,
nor merely by its being known.
But it has indeed been known;
for although it is known by way of being remembered, it is not known as something common to trees and the like,
but rather as a logical mark (liṅga).

Thus, having raised the objection that the statement of the reason (*hetu*) and the application (*upanaya*) are indeed purposeful—since they serve to remind one who has already cognized the nature of the mark (*liṅga*) and its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), acting as reminders of the mark for another, or generating a desire to know it for that other—one says:
"If... (*yadīti*).
If it were merely a means of recollection, there would be no purpose for the one who remembers it here.
The term "of everything that has been stated" is an elliptical expression for its function as a reminder (*smārakatva*).
By the inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*), it excludes the capacity to convey new meaning (*pratyāyakatva*);
the remainder of the sense is "such as the reason (*hetu*) and so forth."

And regarding the phrase "of the mark (liṅga) endowed with the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharma)," the words "it would be" (syāt) and thereafter "not because of that" (na yataḥ) must be supplied [to complete the sense].
The term "smṛtau" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Here, in this statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is a locative case used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta-saptamī*).
And regarding the phrase "in the case of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth":

if it is argued that, just like the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the reason and other members of the syllogism should also produce the desire to know by generating the recollection and synthesis of the logical mark (*liṅga*) as being endowed with the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), that is not the case.
The construction is as follows: since for one who possesses the recollection of that [pervasion] by means of the statement of pervasion itself, there is no need for the reason (*hetu*) and so forth.
This is what is meant:
if the reason and so forth were to convey the meaning through the form of a sentence, then the consideration of their capacity would be useful.

But when it is employed solely as a reminder (*smāraka*) and so forth, then some factor such as similarity (*sādṛśya*) or a relationship (*sambandha*), which serves to awaken the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), must be sought.
This is the same even in the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

For when it is stated, "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire," the very form of inference (*anumāna*) is manifested here; indeed, one understands that the state of possessing smoke is the pervaded (*vyāpya*).
Consequently, how could one who possesses the recollection of that [reason's] presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) and so forth not also possess [the knowledge of] pervasion?
Alternatively, one who asserts that the instruction by another must necessarily consist of five members should be asked:
"Is this five-membered statement [sufficient] for the sake of the pervasion and the presence in the subject (*pakṣadharma*) as authoritative tradition (*āgama*)," or...
Is it a sign that makes the deceased known,
or merely something that reminds one [of him] and so forth? If it were the former, then this [would be the case].
According to the method explained by others, a sentence (*vākya*) is somehow a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
however, that [position] is not tenable.
Because there is no mutual trust between the proponent and the opponent;
or, if there were such trust, then since the matter would be established by the mere statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*), the formulation of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth would be useless.
Regarding the second case, he says: "If... (*yadīti*).

If it is admitted that the statement of another serves merely as a cause for recollection and so forth, then, since the recollection and so forth of the one who remembers arise from the very statement of the pervasion (vyāpti) when that statement exists, there is no purpose for any word other than this statement of the pervasion; thus, it need not necessarily be uttered. Indeed, in the world, it is observed that the recollection of the meaning of a word and so forth occurs even from a mere portion of a word.
Furthermore, even in the treatises there is the practice of employing a mere portion of a sentence.
If it is argued that [the listener] follows [the argument] because they have ascertained the speaker's reliability (*āptatva*), whereas that is absent in the case of the opponent, let it be so;
for it has already been stated that this [portion] does not convey [the meaning] by way of being a scripture (*āgama*).

Otherwise, even the purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) formal argument used in common practice (*sāṃvyāvahārika*) should not be pursued, because it has been demonstrated that the actual scope of formal arguments is otherwise.
If it is argued that, were such an argument pursued against an opponent, the pointing out of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) would not occur; [we reply: no.
Because there would be room for such an objection if one were to transgress worldly and scriptural conventions;
otherwise, even the failure to mention what has entered into the context and so forth would become a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
For the doubt—whether this person does not speak because it has entered into the context, or because of a lack of comprehension and so forth—is equal even in the case at hand. *5,402*
Another says:
"The presentation of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is indeed for the purpose of ascertaining the object of cognition (prameya);
and the ascertainment of the object of cognition is that cognition [of it] which is free from dispute."
And that [ascertainment] does not occur merely by demonstrating the essential nature of the means of valid cognition;
rather, it occurs also through the elimination of what appears to be such [but is not].
Otherwise, the validity of that very [means of cognition] would itself be non-terminating.

Thus, having introduced the subject matter by means of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*), and having demonstrated the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein by means of the reason (*hetu*), the exclusion of contradiction (*viruddha*), non-establishment (*anadhyavasita*), and inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) is effected by the statement of the example (*udāharaṇa*).
Non-establishment (*asiddhi*) is discarded by the application (*upanaya*).

By means of the conclusion (*nigamana*) as well, through the restatement of the reason (*hetvanuvāda*), the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*)— namely, that [the subject] is [the locus] of that [fire] alone and not of anything else— is set aside. By means of the restatement of the probandum (*sādhyānuvāda*), however, the rejection of sublation (*bādha*) and its counter-argument is effected, [showing] that it possesses fire alone and is not devoid of fire.
Thus, it is argued that a five-membered syllogistic statement is necessary for the sake of establishing the object of proof while dispelling disputes;
however, this is incorrect.
For by speaking in this manner—
It would follow that "instruction for another" (paropadeśa) is defined as whatever brings an end to a dispute;
and thus, it is incorrect to say that a five-membered statement is "instruction for another," because even when the five members are stated, the end of the dispute may not yet have been reached.
However, with the intention that it must be stated that "instruction by another" continues until the completion of the discourse, he says: "No."
And even when the five-membered syllogism is stated, there would be no end to the dispute.
The determination of the dispute is the cognition of the probandum (sādhya) accompanied by the conclusion of the dispute.
But is this not improper?
For the removal of fallacies has already been accomplished by means of the three members beginning with the example (udāharaṇa).

Since the dispute would persist even if all possible means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were set forth and refuted, because that same consequence would apply in every respect, he says: "In the case of examples and so forth... (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.1.34ab):
"And in the case of examples and so forth, the proof would likewise have to be stated once again. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.1.34ab)
By the word "example" (dṛṣṭānta), he indicates the meaning of the illustrative instance;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the meanings of the application (upanaya) and conclusion (nigamana) are included.
This is a locative of domain (viṣayasaptamī).
Thus, as in the case of a past object [already] asserted, the proof must be stated; this is the ellipsis. The connection is with the words "it would indeed be so."
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "because.
This is the meaning:
it is true that the ascertainment of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) occurs from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose appearance has been extracted.
However, we maintain that even by means of all five members of the syllogism, such a cognition of the valid means of knowledge does not actually occur;

for when there is disagreement regarding the purpose of the example and other elements intended to exclude fallacious appearances, the proof for those [elements] must also be stated. And it is not the case that one should not engage in such debate.
Nor can that cessation [of doubt] occur through mere words,
because such words share the same status of security or insecurity as the subject of the thesis itself;
furthermore, there is no cause for the removal of all doubts within the examples and other members of the syllogism alone.

Because [the object] is not perceived; for it would follow that a formal debate (*kathā*) would necessarily consist of five members. Therefore, since the application of inference is limited by the determination of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), a restriction to five members is not tenable.
Rather, one must accept that the limit is simply the completion of the discourse (*kathā*).
It is true that the cessation of dispute does not occur in its entirety even when the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava*) is employed;
nevertheless, because it satisfies intermediate expectations, the intermediate statement consisting of the five members is completed. Therefore, he says: "By the mark" (*liṅga*), etc.
And even when the mark (liṅga) is explicitly stated, the ascertainment through inference would likewise be certain.
The word "co" (ca) has the sense of "because. The term "anumeti" (it is inferred) indicates the statement concerning that which is related [to the probandum].

This being so, even when the statement of the mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "smokeness"—has been made as the cause for satisfying the intermediate expectation, "What is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here?", the completion of the intermediate sentence necessarily occurs; therefore, that alone [is required].
The statement must be accepted,
but not the restriction that it must consist of five members.

As for what was said— that the utility of the statement lies solely in its being a cause for recollection and so forth, and since that is accomplished by the mere statement of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), only the pervasion itself need be stated— that is incorrect.
If that were the case, it would follow that even the mere statement of the logical mark (*liṅga*) should be employed [as the proof],
for even that can serve as a cause for the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*), its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), and so forth. Thus,
he either addresses the objection of one who does not understand the intended meaning of what was said, or he refutes it, with the words "the logical mark" (*liṅga*).
Just as it is certain that there is an inferential conclusion upon the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*), so too it would be certain upon the statement of the logical mark (*liṅga*).
The meaning is that this is intended as a reductio ad absurdum (*iṣṭāpādana*).
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include other previously mentioned positions, such as the view that [the syllogism] contains both the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*).
Nor does this imply that the restriction "it is only pervasion" is untenable;
for the intention is that, by whatever means the recollection of pervasion and so forth occurs,
the exclusion of such a restriction is accepted there with respect to each and every conventional [cognition].
By this, it should be understood that the inclusion of the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*) within the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) is also established.
Thus ends the examination of the definition of inference (*anumāna*).
It was stated that inference is reasoning (*yukti*) which includes the state of being free from defects.
Since reasoning devoid of those faults is easily understood only through the thorough knowledge of those faults, the defects of reasoning must be examined.
Even though smoke and the like produce the cognition of fire and so forth, there is a reason why a certain object does not produce the cognition of another object.
Or if it produces doubt or error, that is a fault of reasoning (*yuktidoṣa*).
It is of two kinds.
It is both explicitly stated and implied by the wording.
Of these, he first indicates the former by way of classification: "contradiction" (virodha).
Contradiction (*virodha*) and inconsistency (*asaṅgati*) are direct refutations of reasoning.
Since contradiction is generally subsumed within the faults of inference (*anumāna-doṣa*),
it is mentioned first by virtue of its predominance.
The word "thus" (eva) excludes any further enumeration or excess,
because all existing defects are included within these very [categories],
and because anything not so included is excluded from being a defect.
"Directly" means:
The capacity of what has been stated follows from the reasoning already expressed; it is established in its meaning even without the addition of further words.
As for the word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "the refutation, however" (*dūṣaṇaṃ tv iti*), it is connected with the word "but."
Or, [it means] "directly":
regarding the logical reason (*yukti*) and that which is intended as a logical reason;

and regarding the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), even when the object intended as the probans is such that its cognition is merely presumed by the object intended as the probandum.

Intending that the students themselves should infer that "incompatibility" (virodha) is unfitness characterized by sublation (bādha), he defines "irrelevance" (asaṅgati) with the words: "In the proposition... (pratijñāyām).
For it has been stated that an inconsistency in reasoning consists in its lack of connection with the thesis.
The meaning of that [proposition] is indicated by the term "pratijñā" (the thesis). This is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*).
Here, "non-connection" (*asambandha*) refers to the absence of a connection characterized by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
In this case as well, the term "reason" (*yukti*) is used in a figurative sense.

Since "non-connection" (*asambandha*) and "inconsistency" (*asaṅgati*) are synonyms, the word "stated" (*ukta*) is used to indicate that [the inconsistency] is to be established through conventional usage.

He expresses this with the particle *hi*, implying: "Since the nature of contradiction and inconsistency is clear and has been demonstrated by others, what is the point of providing an example here? *5,413*

Now, one might ask: "How can there be only two types of fallacies of inference, given that there are many others enumerated by others, such as 'unestablished' (asiddha) and so forth? In order to demonstrate how these are included within these two, he states the classification of contradiction:
"Contradiction also... and so on.
Conflict, moreover, may likewise be of three kinds... // MĀnUV 2.1.36a //
The word "api" (also/even) serves to conjoin the specific classification with the general classification.
Alternatively, incongruity (*asaṅgati*) is of many kinds, and it is not merely threefold—otherwise, the subsumption of [fallacies] such as the unestablished (*asiddhi*) would be difficult to achieve.
Or rather, it is intended to refute the notion that there are only as many varieties of fallacious inference (*anumānābhāsa*) as have been enumerated by others.
The word "eva" (only) is used for the purpose of restriction, because all [other types] are included within these very [three].
It demonstrates their threefold nature by stating: "the meaning of the proposition," and so forth. *5,414*
... contradiction with the meaning of the proposition;
lack of a logical mark (liṅga); and non-pervasion (avyāpti) ... // MAnu 2.1.36bc //
The subject (dharmin) as qualified by the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā).
Its opposition to that [proposition] is contradiction (viruddhatā).
Where the cognition of the mark (liṅga) is useful for the establishment of the property to be proven, the absence of that [mark] in that object constitutes the lack of the mark (liṅgarāhitya).
Non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) is the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The word "iti" is to be supplied [at the end of the compound].

For indeed, the lack of fitness for the relationship of the probandum and the probans occurs when there is an impossibility of that relationship between those two things which are intended as the probandum and the probans.
Furthermore, even if that [property] exists in the means of proof (*sādhana*), it is not possible for a contradictory property to be the probandum (*sādhya*);
for instance, although an axe is sharp, space cannot be cut by it.
Nor, even if the probandum could exist in such a manner, can that which is incapable [of it] be so.
It is established as a means [of proof],
because even though wood is something that can be cut, a blunt axe lacks the capacity to cut it.
Therefore, it is logical that contradictions such as being contrary to the meaning of the thesis (pratijñārthaviruddha) constitute a fault.
Granted that the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and the fault of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) are defects of reasoning;
however, how can the contradiction with the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaviruddhatā*) be a defect of it?
If you say it is because of its connection with the probandum (*sādhya*), we say no.

Because if the existence of that [probandum] is impossible for what is intended as the probandum, then the intended probans would be operating outside its proper domain. But if this were the case, then even "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhanatā*) would be a contradiction;
for it is not possible for that which is already established to be a probandum.

Nor should it be said that "let it be so," because it is not included within the three aforementioned modes; furthermore, it would contradict one's own statement that "that which proves what is already established is incoherent."
Not so;
for contradiction (*virodha*) consists in the incapacity for syntactic connection (*anvayāyogyatva*) when there is an expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*).
Since a proven conclusion (*siddhasādhana*) lacks such expectancy, it is not included within contradiction.

But is it not the case that elsewhere, by stating "there are three kinds of contradiction" and so forth, the author—treating the absence of the mark (*liṅga*) and the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) as one—has accepted the third type of contradiction of the example (*dṛṣṭāntavirodha*) as the failure of the example to conform to either the probandum (*sādhya*) or the probans (*sādhana*)?
He will state here too that the example lacks both the probandum and the probans.
How then is this [present case] to be understood?
Nor is it appropriate here to provide an explanation by supplying that [term] in the same manner;
for it is untenable that a flaw in the example (dṛṣṭānta) should constitute a flaw in the inference (anumāna),
since an example is not itself an inference.
Even so, let it be a defect of inference by virtue of its subverting the pervasion (*vyāpti*) which is a constituent of inference:

for when the example lacks the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*), the means of proof (*sādhana*) abandons the probandum; whereas when the example lacks the means of proof (*sādhanavaikalya*), the pervasion cannot be demonstrated. If this is argued, we say no.
If that were so, since it would already be subsumed by the pervasion itself, its status as a third [type of evidence] would be untenable.
To this it is replied:

in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) arises merely through the establishment of the mark (*liṅga*)—whose pervasion has been perceived—in the specific locus intended.

Thus, with the intention that these are defects which obstruct [the proof], there is here the inclusion of "contradiction of the meaning of the thesis" (*pratijñārthaviruddhatā*), "absence of the probans" (*liṅgarāhitya*), and "lack of pervasion" (*avyāpti*).

However, even in the case of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), although the defect of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) is also instrumental for establishing pervasion, it is stated elsewhere that there are three types [of defects] including that [example-defect] as well, in order to make known that it must be pointed out in exactly the same way because it is perceived as residing therein; thus, there is no contradiction.

Alternatively, some speak of eight defects of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*), namely those lacking either the probandum (*sādhya*), the probans (*sādhana*), or both, as well as those lacking a substratum (*āśraya*) for either the probandum, the probans, or both.
To exclude these, the defects of the example are mentioned separately.
For instance, that which is deficient in both [the probandum and probans] cannot even be enumerated.

For a [logical] example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is vitiated by the deficiency of either one [of its two required characteristics], since it would otherwise follow that there is an overabundance [of requirements] when [the deficiency] is not established; otherwise, it would be impossible to exclude those cases where each one is deficient.
If it is asked, "How then can it be both positive and negative (anvayavyatirekin)?"— it has already been stated that it is not so in any way.
Furthermore, the fact that the example does not pervade the probandum and so forth is actually a merit of the example, not a fault.
For an example must be sought to demonstrate the pervasion of the existent by existence.
If it is argued that this is a defect of the example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), then for what purpose is such an example used at all?
If it is said that it is for the sake of making known the negative pervasion (*vyatireka-vyāpti*), we say no.
Since it has no direct utility,
and its indirect utility consists in nothing other than being a similar instance (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta), what is the point of mentioning it separately?
Furthermore, that which is excluded from neither [the similar nor the dissimilar instances] is already rejected by virtue of its redundancy.
A "devoid of a locus" (*āśrayahīna*) fallacy, however, shares the same status as the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*); thus, there are only two types of fallacies regarding the example.
Furthermore, the fallacy of the example is not universal;
for there is no rule that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) must always be demonstrated by means of an example alone.
Because there is no dependence on inference or scripture for the pervasion [in this case],
it might be argued as follows: "Indeed,

the 'mistimed' (*kālātīta*) and the 'neutralized by the context' (*prakaraṇasama*) fallacies are subsumed under the category of being contradictory to the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaviruddha*)."
The absence of a mark (*liṅga*) constitutes the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*).
Furthermore, there are three types of underpervasion (*avyāpti*):
the absence of a relationship between the probans (*sādhana*) and the probandum (*sādhya*).
Even when a relationship exists, there is also a relationship by virtue of its absence, namely,
being pervaded by the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavyāptatā*).
These three [conditions], taken in order, receive the designations of the "unascertained" (*anadhyavasita*), the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*), and the "contradictory" (*viruddha*).
And thus, this would merely be a condensation of a prosodic expansion (prastāra) defined by another;
yet there is no purpose for this.
Otherwise, since other methods of procedure would also find scope due to the manifold diversity of human intellects.

Nor should it be said that this exposition follows treatises on logic such as the *Brahmatarka*, for in the absence of a specific purpose, one would fall into a blind tradition. To this, it is replied:
There is a purpose for employing this alternative method of analysis;
for it will be stated that by way of contradicting the meaning of one's own proposition, one also includes the contradiction of one's own statement.
Nor can that [fault] be established by means of "missing the proper time" (*kālātītatva*) and so forth;
moreover, even in terms of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), it is established as being contradictory to the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*),
not by means of "missing the proper time" and so forth.
Because it would result in futility (*vaiyarthya*).
This [reason] is non-probative because it is "mistimed" (*kālātīta*).
The meaning of "because it has a counter-argument" (*satpratipakṣatva*) is that it is contradicted by a stronger or equally strong means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, there is no purpose whatsoever for this qualification here,
because that which possesses deficient strength is already excluded by the very term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).

Indeed, the application of the word *pramāṇa* occurs precisely in the context of distinguishing between a means of valid cognition and its semblance (*tadābhāsa*), and not when there is certainty regarding invalidity.
Or, since the qualification [of the probans] by way of its not being devoid of strength is possible, the inclusion of its sub-varieties would be entirely purposeless;
and thus this would constitute only a single refutation.

Furthermore, by the mention of "absence of indicative marks" (liṅgarāhitya), there is obtained the exclusion of those things enumerated by others as refutations—which are actually non-refutations—namely, the fallacies of the locus being different from the subject (āśrayavyadhikaraṇa) and the probandum being otherwise established (sādhyānyathāsiddhi), provided that "otherwise-established-ness" (anyathāsiddhi) is indeed a refutation.
Furthermore, since other types [of fallacies] will be mentioned later, one might ask:

"Does the distinction between *anadhyavasita* (unascertained) and so forth even occur in the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*)? Is this [distinction] to be enumerated for that reason alone, or because it is useful for conventional practice?
It is not the first case.
Because the demonstration of what is useless would lead to an over-extension;
nor is the second [alternative] possible,
because it would entail futility.
"This is not a proving [reason] because of its inconclusiveness" means that while it occurs in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it also occurs in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).
And here, there is nothing whatsoever to be excluded by the qualification.
Likewise, "because of its contradictory nature" means that while it does not occur in the similar class, it occurs in the dissimilar class.
And thus, it is indeed redundant;

for even in the case of "because of being pervaded by the opposite of the probandum" (*sādhyaviparyayavyāpyatvāt*), if the purpose is fulfilled by the mere relation, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is entirely useless.
In this way, the demonstration of internal subdivisions is also refuted.
Since providing an exposition for the sake of clarifying the student's intellect is indeed accepted [as permissible], there is no contradiction with one's own conventional usage.
Just as with contradictions (*virodha*), the various subdivisions of incoherence (*asaṅgati*) should likewise be inferred by oneself.
Having thus stated the fault of reasoning (*ukti-doṣa*) directly, he states the verbal fault (*vācanika-doṣa*) [with the verse beginning] "deficient" (*nyūna*).
But in the case of verbal [offenses], there is deficiency or excess.
The word *nyūna* (deficiency) has the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*).
The term "refutation of the reasoning" (*yukter dūṣaṇam*) is understood from the context.
Deficiency (*nyūnatvam*) is the failure to complete that which must necessarily be stated.
The state of having accomplished the task constitutes superiority.
Since the reasoning presented by that [superiority] would also be flawed due to defects in the statement, these two possess the character of being based on verbal expression (*vācanikatva*).
Now, one might object: "Is this distinction not illogical?"
For contradiction and inconsistency are also merely verbal;
indeed, being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is not defective in itself,
because if it were, the same consequence would apply even to its proving impermanence (*anityatva*).
If you argue that it is the same in the case of fire being cold and so forth,
then does "being produced" (kṛtakatva) or "fire being cold," or even "the permanence of sound," proceed of its own accord to prove [their respective conclusions],
such that they would be subject to refutation therein?
What indeed is that which is shown by the word as being the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)?

The word "but" (*tu*) is used for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that even when there is such an inconsistency characterized by proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) and so forth, it should still be stated [as a fault].
For deficiency and excess are only matters pertaining to the explicit statement (*vācanika*).
The meaning is that contradiction and irrelevance [are not faults] because they are observed even in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
Well then, let these faults belong only to the cognizer and the communicator.
Just as a person who employs a sharpened sword against fire or cold might alone be at fault, and not the "producedness" (kṛtakatva) and so forth [of the weapon],
it is not so;
for if producedness and the like are not defective, it is impossible for there to be fault even in one who employs them.

Otherwise, even one who employs [a reason] to prove the eternity of sound would be at fault. Therefore, it must be accepted that defects residing in both the object and the word—such as the unsuitability of "coldness of fire" as a probandum, or the incapacity of "being produced" for proving "eternity" and so forth—are indeed defects. For a defect does not cease to be a defect simply by being included within a qualifying condition (*upādhi*).
If that were so, it would lead to many logical inconsistencies.

Now, one might ask: "How can these alone be the defects of inference, given that 'having a limiting condition' (*sopādhikatva*) exists as an additional one? To this, he states its inclusion within the aforementioned [defects] by restating its nature: "The probandum... (*sādhyeti*).
The non-pervasion of the probans consists in its absence from that which pervades the probandum.

The non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the means of proof (*sādhana*) is its contrariety (*vaiparītya*) to that which pervades the probandum (*sādhya*). By the word "and" (*ca*), it is also implied that there is a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣatā*).
This refers to a property such as being prohibited (*niṣiddhatva*), which pervades the probandum, such as the state of being a means for what is not dharma (*adharmasādhanatva*).
Because of the rule that wherever there is the status of being a means to unrighteousness (*adharmasādhanatva*), there is the status of being prohibited (*niṣiddhatva*);

therefore, the "contrariety" (*vailomya*) of the means—such as the nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*)—in relation to the probandum (*sādhya*) means its "reversal," which is to say its lack of pervasion (*avyāptatva*).
This is because there is no such rule as "wherever there is the nature of violence, there is the status of being prohibited."

For even though ritual killing (*vaidhahiṃsā*) possesses the nature of violence, it lacks the quality of being prohibited. By this, the essential nature of a "limiting condition" (*upādhi*) has been stated: a limiting condition is indeed a property that, while pervading the probandum (*sādhya*), does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*).
And "possessing that" (tadvattva) for the probans consists precisely in not being non-pervaded by the pervader of the probandum.
Prior to this inference, at the time of grasping the pervasion, there is indeed no non-pervasion;
for one who abandons the pervader of the probandum necessarily abandons the probandum itself.
For it is not logical that one who does not abandon the probandum (sādhya) would abandon its pervader (vyāpaka);
moreover, the abandonment of the probandum is itself non-pervasion (avyāpti).
Others, however, maintain that pervasion (vyāpti) is a relation free from limiting conditions (nirupādhika).
However, some maintain that if [the relation] were qualified by a limiting condition (*sopādhika*), there would be an absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*) due to the absence of a definition;
this is incorrect.

For the knowledge of the limiting condition depends on the knowledge of pervasion, the knowledge of the absence of a limiting condition depends on that [knowledge of the condition], and the knowledge of pervasion depends on that [knowledge of the absence of a condition]; thus, because of the fallacy of a circular argument (*cakraka*), it is untenable for that [conditioned relation] to be the definition of pervasion.
Is it then the case that pervasion exists even for that which possesses a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)?
Not so;

for although pervasion and the absence of a limiting adjunct are coextensive (*samaniyama*), it has already been stated that the absence of a limiting adjunct cannot constitute a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), because it is not an integral factor in the cognition of pervasion.
If this is so, one might ask: how can there be the conventional usage of "probandum" and "probans"? We reply: it is by reference to the possibility of what will occur in the future.
In reality, however, it must simply be stated that when a given property (dharma) is not pervaded by that which pervades another, the former is not pervaded by the latter.
However, subsequent to the operation of the inference, there is indeed a counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatā*).
For the abandonment of the pervader of the probandum by the probans must occur either elsewhere than in the subject (*pakṣa*) or within the subject itself.
It cannot be the first case.
This being the case, since there would be no occasion for pointing out a limiting condition (*upādhi*) by abandoning a clearly manifest deviation;

whereas in the second case, the exclusion of that which pervades the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*) from the subject (*pakṣa*) necessarily excludes the probandum as well, and thus it is simply a case of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*).
By this, it follows that if the absence of the limiting condition constitutes the counter-argument, the limiting condition itself cannot be a flaw (*dūṣaṇa*).

The argument that "it is not logical for that which is the absence of something to be a flaw in a certain case, yet that very thing [the presence of the probans] should also be a flaw there, because of contradiction" is refuted; for [the upādhi] is defined precisely by its predominance in excluding the subject (pakṣa). And for this purpose, one should construe it thus: the contrariety of the pervader of the probandum (sādhyavyāpaka) consists in its exclusion from the subject, while the counter-balancing of the proof (satpratipakṣatā) consists in the [upādhi's] presence where the probans is present.
Indeed, we accept that there is no fault in a statement where the abstract state (bhāva) is the primary focus.

But one might object: "Even prior to the inference [of the conclusion], there would be a counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatā*), or else, following the inference, why would there not be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*)?
Do not say so.
For it is only when the probandum has been applied to the subject (*pakṣa*) that there is occasion for a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*).
Since the distinction between the subject and so forth does not exist at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), how could there be a state of being a counter-argument then?
It must be explained how there could be a lack of pervasion after the inference [has already occurred].
If it is argued that an *upādhi* (limiting condition), which pervades the probandum (*sādhya*) and excludes itself from the subject (*pakṣa*), also excludes the probandum [from that subject];
and thus, since the probans (*sādhana*) exists in that [subject] which is devoid of the probandum, the probans deviates (*vyabhicarati*) from the probandum—[we reply:
no, for if that were so, it would follow that even in cases of sublated (*bādhita*) and counter-balanced (*satpratipakṣa*) arguments, there would be deviation.
If it is argued that [the reason] is not [inconclusive], we say no, because it will be refuted later.

If it is asked: "Since the invalidation of an inference can occur through sublation (*bādha*) and the presence of a counter-inference (*pratipakṣa*) alone, what is the use of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*), which depends upon those?"

In that case, since the inference has already been refuted by the exclusion of the pervader (*vyāpaka*)—which is its very counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*)—what is the use of an "inconclusiveness" (*vyabhicāra*) that depends upon it? This is the same [as the previous point]. Furthermore, is the inconclusiveness in the subject (*pakṣa*) certain or doubtful?
Not the first.
Because the conceptual construction is untenable;
for instance,
is the absence of the probandum in the subject ascertained or not?
Regarding the first [alternative], is it by means of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or by the exclusion of a pervading condition (*upādhi*) of the probandum?
In the first case, since the inference would be sublated by that very [means of valid cognition], what is the use of an *upādhi*?
It is not the second [case].
Because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatva*):

namely, that the certainty of the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) depends upon the certainty of the exclusion of the probandum through its exclusion, and this [certainty of the condition's pervasion] exists only when that [exclusion of the probandum] exists.
In the alternative view that this is not the case, there is no certainty regarding the limiting condition’s pervasion of the probandum.

How could there be a certain deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the probans (*sādhana*) from the subject (*pakṣa*) through its exclusion [from the similar instance]? However, a doubtful deviation from the subject is established by itself; it does not depend on the inspection of a condition (*upādhi*). Moreover, such a deviation would be the cause for the total annihilation of all inference.
Therefore, it is appropriate that there is indeed a counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatā*) subsequent to the inference;
it is with this very intention that the statement was made: “That very thing is also the fault of the limiting condition (*upādhi*),” and so forth. (5.439)

If it is argued that when the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) is ascertained through favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) and the like, there is established the certainty of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) within the subject (*pakṣa*), we say no.

For the exclusion of that which is ascertained to be a pervader of the probandum functions as a sublation (*bādhaka*); thus, once the inference has been refuted by that very fact, the mention of deviation is redundant.
If it is further argued that even so, the position remains that the fallacy is "having a limiting condition" (*sopādhikatva*) or "having a counter-inference" (*satpratipakṣatva*), we say no.
Because one does not accept the existence of the counter-argument for as long as life lasts;
it is only when the capacity [of the reason] has not been determined that there is a "counter-balanced" (satpratipakṣa) argument,
but once the capacity has been determined, it must be either a sublation (bādhaka) or [another valid proof].
Who indeed would not accept that [the probandum] is sublated?

While one ought to say here that it possesses a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*), the statement "contrariety to the pervader of the probandum" (*sādhyavyāpakavaiyadhikaraṇya*) is intended to demonstrate the definition of a limiting condition as well.
That too is for the purpose of rejecting the position that [the condition] is co-extensive with the probandum (*sādhyasamavyāpaka*).
But surely this position has been accepted by the author of the Ṣaṣṭhīṭīkā?
Not so;
for it is merely a restatement of another's view.
Otherwise, Udayana’s citation of the statement "the inseparable connection with one probandum" would be purposeless. The refutation, however, is not stated here because it is obvious;
for instance:
Is the term *samapada* (equal locus) intended for the purpose of excluding [reasons] with unequal pervasion (*viṣamavyāptika*), or for some other purpose?
It is not the first [option].

For in such arguments as "The color and so forth of an earth atom are eternal, because they are specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of an atom, like the color and so forth of a water atom," even the absence of being a specific quality of earth—which has unequal pervasion—is treated as a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Because the exclusion of that [upādhi] is improper, and because it constitutes a flaw due to the possibility of suggesting a counter-argument.
If it is argued that if an upādhi with an unequal distribution were admitted, then "being other than the subject" (pakṣetaratva) would also follow as such an upādhi; [we reply:]...
Is that [probans] endowed with the two aforementioned qualifications or not?
If it is not, then for that very reason it lacks the status of being a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
