But if it is the first case—that is, if it is endowed with those qualifications—then what fault is there in its being a limiting condition as well?
If it is argued that this is not the case because properties such as "being other than a mountain" can exist everywhere, we say no;

for when there is the strength of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth of the inference, the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) is destroyed.
And in the absence of that [strength], the destruction of the inference is precisely what is intended.

Otherwise, in such cases as "Sound is denotable because it is knowable, like a pot," there would be the undesirable consequence that the "other-than-the-pakṣa" (pakṣetara) which possesses equal pervasion—such as "non-sound-ness"—would not be excluded. Thus, this [definition] abandons what is intended and accepts what is unintended; therefore, it is not a valid qualification. Furthermore, that which was stated is also incorrect.

“That which, by virtue of its own connection, imposes its own property upon another is a *upādhi*, just as in the world a hibiscus flower or the like [imposes its color] upon a crystal or the like. Here too, it is that which causes the error of perceiving the pervasion of the probandum when there is actually no pervasion of the reason.”
Regarding the statement, "In that case, there would be co-extensiveness of that [probans] with the condition (upādhi) if it were to exist," it must be asked:
what is actually being asserted by this?

Is the word *sama* (equal) used to exclude that [fallacy], on the grounds that it is not a fault because there is no actual pervasion for that which has an unequal pervasion (*viṣamavyāptika*), since a misconception of pervasion in the proposed probans (*sādhana*) by means of such a relation is impossible; or is it for the sake of making the term *upādhi* (limiting condition) etymologically meaningful?
It is not the first case.

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because when a point can function as a refutation by way of leading to a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*), the absence of the manifestation of one's own internal pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not a fault; furthermore, since the delusion of pervasion (*vyāpyatā-bhrama*) can arise simply through the observation of concomitance with the probandum (*sādhya-sāhacarya*).
Because the connection with the term "limiting adjunct" (*upādhi*) is merely a fabrication of one's own imagination,
for this very reason the venerable master [Dharmakīrti], instead of using the expression "having a limiting adjunct," stated "the contrariety of that which pervades the probandum.
However, conventional usage must be maintained even by means of designations established by others.

Alternatively, since it possesses the nature of being a pervader of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpyatā*) in some instances, the designation "upādhi" is applicable elsewhere as well by way of secondary usage (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*).
For this very reason, the second [alternative] is also not tenable.
Now, one might object: "It is impossible for that which has an asymmetrical pervasion (*viṣamavyāptika*) to bring about a counter-inference (*pratipakṣonnāyakatva*)."
"In some cases, [the reason] is inconclusive because its exclusion from both the similar and dissimilar classes is uncommon (*asādhāraṇatva*).
This is not so;
for it is not accepted that "uncommonness" constitutes a logical flaw (*dūṣaṇa*).
Or rather, because it is established that there is an absence of being a qualifying condition (*upādhi*) in those two cases [of the *sammata*].

Where a qualifying condition is excluded from one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśa*), how could there be a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*)? For that would entail the fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*).
Nor is this not a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*),
because it is possible for it to be non-pervasive of the probans even by its exclusion from a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśa*).
Furthermore, this fault does not exist in the view that accepts equal pervasion (*samavyāpti*).

Because it is appropriate to take only the other part as the subject (*pakṣa*), setting aside that [part] where the presence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is necessarily restricted to a portion of the locus possessing the limiting condition (*upādhi*).
It is replied:
By us as well, [only] the exclusion of the limiting condition (*upādhivyāvṛtti*)... [is accepted].
A single part [of the subject] is not made the subject (*pakṣa*).

If there is agreement regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) even in another part, then that very part is indeed not made the subject; however, if there is no such agreement, then there will simply be a different fault in that case—so what is untenable about this?

If it is objected: "How can there be a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*) when the condition (*upādhi*) is suspected? For, due to the consequence of being doubtful-unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddha*), it would lack equal strength," we say no.
This is because doubt—the result of a true counter-argument—cannot be prevented by the mere partial establishment of one side and so forth.
What is intended by "lack of equal strength" is precisely the fact that [the suspected condition] is not a constituent factor of doubt. *5,453*
It might be argued as follows:
Is "being a non-pervader of the probans while being a pervader of the probandum" the general definition of a *upādhi*, or is it its specific definition?
It cannot be the first.

In the argument "inherence is inherent because it is a relation, like conjunction," there is no pervasion by the *upādhi* "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), which is a pervader of the probandum as delimited by the probans.

Furthermore, in the argument "air is tangible because, while not being the locus of unmanifested color, it is the locus of perceived touch, like a jar," there is no pervasion by the *upādhi* "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*), which is a pervader of the probandum as delimited by "substantiality" (*dravyatva*).
Nor should it be said that something which is a pervader of the probandum as delimited by the probans, or a pervader of the probandum as delimited by some [other property], cannot be an *upādhi*.
The second [alternative] is not tenable, because it has been accepted by the teachers in various contexts and because the counter-positive adjunct (*vyatirekopādhi*) does not pervade [the probandum].

Otherwise, it would follow that another general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) must be stated. Nor should it be said that its nature consists in being a property that follows positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka),
because it lacks the capacity to serve as the cause for the conventional usage "this is a limiting adjunct (upādhi) here."
"And because, if that were the case, the definition would be redundant.
To this we reply:
this very [definition] is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
This is because the term "sādhya" denotes both the sādhya as delimited and the sādhya as undelimited; nor is it impossible for a counter-argument (pratipakṣa) to exist in that case,
since it is logically possible for the absence of that which is qualified by the upādhi— namely, the exclusion of whatever upādhi delimits the sādhya— to serve as the probans (hetu).
Just as inherence (samavāya), while being a relation, is devoid of the property of being inherent because it is not an effect, like space;
or as air, while being a substance, is devoid of the property of being tangible because it is not visible, like space.
Nor is there here any pointlessness in the qualification of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣaṇavaiyarthyam*).

[The reason] "because it is not preceded by qualities of its own causes" [is used] in cases such as "sound is not a specific quality of that which possesses touch, because while being perceptible, it is not preceded by qualities of its own causes," for the purpose of avoiding deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
This is because in some instances, the absence of the *upādhi* (limiting condition) qualified by the delimiting factor of the probandum (*sādhyāvacchedaka*) serves as the logical reason (*hetu*).
For example: "Air is not tangible, because while being a substance, it is invisible."
Regarding negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*), however, the answer has already been stated.
Furthermore, since the terms "probandum" (*sādhya*) and "probans" (*sādhana*) refer specifically to those under discussion, there is no minor flaw whatsoever.
The meaning of this [statement]—namely, "whatever is pervasive of that probandum and non-pervasive of that probans"—is thus entirely sound. *5,467*

But is it not the case that even if the presence of an *upādhi* constitutes a counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣa*), it nonetheless constitutes an additional defect of inference by that very fact?
Not so;

for by the term "contradiction of the meaning of the proposition" (*pratijñārthaviruddhatā*) itself, the characteristic of being "mistimed" (*kālātīta*), defined as contradiction with a stronger means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is already established.

Because the contradiction with the measure of the subject's strength (*vatsamabalapramāṇaviruddhatā*) as well as the existence of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatā*) are both included [within the category of contradiction].
For it has been stated that the mere presence of a rival [reason] constitutes a contradiction with the meaning of the thesis.
If that were the case, then even a contradiction with a weak [reason] would constitute a contradiction with the meaning of the thesis.
Because it possesses the characteristics already described, he says: "by the weak one."
Even when there is a conflict with that which is weak, a means of valid cognition is not non-probative.
This is the meaning:
it is well known that even general terms function with reference to a specific instance by virtue of context and other factors.
For example, when it is said at a particular occasion, "Bring a man," it is a specific man who is brought, and not just any man whatsoever.
In the present context, there is an enumeration of the reasons why inference is not a means of proof.
Furthermore, an inference does not fail to be a means of proof merely because it is contradicted by something weaker;
for it is only when there is a contradiction with something stronger that the inference itself becomes fallacious.

For example, in the case [of the argument]: "The person under dispute possesses direct knowledge of form because he possesses eyes," [the counter-argument] "The person under dispute is blind because he is a human being" [is presented].

Therefore, even though there is a conflict with a weaker [reason] regarding what follows from a general term, this does not constitute a contradiction with the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaviruddhatā*)—[provided it is not a contradiction with that which is delimited by the probandum established by inference].
However, [the contradiction] consists precisely in being opposed by a stronger or equally strong means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[Objection: Even if redundancy is thus excluded, the threefold division of contradictions with inference is not possible;
for contradiction with the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*) is already included within the category of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*).

Only through contradiction does a reason that exists in a subject (pakṣa) lacking the property to be proven (sādhya) incur the fallacy of non-pervasion (avyāpti). Indeed, there is no example of contradiction that is not conflated with non-pervasion;
for wherever contradiction is possible, it is non-pervasion—whose capacity has been ascertained elsewhere—that constitutes the defect.

He dispels the doubt— that the contradiction has fulfilled its purpose by giving rise to a lack of pervasion (avyāpti)— by means of the "spreading the feet" logic (*bhikṣukapādaprasāraṇanyāya*), stating: "by one's own statement."
Even if there is a contradiction with one's own statement, it will certainly not attain the status of a proof.
The term "valid means of knowledge" (pramāṇam) carries over [from the previous context].

Not only when there is a contradiction with a valid means of knowledge, but even when there is a contradiction with one's own statement, that [statement] will certainly not attain the status of a valid means of proof.
By the word "eva" (only/just), he shows that this point is established even for opponents.
As it has been said:
"Because of the inclusion of the term 'non-contradictory,' those [reasons] that contradict perception, inference, scripture, one's own treatise, or one's own statement are excluded. (*5,472*)
This is what is meant:
contradiction of the meaning of the thesis is twofold,
namely, contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and contradiction with one's own words (*svavākya*).
Among these, the first [type of contradiction] is twofold, consisting of contradiction with a stronger authority and contradiction with an authority of equal strength.
The second is also twofold, distinguished by the categories of *apasiddhānta* (departure from tenets) and *jāti* (futile rejoinder).
And *jāti* is threefold, distinguished by contradiction with one's own words, contradiction with one's own logic, and contradiction with one's own action.
In this regard, let the contradiction with valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) be set aside for now;
rather, the inclusion of contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) must be treated separately,
because it lacks the capacity to function in the production of a fallacy of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*).

For in the case of a contradiction with one's own statement, would the deviation of the proof occur because of what is accepted by both parties (in the subject), or because of what is accepted by the other?
Not the first,
because the validity of one's own statement is not accepted by both parties.
Not the second.
Because it is established by itself, it does not depend on contradiction with its own statement;
and because it is free from defects,
[the reason] does not function where there is no subject (*aviṣaya-vṛtti*).
Therefore, the contradiction with the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaviruddhatā*) must be enumerated separately as well.
Furthermore, this fault does not belong solely to inference, which functions in dependence upon pervasion (*vyāpti*);

rather, it applies to perception and other means of knowledge as well, since they do not depend on it. Thus, with the intention that the independence of inference is established even when its capacity has been observed elsewhere, [the author] proceeds to state "inference" (*anumāna*) in the context at hand.
The term "valid means of cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is the subject under discussion.
By this, the following [objection] is also refuted:
let the contradiction within one's own statement (*svavākyavirodha*) be considered a distinct fault, since it is impossible for it to give rise to a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).
Contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*), which consists in sublation or opposition, is not an independent fallacy;
for when there is contradiction with a means of valid cognition, the reason would either lack the property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) or be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*),
since the subject whose property one wishes to know constitutes the "thesis" (*pakṣa*).

Furthermore, because that which possesses a property contradictory to the probandum as established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be the subject (*pakṣa*), there is a rule that such a property is not a "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*).

For [the reason] would be shown to be deviant (*vyabhicāra*) by its observation in a locus of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*) that possesses a property contradictory to the probandum as presented by valid cognition.

Nor is it correct to say that only the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*)— and not the subject (*pakṣa*)— are the objects for observing the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

For if the inseparable relation were understood only externally, apart from the subject, then even a reason that is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) would not establish the probandum (*sādhya*) within the subject by virtue of external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*),
because its pervasion with the probandum would remain unestablished therein.
Therefore, the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) must be understood by means of a universal synthesis, whether internally or externally.
And in this way, the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) within the subject (*pakṣa*) is established. [Objection:
But how is it in the case of a counter-argument (*pratirodha*)?
In that case as well, there is the predominance of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Since, even when a means of valid cognition exists for both [the probans and the contradictory], it is included within the "unestablished due to lack of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*), it is appropriate to accept that the same applies to inference as well; for contradiction with a means of valid cognition is understood to function as an independent refutation by virtue of its operation upon a domain other than that of another means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), would there be a contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*) that presents non-pervasion (*avyāpti*),
or [would it occur] even after the operation of the inference?
As for the first case, it is indeed accepted.
Because it will be stated later that "it would not exist when pride is destroyed," the second [alternative] is not tenable.
Because it is illogical to accept that which depends [on something else] while abandoning that upon which it depends;

furthermore, if that which contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*), then even a "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) would likewise not be so,
for the same logic applies.
If it is argued that [this is not so], we say no;

for even in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) would result. Indeed, the non-establishment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is not a fault only in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*).
Therefore, because it is not desired by others, the charge of "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) is indeed irrelevant.
Thus concludes the examination of the fallacies of inference.

Having thus examined the fallacies of inference, [the author], as an incidental discussion, states that all points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) defined by others are also included within contradictions and the like, beginning with the words "In agreement... (*saṃvāda*).
And these very points, when combined with the failure to state the response, constitute the grounds for defeat.
"Points of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*) are so called because one is "restrained" (*nigṛhyate*) or "defeated" (*parājīyate*) by means of them.

Now, one might ask: how can defects of the speaker, such as the abandonment of a thesis (*pratijñāhāni*), be included among the defects of the statement of meaning—namely, contradiction, incoherence, deficiency, and redundancy? To this, it was said: "connected with non-correspondence and non-statement.
Yet, even so, the objection remains unrefuted.
This is because the fourfold set beginning with contradiction (*virodha*) has been stated to be a fallacy of inference (*anumāna-doṣa*),
and because points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) do not necessarily depend upon inference;
for indeed, repetition (*punarukti*) is not possible only within the context of inference.
He states with the word "tu" (but) that there is a distinction here because [the refutation] is applicable even in the case of a formal debate (*praśna*) and so forth.
For the fourfold set beginning with contradiction (*virodha*) is of two kinds: common to all forms of discourse, such as those bound by formal agreement (*samayabandha*), and uncommon.
In that regard, it has been stated that all defects of inference, such as contradiction (*virodha*) and so forth—which are unique (*asādhāraṇa*) to inference—fall within the scope of inference alone;
however, in the case of what is common (*sādhāraṇa*), all points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) apply. Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Alternatively, the word "but" (*tu*) serves to exclude these [defects], such as those occurring outside of formal debate (*kathābāhya*), from being considered points of defeat.

Now, in response to the inquiry, "What indeed is this thing called *kathā* (discourse)? the author, defining its essential nature, states its general definition, its divisions, and its enumeration: "Vāda" [and so forth].
For those who understand, there are three types of discourse: formal debate (*vāda*), informal discussion (*jalpa*), and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*). (Manu 2.1.39ab)
In this context, the word *kathā* (discourse) is the subject term and should be repeated;
it should be supplemented by the phrase *vicāragocare* (within the scope of investigation);
and *vijānatām* (of those who know) is used in the plural to denote a class (*jāti*).

Thus, a composition of sentences (*vākyasandarbhah*) consisting of a discourse that is the object of investigation by many learned authors and speakers is established as the general definition of "narrative" (*kathā*).
And those discourses (*kathā*) are threefold, meaning they are divided into three types by way of debate (*vāda*) and so forth;
or, according to the opinion of those who understand [the matter], there are three.
By this, it is stated that a statement of a number either less than or greater than that would be improper due to its contradiction with that [threefold classification]. *5,488*
He states the definition of debate (*vāda*) as follows: "for one's own purpose" (*svārtham*).
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, it is the means for determining the truth.
But it is merely a story, a mere dispute... // MAnu 2.1.40a //
The phrase "the means for determining reality" (tattvanirṇayasādhanī) serves to exclude *jalpa* (contentious debate), *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), and other such discourses;
nevertheless, because there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to certain specific forms of *vitaṇḍā*, the word "only" (*kevalam*) is stated to exclude those.
This [word "only"] has the sense of "directly."

The word "tu" (but) is used to show that [this type of debate] is distinct from the specific kind of *jalpa* (wrangling), which is a means for determining reality, because it differs in its purpose and the motivation for engaging in it.
For when two persons who have realized reality and are free from passion engage in a discussion at the request of others who have not realized reality, this definition does not apply there;
yet, that too is indeed *vāda* (discourse).
Because it would contradict the statement that there are "three" if they were not included elsewhere, it was said: "either for one's own sake or for the sake of others."
The word "api" (also/even) has the sense of a conjunction expressing both meanings.
He states the definition of *jalpa* (disputation): "It is called *jalpa*."
... Discourse that takes into account the meaning and so forth is to be known as the conversation of the virtuous alone. ... // MAnu 2.40bc //
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [the categories of] renown and so forth are included.
The phrase "in dependence upon the object and so forth" (*arthādivyapekṣayā*) is for the purpose of excluding [the definition from applying to] debate (*vāda*).
Since even debate can incidentally serve as a means for establishing the object and so forth, the term "dependence" (*vyapekṣā*) is employed [to distinguish it].
The phrase "only by those who exist" is intended to exclude cavil (*vitaṇḍā*).
If one were to say simply "by those who exist," the exclusion of cavil would not be established; for even in cavil, there is still one party who exists.
Because the plural number has the sense of a genus (*jāti*), it is stated as "only that.
He defines *vitaṇḍā* [sophistry] with the words: "vitaṇḍā."
But cavil belongs to the wicked, not to the virtuous.
Without disclosing one's own established doctrine, one should refute the positions of the wicked.
The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude *vāda* and *jalpa*.
The term "kathā" (discourse) is understood to carry over [from the previous definition].
Since there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if discourse were differentiated merely by a difference in speakers, he states another definition: "not making manifest," and so forth.
The meaning is that *vitaṇḍā* is when the virtuous (sadbhiḥ), without revealing or establishing their own doctrine, merely perform the refutation of the position of the wicked (asatām).
It is said that *vitaṇḍā* is a discourse that culminates solely in the rejection of the opponent's position, without the proponent establishing their own position through proof. [Objection:
But for what reason is this so?
We say that [the determination of truth] depends upon the judges and others.
If it is asked, "Why would they establish such a rule?"— it is not so—

because if the virtuous were to establish their own tenets for the sake of those who are unworthy of knowing reality and are non-existent [in the sense of being spiritually unready], it would follow that the production of knowledge of reality would occur for them.
And with the intention that such [an object] is prohibited, it was stated "of non-existent things.
By this, the justification for the first definition should also be understood. [Objection:
But surely this definition is impossible.

For the refutation of an opponent's position can only occur through the refutation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish it; and this is not possible in *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), which is devoid of any proof for one's own position. Therefore, he says: "It has been stated."
When they have first stated their proof, its refutation must be stated.

When those who are non-existent (the false) have first stated a means of valid cognition (*māna*) for the sake of establishing their own position, the existent ones must state a refutation of that means of valid cognition.
It is said that the non-existent one, acting as the proponent (*vādin*), must perform both the establishment of his own position and the refutation of the opponent's position;
whereas the existent one, as the respondent (*prativādin*), achieves his purpose solely through the refutation of that [proponent's] means of valid cognition.
The half-verse beginning with "kvacit satām eva" is read after the section on *vāda* and *jalpa*;
therefore, the commentator has explained it in that very place by relying on this same connection.
Furthermore, even those whose learning is not equal, such as teacher and disciple, are qualified for debate (*vāda*).
This is because [the debate] aims at the determination of reality (*tattvanirṇaya*).
However, the qualification for *jalpa* (contentious debate) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) belongs only to those who are equally proficient in knowledge.
As it is said: "Only between those whose wealth is equal, and only between those whose learning is equal..."
For there is a traditional legal authority (*smṛti*) stating: "Marriage and debate [are never] between the highest and the lowest classes";
here, "debate" (*vāda*) refers to the dispute characterized as *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*.

Otherwise, even one who is extremely inferior might, through audacity, attempt to contend with one who is most excellent; and if he were to overcome what depends on fate, he would acquire a false reputation.
Furthermore, there would be a lack of discernment among the judges and others, as well as a transgression, according to the saying:
"Where one who is unworthy is honored."
Thus, there is a distinction between *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) based on this definition.
Now, one might object: "This is incorrect, because since the mind of another is not perceptible, it is impossible to know whether their knowledge is equal or unequal. To this we say: no.
Because a definitive conclusion can be reached by examining the equality of knowledge and other factors between those who seek debate (*jalpa*) and those who seek wrangling (*vitaṇḍā*), he says this:
"Knowledge... [and so forth]. Only after the examination of knowledge do wrangling and debate indeed take place. (Manu 2.1.42ab)
That which has the examination of knowledge as its preceding cause is described as such.
Only when both parties have been determined to be equal through the examination of knowledge should the *vitaṇḍā* (destructive criticism) be employed, not between those of unequal knowledge.
And it should be explained that debate (*jalpa*) likewise must be preceded by an examination of knowledge.
The second particle "eva" (only/just) is for the purpose of excluding formal debate (*vāda*).
This restriction—that [debate] occurs only between those of equal knowledge—does not apply to formal debate.
Now, one might object: "Is this investigation to be carried out through debate for those who seek jalpa and vitaṇḍā, in order to determine things such as superiority or equality, or otherwise?
It cannot be otherwise;
for without mutual friction, that [determination] cannot be established."
Even in the first case, is it by means of *vāda*, or by *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*?
Not the first,
because a formal debate (*vāda*) is impossible between two parties who desire fame and the like and are engaged in rivalry.
If it is argued that the second [alternative] is not tenable because it would lead to an infinite regress, we say no;
for our intention is that the examination of knowledge (*vidyā*) is indeed desired by means of debate (*vāda*), and thus debate serves as the instrument for that examination of knowledge.
Having stated the introduction in order to establish the nature of [the relationship] through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), he says "ucca" and so forth.
For it is from the determination of high and low status that victory and defeat arise.
The meaning is that victory consists precisely in being determined as superior by means of knowledge (*vidyā*), while defeat consists in being determined as inferior.
Thus, "the examination of knowledge through debate" is to be connected with what will be stated hereafter.
Having thus stated the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "even without."
Without a definitive determination of the truth, there can never be a discernment of superiority or inferiority through mere disputation and the like; such is the examination of knowledge.
"By means of this, it is determined"—thus it is *nirṇīti*; "the determination of reality" (*tattva-nirṇīti*) means debate (*vāda*).

If one were to say simply, "Without the determination of reality, there is no knowledge of superiority and inferiority," there would be a contradiction with what is stated later, namely, "without debate.
Therefore, it is said, "by means of *jalpa* and so forth."
The word *iti* has the sense of "therefore. The examination of knowledge by means of debate (*vāda*), which will be explained later, is also connected here.

Although the discernment of the superior and inferior status of the two disputants also occurs in the case of *jalpa* (contentious debate) when a valid proof is perceived, [it is specifically established here].

Nevertheless, because one does not engage [in the activity] with that as the objective, and because its being for that purpose (*tādarthyam*) is not initially determined, it is not possible to give a verbal expression (*jalpa*) for that purpose.

Since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) serves only as the cause for determining that something belonging to another is not the cause, he states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in order to ascertain the status of debate (*vāda*) as the cause—namely, "by means of debate" (*vādena*).
And through debate, the clear discernment of superiority and inferiority arises.
The word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin [the present] with the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
He concludes the matter established through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the word "iti" (thus).
Regarding the phrase "iti vādasya pūrvatvam": [this refers to the priority of the aforementioned discourse].
Thus, this establishes the priority of that [vāda] discussion;

the meaning is that it must be practiced first for the purpose of examining the reasons for determining the equality of knowledge and so forth between those who seek *jalpa* (wrangling) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).
This is what is being said:
Debate and cavil occur only between those of equal learning,
and equality of learning is to be determined through examination;
and this examination is to be conducted by means of formal discussion (*vādakathā*).
Not by means of frivolous talk or cavil;
for superiority in knowledge is to be determined by victory,
and its inferiority by defeat.

Furthermore, victory (*jaya*) and defeat (*parājaya*), characterized by the capacity or incapacity to establish the subject matter under discussion through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), are expressed by the terms "high" and "low" in relation to the determination of the issue; these two are relevant only to the formal debate (*vāda*), and not to the contentious debate (*jalpa*) or the destructive debate (*vitaṇḍā*).
This is because in those latter cases, the determination of victory and defeat occurs merely by the production of some incidental point of defeat (*nigraha*).

Therefore, since there is no request for debate (*jalpa*) or wrangling (*vitaṇḍā*) for the sake of debate or wrangling, there is no infinite regress. When those seeking debate or wrangling have already conducted an examination of knowledge through formal discussion (*vāda*), what remains to be done? It has already been stated that if there is the possibility of them being equal in learning, they should engage in debate or wrangling.
In response to the inquiry as to what should be practiced when there is an apprehension of erroneous knowledge, he says: "Upon its establishment."
... when that [knowledge] is established, the other two are useless. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.1.44d)
Since that distinction between high and low status is established by debate alone, the other two—wrangling (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*)—are rendered useless;
consequently, the meaning is that they should not be practiced.
Thus, one should desist from them by means of debate for the sake of investigation.
But when the state of being a master of many sciences has been established, there is no longer even a dispute... // MAnu 2.1.45ab //

Regarding the statement that "the formal debate (vādakathā) should first be granted for those seeking to examine knowledge through sophistry (jalpa) or cavil (vitaṇḍā)," he states an exception to this: "if [the opponent] possesses extensive learning," and so forth.

If, prior to the formal examination, through worldly consensus and other means, the status of one party as possessing superior knowledge is established in relation to the opponent, then even a *vāda* (debate) should not be granted;
how much less so a *jalpa* (contentious debate) or a *vitaṇḍā* (cavil)?
Why? To this he says: "The reason."
...is the cause. (Manu Smṛti 2.45b)
The phrase "of the examination of knowledge" is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the object].
The term "debate" (vāda) is carried over [from the previous context].
For debate should be understood as the means for the examination of knowledge, and not out of a mere addiction to it.
Since that fruit [of victory] arises from something else entirely, what is the use of investigation, or what is the use of debate as its constituent?
As for the statement that debate cannot occur between two rivals who desire fame and the like,
this is because the employment of fallacious proofs and rejoinders is inevitably unavoidable therein.
And because it would otherwise be impossible to determine the equality or inequality of their knowledge, he says in that regard: "Together with [the body]. (Sabhā)
But for those who are rivals, it shall be preceded by the assembly, the assembly president, and the assessors.
... indeed, it is debate alone. // MAnu 2.1.46a //
The suffix *īka* should be stated [to be added] after the word *praśna* in the sense of "he makes";
the plural number in *spardhinām* is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*).
The word *eva* is to be construed with the supplied verb *yujyate*.
Since it is preceded by an assembly (*sabhā*) and so forth, debate (*vāda*) is indeed appropriate even for opponents;
the word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of a reason.

The meaning is that because the members of the assembly (*sabhya*), the presiding officer (*sabhāpati*), and the judges (*prāśnika*) ensure that the two parties refrain from employing fallacious proofs (*asat-sādhana*) and other such errors. *5,505*
As for what was stated— "Once that [truth] is established, the other two are useless"— that is incorrect;
for even when the determination of reality is achieved through debate, wealth and the like are not thereby established.
Thus, that which was desired has not been accomplished, while that which was undesired has been accomplished; regarding this, he says: "Both," etc.
...it would serve the interests of both parties and bring about a definitive victory.
The term "debate" (vāda) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. "Determination" (nirṇīti) is its explanation.
He is not merely the one who effects the decision, but also the one who effects victory.
By the word "victory" (jaya), the wealth and other benefits resulting from it are implied.
The sense is that in a debate for the purpose of examining knowledge, the presiding officer must also provide the victor with wealth and such rewards.

If that is the case, then there would never be the engagement in *jalpa* (disputation) or *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), because the reasoning—namely, "the two [types of debate] are practiced for the sake of something useless"—is the same [for all].
For just as in the determination of differences in knowledge, the one who wins obtains wealth and other benefits as a matter of course; [so too would it follow for cavil].
Likewise, when those two are equal, the attainment of wealth and other benefits is indeed possible for both;

nor is there any further result by which one would again undertake *jalpa* or *vitaṇḍā*. Therefore, he says: "The non-revelation of reality alone is the sole fruit of *vitaṇḍā* and *jalpa*. (MAnu 2.1.46cd)
The phrase "non-illumination of reality" refers to the capacity for deceiving others;
by this, the attainment of wealth and so forth achieved through that means is indicated.
This is what is meant:

Although the determination of victory or defeat may occur through the equality or inequality of knowledge, these are nonetheless merely the fruits of a discussion concerning ultimate reality (*tattvika-kathā*).

However, when two individuals of equal learning engage in *jalpa* (disputation) or *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), it is for the purpose of gaining wealth and other benefits by employing skill in concealing one's own [ignorance] from others.
Such engagement does not occur between those of unequal learning.
This is because the consequence of [the argument] being subject to sublation has already been stated.
Alternatively, debate (*vāda*) has the determination of truth as its fruit, whereas disputation (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) have wealth and so forth as their fruits;
thus, a distinction between types of discourse (*kathā*) has been stated based on the difference in their fruits.
That [position] is untenable;
for if that were the case, it would follow that discourse would be endless due to the differentiation of objects and so forth. Therefore, he says: "In reality... (tattve).

Although the purposes (*artha*) and so forth are distinguished by their internal subdivisions, nevertheless, the non-illumination of reality (*tattvāprakāśa*) alone is the fruit of both *vitaṇḍā* and *jalpa*.
Since the purposes and so forth are one insofar as they consist in being either the determination of reality or its opposite, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
The point is that the desire to express their internal subdivisions is indeed useless. *5,507*
Thus, the position that the examination of knowledge occurs through conversation has been supported.
Now, supporting the position that it occurs "otherwise" as well, he says: "Without... (vinā).
If it were possible to examine knowledge without debate, then frivolous talk and the like might also be found somewhere [to serve that purpose]. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.1.47a–c)
The phrase "by means of the undisputed consensus of the learned and so forth" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The word "kvāpi" (in some cases) connects with the first half-verse.
The meaning is that, in such a case, even at the outset, a specific type of debate such as *jalpa* and so forth should be conducted between those of equal knowledge.
In that case, there would be a contradiction with the statement that "the examination of knowledge is by means of debate" alone; therefore, he says: "or rather (vā eva)."
... otherwise, the doctrine itself would become something else.

As for what was stated—that debate (*vāda*) must first be undertaken—that is not contradictory, because it is impossible to examine learning without debate. Let it be so that, in the absence of other means, the examination of learning occurs through speech alone; however, on what basis is that [speech] called "debate" (*vāda*)?

If it is argued that [only debate] exists because those seeking the determination of reality (*tattva-nirṇaya*) possess the requisite qualification (*adhikāritva*) and because that [determination] is its fruit—[we reply: no, for it is not so.

If that were the case, then since those desiring victory (*vijigīṣu*) also possess the requisite qualification and since [victory] is its fruit, and since it is endowed with the members of an assembly (*sabhā-aṅga*) and so forth, then even *jalpa* (contentious debate) would exist [as a distinct category]. *5,508*
Does it here merely attain the status of being denotable by the term *jalpa* (wrangling),

or is it the absence of the status of being denotable by the term *vāda* (discussion), or rather is it a different type of discourse consisting of a combination [of both], or else, when two causes coincide, is there simply an impossibility of applying the term *vāda*?
He provides the answer for all cases as well: "It is mere verbal expression."
But for such a debate as this, there may even be the name "disputation" (jalpa).
By accepting that "jalpa" (contentious debate) is the name for such a [discourse] endowed with these two characteristics, the first [position] is refuted.
By the word "api" (also), the claim that it is denotable by the term "vāda" (formal debate) is asserted; and by the phrase "of such a kind," the reason is stated.
By this, the second [position] is also rejected.
It is not logical that the expressive word should fail to function when its cause is present,

for the same applies to the word *jalpa*. Therefore, in the case of the scale (*tulā*), it would possess a different mode [of operation] than that of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth.
It is indicated that while "vāda" (debate) may also be called "jalpa" (wrangling), the designation "vāda" is primary, whereas the designation "jalpa" is secondary;
by this, even the fourth [position] is refuted.
In that regard, he indicates the existence of a specific reason for this with the word "tu" (but).

For instance, although the two disputants may initially be desirous of victory, nevertheless, once their desire for victory has been set aside by the members of the assembly and others, only the pursuit of determining the truth becomes relevant to the discussion.
Furthermore, while gains such as wealth may be obtained incidentally, they were not aimed at from the very beginning; thus, they are merely secondary.

For this very reason, when it was previously stated that "it would serve both purposes," and the possibility arose of perceiving them as equal, the detailed explanation was provided to demonstrate the primacy of the determination of truth by stating that [the *vāda*] "is the cause of the determination of victory.
Otherwise, since the two fruits of the debate would already be understood through the word "both" (*ubhaya*), the explanation would be redundant.
Even by one who points out an exception to the grammatical rule *alpāctaram*, this very point has been indicated.
Otherwise, he would have stated that [the purpose] is "to determine victory.

Furthermore, the concealment of the members of the assembly (*sabhyas*) and others is for the sake of avoiding humiliation in the desire for victory; thus, this only reinforces the primacy of the debate itself.
Moreover, distinctions such as the difference in qualified participants (*adhikāribheda*) differentiate the types of discourse only as external factors.
The internal factor, however, is simply the mode of engagement;

and since that exists in this discourse only as something connected to debate, the intention is that "debate-ness" (vādatva) alone is primary. With this in mind, he says: "the proposition" (pratijñā).
Even the state of being established by mere assertion might occur, as in the case of Yājñavalkya.

In a discourse intended for the examination of knowledge, regarding any object of cognition, the state of being a thing to be proven (*sādhyatva*) would have to be made known by a mere proposition (*pratijñāmātra*), that is, by a statement devoid of the presentation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Why is this so? Because when Śākalya asked, "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? [the answer was given as follows].
Since Yājñavalkya has already provided the instruction by the mere statement "thirty-three," it is established—
by considering the context of the introduction— that this [subsequent] dialogue is for the purpose of examining his knowledge.
By the word "Yājñavalkya," his discourse is indicated;
the suffix -vati is used in the sense of the locative case.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "The dialogue."
In any debate between two disputants... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.48a]

For such a state of affairs can only exist when there is mutual trust in the reliability of the proponent and the opponent during their dialogue; for that trust is possible only in *vāda* (formal debate), not in *jalpa* (wrangling).
This is because one who desires victory must, by all means, employ valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) while avoiding fallacies such as deviating from one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
Therefore, this is indeed *vāda*.
"It is known.
[Objection: If that is the case, then an investigation of knowledge (*vidyā*) is not possible;
for such an investigation would occur only through the presentation of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), followed by its support or refutation.
But it is not by mere acceptance of the question and the proposition; therefore, he says: "In dispute."
...is accepted as the ground for a dispute. (Manu 2.48b)
The term "cause" (*hetu*) is an indicator for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in general,
or it may mean the cause of valid cognition.
The intended sense is that there is no rule stating that what is established in one instance must necessarily be established in all instances.
Yājñavalkya, too, has indeed provided authoritative citations on various occasions; thus, everything is consistent.

Regarding the desire to know the nature of the members of the court—the assessors (*sabhyas*), the presiding judge (*sabhāpati*), and the legal experts (*prāśnikas*)—who are the subject at hand, he says: "The court... (*sabheti*).
The assembly, the president of the assembly, and the assessors shall indeed be Vaiṣṇavas,
free from passion and hatred.
The two instances of the word "ca" (and) serve to conjoin the assembly halls and so forth with one another;
the third serves to conjoin the qualifiers.

The two words *eva* (only/indeed) are connected respectively with "the Vaiṣṇavas alone" and "those who are indeed devoid of passion and hatred. Otherwise, their purpose would be to indicate the impossibility of the narrative.
The word *syuḥ* (they may be), which is to be mentioned later, applies here as well.
It is connected [to the previous].
He states another qualification for the *sabhyas* and the *prāśnikas*: "they should be... and so forth.
... they shall be members of the assembly, all-knowing.
The assessors (*prāśnikas*)... [MAnu 2.1.50a].
By the word "all" (*sarva*), there is an inclusion of the observation of the plaintiff and defendant, as well as grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and other sciences useful for the discourse.
The repeated mention of the "members of the court" (*sabhyas*) and "assessors" (*prāśnikas*) is for the purpose of excluding the presiding judge (*sabhāpati*).
Because there is no utility in discussing that [alleged] omniscience;
the logical connection is that the members of the assembly and the judges would themselves have to be omniscient.
Now, one might ask: what is the utility of the judges?
We say that [the function of the members] is for the purpose of ascertaining the merits and defects of two parties in dispute.
If this is so, then those [disputants] alone should suffice; what is the need for the members? To this he says: "This... (etad).
... and if this is unknown, the members of the assembly [are also at fault]... // MAnu 2.1.50ab //
He refers to the aforementioned judges by the word "these" (ete).

The connection is with what will be stated later: when there is ignorance regarding another cause in some subtle object of knowledge, the members of the court (*sabhyas*) shall also be the authority for determining the merits and defects of the two disputants.
This is a metaphorical application of the term "authority" (*pramāṇa*) to those who are the locus of authority.

If, on these grounds, there is the selection of court members (*sabhyas*) due to the suspicion that the judges (*prāśnikas*) might be ignorant, then others must also be selected for those [members] due to the suspicion that they too might be ignorant;
otherwise, because there would be no final determination, the debate would result in futility.
Thinking that the same applies to those as well, he says: "And of these..."
And among these, those who are far removed [from the case] may serve as authorities for reaching a definitive decision.
And when these members of the assembly are ignorant, they are "far away," meaning situated in another country;
yet the concealment of the members is not useless for that reason,
because beyond that point, the suspicion of ignorance generally does not arise.
And because this matter is worldly,
he specifies "the thesis" (*pakṣa*) in order to establish that it is capable of being determined even from a distance.
... free from partiality. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.50d)
By mentioning one part [of the definition], he extends by analogy (*atideśa*) the previously stated characteristics of the *sabhyas* (court members) and so forth.

Since the definition of *vitaṇḍā* was stated as "without disclosing one's own tenet" (*aprakāśya svasiddhāntam*), how does this distinguish it from *vāda* and *jalpa*? To this, he says: "From both. (*ubhābhyām*) [5.521]
And by both [of these], there is indeed the establishment and the refutation in debate and wrangling.
In both formal debate (*vāda*) and contentious discussion (*jalpa*), both parties must establish their own position and refute the opponent's position;

it is not the case that the respondent fulfills his purpose merely by refuting the opponent's position. However, if the half-verse beginning with "only those who are virtuous" (*satām eva*) were inserted here:
The *vāda* and *jalpa* have been defined;
now, wishing to state the two definitions of *vitaṇḍā*, [the author] first states what is relevant: "By both," and so forth.
"Discourse" (kathā) is characterized by debate (vāda) and wrangling (jalpa).
By this, the over-extension [of the definition] of wrangling to cavil (vitaṇḍā)—which was mentioned in the statement "wrangling depends on the object and so forth"—is also avoided;
for discourse that depends on an object and so forth has been specified as being "possessing the means of proof for both sides" or "having a single subject matter."
To explain what was meant by the statement "only for the virtuous," he states the definition of *vitaṇḍā*: "But *vitaṇḍā*... and so forth.
The word "kathā" (discourse) carries over from the previous context.
Regarding what was stated by the phrase "by both," he states another definition of that: "not illuminating" (aprakāśya).
When they said, "As before," it was stated that "the proof is by means of both," and so forth. In that regard, what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) should be employed for the sake of proof?
Where something exists, it is indeed that very thing [which must be stated].
True.
But how is it in the case of the convergence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-samplava*)?
In response to the inquiry—"Is it all [the teachings] or only one, and even there, which one?"—he says: "by the virtuous" (sadbhiḥ).
The virtuous should employ only the traditional scripture (*āgama*) as the means for achieving their desired goal;
it is "only one," for there is no possibility of employing everything [at once], as that would lead to the undesirable consequence of excessive complexity.
And that [means] is indeed the traditional scripture—thus it should be construed.
Alternatively, the word "one" (*eka*) has its primary sense; thus,

with respect to objects of knowledge such as the Lord (*īśvara*), it must be stated that scripture (*āgama*) alone— such as the Vedas— is primary (because it functions independently as a factor for establishing what is to be proven),
and not inference (*anumāna*).

Now, one might object that for a non-Vedicist, the adoption of scriptures such as the Vedas would constitute an abandonment of one's own tenets (apasiddhānta); therefore, it was said: "by the virtuous" (sadbhiḥ).
To the question, "Whence comes the rule for the application of the Vedas and so forth? he says: "abhīṣṭya" (by means of what is desired).
The word "yataḥ" (since) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Indeed, inference is not intended as an independent means for proving God and so forth,
because in every case, both the presence of limiting conditions (upādhi) and counter-instances (pratipakṣa) are possible.
For that purpose, one must follow the traditional authority (āgama) even at the very end;
therefore, it is better to state the authority at the very beginning,
because it serves as an independent factor for the establishment of what is to be proven.
But how can this be done for one who is non-Vedic?
One must establish its authority by employing scripture (*āgama*).
What indeed should be said to those who are not [Vedic] adherents?
First of all, it is not perception,
because that is impossible regarding what is beyond the senses;
nor is it scripture.
Nor is there inference [as proof], because there is no mutual agreement on the validity of one's own or another's scriptures,
and because there is no agreement on the scope of logical application.
For instance,
if the Buddhist were to employ a syllogism consisting of two members, he would then be defeated by the Naiyāyika on the grounds of deficiency;
or, even if not defeated, the opponent would neglect him by failing to point out the required member.

However, if one employs more than five members, one would be defeated by the fault of excess; likewise, if one accepts [more], one would be defeated by the fault of contradicting one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
Furthermore, if there were a deviation from the fixed number of members and so forth, there would be no *vitaṇḍā* at all. Therefore, he says: "according to one's own tenet" (*svasiddhānta*).
For it is according to their own tenets that those who hold [erroneous views] infer what is non-existent.

The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is as follows: it must be stated according to one's established tenet (*siddhānta*), because prior to the formal regulation [of debate], the introduction of deficiencies and so forth occurs only in relation to the number of members of the syllogism determined by one's own tenet; otherwise, [such a debate] would be untenable.

It is not correct to say that "the scripture must be stated by the virtuous," because for a Vedic opponent, to refute it would constitute a departure from their own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), while to fail to refute it would result in the collapse of the debate due to the non-refutation of the opponent's position; therefore, he says: "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
But by relying on the incompatibility with perception and scripture, [the opponent's position] is shown to have a different meaning altogether.
In this case, the fault to be observed in the traditional scripture (āgama) is the inconsistency of gender.
But when a scripture has been adduced by the proponent, the Vedist opponent must demonstrate that it has a different meaning;
he should not, as in the case of inference, point out its lack of authority,
for that would constitute an abandonment of one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
For this very reason, one may also effect the refutation of the opponent's position;
for by demonstrating that the scripture has another meaning, it is shown to deviate from the meaning intended by the opponent.
Indeed, there is no refutation of a means of valid cognition other than its failure to establish the object required [by the proponent].
But if this is so, how can the debate reach a conclusion?
Since there would be no means for either party to grasp their own intended position or to cause the other to abandon theirs, it was therefore said: "Perception," and so forth.
In this regard, one should rely on the contradiction with perception and scripture concerning the opponent's intended meaning;
moreover, it is not merely this,
for here the fault of the reversal of indicators such as the introduction (*upakrama*) and so forth must also be demonstrated.
In this context, the intention applies to any one [of the factors] alone;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of redundancy. *5,527*

"But surely, even by this much, the discussion is not concluded; for the establishment of one's own intended object does not follow merely from the impossibility of the opponent's intended object. To this he says, "It is true," beginning with the word *liṅga*.
Conformity with the gender of the word and the favoring of the direct meaning by the direct statement (śruti) and the other means of proof.
The term "darśanīya" (visible/observable) follows [the previous context].
This is because *śruti* and the others—namely *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *samākhyā* as mentioned among the Vedas and so forth—are already included by the mention of *liṅga* alone.
Furthermore, this is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be understood that one must demonstrate the absence of both conformity with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the welfare of others and its opposition regarding one's own welfare.
The formulation of a statement for inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) must be carried out without exceeding the proper measure of the application of one’s own established tenets;
and when this is done, there is no room for defects such as deficiency (*nyūna*).
It has been stated that the very transgression of that [rule] constitutes its scope.
Another says:
one should apply [the rule] according to the actual state of affairs.

Nor should it be argued that because disputants disagree regarding the very nature of reality (*vastutattva*), there is a possibility of the introduction of deficiencies and so forth, which would result in the non-application [of the reason];

for when someone has the conviction that something is real, after they have employed it and another person points out a deficiency or similar fault, it must be proven that the thing indeed possesses that specific form (*tathārūpatā*).
Nor does this entail the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*).
[The opponent claims: "This is because, just as when one points out that a reason is unestablished for either party, there is a utility for the present context in demonstrating its establishment.
This is incorrect, because it has been established that all positions—whether consisting of two, three, five, or more members—are indeed real.
If one were to accept that each person’s own specific rule is the ultimate reality and admit its application without transgressing it, then all discourse would necessarily come to an end;
for when an opponent disputes the ultimate reality of such a rule, they must inevitably point out defects such as deficiency (*nyūna*) and so forth.
Now, it might be argued here: "One's own conceptualization of the constituent parts must simply be established against the opponent."
That was poorly stated, because it is impossible to justify it; thus he says: "three and five" (*tripañca*).
[This refers to] that which possesses exactly three or five members, even though it consists of an even number of members.

One might say to him who asserts that inference [occurs] by necessity: "If it is of such a nature, then why is it not called inference? In that case, on what basis could there be the conceptualization of parts within the object to be proven? (MAnu 2.1.54)
That which has three or five members—namely, the proposition, the reason, and the example;
or the example, the application, and the conclusion; or the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion—is called "that which has three or five members."
By the word *eva* (only/just), he states the restriction to two alternatives.
That which possesses the two members—the example (*udāharaṇa*) and the application (*upanaya*)—is "that which has two members" (*yugmāvayavinī*).
The word "by restriction" (*niyamāt*) is connected only with what is immediately adjacent [to it].

The term *anumeti* (it is inference) is used because it serves that purpose (*tādarthyāt*), for the Vaiśeṣikas and others employ the term in that very sense. The remainder of the sentence is: "one should state that [inference] if the opponent is an advocate of non-restricted [or indeterminate] doctrine."
Alternatively, it should be understood as follows: if a Mīmāṃsaka or a Tārkika and others were to assert that inference consists of exactly three or five members,
and a Buddhist were to assert to them that it consists of two members by way of a fixed rule,
[the former] might say, "If such [an inference] is not an inference consisting of three or five members," and so on.
The same applies even by way of reversal;
the remainder of the statement is that such [a thing] is not inferred because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is what is meant:
When a Naiyāyika has formulated an argument consisting of five members against a Saugata, the Saugata might rebuke him, saying, "This is redundant.
Thereupon, the Naiyāyika must state that this is not so, because the employment of the five-membered syllogism alone is the reality.
To this, the Saugata would surely reply, "This is not the truth, because it lacks valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
Then, when the Naiyāyika, asserting that [the opponent's position] lacks epistemic warrant (*aprāmāṇikatva*), asks the Saugata "How so?", [the latter replies:
"By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could one's own construction of the five-membered syllogism be established?
For it is not within its scope."
For the relation of cause and effect is never an object of direct perception, nor is it [known] through scripture,
because such scripture is absent.

If it is argued that there exists a statement in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts stating, "one who knows the merits and defects of a sentence consisting of five members [is a logician]," we say no; for in that very same context, it has been explained otherwise by such passages as, "subtlety, number, sequence, determination, and purpose."
Nor [is it established] by means of analogy or non-apprehension, because these have restricted objects; nor is it established by presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
Because of the absence of that [whole],
and because there is neither deficiency nor excess of the parts;
*5,531* let it be that the establishment of the conceptualization of parts does not occur through perception and other means of valid cognition.

If it is argued that inference will indeed occur because the cognition of a logical mark (liṅga) endowed with pervasion (vyāpti) and presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatā) follows the hearing of a five-membered syllogism and conforms to positive and negative concomitance— [we reply:
first of all, this inference revolving in your own mind is not a means for communicating [the truth] to another.
What indeed is being employed here?
In this regard, will a five-membered syllogism be prescribed for it, or rather a two-membered one?
He says "not even both" with the words "niyata" (fixed).
When the constituent parts [of a syllogism] are not established as necessary... // MAnu 2.1.57a //

The remainder of the argument is that since it has not been established that a syllogism with a fixed number of members— whether five members or two members— is conducive to understanding for the Buddhists and the Naiyāyikas respectively,
the postulation of such members is not established even by means of inference.
Alternatively, this is a restatement in the subsequent sentence of the phrase "because the members [of the syllogism] are not fixed";
from that, it follows that "because the members are not fixed," since the opponent has pointed out an excess [of members] in the employment of the five-membered syllogism.
The meaning is that when both members of the syllogism are employed, one must point out either the deficiency of one of them or a departure from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "By mere pervasion (*vyāpti*) alone is there proof. (*5,532*) ... [Proof] by means of mere pervasion.
He must certainly perform that very duty... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.1.57bc //
Since there is no other means [of proof] in this way, for that reason—
by that very logician, through mere pervasion (vyāpti) alone, namely by the mere statement of pervasion such as "whatever follows the presence and absence of another is its effect," and so forth.
This is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa).
It should also be understood that [the proof] must be formulated according to any one of the modes previously explained in the passage beginning with "liṅgoktau" (when the logical mark is stated),
which is the rule regarding the five-membered syllogism.
This [proof] ought to be performed.
The follower of the Sugata must also follow that [reasoning];
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even for him, the application [of the argument] would be untenable.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).
... therefore, that alone is considered inference. MAnu 2.1.57d.

Because the establishment of the extent of the formal argument (prayoga) is only possible when either the proponent or the opponent abandons their own view and accepts the view of the other— and not otherwise—
therefore, that very [acceptance] is considered inference (anumā).
In all cases, it should be understood that the statement of pervasion (vyāpti) and so forth alone constitutes the formal argument for the sake of others (parārthaprayoga).
This is what is meant:
when a Naiyāyika establishes the restriction of five members by means of two members,
does he himself consider those two members to be ultimately real, or not?
If the latter position is taken, he would be a deceiver;
if the former, why would that [logical structure] not also apply elsewhere?

Thus, even the Buddhist, fearing the consequence of the absence of discourse, must consider whether he regards as "truth" the necessity of two members [of a syllogism] within a five-membered one, or not.
In the second case, how could one proceed from that?

In the first case, why would it not be so even elsewhere? Therefore, since all types of established tenets are ultimately real, it is appropriate [to proceed] according to one's own established tenet.

Fearing this very predicament, Udayana stated that one must speak according to the facts, or else one must speak according to one's own established tenets; having thus established a rule, he declared that once the debate has commenced, there shall be no introduction of deficiencies or other such faults—this is another position he asserted. Thus, the section on inference is concluded. *5,535*
Scripture is a statement that is free from fault.
It is of two kinds: human and non-human.

In this context, the Veda is authorless (*apauruṣeya*), while other [scriptures] are authored (*pauruṣeya*); this is not explicitly stated here because it is well known. Some, however, maintain that a sentence is an inference regarding the meaning of the sentence.
That is untenable,
because there is no positive or negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) between a sentence and its meaning, whether in terms of space or time.
If it is argued that "this sentence possesses its meaning because it is a sentence," [that remains unproven].
In this regard, is it merely the sentence-meaning that is being established, or its specific qualification?
It cannot be the former, because it would follow that the cognition of the specific qualification would be without a basis.
Regarding the second [alternative], is that specific qualification perceived or not?
In the first case, the statement is redundant;
in the second case, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*).
Furthermore, because the specific property (*viśeṣa*) does not exist elsewhere, there is also the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntya*).
And what is the meaning of the possessive suffix *matup*: is it the relationship between the signified and the signifier, or some other type of relation?
In the first case, it would be either as a direct mark (*liṅga*) or [otherwise].
It is not the first,
because inference would be redundant.
Furthermore, it would involve an abandonment of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

In the second case, however, this is not an inference of the sentence-meaning; rather, it is simply an inference of the sentence’s status as a logical mark (*liṅga*) with respect to an already established object.
And in that case, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is deficient in the probandum (*sādhya*) for at least one of the two parties.
Not the second [alternative],
because it is sublated by the absence of that [nature].
Now, if it is formulated in this way:
"The words under dispute are preceded by a cognition of the connection with the meanings they respectively recall, because they constitute a collection of words possessing expectancy and so forth.
This is incorrect;
for there is an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntya*) even in the absence of a cognition of connection, in the case of words possessing expectancy and so forth that happen to be uttered by chance.

If the reason is qualified by being "employed by a reliable person" (*āptaprayuktatva*), it would entail the fallacy of the probandum (the property to be proven) entering into the meaning of the reason itself; furthermore,
since being employed by a specific person is found to deviate in the case of texts taught by mere instructors,
such a qualification is untenable even when inferring a foundational authority for the Vedas.
This is because its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) has already been established.
Others, however, while accepting that scripture (*āgama*) is non-human in origin, maintain that what is of human origin is subject to inference (*anumāna*).
For them, however, there is a manifest contradiction regarding the Veda.
Furthermore, words possess the power to denote their meanings as already connected; moreover, the sentence is nothing other than the words themselves;
and there are no worldly words that are distinct from Vedic words.
But the speaker is required only for the cognition of the words;
so how could there be a difference in the manner [of usage] between the worldly and the Vedic?
Furthermore, how [could this be explained] in the case of worldly sentences being recited in accordance with the Veda?
The cognition of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) certainly arises;
what then is removed by the knowledge that [the Veda] is of human origin?
If that is the case, then the knowledge of the sentence-meaning arises from the sentence itself.
However, it follows that one must rely on the speaker and other factors in order to ascertain its validity; let this suffice for now.
Thus, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have been defined both generally and specifically.
In this regard, by establishing our own general definition, the general definitions stated by other proponents are effectively refuted by implication.
Nevertheless, because there remains a specific point to be addressed regarding the object of memory, he specifically refutes the Prābhākara definition with the words: "anubhūtiḥ" (perception).
If direct experience is the means of valid cognition, by what is memory sublated?

“Then it must be asked: ‘Is memory a valid means of knowledge (pramā) or not? In the first case, the consequence is ‘contradiction of one’s own tenet’ (apasiddhānta); this is the remainder [of the argument].
Regarding the second case, he says: “By what? (keneti).
If memory is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*), then memory must be excluded by the definition;
otherwise, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Why, then, is memory set aside and excluded?
Memory is not anything that excludes [the definition];
that is to say, it is not present in the definition.
[Objection: But surely, by stating "experience" (anubhūti), there is already no over-extension to memory.
This is because it is stated that cognition distinct from memory is "experience" (anubhūti);
for memory cannot be something other than memory.
This is not so.
Because it is possible for one memory to be distinct from another memory, [the term "memory"] cannot serve as a differentiator.
If you argue that "experience" (anubhūti) is a cognition that does not have "memory-ness" (smṛtitva) as its locus,
then what is this "memory-ness"?
First of all, it is not a genus (jāti),
because genus is not admitted in the case of qualities (guṇa).
Nor is it possible for it to be the state of being a cognition produced solely by mental impressions (saṃskāra).
Because it is produced by unseen factors (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth;
and even when there is an intention to specify the uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*), the same applies,
since it will be stated later that memory is mental in nature (*mānasatva*).

By this same rule, it should be understood that "the state of being a fresh experience produced by a unique present cause" is also a defining characteristic [of perception], because even memory—which is produced by mental perception—is likewise [an experience]. Furthermore, although the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is a cause, it does not produce memory by its mere existence; rather, it produces it only when it has been awakened.

And thus, how could it not be produced by its own specific, presently existing causes? Otherwise, one might as well deny that even experience, which arises based merely on the sense organs and so forth, is produced by such causes.
Furthermore, it is indeed possible for some memory (*smṛti*) to be produced by a presently existing mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
Moreover, a restriction cannot be known without a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).
Alternatively, if experience (*anubhūti*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the [definition] does not extend to memory; this is the remainder of the sense.
Now, one might object: "Memory is not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) at all; so how can there be the fault of non-pervasion (avyāpti) in that case? To this, he says: "By what? (keneti).
The meaning is that memory is not set aside or excluded from the category of valid cognition by any cause whatsoever.
To explain: is it because it is non-conformable with reality?

Whether it be because, despite being in accordance with reality, it lacks the nature of experience; or because, despite lacking invalidating factors, there is no proof for its validity; or because, despite having proof for its validity, there exist invalidating factors—he refutes the first [alternative] with the words "by what? (keneti).

By what powerful means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is memory sublated (*apodyate*) or contradicted (*bādhyate*), such that it would not be in accordance with reality? Since there is no sublater, one must not claim that memory is non-conformable to reality.
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "By what? (keneti).

Is it on the grounds that "being an experience" (*anubhūtitva*) is the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and thus memory (*smṛti*) is called invalid because it lacks the nature of experience, or rather by relying on examples such as a jar?
In the first case, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*).
And if so, by what means would memory be set aside?
In the second case as well, what is it that subverts memory itself?
Why is experience not subverted by its being non-memory, since there is no distinction [between the two]? He refutes the third [position] with the words "pūrva... (the former...).
If it is asked, "What is the means of knowledge regarding what was previously experienced? what would be the answer?
If memory were not a means of valid cognition (apramāṇa), then the question "What is the means of knowledge regarding what was previously experienced? would be without answer;
for there exists no means of valid cognition other than memory to establish that.
And in that case, worldly transactions such as those involving witnesses would be subverted.
If it is argued that Smṛti alone is the means of valid knowledge, but only by way of being an inferential mark (liṅga), we say no;
for there is an absence of such experience.
Otherwise, one might as well claim that there is an inference of a jar (and so forth) from its direct perception, its effect, or its status as an object of action (*karmakāraka*).
He states the fourth [alternative] with the words "pūrva" (the former).
Indeed, one should simply say "recollection" (*smṛti*).
The meaning is that since experience is inferred from the verbal report, worldly convention itself is the authority (*pramāṇa*) in this matter.
