Now, if recollection were a valid cognition (*pramā*), it would follow as an undesirable consequence that its cause—the mental impression (*saṃskāra*)—would also be a valid means of knowledge (*anupramāṇatva*).
In that case, the threefold nature of valid cognition (anumāna) would be undermined;

for mental impression (saṃskāra) is not included within perception (pratyakṣa) and the other means of knowledge, because it does not involve sense-object contact and because its instrument is unknown. Thus, he refutes the fifth [type of cognition] by stating "mental" (mānasa).
For that consciousness is indeed mental.

For since that recollection is mental (*mānasa*) and arises from mental perception (*manah-pratyakṣa*), it does not have the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) as its instrument; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply—this is the remainder of the argument.
Since it is not of the nature of direct perception (*asākṣātkāra-rūpatva*), it cannot be the fruit of perception; hence it is stated: "cognition" (*vijñāna*).
The meaning is "direct perception.
To the question, "How can recollection possess both the nature of being mental and the nature of direct perception? he says: "And that..."
... and that is based on the authority of witnesses. (Manu 2.59b)
The word "that" (tat) refers to its being mental;
by the word "and" (ca), its being direct perception is also included.
Alternatively, both [properties] are referred to by the word "that."
The word "ca" (and) serves to connect with the current context.

Now, one might object: since there is a rule that the sense organs function only by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*), and since it is impossible for the mind to reach a past object, how can memory be said to arise from mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*)? To this, he says: "atīta... [past].
Just as the past and the future are perceived directly by yogis,
so too is that which was previously experienced understood by the mind alone.
There indeed exist yogins endowed with supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and others, who perceive the past and the future, and who are well-known from the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Itihāsa*, and *Purāṇa*.
This is because it has been established that the *Śruti* and other sources possess authority regarding matters already accomplished (*siddhārtha*),
and because the injunctions concerning yoga share the same status and security as the injunctions concerning ritual action (*karma*).
Nor is that knowledge non-perceptual, because its status as direct perception (*sākṣātkāratva*) is understood through scripture and other means.
For instance, the Śruti says: "O Viśvakarman, with pure vision, I beheld this world placed within you by your creative power (*māyā*) at the beginning."
And the Purāṇa says, "By the grace of Nārāyaṇa," and so forth;
the Itihāsa also says, "I give you divine vision," and so forth.
This very point has been stated by the word "directly" (añjasā).
The meaning is "directly.

And thus, just as for yogins there is a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of past and future objects by means of the sense-faculties themselves, so too there is recollection of the past by means of the mind; what fault is there in this?
Now, it is not a fixed rule that the "attainment" (*prāpti*) of an object by a sense-faculty must be either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*).
But it is merely proximity;
and that [proximity] exists for the sense faculties of those yogins, characterized by being assisted by the specific dharma born of yoga which reveals each respective object. If this is argued:

If that is the case, then even for the mind there exists a proximity with a past object, characterized by the assistance of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by prior experience; it is with this intention that it was said: "and what was previously experienced.
This is what is meant:
if "attainment" (*prāpti*) is intended to mean something characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, then its absence [in the case of the mind] would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

However, if one intends to express mere proximity, then [the reason] is unestablished (asiddhi). The statement of the example, moreover, is intended to suggest that mere proximity can be the cause of direct perception,
and to show that this conceptual construction— based on the observation of the effect— is not subject to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
By this, the objection that if memory were mental it would arise even with respect to what has not been experienced—since it would not be born from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—is refuted;
for the latent impression is accepted as functioning in the place of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*). *5,557*
He demonstrates by means of a gesture that which was stated—that the mental nature of memory is established by the Witness—by saying: "It is known."
"Even this [act] previously cognized by the mind as 'this was done by me' is established through direct experience. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.60a–c)

"This was done by me previously"—this is known by the mind and is also remembered as "I remember. Thus, the fact that remembrance is mental is established by direct experience, specifically through the experience of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).

As for what has been stated by others—that remembrance, which has as its object an entity delimited by a previous experience, does not itself correspond to reality even while conforming to the truthfulness of that [original] experience—that is incorrect.

It has been stated, "I have done this," in order to show that the fact of having a pure object as its content—just like [the content of] experience—is also established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).
Now, one might object: since the mind (*manas*) is not itself perceptible, how can the fact that memory is mental be known through the perception of the witness?
This is not so, because it will be explained later that the mind is indeed cognizable by the witness.

If it is argued that, nevertheless, the relation of cause and effect is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), we reply: no, because the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), assisted by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), is admitted to have authority in that regard.
If it is argued that cognition is always to be inferred, we say no, because the state of being known (*jñātatā*) will be refuted later.
If it is argued that [consciousness] is self-luminous, we say no; because it would follow that it is not a substance, like a jar.
With the intention of refuting its being cognizable by the mind, he says: "How indeed?"
"...how indeed could it be set aside?
[He states] the application of what was said starting with "yāthārthyam eva" (the state of being exactly as it is) to the subject at hand: "evam" (thus).
Thus, regarding the three means of knowledge characterized in this way, with respect to entities such as Brahman and the rest, the Veda alone is the authority.

Since the three means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) possess such characteristics, the Veda alone is the authority regarding entities such as Brahmā; there is no room for reasoning (*yukti*) or other means therein.
For the sense organ operates only with respect to substances possessing form and so forth, and Brahmā and the like are not of that nature.
Furthermore, inference depends upon pervasion (*vyāpti*);
and for that [inference] which is independent of the Veda, there is no application to Brahman and so forth,
because pervasion cannot be ascertained due to the possibility of both adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) and counter-examples (*pratipakṣa*) existing everywhere.

However, in the case of following the Vedas, it is necessary that [the reason] be either non-pervasive of the probandum (*sādhyāvyāpaka*) or have a sublated object (*bādhitaviṣaya*). Since human scripture (*pauruṣeyāgama*) is entirely dependent on other factors,
he says "and its validity" (*tatprāmāṇyam ca*) to explain what follows from this.
And its authority has been established. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.61d)

Therefore, since there is no scope for reasoning within the domain of the Veda, it is logically consistent that the contradiction [of the Veda] has been stated as being precisely that [lack of scope].
Thus, because the Veda is free from contradiction with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its authority has been established.
As was stated previously: "Therefore, the authority of the Veda is accepted."
Thus, the meaning is that this has been established.
Thus ends the section on "Not Being of a Different Character" (*na vilakṣaṇatva*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
[======= JNys_2,1.III: Section on the Possessor of Pride (Abhimāny-adhikaraṇa) =======] *6,1* // Now begins the fourth part of the illustrious Nyāyasudhā: (The Section on the Possessor of Pride).
// Oṃ. But there is a designation based on the presiding deity, because of specific distinction and common usage. Oṃ.//
This [section] is commenced in order to resolve the contradiction of the Veda with other logical arguments.
It might be argued: "Should these contradictions with logic be resolved individually?"
[This is] by way of an illustration.
It is not the first [alternative],
because it would entail the consequence that the treatise could never reach completion due to the infinity of fallacious arguments to be refuted.
Furthermore, it would contradict its status as a *sūtra*.
In the second case, however, there would be no commencement of this section at all;
for by the very preceding section on "immediately past," all contradictions with reason have already been resolved through implication (*upalakṣaṇā*).
"Not so;
since that [objection] is possible due to the existence of a suspicion of something additional, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), intending this, first states: 'Even so...'"
"But there is a designation based on the presiding deity, due to distinction and conformity.

(BBs 2.1.5) "Nevertheless, since [terms like] 'clay' or 'water' denote the intellect, speech, and so forth, how could they be authoritative in that regard? For it would contradict observed pervasion. (MAnu 2.1.62)
The meaning is: "even though," although the contradiction regarding the Vedas' failure to produce results and so forth has been resolved;
by the phrase "of clay, water, etc.," the word "etc. includes fire and the rest;
"buddhi" means cognition.
"Speech" refers to the faculty of speaking;
by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," the faculty of hearing and so forth are also intended.
The term "knows" (veda) is understood to carry over from the previous context.
That reasoning for which the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been seen and ascertained is described as such.
The mention of "grasping the pervasion" is also an indicator for the property of being present in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
In some cases, because that [presence in the subject] is not accepted as a necessary rule, it is not explicitly mentioned by its own name.
Because it is contradictory with that;
in this regard, [the question] "how" is used as an objection concerning clay, water, and so forth, in relation to the intellect, speech, and the rest.
The remainder [of the argument] is that there is no other thing to be established, because it is not perceived.
This is what is meant:
"The earth spoke," [and so forth].
The waters said; that fire reflected; those waters reflected.
"Listen, O pressing-stones,
you who breathe after the wise;
we have disputed over what is better."
The Veda beginning with "The waters, indeed, desired" is not an authoritative means of knowledge,
because it expresses matters that contradict reason.
It is like the expression "the blue sky.
Indeed, the meaning of this [statement] is that earth, water, and so forth possess intellect, speech, and the like;
however, that [meaning] is contradicted by such reasoning as: "The subject under dispute is not a speaker, because it is earth, like earth that is commonly acknowledged [to be non-speaking]."
And thus, lack of authority would be inferred even in other Vedic statements.
[Objection: But surely this contradiction too should be resolved by the very same reasoning expressed in the sūtra, "Not so, because of the difference in nature" (BrSū 2.1.4).
Not so;
for that [reasoning] does not fall within the scope of the application of that logic.

For in that case, even if the practice is performed as described, if there is a deviation regarding the result, then, at first glance, the reason is unestablished due to a doubtful qualification (*sandigdhaviśeṣaṇāsiddhi*).

Since defects in the agent and other factors are also possible, if the authority of the Veda is established on the basis of its eternality, there is simply the certainty that the qualifying attribute is unestablished (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*).

However, if the mere deviation from the result were taken as the reason, it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); thus, by demonstrating the absence of both pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), the contradiction with reasoning (*yuktivirodha*) is avoided.
Nor is this reasoning connected with a deficiency in its constituent parts, such as the lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*),
because it is observed to be so in the case of well-known examples like clay;
yet even there, the presence of consciousness (*buddhi*) and so forth does not exist.

Nor is it the case that [the reason] is deviant even though it is connected [to the probandum], because no deviation is observed. This is because the effect of that [probandum] is never seen [in the absence of the reason]. Because we observe the activity of non-agency;

Therefore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of earthiness and other such properties by non-speakerness and the like is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends concomitance, which is supported by favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) and assisted by the non-observation of the deviation of the limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Nor is it logical to claim that the nature of clay and so forth does not exist in things such as clay; for that would involve a contradiction.
And because of such usages as "the clay spoke" (*mṛd abravīt*), the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is also established.
Now, one might object: once the authority of the Veda is established by its eternity, it is only logical that reasoning which contradicts it should itself lack authority.
Not so;

for even reasoning endowed with pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) would find no scope [in this case]. Consequently, because it lacks the power of ascertainment due to being counterbalanced by an opposing argument (*satpratipakṣatā*), the Veda would lack authority.

Is it not the case that if well-known clay and so forth are taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) and an absence of distinction between the subject and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)? And if another similar instance is admitted, then the property of being clay and so forth would be absent from it.
If, however, insentience (*jaḍatva*) were made the reason (*hetu*), there would be the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*).
Therefore, clay and so forth existing from the beginningless past must be taken as the subject (*pakṣa*).
And since that is not established by perception or other means of knowledge, the Veda alone is to be relied upon.

If it is argued that, therefore, the reasoning (yukti) lacks validity because it contradicts the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (dharmigrāhakapramāṇa), we say no; for such a contradiction is impossible in the case of a reasoning endowed with universal concomitance (vyāpti) and other necessary factors.
This is because the apprehension of the subject is established by another scriptural statement concerning the nature of primordial clay and so forth, together with the visible mark of the effect.

By this, the argument that there is no scope for reasoning regarding Vedic matters and therefore reasoning cannot contradict them is refuted. Thus, if Vedic statements such as "The clay spoke" are invalid because they contradict reasoning, then other Vedic statements such as "From which indeed these [beings arise]" would also be invalid due to their being part of the Veda; consequently, the status of Brahman as the cause of the world could not be established through the systematic coherence (*samanvaya*) of the Vedas. *6,13*
He states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "From that" (tataḥ).

By the phrase "in contradiction with reason and scripture," he indicates an *arthāpatti* (presumption).

"In the third case, that [effort] would be futile, because it is possible for it to operate in another location just like a region not presided over by it.

Regarding those who possess such conceit (*abhimānin*), since their being localized (*prādeśikatva*) and being bodiless (*videhatva*) would result in the impossibility of speaking and so forth, and since their being pervasive (*vyāptānām*) while possessing bodies would be contradicted by non-perception (*anupalambha-bādha*), the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "by specific [perception] and following [the general rule]" (*viśeṣānugatibhyām*) has been explained by some others as having the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of providing a refutation of these [objections]. *6,23*

... their power is said to be especially superior to that of others. // MDh 2.1.65ab //
"Specifically" means "with excellence. The connection is that "pervasion is also stated" [to be superior] to others such as ourselves.

Nevertheless, by following the rule that the word with fewer syllables should be placed first (*alpāctara-pūrvanipāta*), the author has followed the established grammatical sūtra, even though this breaks the logical sequence.

This contradiction would arise if power and pervasion were here asserted to be unlimited;

This is because it is accepted that the capacity for invisibility and so forth, as well as the pervasion of desired objects, are to be established in accordance with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, having accepted the non-perception of those who possess such pride from our own perspective, the objection based on that [non-perception] has been refuted.

This is established both through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) and through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). having said this, he will further address those who are mistaken even regarding that point by saying, “and also the world.

Furthermore, its application is not found in that which is merely insentient;

And it is not possible for that [Veda] to be devoid of composition; enough [of this].
[Objection: Even so, the lack of authority characterized by non-cognitiveness in the Veda—such as in the passage "the clay spoke"—is difficult to avoid.
For instance:

Although words that constitute a sentence convey the meaning of the sentence— which is an unprecedented (*apūrva*) specific mutual relation of word-meanings— even so, they depend upon a linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) characterized by the comprehension of the relationship between signifier and signified (*vācya-vācakabhāva*) among those word-meanings, since this is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

But that is not the case.
However, it is precisely the substratum (*dharmin*) that possesses the status of being negated, and not through the medium of its property (*dharma*).
And this [status] certainly exists for both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*),
because although these two possess the status of being affirmed through the medium of their properties, the status of the two substrata being negated is established for both parties.
And it is excluded from the dissimilar class, such as the potter;
for although that [exclusion] is a negation in terms of its property (*dharma*), the substratum (*dharmin*) is affirmed.
"Not because it is not a negation.
Now, how is this obtained?
It is said:
For the word *mātra* signifies totality (*sākalya*),
and that is not possible in any instance; moreover, the opponent himself has stated that even in a negation, there exists a positive injunction.
Consequently, the word "mere negation" indicates the non-priority of the positive injunction, just as the expression "only rice was eaten" [indicates that other foods were not].
And this applies to both the property and the substratum.
The property (dharma) is subordinate, while the substratum (dharmin) is primary;
therefore, it is established that the negation belongs to the substratum, and its nature is that of a mere negation.

It has been stated that because the intellect (*buddhi*), which pervades activity (*pravṛtti*)—which consists of desire, effort, and so forth, and is synonymous with agency—is absent [in the insentient], it excludes that [activity] as well.
To the question, "In that case, why is there an exclusion of the intellect precisely due to its absence? he says: "The intellect... (*buddhi...*).
... that is indeed a lack of intelligence. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.1.73d)
Therefore, the meaning is that because it is a mere negation, the non-existence of cognition is established just like the non-existence of a jar.
For the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is of two kinds: independent (*svatantra*) and dependent (*paratantra*).
The dependent is also of two kinds: existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*).
Existence, too, is twofold: conscious and unconscious.
And thus, when even some form of existence lacks consciousness, what can be said of consciousness in its absence?
If it is argued that some non-entity might be intelligent, we say no;
for, disregarding an essential (nirupādhika) relation, a groundless suspicion leads to over-extension (atiprasaṅga). [As it is said:
"It made that mind."

If it is argued that this is so because of the Vedic scripture, we say no; for [the scripture] is established otherwise. Furthermore, one would not even accept the status of being a mere negation in the case under consideration.
The designations "that is non-existent" and "Brahman" are merely differences in terminology;
for even the opponent must relinquish [the notion of] multiplicity and so forth,
since the arising of an effect is impossible if there were multiple independent [causes].
Should this not have been stated right there?
True;
[it was intended as] a negation.

This is stated here because, once mere-ness (*mātratva*) is known, it is easy to realize the absence of cognition (*buddhi*). However, the commentator says that this is stated here because there would otherwise be room for the objection: "If positive properties such as knowability (*prameyatva*) are admitted, why should cognition not also be [admitted] in that same way? [Verse 6.80:
The absence of a thing is its property.

Furthermore, it is untenable that even the existence of non-existence is a property (*dharma*) [of things]. (It is untenable that existence has non-existence as its property, and that non-existence has existence as its property.
This is because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for existence and non-existence to possess the properties of non-existence and existence respectively.
And because there is an absence of a relationship:

for it is only between two related things, such as whiteness and a cloth, that the status of property and property-possessor is observed, not between unrelated things like the Maru desert and Mount Mandara;
and no relationship exists between existence and non-existence.
Because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) are restricted to existing entities,
and because they possess contradictory natures;
for it is only when quality (*guṇa*) and possessor of quality (*guṇin*) possess non-contradictory natures that they are perceived as property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*).
A horse and a buffalo do not possess contradictory natures;
yet existence and non-existence do possess contradictory natures,
because they consist of affirmation and negation.
And because there is no difference [between them]:
for a jar cannot be its own property.
And since it has been stated that the property and the substratum are one, he says: "It is merely the state of being qualified."
The state of being a subject (dharmin) consists precisely in being that which is qualified... // MAnu 2.1.74a //

It should also be understood that being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is itself the state of being a property (*dharmitva*). For that which is qualified— that is, that which is distinguished or excluded— is the substratum (*dharmī*) of that [property], while the other is the property (*dharma*).
Because no other alternative can be defined,
and yet the relationship between qualifier and qualified is perceived between existence and non-existence;
otherwise, such linguistic usages as "a jar is not a cloth" and "non-existence is an object of cognition" would be untenable.
Therefore, how could there not be a relationship of property and property-bearer between existence and non-existence?
Furthermore, the relationship of property and property-bearer between a cloth and whiteness is not caused by a [physical] connection;
nor is the absence of that relationship between Mount Meru and Mount Mandara caused by the absence of a connection.
However, it consists in the absence of that [relation] precisely by virtue of its own nature (*svabhāva*), because of the relationship between the qualified and the qualifier;
for even in the case of a jar and a cloth which are related, that absence exists, whereas in the case of the ground and the absence of a jar, that [relation] exists. (6.82)
In this very way, the non-difference between contradictory natures is also refuted;

for we observe that even though the quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) possess contradictory natures—either by virtue of being with-qualities and without-qualities, or by virtue of being eternal and non-eternal—they nonetheless share the common property of being "cloth" (*paṭatva*). Conversely, we do not observe such a commonality between "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*) and "whiteness" (*śauklya*).
Moreover, that state [of identity] is observed even in the case of non-difference,
because others accept that properties such as existence and nameability are non-different from the substratum.
Furthermore, that state is not perceived even among things that are distinct.

Thus, even though existence and non-existence are unrelated and possess distinct intrinsic natures, their relationship as subject and attribute— characterized by the state of a substratum (dharmin) and its property (dharma)— is indeed logical due to a specific causal capacity (*viśeṣa-śakti*), despite their non-difference. If this were the case, such that non-existence and existence were the attributes of a single substratum and there were no difference between the property and its substratum,
then existence would also be non-existence, and non-existence would be existence.

The restriction that things such as jars possess only positive existence (bhāvatva), while prior non-existence, posterior non-existence, and absolute non-existence possess only negative existence (abhāvatva), would be without foundation.
Nor should it be said, "Let it be so," for that which is established by the consensus of all the world cannot be otherwise; therefore, he says: "First... [and so forth].
In these initial practices,
the nature of both affirmation and negation consists here in the existence and non-existence [of the object].
The word "form" (rūpa) denotes the substratum (dharmin).
The phrase "the state of being existence and non-existence" is to be connected as appropriate.
This being so, even in this case:
The word "hi" indicates what is well-known.
This is the meaning:
is it the nature of the object of cognition that is being sought as the basis for existence and non-existence, or is it the means of valid cognition?
The latter half of the first [verse] provides the answer:
although jars and the like consist of both existence and non-existence, as do prior non-existence and the other types of non-existence,

nevertheless, within this collection of categories (*padārtha-sārtha*), that which is a concrete entity (*piṇḍa*) characterized by affirmation (*vidhi-dharmika*), such as a jar, is "existence" (*bhāva*).
As for that which is characterized by negation, such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the like, its status as "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is logically established.

It has already been stated that even when there is no difference [between the entity and its absence], the relationship of property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) is consistent through a specific capacity (*viśeṣaśakti*).
The response to the second [objection] is: "in the first cognitions."
That which is first perceived as a positive affirmation (*vidhi*) without having the nature of excluding another is an entity (*bhāva*), such as a jar.

However, that which is perceived as a negation (*niṣedha*) by way of excluding another, such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, is a non-entity (*abhāva*). This is to be construed as a single syntactical unit with the second half of the verse.

For a jar is first perceived as a positive affirmation in the form of a substratum (*dharmin*), and subsequently it is perceived as having the nature of the negation of a cloth, in the form "it is not a cloth."

He indicates by means of the plural number and the word "hi" that it is established for all cognizers that even antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the like are first understood as a negation— that is, as the very nature of the locus— and are subsequently understood as the object of cognition (*prameya*) in a positive sense.
The use of the locative case is intended to express the relationship of locus and located between the subject and the object,
since it is established that among the grammatical factors (*kārakas*), there is no intention to distinguish between the primary and the secondary.

Thus, the contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been demonstrated regarding the meaning obtained from the collection of proofs imagined by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).

Now, wishing to specifically refute the inference that "the effect is non-existent [prior to its production] as it is observed [in the world]," the author of the Sūtras introduced the following aphorism by way of introduction: "Oṃ, [this view is] inconsistent because of the consequence that [the cause] would be like that [effect] at the time of dissolution.
This doctrine—that the universe has a non-existent entity as its creator—is inconsistent.
Why?

Even if one were to accept that non-existence (*abhāva*) itself is the creator of the world, it would follow— upon dissolution or pralaya— that [the world] would likewise become non-existent; for everything, including God and so forth, would then possess the nature of non-existence.
This means that it would entail the undesirable consequence of having to accept the existence of [other] entities.
For, while God and the like exist, it is impossible to determine that non-existence (abhāva) is the creator of the world by setting them aside.
Now, one might object: we do not accept this; for God and the like must be non-existent during the dissolution (pralaya).

Regarding the argument that because [the world] possesses existence it must be like a jar, and thus one accepts the non-existence of everything—including Īśvara and so forth—at the time of dissolution, the author of the Sūtras has stated: "But not so, because of the existence of examples.
It is not at all appropriate to accept the non-existence of everything at the time of dissolution.
Why? Because of the existence of examples.
Regarding the term "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*), it refers here to inference based on a pervasion (*vyāpti*) that has been ascertained therein;
for a mere example is not a constituent part of either proving or refuting.
And thus, [regarding] the existence of the Supreme Lord and so forth at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*).
The meaning is that it is possible through the inference of the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
To the question "What is that inference?", the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) says: "Even in the case of the destruction of all [things]... (BBs 2.1.8):
"Because of the consequence that [the world] would be like that [Brahman] at the time of reabsorption (*apīti*), [the doctrine] is inconsistent. (*asamañjasam*)

Since he always remains as a survivor even when all else is destroyed, this destruction, though it may seem otherwise, must leave a survivor as its agent, because it is a destruction [of something]. (Manu 2.1.75)
The particle *api* is used in the sense of pervasion (*abhivyāpti*).
Since the word "all" (*sarva*) might otherwise be intended to refer only to the present time, the term "always" (*sadā*) is stated;
this is mentioned in order to avoid the charge of inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*).
"Of us" refers to the person (*puruṣa*).
"This very one" is explained as "the subject of dispute" (*vimata*).
Here, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is stated by the first half-verse.
By the second half [of the verse], the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) are stated.
This is what is meant:
the destruction characterized by the great dissolution must possess a residual person (*puruṣaśeṣavat*), because it is a destruction, like that which is commonly accepted (*sammata*).
Regarding the phrase "like destruction":
here, what is to be proven is merely the persistence of the person (puruṣa) alone;
it is not, however, the persistence of the person who is the agent of destruction.
For this very reason it was said, "of whomever";
the meaning is: "whether of the agent of destruction or of one who is not the agent.
Nevertheless, by saying "possessing the remainder of the agent," this is what is intended.

Since the dissolution [of the world] is established as consisting merely of the existence of the Puruṣa, the opponent's inference is already refuted. Furthermore, the opponent's position that the world is produced by a non-existent agent is likewise discarded for this very reason.
Since the status of being the creator of the universe is possible for a specific person who remains [as a viable candidate], there is no occasion for postulating an absence [of such a person];
for a postulation must follow what is observed.

For in the world, it is not observed that prior to its production, the non-existence of the potter and other such factors is the maker of the jar; rather, it is the potter himself who is so. Not understanding this intention, one who holds the view that the agent is a residual entity (*kartṛśeṣavān*) speaks and, being deluded, objects: "In a case where, by the logic of Sunda and Upasunda, all persons have perished, the reason 'being a cause of destruction' is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*)."
To this, he says: "And not... (naceti).
Moreover, the destruction of all men has never been seen, nor is it observed anywhere.
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis.
Since the destruction of all men has never been seen anywhere, there is a negation of what is past; and since it is not seen [now], there is a negation of what is future.
"Or else, that which is being seen does not exist at all"—this refers to the present.
What is meant is this:
for "inconclusiveness" (anaikāntikatva) must be asserted when the reason (hetu) is present in a proven counter-example (vipakṣa).
It is not unmeasured;
for if that were so, it would follow that the mere measure of non-measure itself is annihilated.
Furthermore, the destruction of all persons across the three periods of time has never been measured.
Otherwise, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the property of perishability in that case.
Furthermore, if its being known (*pramitatva*) is admitted, then since only the knower (*pramātṛ*) remains, there would be a contradiction (*vyāghāta*).
Nor is it intended that the person who is the agent of destruction remains as the probandum (*sādhya*).
It is not by means of [the example of] Sunda and Upasunda and others that [the point] would be countered;
rather, it is merely the state of being a particular person (*puruṣaviśeṣavatva*). (6.97)
By this, the following inference is also indicated: "The time of dissolution possesses a Puruṣa, because it is time, just like the present time.
Nor is there a fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) due to the absence of time at that point; for if that were the case, it would be impossible even to say "at that time" (*tadā*).
Furthermore, in the opponent's inference, the qualification "at the time of dissolution" (pralaya) is untenable. Even if one were to ask here: "Is time admitted [as a locus] or not?
In the first case, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) of the reason 'being an entity' (bhāvatva) precisely in that [time]."
In the second case, the qualification "dissolution" (pralaya) is untenable; for dissolution is defined as time characterized by the destruction of all effects.

Alternatively, if dissolution were simply the destruction of effects, even then, because there is no relationship between the non-existence of God and that [destruction], the meaning of the proposition—that God and so forth do not exist during dissolution—is untenable.
If one accepts a connection by way of place (*deśa*) and so forth, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the state of being an entity (*bhāvatva*) in that very case.

As for the abandonment of the qualification "at the time of dissolution" (*pralaya*), let it be inferred by the students themselves; therefore, it was not explicitly stated by either the author of the Sūtras or the author of the Bhāṣya.
Furthermore, it was indicated by the author of the Sūtras in the words "in absorption" (*apītau*).
"Even the author of the Bhāṣya has said: 'If [the self] were grasped, what pride could there be?
This very inference has been stated as being common to both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)."
Now, he states an inference that establishes the existence of the individual soul (*jīva*) during the dissolution (*pralaya*): "Dharma... etc.
Even though he must be accepted as the substratum of dharma and adharma, man [merges] into dissolution.
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: it is not only by the aforementioned inference, but also by virtue of being the substratum of dharma and adharma;
"man" (nara) refers to the individual soul (jīvātman).

The formal argument here is as follows: A property existing at the time of dissolution has a substratum, because it is a property, like a property existing at present. In this same way, one should formulate the argument by taking non-dharma (adharma) as the subject as well.
Furthermore, no substratum for merit and demerit other than the individual self (jīvātman) is possible;
thus, since the individual self exists during the dissolution (pralaya), the proof that non-existence consists merely in the absence of being is untenable.
This is where the proof for the existence of the Lord (īśvara) [is established].
Because the word "substratum" (āśraya) has the sense of a "presiding agent" (adhiṣṭhātṛ), the formal argument (*prayoga*) in this case is as follows:
virtue and non-virtue existing at the time of dissolution are presided over by someone.
Because, while being a cause, it is insentient,
like an axe or similar tools;
and it is not possible for anyone other than the Lord to be the supervisor of merit and demerit, which are beyond the reach of the senses.
Therefore, even as the presiding authority over dharma and adharma, the Supreme Person must be accepted as existing at the time of dissolution (*laya*).

[Objection: But for me, who accepts that at the time of dissolution there is the non-existence of all things whatsoever, dharma and adharma do not exist either; thus, there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
To this, the following must be said here:

Is it asserted that the non-existence of that [unseen force] at the time of dissolution is maintained while accepting that there exists an unseen force designated as merit and demerit which serves as the cause for every effect;
or is it maintained that although it exists, it is not a cause; or is it accepted that such a thing does not exist at all?
He refutes the first [position] with the words: "the state of being beginningless."
How could there ever be a cause that is itself without a beginning, if it were not observed [to exist] without a beginning?
"Being as if beginningless" means being existent during the dissolution (*pralaya*).
"In some cases" refers to the time of creation.
If the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) did not exist during the dissolution, then it could not be the cause of effects belonging to the initial period of time.
Because that which is non-existent cannot function as a cause;
thus, the accepted position that [the Lord] is the efficient cause (nimitta) of all things that arise is refuted—this is the meaning.
This might be so.
My position is that present-day effects have an unperceived cause (*adṛṣṭa*), but those belonging to the beginningless past do not.
To the objection, "What then of the existence of the unperceived at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*? he replies: "beginninglessness" (*anāditva*).
Without beginninglessness, and consequently without the absence of a cause for the body at the initial moment of time, how could there be a cause for any present effect that has not been observed?
It could not be so in any way;
a present effect does not have an unobserved cause.
This is because the inference "because it is an effect, like an effect belonging to the initial time" is possible;
for one might argue that, just as this [present] case, that [initial] case too must be accepted as having an unperceived cause (adṛṣṭa).
Alternatively, let there be no unperceived cause for the effect belonging to the initial time.
Nevertheless, its existence during the dissolution must be admitted.
Why?
Because its beginninglessness implies its presence during the dissolution.
How could there be a cause for any effect, even in the present, if it were not perceived?
This should be understood as meaning that it is impossible for the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) to arise in the interval [between destruction and creation].
Now, one might object: even if the unseen force is the cause of all things that arise, its existence at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) need not be admitted.
"Because it is possible for that which has arisen at the very beginning of time to be the cause of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest.
To this, the following must be said:
Does that unseen force (adṛṣṭa) which possesses birth at that initial time arise from an unseen force prior to it, or not?
He introduces the first [point] with the words "previously."
If that which is seen later is not at all superior to what was seen before, why [should it be accepted]? (2.1.77cd)
The word "is born" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He refutes this, saying: "Not at all."

In that case, we do not take as our subject (pakṣa) the unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa) produced at the beginning of time following that [dissolution]; rather, we take as our subject only the prior unseen merit/demerit existing at the time of dissolution, which is the cause of that [new creation]. Therefore, how can there be the fallacy of the unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi)?
He takes up the second [alternative] with the words "pūrva" (prior).
The ellipsis is "it does not arise at all.
He refutes [the opponent's position] with the word "uttaram" (the answer).
In that case, from what would that initial adṛṣṭa (unseen force) at the beginning of time arise? From nothing at all;
the meaning is that since there is no adṛṣṭa to serve as the cause for anything that originates, the very production of the initial adṛṣṭa would be impossible.

We do not say that every effect is produced by the unseen (adṛṣṭa). What then? At the beginning of time, the cause of the great [elements] and so forth, which possesses birth, is something other than the unseen; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Having raised this objection, he refutes it with the words "pūrva... (beginning with the previous...).
If that which is perceived by others at the beginning of creation does not arise from a previously unperceived *adṛṣṭa*,
but rather arises entirely independent of *adṛṣṭa*,
then one must likewise accept that the subsequent effects, such as the *mahat* and so forth, also arise from something other than *adṛṣṭa*.
For it is possible that even for that [unseen force], there may be independence from an unseen force, since it too possesses the nature of being unseen.
Otherwise, because it is an effect, one would have to admit that even the unseen force requires another unseen force.
Let us then accept the second position: that the unseen force is not a cause at all.
Or else, the third [position] is that the unseen (adṛṣṭa) simply does not exist, because neither of the two [the seen nor the unseen] is perceived;
and thus, fearing that the "unestablished basis" (āśrayāsiddhi) fallacy would be unavoidable, he says: "The unseen... [and so forth].
If the unseen principle (adṛṣṭa) were not the cause, what would be the basis for dissolution and for measurement?

If that which is unperceived were non-existent simply because it is not apprehended by direct perception, or if even an existing cause were not to exist [for that reason], then what proof would there be for dissolution?
Even dissolution (*pralaya*) would not exist because it lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For even that is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Consequently, since God and so forth must be non-existent during dissolution, the thesis (*pakṣa*) of the opponent would likewise involve an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*).
Now, it might be thought:
although dissolution is not perceived due to the vastness of time, it must nevertheless be accepted because it is established by inference.
For instance:
this continuum of the universe is composed of constituent parts that are devoid of a continuum of visible objects,
because it is a continuum, like the continuum of fire produced by friction.
The atoms of the present universe have previously produced other homogeneous successions, because, while being eternal, they are initiators [of such successions], like the atoms of a lamp.
All successions are at some time completely cut off, because they are successions, like the succession of a lamp.
All atoms are at some time devoid of a continuous series of complete effects, because they are initiators, like the atoms that initiated a wind that has ceased.
The continuity of the terrestrial globe is at some point completely severed, because it is a continuity, like the continuity of a lamp-flame.
This action [of cessation] occurs at some time not co-located with its own constituent parts, because it is an action, like any other action.
If that is so, then merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), though unperceived due to being remote in their essential nature, [nevertheless produce effects such as] Devadatta’s body and so forth.

By means of such inferences as: "It is produced by a specific quality of Devadatta, because, while being an effect, it is the cause of Devadatta's experience, like a garland and so forth produced by Devadatta's effort," and because diverse effects would otherwise be inexplicable, [it is established that there is a creator];
and [from the Vedic injunction]: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma."

"Whoever should raise a weapon against a Brahmin, him one should punish with a hundred [strokes]"—since this is established by the fact that the relationship between the means and the end as heard in such scriptural passages would otherwise be untenable, these two must be accepted; thus, the resolution is the same.
Now, you might think:
The establishment of dharma and so forth does not occur through inference and the like, because those [means] are fallacious. For instance:
Is the fact that Devadatta’s body and so forth are produced by the specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) of Devadatta to be proven as being direct, or indirect? Not the first,
because it is accepted that merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma) also function only in the form of initiators (ārambhaka) and impellers (preraṇā), etc.

Furthermore, there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*): "Devadatta’s body is not directly produced by a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of Devadatta, because it is a body, like Yajñadatta’s body.

As for the second [reason], since it can be explained through the mediation of a deity propitiated by efforts in a previous birth, it results in proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntaratā*).

Moreover, even without being produced by a specific quality of Devadatta, it is possible for Devadatta’s body to be the cause of his experience through the will of the Lord (*īśvara*), just as space is; thus, the reason is non-conclusive (*aprayojakatā*).
Furthermore, the diversity of effects is accounted for solely by the diversity of observed causes;
and as for the primordial time, that diversity is accepted as residing precisely in the respective prior non-existences (*prāgabhāva*) of those effects.
Moreover, the scriptural statement regarding the relationship of means and end between one's own body, speech, and so forth, is simply unestablished due to a lack of functional capacity (*yogyatā*).
If it is accepted on the basis of the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), [the argument] is not otherwise established,
because the attainment of heaven and so forth is possible through the mediation of deities who have been propitiated by sacrifices and other rites, even if they remain unknown.
Thus, in that case, [the same applies to] the inferences that establish dissolution (*pralaya*).
The rebuttal is the same: that it is not established by those [reasons] because they are merely appearances (*bhāsa*).
For instance: "The subject under dispute (the time in question) is devoid of parts, because it is time, like the present time."

The collection of inferences previously stated—such as "the disputed Brāhmaṇa was preceded by a Brāhmaṇa because he is a Brāhmaṇa, like one who is universally accepted"—is countered by a *satpratipakṣa* (an opposing argument with equal force).
Now, [one might object]: "If the period of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*) is made the subject (*pakṣa*), there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*);
otherwise, it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)."
If it is argued that there is a fault in treating [the subject] as a "non-Brahmin" (abrāhmaṇa) and so forth in this way, and otherwise as well, we say no;

for then, since in cases such as "the mountain possesses fire" (*parvato 'gnimān*), it would be possible to refute the subject by means of its being "possessing fire" or "not possessing fire," there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of all inference.
Now, one might object: "The mountain and so forth possess a specific nature (*svarūpa*) even apart from their possession of fire and the like."
And it is possible to determine [the time] by means of another particularity.
If it is asked, "In that case, how is there room for an objection?",
then is it that the very nature of the specific time does not exist apart from its connection or lack of connection with the whole (avayavin)?
Or, having set aside the present and non-present states of a particular Brahmin,
the restriction [of time] will occur through such factors as the fact that [the world] arises subsequent to the dissolution of Hiraṇyagarbha. (6.126)
Furthermore, in the initial application [of the argument], what is intended by the word "universe" (viśva): the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) or all effects?
Not the first, because the locus is unestablished (āśrayāsiddhi).
This is because one who does not accept dissolution (pralaya) cannot admit the existence of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa);
furthermore, even in the absence of a cosmic egg, dissolution is unproven since it is possible for other effects to persist.
If it is argued that such persistence as another effect is impossible—just like the body of a mosquito existing within the interior of a fig fruit inside the cheek of a monkey—we say no.
Because [the dissolution] would be established like that of a jujube fruit in a pit;
and because the process involving Kālāgnirudra and others is unproven.
Even in the second case, the dissolution is not established.

For just as there is no dissolution of the present series of flames and winds even when they cease sequentially, so too, although the series of trees, mountains, bodies, and so forth may be established as beginning sequentially, a time devoid of composite wholes is not thereby established.

If, on the other hand, the qualification "simultaneously" were employed, then there would be a logical deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the series of flames, winds, and so forth, which begin sequentially.
If the qualification of the reason is "when there is a completeness of causes for a single commencement," then that qualification is unestablished (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*).

Furthermore, since the commencement [of creation] is accepted as occurring through a sequence beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of contradiction and so forth.
By this, the second inference is also refuted.
Because the existence of a cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is not accepted;
and even if it were accepted, because production and destruction are accounted for simply through the addition and removal of constituent parts,
and because the persistence of other effects is thereby established.
In the third case as well, there is an abandonment of the tenet (*apasiddhānta*),
because the destruction [of things] is admitted to occur sequentially.
In the fourth case too, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to cloth and other objects [being produced] from threads and so forth that have already perished previously.
Even if the reason is qualified by the term "atomicity" (*paramāṇutva*), the probandum remains doubtful in the example because the existence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth is possible.
Regarding the fifth [reason] as well, are the terrestrial globes themselves being referred to by the word "continuum" (*saṃtāna*), or is there something distinct from them?
In the first case, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Because the continuous arising and destruction [of the whole] is established through the insertion and removal of its constituent parts;
in the second case, however, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*);
and the sixth [case] is to be disregarded because it shares the same logical status as a fallacious argument (*ābhāsa*).
Now, even if the proof of dissolution (*pralaya*) does not occur through inferences, it will nonetheless occur through scriptural authorities (*āgama*),
since their validity has been established even with respect to already established facts (*siddhārtha*).

If you then argue that there is no such thing as an "unestablished qualification" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), then for us as well, the establishment of *dharma* and so forth will proceed from scripture (*āgama*); how then can there be a "non-establishment of the locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*)?

Thus, by one who seeks to prove the existence of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), the existence of *dharma* and so forth is also proven; therefore, it is not logical to attempt to prove the non-existence of mere entities at the time of dissolution.

Having thus taken such an initial effect as the subject (*pakṣa*), one should also observe that in proving its possession of a material cause (*sopādānatva*), the establishment of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth follows as well.
In the first sūtra, an inference was stated for the purpose of refuting the agency of non-existence (*abhāva*). Now, for this reason as well, the world is not created by non-existence.

Intending another commentary on the sūtra, "Because of the absence of an example [for] having a conscious agent as the author," he states the inference for the state of having a conscious agent as follows: "In the case of origination... (utpatti).
For a wise man is seen in some cases to be the cause of both the production and the destruction [of things].
Why, by that same analogy, is an agent not inferred everywhere?
The meaning is that one who brings about production and destruction through intelligence acts with prior deliberation;
this refers to certain things such as cloth,
and to every disputed effect.

If it were stated merely that "the effects beginning with the Mahat [are produced by an agent]," a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) might be suspected in the case of sprouts and the like; therefore, the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) is used to include those as well within the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*).
The remainder of the sentence is "the agent is intelligent."
Because it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) against one who maintains that [the self] is the agent of transformation (*anyathābhāva*).
What is the purpose of this objection?
There is no reason whatsoever for non-inference;

the meaning is that because there is an absence of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), a counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) is impossible. By this, [the phrase] “and because of the defect in one's own position” [is explained].
Thus, the Sūtra is also explained.
This is the sequence of the formal argument (prayoga) here:
the subject under dispute is an effect produced by a conscious agent, because it is an effect, like a jar.
And its destruction is caused by volition (cetanā) for that very same reason and in that very same way.
Furthermore: the arising under dispute has volition as its agent, because it is an arising, like the arising of a cloth;
and the destruction under dispute has volition as its agent, because it is a destruction, like [the destruction of] what is commonly accepted.
In this context, the proof that destruction has a conscious agent as its creator is incidental.

Alternatively, some maintain that because they observe the birth of sprouts and the like from the destruction of causes such as seeds, and the destruction of cloth and the like from the destruction of threads and the like, it is non-existence in the form of "destruction" (pradhvaṃsābhāva) alone that acts as the creator of the world’s birth and destruction;
as it has been said:
"Because it does not arise without having crushed [its cause]"—this is intended to show that that view has been refuted here by such sūtras as "that which is non-existent," etc.
As for the absence of an illustrative example, it should be inferred by oneself. *6,138*

But is this proof of the Lord’s authorship of the world by means of inference not contrary to what the author of the Sūtras has stated? For, in the sūtra *śāstrayonitvāt*, he himself has rejected the validity of inference regarding the Lord. To this, he replies: "By scripture... (*āgama*).
But when supported by traditional scripture, it is authoritative... // MDh 2.1.79cd //
The word "anumeti" (inference) is connected here as well with what is about to be stated.

It is not that the author of the Sūtras has rejected inference as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the Lord in every respect; rather, he has rejected it when it is not supported by scripture (*āgama*).
However, inference supported by scripture (āgama) is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) regarding God;
otherwise, one would not undertake the inquiry (jijñāsā) consisting of the application of reasoning toward the meaning of the Vedic statements.
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "This... [eṣā].
... this is the inference. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.79d)
The phrase "supported by scripture" (āgamānugṛhītā) continues [from the previous context], as does the word "means of knowledge" (mānam).
Although this [inference] has just been presented, it is [the inference] that [proceeds from the consideration]: "Or, from these [elements], these beings [arise]."
Thus, being supported by scripture (*āgama*),
there is no contradiction whatsoever in the resulting inference (*māna*) regarding Īśvara.
In this way, having raised the doubt that the universe might be created by non-existence (*abhāva*) through inference, its being created by Īśvara has been established by means of inference itself.

Having raised this objection from another perspective, the Sūtra provides the resolution: "Oṃ. If it be argued that there is something else to be inferred because reasoning is not final, even so, there follows the consequence of no liberation, Oṃ."
In this context, the meaning of the objection is as follows:
this prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) does not become established by means of inference, nor does the final conclusion (siddhānta) become established by means of a valid cognition (pramāṇa);
for there is no such thing as inference that constitutes a valid cognition.
(Why so?
Because it can be inferred otherwise as well;
for those who maintain the validity of inference must accept that "the absence of a counter-argument" (*asatpratipakṣatva*) is a constituent factor (*aṅga*) of inference.
Because it is never observed that a blocked instrument produces an action;
furthermore, an object of inference established through inference can be inferred even in another way.
Why?
Because reasoning is not firmly established,
one should infer in this very way and not otherwise.
Thus, because there is no fixed determination of reasoning (*tarka*),
it has been said:
"Where indeed are the [concepts of] 'limiting condition' (*upādhi*) and 'counter-argument' (*pratipakṣa*) so utterly difficult to express?"
But is this not a case of a misplaced reason (*vyadhikaraṇa*),
since reasoning is unstable and the object of inference might be otherwise?
Not so.
By this, the author of the Sūtra makes it known that "reasoning (tarka) is not distinct from inference (anumāna).

Alternatively, because reasoning— inference— is unstable and lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (apramāṇa), the presentation of the prima facie and final positions (pūrvottara-pakṣau) by means of inference is not tenable.
"How [is it established] because of its being non-authoritative?"—the construction is that "otherwise, it would be inferable.

In this regard, in order to bring together the sutra containing the solution, the author of the commentary first provides the answer, even though it goes beyond the literal text of the sutra, saying: "By scripture... (āgama).
If it is argued that, because reasoning is not firmly established, the object of inference must be otherwise, even so, there follows the consequence of no liberation;
for in the absence of the support of scripture, reasoning would not be firmly established. (Mānuṣa 2.1.80ab)
The mention of "scripture" (*āgama*) is an illustration for all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in general.
For this very reason, that which is born of the senses (*akṣaja*) is also included in the latter half [of the verse].

By the two terms "concordance with a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇānugraha*) and "being rooted in a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇamūlatva*), it is expressed that [the teaching] possesses a well-established validity through its possession of a logical mark (*liṅga*) whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) and subject (*pakṣa*) have been ascertained by other means of valid cognition, as well as its concordance with those [other means of valid cognition]. (6.142)
In this regard, the meaning of the first interpretation is as follows:
the claim that because inference is not definitively established, a counter-inference (praty-anumāna) is possible in every case, is untenable;
for without the support of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), reasoning (tarka) would have no foundation.
However, its establishment must be based solely on valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is what is meant:
would your counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*) be devoid of the support of valid means of cognition?
Or is it rooted in that?
But how could the first [position], being itself of an unstable foundation, refute another?
For a young fawn is no match for a hyena.
However, it is sublated by the very first root of valid cognition;
whereas the second would indeed be a valid cognition and would itself sublate the first.
In either case, it is not the case that all inference is invalid.
However, when there is doubt regarding the foundational validity of both [the opposing arguments], then let there be a stalemate;
but this is certainly not the case everywhere.
But regarding the restrictive sense (*avadhāraṇā*), the previous explanation alone is the way. However, in the second interpretation, it must be asked:
is inference devoid of the support of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) non-authoritative because it is sublated by a counter-inference?
Or is it based on that [scripture]?
Regarding the first case, he states the answer of agreement: "By scripture," etc.
Nevertheless, the point is that this is not the case everywhere. [The word] *pratiṣṭhita* means "established as a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇabhūta*).
Regarding the second [case], however, he says: "arising from the senses" (*akṣaja*).
The foundation of this [dharma] must indeed rest upon the root of the Vedas, which are born of the senses.
The validity [of the first cognition] is established;
for by that very [cognition], the counter-application is sublated,
since it is impossible for both to be rooted in real means of valid cognition— this is the intended meaning.

But for one who, not accepting this established rule, thinks that there is room for a counter-argument everywhere and thus considers all inference to be invalid, the author provides the answer as it is set forth in the Sūtra: "Otherwise... (anyathā).
Otherwise, its lack of foundation would indeed be contradicted by one's own words.

Even when this has been established in such a manner, for one who does not think thus, there follows the consequence of non-liberation due to a contradiction with one's own words; this application of the aphorism (*sūtra*) has been indicated.
For instance:
"Is your own inference—that all inferential means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are sublated by their opposites—sublated by its opposite and thus invalid, or is it not?"
In the first case, it is not by this [reason] that the invalidity of everything is established;
in the second case, however, there is sublation (*bādha*) precisely here. Otherwise, if one were to abandon the aforementioned systematic arrangement, [the argument would fail].
"The lack of foundation— that is, the lack of validity— of all this inference is contradicted by one's own words.
Others, however, [cite the argument] "because of the difference in characteristics."
They explain such sūtras as being intended for the purpose of raising and resolving objections regarding Brahman’s status as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world;

however, this has already been refuted in the very section concerning "Its Nature" (*tatprakṛtyadhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, they interpret the phrase "on account of the instability of reasoning" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt*) in this sūtra by splitting it [from its context] and presenting it as their own final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

He refutes that very point with this verse. For one who asserts the instability of reasoning must be asked: is it reasoning devoid of the support of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is it that which is rooted in it?
Regarding the first [point], he provides the answer with a hidden intention: "By scripture," etc.
This is the intention:
this is true;
nevertheless, the Sāṅkhya does not consider his own reasoning to be devoid of the support of scripture and other such authorities.
If this is stated according to one's own view, there is tautology [with the following]:
"Because it has the Veda as its source," and "Because of seeing, [Brahman] is not that which is not based on the Veda."
Because this point has already been stated by the passage beginning with "ānumānikaṃ" (inferred),
he refutes the second [position] with the words "akṣaja" (arising from the senses).

The point is that it is not logical to claim that there is no validity for an instrument of knowledge which has grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and which is free from the stain of doubts such as deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—the causes of invalidity.
He states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) for the opposite case [of its being invalid] with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*).

Otherwise, by not accepting what has been stated, the author of the Sūtras would himself be contradicting his own words through this inference, even though it is rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For how could the author of the Sūtras—who himself undertook the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* consisting of the investigation of reasoning (*yukti*)—be a speaker of contradictions while asserting the invalidity of reasoning even when it is rooted in valid means of knowledge?
As for what was said by the commentators (*vṛttikāras*): “One logician refutes an argument conceived by another logician;”
"Therefore, since another person might even imagine something else, reasoning (tarka) born from the manifold nature of human intellect would be unstable.
This, however, is incorrect.

Since, whether this reasoning (*tarka*) is valid or invalid, its lack of foundation is already contradicted by [the proponent's] own words, this division of statements is not tenable; thus the meaning of the Sūtra has indeed been stated.
Regarding this, the Sūtra says: "Oṃ, by this, those who do not accept [a system] are also explained."
Regarding this, some explain as follows:

by means of this present [sūtra], beginning with "Not so, because of the lack of difference" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*), there is the refutation of the doctrine of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause— which had been partially adopted by certain disciples— through the discussion at hand.

One should understand that those theories of atomic and other causes, which have not been adopted even in part by any of the disciples beginning with Manu and Vyāsa, are also to be explained [and refuted].
He refutes this as follows: "And not... (na ca).
By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned are also explained.
And it is not the case that the doctrine of a non-existent Lord is unaccepted by students simply because it is the doctrine of one who speaks of a Lord [who is actually non-existent].
Let alone the manner of the suspicion regarding superiority and the manner of the extension of the refutation;
as for what was stated: "the fact that [this system] is grasped by disciples even more than by the Sāṅkhyas, the Vaiśeṣikas, and others."
That is highly contradictory;
for the Sāṃkhya system is atheistic,
whereas the Vaiśeṣika and other systems are theistic.
Because the opposite is indeed more appropriate;
for here, the conflicting views regarding Brahman being the cause of the world are refuted.
Among those, the Sāṅkhya does not even accept that there is a Brahman.
"How could he possibly possess the status of being the cause of the world?"—because of this extreme contradiction with the Vedāntic doctrine, he was not accepted by the disciples.

As for the Vaiśeṣika and others, however, since they accept that Brahman is the efficient cause (nimitta) of the world but do not accept its status as the material cause (upādāna), there is only slight contradiction; thus it is logical that they were only slightly rejected by the disciples.
However, [the doctrine of] the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) and so forth is entirely irrelevant to the present context;
otherwise, there would be a reversal [of the argument] due to the prohibition of violence in sacrifices and the like.
Now, this [distinction] might be based on the abundance or scarcity of corroboration by the Veda.
Not so;
for that [is not the case], because the principles (*tattva*) to be explained are innumerable. (6.153)
What, then, is the subject matter of this sūtra? To this he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ).
What is negated here is the agency of the remaining entities, such as the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, with respect to the purpose [of creation].
The meaning is that any other [alternative] sense has been refuted.
The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is stated to indicate that this is not irrelevant, since the refutation of misinterpretations serves the purpose of strengthening one's own interpretation.
As for the remaining [point], namely the agency of non-existence which has already been refuted, [it is as follows:]...

The agency of the soul and so forth [belongs] to the world— this is the ellipsis. By this, it is explained that the remaining doctrines not accepted by the Vedas, which were set aside [previously], such as those concerning the soul, primordial matter (pradhāna), non-existence, time, and inherent nature (svabhāva), are thereby refuted.
In that context, if one were to say merely "the disciples," the doctrine that Brahma is the cause would also be included. To exclude that, the term "those who do not accept [a creator]" was stated.
However, if only that were said, the doctrine that non-existence (abhāva) is the agent would also be grasped.
Otherwise, there would be both redundancy and the impossibility of the extended application (atideśa).
Therefore, it is said "the students" (śiṣyāḥ).
Furthermore, in order to justify the commencement of the Sūtra by indicating the existence of further doubts, those recognized as students are referred to as "students."
"But not because it has been refuted by that very [reason].
[Objection: But surely, by the mention of "the living being" (*jīva*) and so forth in the phrase "if it were non-existent," the fact that it would have a non-existent creator was already grasped.
Regarding that, [it is said]: "If [you say] 'non-existent'..."
Since [the objection] has already been refuted by such statements as "because of the consequence of tautology," he says: "That mind... (tanmanaḥ).

The birth of the mind from non-existence, as expressed in the passage beginning "He made that mind," is precluded by the preceding statement, for [the mind] could not have arisen "all at once" (akasmāt) without that [prior cause].

"Because of such authoritative sources as [Manu 2.1.83ab]: 'The production of the universe from that which is non-existent is here prohibited due to doubt,' the word 'suspected' (āśaṅkita) is to be supplied [as the object of the prohibition]."
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), the previously stated reasoning is understood.
Of the non-existent— that is, of absence—
[the cognition] is by means of the mind.
The origination [of the world] is from knowledge, desire, and effort;
"of the world" is the ellipsis.
The connection, however, is with the preceding [verse].

The word "hi" (for) indicates that this is clearly understood from the passage beginning with "And because it is a mere negation," as well as from the Śruti text beginning with "For this [world] appeared suddenly.
That [world], namely the mind, [appeared] without [a prior cause].
"From the non-existent" means from the void (*śūnya*).
This is what is being said: previously, the status of the prior non-existence (*pūrvabhāva*) as the cause of the world was refuted; now, however, that of the void is refuted.

Furthermore, since it was previously [stated] that there is an agent, whereas now it is stated that there is no agent, there is no tautology or similar fault. Alternatively, according to the perspective of the *Bhāṣya*, the arising of the world here was suspected to be without a cause; thus, there is no tautology or similar fault. The presentation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that brings about this suspicion, however, is for the purpose of establishing this very distinction in the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
By this, an even greater doubt is also indicated;
for instance: let it not be that the world has non-existence as its agent.
Nevertheless, it may arise from the individual soul (jīva) and so forth; for instance:
"Beings arise from the individual soul," or "This was produced from primordial matter (pradhāna)."
This is because of examples such as the pot, the curd, and the sharpness of the sword's edge, which are supported by scriptural passages such as, "For this [world] appeared suddenly from nowhere";
for the individual soul (*jīva*) and other entities do not consist of mere negation.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the reasoning already stated.
If it is argued that this is merely an illustration of [properties] such as non-existence and insentience,
then is it being said here that non-existence and so forth do not possess even the mere status of being a cause?
Or what is this agency? It cannot be the first [option],
because there is deviation from the examples already mentioned.

Not the second [alternative], because we do not accept [the existence of] agency (*kartṛtva*). For this very reason, in all these instances, the word "agent" (*kartṛ*) should be understood as referring merely to causality (*kāraṇatva*). *6,165*
Now, is it merely the status of being the cause of the universe that is suspected here in regard to the individual soul (jīva) and others, or is it that very [status] itself?
In the first case, there is no contradiction with our established doctrine (siddhānta).

For it is already accepted that the individual soul (jīva) is the efficient cause by virtue of being the substratum for the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), while primordial matter (pradhāna) is the material cause.
Nor is the second alternative [tenable],
because there is no means of establishing it.
And because one observes the rule that every effect must have an agent, he says: "that which brings [the object] about."
But a mere statement that brings about [the attainment]... // MAnu 2.1.83c //
Only the second [alternative] is suspected;
and its proof is: "There is no cause higher than the Jīva," and "No other cause is recognized."
Such is the statement.
Nor is there a contradiction with worldly usage;

for the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) maintains that when a matter is established by the mere word of scripture, one must accept exactly what is conveyed by that [scripture], and not conform to worldly usage.
But surely, the views asserting the Pradhāna as the cause and so forth will be refuted in the second chapter (pāda);
if they were refuted here as well, there would be the fault of tautology. Therefore, he says: "It is the means of attainment."
The meaning is that here there is merely a statement that gives rise to doubt, but not an established tenet (*samaya*).
This is what is being said:
here, the status of the *pradhāna* and so forth as the cause, which was suggested by reasonings supported by scripture (*śruti*), is refuted.
But later on, it will be obtained through the conventions of the Sāṃkhya and other schools;
therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply here either.
