[Objection: If that is so, then how can there be an extension (*atideśa*) by means of this [sūtra], since the stated refutation has already been countered by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*)? To this, he says: "The refutation... [is as follows].
...the exception has been specified. // Manu 2.83d //
Although the status of being a mere negation is unestablished in the case of the Pradhāna and other such causes,
and the lack of consciousness and so forth is inconclusive regarding the doctrine of causality in general,
nevertheless, it has been indicated in a general sense that the prima facie positions (pūrvapakṣas) are contradicted by reason, because they consist of mere negations and lack supporting examples.
And as for the lack of authoritative status due to the defects in one's own position, that same rebuttal applies here without distinction;
thus, the extension [of the argument] is appropriate—this is the meaning. *6,167*
Now, one might ask: how is it that the doctrine of the world having a living being as its creator and so forth is contradicted by reason? To this, he says: "In some places... [etc.]
Having observed in some cases that a form is produced by a living being, and in others that it is produced from consciousness alone,
one infers in other instances that it is likewise [produced by a creator], because of its substantiality and because of scripture.
"In some place" refers to a location and so forth; alternatively, "in some [being]" refers to a living being and so forth.
Furthermore, the term "uncreated" (*akṛta*) is an expression in which the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary focus.

In this context, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) concerns mere causality and not agency; therefore, the ablative case is employed in the phrase "from the insentient" (acetanāt). By stating "having seen [it] produced from the insentient," the word "even" (eva) indicates that the probanda of the examples are beyond doubt.

*Anumā* means inference (*anumiti*). Otherwise, since "being a real entity" (*vastutva*) itself would constitute the inference, the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) would not be possible; the words "of being uncreated by a living being," etc., are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Except for [the case of] the Great One (mahat) and so forth;
here are these formal arguments (prayoga):
"The effects such as the Great One are not created by a living being (jīva), because they are real entities (vastu), like the living being itself."
"The subject of dispute is not the effect of Pradhāna, because it is a real entity, like Pradhāna itself;
the subject of dispute is not a non-existent effect, because it is a real entity, like a jar.

Although it is indeed accepted that the world has its cause in both the individual soul as the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and Pradhāna as the material cause (*upādāna*), there is no contradiction here, for this statement is made with the intention of denying [the soul's] independence.

But if this were so, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), since one could also employ the following argument: "The subject under dispute was not created by Īśvara, because it is a real entity (vastu), like Īśvara himself. To this, he says: "On account of scripture" (śruteḥ).
“Since scriptural passages such as ‘He created all this’ establish that the mahat and other principles were produced by the Lord, inference based on over-extension is invalid due to being sublated.
[The opponent replies: “Then this same [objection] applies equally to your own inferences.”
Because of such scriptural passages as "From the living self (jīva) all beings arise," he says: "On account of scripture."
The designation is one in which the abstract state (bhāva) is predominant.
The meaning is that there is no contradiction with the Śruti, because words such as "jīva" and others are Śruti-designations of Brahman and are thus names of Brahman.
To the question "Why is that?", he says: "Because of the Śruti."
"Into Him all names enter," according to such scriptural passages;
the remainder is in the commentary.

Now, one might object: "Even if the soul and so forth are the cause, since an inference is possible by relying on examples such as a jar, how can it be said that [the claim] lacks authoritative basis? To this, he says: "From scripture" (śruteḥ).

“Because such scriptural passages as ‘There is no other agent besides Him’ have their subject matter sublated [by direct perception], and because the illustrative examples lack the property to be proven (sādhyavaikalya), these inferences lack validity.
By this, the claim that ‘non-producedness’ (akāryatva) is a limiting condition (upādhi) in our inference is also refuted.”
(Independently,) because even in the case of a jar or similar objects— which are not produced by a living being (*jīva*)— there is no absence of being an effect;
and because the opposing view would entail defects such as contradiction (*bādhā*), everything is well-established.
Thus ends the section on the non-existent (*asadadhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.

[======= JNys_2,1.V: The Section Concerning the Enjoyer =======] *6,170* // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section concerning the enjoyer: // Oṃ. If it be argued that there would be no distinction because of the attainment of the state of being an enjoyer, [we reply] it would be as in the world. Oṃ. //
In the preceding section, the contradiction regarding Brahman’s status as the cause of the world’s origin and so forth was resolved by means of a powerful reasoning that is in harmony with the Śruti.
Now, however, the contradiction is resolved by means of a powerful reasoning based on the indicative marks established by the Śruti.
For instance, it is not possible for Brahman to be the cause of the world in a real sense;
[otherwise] there would be no liberated soul (mukta-jīva) who is not the cause of everything.
Because they are not absolutely non-different.
For it has never been observed anywhere that something which is absolutely non-different from another can, in reality, possess a nature opposed to it.
Nor is the fact that the liberated one is not the cause of all things unestablished.
Because [the state of being] the cause of everything is not observed in saṃsāra;
for liberation is indeed the disappearance of some form that is perceived in saṃsāra, and not the production of a previously non-existent form.
Because it would follow that [the Self] is impermanent.

Nor should it be argued that the non-perception of its being the cause of all things is due to its being concealed by ignorance while still existing— just as bliss and other qualities [of the Self are said to be concealed]—
for there is a lack of evidence for such a claim.
Furthermore, because Ānanda and the like are perceived even slightly as the object of supreme love and so forth;

nor is it reasonable to assume that the causality of the world—which, though not perceived in its entirety within transmigratory existence, is heard in scripture regarding Brahman—should be postulated for the sake of the world.
For the scripture remains consistent even if it merely restates a conceptually constructed causality of the world.
Nor should it be argued that the definition must be exactly as described;

for that is not accepted, and because there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since a causality of the world that is merely conceptual could also exist in relation to *pradhāna* and other such entities.
It might be argued that the very identity of the liberated soul with Brahman is unestablished;
but this is not so.
This is because it is established by such scriptural passages as: "The karmas and the self consisting of consciousness all become one in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman].

This very point was stated by the author of the Sūtras: since scripture declares that the individual soul (jīva), the enjoyer, attains the state of Brahman upon liberation, there is non-distinction—that is, the absence of difference—between the two.
And consequently, it would follow that Brahman’s status as the cause of the world is not logically tenable in reality.
This being the position reached, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is stated:
all this [objection] might hold true if the identity of the liberated soul with Brahman were indeed established by valid means of knowledge.
This is not the case;
rather, the scriptural usage of "becoming one" (ekībhāva) would be like that in common worldly usage.
Just as in the world, the conventional expression regarding the "becoming one" of water with water is based on their occupying the same location.

Or, just as Brahmins who were previously divided have now become one, based on the unity of their thought; so too, individual souls (*jīvas*) who were previously in different places and possessed different thoughts become one with Brahman in liberation. It is thus logically established that they come to occupy a single place and possess a single thought.
Therefore, this is a proof of the unestablished by means of the unestablished;
that is incorrect, because there is no sublation regarding the primary meaning.

Furthermore, because there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) if one were to resort to a secondary sense in the absence of a subverting factor (bādhaka), he explains the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "syāl lokavat" as being intended to demonstrate the reasoning that subverts the primary meaning: "nānyat" (not otherwise).
If it be argued that there is no distinction because of the identity of the enjoyer, as in the case of the world; [we reply:
nowhere has anything ever been seen to have attained a state of being other than what it is.
Therefore, the individual soul could never become Brahman. (Brahmasūtra 2.1.13; Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 2.1.85) *6,176*
In this regard, one who accepts the primary meaning [of the scripture] must be asked:
Is it stated by this that the soul, which was previously non-different, attains unity with Brahman upon liberation; or is it [the unity of] one that is different; or rather—
Regarding that which is both different and non-different:
not the first [alternative], because the suffix *cvī*, which signifies the state of becoming what one was not (*abhūtatadbhāva*), would be untenable in the sense of "becoming one";
for this very reason, the third [alternative] is also not tenable.
Because identity is already established prior [to the statement];
because, if it were intended for the purpose of negating difference, it would result in a figurative meaning;
and because [this view] has been refuted by the rejection of the second alternative.
But in the second [case], this alone presents itself, and nothing else;
the word "hi" (for) indicates the reason, because in the world there is another object.
Difference has never been observed at any time, in any way, or by any means to have attained non-difference with another entity.
Therefore, by that same analogy, even upon liberation, the state of being Brahman—the identity with Brahman—would never belong to the individual soul (jīva). Herein lies the formal argument:
the individual soul will not attain unity with Brahman even at another time.
Because it is absolutely distinct from that [prior state];
for whatever is at any time absolutely distinct from something else never attains identity with it,
just as a jar is [distinct] from a cloth.
Alternatively, there is a difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman; this difference, existing between two real entities, is not subject to cessation,
because it is a difference, just like the difference between a pillar and a jar.
If it is argued that this [position] is contradicted by scripture (āgama), we say no;

for scripture can subvert inference only when its primary sense is possible, whereas the primary sense of scripture is established only once the inference has been subverted— thus there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (parasparāśrayatva).
And because there is a counter-argument;
for instance, there is a scriptural passage beginning with "Just as water... and so forth.
Prahlāda also said: "The union of the supreme self and the individual self is held to be the ultimate reality;
for this other [world] is false, since one substance does not become the nature of another substance. (6.182) Now, suppose this is the view:
There is no contradiction with reason here,
because it is accepted that even prior [to liberation], the individual soul (jīva) is indeed non-different from Brahman;
nor is there any impossibility regarding the suffix cvi.
Because that [identity] is established through dependence upon [the state of liberation];
this individual soul was previously seen as distinct from Brahman,
but now, in liberation, it is seen as non-distinct.
"Therefore, it is said that they become one.
To this, the following must be addressed:
Is the prior perception of a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman an error, or is it valid knowledge (pramā)?
Not the first [alternative],
because there is no sublation.
For the scriptural passages, their meanings not yet being definitively established, do not attain the status of sublation.
Regarding the second [objection], he says: "In some cases... "In some cases it is seen as distinct; how then could it be seen as non-distinct?
For such a thing has never been seen before, nor is it seen now. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.1.86)
The meaning is: how could an object that has been cognized at one time as distinct from something else be cognized at another time as non-distinct from it? It could not be so in any way.
Why? To this he says: "For it has never been seen before."
That which was previously cognized as distinct is now being cognized at a later time as non-distinct.
This is the formal argument:
the individual soul (jīva) has never been an object of valid cognition as non-different from Brahman.
Because it is cognized as being absolutely distinct;
for whatever is thus [distinct] is so, just as a jar is distinct from a cloth. But as for one who does not admit the cognition of difference anywhere at all, [the following applies]:
That single entity, in which difference has been superimposed, should be stated as the example of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
And thus, even by relying on such conventional cognition, the use of the particle *nañ* (the negative particle) is justified.
This should also be applied with the phrase "it would be as in common worldly usage" (*syāl lokavat*), for that very purpose.

Thus, just like the scriptural passage concerning stones floating [on water], since the primary meaning of the scripture is impossible due to its contradiction with reason (*upapatti*), one must accept only the secondary meaning (*amukhyārtha*).
Consequently, because the opponent's reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), it is proven that there is no conflict with logic regarding Brahman’s being the cause of the world.
Some explain this Sūtra otherwise.

Previously, it was indeed stated that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), consisting of both sentient and insentient beings, is non-different from Brahman because Brahman is its material cause (*upādāna*). This sūtra is intended to challenge and resolve that point;
for instance:

If the world, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, were non-different from Brahman, then this distinction—that the conscious is the enjoyer and the unconscious objects are the enjoyed—would not exist.
Why?
Because the object of enjoyment would also necessarily become the enjoyer.
[Otherwise] the enjoyer would also fall into the state of being the object of enjoyment;
and this distinction must indeed exist, because it is established by perception and other means of valid cognition— if this is argued:
It would be as in the world.
Just as in the world, although foam, waves, and so forth have the ocean as their essence, there is no destruction of their distinction through the mutual transformation of one into another;
or just as the spaces within jars, huts, and so forth, although they have the great ether as their essence, [do not lose their distinction].
"Likewise, it might be so in the present case as well"—
this [objection] he refutes with the words "bhoktṛtva" (the state of being an enjoyer), etc.
As for the opinion that [the world-soul] would become an enjoyer, why did Hari say, "Because of the attainment of being an enjoyer" (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.87)? ... [Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 2.1.87a-c]

If the author of the Sūtras had intended the explanation "because of the attainment of being an enjoyer" (*bhoktṛtvāpatteḥ*) for the phrase "because of the attainment of being an enjoyer" (*bhoktrāpatteḥ*), then why did Hari, the author of the Sūtras, say "because of the attainment of being an enjoyer" (*bhoktrāpatteḥ*)?
He would have simply said "because of the attainment of being an enjoyer" (*bhoktṛtvāpatteḥ*).
And since he did not speak in this manner,
this is therefore not the intention of the author of the Sūtra;
even though, in this regard, there is an equality of ellipsis between our opponents and ourselves.
Nevertheless, for the opponent, there is the further deficiency that the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) would be absent.

As for those who explain: "If Brahman has both sentient and insentient entities as its body, then, like the individual soul (*jīva*), it would follow that He is an enjoyer of pleasure, pain, and so forth; thus, there would be no distinction between the natures of the individual soul and Brahman. To this, [the reply is]: "No. Just as, even for one fallen into a wilderness..."
"Likewise, for the king as well, there would be no affliction from gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like";
this same fault regarding the word applies to them as well. [Objection:
But surely, it is frequently observed that in various instances, grammatical expressions have the abstract state (bhāva) as their primary referent.
How, then, can this fault be alleged?
This is the intention (*abhisandhi*) of the author of the *Bhāṣya*:
once the object to be established is settled, one must somehow follow the figurative nature of the word by the force of that [established fact].
Furthermore, this is not established as the intended meaning of this Sūtra;
for since the world's being the material cause was not previously stated, it would result in the fallacy of criticizing what was not asserted.

Moreover, although the world's being the body [of Brahman] was raised in the section concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa), that objection was already refuted by the very statement that [the Lord] possesses the enjoyment [of the world].
If it is argued that while the status of being an agent and enjoyer— which was previously [erroneously] attributed to the soul as residing in the body— has been refuted there,
it is not refuted here because the world is His body, we say no.

Since there would be no justification for the commencement of the sūtra if there were no distinction between the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the final (siddhānta) positions, it follows that even a verbal defect (*śābdadoṣa*) that lacks a basis should not be pursued. Alternatively, this very meaning of the sūtra has already been stated: the subsequent passage beginning with "kathaṃ ca" should be construed here as well in order to explain this point.
Thus concludes the section concerning the enjoyer (*bhoktradhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
[======= JNys_2,1.VI: The Section on Origination (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa) =======] Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section on origination:
*6,188* // Oṃ. Its non-difference [from Brahman] follows from the words concerning "origination" (ārambhaṇa) and so forth. Oṃ. //
The contradiction regarding the stated matter has already been refuted by means of powerful reasoning based on its being rooted in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its consistency with it;
this present section is now commenced to resolve the contradiction posed by the reasoning characterized by its abundance.

Regarding this, the proponent of the theory of Brahman’s transformation explains: “In the immediately preceding section, having accepted the non-difference of the cause—which is established in the world—by not denying the specific differences of individual forms that are established through the transformation of the class of objects of enjoyment, it was stated that [the Sāṅkhya] refutes by means of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) the objection raised according to the Sāṅkhya tenet: namely, that if the class of enjoyers is naturally non-distinct from Brahman according to the scripture, then the objects of enjoyment would likewise attain the status of being enjoyers, just as they possess oneness with Brahman.”

Now, the non-duality of Brahman regarding the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is challenged and subsequently resolved by means of the Vaiśeṣika and other systems, which— through distinctions such as essential nature, function, and designation— fail to establish that the effect is identical in essence to its cause.
To explain:
"Non-difference from that" means non-difference from that Brahman, [the cause], on the part of the effect.
Why? From such scriptural passages as "origination" (*ārambhaṇa*), etc.: "Just as, my dear, when a single lump of clay has been known, all that is made of clay becomes known;
modification is a mere name arising from speech, while 'clay' alone is the truth."

From the word "and so forth" (*ityādi*); by the inclusion of the term "etc. (*ādi*), [it refers to] "all this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*) and "that which is this self" (*yad ayam ātmā*).
"Indeed, all this is Brahman"; such is the acceptance of the scriptural texts that teach identity.
However, the proponent of the theory of illusory manifestation (vivartavādin) explains: "Having provisionally accepted this empirical distinction characterized by the enjoyer and the enjoyed,"
“The [world] is like [the case of] the world,” thus was the rebuttal stated; however,
this distinction does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Because that non-difference of the effect, such as space and so forth, from the cause, Brahman—that is, its ultimate non-difference or its non-existence apart from it—is understood;
for what reason? "From the word 'origin' and others" (BrSū 2.1.14). *6,193*
Therein, he first refutes the initial explanation with the words: "And how?"
The non-difference of that [effect] from that [cause] is established on account of the words concerning "origination" (ārambhaṇa) and so forth.
And how is there this non-difference? 2.1.87.
Regarding the objection "How so?",
the word "ca" (and) serves to connect this [objection] with the objection against the misinterpretation of the preceding sūtra.
The term "of the world" (*jagataḥ*), which is to be mentioned later, is also connected here.
The phrase "it should be established here" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
This is the intended meaning:

for he who, while accepting that the world has Brahman as its material cause (*upādāna*), nevertheless maintains its difference from it, is the one to be treated as the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) in this context.

And since the Vaiśeṣikas and others do not hold such a view, there is no occasion for the statement regarding their non-difference from it, as there is no such attainment [of that status]. Rather, against one who does not accept Brahman as the material cause (upādāna), it is precisely that [status of being the material cause] which must be established,
and not their non-difference from it.
This is because its establishment depends upon that [previous argument].
If it is argued that the status of Brahman as the material cause (*upādāna*) is also being established here, we say no;
for if that were the case, the section concerning *prakṛti* (the "Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa") would become redundant.
If it is argued that the opponent here accepts that [distinction]— which was established by the logic of the *prakṛtyadhikaraṇa*— and yet maintains that they are different, we say: no.

What is this "having Brahman as its material cause" (brahmopādānatva) that has been accepted by the opponent— is it inherence in Brahman (brahmasamavāyitva), or is it being a transformation of Brahman (brahmapariṇāmatva)?
The first alternative is not tenable, because it contradicts its non-difference [from the substance],
and because inherence will be refuted later.
In the second case, effort would be entirely futile;
for no one who accepts the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda) admits an absolute difference between the body and its cause, such that this [effort] would need to be undertaken against him.
Alternatively, how can that non-difference of the world be asserted?
For non-difference is the absence of distinction; that is to say, absolute identity.
Furthermore, difference and non-difference are both accepted by the opponent;
therefore, one would have to say that there is identity [between them].
This is not a fault.

If it is argued that difference and non-difference are thus accepted because there is indeed non-difference of the effect from the cause, while there is indeed difference of the cause from the effect, we say no.
If Brahman were indeed something other than the world, then how could the non-difference of the world from it possibly exist?
For it is not possible that what is absolutely distinct from something else could be absolutely non-different from it.
"Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Alternatively, how could that non-difference be logically asserted?
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "because there is an absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)."

If it is objected: "But since it has been stated that [the world is non-different from Brahman] on account of such terms as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa-śabda) and so forth, how can there be an absence of proof?"—to this it must be replied:
First of all, does the term 'originating' directly declare the non-difference of the world from Brahman?
Or, is it that the modification is non-different from the object modified? If the former, how could this world be non-different from That?
To this, the answer is: "Just as, O Somya," because the lump of clay and so forth are the subject under discussion.
In the second [case], let it be granted that the modification is non-different from the modified; however, how is the world non-different from that? (*6,197*) [Objection:
Even if the non-difference of the modification from the modified has been stated by him, the non-difference of the world from Brahman is nonetheless established.
Because that [unmanifest] is also a modification of that [Self], he says: "But of the world... etc.
But when the immutability of the world has been established by the reasoning already stated, [Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 2.1.88ab].

"In the state of being unchanging" means in the absence of being a modification of Brahman; the phrase "by the aforementioned reasoning" is to be understood as completing the sense of the passage beginning with "And [the Self] is not the material cause."

The syntactical connection is: "When [the world] has been established [as real], how can there be non-difference from that [Brahman]? Alternatively, it connects with the preceding word "of the world" (*jagataḥ*);
the ellipsis to be supplied is "in Brahman being changeless."
That which has no modification is "unchanging" (*avikāra*).
Its state is its "reality" (*tattva*), and it is in that [state]. Now, here, regarding the word "commencement" (*ārambhaṇa*)... [6,198] Indeed, here, the word "commencement" (*ārambhaṇa*)—
If it is argued that the Śruti passage beginning with "Did you ask for that instruction? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.2) is indicated,
and that upon examining its purport, the world is understood to be a modification of Brahman and not different from it, we say no.

Because this [word "Brahman"] lacks the status of being the introduction to a great sentence (*mahāvākya*) or a subordinate sentence (*avāntaravākya*), and because it does not denote the primary subject, there is no reason to include it by way of indicating the *śruti* (the Vedic text).
Even granting that it functions as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), he says: "In the state of being unchanging" (*avikāratve*).

When it is established—by the logic already stated—that similarity and so forth belong to something other than the transformation itself, how could that non-difference be proven through an examination of the purport of the scripture?

Furthermore, as for the claim that the non-difference of the effect is established from the statement "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*) and other such passages included by the word "etc. (*ādi*), that too is incorrect;
for it is illogical to include other scriptural passages under the term "etc. (*ādi*).
If that were the case, it would follow that these [other passages] would also be included under the term "and so forth" (ārambhaṇādi-śabdāt), since they too possess the nature of being words;
or, let it be granted somehow that those sentences are indeed included by the word "and so forth."
Nevertheless, their non-difference from that [cause] is not established by these [arguments], because it contradicts logical reasoning; with this intention, he asks: "And how?"
How and of what nature is that non-difference of the world from That (Brahman), which was asserted by the author of the Sūtras and established by the Śruti?
Is it characterized by identity, as in the expression "the cuckoo is the *kokila*," or is it characterized by modification, as in "the clay is the jar"?
The meaning of the question is that [the self] has the characteristic of being subject to modification.
He raises the first point by asking: "And how?"

But how could the author of the Sūtras assert that the world is non-different from That, characterized by oneness? And how could it be established by the Śruti texts? The meaning is: "in no way at all.
He states the reason for this: "because of its immutability."

The sense is this: once it has been established by the aforementioned reasoning that Brahman is changeless, while the world is established through perception and other means of knowledge to be of the nature of a modification (*vikāra*), [the two] would possess contradictory attributes.
He raises the second objection with the words, "And how? (*kathaṃ ca*).
The phrase "consisting of the nature of the transformer and the transformed" is to be supplied as the remainder. He states the reasoning for this objection: "But of the world... and so forth.
The explanation is as before.
Now, one might object: "In that case, even though it contradicts reason, the non-difference of the world from Brahman must be accepted;

otherwise, there would follow the consequence of invalidating such scriptural passages as 'All this has that as its self' (*etadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*). To this, he says: 'And how... (*kathaṃ ca*) [referring to the following verse].

Even though [Brahman] is changeless, since it is established— by the logic stated as "because of being a modification," "because of its dependence on another," and so forth, regarding the meaning of the scripture, as well as "independence" and "distinctness"— that it is distinct from that [world], how is it appropriate to accept non-difference from it? Furthermore, even a meaning perceived through a scriptural passage that allows for an alternative interpretation must be abandoned if it contradicts an argument that admits of no other possibility.
The meaning is as stated in the section concerning overestimation (*abhimāny-adhikaraṇa*).
He refutes another interpretation as well with the words "And how? (*kathaṃ ca*).
The phrase "so he said" is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
If the author of the Sūtras had intended here that the mere proliferation of effects (*kārya*) is unreal,
then he would have simply said "unreality."
How can it be said that "it is non-different from that"?
For the term "non-difference from Brahman" does not denote unreality;
if it did, it would follow as a logical consequence that Brahman itself is unreal. (6.204)
But has it not been explained that non-difference from that means its non-existence apart from it?
True;
nevertheless, even so, the status of being unreal is not thereby established.
When it is stated that [the world] does not exist apart from That, it is understood that it exists as That;
however, it is not the case that it is entirely unreal.
Otherwise, the individual consciousness (jīvacaitanya), being non-existent apart from Brahman, would also have to be entirely unreal.
And this is well known:
that a negation whose object is qualified transfers its restriction to the qualifier.
True;
nevertheless, if it is argued that this was stated only to make known that [the world] is an illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, [we reply:
no, for if that were the case, [the world] would be merely superimposed (*āropita*) upon it.
Because it must be stated [in this way]:
for when it is to be said that "silver is superimposed upon a fragment of mother-of-pearl," one does not employ the expression "it is non-different from that.
Now, if this world exists only through the existence of Brahman, [then...]

If it is argued that the purpose of this [statement] is to make known that there is no other existence for it, then it follows that this is indeed ultimately real; so how can it be unreal? Or, if it is argued that what is understood as existence within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is made known by this [statement] to be merely superimposed upon Brahman, which is its underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Just as for the proponent of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory that there is a misapprehension of one thing as another), so too for the proponent of *anirvacanīyakhyāti* (the theory that the object of error is indefinable), it is necessary that the superimposed form must have ultimate reality elsewhere.
If that were the case, then even properties such as "being space" (*ākāśatva*) would have to be admitted as ultimately real in Brahman,
and properties such as "being silver" (*rajatatva*) would have to be admitted as ultimately real in mother-of-pearl.

Alternatively, the construction is as follows: having asserted the reality of the manifold of enjoyers and enjoyed through the aphorism "Or it may be as in the world," the author now states its opposite—its unreality—in the phrase "And how [is there] non-difference from that? One might object: "But the author of the Sūtras stated 'non-difference from that' with the ultimate truth (paramārtha) in mind, whereas he said 'it may be as in the world' with the conventional usage (vyavahāra) in mind."
If it is argued that there is no contradiction, how can that be? For [if there were], it would follow that he is a deceiver; otherwise, he would have rejected [the doctrine].

If it is argued that [the Sūtrakāra], without rejecting the manifoldness of effects (*kāryaprapañca*), resorts to the process of transformation (*pariṇāmaprakriyā*) because it will be useful for meditations on [Brahman] with qualities (*saguṇopāsana*).
Are the subject matter and purpose of the meditation on the qualified [Brahman] conducive to the subject matter and purpose of the present topic, or are they opposed to them, or are they indifferent?
Not the first [alternative],
because it has difference as its object and because its fruit belongs to saṃsāra.
For the latent impression of duality is extremely firm; it would only strengthen that very [duality]. For this very reason, the third [alternative] is not possible, nor is the second.
"Because the state of being unauthoritative has not been avoided.
Alternatively, let us set aside for now this consideration of the straightforwardness of the text;
how could that non-difference from [Brahman], characterized by unreality, be logical for the world?
"It is not in any way" is to be supplied [to the previous statement].
He states the reason for this: "of the world."
If there were no illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, there would be no changelessness;
this is according to the logic previously stated, beginning with "that which is unmodified.
Thus, it should also be explained as before, in the sense that there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāva*). *6,209*
If that is so, what then is its meaning? To this he says: "independent" (svatantra).
For by that [reasoning], the existence of an independent cause is here negated.
The meaning is: "by that [reason]"—namely, because the non-difference of the world from Brahman, though manifold, is not what is to be established here.
By this, he reminds us that the refutation of misinterpretations is not irrelevant, as it serves the purpose of strengthening his own interpretation.

Indeed, the creation of jars and the like is observed to depend upon another cause that possesses a power and existence not dependent on an agent. Therefore, the creation of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest also depends upon an independent cause distinct from an agent, because it is a creation, just like the creation of a jar;
or else, the Great Principle and the rest are dependent upon an independent cause distinct from an agent, because their production is contingent, just like a jar.
Alternatively, primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth are independent because they possess causality, like clay and other materials;
or else, God is dependent on another independent cause because He possesses agency, like a potter and others.
Because it contradicts reason, that which was intended in the *Janmādi-sūtra*— the independence of the Supreme Brahman alone— is untenable;
yet there is no contradiction with the Śruti,
for the Śrutis have as their sole purport the fact that Brahman is the cause of the world.

Because there is no scripture (*śruti*) that excludes other independent causes; and even if such scripture existed, since it is non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*), it would possess the same strength as scripture, and thus reasoning (*yukti*) could also possess great strength due to its abundance, thereby rendering the scripture subject to counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*).
Thus it follows that the determination of what is intended [by the opponent] is untenable;
namely, that Brahman is distinct from independent causes—that is to say, that there exists another independent cause.
This is the conclusion reached in this section (*adhikaraṇa*).
By the phrase "non-difference from that" (*tadananyatvam*), this is negated:
namely, that the independent cause of the creation of the great principle (*mahat*) and so forth is non-different from that [effect].
If one were to say here simply that there is an absence of an independent cause, [the point would not be established].
In that case, even the independence of Brahman would be negated;
for when it is stated that "there is non-difference from That" regarding the independent cause, it follows that the independent cause is That alone and nothing else.
To establish this, [the Sūtra] states: "On account of the word 'originating material' (ārambhaṇa) and others."
Thus, the proof for one's own position has been stated;
and as for the absence of proof in the opposing position, namely the argument "and because [the object] is perceived when it exists," the word *hi* indicates both of these points.
Should it not rather be stated as "on account of the objection regarding the 'merely a name' passage and so forth, and on account of the words and so forth"?
True;
however, there is no fault, because this very same meaning is conveyed through a secondary indication based on a primary indication (lakṣitalakṣaṇā).
Even so, if it is argued that the selection of a material cause (*upādāna*) is appropriate in accordance with the Vedic injunction, "What was the foundation? (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.81.2), we say no;
for the primacy of the actual meaning is more powerful than even the literal word.
Because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) that "the most effective instrument is the *karaṇa*.
Now, one might object: having asserted the non-difference of the independent cause from Brahman, the presentation of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the absence of any other cause is irrelevant.
Not so.
There is an underlying intention here; for it will be stated that there exists a cause such as primordial matter (prakṛti) and so forth, which is distinct from Brahman.
The absence of that [independent cause] is understood from the words regarding "commencement" and so forth;

therefore, by stating that there would be the consequence of its perception through means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) if another independent cause existed—which is not the case—he asserts the absence of such a pramāṇa.
He thinks as follows:

Even though there are many dry arguments, because numerous arguments supported by scripture (*śruti*) are more powerful, the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that contradict them lack authority.
One might object:
"How can there be no perception of an independent cause other than Brahman, given such statements as 'He was born from water'?"*6,215*

Nor should it be argued that independence is not heard of here [in the scripture]; for in the absence of a statement regarding dependence, independence is established simply by following worldly convention. To resolve this, the Sūtra states: "Om, and because of the existence of what is subsequent. Om.
This is its meaning:
this fault would arise if we were to say that there is no cause whatsoever other than Brahman;
but it is not so.
"Because there exists a cause such as primordial matter (prakṛti) and the rest, which is subordinate and dependent upon that [Iśvara].
This is not sufficient as a rebuttal,
because the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) has stated that, since dependence was not mentioned, it follows that [the effect] must be independent.
Otherwise, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) would fall into the error of being groundless;

therefore, demonstrating the evidence that the entire collection of causes, such as primordial matter (prakṛti) and the rest, possesses an existence dependent upon God, he explains the Sūtra with the words: "Substance" (dravyam).
And because of [the mention of] *sattva* and another [quality].
(BBs 2.1.16) If it is argued that [it is] not so because of the designation of non-existence, we say no; for [it refers to] another quality, as is clear from the remainder of the sentence.
(BBs 2.1.17) Substance, action, time, intrinsic nature, consciousness, and fortitude.
"By whose grace these things exist, and by whose neglect they do not exist"—
because it is heard thus, the state of being [of all things] is dependent upon Him.
Living beings possess consciousness;
the sustaining power (dhṛti) is the nature of consciousness, according to the scripture which states, "because it is that which sustains."
The existence of that which is subject to [the power of] primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth is accepted;

therefore, even in the case of the scriptural statement "born from water" (*adbhyaḥ sambhūtaḥ*), since independence is not established, non-perception is not a valid [reason for denial]. This is the meaning.

Although this point is obtained through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) due to the mutual contradiction between the word "originating" (*ārambhaṇa*) and the Śruti text "born from water," [it is nonetheless established here].
Nevertheless, the example of a clear scriptural statement is given out of consideration for those of dull intellect.
Alternatively, by the phrase "the difference from independent causes is negated," the existence of other dependent causes is indicated;
otherwise, he would have simply said "the difference from causes."
Since the existence of dependent causes has been established, he says: "Substance" (*dravya*).
The word "existence" (bhāvaḥ) is to be understood as the subject;
here, its dependence on that [the cause] is the predicate to be established,
since the existence of a cause is admitted even by the opponent.

// Oṃ. If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the subject of the statement] because of the designation of non-existence, we say no; for there is another attribute [intended], as is clear from the remainder of the sentence. Oṃ.//
Thus is the Sūtra.
In this regard, the meaning of the objection is as follows:
"Neither non-existence existed, nor did existence exist at that time."

Thus, since there is a designation of the non-existence of everything— including both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*)— during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), neither the objection regarding the perception of a cause nor its resolution by accepting that [effect] is under the control of God (*īśvara*) is tenable. Nor is this position [acceptable] if one says, "It is non-existent."
It has already been refuted by such [arguments] as those,
because even Īśvara is not accepted there;
whereas here, however, having accepted Īśvara, other causes are refuted.
Nor is there any contradiction with such passages as "He was born from the waters," because in this context,
no other cause is heard of during the great dissolution (mahāpralaya).
And because [the texts] are intended to establish the existence of causes such as water in creations that have an agent other than Īśvara;
and thus, the words regarding "originating" (*ārambhaṇa*) and so forth also become consistent.
Here, he explains the portion of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) beginning with "not so"—namely, "substance" (*dravya*).
It should not be said that there is an absence of other causes during the great dissolution; rather, it is precisely because of its dependence on that [cause] that they exist.
If it is asked, "From what does its dependence on that arise? [the answer follows].
"Because of the scriptural statement, 'It was substance' (dravya).
Now, [one might object]: "It was not non-existent" (nāsad āsīt).
Since everything is thus designated as non-existent, how can it be said "no"? To this it is said: "by means of another property.
He explains that: "of that which is under its control."
And this [statement] is restrictive:
existence at the time of dissolution belongs only to that which is dependent on Him, not to that which is independent.
Therefore, with the intention of referring to the specific property characterized by independence, the designation "non-existent" is appropriate;
this is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa),
as it has been stated in the Bhāṣya.

Indeed, that which is dependent (*paratantra*), unmanifest, and not directed toward its effect is designated as "non-existent" (*asat*). Why? Because of scripture (*śruti*). How can a non-primary meaning be accepted by abandoning the primary meaning?
[It is so] because of the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) beginning with, "Darkness existed."
Nor is darkness Brahman, because its existence is stated separately in the passage, "It breathed, windless."
Moreover, it is not logical for infinite light to possess the nature of darkness;
rather, it belongs to primordial matter (prakṛti) alone,
because of its quality of being an obscuring agent and so forth.

If it is asked: "But if primordial matter (prakṛti) and the rest remain during the dissolution (pralaya), how could they lack attributes such as independence (svātantrya), such that [the Lord] is explained in this way?
We reply: It is by means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) alone, because there is a contradiction between the opening of the passage and its conclusion.
Intending to show that [the fact] is clearly heard, he explains the phrase "from the remainder of the statement" (*vākyaśeṣāt*) by means of another method: "not another" (*na paraḥ*). ...
from the words "not another" (*na paraḥ*). (Manu 2.1.89f)

The meaning is this: from the supplementary statement, "Therefore, other than that [Brahman], there is nothing else whatsoever," it is understood that during dissolution (*pralaya*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the rest lack independence and other such attributes.

For here, by the phrase "other than that Brahman, there is nothing else whatsoever"—meaning nothing else characterized by attributes such as supreme independence—the state of being "other" (*paratva*) is negated through the acceptance of the existence of that [Brahman].
"Otherwise, the word 'other' would be redundant.
This might be argued:
having admitted the existence of other causes, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) who asserts their dependence on God must state this [following point].
Does the Lord sometimes perform creation and so forth even without primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the other [causes], or is there a rule that he does so only with them?
In the first case, how can they be considered causes, given their lack of necessity?
Otherwise, even a donkey would be a cause of a jar.
Otherwise, [God] would fall into the state of being a cause.
But in the second case, how could there be independence for God, who never acts without abandoning those [auxiliaries]?
And how could there be dependence on those auxiliaries which are invariably required?

Thus, does [the Creator] create by sometimes setting aside the rule that "from Primordial Matter (prakṛti) itself [comes] Mahat, and from Mahat [comes] Ahaṅkāra," and so forth, or rather according to this very rule?
In the first case, because of the lack of regularity, it would follow that [the Creator] is not the cause.
In the second case, however, the independence of the Lord and others would be untenable.

Likewise, if it is held that [the Lord] creates by taking primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth as the material cause (*upādāna*) and time and so forth as the efficient cause (*nimitta*), then the same faults mentioned above would follow both in the case of regularity and in the case of irregularity.
Therefore, since this position is contradicted by reason, it is more appropriate to hold that the Blessed One performs creation and so forth entirely independent of any other cause.
In this way, his unimpeded sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) would be fully established.
Nor is there any contradiction with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This is because it has been stated that passages such as "He was born from the waters, from the essence of the earth" refer to intermediate creations whose agents are not the Lord (*īśvara*).

Furthermore, although darkness and other elements are heard to exist during the dissolution (*pralaya*) in texts such as "Darkness existed," they are not heard to be the causes in a creation whose agent is the Lord. To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra states: [Sūtra 2.1.35]...
Oṃ. [The self is distinct from the body] because of reasoning and because of another scriptural statement. Oṃ.
Thus, this is the meaning:
one should not accept that the Blessed One is devoid of other causes on the grounds of contradiction with the aforementioned reasoning.

Even if one admits the existence of other causes, such as primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth, the causality of these and the independence of God (*īśvara*) and so forth are established by reason.

Nor should it be said that, in that case, there is a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamana*) for [identifying] the cause; for this is known from other scriptural passages, such as "Hiraṇyagarbha was born from the waters."
A sound that is distinct from the sounds previously cited is a different sound (*śabdāntara*).
By this it is meant that,
although the sounds cited earlier might somehow be interpreted otherwise, [this one cannot].
Nevertheless, this is not so;
for in this very creation whose agent is Īśvara, there is heard mention of the existence of other causes.
Indeed, the creation of Hiraṇyagarbha is not one that has a non-divine (anīśvara) creator.
"Because that alone is the first-born.

Regarding this, in response to the inquiry as to how the reasoning (*yukti*)—namely, the statement concerning the compatibility of being the cause and so forth within one's own position—is established, he says: "Even though capable," and so on.
This is due to both reasoning and another scriptural passage (*śabdāntara*). (BBs 2.1.18)
For although Hari is capable of acting otherwise, he always creates this world through fixed causes alone, in accordance with the constraints of his own will.

Otherwise, although Hari is capable of acting even without causes, he creates this world always by means of causes alone, due to the restriction of his own will, thinking, "I shall act only by employing other causes.
Thus it is otherwise.

From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the ego (ahaṅkāra), and from the ego comes the Great One (mahān); thus, although [the Lord] is capable of acting by taking primordial nature as the instrumental cause (nimitta) and time and so forth as the material cause (upādāna), he acts according to the restriction of his own will, determining that "having taken this very thing as the material cause, I shall create this," through factors that are fixed and established.
The construction is as follows: He always creates this world by means of causes that are themselves fixed and possess their own fixed existence, power, and so forth.
This is what is being said:
regarding the question raised as to whether or not there is a restriction concerning God’s causes, material substrata, and so on.
To this we reply: it exists.

And thus, it is logical that primordial matter (prakṛti) and the other factors possess causality. Furthermore, that necessity is not based on a lack of capacity—such as that of a potter—to act otherwise or to act by setting those factors aside.

By this, his independence and their dependence would not exist; rather, [the world] would indeed be subject solely to his own will. Therefore, even [the concepts of] independence and so forth are logical.
Nor do they possess independent existence, power, and so forth, by virtue of which their sovereignty would not be unrestricted; rather,
their existence and other attributes depend entirely upon the Blessed Lord alone.
Therefore, that assistance is nothing other than an indicator of supreme sovereignty.
As it has been said: "When the efficacy of the means of accomplishment is held to be dependent upon the Self, then the perfection of those means becomes an indicator of sovereignty."
If it is asked, "But why does even the omnipotent Lord have the desire to follow those rules?",
do you ask for the cause or for the evidence?
In the first case, we say that this is simply His nature.
But in the second [case], it is because of its being well-known from scripture;
this is what is indicated by the word "hi" (for),
and he will cite the scripture.
By this, it should be understood that the sūtra "and because of another word" (śabdāntarācca) is explained by way of another method.
Furthermore, "another word" (śabdāntara) means a specific word; that is to say, a word that conveys the intended meaning.
The phrase "and like cloth" and "just as breath and so forth" are explained in the Sūtra;
this is made clear in the Bhāṣya itself (*6,229*). Others, however, explain these Sūtras in a different manner.
For it is thus:
"And because [the effect] is perceived when the cause exists. Since the effect, such as a jar, is perceived only when the cause, such as clay, exists, the effect is non-different from the cause.
For that which is distinct from something else is not perceived as being of the very nature of that thing;
indeed, a horse, being other than a cow, is not perceived as being of the nature of a cow.
Furthermore, regarding the existence of causes such as sesame seeds and the like:
Oil and so forth are perceived [within sesame seeds],
and gold and so forth are perceived within their effects such as earrings;
therefore, the non-difference between them is established.
"And because of the existence of the subsequent.

Because of the determination of existence in the statement, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," prior to the arising of the body belonging to a later time, there is non-difference of the effect from the cause. *6,230*
“If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the cause] because of the designation of non-existence, we say no; for there is another attribute [intended], as is clear from the remainder of the passage:
‘In the beginning this was indeed non-existent,’ and ‘In the beginning this was verily non-existent.’”
If it is argued that [the effect does not exist] because of the designation of the non-existence of the effect prior to its production, we say: no;

for this would be the case only if this designation were intended with reference to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the effect. However, it is intended with reference to another attribute characterized by manifestness (*vyaktatva*).
Why?
On account of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).

Having first indicated [the subject] with the word "non-existent" (*asat*) in the opening statement, "In the beginning this was indeed non-existent," the remainder of the sentence subsequently indicates it again as "That became existent" (*tat sad āsīt*).
And even in the passage "It became non-existent," there is the further statement, "It made itself by itself."
By this it is known that the effect is not non-existent; rather, the designation "non-existence" refers to its state as a different property (dharma).
This is understood both from reasoning and from another scriptural passage.
From reasoning, it is understood that the body exists prior to its production and is non-different from its cause.
And from another scriptural passage:
the reasoning has been stated by the Sāṃkhyas as "because that which is non-existent cannot be a cause," and so forth;
and that stated by the Buddhists consists of the impossibility of the alternatives regarding subsistence, and so forth.

And there is a difference in terminology because of the designation of "being" (*sat*); for instance, there is the designation of "being" in such passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone.
And it is like the case of a cloth.

This non-difference of the effect from the cause, as well as its existence prior to production, is to be understood through the analogy of a cloth that has been folded and then unfolded. [6.238] Intending that the disciples themselves should carry out the investigation into whether the words of the Sūtra are straightforward or not, he proceeds to refute for now the claim that the effect is non-different from the cause; for what has been established by this entire section? Has the non-difference of the effect from the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) been demonstrated?
Keeping in mind the conceptual alternative that [the effect] is non-different from its material cause, he first refutes it with the words: "eternal difference."
For constant differentiation [occurs] by means of a cause...
The word "always" (nitya) is for the purpose of restriction;
[it means] "only in the case of difference.
The words "of the effect" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The word "hi" indicates that this is established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
thus, all of this has its object sublated.
The second [alternative] is not [the case].
Because it is irrelevant to the present subject.
Indeed, this [argument] was introduced precisely to establish that the manifold world (prapañca), beginning with space, is non-different from Brahman.
Even if the effect were non-different from its material cause, what would that have to do with the matter at hand?

Thinking that it has already been largely established that Brahman is not the material cause of the phenomenal world (prapañca), he states another objection with the words: "By the material cause... (upādānena).
But by means of clinging, however, there is a duality.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is carried over [from the previous verse].
By means of the material cause (*upādāna*), both difference and non-difference of the effect are cognized.
Therefore, even in this position, there is the fault of the subject matter being contradicted (*bādhitaviṣayatva*). *6,241*
How is it known that the effect is both different and non-different from the cause? To this he says: "Non-existent," etc.
For that which is non-existent in the form of an effect does indeed exist by virtue of being the nature of its cause.
Since that very thing, such as a jar, which is cognized by the opponent and accepted by him as existing prior to its production in the form of its cause, such as clay,

is indeed non-existent prior to its production in the form of an effect— characterized by features such as a broad base and a belly— it is therefore determined to be both different and non-different from its material cause (*upādāna*).
This is what is meant:
for the opponent indeed accepts the existence of an effect, such as a jar, prior to its production;
one must then state whether that [existence] is something entirely separate or whether it consists of the nature of the cause, such as clay.
Not the first,
because it is not accepted [by us] and because it is unperceived.
In the second [position], however, the non-difference of the effect from its material cause is indeed accepted;
yet there is no absolute identity,
because prior to its production, the jar and other effects do not exist in the form of the effect.
For if the jar and so forth were absolutely non-different from the clay and so forth,
then the jar and so forth would exist even prior to its production, because the clay and so forth exist at that time.
But this is not the case.
Therefore, we know that the jar and so forth are both different and non-different from the clay and so forth.

As for the establishment of difference and non-difference, as well as the resolution of contradictions against those who maintain that the effect is absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsatkāryavāda*), these will be set forth later. *6,243*
And as for that existence of the effect prior to its production which was asserted, that too is not tenable; thus he says: "non-existent" (asad).

If it is argued that since we both agree that things such as a jar exist prior to their production, yet at that same time they are non-existent, and therefore they must be existent [prior to production], the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is simply untenable;
for it is a contradiction for that very same thing to be both existent and non-existent at that very same place and time—if this is said, we reply: no.

With the intention that there is no contradiction due to the difference in form, it was stated [by the author] that [the effect exists] "as the nature of the cause" and "in the form of the effect. [Objection:
If this were so, some things would be existent, some would be non-existent, and nothing would be both existent and non-existent. [Reply:
It would not be so.
"Because there is no absolute difference between those two forms either.

This might be argued: "If the effect were non-existent prior to its production, that would be so; but why is it so? For the effect is thus absolutely non-different from its material cause (*upādāna*). Therefore, by demonstrating a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the opposing view, he establishes both the non-existence of the effect prior to its production and its difference from the material cause: "It would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)."
Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress in all cases of arising and destruction.

Otherwise, if it were admitted that the effect exists absolutely even prior to its production and is absolutely non-different from its cause, there would be an infinite regress and a lack of determinacy regarding production and destruction everywhere.
For instance, just as a cloth, being essentially identical with the threads, would exist even before [its production].
Likewise, since even threads exist only as being of the nature of their own causes, by this sequence everything would possess absolute existence by virtue of being of the nature of the root cause.
And since the root cause neither arises nor perishes, there would be no arising or perishing for cloth and the like either.

Consequently, the established distinction between the arising and perishing of things such as cloth—which possess them—and the self and so forth—which lack them—would not exist, as this is well-known in both worldly experience and the Vedas.
This is also an illustration;
it should be understood that if there were no arising and ceasing of cloth and other such things, there would be a deficiency in the activity of their causes.
Alternatively, by the terms "arising" and "ceasing," existence and non-existence are indicated.
And from this, the following is the meaning:
if the cloth were identical in nature to the threads and existed even prior to its production, then it would be perceived at that time as well, just like the threads.

If, on the other hand, something were accepted as existing even though it is not perceived, then there would be an infinite regress regarding the existence and non-existence of arising and destruction in all cases.
The universally accepted distinction—that things such as jars which are perceived exist, while things such as a donkey’s horn which are not perceived do not exist—would not hold. (6.247)
Alternatively, the terms "origination" (utpatti) and "destruction" (vināśa) are indicative of the demonstration thereof.
Thus, the construction [of the argument] is as follows: let alone anything else;

in the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda), for every student or opponent, there is an absence of an infinite regress even in the demonstration that origination and destruction take the form of "the non-existent does not originate" and "the existent does not perish."
It may be so;
for it must be stated: for what purpose is this proof?

If it is argued that [the means such as debate and disputation] are for the sake of producing knowledge in disciples and others, or for the destruction of ignorance, whereas in debate (*vāda*), wrangling (*jalpa*), and so forth, they are for the sake of producing fame and the like—
[we reply: that knowledge and so on, being existent, cannot be produced, because of its existence, just like the self (*ātman*).
That which is non-existent cannot be produced, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the collapse of the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
Likewise, if ignorance were existent, it could not be destroyed.

Otherwise, it would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*). If [the cause] were non-existent, then [the effect] could not arise at all, because [the cause] would be eternally absent.
Therefore, it is impossible to establish [the object] in any way whatsoever;
or rather, the phrase "of arising and destruction" is an indication of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharma*).
For instance:
If the effect were identical in nature to its material cause and were already existent prior to its production,
then there would be no end to the properties of production, destruction, and so forth;
for the threads, being already existent even beforehand, would not be produced at this time.
The cloth arises;
yet while the threads have not even perished, the cloth perishes.
The threads are many, whereas the cloth is one.
In this way, the distinction between the forms, the designations, the cognitions, and the effects should also be understood;
otherwise, this established order would not exist.
[Objection: But is not all of this, like a cloth, [merely a collection of parts]?
Just as [the objection] beginning with "like breath and so forth" was refuted by relying on both manifestation (*vyakti*) and non-manifestation (*avyakti*),
so too is it appropriate that the production of cloth and other such things occurs in relation to manifestation, while their destruction occurs in relation to non-manifestation.
Furthermore, causal factors (kārakas) are employed solely for the purpose of manifestation and non-manifestation;
it is precisely through manifestation and non-manifestation that perception and non-perception occur.
For this very reason, the process of communication is logically consistent.
Contradictory properties abide precisely in the form of the manifest and the unmanifest;
for just as a cloth that has been rolled up is not clearly perceived as "cloth," it cannot be used for covering nor does it dispel the cold.
It does not pervade many locations; however, when extended, it possesses clear cognition and so forth. Yet, there is no difference [between the two states] on account of this.

Nor is it the case that what was previously non-existent becomes manifest when extended. Just as the bodily air, when restrained by breath control (prāṇāyāma), performs only the function of sustaining life and not actions such as lifting, but performs those too once the restraint has ceased and its manifestation is attained; so it is here.
It is not differentiated by that much alone,
nor was it previously non-existent;
likewise, this [distinction] is also consistent with respect to manifestation and non-manifestation.
To this we reply:
what is this non-manifestation of the cloth prior to its production and after its destruction, and what is its manifestation in the interim?
If it is argued that non-manifestation is non-perception and manifestation is perception, to that he says: "anavasthā" (infinite regress).
If perception and non-perception themselves were arising and destruction,
then there would be an infinite regress regarding arising and destruction in all cases;
that is to say, whatever is perceived would have to arise at that very moment, and whatever is not perceived would have to be destroyed at that very moment.
Furthermore, if the cloth exists prior to its production, why is it not perceived, and how is it perceived afterwards?
One who offers the answer to this question—that it is simply due to perception and non-perception—would be a "beloved of the gods" (a fool) whose wisdom is truly to be praised.
Moreover, since the threads are perceived both before and after, how could the cloth, which is nothing more than those [threads], fail to be perceived while existing?
Otherwise, that [manifestation and non-manifestation] would also apply to the threads themselves.
Now, if manifestation and non-manifestation are indeed properties of the cloth,
then do those two also exist in the threads or not?
If it is argued that there is no absolute identity between cause and effect, and that they do indeed exist [as distinct], he replies: "Infinite regress" (anavasthā).

If manifestation and non-manifestation were the causes for the conventional designations of arising and destruction even in the case of threads, then there would be an infinite regress of arising and destruction everywhere.
[For it would follow that] the threads neither arise nor perish, but rather only the cloth does; thus, the established distinction between arising and destruction would not exist. (6.252)
Furthermore, if this manifestation is posited as the cause for conventional designations such as "arising" and so forth,
does it arise— being previously non-existent— through the potter's wheel, the cloth, and other such factors, and perish through the blow of a hammer and so forth;
or rather, is it already existent even prior to these, and indestructible?
In this way, is non-manifestation (*avyakti*) also previously non-existent and produced by the blow of a mallet or other such causes, or is it already existent even prior to that?
He refutes both of these initial positions with the words: "anavasthā" (infinite regress).
If both the manifest and the unmanifest were subject to arising and destruction, there would be an infinite regress of arising and destruction everywhere, resulting in a lack of systematic order.
The meaning is that this would constitute a contradiction (or abandonment) of the established tenet: "Nothing non-existent arises, and nothing existent perishes."
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "anavasthā" (infinite regress).
If manifestation and non-manifestation were always present, there would be an impossibility of establishing production and destruction anywhere.
For instance, it would not be possible to say, "The jar was unproduced for all this time, but has now been produced."

Because manifestation exists even prior to [the pot's] conventional usage as "arising," there would likewise be the conventional usage of the pot's existence even at a time subsequent to the blow of a mallet and so forth,
since its cause— manifestation— has not perished.

Likewise, even the expression "the jar has now perished" would not be possible, because the cause for the conventional usage of "destruction" has not manifested, and [the jar] continues to exist even prior [to that usage]. Thus, the futility of the operation of causal factors remains evident. *6,253*

Now, if in order to avoid this fault, manifestation and non-manifestation are themselves admitted to have further manifestations and non-manifestations, then those two would likewise be subject to the aforementioned faults resulting from such alternatives.
If, moreover, one were to admit yet further manifestations and non-manifestations for those as well, there would be an infinite regress; thus he says: "infinite regress" (anavasthā).
The locative case in "utpatti-nāśayoḥ" (at the time of arising and destruction) denotes the object.
Let there be infinite manifest and unmanifest entities;
since there is no destruction of the root, the fault of infinite regress does not apply—to this he says: "anavasthā" (infinite regress).

Otherwise, if one were to accept an infinite succession of unqualified individuals and non-manifestations, there would result an untenable infinite regress regarding the production and destruction of every jar and so forth.

For it is only when each subsequent individual and non-manifestation is established that the preceding individuals and non-manifestations can serve as the basis for the conventional usage of "production" and "destruction.
Consequently, because it leads to the exhaustion of all purpose, this infinite regress is indeed a logical flaw.
But is this not the same for you as well?
For "origination" is held by you to be the inherence of existence (*sattā*) in that which previously did not exist;
and since things would always exist due to the inherence of existence, origination would occur even before [the thing's production] and after its destruction.
And because there would be no destruction [of the series], he says: "infinite regress" (anavasthā).

This is the established principle that there is no infinite regress regarding production and destruction in all cases; otherwise, it would indeed follow that inherence itself must be admitted to have been produced.
This is not our position, because production will be explained in another manner later on.
Now, is origination (*jani*) existent prior [to the operation], or is it produced by the activity of the causal factors (*kāraka*)?
In the first case, the very same fault already mentioned applies.
In the second case, there would be an infinite regress, since the origination of origination would likewise require another origination, and so on.
Since destruction is likewise [untenable], he says: "infinite regress" (anavasthā).
In all cases, this infinite regress regarding arising and destruction has been stated;
otherwise, one would have to accept that the arising of a jar is distinct from the arising of that arising itself,
yet such is not accepted.
Rather, the very birth of the jar is itself the birth of birth.
As they say: "Just as the birth of birth is not other [than birth], so the birth of that [birth] is the birth of the entity.
For the identity of meaning between "the jar is born" and "the birth of the jar is born" is indeed accepted by both worldly convention and the investigators of reality.

Nor is it appropriate to accept such a distinction between manifestation (*vyakti*) and non-manifestation (*avyakti*), because apart from birth and destruction or perception and non-perception, manifestation and non-manifestation themselves lack any basis in valid cognition (*aprāmāṇikatva*).

[Objection: But if that which is non-existent were to arise and that which is existent were to perish, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding arising and destruction everywhere.
For if that were the case, even the horn of a hare would arise, and the self would perish; therefore, he says: "infinite regress" (anavasthā).

Otherwise, if one disregards the power of causes, there would be an infinite regress regarding both arising and ceasing. But this is not the case; rather, that which has a cause for its arising arises even though it was non-existent, and that which has a cause for its destruction ceases even though it was existent.
Furthermore, since there is no cause for the production of a donkey’s horn or for the destruction of the self, there is an absence of their production and destruction.

However, if the nature of the cause does not persist [in the effect], then this same over-extension (atiprasaṅga) applies even to the proponent of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (satkāryavādin).
Alternatively, this infinite regress would occur only if we were to assert that what is absolutely non-existent is produced, or that mere existence perishes.
It has been stated that "only what exists and what does not exist arises," and likewise, "it perishes just like that which possesses a cause of destruction. Furthermore,

as for the statement "because it is perceived when there is existence," which was presented as the meaning of the Sūtra, that is established only through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva*), and it does not prove absolute non-difference.
Now, suppose it is held that what is intended here is either a cognition colored by the cause (*kāraṇoparaktabuddhi*) or a cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyabuddhi*).
Even that, being satisfied by mere non-difference, is not capable of proving absolute identity.
Furthermore, this is already included within the phrase "and because of this reasoning" (*kiñcaitadyukteśca*), and thus need not be stated again.
Now, if direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is adduced by this [opponent], that too does not prove absolute non-difference.
For this very reason, the modification of the sūtra as "and because of existence" (*bhāvāt*) and "because of apprehension" (*upalabdheḥ*) is also refuted.
If the reasoning is "and because of being" (*sattvāt*), its meaning is already covered by the phrase "and because of reasoning" (*yukteśca*).
This is established by the [sūtras] "Because of scripture" and "And because of another word.
However, the objection based on the "designation of non-existence" (*asadvayapadeśa*) is entirely irrelevant;

for while the [scripture] ultimately intends to establish Brahman as the cause, it does not, even at first glance, convey the non-existence of the effect, since it merely appears to teach that the void or non-being is the cause.
As for the argument regarding "reasoning," we shall refute that reasoning later on.
Furthermore, the other teacher has explained the term "different word" (*śabdāntara*) quite differently elsewhere.
