Moreover, since cloth and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth do not lack the arising of specific qualities, they are not suitable examples at all; enough of this prolixity.
He establishes both that which was stated—"even though he is capable"—and that which was stated—"as if there were eternal difference"—by means of scripture as well: "even though he is capable."
Although the Blessed Viṣṇu is capable of not acting or of acting otherwise, [he does not do so].
"The Unborn creates the universe, which is non-different from Himself and yet differentiated by being non-different from His cause"—
thus is the meaning stated in its entirety concluded according to the Śruti.
Even though he is capable of not acting, he acts;

otherwise, even though he is capable of acting by means of fixed causes through that very reversal [of non-action] without other causes, it should be understood that he acts by means of fixed causes according to his will.
This is distinct from its own efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
It is both non-different and different from its material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).
For transmigrating beings, like those seized by a poison, are impelled by the Lord and are unable to remain without exerting the effort of sustenance, even against their will.
But it has been stated that the Blessed One is not like that; thus, although he is capable of acting, he is able to refrain from acting as well.
The meaning is that [the matter] has been stated in its entirety both previously and now, and not merely as something proximate.
Thus ends the section on "Origination" (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa) in the venerable Nyāyasudhā.
[======= JNys_2,1.VII: Itaravyapadeśādhikaraṇam =======] *6,265* // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section concerning the designation of the other (Itaravyapadeśādhikaraṇam).
// Oṃ: Because of the designation of [the Self] as other [than the body], there would follow the defects of not performing what is beneficial and so forth. Oṃ.//
Regarding this section, the Commentary states: "The position that the individual soul (jīva) is the agent—which is [prima facie] supported by scripture—is refuted in detail.
Here it must be asked: Is the agency of the soul being refuted here in every respect?
If one were to accept that [the soul's] independence consists merely in its being subject to Īśvara,
the first [alternative] is not tenable;
for if that were so, it would result in a contradiction with what will be stated later, such as "He is the agent because He possesses the purpose of the scripture."
Furthermore, because it would entail the absurdity of the futility of qualifiers such as "the impossibility of self-agency" and so forth,
the second [alternative] is not tenable;
for although the sūtras beginning with "because of the consequence of defects such as performing what is beneficial" can be interpreted as being intended to refute independence (*svātantrya*).
Because this sūtra is impossible to explain— whether it be taken as "the consequence of [the Self] being entirely affected" or "the contradiction with the scriptural texts on its partlessness"—
for this sūtra is clearly perceived as refuting agency in every respect. To explain:
Agency is pervaded by either being total or partial.
In that regard, if it were total, there would be a contradiction with experience;
and if one were to admit it to be partial, [it would contradict the scriptural statement]: "Now, that which is the individual soul (jīva) is eternal and partless."
Thus, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural teaching that [the self] is partless (*anaṃśatva*).
For us, agency—which is synonymous with capacity (*sāmarthya*) and consists of effort (*prayatna*) and so forth—is not distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*);
such that even if that [agency] were manifold, the partlessness of the soul would not be undermined.

Therefore, by the cessation of the pervader, the pervaded agency would also cease; thus, even though the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses diversity, its partlessness (*niraṃśatva*) would not be contradicted.
Consequently, it is understood that the intended meaning here is that by the cessation of the pervader, the pervaded agency also necessarily ceases.
This is because a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) must necessarily terminate in its contrapositive.

Now, if it is argued that these two reductios were stated not regarding agency in general, but rather specifically regarding the non-acceptance of the fact that the soul's agency is dependent upon God—
and thus, by obtaining its termination in the contrapositive, it will simply mean that [agency] is dependent upon God— this is not so.
This might be so if these two undesirable consequences could be resolved by accepting that the soul's agency is dependent upon God;
however, it is not so, for even when dependent on another, this [agent] must act either in its entirety or in part,
as there is no third possibility.

Alternatively, since agency is logically possible even when there is no dependence on another due to that very [independence], this interpretation—which fails to reach a definitive conclusion—is not tenable; rather, the intended meaning is precisely the absence of agency. And thus, there would be a contradiction with what is to be stated later.
Now, if it were the case that the soul has no agency at all in reality, but that agency is merely based on conceit, there would be no contradiction;
but this is not so.

Since its reality will be established by means of the passage beginning with "vihāropadeśāt" (*6,266), this present topic is difficult to resolve; therefore, accepting the second position, I shall explain the two undesirable consequences (*prasaṅga*) regarding the dependence of the individual soul’s agency upon God. First, regarding the acceptance of such dependence on God, I shall demonstrate the manner in which those undesirable consequences are avoided by citing scriptural statements.
He demonstrates this with the words: "Even of that which is partless."

"Because of the designation as something else, there follows the defect of not performing what is beneficial and so forth. (BBs 2.1.21) "To him who truly bestows some measure of power upon the partless individual soul for its various tasks—to that Self-existent One, I offer salutation. (MAnu 2.1.94)
"By the application of some capacity," because of the employment of a capacity corresponding to the task;
"to the Self-existent One (svayambhuve)," that is, to the independent one (*svatantrāya*);
by this statement, it follows that this intended meaning is established. This is how the text continues.
And from this, the following is meant:
if the individual soul (jīva) is accepted as an agent by virtue of its dependence upon the Supreme Lord, then its status as an agent is indeed logically established.
Because the two undesirable consequences (*prasaṅga*) can be resolved:
for by accepting that [the cause] is partless (*anaṃśatva*), there is no contradiction with the term "partless" (*niravayavatva*).

Even though it is partless, since it is possible for it to exercise a capacity corresponding to its effects through the power of the inconceivable might of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), there is no consequence of the whole being consumed (*kṛtsnaprasakti*).
This will become clear immediately following this point (*6,271*).

Having thus explained the logical possibility of the conclusion being the opposite through the method of introduction (*upodghāta*), he now applies the Sūtra to the intended meaning, beginning with "If" (*yadi*).
If Hari were not to apply His own power through a portion to the various tasks, then He would have to exert His entire effort everywhere, or else He would be subject to partiality.
"By a portion" means by a part corresponding to the task to be performed.

Here, although it should have been stated that "if [the agent] were not dependent on God," the statement beginning with "by a portion" is for the purpose of clarifying the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) and for the purpose of elaborating upon the manner in which [the agent] is dependent on God.
Otherwise, it would follow that even in the case of picking up a blade of grass and such, the effort would have to be either entirely complete or only partial;
and thus there would be a contradiction with both experience and scripture.
Therefore, the remaining conclusion is that the individual soul (jīva) is an agent only insofar as it is dependent upon the Supreme Lord.
Nor can the agency [of the Self] be established as being merely illusory through the postulation of parts created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);

for it is improper to abandon what is proven by valid means of knowledge— namely, that which is established by such authorities as "even though it is partless"— and instead accept what is neither authoritative nor logically tenable.
[Objection: "Surely this can be accomplished by the power of the individual soul (jīva) alone.
[Reply: Not so;
for that [individual soul] lacks the inconceivable power capable of accomplishing the impossible.
Alternatively, if [the soul were the agent], there would follow the fault of its not performing what is beneficial and so forth.

For in this context, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) has not suspected that the individual soul (jīva) is the agent of all effects such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest; rather, he has suspected only its agency regarding jars and the like.
First of all, because it is established by direct experience, the agency of potters and others cannot be abandoned.

In that regard, if one were to admit the Lord's agency as well, there would be the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (kalpāgaurava); therefore, the Lord does not possess universal agency. And so, how could there be any possibility of His possessing inconceivable power?

But surely the author of the Sūtras himself will state the manifold nature of the individual souls through the example of "smell" in the sense of their distinction [from one another], and he will also state their atomicity in the Sūtra: "Because of their passing out, going, and returning.
And since a manifold nature cannot belong to an atom simultaneously except by way of having parts, their possession of parts is also established from that very same [statement].

"How then can there be a contradiction with the term 'partlessness' (niravayavatva) here?"—anticipating this doubt from one who speaks with a hidden intention, [the author] refutes it without yet revealing that intention, by saying "For of the whole... and so forth.
In two and a half verses:

"For those things such as cloth which are the possessors of parts are called 'possessors of parts' because their parts are indeed distinct from one another; but consciousness is not like this at all. (Manu 2.1.96)
Therefore, the Vedic revelation applies the term "partless" to these [entities],
even though they possess multiple natures, solely on account of their specific [essential] nature.
For indeed, the possession of parts (sāṃśatā) exists in those [atoms] precisely because they possess multiple natures.
In this context, by the phrase "called the state of having many forms," he accepts what is about to be stated.
The word "many" (*bahu*) is an indicator of multiplicity.
It is called "the state of having many forms" (*bahusvarūpatākhyā*) because it is manifested as having many forms.
The word "tu" (but) indicates the superiority of that which is prohibited by the Veda.
[The locative] "teṣu" means "among those sentient beings.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates establishment through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For this very reason, there is the restriction "it certainly exists.
Consequently, the meaning is as follows:

it certainly possesses the manifold natures that will be described hereafter, as well as atomism, and its possession of parts—which is established through the impossibility of [those natures] otherwise.
Because that which is authoritative cannot be abandoned; if so, how is it that its opposite has been stated here? To this, it is said: "Of the whole," and so forth.
The first word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that [the fact] is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); the second has the sense of "because.

Those well-known wholes (*aṃśin*), such as cloth and the like, are said to be wholes composed of parts (*aṃśa*)—such as threads and so forth—which are mutually distinct from one another, yet distinct-and-non-distinct from the whole in the manner to be described; they are not, however, wholes composed of parts that are absolutely non-distinct.

But consciousnesses (*cetanā*) are not related to their parts as a whole is to its parts in the manner described for cloth and the like; rather, they are absolutely non-different from one another and from the whole.

Because this is so, due to their dissimilarity to established wholes, the scriptural term "partless" (*anaṃśin*) applies to these consciousnesses, even though they possess multiple natures and, for that very reason, are possessed of parts.
But this is not with the intention of asserting a total absence of parts;
therefore, there is no contradiction.
[Objection: If there is no difference, how then can there be multiplicity, since multiplicity is pervaded by difference?
And how is there "possession of parts" (aṃśitva)?
Because the sense of possession (matvartha) is untenable without difference, it was therefore stated: "precisely because of the distinction.
Even in the absence of difference, the construction is: "precisely because of the distinction that serves as its substitute, [the term applies] to those things of manifold natures."

Alternatively, by accepting the point that will be stated in the phrase "even in those of manifold natures," the contradiction [raised] by the words "of the possessor of parts" (*aṃśinaḥ*) and so forth is resolved. In that regard, one might raise the objection: "If there is no difference, how can there be multiplicity and the state of being a possessor of parts? To this [the author replies]:
He refutes this with the three quarters beginning with "viśeṣād eva" (specifically because...).
Even without any distinction whatsoever, there exists within them a multiplicity of forms and a state of having parts as they appear;
how so?
"Specifically because of this.
From what is this inferred?
He states by means of the word "hi" (for/because) that it is precisely because of the contradiction between two scriptural passages.

Although the subject under discussion here is "of the individual soul" (*jīvasya*), the fact that it is stated in general terms as "that which is sentient" (*yaccetanā*) indicates that this same principle applies even to mere sentience in general. Alternatively, [the author] uses this to illuminate the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of insentience, [showing that] if these individuals were the possessors of parts (*aṃśin*), they would necessarily be like cloth and other such things. *6,281*
Now, if this is so, what is the purpose of postulating that the soul's agency is dependent upon God?

For even in the absence of such dependence, since manifoldness exists inherently [in the soul], the performance of action is possible through one part; thus, there is no risk of the entire [soul] being simultaneously engaged.
Furthermore, because there is no distinct division of parts, the contradiction with the scriptural term "partless" (*niravayava*) is also avoided.
When the opponent has revealed his own intention by stating that no activity of God is observed beyond this, [the author] says: "By way of multiplicity."
Due to the necessity of inseparable concomitance with multiplicity, there must be distinctness by way of a fixed rule.
If the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, had not established such a rule.

If the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, were not thus the establisher of rules— that is, if He were not the author of the systematic order so that there might be no diversity among individual souls despite their plurality—
then, by reason of that very plurality, diversity would exist even among the souls.
This is because of the rule characterized by the inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between the number "plurality" and "diversity."
As it has been said: "Because of following after that [the Lord], there is distinctness.
This is what is meant:
if the agency of the individual soul (jīva) were admitted independently of the Supreme Lord, the two aforementioned undesirable consequences could not be avoided in any way.
To explain: first of all, how is the consequence of total pervasion (kṛtsnaprasakti) to be avoided?
If you say it is by virtue of the existence of multiplicity, [we reply:]...
In that case, since plurality in the world is invariably concomitant with difference, the multiplicity of the individual soul (jīva) would entail its differentiation as well;
and thus, the wicked soul's violation of the scriptural teaching on partlessness would be difficult to avoid.
If, on the other hand, difference is not admitted in order to avoid that [consequence], then [multiplicity] cannot be maintained.
In that case, since the cessation of the pervader necessarily entails the cessation of the pervaded, even the number "plurality" would have to be abandoned;
and thus, once again, that same undesirable consequence—the contingency of everything being one—would follow.
Now, if it is argued that the rule is that plurality exists only among insentient things and not among sentient ones;
Why is this so?
If it is argued that it is because it is seen to be thus, we say no;
for this is a question concerning the causal agent (kāraka), not a question concerning the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
If it is argued that this is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of things, we say no; for that would lead to the extension of the doctrine of non-divine causality (*anīśvaravāda*).
Furthermore, how can something be both "inherent nature" and "contradictory"?
For it is not logical that one and the same thing should be accompanied by a second of its own accord;
as for the claim that there is no contradiction because this is established by valid cognition, that has already been refuted.
If it is argued that this is possible through the power of consciousness (*caitanya*), [we reply: no.
Let it be that some thing possessing smoke might be devoid of fire.
If you argue that this is possible due to a specific power [of the fire],
then let it be possible for the pot as well.
It is not that there is no distinction therein;
if you argue that it is due to the variety of distinctions, then from where does that [variety] itself arise?

Therefore, the Blessed Lord alone, acting as the regulator of the specificities of His own form and nature, having established consciousness as the delimiting factor and making the particularity the instrumental cause, brings together even the contradictory [qualities] of non-duality and multiplicity; by means of non-duality, He sets aside the contradiction regarding partlessness, and by means of multiplicity, He overcomes the contingency of total pervasion, [manifesting] a specific capacity corresponding to the effect.
"One must accept that [the Lord] causes [the soul] to act by joining it with the individual soul (jīva).

Now, one might object: "Since all this is impossible to accomplish through the power of the individual soul and so forth, how could even the Blessed Lord accomplish it? To this, he says: "But for him... "But for him, because of his possession of all powers, everything is indeed possible. (Manu 1.99cd)
Thus, it is established that there is no contradiction whatsoever when the purport of this sūtra is explained in this manner.
Thus ends the section on "Designation as Another" (*itaravyapadeśādhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
[======= JNys_2,1.VIII: The Section on Having Scripture as its Source =======] *6,287* // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section concerning having scripture as its source.
Oṃ. But it must be heard from scripture, because [the Veda] is the source of verbal knowledge. Oṃ.

But surely, the agency of God also is not tenable, because, like the individual soul (jīva), it would entail the consequence of His being entirely consumed [in the act]. For [if He were to create], the entire cosmic egg— or even an anthill— would [be produced by Him].
One who employs equal capacity in creation is a discerning person.
If it is argued that there is no fault because there is no other alternative, we say no; for that would contradict his status as the Lord (Īśvara).
If, as a means of avoiding this [objection], partial activity is admitted, then there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning partlessness, such as "There is no diversity here";
furthermore, because of being devoid of body, senses, and so forth, there could be no agency.
For no agent devoid of a body and so forth has ever been perceived;
moreover, [an agent] would be deprived of a substratum such as the earth.
Thus, even though it is so difficult to establish, if God were to possess agency, why then could it not belong to the individual soul (jīva) as well?
Because no specific distinction is perceived, and thus the capacity for universal agency is completely cast aside, this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is refuted in this section.
He states its purport: "But of that... and so forth.
But because the Veda is the root of verbal testimony,
and because it possesses all powers, it is logical that it should indeed possess all properties.
The word "tu" (but) indicates the distinction [of the Lord] from the individual soul (jīva).
The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the reasons.
Since the scripture declares that the Lord is transcendent to the world, He is accessible solely through sacred tradition (āgama), and thus there is no room for contradiction with reasoning (yukti).

Furthermore, this is because the possession of diverse and infinite powers is understood from such scriptural passages as, "The Puruṣa possesses manifold powers," and "That deity is endowed with all powers."

Even for that which is devoid of distinct parts, there is no consequence of its being entirely involved in all its effects; even though there is a multiplicity of constituent aspects of its own nature, there is no actual division; and even when performing an action through one aspect, there is no contradiction with the scriptural description of it as being partless.
It is argued that the establishment of agency even for one devoid of a body and so forth is logical.

Now, an objection may be raised: was it not stated in the previous section (*adhikaraṇa*) that even the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*), though difficult to accomplish, is made possible through the power of the Lord (*īśvara*)?
If that is so, how can there be any room here for a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
For it is inconceivable that one who desires to connect what has been cognized elsewhere should not desire to do so with respect to his own [self].
It is said in reply: this point was not stated by the author of the Sūtras in the section concerning the past (atītādhikaraṇa).
However, keeping a future point in mind, the refutation of the doctrine that the individual soul (jīva) is the agent was specifically performed.
But the Commentator, desiring the welfare of his disciples, has drawn forward even a point yet to be stated in order to resolve the contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

Those who follow the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) and those who follow the theory of illusory appearance (*vivartavāda*) explain that the fact that Brahman is the material cause of the world is first challenged by the argument "the entire [Brahman] would be consumed," and then resolved by the passage beginning with "But on account of scripture" (*śruteḥ*).
For instance: Brahman is not the material cause of the world;
because if that were the case, it would follow that the entirety of Brahman would assume the form of its effects.

Furthermore, if Brahman were non-existent during its state of persistence, there would follow the futility of teaching the vision of it. Now, if— seeking to avoid this fault— it is asserted that Brahman transforms in one part while persisting in another part, then the scriptural texts concerning its partlessness, such as "It is without parts, tranquil," would be contradicted.
To this it is replied: this is not a fault, for [the scripture says],
"He made himself by himself."

This is because such scriptural passages as these establish that Brahman is the material cause of the world and that there is no total transformation [of its nature]; furthermore, since this is based on the authority of the Word (śabda), there is no room for contradiction with reason (yukti).
Moreover, the Supreme Deity is heard in scripture to be endowed with all powers.
“[Brahman is] the agent of all actions and the possessor of all desires,” and so forth;

consequently, it is argued that even though Brahman is partless, its status as the material cause of the world is established precisely because there is no possibility of its being entirely transformed [into the effect], and so on.
This interpretation is untenable.
This being the case, it would follow that these sūtras lack the logical connection characterized by inclusion within this particular chapter.
To address the question "How so?", he says: "Contradiction" (*virodha*).
Contradiction is that which is refuted in the second [chapter], regarding the preeminence of all [the qualities].
But in the chapter on Nārāyaṇa... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.100a–c]
The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis.

Whatever contradiction with reason and other means of knowledge there may be regarding the superiority, distinction, supreme excellence, and absolute transcendence of Nārāyaṇa from the Supreme Brahman over all that is sentient and insentient— that very contradiction is refuted here in this second chapter.
However, being the self of all by virtue of being the material cause of the entire world does not entail being qualified by everything;
nor is that even useful for the purpose at hand;
on the contrary, it is indeed contradictory.
How, then, can the resolution of that contradiction be included within this?
[Objection: Is it not the case that Brahman possesses all excellence precisely because it is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world?
For the world is not the material cause of the world. If this is your thought:
In that case, do you maintain a difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*)?
If so, there is a contradiction with the stated principle that "it is not different from that" (*tadananyatva*).
If you argue that the world is not different from Brahman, but Brahman is different from the world, we say no.
Because the answer has already been stated (*uktottaratvāt*).

Since it was not previously asserted that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*), the objection regarding the consequence of the whole being transformed (*kṛtsnaprasakti*) and so forth has no basis.

Furthermore, since there is no scripture (*śruti*) establishing transformation (*pariṇāma*), and because it is impossible for the world-phenomenon (*prapañca*) consisting of space and so on to have its root in words—which would otherwise be impossible for [an unchanging Brahman]—the proposed resolution is also untenable.
In the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*), however, this doubt finds no room whatsoever.

It has been clearly stated in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* that, just as mother-of-pearl and the like are the substrata for the superimposition of silver and so forth, Brahman is the substratum for the superimposition of the world through ignorance (*avidyā*).
In that case, how could there be an inquiry into whether [the cause] is destroyed in its entirety or in part?
If it is argued that [the world] is called a "horn" because it has not been previously stated [to exist], then one must say that it was stated [in the form of a command]: "Remember!
Furthermore, the fact that the phenomenal world (prapañca) is superimposed upon Brahman must be clearly established.
What is the connection of the passage beginning with "But because of scripture" (*śruteḥ*)?
Someone, whose mind is bewildered by not seeing a refutation, says:
"Indeed, Brahman conjoined with ignorance (*avidyā*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world."
In this regard, this objection concerning the fact that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the material cause (*upādāna*), and its refutation,
are both extremely weak;
for even the status of ignorance as a material cause is not real.
This is because it is itself an object of doubt precisely due to its lack of deliberative cogency.

Furthermore, what will the arguments regarding the total pervasion [of the cause by the effect] and the possession of parts avail against ignorance (*avidyā*)? Any proposed solution is entirely inconsistent.
By this, it should be understood that the objection and its refutation based on "the state of being a modification" (*vikaraṇatva*) are also irrelevant;
for the status of being the substratum of an illusion does not depend upon a body or the like.
If it is argued that "that [status] pertains to the Lord (*īśvara*)," we say no.

Since there is no implication [of the former] due to the absence of its being a ray (*kiraṇa*), students should understand for themselves such points as these; thus, the Teacher has stated that there is indeed no inconsistency. This would indeed be an inconsistency if the resolution of the contradiction regarding Brahman’s possession of all qualities were to require textual supplementation (*adhyāhāra*). Why is that so? To this he says: "Other than that... ... "Others than those, who go here and there" (Manu 2.1.100c).
Therefore, other contradictions than those concerning all specificities have been addressed and resolved within their respective topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*).
This is what is meant:
it is generally accepted that the second chapter has non-contradiction as its defining characteristic.
Since the resolution of contradictions is not appropriate when the subject matter has not been stated, the non-contradiction [of the Vedas] constitutes the subject matter of the second chapter.
In the first chapter, by means of demonstrating the subject matter and purpose of the scripture through its opening sūtra, the necessity of the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) was established.
That [inquiry], however, is to be completed across all four chapters and does not conclude in a single one.

Then, when there arises a desire to know its essential nature— asking whether that Brahman is the individual soul (*jīva*) or the insentient (*jaḍa*)— it cannot be pointed out by directly grasping it like a horn.
Therefore, in the second aphorism, it is established that it is superior to all and distinct from everything by demonstrating its difference from all else.
Because a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which cannot be conceived as belonging to either similar or dissimilar classes,
and because its purpose is the exclusion of everything else;

having stated in the third aphorism that the scripture (*śāstra*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that [characteristic], its objective domain— consisting of a reality excluded from all sentient and insentient things both generally and specifically— is established through the subsequent discourse.
And thus, two types of contradictions are to be resolved:

those concerning all the specific attributes established in the second Sūtra, and those concerning the reconciliation with the Śāstra. Among these, the latter have been resolved in their respective sections by means of [the arguments] beginning with "because of the word for modification" (vikāra-śabdāt) and so forth; therefore, by process of elimination, it is understood that the purpose of the second [Sūtra] is precisely the resolution of the contradiction regarding all the specific attributes.

[Objection: But has not the mutual contradiction among the Śrutis also been resolved in the second chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras] by such passages as "Because of the non-hearing of ether" (*na viyadaśruteḥ*)?
So how can it be said that the contradiction regarding the preeminence of Brahman over all is refuted in the second chapter? To this, he says: "In the section on creation" (*sṛṣṭau*).
The mutual non-contradiction of the statements concerning creation and dissolution, as well as those denoting the nature of the individual soul (jīva), is the subject matter of the second chapter.
This refers to those statements that designate the form of the living being (jīva); it should also be understood as including those concerning the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth.
The qualification "creation and so forth" is intended to indicate the logical justification [for the inquiry].
The word "but" (tu) serves to specify a distinction.

Furthermore, that mutual contradiction among scriptural passages which was the subject matter of the second chapter is likewise resolved precisely by the removal of contradictions regarding the supreme Lord's possession of all distinctive attributes.
However, the distinction is that in the first and second quarters [of the verse] it is direct, whereas in the third and fourth it is mediated.

To explain: does the resolution of mutual contradictions among the Śrutis have as its sole fruit the determination of their authority (*prāmāṇya*), or rather the determination of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*)?
Not the first [alternative],

because it would follow that Mīmāṃsā is a treatise on logic (nyāyaśāstra). Furthermore, if this were the case, why would one even attempt to resolve contradictions with scriptural passages concerning the creation of ether and so forth?
For even sentences concerning the *uditahoma* (the offering after sunrise) and so forth can be justified as *upādāna* (inclusion) according to the principles of the *Nyāya-darśana*.
Furthermore, the sequence beginning with ether (*ākāśa*) and air (*vāyu*) is not of absolute necessity here.
In the second case as well, is the very sequence of creation and so forth the object of knowledge (*prameya*), or is it something else that constitutes its primary constituent (*aṅgin*)?
Not the first [alternative],
because its own nature is not the motive [for inquiry]; thus,
it is not what is to be presented at the outset.
Otherwise, one would also have to resolve the contradiction with statements regarding the re-offering of oblations (*uditahoma*) and so forth;
furthermore, the extraction of the subject matter concerning the creation (*sṛṣṭi*) and other topics would be without a basis.
Therefore, the second [alternative] alone remains.

Nor is there any other object of knowledge, such as creation and so forth, that could serve as the primary subject (*aṅgin*) apart from Brahman—the subject first mentioned in the second aphorism—because [Brahman] possesses all attributes.
Therefore, what was stated is correct.

Thus, it is established that the meaning of the aphorism as explained by the opponent is untenable, because it lacks the logical connection (*saṅgati*) characterized by inclusion within the second chapter and because it is contradictory; hence, the meaning of the aphorism as we have stated it is proven. *6,302*
This sūtra is intended to resolve the objection that the Lord's status as an agent is untenable because he is devoid of instruments such as a body and sense organs.
If it be argued that [the Lord] is not [the cause] because of His being devoid of organs, that has already been answered. Om.
Thus [it is said]:
this is not to be undertaken,
because it is redundant.

For by the very sūtras— "On account of scripture, [Brahman] has sound as its root," "And thus also in the case of the Self," "And [the Lord is] endowed with all [powers], for it is seen [in scripture]," and so forth— the resolution of every apparent inconsistency is achieved through such arguments as its supramundane nature, its being cognizable solely through the Word (śabda), and its possession of diverse and infinite powers.
For that which is not desired as the substratum of direct perception requires the mediation of a body;
and for that whose knowledge is adventitious, it requires the sense organs for that purpose;
and that which is heavy-bodied and cannot remain [unsupported] requires a support such as the earth.
But since the Blessed One is omnipotent and omniscient, why would he depend on anything else?
Nor is there any further doubt remaining for which a new undertaking would be necessary; therefore, he says: "māna... (pride, etc.).
If it is argued that [the Lord] does not [act] because He is devoid of instruments (*vikaraṇatva*), that has already been answered.
Furthermore, there is no tautology due to the distinction between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyaviśeṣa*). (BBs 2.1.31; MAnu 2.1.102ab)

Just as in passages such as "prāṇa" and so forth, there is no fault of tautology despite the identity of the means of knowledge because of the distinction of the objects to be known, so too here, despite the identity of the object to be known, there is no fault of tautology because of the distinction of the means of knowledge.
This is what is meant:
is the mere statement of an already expressed meaning the fault?
Or is it a restatement of what has already been said? Not the first,
because that would entail the persistence of the fault even in the statement that extends the refutation of what was previously stated.
The second [position], however, is not established in the present context;
for even when the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is identical, there exists a distinction between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Indeed, in this case, although the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*), who possesses a divine, auspicious form consisting of consciousness, bliss, and so forth, lacks a material body and the like, His agency regarding all effects has been stated by relying on such scriptural passages as "without hands or feet" (*apāṇipāda*).
Alternatively, it should be construed as "specifically regarding the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge.
And thus the meaning is this:
by means of the preceding sūtras, relying upon the means of knowledge whose objects are general, a general resolution of all inconsistencies has been provided.

But here, since the resolution of the impossibility of the particular is effected by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that has the particular as its very object, how can there be any room for the fault of tautology?
If it is argued that even so, the objection is not tenable, we say no;
for it is justified by the desire to know the particular.
Thus concludes the section on "Having Scripture as its Source" (*śabdamūlatva*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
[======= JNys_2,1.IX: The Section on the Lack of Purpose =======] *6,304* // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section on the lack of purpose (naprayojanādhikaraṇam).
// Oṃ. [The Lord] does not [act] because He has a purpose. Oṃ. //

Oṃ. "As in the world, [the Lord's activity] is mere sport (līlā), for it is absolute (kaivalya). Oṃ. This section is commenced to resolve the objection that because He lacks a purpose for creation and so forth, He would be deficient and therefore incomplete. However, this appears to be untenable.
For instance:
if the proponent's intended aim were to establish the existence of a purposeful agent in order to prove the world's imperfection, then the first sūtra would be inappropriate;
for, with respect to one who seeks to prove imperfection, the reason "possessing a purpose" would be unestablished (asiddha).
Now, if it were intended to establish that "if the agent were to have a purpose, he would consequently be incomplete," then this Sūtra would be entirely redundant;
for the opponent himself has already admitted that one who is incomplete cannot possess a purpose.

Otherwise, there would be no resolution of the contradiction. Furthermore, the second sūtra, "But as in the world, it is mere sport," is inappropriate for both positions, because the refutation consisting in the reduction of the means of proof has not been raised.
Not so;
for does the Lord have a purpose in creating and so forth, or not?
In the first case, it would follow that he is incomplete.

In the second case, however, agency is untenable because he would be occupied with a purpose; thus, in both ways, the opponent intends to show that God’s agency in the creation of the world and so forth is untenable.
Therein, with the first sūtra, he presents the position regarding the absence of a purpose along with its supporting arguments.
Then, the second sūtra is intended to refute the defects stated therein.

Alternatively, the proponent (siddhāntin), having raised the dilemma as to whether "this" refers to the wealth itself as the object of the agent's purpose— which implies incompleteness— or to its acquisition, refutes the first alternative with the first [part of the verse]:

"Being possessed of a purpose is not to be proven by way of agency," because it is certain that there is an absence of purpose precisely due to the state of having already accomplished what was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatva*).

Nor is the reason unestablished, for scripture declares: "This indeed is the supreme bliss, free from desire and free from blemish. As for the inference that [Brahman] is incomplete because it possesses a purpose, that is refuted by its very miscarriage.
Stating another refutation of the first [position], he refutes the second by means of the second [point].
Now, it was said here that according to the sūtra "as in the world," no refutation whatsoever is raised against the proof (*sādhana*) or the application (*apādana*).
This is not so.
Intending to show that [the opponent's position] arises from the manifestation of sublation and so forth, he states the purport of the second sūtra: "sadā" (always).

[The world] is not [created] for the sake of some purpose; rather, it is like the world [in general], being solely a sport (*līlā*). The constant activity of the Lord proceeds from his very nature alone. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.102cd) *6,309*

Just as in the world the activity of fire, wind, and so forth is observed, so too the Lord’s activity at the beginning of creation and other times is established as proceeding solely from His own nature, even without a purpose; this is the remainder [of the argument].
Thus, it is stated that the proof of a purpose through the Lord’s activity is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and its object is sublated (*bādhita-viṣaya*).
Furthermore, the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is shown to be devoid of pervasion (*vyāpti-vikala*) and not to lead to a necessary conclusion (*viparyayāparyavasāyin*).
Now, one might think:
"The activity of volition is never observed without a purpose;
therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (anaikāntya) and so forth."
That too is not the case;
for we observe that even one who is intoxicated engages in dancing, singing, and so forth, precisely because of an excess of pleasure.

Now, it may be argued that the activity of a discerning person is never observed to occur without being directed toward a purpose, and this [activity of the intoxicated person] is indeed the activity of a discerning person.

Therefore, [the treatise] must possess a stated purpose; thus, having established that it has both a goal to be proven (*sādhya*) and a consequence to be reached (*āpādya*), he says: "The limb... and so forth.
Just as certain gestures of a man's limbs may be devoid of any specific purpose.
Some [actions], such as the movement of fingers during an exposition and so forth,
are devoid of instruction— that is, they are devoid of an instruction regarding a specific purpose—
and likewise the activity of the Lord [is also such]; this is the connection with what precedes.
Nevertheless, the sense is that there is no escape from fallacies such as inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*).
Regarding what was stated—that the activity of the Lord is known to proceed from his very nature even without a purpose—he now states the proof for that: "Of the God," etc. (*devasya*).
"The Śruti declares directly: 'This is the very nature of the Divine.'"
"The scripture clearly states the meaning in these words: ‘This is the very nature of the Lord; what desire can there be for one whose wishes are already fulfilled?
This refers to the Lord’s will regarding the objects of creation and so forth."
That is to say, activity is preceded by that;
it is simply the intrinsic nature [of things],
not for the sake of a purpose.
The meaning is: "From where [could it arise]? Because for one whose desires are fulfilled, the longing for a purpose is impossible.
Some explain this sūtra otherwise:

"Just as in the world, even for a great king who rules over the earth with its seven continents and possesses complete skill, heroism, and prowess, undertakings such as playing with a ball are seen to have mere play as their sole purpose."

In the same way, for the Supreme Brahman as well, whose creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world are brought about by His mere volition, play (*līlā*) alone is the motive; he refutes this very point with the words "play" (*krīḍām*).
If one were to regard play as the motive for creation, such a theory would contradict the Veda.
"Others say creation is for the sake of enjoyment, and others that it is for the sake of sport.

Having thus made the opponent's position—that the Lord’s engagement in creation and so forth has sport as its motive—the established conclusion (siddhānta) was reached through scripture and reasoning: that this is simply the very nature of the Divine, and thus there is not even a trace of a [separate] motive.
Therefore, because this contradicts the Śruti, it is indeed a false interpretation; moreover, he states that this interpretation does not conform to the words of the Sūtra with the word "iti."
Thus, it has been determined by the Lord himself that this is merely sport.

Since it has been stated thus: "Making play the motive, creation is contrary to the Śruti," therefore, for the Lord who follows the Śruti, it is determined that His engagement in creation and so forth is solely for the sake of sport (*līlā-kaivalya*).
It is not "for the sake of sport" [as a purpose]; hence, this interpretation is also untenable.
Alternatively, the reason stated in the preceding sentence is the subject to be proven (*sādhya*).

Since creation, if it were made with sport as its motive, would contradict the Śruti, therefore in this Sūtra the author has determined and explained that it is mere sport alone, and not that it is for the sake of sport.
Furthermore, one who seeks to establish or bring about the possession of a purpose through the agency of a creator must be asked:
is the intended purpose related to oneself, or is it related to another?
Now, regarding the common [fallacy]:
in the first proof, there is inconclusiveness (anaikāntya);
in the reductio ad absurdum (āpādane), there is a lack of pervasion (vyāptyabhāva).
In the case of the opposite conclusion, there is indeed a deviation [from the rule].
For we observe compassionate persons who act solely for the sake of another's purpose without aiming at their own benefit.
Nor should it be argued that they do not act for the sake of an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha).
For we observe that animals and those who are like animals engage in activities such as protecting their offspring;
yet it is impossible for them to possess either a purpose-oriented intention or compassion.
In the second case as well, there is simply the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) and so forth.
Because it is frequently observed that activity proceeds for the sake of one's own purpose;

and because even in the case of the Blessed One, although he lacks a personal purpose, since he accepts [activity] with the aim of another's purpose, there would follow the consequence of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) and the fallacy of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhatva*) through gradual application.
For this very reason, the third [alternative] is also not tenable.
For this very reason, the qualification [of agency] by means of any [particular agent] is refuted, as is the over-extension that [if it] had the nature of activity, it would always be active. *6,314*
This might be so, provided that there were a reference to another's purpose in the activity of God; however, such a thing is not fit to be accepted.
For it has been refuted in every way by the Śruti with the words "What desire could He have? and by the author of the Sūtras with the word "No" (na). To this, he says: "The Self" (ātma).
The Śruti has forbidden desire for the sake of one's own personal interest.
The term "Śruti" is also an elliptical designation for the author of the Sūtras;
the implication is that he indeed accepts [the Veda's] being for the sake of another's purpose.
To the question, "How is this understood?", he says: "Not... (neti).
Since [the world] does not exist by virtue of having a purpose, the Teacher of the World said: [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.1.105cd].

Since he accepted the purpose of others and thereby prevented it from being directed solely toward his own purpose, for this very reason he stated the logical reason there as "because it possesses a purpose"; otherwise, he would not have said this. This is what is meant: [The text continues: "If the Blessed One had been one who sought only his own benefit, he would not have taught the Dharma to others; for how could one who seeks only his own benefit teach the Dharma to others? Therefore, because he taught the Dharma to others, it is understood that the Blessed One was not one who sought only his own benefit. Thus, by means of the reason "because it possesses a purpose," he established that the Blessed One was not one who sought only his own benefit. Furthermore, he stated the reason: "Because he taught the Dharma to others. If he had been one who sought only his own benefit, he would not have taught the Dharma to others. Therefore, it is understood that the Blessed One was not one who sought only his own benefit. This is the meaning. Furthermore, he stated the reason: "Because he taught the Dharma to others. If he had been one who sought only his own benefit, he would not have taught the Dharma to others. [======= JNys_2,1.X: The Section on Partiality and Cruelty =======] *6,359* // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, begins the section on partiality and cruelty.

Does the Lord, in producing for living beings their various bodies, sense organs, and objects, as well as their results characterized by pleasure and pain, depend upon their karma in the form of merit and demerit, or not? In the first case, his sovereignty would be lost.

In this section, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is refuted.

The particle *hi* indicates that the dependence of everything upon the Blessed Lord is well-established through scripture (*śruti*) and other authorities.
Regarding the objection "How so?":
for an object is not attained in two ways—
either due to a lack of independence or due to a lack of desire to obtain it.
And he does not lack [sovereignty] in two ways:
either due to a lack of independence or due to a lack of the desire to abandon [defilements].
Indeed, the Lord possesses independence in all respects.
Furthermore, because he is a person of discernment, he possesses the desire: "May I always be endowed with qualities such as bliss and be free from defects such as suffering.
Therefore, how could it be that he does not possess the fullness of qualities like bliss and remain far removed from all defects such as suffering?
In this regard, there are these formal arguments:
God is complete with all virtues and far removed from all defects,
because he is independent.
By way of contrast, like Yajñadatta:
God possesses the qualities of one who is subject to misconception, because he is independent while possessing the desire to obtain [certain ends].
Whoever is independent with respect to something while desiring it possesses that thing, just as is commonly admitted.
God does not possess the defects under dispute, because he is independent while desiring to abandon them.

"Whoever is independent with respect to something while possessing the desire to abandon it, lacks that thing; as, for example, is commonly accepted. For all phenomena are established by such statements as well.
The Blessed Lord Hari is determined to be free from all defects and possessed of every perfection.
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the *Śrī-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.

Thus, by means of the logical justification (*upapatti*) that pertains to and establishes all dharmas, qualities, and absences of defects in the manner described, the word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates those well-known [scriptural passages] such as "His qualities are heard," which serve to establish the fulfillment of all qualities and so forth.

Thus, by the very act of stating the proof for his own position, he has demonstrated that the arguments of the opponent are "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) and are vitiated by the fallacy of being dependent on a limiting condition (*upādhi*), namely the lack of independence.

Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in this commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Anuvyākhyāna*— the work of the venerable teacher Pūrṇaprajña— composed by the ascetic named Praguṇajayatīrtha, which provides an explanation of the meanings of difficult words and sentences.
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
*** Adhyāya 2, Pāda 2:
[The Section on the Impossibility of Composition (Racanānupapattyadhikaraṇa)]
Now begins the section on the "Impossibility of Composition" (*racanānupapattyadhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.

Regarding the concordance of all the Vedas with Viṣṇu—the Supreme Brahman, who is the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire universe, who is replete with all auspicious qualities, and who is entirely free from even the slightest trace of defect—a doubt may arise that this [concordance] established in the first chapter might be otherwise due to conflict with the doctrines of the Sāṅkhyas and others; therefore, this [section] is commenced for the purpose of refuting that.
The second quarter [of the chapter] begins in order to refute the objection [expressed by the word] "ṅkāṃ. Now, one might object: "This quarter is indeed not to be commenced;
for it may be suspected that the doctrines of the Sāṅkhyas and others contradict the meaning already stated by way of being Smṛtis."
Is it by being endowed with reasoning, or by being endowed with scripture, or perhaps by being endowed with direct perception?

Not the first, because it has been established in the first pāda that those [texts] are not authoritative smṛti due to being contradicted by direct perception and the absence of any means of ascertaining their authoritativeness.
For this very reason, not the fourth. Nor the second.
For it has been demonstrated in that very same place that all arguments contradicting the stated meaning are merely fallacious.
If it is argued that what is being refuted here is a contradiction with powerful arguments, we say no;
for the power of arguments consists in their being rooted in authoritative means of knowledge such as the Vedas (*śruti*).
Whether by virtue of its being in agreement with that [scripture] or by virtue of its multiplicity,
in every respect there is no room for further suspicion.
This is because many arguments that accord with the Vedas and other authorities, which are rooted in those [scriptures], have been refuted in that very [work].
If it is argued that only some [arguments] were rejected there and not all, we say no;
for the aphorisms (*sūtras*) are intended as illustrative examples.

Otherwise, because fallacious arguments (*yuktyābhāsa*) are infinite, there would be no finality; furthermore, in that case, there would be no distinction between the [four] quarters. Nor is it the third [alternative], because it has already been stated that all the scriptures (*śruti*) are in harmony (*samanvaya*) with Brahman.
On this point, someone says:
"Determination occurs precisely through the establishment of one's own position and the refutation of the opposing position.
In that regard, in the first chapter, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for one's own position was stated."
The contradiction with reasoning regarding that second [position] has been refuted by the first quarter-verse.
Thus, once the establishment of one's own position has occurred, this debate is commenced for the purpose of rejecting the positions of others;
however, that is incorrect.
For the refutation of the opposing position consists of nothing other than the rejection of its proofs;
and the proofs are precisely memory and the rest.
Since all of those have already been rejected in the first chapter, what function remains for this [second chapter]?
Furthermore, if this were the case, the purpose of the chapter—which is the resolution of contradictions—would not be fulfilled.
Another [teacher] says:

even though it has been established that there is no contradiction with Smṛti or reasoning regarding the stated meaning, there remains a doubt as to whether there is a lack of concordance (samanvaya) with respect to Brahman.
How so?
Although inference is not capable of subverting Brahman’s status as the cause of the world,
it is nevertheless capable of establishing another cause for the world.

Furthermore, since conceptual alternatives regarding the nature of reality are untenable and there is no evidence to favor one over the other, it is impossible to determine with certainty that Brahman alone is the cause of the world;

on the contrary, because inference is reinforced by the fact that [the world] was composed by an omniscient author, the notion might arise that the Pradhāna or some other principle is the cause of the world, and not Brahman.
Therefore, inference is not only unable to refute Brahman’s status as the cause of the world, but cannot even establish it.
However, the second quarter is commenced in order to demonstrate that [the previous reason] is also incapable of establishing another cause.
This too has been stated; for instance:
What could have been meant by this?
[It would mean that] if, previously, one's own position was established by removing contradictions with reasoning regarding the intended meaning,
then now the refutation of the opposing position is being set forth.
Therefore, the very same answer has already been stated.

Alternatively, if the purpose of the two quarters is precisely the removal of contradictions with reasoning (*yukti-virodha-parihāra*), then the refutation of reasoning that contradicts one's own position occurs in the first [quarter], while...

As for the claim that in the second [chapter] there is a refutation of the arguments proving the opponent's position, that is not correct; for by the same logic, those [arguments] too can be refuted. Furthermore, the omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) of the authors has already been rejected previously. *7,5*
Therefore, this quarter [of the verse] is not to be commenced; thus he says: "Mindfulness" (smṛti).
Memory, reasoning, sacred revelation, and the qualities of virtue—these four types of arguments are not at all contradictory when applied toward the same conclusion. (Manu 2.1)
Although the matter has been settled by the first quarter-verse,
the dull-witted person entertains doubt once again because various philosophical systems continue to prevail due to their persistent application.
Those whose Vedic scriptures have the teacher as their subordinate element are described as such.
There are four kinds of contradictory cognitions.

The meaning is that they cannot subvert the reality established by the concordance of the Śruti, namely, that "they are not contradictory with respect to the underlying unity" (anvaya). "Abhiyoga" means insistence.
"Darśanas" are the systems of Sāṅkhya and other schools, so called because "the objects of knowledge are perceived through them."
This is what is meant:

although, in the ultimate sense, the establishment of our own position and the refutation of the opposing positions have already been accomplished by demonstrating that the arguments for the opponent's view and the objections against our own view—such as memory and so forth—are merely fallacious;
nevertheless, a person still harbors doubts regarding the matter already explained.
Is this so, or otherwise?
Why?
Because of application (to the various views).
"Because the [other] doctrines have come into existence and because those [doctrines] are perceived.

[Objection: But surely the Vedic scriptures (*śruti*), being of non-human origin, are free from any suspected defects; their meanings are established by numerous (and powerful) reasonings, and all opposing views have been refuted.
Therefore, how could there be a suspicion of otherwise-ness based merely on observing the activity of exertion toward an object that has already been established as being possessed [of that quality]?
For that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
But was it not said for this very reason that [the opponent] is "dull-witted"?
Not so;

for one who suspects without considering the established tradition (*prāpti*), being subject to unfounded doubt, has no authority regarding the scripture. Therefore, he explains the cause of the aforementioned suspicion by stating that "the systems have proceeded from application":
"Indeed, the conventions (*samaya*) have existed since beginningless time as a continuous flow."

"There is no annihilation of anything at any time... [Mānavadharmaśāstra 2.2.3]. Since there is a recollection of founders such as Kapila and Kaṇāda, how can there be beginninglessness? To this it is said: "by way of a continuous stream."

For Kapila and others, having understood through the power of their own asceticism and other means those very treatises previously composed that had been lost due to the force of time, set them forth again by composing new works.
In this way, since the predecessors were likewise [recovered] by those even more ancient, there is no fault because of this beginningless continuity.
"And likewise, there are recollections"— thus,
the connection with what precedes is "suspected for this reason.
This is what is meant:
For invalidity must indeed be postulated on account of defects in the instrument [of cognition] or subverting cognitions;
otherwise, there would be an over-extension [of the principle].
In that regard, since the Vedas are beginningless, there is an absence of defects in their instrument.
The same applies to the conventions (samayas) as well;
the only difference is that while their own nature is beginningless, their continuity is beginningless,
since there is equality in both cases regarding the absence of the transmission of human defects.
Just as there is no sublation of the Vedic scriptures because they continue without interruption,
so it is with the traditional codes (samayas) as well.
If these were accompanied by defects in their instruments of cognition or by subverting cognitions, then, like the words of a madman, they would be unprecedented and subject to total annihilation.
But this is not the case;
therefore, how could they incur invalidity?
And just as the Vedic scriptures have meanings supported by powerful reasoning, so too do the established traditions (samayas).
Nor should it be argued that those [scriptures] have been declared to be fallacious;

for since we have not ascertained all those who follow them, there remains the possibility of refuting them. In this very same way, the lack of opposition among the scriptural traditions (*samaya*) is rendered possible, just as it is with the Vedas (*śruti*).

Otherwise, how could the foremost authors of the Sūtras, such as Śauddhodani and others, have composed them through diligent effort? And how could many discerning people have accepted them through such diligent application?
Thus, they are equal to the Śruti.
For one who considers the security and well-being of the conventions, there would indeed be doubt regarding the stated meaning.
[7.17] Now, if this were the case, it would not be possible for multiple mutually contradictory [statements] to possess authority, because that would entail the fallacy of the object being manifold.

Thus, since one must necessarily resort to the authority of at least some [scripture], and since other [systems] are established otherwise—given that [the Veda] has been continuous from beginningless time and so forth—it is indeed possible to conclude the lack of authority of the systems of the Sāṅkhyas and others, in accordance with the stated direction: "and because the others are not perceived. Therefore, how can there be any further doubt regarding the meaning established by the harmony of the Śruti?
It is said:
"For that which is [the reason] because of the non-perception of others," this is the logic stated in brief for the sake of refuting [the opponent].
This applies specifically to one who is capable of conceiving of the various objects of cognition as they are conceptually constructed;
however, for one who is not so capable, as long as this summary is not elaborated upon, that person— being unable to grasp the single [truth] while abandoning the others— will certainly harbor doubt.
And it is not the case that such a person would not be qualified for the treatise, for that would entail the consequence of the destruction of both compendium and detailed exposition.
Thus it has been said: "The dull-witted one entertains this doubt."
If this is so, what follows from it? To this he says: "From this" (ataḥ).
Therefore, he is all-pervading.
He clearly demonstrates individually that these [perceptions] have their root in error.
The term "state of delusion" (bhrāntipada) is also an indicator for "deception" (vipralambha);
[this is explained] separately and in detail.
It is clear and easy to understand.

The lack of authoritative status and the contradiction with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the matters taught in those respective [heterodox] systems were previously stated briefly and not clearly;
here, by demonstrating them in detail and clearly, the meaning is that he makes known their basis in error and so forth.
By this, the relationship between the preceding section and this section—characterized as that of the "expounded" and the "expounder"—as well as the purpose of the exposition, have been stated.
This is what was expressed by the commentary beginning with the words, "Of the others," and so forth. (7.19)

But surely this is impossible, because their own objects of knowledge are established by firm reasoning and scripture, and because the reasoning and so forth of others have been refuted; to this he says: "by reasonings" (*tarkaiḥ*).
By means of the most firm arguments and the words of those who propound traditional scripture.
The word *tarka* (reasoning) refers to inference (*anumāna*) along with its auxiliary factors;
it consists of those most firm refutations of the reasoning of others, as well as those [reasonings] that cannot be subverted by them.
And it is connected with the words "by means of very firm [statements]";
this is the connection (anvaya) with what precedes.
To the question of how the Vedic and other statements can be presented as evidence against one who does not accept their authority, it is said: "of those who maintain the authority of scripture."
The connection is with "the systems of those persons who accept the authority of scripture (*āgama*), such as the Vedas.
Alternatively, it means "of those who maintain the authority of their own scriptures.
Consequently, the implication is that by the same logic used to accept the authority of their own scriptures, they must also admit the authority of the Vedas and so forth.
Alternatively, the phrase "with regard to students" is to be understood as "students who assert the authority of scripture such as the Veda";
thus, there is no contradiction with the *Bauddhādhikaraṇa*.
Although this will be demonstrated immediately hereafter, [it is mentioned now for the sake of brevity].
Nevertheless, it was stated [in that way] for the sake of concentrating the minds of the listeners.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that for those conventions (*samaya*) which proceed without interruption throughout beginningless and endless time, it is not appropriate to say they are rooted in error and so forth?
For there is no persistence of such things as the words of a madman throughout beginningless and endless time."
Therefore, the formal argument is as follows:
the systems of the Sāṅkhyas and others are authoritative;
they do not arise from error and the like.
Or they are fundamental (mūla), because they persist at all times, or because they are accepted by the great multitude of people,
just like the Vedas.
And thus, the reasoning (tarka) and so forth to be mentioned hereafter would have a sublated object (*bādhitaviṣayatva*).
This is not so.
For in this case, is it the validity and so forth of all systems that is to be proven, or that of only one?
Not the first [alternative],
because in establishing validity and so forth for mutually contradictory [positions], the subject matter is sublated by the consequence of a dilemma regarding the nature of the entity;
and because they constitute a "counter-balanced" argument (*satpratipakṣa*) due to their being of the nature of mutual exclusion.
Not the second [alternative],
because if one accepts the validity and so forth of that which is other than the subject under consideration, the previously mentioned faults would follow;
and if one does not accept them, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in that very case.
If one accepts the authority of the Vedas and so forth, there is an inconsistency with the thesis;
if one does not accept it, there is a defect in the illustrative example. This might indeed be the case.

Since the root cause—delusion and so forth—is the same [in both cases], one might ask with friendly intent: "If that is so, what is the cause for the persistence of these very [false views] throughout beginningless and endless time, while it does not exist in the speech of a madman? In response to this, he says:
"Because of the rarity...
(7.22): "Because of the rarity of those with pure intellects and the abundance of those who know little."
And because the world is characterized by darkness (tamas), it is prone to false knowledge.
Because the men who promulgate systems are gripped by dogmatic prejudice, their systems persist forever;
no unity exists in the words of a madman. Now, as to the question "What is the cause even of this prejudice?", it is said: "Out of hatred."
Out of malice toward the supreme reality and toward those who know that reality, [one incurs sin] constantly.
In that case, let it proceed immediately after the arising of hatred; how then can it be said to be "always"? To this, it is said: "unceasingly" (aniśam).
Now, one might ask: how can those who desire the goals of human life engage in injustice due to a persistent attachment rooted in aversion? To this, it is said: "beginningless" (*anādi*).
Due to the connection with beginningless latent impressions, because of the great number of asuras,
and because they are seized by perverse dogmatism, these systems of doctrine persist forever.
The sense is that, by the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they find pleasure in those very things.
Now, one might ask: why does even beginningless latent impression not cease through powerful effort? To this, it is said: "of the Asuras."
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "of those who, such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth, identify with [the self] and impel [actions] through perverted efforts.
Now, one might ask: since they are restrained by virtuous and wise people, why do they not desist? To this it is said: "Because of their rarity" (daurlabhyāt).
[This refers to] those of little knowledge who know only the nature of the substratum of delusion and who promulgate [their own] conventions.
To the objection that "then the world, including kings and others, will prevent [this]," it is said: "because of their being characterized by darkness (tāmasatva)."
For that very reason, there would also follow the occurrence of false knowledge caused by wicked scholars;
furthermore, these causes do not exist even in their own nature within the beginningless Veda. Although this point ought to have been stated at the end of this section, [it is stated here].
Nevertheless, this has been stated here as it arose in the context [of the discussion] for the purpose of settling the intellect.
If that is so, then since it is impossible to completely uproot these conventions that are so firmly established, this refutation is useless; to this he says: "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).
Nevertheless, for those of pure intellect who are joined with the grace of the Lord,
reasonings consistent with the scriptures shall always destroy darkness.
Thus Vidyāpati thoroughly refuted the [false] interpretations of the rules... // MAnu 2.2.8a-c //
Although they cannot be completely eradicated by Kusumā, nevertheless,
"tamas" means ignorance.
The explanation of being well-reasoned is that [the teachings] always follow the authentic scriptures (*sadāgama*).
"Endowed with pervasion and so forth as established by valid cognition, and endowed with corroboration by that"—this is for this purpose.
This is what is meant: [the following].
This effort is not for the purpose of utterly destroying the systems of the Sāṅkhyas and others,
which would entail the aforementioned fault; rather,
it is [intended] to remove those various misconceptions instilled in certain persons by those respective systems.

[The opponent says: "It is intended that, by generating the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) through reasonings accompanied by scripture, one may remove ignorance (*jñāna*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), and error (*viparyaya*).
But this too is unreasonable:
how can beginningless ignorance, which is bound up with extremely deep-seated and dense latent impressions (*vāsanā*), be removed by the knowledge of reality produced only now?"

However, because it arises again through the power of one's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), overriding the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), and sets in motion its own appropriate effects, it is said: "of those with pure intellects."
This refers to those whose nature is knowledge of reality as it is and who are fit for liberation.
The point is this:
it will be stated that some sentient beings are fit for liberation while others are not.
In this regard, the undertaking is not for the purpose of removing ignorance from those who are unfit, but rather for those who are indeed fit;
and they are of the nature of pure consciousness.

And thus, although this state of being a mental modification has just now arisen through the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it— being reinforced by the knowledge of one's own pure nature, which is its internal cause— destroys, root and branch, even the external ignorance along with its latent impressions (*savāsanājñāna*),
despite its beginninglessness; for one's own true nature is stronger than anything else.
Nor is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) thus rendered useless, because it is only when one's own nature is assisted by external effort that it produces its effect.
As it has been said: "Without effort, there is neither force nor action."
Furthermore, it is well-established that the grace of the Lord is more powerful than anything else;
moreover, it will be explained later that this grace has existed from time immemorial in those individual souls (jīvas) who are fit for liberation.
And thus, this auxiliary knowledge of the Vṛtti, though beginningless and bound by extremely deep and dense latent impressions (vāsanās), indeed eradicates that ignorance along with its very root.
Therefore, with the intention that the refutation of [false] doctrines is not in vain, it was said: "for those endowed with the grace of the Lord."
Nor should it be argued that the cessation of ignorance will occur from that [devotion] alone, rendering knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) unnecessary;
for the grace of the Lord has the inherent nature of producing its fruit only in accordance with human effort.
Thus it has been said: "Vāsudeva is the bestower of the fruit of everything."
The meaning is that [the Lord's effort] pertains to the entirety of the fitness and exertion of all [beings], and not to each one individually.

If this were so— that the Blessed One refuted the systems of those who hold wrong views in order to remove the ignorance instilled by the flowers of the wicked— then this [teaching] would be disregarded by Brahmā and the others.
Because ignorance has not been instilled in those [entities], there is no purpose [for such sūtras] among them;
thus, since there would be a contradiction with the scripture stating, "Having composed sūtras of this kind," he says: "nijā... (intrinsic...).
...for the purpose of sharpening the intellect of his own devotees.

For the sake of establishing the whetstone-like quality of the arguments of Brahmā and others—who, though adorned with flowers, have not yet applied their knowledge—one must use the whetstone of reasoning; that is to say, for the purpose of achieving the extreme sharpness of the sword of knowledge.
This connects with what was stated previously.
[The word] *kusumayā* is [to be understood as] *kusumayā(hitā)*.

The intention is that even though there is no purpose for the refutation of knowledge, this [work] must be respected by them because the purpose of clarifying knowledge does exist. // Oṃ. And because the arrangement [of the world] is untenable, there is no inference. Oṃ.//
Thus, the commencement of the [first] chapter has been established.

In that regard, in the first section (adhikaraṇa), the Sāṅkhyas who deny the existence of a Lord (nirīśvara) are refuted. Since a refutation is not easily understood without knowledge of their own system, he first shows the position of their doctrine, beginning with the words "cetanā" (consciousness).

"And because the formation [of the world] is untenable, there is no inference [for a creator]; the atheistic [Sāṃkhyas] say that there are only two principles, the sentient and the insentient... (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 2.2.9a-c). *7,32*
"Cetanā and acetanā" is a dvandva compound treated as a singular;
"they say" is the ellipsis for "the enumerators (saṅkhyā).
Now, one might object that since no other alternative is possible, only two principles should be asserted by those who follow authoritative means of knowledge.
If one asks why their inequality is stated, it is for this reason that it was said: "without a Lord."
The meaning is that, without accepting an Īśvara, they assert only two principles consisting of the sentient (jīva) and the insentient (jaḍa).
Now, the Sāṅkhyas consider that,
in brief, there are four categories of principles.
Some entity is a primary cause (prakṛti) alone; some entity is a transformation (vikṛti) alone;
and some entity is both a primary cause and a transformation.
Some [hold] that there is neither [of these two].
