In this regard, the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is *pradhāna*; it is indeed *prakṛti*.
For she is the root of the entire universe of effects.
But for this [mahat], there is no other root;
rather, the seven—mahat, ahaṃkāra, and the five tanmātras—are both prakṛtis and vikṛtis.
They are both primal causes and transformations.
For instance:
the principle of Mahat (the Great One) is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*) and the evolved effect (*vikṛti*) of the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*).
Likewise, the principle of the ego is the material cause of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the sense organs, and the evolved effect of the Great One.
Thus, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are the *prakṛtis* of the gross elements (*bhūta*), such as space and the rest,
and they are the *vikṛtis* of the *ahaṅkāra*.

The group of sixteen— consisting of the five elements and the eleven faculties— is indeed a transformation (*vikṛti*). Although cows, jars, trees, and so forth are transformations of earth and the other elements,
likewise, milk, seeds, and so forth are specific varieties of those transformations.
Their [products] are curd, sprouts, and so forth;
nevertheless, cows and the like, or seeds and the like, are not a different principle from earth and the other elements,
because they share the common characteristics of being gross and perceptible by the senses.
And here, "being the material cause" (prakṛtitva) is intended to mean being the substrate of reality (tattvopādānatva).
The Puruṣa, however, is neither of these two; it is neither the material cause nor the transformation.
Thus, in detail, there are twenty-five principles (tattvas).
As it has been said:
"The root nature is the unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both natures and evolutes;
the group of sixteen is the evolute alone; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor evolute."
How then is it said that "they speak of only two realities"? He says: "That" (tad).
... that which exists as the fivefold division of the five [elements] is insentient; [but] the sentient... // MAnu 2.9c-e //
Five and five times five; the state of those [groups] is "five-fiveness" (pañcapañcatvam),
and that is the division.
Thus it is observed that [the Self] abides as the division of the five pentads;
that consists of two principles, the conscious and the unconscious,
which in brief are fourfold.

They say that, in detail, there are twenty-five divisions; therefore, there is no contradiction. Now, one might ask: "Since they perceive both the sentient and the insentient as innumerable through means of valid cognition such as direct perception, how can they speak in this way? To this, he says: "That... (tad).
... that is incalculable ... // MAnu 2.2.9e //
The word "that" (*tad*) refers to both [categories].

The meaning is that even though they speak of twenty-five divisions by including the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), they state that there are two principles (*tattva*) when considering the intermediate subdivisions.
Although there is a commonality in the fact that both sentient and insentient things are individually innumerable, there is no equality between the two in terms of their being distinct entities.
To the question "What then?", he says: "It is distinct."
...the dissolution would be something else, distinct [from it]. "The conscious" is the ellipsis;
they say that the conscious is distinct from one another.
As it has been said:

"The plurality of spirits (puruṣa) is established by the specific determination of the causes of birth and death, by their non-simultaneous activity, and by the variation in the three constituents (traiguṇya)."
They say that whatever is other than consciousness is distinct as non-consciousness.
[Objection: But surely, if a Lord (Īśvara) is not accepted, the activity of anything whatsoever would be untenable.
Since creation and so forth would otherwise be impossible, a third principle called Īśvara must be accepted.
To the question of how they do not accept this, he says: "Of the insentient...
[Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.10ab]: "The agency of the insentient is asserted as being independent."
The word "it is said" implies that this is the position of the Sāṅkhyas.
For instance:
"The conscious [Self] exists because composite objects exist for the sake of another," and so forth—this is established as a reason.

They hold that the manifest (vyakta) is established by perception and other means as being insentient, and the unmanifest (avyakta) is established by reasons such as the distinction between cause and effect;
furthermore, there is no proof for a Lord (Īśvara) that is not otherwise established,
because the beginning of creation is possible through the agency of the insentient Pradhāna alone, and thus the postulation of an unseen Lord is untenable.
Now, it is observed that nothing insentient, when not presided over by a sentient being, ever exhibits activity;
therefore, there must be a Lord as the presider of the Pradhāna. To this, it is said: "by its own independence."
The meaning is "without the basis of volition.
As it has been said:
"Just as the flow of milk from the insentient [cow] occurs for the sake of the growth of the calf..."
"The activity of the Pradhāna is for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa"—
this has been stated as a different [view],
but it is incorrect.

Since even for insentient things, their mutual distinction from one another is established through perception and other means of valid cognition as if they were sentient, he says: "mutually... [and so forth].
And mutual discord among undertakings would become their ruin.

It is said by them that the storehouse-consciousness (*ālaya*) lasts until the end of dissolution, and that there would be a mutual differentiation among its effects. This is what is meant: *7.45* This is what is being stated: [the storehouse-consciousness persists] until the final dissolution, and a mutual distinction among its effects would come to be. This is what is intended.
The effect exists even prior to the operation of its causes, because that which is non-existent cannot be produced;
for if it were non-existent before the operation of the causes, its existence could not be brought about.
For even by a thousand artisans, blue cannot be made yellow.
Furthermore, is a cause that produces an effect connected with that effect, or is it unconnected?
In the first case, existence must be admitted because a relation with what is non-existent is untenable;
the second case is not [possible] either, because since there is no difference in being unrelated, it would follow that everything could arise from everything.

If it is argued that even though there is no connection, that very cause acts in such a way that it produces only what it is capable of producing—and therefore there is no over-extension of the principle—then we ask: does that capacity have a specific object or does it apply everywhere? If it applies everywhere, then the same lack of restriction remains.
But if the effect were non-existent at the outset, how could it have that [cause] as its object? Therefore, the effect must be existent.
Furthermore, since no effect is perceived as existing apart from its cause, one must accept the non-difference between cause and effect.
Moreover, the cloth is not different from the threads, because it possesses the properties of the threads.
Whatever is distinct from something else cannot be a property (dharma) of that thing, just as a cow is not a property of a horse;
and because of the relationship between material cause and its effect (upādānopādeyabhāva).

Between two things for which there is no difference in substance, there can be no relationship of material cause and its effect, as in the case of a jar and a cloth; this is also because there is an absence of conjunction and non-attainment [between them].
For conjunction is observed between distinct entities, such as a bowl and a jujube fruit,
or non-attainment [is observed] between them, such as between the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains; yet neither conjunction nor non-attainment exists here.

Therefore, there is no difference in substance. Furthermore, because the distinct downward bending caused by another weight is not perceived, even though effects differ from one another, they are non-different from their respective causes; thus, when they have sequentially reached the state of the fundamental cause at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), there is indeed non-difference.
With this intention, it was stated that "something else is produced.

And that has been said: "The effect exists [prior to its production] because what is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is the grasping of a material cause, because everything is not possible from everything, because an efficient cause produces only that for which it is capable, and because there is no destruction of the cause" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 9).
Regarding these as well, he states a difference of opinion: "the state of being an enjoyer," and so forth.
Some say that it belongs to the conscious enjoyer, while others say it does not even belong to him.
All Sāṅkhyas likewise do not admit the agency of the *puruṣa*;
for agency consists in the engagement in action,
and an action characterized by physical motion is not possible for the self.
Nor is it characterized by effort, because that [effort] is a function of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), whereas [the self] is all-pervading.
Nor is it characterized by modification, because it is changeless,
as has been stated.
"And because of that absence of error, the witness-hood of this Puruṣa is established,
as well as his isolation, neutrality, state of being a seer, and lack of agency. Regarding this,
some assert that the conscious [Puruṣa] possesses the nature of an enjoyer.

Others do not even accept that [position], saying: "Therefore, no one is bound, no one is liberated, nor does anyone transmigrate. As it is said: "Because there is no state of an experiencer... and so forth.
"Prakṛti, having various substrates, is bound, transmigrates, and is liberated.

[Objection: But if there is an absence of agency, how can there be enjoyership? For that too consists in being permeated by action. To this, he says: "By its own nature... (*svarūpa...*) and so forth.
And the state of being an enjoyer [is established] by virtue of the power of the consciousness of its own nature and because it is self-luminous.
For they say that being an enjoyer consists in being the experiencer of pleasure, pain, and so forth; therefore, it was stated: "because of its self-luminosity."
The meaning is that the state of being an experiencer of pleasure and so forth is established by one's own direct cognition.
As it has been said:
"And the capacity for being an enjoyer is the consciousness (caitanya) of the Puruṣa."
Nor is it appropriate to accept agency in this way as well;
for since the cognition of agency is sublated by reasoning, it is of the nature of a superimposition (*adhyāsa*).

[Objection: If that is so, then why do others not also accept the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), which is established by cognition? To this he says: "And because of primordial matter" (*prakṛteśca*).

But those who maintain that there is no experience [of pleasure and pain] say that what is called "experience" is simply the failure to grasp the distinction between the self and the nature of primordial matter (prakṛti). ... MAnu 2.12a-c.
"Enjoyment" refers to the cause of the activity of enjoying;
this is their intention.
For the state of being an enjoyer is not the inherent nature of the person (puruṣa).
Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that liberation (apavarga) is impossible;
moreover, it is not tenable for [the self] to be subject to adventitious qualities,
because it is unchanging (apariṇāmin).
Therefore, just as agency, so too enjoyment cannot be accepted as belonging to the self;
nor is there any contradiction with experience, because such an experience does not exist.
For it is merely in conventional usage that the experiencer is called the "Self," and this [usage],
like the conventional usage of being an agent, is based solely on the failure to grasp the distinction between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa).
This might be so.

For those who hold that the person (puruṣa) is the enjoyer, there would be an absence of liberation; for they admit that the enjoyment of the person is caused by its conjunction with primordial nature (prakṛti). [As it is said:
"For the sake of the Person's vision, and likewise for the sake of the isolation (kaivalya) of Pradhāna..."

Because of the statement, "The conjunction of both is like that of the lame and the blind; from that [conjunction] proceeds creation," one might think that the conjunction of primordial matter (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) never ceases, whereby liberation for the person would be impossible. To this, he says: "from the apprehension of difference."
... because of the apprehension of difference between those two. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.12d)
Liberation is declared for those who possess enjoyments... // MAnu 2.13a //
Regarding these two, primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), this is the intention of those who accept the experience of the experiencing person:
the conjunction of the person with primordial nature is not for the sake of experience alone.
And what is the name of that which has liberation as its purpose?
In this regard, when accompanied by the non-apprehension of discrimination (*viveka*), it leads to enjoyment;
but when there is the apprehension of discrimination, it leads to liberation.
Granted that Prakṛti may repeatedly provide enjoyment of sound and other objects;
however, by this [enjoyment], discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) has not been accomplished.
But one who has accomplished discriminative discernment no longer causes the enjoyment of sound and the rest.
For that experience is bound by the non-discrimination of [Purusha from Prakriti]; in the absence of that bond, it cannot exist.
And this has been said: "The one [Purusha] remains indifferent, thinking 'I have seen [it].'"
"I have been seen"—with this thought, Nature ceases entirely; even when there is a conjunction between the two, it serves no further purpose for creation.
Thus: "Just as a dancer, having displayed herself to the audience, desists from her dance," so does Nature cease.
"Having thus revealed herself to the Puruṣa, Prakṛti desists.
Nor should it be suspected that she, though having desisted, will begin again;
for there is no purpose remaining.
And it has been said: "It is my conviction that there is nothing more subtle than primordial nature (prakṛti), for even that ceases by its own accord. [Objection:
But for those in whose view the Spirit (puruṣa) possesses no experience at all, how can there be liberation?
Because there would be an absence of bondage, the instruction on yoga would likewise be rendered useless; therefore, he says: "That very [consciousness]."
... that very same [result] belongs to those who advocate for the exertion [of effort]. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.13b)
The apprehension of difference itself is intended as liberation;
for bondage is indeed delusion based on the non-apprehension of difference,
and that [delusion] ceases when there is the apprehension of difference— that alone is liberation.
However, because there is no other [state], it is said that "it is that very [state].
Yet, the apprehension of difference itself is not liberation,
since even that must be brought to cessation.
"Nor [is it established] by the discriminative discernment (vivekakhyāti)," because this has already been stated.
Thus, the position thus presented must now be refuted.
In that regard, the author of the Sūtras, intending to state the sequence, said: "And because the arrangement [of the world] is impossible, there is no inference [of a creator]."

Thus, having first formulated the refutation of the opponent's position (*parapakṣopālambha*), he subsequently established the proof of his own position (*svapakṣasādhana*) with the words "And because of [the necessity of] activity" (*pravṛtteśca*).

However, the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), considering that the means of proof (*sādhakapramāṇa*) is an internal factor for the realization of reality (*tattvapratipatti*), maintains that its presentation should come first.

Desiring to establish the sequence as well— showing that the presentation of that [reason] follows immediately after the previous one because it is an external factor for the purpose of refuting the opposing view—
he explains [the sūtra] by way of transposition, stating the introductory meaning of the sūtra "And because of activity" (pravṛtteśca) with the words "Of the Lord" (īśasya).
Because the Lord is beyond all grasping, both of those [theories] are likewise untenable.
Because of being neither included nor accepted;
the word "evam" (thus) indicates the intensity of this fault.
Both of those—whether the person is the enjoyer or the non-enjoyer—are positions regarding the person. (7.58)

Now, one might ask: "If an unproven God is not accepted, how can it be considered improper? To this end, he states the proof for God as the meaning of the sūtra *pravṛtteśca* (and because of activity): "Cetanā... [etc.].

"When the production of a cloth is seen to follow from volition and desire, by what means can such a nature of another thing be prevented, given its status as a real entity? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.14).
"When" (*yadā*) means "because" (*yasmāt*).
Therefore,
it is understood that "being such" means arising in accordance with the will of a conscious agent, like a cloth; [this applies] to other things, such as the *mahat* and so forth.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "it is inferred because of its being an entity and because of its being an effect. To the question "By what [is it inferred]?",
the following formal argument (prayoga) is presented here:
"The Great One (mahat) and the rest have their production dependent upon the will of a conscious being, because they are effects, like a cloth.

Alternatively, one should formulate the argument as: "The emergence of the Great One and the rest is dependent upon the will of a conscious being, because it is an emergence, like the emergence of a cloth.
Having stated the example of the emergence of a cloth to indicate these two syllogisms, he states the reason (*hetu*) "because they are entities" (*vastutvāt*).
When this has been stated, it should be understood that the status of being an "indirect indicator" (*upalakṣaṇa*) applies to both cases. Furthermore, this is merely an indirect indicator;

one should also consider such arguments as: "The primordial material cause (*upādāna*) consisting of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest is presided over by a conscious being, because it is a material cause, like a thread. And so forth.
And since no other conscious being could possibly be such [an agent], it is established that the Supreme Person, the Lord (Īśvara), alone is the one who transcends all.
This might be argued:
"The Great One (mahat) and the subsequent principles are not established by direct perception."
Because it is unmanifest,
its comprehension must be admitted to arise either from the words of the Sāṅkhya teachers or from the inference employed by them.
However, since they have both spoken of and inferred it as being precisely not of such a nature, there is a contradiction.
"Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of an unestablished substratum (āśrayāsiddhi).
Not so;
for that [substratum] is understood from the Veda.
For this has been stated: the Śruti passage beginning with "the one unborn" (*ajāmekām*) also establishes the Pradhāna.
But surely the Puruṣa is conscious, whereas the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is not?
If it is argued that desire is a property of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and not of the conscious, unchanging [Self],
and therefore there is either a lack of proof for the qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*) or a contradiction (*bādha*),
and furthermore, because cloth and so forth do not possess such a nature, the example lacks the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*), we say: no.
Because it will be stated that the possession of desire belongs to the self alone.
Nevertheless, "arising" (*udbhava*) means either production (*utpatti*) or manifestation (*abhivyakti*).
It cannot be the first.

In the first formulation, the qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). In the second, there is a lack of a substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

This is because I accept the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*). If it is argued that even in the second case these same faults apply because you do not accept manifestation (*vyakti*), we say no.
Since the theory that the effect is non-existent (asatkāryavāda) has been established and because there is a lack of evidence for the theory that the effect is existent (satkāryavāda),

one must consider whether, by such arguments as "because that which is non-existent cannot be produced," it is merely the existence [of the effect] prior to the operation of the causal process that is being proved, or its absolute existence.
In the first case, there is the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*),
because [the opponent] accepts both existence and non-existence.

In the second case, however, just as in the argument "because that which is non-existent is not produced" (*asadakaraṇāt*), the argument "because that which is existent is not produced" (*sadakaraṇāt*) is equally applicable.
For the existent self is not produced by anything.
[Objection: But how can that which is non-existent be an object (*karman*)? [Response: How can that which is existent be an effect (*kārya*)? This is equally [applicable].
By this, the claim that "the jar is born" is also refuted.
If so, what is the meaning of such expressions as "he makes a jar"?
It means "he transforms the clay into a jar."
If it is asked, "Since clay becomes a jar, why does a donkey's horn not also arise from what is non-existent?
we reply: because there is no material cause (upādāna) that has the nature of such a horn.

Otherwise, if that which already exists were to arise, why would the self (*ātman*) not also arise? This is the same [logical difficulty]. Furthermore, it was asked whether the cause produces the effect while being connected to it, or while being entirely unconnected.
In this context, by the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*), is either the material cause (*upādāna*) intended, or the efficient cause (*nimitta*)?
In the first case, it is not accepted that [the cause] produces [the effect];
rather, the efficient causes bring that [effect] to the state of being an effect.
In the second case, however, the answer is that [the effect], while unconnected with the form of the effect, is connected with the form of the cause.
For this very reason, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
Furthermore, the causal capacity of causes has both existent and non-existent things as its objects;
otherwise, it would follow that it is devoid of an object.
For it is not possible to make that which already exists [into something else].

Furthermore, regarding the inference of non-difference between the threads and the cloth, if one seeks to prove mere non-difference, it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*),
because both difference and non-difference are admitted.
In establishing absolute non-difference, the property of being a quality of the threads (*tantudharmatva*) is first of all unestablished;
for a thing itself cannot be its own quality. Furthermore, metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is not a factor for the operation of inference.
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument].
And how could the cloth have the threads as its nature? If you say it is because the threads are its qualifiers, no; for that is not so.
Because there is a deviation [of the reason] in the case of a staff and so forth, which are qualifiers of a person and the like;
if it is argued that [the reason is] "being dependent upon that," we say no,
because it would result in the fallacy of unestablishedness (*asiddhi*) due to non-difference.
Furthermore, there is a deviation [of the reason] in the case of jujube fruits in a pit and the like.
If it is argued that [the reason] consists in being of the same nature as that [the probandum], we say no; for this would result in the reason being indistinguishable from the probandum itself.
If it is argued that non-difference is established by the absence of difference, we say no;
for non-difference is not admitted as something distinct from the absence of difference, and even if it were admitted, it would be contradicted by logical sublation (*bādhāt*).
Thus, the relationship between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*) is likewise unestablished;
for it is not logical that something should be both the material cause and the effect itself,
since the states of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) and an object (*karmatva*) are necessarily distinct.
The absence of conjunction and non-attainment will be established because there is no absolute difference [between the two].
Furthermore, the non-perception of the effects of another weight will occur through the acceptance of their non-difference.
By this, if it is argued that "being an effect" means "coming into existence after not having existed," then that is unproven for us.
And the claim that [the self] possesses the property of being manifested has already been refuted;
this is what was meant by the statement: "By whom is this prevented?"

Thus, having established his own position by showing that since the activity of a conscious weaver or the like is observed in the production of cloth and so forth, the production of the "Great Principle" (mahat) and the rest must likewise depend on the will of a conscious being—using that as an analogy—he now prepares the foundation for explaining the aphorism, "And because of the impossibility of arrangement, [the Primal Cause] is not inferred," in order to refute the opposing view, with the words: "And not... (na ca).
"And there is no proof for the object asserted [by them]... (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.15a).

Not only is there the existence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in our own view, but furthermore, there is no proof whatsoever for the object asserted by the Sāṅkhyas—that the *pradhāna* is the independent cause of the world.
For instance: what would be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here—is it perception (*pratyakṣa*), or scripture (*āgama*), or else inference (*anumāna*)?
Not the first.
For that [object] belongs either to people such as ourselves or to yogis;
it cannot be the first case,
because this object is beyond the reach of the senses.
Not the second [alternative],
because it is unestablished;
for we have no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to the effect that yogis do not perceive things in this manner.
Nor is there scripture [to support this], for that would have to be either non-human (apauruṣeya) or human (pauruṣeya).
It is not the first case, as he says: "It is only revelation" (*śruti*). *7.75*
...for us, indeed, revelation alone is the authority. Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.15b.
In our view alone, scripture (*śruti*) is indeed the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramā*).
For all scripture establishes that the Lord alone, in His sovereignty, is the cause of the entire universe—omniscient and omnipotent.
And the primordial matter (*pradhāna*), whose existence, cognition, and activity are dependent upon Him, is merely the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world under His governance.
For instance: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving";
"He who alone presides over the source," and so forth.
And thus the Śruti stands as the very opponent of the other [position].
Furthermore, is the human-authored [scripture] characterized by the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas, or is it that which was composed by the teachers of Sāṅkhya?
Not the first,
because that too follows our own view:
"Having entered both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, the Supreme Person..."
"the omnipresent Lord agitated [the waters] for the sake of the creation of the world," and so forth; thus,
the second alternative is not tenable.
If it is argued that its validity is established by the fact that it was spoken by a reliable person (āpta), he says in response: "Reliability... [and so forth].
The authoritativeness of the speaker is not at all established by the aforementioned path;

that is to say, because he speaks in contradiction to the Śruti, according to the stated method that "only the Śruti is indeed the means of valid knowledge. The "speaker" refers to the founder of Sāṅkhya.
Or rather, it is according to the path already stated, namely "and because of the non-perception of others.
For even in the Sāṅkhya treatises, many matters set forth in its narratives are demonstrated to be sublated by the non-perception of what is otherwise possible.
Alternatively, [the definition is]: "Non-deceptiveness is the knowledge of that [object]."
The meaning is that there is an absence of any valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to ascertain his status as an authoritative person (*āpta*) according to the path described above. [As it is said:
"Kapila, known as Vāsudeva, proclaimed the *Sāṅkhya* system to the gods beginning with Brahmā, and likewise to Bhṛgu and others."
In the same way, another Kapila proclaimed to Āsuri the Sāṅkhya system, which is augmented by the meaning of all the Vedas yet contradicts all the Vedas,
being further bolstered by fallacious reasoning.
Or rather, [it means] "according to the path taught in the Purāṇas.
By this, even the citation of the Śruti passage beginning with "the seer Kapila, who was born... is refuted.

By this very [argument], the claim that "scripture is understood through the direct perception of yogins" is refuted. Not only is the impossibility of [the teacher's] being an authoritative person (*āpta*) established by the path already stated; [it is also refuted here].
He says "aprāmāṇya" (invalidity) because it is also spoken by one who has not attained [the state of] a Kinnara.
"Also because of the acceptance of the intrinsic nature of invalidity... (Mānava 2.2.16ab).
By the word "also" (*api*), [the author] includes the intrinsic nature of validity as well.
The Sāṅkhya accepts that the validity and invalidity of cognitions arise depending solely upon the causes of the cognition itself.
And since that [position] is untenable, he is therefore not an authoritative person (*āpta*).
To explain how the self-validity (*svatastva*) of both validity and invalidity is untenable, he says: "like a magician" (*māyīvat*).
... like a magician;
he would be one who negates everything he himself has taught. // MĀnuv_2.2.16bc //

If both validity and invalidity were produced solely by the causes of cognition, then according to the Sāṅkhya position, a cognition that has arisen would have to be of a dual nature— both valid and invalid— or, due to their mutual contradiction, it would arise as a mere cognition devoid of both; or else,
because a cognition lacking an intrinsic nature is impossible, it would not arise at all.

In the first case, the proponent of Māyā, who considers the universe to be distinct from both existence and non-existence, himself negates the non-existence that follows from his own statement "distinct from existence" by saying "distinct from non-existence";
and he himself negates the existence that follows from his own statement "distinct from non-existence" by saying "distinct from existence."
Likewise, Sāṅkhya too would be a negator of everything it has itself asserted;

for if the knowledge produced by its statements were to correspond to reality, then the very meaning obtained— namely, that *prakṛti* is the cause of the world and so forth— would, in the case of that knowledge being non-correspondent to reality, be what is negated.

The meaning is that since non-reality does not exceed the category of the misapprehension of the object, it would follow—were both [the real and the unreal] inherent in the thing itself—that the entity would be embraced by two contradictory forms.
The word *māyī* is grammatically correct because the term *māyā* belongs to the *vrīhy-ādi* group. (7.80)
Now, even if this is so, the point that "primordial matter (prakṛti) is the cause of the world" and so forth is established according to reality; to this he says: "And not... (na ca).
And nothing at all is established.
The sense is that nothing at all is established when there is mutual contradiction.
If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of validity? [the answer is: Let your gaze be directed toward invalidity as well.
He states the fault in the second [case] with the words "And not... (na ca).
For knowledge must take as its object an entity either as it actually exists or as it does not exist,
since no third mode can be determined.
Consequently, a cognition devoid of both validity and invalidity would be entirely without an object, like an iron rod [without a point].
And thus, nothing at all would be established from the Sāṅkhya statement; moreover, in the third case, there would be total blindness for the world. Thus he says: "Nor... (na ca).

It might be argued as follows: when the cause of cognition is endowed with excellence (*guṇa*), then, since the capacity to produce non-validity (*aprāmāṇya*) has been obstructed by that excellence, only valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*) arises. But when it is endowed with defect (*doṣa*), then, since the capacity to produce validity has been obstructed by that defect, only non-valid cognition arises.
For no instrument is possible that is simultaneously endowed with both or devoid of both.
[If it is argued] that "thereby the aforementioned fault would ensue," we reply:
for what purpose is this [position] thus imagined?
If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of cognition having a dual form,
then why should that consequence not also be accepted?
If it is argued that this is for fear of contradiction, [we reply:]...
Even regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*), why do you not fear the contradiction of its possessing two opposing powers?
(*7.81*) Furthermore, even that instrument which produces two contradictory effects possesses only such powers as are conferred by its association with auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*).
And if one accepts this in the present case, it follows that both [the cause and the effect] would be dependent on something else (*paratastva*).
Furthermore, what are the merits and defects of speech?
If it is argued that they consist in being composed by an authoritative or non-authoritative person,
then— since both [authoritativeness and non-authoritativeness] would be absent in the case of Vedic sentences— a cognition characterized by both or neither would arise from them.
Or it might not arise at all.

If you argue that being composed by one who is untrustworthy is a merit, then why should being not composed by one who is trustworthy not also be a defect? That same logical consequence remains. (7.82)
By this, the Sāṅkhya teacher’s statement—that a word is inherently authoritative (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*) and does not require certainty regarding its source of trust (*āpti*)—is also refuted;
for if non-authoritativeness were also held to be inherent, all the aforementioned faults would follow.
If it is argued that the certainty of its authority arises from its acceptance by the great masses (*mahājana-parigraha*), we say no.
Because [the reason] is unestablished if it means "being worthy of worship," and because it is inconclusive and subject to doubt if it means "having many objects.
Let it be that perception is not a valid means of knowledge for the world being produced from primordial matter (*prakṛti*).
And let there be no scripture;
however, there shall be inference,
as it has been stated.

"Because of the finite measure of differentiated objects, because of their homogeneity, because of the activity [of the world] proceeding from power, because of the non-distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-differentiation of the manifold universe"—
this is the meaning.
Because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-distinction of the manifold universe, there exists an unmanifest primal cause;
just as the limbs, which already exist within the body of a tortoise, emerge from it and then become unmanifest within that very same body.
In this way, effects such as jars and crowns are differentiated from their causes, whether a lump of clay or a lump of gold;
and the elements such as earth exist indeed from their cause, the subtle element (tanmātra);
and the subtle elements exist indeed from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
The ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) exists only as an effect of the Great One (mahat), and the Great One exists only as an effect of the supreme Unmanifest (avyakta). Thus,
this is the sequential differentiation of the entire universe of effects from its cause, the supreme Unmanifest, during the process of re-absorption (pratisarga).

Just as a clay lump or a gold lump, when entering into the forms of jars, crowns, and so forth, becomes unmanifest—thereby becoming "unmanifest" with respect to those effects such as jars and crowns which were previously unmanifested—the same applies here: earth and the other elements, upon entering the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), render those *tanmātras* unmanifest with respect to themselves.
Likewise, the *tanmātras*, upon entering the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), render that ego unmanifest.
In this way, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), entering the Great One (mahat), renders the Great One unmanifest;
the Great One enters its own cause, which is primordial nature (prakṛti);
but since primordial nature has no place of entry anywhere, it remains the unmanifest of all effects.
This is the non-differentiation of the multiformity—that is, of the effect in its various forms—within the primal nature (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, because the effect exists within the cause through both differentiation and non-differentiation, the unmanifest cause exists.
(7.84) For this reason as well: "because of activity proceeding from power."
For an effect proceeds from the power inherent in its cause,
since an effect cannot arise from a cause that lacks power. Furthermore, this power residing in the cause is not something other than the unmanifest state of the effect itself.
Let it be, then, that the Great Principle (mahat) alone possesses supreme unmanifestness; to this it is replied: "Because of the finite dimension of differentiated entities.
The meaning is that because the Great Principle and the others are not all-pervasive, they must have an unmanifest cause, just like jars and other such objects.
Furthermore: "Because of homogeneity" (samanvayāt).
For all effects are endowed with the experience of pleasure and pain;
and those things which conform to a particular form are unmanifested as that very nature.
Just as jars, crowns, and the like, which conform to the forms of clay or gold, are unmanifested as lumps of clay or gold.

Therefore, there exists the unmanifest (avyakta), which is the state of equilibrium of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, whose nature consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and which is the cause of all differentiated effects.
Although these inferences establish the essential nature of the unmanifest,
it is established by them specifically as the cause of the Great One (mahat) and the subsequent principles.
Here it must be asked: is the unmanifest established by these inferences merely as the material cause of the world, or also as an independent entity?
In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*),
because we also accept that *pradhāna* is the material cause of the universe;
[the term] "having the form of a body" [is redundant].
For it has been said thus; and in order to refute the second [position], the Sūtra states: "And because the arrangement is impossible, there is no inference."
He explains that with the words "this" (idam).

"This [world] is not under the control of insentient matter, because it is a functional entity, like a perceived object"—since this very [argument] has been refuted, how could there be a fundamental inference for it? (MAnu 2.17)
The meaning is that it is the great effect, such as the primordial matter (mahat) and so forth;
"under the power of the insentient" means having an origination dependent upon an independent insentient principle, just like [the objects] already mentioned.
Like the case of *pradhāna*.

Let other refutations be set aside for now; the remainder [of the argument] is this: by what capacity could the original inference (*mūlānumā*) be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the independence of *pradhāna*, which has already been refuted by the counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*)?
Or rather, it should be understood as "following from the root" (*mūlānumā*). What is the purpose of this objection?
If it is argued that "the state of not being an effect" (*akāryatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*) here, we say no.
Because [the reason] does not pervade the probandum in the case of cloth and the like;
for it is observed through positive and negative concomitance that cloth and such things have as their material cause threads presided over by weavers and others.

Keeping in mind the construction of the words of the Sūtra—namely, that since the activity of the Pradhāna as an independent agent in the fashioning of the world is untenable due to its contradiction with inference, inference is not a valid means of knowledge regarding it—the intended meaning of the Sūtra has been stated.
Now, explaining that very point, he states another counter-argument: "Independent" (svatantra).
And how could that composition exist in an insentient being if it were independent? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.18ab)
The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate other forms of inference; the connection [of the phrase] is "how much more so? The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows:
Pradhāna lacks independent activity because it is insentient, like threads and so forth.
[Objection: Even though pradhāna is insentient, let there be independent activity; what contradiction is there?
And thus, because there is no subverting argument (bādhaka) against the contrary case (vipakṣa), this reason (hetu) is non-conclusive; to this he says: "the state of being insentient" (acetanatva).
And the claim that insentience constitutes independence is contradicted by the very nature of the self.
For one should only suspect that which, when suspected, would not give rise to a contradiction with one's own words, one's own actions, logic, or other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Indeed, no one suspects:
"Could even a mute person not be a speaker?"
Why would a word not be non-expressive?
Since it is an inference, why should mere inference not be invalid?
Why, then, should fire not be non-hot?
For this demoness of doubt never attains peace;

therefore, one who harbors such a suspicion is neither a worldly person nor an investigator, and should be disregarded like a madman. Furthermore, in the case at hand, the lack of sentience and independence [of the body] are sublated by the valid cognition of the self.
[The opponent's position] is self-contradictory and contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, the very doubt that "let there be independent activity of the Pradhāna even though it is insentient" ought not even to arise; so what is the point of presenting an objection here? [The author replies:
But how is there self-contradiction when one suspects the independence of something insentient?
For independence is not what constitutes consciousness,
nor is dependence what constitutes insentience.
And how could there be a contradiction with valid cognition?
Therefore, in order to first demonstrate the self-contradiction, he explains independence as follows: "By his own will... and so forth.
For the wise know that sovereignty is indeed the state of acting according to one's own will.
The word "in [the case of] activity" (*pravṛttau*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
By the phrase "those who know know," he states that this is the consensus of all learned people.

For this very reason, because there is an absence of independence (*svātantrya*), everyone accepts that the conventional usage of agency in expressions such as "the tree stands" is figurative (*gauṇa*). (7.97)
Nevertheless, how is there self-contradiction?
For "insentience" does not mean the absence of desire; rather, it means the absence of consciousness. To this, he says: "Why? (kutaḥ).
Whence [could there be] volition for one who lacks desire? ... // Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.19c //
From what cause does desire arise in that which is insentient? From nothing at all;
for the meaning is that knowledge alone is the generator of desire.
Nevertheless, as to why this is so, he says: "If [it were] by its own will... (*secchaṃ cet*). ... "If it were by its own will, how could it be insentient? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.19cd).
If that [activity] is admitted to be spontaneous (*svacchanda*), then the meaning is: how can that which is insentient (*acetana*) be sentient?
This is what is being said:
by one who asserts that the insentient *pradhāna* possesses activity through its own independence, it would be as good as saying that the insentient possesses desire (*icchā*).
This is because it is universally accepted that the meaning of the word "independence" (svātantrya) is the state of acting according to one's own will;
furthermore, by one who accepts that an insentient entity possesses will, sentience must also be admitted for it,
since it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that will is an effect of consciousness residing in the same substrate as itself.
Because it is improper to accept the effect while rejecting the cause,
and because the claim that "the insentient is sentient" is a manifest contradiction;
by this, the following point is also refuted.

If insentience (*acetanatva*) and independence (*svātantrya*) are mutually contradictory, then in establishing the absence of independent activity by means of insentience, there would be the fault of the reason being non-different from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatā*).

For we have not asserted a direct contradiction between insentience and independence— like saying "the barren woman has offspring"— but rather that, by the force of independence, consciousness (*caitanya*) must be accepted by the opponent.

Having thus stated the subverting argument—that if one accepts independence for that very [insentient entity] after having caused it to act, its lack of sentience would be untenable—he now demonstrates the contradiction with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the acceptance of independence for the insentient: "I desire... (*icchāmīti*).
For it is by the constraint of one's own experience that one says, "I desire";
thus, desire is absent from that which is insentient. 2.20.
By the word *hi*, he indicates that this inference is well-known to all people.
The word *eva* connects with "is indeed gone.
One's own experience (*nijānubhava*) is the experience of direct perception (*sākṣyanubhava*).
In the cognition "I desire," the desire related to the self is first experienced by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*);
nor is it possible for that [desire] to have two agents,
because nowhere is a single operation observed to have two agents.

Consequently, since the admission of desire in that which is insentient contradicts the experience of consciousness, it follows that desire is absent in the insentient; that is to say, it does not exist.
The sense is that in the absence of desire, independence—characterized by acting according to one's own will—is utterly cast aside.
Now, it may be argued: "There is no such experience; rather, there is merely the conventional usage of 'I desire'."
The cause for that [error] as well is the non-apprehension of difference.
For the Self is eternal and changeless, its nature being pure consciousness alone; therefore, it is impossible for agency such as desire to be adventitious to it.
Rather, such qualities belong to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone, because it possesses the property of production.
And due to the non-apprehension of the difference between these two— the self and the internal organ— the practical usage of each other's attributes proceeds.
And the cause for this non-apprehension of difference is proximity,
as it has been said:

"Therefore, through union with that [Puruṣa], the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears as if it were sentient; and likewise, while the Guṇas are the actual agents, the indifferent [Puruṣa] appears as if he were the agent.
For this reason, the claim that—on the strength of experience—the possession of desire belongs only to the sentient and not to the insentient is incorrect; thus, he says: "If..."
...and if there is also a non-apprehension of difference here. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.20d)
How could that [destruction] not belong to the jar? ... // MAnu 2.21a //

If it is thus the case that there is no actual experience at all, but only mere conventional usage, and if it is asserted that the non-apprehension of difference is the cause for this conventional usage, then why would that non-apprehension of difference not also apply to a jar?
The phrase "the cause of worldly transaction" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
This is what is being said:
first of all, there is the fault of denying self-luminous experience.
Furthermore, there is no basis for linguistic usage [in that case],
nor is there a non-apprehension of difference;
for it is a rule that specific linguistic usage has such a cognition as its necessary effect.
Otherwise, even a jar and a cloth would not apprehend their mutual difference, and there would consequently be the practical usage of the "intermixture of each other's properties. [Objection:
But surely, it is the apprehension of difference between two objects being apprehended that is the cause of such practical usage, and not the mere non-apprehension of difference.
Furthermore, since a jar and a cloth do not apprehend their own intrinsic natures [in this context], how can there be such an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)?
Is this non-apprehension of distinction (bhedāgraha) a property of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), or of the self (ātman)?
Not the first,
because since it is insentient, the apprehension of its own nature is impossible.
Or, even if it were so, why would that specific non-apprehension of difference not exist for the jar?
And in that case, there would also be practical usage [regarding it].
But surely, the superimposition of consciousness exists in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), not in the jar.
If it is argued that there is therefore no over-extension [of the definition],
what is its cause?
If it is argued that it is "proximity," then...
In that case, since the presence of the omnipresent self exists even in a jar, why would it not belong to the jar?
[Objection: But conjunction alone is not the cause;
rather, it is when there is a relationship of benefactor and beneficiary.
If it is argued that this [connection] exists between the self and the internal organ because it was stated to be for the sake of the Puruṣa’s perception,
then since a jar also assists the Puruṣa, why should it not belong to the jar as well?
Regarding the second [alternative], does the empirical transaction belong to the Self or to the internal organ?
Not the first,
because it is untenable for that which is changeless to engage in the activity of empirical transaction.
Or rather, what fault is there in [the existence of] a desire for rebirth?

If, in the second case, the conventional usage of one thing is applied to another due to a non-apprehension of difference when [the cognition] has gone toward something else, why would that [usage] not apply to a jar as well? (7.109)
Furthermore, if it is accepted that desire— which is actually a property of the internal organ— is designated as belonging to the self due to the non-apprehension of their difference,
then why would there not also arise the designation "I am pot-shaped, with a broad base and belly," since there is likewise a non-apprehension of the difference between a jar and the self?
This is the answer from one whose intention is hidden.
Alternatively, the intended meaning here is that even though the difference between the self and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is clearly manifest;

[the question is]: if there were a non-apprehension of difference, then why would that non-apprehension of difference not also exist between the jar and the self? This is the construction [of the argument]. Or rather, one who speaks thus should be questioned as follows:
Is the non-apprehension of difference the opposite of the apprehension of difference, or not?
If the position is that it is not, the answer is: how could that [apprehension] not exist with respect to a jar in its own nature, or with respect to a cloth and so forth?
[Objection: But surely, the apprehension of difference is the opposite of the non-apprehension of difference.

Since that pot exists, how could there be a non-apprehension of difference therein, or the linguistic usage prompted by it? Anticipating this second position from one who does not understand the hidden intention, he says: "The mind... [mana iti].
... because of the distinction that "the mind is I," since even the mind is grasped [as the self]... // MAnu 2.21bc //
In the word *bhedataḥ*, the suffix *-tasi* has the sense of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārtha*).

If it is argued that the apprehension of difference is opposed to the non-apprehension of difference, and therefore when a jar is apprehended as distinct [from others], there is no non-apprehension of its difference [from itself], then—

since the mind (*manaḥ*) is also apprehended as distinct [from the self] in the cognition "this is my mind"— there would likewise be no non-apprehension of the difference between the mind and the self.
And thus, it is incorrect to say that the conventional usage "I desire" is caused by the non-apprehension of difference;
rather, it is caused solely by direct experience.
For this very reason, it is also logical that there is no superimposition of the attributes of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) upon the Self.
Because, given the actual existence of the apprehension of difference, it is impossible for there to be a non-apprehension of difference— which is the cause of superimposition.
For that which has its difference unknown cannot be apprehended as being related [to another],
as this would lead to the absurd consequence that even the self [could be so apprehended].
By what means, then, is the mind apprehended?
We say: by the witness.
For it is thus:
Nor can there be comprehension of that [self] by means of the eyes and so forth,
because it is a substance devoid of form (arūpidravya),
and because it is perceived even when the eyes and other [senses] are not functioning.
Nor can it be established by inference, because there is no inferential mark (liṅga). [Objection:
But surely the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the inferential mark of the mind.
For instance, even when the external sense-faculties are simultaneously in contact with their respective objects and are presided over by the self, cognitions do not arise all at once.
Therefore, it is known that there exists something else besides these [faculties] which acts as a cooperative cause.
Because the sequence of cognitions proceeds by virtue of the sequence of their conjunctions.
Regarding this, someone says:
since such a capacity can be postulated for the self alone, the inference is established otherwise;
furthermore, it is inconclusive with respect to the mind, which, in its sequential engagement with each respective sense organ, is devoid of any other cause.
Furthermore, [it would apply] to the conjunctions with space occurring in succession as a fruit falls from a tree onto a hundred [other fruits], to the operation of an axe and so forth,
and to the operation of the sense organs in their conjunction with their respective objects;
therefore, that is incorrect.
For conceptualization follows what is observed;
indeed, an agent is observed to perform various effects simultaneously by presiding over multiple instruments. For instance:
A young student goes, reads, looks at the path, and carries a water-pot all at once;
therefore, it is not logical to postulate that [the self] is a property of the agent.
Rather, because it is observed, it is simply another substance that is non-pervasive.
"But there is no lack of certainty [in our position],
because even in that case, causes such as the sequence of actions and so forth do exist.
To this, it is replied:
To begin with, even those lacking discrimination possess the cognition of the mind,
as evidenced by such common expressions as "my mind has gone elsewhere.
Furthermore, they do not know the non-arising of simultaneous cognitions.
On the contrary, they maintain that cognitions arise simultaneously;
otherwise, if there were a sequence observed in cases of divided attention (*vyāsaṅga*), the opponent’s inference of a sequence in other cases as well would be futile.
Therefore, this mental cognition which exists even prior to the perception of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) cannot have that [mark] as its cause.
Let it be, then, that the mind is established as the substratum of the conjunction that serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of cognition and so forth.
Not so;
for in the case of perceptual knowledge, it is logical that the conjunction between the sense organ and the self alone functions as the non-inherent cause.
In the case of inference and the like, it is the knowledge of the logical mark (liṅga) and so forth;
in memory, it is mental cultivation (bhāvanā); and in pleasure and the like, it is the perception of a desired object and so forth.

If it is argued that this is not the case because there is a rule that eternal specific qualities (*nityaviśeṣaguṇa*) cannot have conjunction as their non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), we say no;
for there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of sound produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-śabda*) and sound produced by sound (*śabdaja-śabda*).
If it is argued that this is avoided by qualifying the reason (*hetu*) with "not being audible" (*aśrāvaṇatvena*), [we reply: no.

If, then, as in the case of words such as "disjunction" (*vibhāga*), one exerts effort at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) for the purpose of excluding other causes because other causes are observed, so too should one exert effort to exclude pleasure (*sukha*) and the like; for the observation of another non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is equal in both cases.
If it is argued that [pleasure] is merely an efficient cause (*nimitta*), we say no.
Because this would result in the definition of an *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause) being over-extended (*ativyāpti*).
Nor is the mind established by its being the instrument for the perception of pleasure and so forth;
for that is established otherwise, since it is already established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). *7,123*
In this way, other forms of inference as well must be refuted;
nor is scripture a means of valid cognition regarding the mind,
for even those who are congenitally deaf possess that cognition.
Therefore, it is established that the mind is apprehended by a witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).

And since that [mind] is apprehended by that very [witness] as distinct from the self, the non-apprehension of difference is impossible; thus, the conventional usage "I desire" is not based on a non-apprehension of difference.
Now, an objection: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, fear, and shame—all these are indeed the mind alone."
Thus, in the Śruti, desire is first understood to be of the nature of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). And it is not proper for the meaning of the Śruti to be otherwise.

Therefore, due to the onset of a powerful subverting factor, one must accept that the expression "I desire" is merely a conventional usage caused by the non-apprehension of difference [between the self and desire].
But there is no experience of a connection with the self's own desire;
nor is it impossible for that [connection] not to be grasped because of the apprehension of difference in the form "my mind," since that is merely a conventional usage,
like the expression "my consciousness."
Nor is there any inconsistency in what has been stated;
for it is said that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the primary effect of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*,
and it possesses three constituent parts (*aṃśa*).
The constituent parts are the coloring by the person (*puruṣoparāga*), the coloring by the object (*viṣayoparāga*), and the entry of activity (*vyāpārāveśa*).
For indeed, there arises the thought, "I am doing this.
Among these, the coloring by consciousness (*cetana*)—expressed as "I"—is unreal (*atāttvika*), like the reflection of a face on a mirror, due to the non-apprehension of their distinction.
The coloring by an object as "this" is a transformation through the channel of the sense organ, like the contact of dirt with a mirror; it is not ultimately real.
Likewise, the engagement in activity depends upon both [the subject and the object].
This same principle applies here in the case of "I desire this"; therefore, he says: "dependent upon both."
... because it possesses the nature of both. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.21d)
But for desire, the mind is the desire... // MDh 2.22a //
The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis;
the word "tataḥ" (therefore) should be supplied [to the sentence].
This is because desire possesses a dual nature.
It is the nature of the self and the nature of the mind;
for this very reason, the scriptural statement that "the mind is desire" is justified.
This is what is meant:
This assumption of the non-apprehension of difference would be possible if the state of having desires were not ultimately real for the self;
but this is not the case.
Because there is no sublation [of this position].
For desire is of two kinds:
one is a property of the self (ātman), and the other is a property of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
In this regard, the Śruti has proceeded with reference to desire as a property of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and it does not negate the fact that the Self possesses desire.
For the statement "Devadatta is rich in cows" cannot negate Yajñadatta’s connection with cows. (7.133)
This might be so,
provided that the twofold nature of desire were established by valid cognition;
but if it is asked, "From where is this established?"— then [the answer follows].
First, by the force of scripture and experience:
even when a thousand ways of accounting for it have been pursued and yet no consistency is found, one must indeed resort to the audacity of denying experience.
And he states another means of knowledge: "The beloved," etc.
... due to the distinction between the pleasant and the unpleasant, a twofold nature of this [world] is observed. ... // MAnu 2.22bc //

"Dear" refers to that which is desired absolutely, while "not dear" refers to that which is desired only for the time being. By means of the object (*viṣaya*), the subject (*viṣayin*) is indicated; this refers to desire (*kāma*).
This is the meaning:

for a man who is a believer and a lover, there is on one hand the desire regarding garlands, sandalwood, women, and so forth, thinking "may this be mine," and on the other hand the thought "I might have to abandon it."
And this is not a single entity,
because its forms are contradictory;
nor are both of them mental phenomena (*manodharma*).
Because of simultaneity;
for it is impossible for [the cause] to produce dharmas of the same kind simultaneously,
yet simultaneity does not fail to exist.
Because it is established by experience and because there is no subverting evidence,
that which has an unpleasant object is a property of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), whereas that which has a pleasant object is a property of the self (*ātman*). (7.134)
Alternatively, by the words "pleasant" (*priya*) and "unpleasant" (*apriya*), liberation (*mukti*) and saṃsāra are expressed;
thus, a twofold nature of desire (*kāma*) is observed through the distinction of their respective relations.
Indeed, there exists in saṃsāra this abundant desire which consists of the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*).
And that [bliss] exists in liberation,
according to such scriptural passages as: "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers," and so forth.
And this [pleasure] is not one and the same [in all cases],
because the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) dissolves upon liberation;
thus, it must be accepted as a property of the self (ātmadharma).
And since there is no connection with adventitious properties in liberation, the twofold nature of desire is established even prior [to liberation].
He states the purpose for avoiding the contradiction with scripture: "Therefore...
[Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 2.22d]: "Therefore, how could there be a non-apprehension of difference?"
Since the contradiction with scripture has been resolved, from what source of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could the non-apprehension of difference be postulated?
And from what [source] could the fact that worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is caused by that [non-apprehension] be established through the denial of experience?
The meaning is: from no source whatsoever.

By this [statement], for those who seek to establish that the insentient *pradhāna* is the independent cause of the world through inference, both self-contradiction and contradiction with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) arise in their assertion;
furthermore, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because the independence of an insentient entity is not admitted anywhere. (7.138)
Summarizing the meaning of the sūtra, he explains the term "inference" (anumāna) by means of another method, stating: "composition" (racanā).
Because the formation [of the world] is impossible, that [world] does not follow from the inference of an omniscient being;
the creator of the world is insentient... // MAnu 2.23a-c //
Therefore,
the inference regarding primordial matter (prakṛti) and so forth, which is derived from the inference of an omniscient being,
is the direct perception of someone.
"Because it is an object of knowledge"—this means that everything is understood through an inference that is not yet established as proof.
That is to say, it is understood through the words of one who is accepted as omniscient, whose omniscience has been established by inference.

Alternatively, because his authority is established by inference and because inference is his primary means, the very words of the one regarded as omniscient are themselves called "the inference of the omniscient."
Furthermore, this is the purpose of the alternative explanation:
it is to make known that what was stated previously—that this matter is not established by yogic perception or by the words of the Sāṅkhya teachers—is indeed indicated by the sūtra itself.

Alternatively, the construction is as follows: when [the nature of] inference is understood through an inference such as "because of the finite measure of distinct objects" (parimāṇāt) and so forth, which is conceived by those who claim to be omniscient.
Then,
the demonstration of the threefold variety is the purpose of the alternative explanation:
[the Lord] is the creator of the world, the cause of the world by virtue of His sovereignty.
It might be argued as follows:
by means of reasons such as finite magnitude (*parimāṇa*), it is understood that there exists some fundamental cause for effects such as the "great" (*mahat*) and so forth.

Furthermore, since there is no evidence for postulating another cause for that [cause] as well, and because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), [that fundamental cause must be accepted].
And its independence consists precisely in not being prompted by any other causal factor (*kāraka*), but not in following its own will—
which would entail the aforementioned fault.
And that [independence] is established simply because there is no other prompting causal factor for it that is supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Nor is that impossible for what is insentient,
because it is observed even among insentient things such as milk and water;
for indeed, milk, though insentient and even without being presided over by another, proceeds toward the growth of the calf.
It turns into the state of curd;
and water, when released from its density, undergoes various transformations in things such as the citron and the coconut; yet it does not depart from its nature as water.
Grass eaten by a cow turns into milk,
and iron moves toward a magnet;
yet it is not the case that "this is under the power of something insentient."
This contradicts such authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the very locations already mentioned;
nor is this accepted by the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādins*).
The aphorism [is presented] for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that this would result in proving what is already established:
Oṃ. If it is argued that [the self] is like milk and water, then to that also: Oṃ.
Thus it is said. He explains that: "And like milk, water, and so forth. (7.143) "If [it were] like milk or water, then in that case too... (BBs 2.2.3).
... nor milk, water, and the like, serve as a [proper] comparison. MAnu 2.23d.
And from these words of the Praśāstṛ, [the nature] of both the conscious and the unconscious [is known].
The comparison [is used] for the purpose of imagining a similar case for one's own position, and [it applies] to the deviation of our reason—this is the remainder [of the sense].
For the purpose of showing that "just as the probandum deviates here, so may the reason also deviate in the subject (pakṣa)," the deviation is pointed out;
however, that is not appropriate in this case.
This is because of the statement of Praśāstṛ regarding the conscious and the unconscious; because of the Vedic revelation (śruti) which establishes the impulsion by the Supreme Lord;
and because the first word "ca" (and) has the sense of "even though it is perceived by worldly people as being independent."
The second [view], however, is that it applies not only to the insentient,
but to both as well;
this is what is meant.
Furthermore, independence characterized by not being prompted by another agent is also not applicable to the primary [agent],
because it is impossible and because it contradicts the aforementioned inference. *7,146*
As for what was stated here—that it is like milk and water—that is incorrect;
for even in that case, [the movement occurs] through the impulsion of the Lord, as in the passage: "Of this very Imperishable..."
This is because it is established by such scriptural passages as these.

For this very reason, the argument that there is a lack of evidence for the Pradhāna being directed by another is also refuted. Furthermore, although the Sūtra mentions "like milk and water," that illustration is not to be taken as authoritative.

The word "etc. (*ādi*) is employed for the purpose of explaining the subsequent sūtra—"Because of the non-existence of negative concomitance and because of independence"—which serves to dispel the doubt that "in other instances, there may be both possibility and deviation.
Alternatively, the word "etc. was stated with the intention that the mention of milk and water is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The subsequent sūtra, however, is for the sake of *kaimutya* (the argument from the obvious):
since even the activity of sentient beings does not exist independently of God, what need is there to mention that the activity of insentient things is dependent upon Him?
To explain this, it was stated: "of both the sentient and the insentient."
Furthermore, the reason "because of limited magnitude" (parimāṇāt) is inconclusive.
For *prakṛti* is defined as the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*;
yet *sattva* and the other qualities are indeed limited in measure.
As it has been said:
"By means of fire, water, earth, ego, the great principle (mahat-tattva), and the three qualities,
[the elements] arise in sequence, each increasing by ten."
(Ādi Purāṇa, Pūrva-khaṇḍa, Māhātmya 2.46).
Nor is it the case that *prakṛti* possesses another unmanifest (*avyakta*) within it; thus, how could there not be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntyam*)?
Furthermore, there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against even a limited entity being the root-primal nature (*mūla-prakṛti*).
Causality belongs only to those things whose non-production of an effect is restricted to all instances, as is observed in the case of threads and the like;
for it is impossible for that which is unlimited to be subject to the alternatives of being either the whole or a part.
But for us, it is established solely through the power of God.
Furthermore, the argument based on "homogeneity" (*samanvaya*) is also untenable;

for the universal rule that "whatever effect possesses a certain following [of qualities] must be endowed with a cause possessing those same qualities" is already refuted by the very admission that the manifest arises from the unmanifest.
The argument that "because activity occurs according to capacity" (*śaktitaḥ pravṛtteḥ*) also does not establish the intended point;
for this would only be the case if it were established that the capacity of a cause is precisely its having the effect already inherent within it (*antarbhāvitakāryatvam eva*),
and that [inherence] is maintained only by the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
For this very reason, both differentiation (*vibhāga*) and non-differentiation (*avibhāga*) are also refuted;

for differentiation and non-differentiation themselves lack existence, being dependent upon the establishment of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). If the object were established merely through one's own system of thought, [one would have to say] "of a gross body such as a clod of earth."

By such statements, [the opponent suggests that] even the theory of atoms as the cause [of the world] might hold, based on the notions of division and non-division imagined by the logicians; let this elaboration suffice.
Now, one might object: "This follows the maxim of 'dawn at the very spot where the house was struck' (ghaṭṭakuṭṭīprabhātanyāya).
For in the case of the claim that 'the possession of will belongs to the Self alone and not to the insentient,' experience was first made the authority."

And there, when a contradiction with the Veda was raised, it was stated that there is no contradiction because desire is twofold—being both a property of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and a property of the self (*ātman*).

Thus, the suspicion that the self alone possesses desire while the insentient [organ] does not has already been abandoned; he now dispels this by means of the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokana*) method: "Even though desire and so forth are twofold, how can the self have ownership over them? (2.24cd)
That which has ascended to the level of direct experience can never be sublated.

The construction is as follows: even though desire and so forth are twofold, how can the Lordship of the Self over desire and so forth—which is established by direct experience—be set aside by any means of valid cognition? It cannot be set aside by any at all. The inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi) is for the sake of referring to the Śruti.
The change to *apoditum* involves a Vedic vowel-sandhi (*samprasāraṇa*).
This is the sequence of the answer here:
it is true that desire is twofold, consisting of a property of the self and an activity of the mind;
therein, even with respect to desire as an activity of the mind, the self alone possesses ownership, not the mind.
This is because it is established by direct experience that "I desire";
however, the mind is merely the material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to desire,
just as follows:
Just as the farmer alone is the owner of the crops that arise from the appropriation of a field, and not the field itself, so it is here.
Nor should it be argued that the mind alone is the master of desire, while the experience "I desire" is merely an illusion or a conventional usage;
for there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka-pramāṇa) to the contrary.
Nor is immutability a subverting factor,
because it is accepted that the internal organ alone is the material cause of desire,
and because immutability remains unimpaired by mere ownership.
Otherwise, there would result the futility of the self, just as that of a miser’s wealth.
This is what was meant by the phrase "in some cases.
Now, let it be that the self alone is the master of desire, and not the mind.

Nevertheless, the contradiction between the earlier and later statements remains exactly as it was; for even in the absence of ownership through desire, some form of possessing desire has been admitted by you in the case of the mind. To this, he says: "Desire," etc.
Mastery over desires alone has been described as the possession of desire, and nothing else.
In the passage beginning with "devoid of insentient desire" (*acetana-icchā-apagata*), the state of possessing desire is said to be simply the ownership of desire;
it does not mean something else characterized by being the material cause (*upādāna*) of desire.
This is what is meant.
There might be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows here:
if that very possession of desire which was previously denied of the mind were now accepted again in this context.
But this is not the case.

Previously, it was stated that the possession of desire—characterized by being the master of desire—belongs to the Self alone and not to the insentient [mind], because that [possession of desire] is what constitutes its agency.

However, since it is now accepted that the mind possesses desire as characterized by being the material cause (*upādāna*) of desire in accordance with the meaning of the scripture, how can there be any contradiction? *7,156*
Alternatively, since the mind also possesses desire due to the twofold nature of desire, its status as an agent would be established; therefore, he says: "Even though there is twofoldness."
Although both [the self and the mind] possess desire, the ownership of desire belongs to the self alone and not to the mind;
for this is established by the experience of an unimpeachable witness.
As for the mind, however, it possesses only the status of being the material cause (upādāna) of desire.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Desire," etc.
