The state of possessing desire (*icchāvattva*), characterized as sovereignty over one's own will (*icchā-svāmitva-lakṣaṇa*), was previously stated to be necessary for agency; it is not, however, characterized as being the material cause of desire (*icchopādānatva-lakṣaṇa*).
For it is the person who desires who exerts effort, and not that which becomes the object of desire.
Therefore, because of the ownership of desire, agency belongs only to the conscious being and not to the unconscious one;
for although the latter possesses desire as its material cause, it lacks ownership over that desire.
It might be argued as follows:
That which is capable of being employed according to its intended purpose is its own name,
such as "cow" and so forth.

And he is called a master who is the director of one's desires as he wishes; however, this does not exist for the self and desire, because even when a believer or a lustful person restrains a prohibited desire, [the desire remains].
If it is argued: "She manifests; yet even for one who exerts effort, the desired object does not arise. Therefore, how can the self possess mastery over desire?"
Is it being said that one's own desire is not subject to control in any way whatsoever? Or is some degree of control admitted?
Not the first.
Because it would contradict experience, and because it would entail the absence of common usage such as "Devadatta desires," [the first alternative is rejected].
Regarding the second [alternative], however, he states that ownership is established: "something" (kiñcit).
Even though he is under her control in some respects, his status as the master remains, just as it does in the world.

Even though desire lacks absolute mastery due to the force of powerful opposing factors, the self’s ownership over it would certainly still exist by virtue of its possessing even a slight degree of mastery.
How so?

Just as in the world, Devadatta’s ownership over a cow is observed despite the cow being entirely beyond his control, provided he possesses even a slight degree of mastery over it; exactly so is this case.
Otherwise, even that would not exist. [Objection: But if this were so, then for one desiring to connect a single [syllable], [the subsequent one would be displaced].

The objection "it follows that [the self] would fall [into the error of being unconscious]" has been addressed. It was established that agency belongs to the insentient [mind] only insofar as the self possesses ownership over desire, and not to the mind itself.
If that were so, then even the Lord (Īśvara) would lack ownership over the mental activity and desire of the potter and others, and thus he could not be the agent of jars and such things.
To the objection that this contradicts the section [sūtra] beginning with "Because there is designation as something else" (tathācetaravyapadeśāt), he says: "The Self of all" (sarvātmā).
How much more so, then, for the Supreme Lord, who is the soul of all tantras and desires?

When even for the individual soul (jīva) there is lordship over desires and so forth, then he is described as such because his desires and so forth are entirely dependent upon him; that is, he whose desire is the primary cause—the "beginning"—of the means (tantra/sādhana) for all souls. What more need be said regarding the supreme Lord’s lordship over desire?
This is what is meant: [the Lord is the ultimate source of all volition].
Both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) preside over the body.

Therein, the Lord, having clearly perceived the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), produces within it the functions consisting of knowledge, desire, and effort by means of His own will, knowledge, and effort; and having presided over the external organs, He brings about the production of jars and other objects. The individual soul, however, remains as one whose lordship has been granted by Him.
As it has been said: "Intellect is knowledge," and so forth. Therefore, sovereignty and agency belong primarily to the Lord alone, whereas for the individual soul (jīva), they are merely secondary.
And so it has been said: "Where this relationship of owned and owner is constant, then that [agency] exists in the Infallible (acyuta) through its connection with the action" (*Ślokavārttika* 7.161).
As for the claim that, by the force of uncontradicted experience, the ownership of desire belongs to the Self alone—that is incorrect.

Since this has already been refuted by the powerful Vedic statement—which is non-human in origin and declares that desire belongs to the mind in the passage, "Desire, volition..."—he says: "And not... (na ca).
Nor is even the Vedic word capable of refuting the fact that sovereignty over objects of desire is experienced [by the sacrificer].... MAnu 2.27a-c.
The ellipsis to be supplied is "the self's sovereignty over desires.

Indeed, by way of restating desire and so forth, this Vedic statement declares that they are of the nature of the mind (*manas*) in order to preclude the view held by the Vaiśeṣikas and others that the self is the material cause [of desire].

Furthermore, since the essential nature of desire and the rest is established solely through the experience of direct perception (*sākṣin*), that [perception] serves as their foundational support (*upajīvya*).
And he (the author) takes as his objects only those things that have himself as their master;
nor can one who depends on another ever refute that upon which he depends.
Even though the Veda is generally more authoritative, it is indeed weaker in comparison to that which it depends upon.
As they have said:
"Among those three, the superior authority of scripture alone is traditionally held; however, when there is a contradiction with that which it depends upon, this [scripture] possesses no validity."
Therefore, it is not logical that scripture should subvert direct experience. If one asks, "In that case, what is the status of scripture? he says: "Therefore... ...
"Therefore, it denotes something other than that. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.27cd)
The meaning is that [the perception] is sublated by a stronger experience because it serves as its basis of subsistence (*upajīvya*).
"Denoting something other than that" means denoting a state of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) for something other than ownership (*svāmitva*).
It is not merely due to the sublation of what is to be relied upon.
But he says "one who desires liberation" because [otherwise] it would contradict the possibility of rebirth.
If there were another who desired liberation from that which is yet to be liberated.
If desire were to have the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its agent, then even the desire for liberation would belong solely to the internal organ.
However, it is well known that liberation belongs to the Self (*ātman*).
And thus, it would follow—which is untenable—that the one who will become liberated is entirely different from the one who desires liberation.
If desire belongs to one person, it must be admitted that the performer of the means [to achieve it] is necessarily another;
for we observe that the desire for a result and the performance of the means [to attain it] reside in a single locus.
And thus, there would follow the fallacy of "the acquisition of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the loss of what was done" (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*). (7.166)
But surely this is not a fault,
because it is accepted that the activity of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) proceeds for the sake of the liberation of the person (*puruṣa*).
For indeed, the activity of people is observed to be for the sake of another's purpose.
In this context, the following is presented: "for one who desires liberation."
Of what use is that to one who desires liberation? ... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.28c //
This is an elliptical indication;
it should also be understood as "one who performs the means of accomplishment.
Indeed, those in the world who act for the sake of another's purpose are generally observed to be pursuing some objective, whether perceptible or imperceptible.
Likewise, here too, there must be a purpose for primordial nature (prakṛti); and the meaning is that such a purpose does not exist.
This might be argued:

Since the activity of primordial nature (prakṛti) for the sake of the liberation of the individual soul proceeds even without pursuing its own purpose—just as it does for you, O Lord, out of compassion—he says: "And for the sake of its own destruction."
"And who would strive for its own destruction? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.28d).
Not only is it not fitting for the activity of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) to be for the sake of another's purpose;
for liberation (*mokṣa*) is indeed the dissolution of primordial nature.
For no compassionate person is ever seen striving for the sake of their own destruction.

Although it should have been stated here that even the state of being benefited is nowhere observed in that which is incapable of receiving an enhancement and is devoid of activity, nevertheless, since this [objection] was raised by his very disciples, this other refutation has been stated while accepting that [position]. *7,168*
Is this not indeed improper? For a conscious being would pursue its own purpose;
and fearing its own destruction, it would turn back.
But how can *prakṛti*, being insentient, be subject to such an inquiry?
If it is argued that she proceeds even while considering her own liberation, then how could she do so?
If you say, "This is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of *pradhāna*," [we reply:]...
In that case, his transmigratory existence would never cease.
If it is argued that the activity of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) for the sake of experience is its inherent nature,
then there would be no liberation.
If, however, it were of the nature of both, then neither would exist due to contradiction;
or, if there were no contradiction, both would exist simultaneously.
Because there would be no one to establish [the rules].
If it is argued that [the practice] is for the sake of liberation once enjoyments have been consumed, we say no;
because enjoyments are infinite and thus can never be fully exhausted.
This is the consequential argument (*prasaṅga*): if the self were not the agent of desire, then there would be no seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*);
consequently, one would not exert effort for that purpose.
And thus, one would not be liberated; for it is illogical that the activity of another could occur regardless of whether there is a purpose for oneself or not.
This illustration is abundant, as is recorded in the tradition; hence, the *parasmaipada* ending is used in the word "yateta" (one should strive).
And so it has been said: "The followers of Candra and others, however, believe that both [agency and enjoyment] proceed from everything.

(7.171) Having thus refuted the non-theistic Sāṅkhya doctrine by means of general objections, he now refutes the view of those who maintain that agency belongs to primordial matter (*prakṛti*) alone, while enjoyment belongs to the self (*ātman*).
"Agency..."—for whomsoever agency exists, for that very one enjoyment is observed. (Manu 2.29ab)
Alternatively, having thus established the self's status as an agent, he establishes its status as an enjoyer by this very same reasoning:

"I, who performed this action, am that very same person who enjoys its fruit. Since there is an experience of the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between agency and enjoyment, if one were to accept their lack of coreferentiality, it would contradict experience.
If it is argued that this experience is erroneous, we say no.
He states "and in the case of division" because there is no subverting evidence [to the contrary].
And upon their division, there would be no measure whatsoever for either of them anywhere.
Regarding those two— agency and enjoyership—
if they were distinct, that is, if they resided in different substrata,
then it would follow that there is the acquisition of what was not done and the destruction of what was done. (7.172)
As for what was stated— that there would be no liberation for the self—
that is a point we accept,
because liberation is admitted to belong to primordial nature (prakṛti) alone.
Nor is it untenable that bondage and liberation are located in different substrata, because bondage also resides in *prakṛti*. To this, he replies: "No.

His intention is that since all the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and direct experience establish that both bondage and liberation reside in the Self, [the opponent's view] contradicts those authorities; thus he concludes with the words "sarva... (all...).
Initiated into the singular, wicked initiation that opposes all the Manavas,
he shall be comparable to a Māyāvādin.
Indeed, that which is a primary, wicked initiation—a corrupt resolve for practice—is in direct contradiction to all [scriptural] authorities.
One who is initiated by such [a resolve], this Sāṅkhya, would attain a status comparable to the Māyāvādins.

For they too, having accepted a mere consciousness (caitanya) that is devoid of all attributes such as agency and enjoyership and is virtually non-existent, attribute the causality of everything and the locus of bondage and liberation to insentient ignorance (avidyā) alone.
And they accept [this].
Therefore, since these [others] accept propositions that contradict all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this Sāṅkhya serves as an illustrative example.
That plurality of puruṣas which was accepted by the Sāṅkhya is indeed also accepted by the proponents of Māyā.
Indeed, that plurality [of Brahman] arises solely from the natural attributes such as being the progenitor and so forth;
there is no mutual distinction whatsoever in its essential nature.
Even the proponents of Māyā admit that difference is based upon limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

Nor is the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) a distinguishing feature [of this system], because the Sāṅkhya school has already refuted the phenomenal body by accepting it as being merely a cause. Thus,
it is stated that even the process of creation, dissolution, bondage, liberation, and their means as conceptualized by the Sāṅkhyas is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
We do not merely state that the Sāṅkhya system is similar to the Māyāvāda;
rather, he says "that" (tat) to indicate that this has also been hinted at by the author of the Sūtras.
...and that [objection] has been refuted by the word "tat" (that). 2.2.30d.

Therefore, because the Sāṅkhya system is similar to the Māyāvāda, it has been refuted by the very same arguments used to refute the Māyāvādin—namely, the argument from the "attainment of the enjoyer" (*bhoktrāpatti*) which leads to the lack of distinction (*avibhāga*), as previously addressed under the aphorism *syāl lokavat*, and the argument from the "impossibility of construction" (*racanānupapatti*) under the aphorism *na anumānam*. This was done by combining these points with the word "and" (*ca*).
Alternatively, he states by this that even the contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*) was not left unstated in the sūtra.
Therefore, it is precisely because of its contradiction with all means of valid cognition (*māna*).
The word "and" (*ca*) is inserted for the purpose of compounding the contradictions with all means of valid cognition; such is the meaning.
Thus ends the section on the "Inexplicability of Composition" (*racanānupapatti*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*. (7.180)
[======= JNys_2,2.II: The Section on Non-existence Elsewhere =======] // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section on non-existence elsewhere.
And because it does not exist elsewhere, it is not like grass and so forth.
Oṃ, and because it does not exist elsewhere, it is not like grass and so forth. Oṃ.
Some explain this sūtra as follows:

"Just as grass, shoots, and so forth, when consumed by cows and other animals, themselves turn into milk, so too does the *pradhāna* transform itself into the form of the *mahat* and the rest. It is said that this very doubt is what is being refuted here.
One should not say that the transformation of the *pradhāna* occurs by itself, like grass and so forth;
for even grass and such do not undergo transformation by themselves.
Why?

"In other cases, it is because [the substance] has been consumed by an ox, and thus that [substance] is absent. Here, the very doubt is untenable, as it has already been refuted by the statement: "If it were like milk or water, then it would be the same there too."
Furthermore, since it is inappropriate to compose a sūtra [based on such a case],
this counter-example is also untenable as a rebuttal.

For by asserting that milk-ness belongs only to that which has been consumed by cows and the like, and not to anything else, one would merely be establishing the presence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) for the material cause (*prakṛti*).
Nor, however, is there dependence upon Īśvara;
therefore, this is not the meaning of the Sūtra. Rather, intending to show that the doctrine of the Pātañjalas is refuted in this section, he introduces it with the words: "Of the Sāṅkhyas."

The Sāṃkhya, however, maintains that there is a Lord who possesses the power to favor the field (kṣetra), who is self-manifested and free from afflictions, karma, and the like. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 12.31)

Since the Sāṅkhya doctrine has already been refuted, one might ask what is the purpose of introducing it again; therefore, he indicates its distinction from that [previous doctrine] by means of the word "but" (tu).
He clarifies that very distinction by saying: "it is with God" (seśvara).
If it is argued that [the Self] is not to be denied because it possesses a Lord (īśvara), since there is no contradiction, it is therefore said: "The field" (kṣetra).
The word "tu" (but/however), which has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), is also to be construed here.
Although it is already established by the phrase "seśvaraḥ" (one who holds that there is a Lord) that they assert that God exists,
nevertheless, this [statement] is intended precisely to enjoin a qualification by way of restating that [assertion].
"Tell us: does that which exists as the Lord possess only the power to favor the field (*kṣetra*)?

In this regard, the 'field' (*kṣetra*) is the material cause (*prakṛti*), so called because effects reside within it in an unmanifest state. It is precisely this power to favor that field which is admitted by you to belong to the Lord."
Therefore, this [position] must indeed be rejected.
To the question, "In the absence of omnipotence, what constitutes his lordship (īśvaratva)? it is said: "Self-luminous" (svayambhāta).
It appears by itself, independent of the sense faculties and so forth;
the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
From this, it follows that [the Lord] is omniscient.
He states another qualification that establishes [the subject's] lordship: "kleśa... (beginning with the word *kleśa*).
The meaning is that he is devoid of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, its maturation (*vipāka*), and latent dispositions (*āśaya*).
Thus Patañjali said: "The Lord (*īśvara*) is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions, karma, its maturation, and latent dispositions."
Likewise: "Having empowered the nirmāṇakāya, he is the promoter of the tradition and the benefactor.
In that context, ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the clinging to existence are the five afflictions (*kleśa*).
Ignorance is the notion of a self in what is not-self.
The conceit "this is mine" is *asmitā* (egoism);
attachment to sense objects is *rāga* (passion);
and anger is *dveṣa* (aversion).
Fear is dogmatic adherence (*abhiniveśa*).

These same five afflictions are designated in other tantras as darkness (*tamaḥ*), delusion (*mohaḥ*), great delusion (*mahāmohaḥ*), gloom (*tāmisraḥ*), and blinding gloom (*andhatāmisraḥ*). Vārṣagaṇya, however, says that they are simply ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Karma" refers to injunctions and prohibitions;
by the word "intention" (āśaya), dharma and adharma are meant.
"Vipāka" refers to its fruit—namely pleasure and pain—and their means.
The word "iti" (thus) connects with each subsequent sentence that follows.
To clarify the contradiction with the Vedic doctrine, he states the term being excluded by the restriction: "In the field... (*kṣetre*).
That very Prakṛti, possessing the power of the field (kṣetra), is... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.32ab //
That which is the material cause of the world is Prakṛti alone, which possesses the power of being a material cause;

however, unlike the proponents of the Veda, it does not hold that even this power is dependent upon Īśvara. He states another point to be excluded [from the opponent's view] with the word "bīja" (seed).
... endowed with the power of the seed;
the individual soul [is like] the rain-cloud... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.32bc //
The word "also" (*api*) is connected here with "in this way" (*evam*).
The potency for arising through connection with the body, sense organs, and so forth is the "seed-potency" (*bīja-śakti*);
he asserts that the living being (*jīva*) alone possesses that [potency].
But [the proponent of the doctrine of principles] does not hold that their seed-potency is dependent on the Lord, as the proponents of the principles do.

If it were the case that the capacity for being the material cause and the capacity for origination belong to primordial matter (prakṛti) and the self (puruṣa) alone, then what would be the use of a Lord acting as a benefactor? To this he says: "Like the rain-cloud."

For just as the powers of being the material cause (*upādāna*) and of being the seed (*bīja*) respectively belong to the earth and to seeds such as rice, even though these powers are under their own control, nevertheless, in the production of the sprout, the rain possesses the quality of being the supportive factor (*anugrahakāraka*) for the earth and the factor that takes hold of it (*grāhaka*).

Likewise, even though both primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) possess powers inherent to themselves, it must be admitted that the Lord possesses the power to grace primordial nature. One might ask: "Is the Lord's role as the gracer of primordial nature to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), like a rain-cloud? To this he says: "By fate," etc.
...the Lord is traditionally held to be possessed of divine power. (Manu 2.2.32cd)
The word *daiva* (fate/divine) expresses the nature of the unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*).
By that, it indicates that [the Lord] is not an object of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
One might ask: "Is the Lord, who favors primordial nature (*prakṛti*), then to be accepted as being entirely without proof? To this, it is said: "He is remembered" (*smṛtaḥ*).
The phrase "in such passages as 'By the presiding Māyā, Nature brings forth the moving and the unmoving'" is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the context].
The term "is recorded" (*smṛta*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The word "also" (*api*) should be understood as including the term "heard" (*śruta*).
To the question, "Why do primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*) possess power inherent to themselves? he says: "Like the earth.
[Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.33a] Like the earth, that primordial matter...

Just as the earth possesses the power of being its own independent material cause (*upādāna*), so too, because it is a material cause, Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) is to be inferred as possessing the power of being its own independent material cause; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, this is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*);

it should also be understood that, like the seeds of rice and other grains, the individual soul (*jīva*) is likewise to be inferred as possessing the power of its own independent seed-nature due to its being a "seed" (*bījatva*).
Now, just as in the world there is someone who performs the sowing of seeds such as rice, so too here there must be someone corresponding to that role;
and no one other than the Supreme Lord can exist for that purpose.
How then is it that Īśvara alone possesses the power to favor the field? To this he says: "The individual soul (jīva)."
...the living soul [is the cause] merely by its presence, like one who performs the sowing of seeds... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.33bc //
Indeed, the life-force of the offspring is seen to be the seed,
while the life-force of the father stands in the place of the sower;
therefore, what is the use of postulating such a power for God?
The meaning is that, regarding the production of an object, there is no dependence on that [soul] at all.

Now, one might object: "If it is thus accepted that the soul of the father produces offspring, would this not constitute a departure from established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*), since the Sāṅkhyas do not admit that the soul is an agent (*kartṛ*)? To this, it is said: "By mere proximity (*sannidhimātrataḥ*)."

They say that primordial nature (prakṛti), in the form of the body and so forth, is itself the producer of offspring; and that due to the non-apprehension of its distinction [from the self] caused by its proximity, the conventional designation of agency is attributed to the individual soul (jīva). *7,188*
Thus, in order to refute that misconception as well, he introduces the Sūtra with the words "herein" (atra).
...herein the Lord himself has declared: (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.33d).
The meaning is that he stated this refutation regarding the subject matter of that view;
"himself" means directly, not figuratively;
and by the word "the Master," he indicates the author of the Sūtras' capacity for refutation.
He explains the sūtra with the words: "Elsewhere."
Elsewhere, there is no power whatsoever independently... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.34ab //
This occurs elsewhere, such as in the primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa),
as well as in the earth and the seeds of rice and other grains.
The term "kāpi" means the power of the field (kṣetra-śakti), the power of the seed (bīja-śakti), and the power of sowing the seed (bījāvapana-śakti).
To the question, "How then [can there be] the status of being a material cause (upādāna) and so forth?", it was stated: "by way of independence" (svātantryeṇa).
To the question "Why does it not exist?", he says: "Īśa" (the Lord).
... for it is Īśa alone who impels those powers directly. ... // MAnu 2.2.34bc //
Since it is well-established in the Śrutis and other scriptures that the Lord alone impels those powers such as Pradhāna and the rest, therefore no power whatsoever exists elsewhere independently.
Nor has it been said that the Lord’s power of impulsion, like that of Pradhāna and the rest, is dependent on another; thus it is said: "Añjaḥ" (directly).
This is an adverbial modifier.
By this, it is stated that the subject matter of the opponent's inference is sublated and that the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*).
Not only do primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*) lack independent power, but their power is also dependent upon the Supreme Lord.
What then? He states the meaning conjoined by the word "and" (ca): "And they are dependent on that."
And they are always dependent upon him. (Manu 2.34d)

And all those perceptions and activities of existence (sattā), the primary principle (pradhāna), and the power of the person (puruṣa)— the first word "and" (ca) has the sense of conjunction with the fact that [Brahman] impels the power by bestowing existence and so forth.
The word "and" (*uttara*) indicates mutual conjunction;
[it refers to] the existence and essential nature of both the primary matter (*pradhāna*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*), as well as their respective powers.

The construction is as follows: all those various cognitions and all those various activities are at all times dependent upon that [existence], meaning that they consist in being objects of valid cognition (*pramā*).
Some maintain that the very nature (*svarūpa*) of an entity is its existence.
Others, however, [define existence] as fitness for being an object of valid cognition; still others, as possessing causal efficacy.
All three of these, moreover, depend entirely upon the Blessed One in the case of primordial matter and the rest. (7.192)
But surely this is incorrect, because the existence of the *pradhāna* and so forth is eternal, and it is impossible for that which is eternal to be dependent on another; to this he says: "eternal."
Because it is eternal by virtue of its eternal nature.
Just as the eternal Lord himself, by virtue of his eternity and eternal power, eternally governs... // MAnu 2.36a-c //
Just as an impermanent thing such as a jar is governed by its impermanent nature,
so too does the Lord govern even the permanent by means of its permanent nature, and He governs it eternally at all times.
Since this is so, the conclusion that what was stated is logical is the proper interpretation.
This is what is meant:
just as jars and other such things, although they have impermanence as their intrinsic nature, do not become impermanent without a cause; [so it is with this].
What is the fault?
Nor is impermanence dependent on another, such that impermanence would only occasionally apply to a jar or the like;
for there is the constant presence of the occurrence of causes of destruction.

Likewise, if the permanence of the eternal were dependent on something else, then, O shameless one, there would never be the consequence of impermanence; for that [permanence] would be restricted by that [dependence]. This is what was stated: "And it is eternal."
And this is not extraordinary,
because the proponents [of the opposing view] themselves accept that the non-arising of evil (*duritaprāgabhāva*) is to be accomplished through obligatory rites (*nityakarman*),
since the persistence [of that non-arising] does not exceed the production of its permanence.
This might be so for that which is not naturally eternal; but if you say it is not so for that which is naturally eternal, we say no.
Because it is not admitted that anything other than Īśvara possesses that nature [of being eternal],
there is this much distinction:
[in our case] there is a certain eternality dependent upon us.

As for the claim that "there is a certain degree of permanence dependent upon Īśvara," why is that not also attributed to us? And how can such a state be dependent on Īśvara? To this it is said: "by means of eternal power."

The word "itself" (*svayaṃ*) is stated in order to dispel the doubt of the dull-witted that this [power] might refer to the power of Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth, since that was the subject under discussion.
As for what was said—that the power of Primordial Matter and the like to act as material causes is not independent, but is impelled solely by the Lord—why is that? To this he says: "Not... (*na*).
"Nothing whatsoever is done by anyone other than you," according to the Śruti.
The remainder [of the meaning] is that what was stated previously is to be understood.
For it is power itself that is called "action."
Regarding that which was stated—the fact that the existence of primordial matter (pradhāna) and so forth is dependent upon the Blessed One—that has been merely suggested as a possibility.
To the question, "What is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for this?", he says: "By its own nature," and so on.
Intrinsic nature, the individual soul, karma, substance, time, the Veda, and ritual action—
by whose grace these exist, and by whose disregard they cease to exist.
Thus, according to scripture, even existence and so forth do not exist apart from Nārāyaṇa.
By the word "karma" (action), individual instances of dharma and adharma are understood; "kriyās" (actions) refers to physical movements;
and "śruti" is the Veda.
The word "exist" (santi) intends all three types of existence; [the suffixes] -tva and -tā [denote] being and so forth, [belonging] to primordial matter (pradhāna) and the like.
"Without Nārāyaṇa" means without his impulsion (*tat-preraṇā*). (7.197)
Therefore, because the power of being a material cause and so forth does not exist elsewhere, and because even the existence of those [causes] depends upon God,
it is not the case that the earth merely acts as a supportive factor for the production of grass and other things, as the rain-cloud does.
In the production of the great principle (mahat) and the rest, Īśvara possesses merely the status of a benefactor to the field (kṣetra); rather, he possesses absolute sovereignty alone— thus,
that which has been accepted by the Pātañjalas is contrary to the Vedic doctrine.

All of that has already been refuted in the very first section (*adhikaraṇa*). With the intention of asking, "Why then this further effort?", he concludes the reason for this [objection] together with the previous argument, saying: "That... (*tad iti*).
The doctrine of Patañjali, Vindhyā, and others does not grant the goal of human existence.
Vindhyā, Anīśvara, and Sāṅkhya—
by the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of their partial adherents such as Pañcaśikha, Īśvarakṛṣṇa, and others;
for even their intermediate doctrines have been refuted.
Alternatively, it is so called because it is the doctrine of Patañjali and Vindhya-vāsin;
for even the Lord accepted by Patañjali is virtually equivalent to one who is without a Lord (anīśvara).
Therefore, the conclusion is drawn together with the preceding section either because of the intention to show their similarity, or for some other reason.
Thus ends the section on "Non-existence elsewhere" (*anyatrābhāvādhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*. [======= JNys_2,2.III:
Section on Acceptance (abhyupagamādhikaraṇa) =======]
Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section concerning the acceptance [of the opponent's position] (Abhyupagamādhikaraṇa).
Even if [the opponent] were to grant this, it would be because of the non-existence of the object.
Oṃ, even if granted, because of the non-existence of the object. Oṃ.
Some explain this treatise as follows:
It was previously stated that the activity of the Pradhāna is not tenable;
now, even if its activity were admitted, it would be so because of the absence of a purpose for that activity.
That is incorrect; for [the phrase] "even if it were admitted" is redundant,
and [the argument] is complete with just [the phrase] "because of the absence of the object."
Furthermore, what is to be established by the non-existence of objects?
Is it the inconsistency of the Sāṅkhya doctrine, or the impossibility of the activity of primordial matter (prakṛti)?
It cannot be the first.
Because they have different loci (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*).
Even if one were to somehow establish a common locus (*ekādhikaraṇatā*), it would still be inconclusive (*anaikāntya*) according to one's own view.
Not the second [alternative].
Because it would contradict the position of the proponent's own admission (*abhyupagamavāda*). For even in the case of an admitted position, that which is admitted is not itself refuted;
rather, by means of the admission, they merely indicate a temporary lack of commitment.
Whether the word is eternal or non-eternal, instruction must nevertheless be given;
therefore, this is not the meaning of the Sūtra. *7,203*
Thinking, "Let it be that an insentient thing has no agency;

for agency is possible for the body itself because it possesses consciousness," the Cārvāka—who objects with this further doubt as to why [agency] should belong to God (Īśvara) and so forth—has his view refuted in this section. With this intention, he sets forth that view, beginning with the words "by the Cārvākas."
The Cārvākas assert that the only means of valid cognition is that which is born of the senses; there is no other anywhere.
The intellect is "beautiful" (cārvī); because of that connection, the teacher is also called Cārvī.
These students of his are the Cārvākas. By them, cognition arising from the senses is declared to be the only means of valid knowledge.

Thinking that this might also be agreed upon by us, [the author] explains the statement "nothing else" with the intention of clarifying that it was spoken as an emphatic restriction. Thus he says: "nāparam" (nothing else).
The meaning is that inference and scripture are not stated to be valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

This too is indeed accepted by us, because we admit that only direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge regarding specific objects of cognition (*prameya*). Therefore, he says: "in some cases" (*kvacit*).
This is what is meant:
the establishment of the objects of knowledge (prameya) depends indeed upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
and the means of valid cognition is exclusively direct perception (pratyakṣa).
There is nothing other than this;
nor do we perceive Īśvara through direct perception.
Therefore, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), Īśvara does not exist.

Now, one might object: "If there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) other than perception, then dharma, liberation, and their means—which are not objects of perception—would remain unestablished. To this, he says: "The body... and so forth.
The body, the self, and the goals of man do not exist without desire and wealth.
Indeed, one who possesses knowledge [is the self], and knowledge is a property of the body;
as it has been said: "Earth, water, fire, and air are the fundamental principles (tattvas)."
The designation "body," "sense organ," and "object" applies to the collection of those [elements].
From them arises consciousness, like the power of intoxication from fermented grains;
thus, the body alone is the self.
And since that [body] is perishable, it follows that because a person existing at a later time does not exist, the absence of the human goals known as dharma and liberation is not undesirable;
for the two human goals are merely desire and wealth,
which can occur through the continuity of the person.

Even in that case, desire (*kāma*) alone is the primary [object], while wealth (*artha*) is a human goal only by virtue of being a means to it; thus, desire is mentioned first in order to make this known.
This is how the connection with the phrase "it is said" (*iti cocyate*) is to be understood.
To explain the aphorism for the purpose of refuting this view, he first states the introductory context (*upodghāta*) with the words: "Since it is thus... (*yadevam*).
Since it is thus... // MĀnUV 2.2.40a //
The implication is that if such a supersensible reality did not exist, then its corresponding scripture would become devoid of both subject matter (*viṣaya*) and purpose (*prayojana*).
If one asks how this is so:
does the author of that scripture establish a subject matter and attain a purpose by means of this scripture? [If there were no supersensible reality, the answer would be no.]
Or perhaps [it refers to] the persons to be converted.
He refutes the first [possibility] with the words: "by seeing."
What purpose would there be in seeing that which is within the range of direct perception?
For it has already been obtained by him through that very [means]. // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.40a-c //
The word *kim* is used in the sense of an objection (*ākṣepa*).
*Artha* means object (*viṣaya*) and purpose (*prayojana*).
*Labdha* means perceived (*upalabdha*) and attained (*prāpta*).
"For it is within the range of direct perception"—
this is the reason [for the preceding statement].
And from this, the following meaning follows:
First of all, no supersensuous object is apprehended by this treatise through its author; for such an object does not exist. Nor is there any object that is accessible to the senses.
Because it is not possible for that [object] to be an object of knowledge by virtue of being within the range of perception;
for "the scripture is purposeful regarding what has not been reached.
Furthermore, it is only after one has apprehended that object through perception that one becomes proficient in the scripture.
Otherwise,
its composition would be untenable;
and thus, how could it be "possessing an object" while merely pointing out that very same object to him?
In this way, the purpose (prayojana) is likewise not supersensible (atīndriya), because such [a purpose] does not exist;
nor is it sensible (aindriyaka).
Because that [person] is sublated by the non-perception of what is possible;
for surely, people feel affection for one who teaches what is beneficial.
If it is argued that "prosperity arises from the affection of the people," this may be so provided there is consideration for the transgression caused by ingratitude;
however, that [affection] has been made to cease by another.
He refutes the second [position] with the words "by men" (naraiḥ).
... by men; what [is there] from the scripture other than delusion? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.40cd)
The word "obtained" (labdha) carries over [from the previous context].
Here too, the response is as before.
This might be so.
The subject matter of the treatise is the non-existence of objects such as *dharma* that are considered beyond the reach of the senses.
Even though these are perceptible, their status as the subject matter is justified because they are tainted by doubts arising from Vedic predispositions (*vāsanā*).
And the purpose is the enjoyment of wealth and pleasure, which had been obstructed by doubts regarding *dharma* and *adharma*.
How then can it be said that men have gained anything from the treatise?
It is not so;
for the attainment of the purpose occurs through the comprehension of the subject matter.

And as for the object [of the treatise], would it present it as the word of a reliable authority (*āptavākya*), or by means of establishing logical reasoning (*upapatti*)? Not the first, because that would entail the acceptance of scriptural authority (*āgama-prāmāṇya*).

It is not the second [alternative], because it would be redundant to state the full extent of the matter merely by saying "there is nothing whatsoever beyond the senses," which would render the elaboration of the sentence useless.
Because it would entail the acceptance of logical reasoning (*upapatti*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that the treatise merely removes doubt,
while the comprehension of the object occurs through perception itself, we say no.
For one who neither presents a point for themselves nor demonstrates it through the exposition of a logical proof lacks the capacity to dispel doubt;
for doubt is either uncertainty or error,
and both are to be removed by a powerful cognition whose object is the opposite of the erroneous one.
It is not by mere command alone.
If it is argued that the elucidation of reasoning is performed by means of a treatise, [we reply:
no, because that too is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This very point is indicated by the author when, while continuing the context of "by seeing," he asks: "What [is gained] from the scripture? (śāstrāt kim?).
Otherwise, he would have said "by men";
the phrase "without deluding" is the ellipsis for both sentences, serving as a jest.
Thus, the author of the treatise, the Teacher of the Gods (Bṛhaspati), has achieved the purpose of deluding unworthy people.
And by others, it is false knowledge;
there is nothing more than this.
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "One's own... (*sva*).
Because they are devoid of the welfare of both oneself and others... // MAnuv_2.2.41a //
The statement "the treatise is fruitless," which is about to be explained, follows [the previous discussion] by way of the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokana) maxim;
and that [statement] is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa).
And it should also be understood that [the mind] is without an object;
for the state of possessing an object and a purpose is pervaded by the possession of an object and a purpose pertaining to either oneself or another,
since there is no third possibility.

Because it does not abide in generality through the relinquishing of every mode [of existence], and because, consequently, there is an absence of the pervading quality of possessing both an object and a purpose for oneself and others, it follows that the state of possessing an object and a purpose—which is pervaded by that [quality]—also does not exist; this is the meaning.
Let it be so: our treatise is indeed devoid of an object and a purpose.
To the question "What follows from that?", he explains the sūtra with the words: "according to his own view."
...is fruitless according to his own doctrine. Why does he himself prattle on in vain like a madman? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.41b–d)
Since it is thus fruitless and devoid of an object even according to its own tenets— not merely because of the arguments advanced by others—
it is therefore in vain, being empty of both subject matter and purpose;
for it has been accepted as such by the Cārvāka proponent himself and by all other opponents alike, due to its lack of subject matter and purpose.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is indeed devoid of both subject matter and purpose.
Since it is in vain, why would a discerning person prattle on about such a treatise? That is to say, it should not be undertaken by one who possesses discernment.

One who undertakes an undertaking devoid of both a subject matter (*viṣaya*) and a purpose (*prayojana*) would be neither a worldly person nor an investigator, and thus should be disregarded like a madman.
Alternatively, "fruitless" (*niṣphala*) is a statement regarding the absence of a purpose,
while "in vain" (*vṛthā*) is a statement regarding the absence of a subject matter.
And thus, the construction of the sūtra is as follows:

the remainder [of the sentence] is that the treatise is not to be commenced not only because of the arguments advanced by others, but also because of the non-existence of its subject matter even according to one's own admission.
The phrase "even in the case of admission" is stated in order to avoid the charge of the reason—namely, the non-existence of the subject matter—being unestablished (*asiddhi*).
But surely, the purpose must conform to the means of valid cognition;
it is not appropriate to accept an object that lacks a basis in valid cognition merely out of deference to the purpose,
for that would lead to over-extension.
And the only means of valid cognition is perception itself, not any other;
nor does this entail the abolition of worldly convention,
for that is established through mere presumptive probability (sambhāvanā).
Furthermore, because of the confidence in its validity arising from corroboration,
and because the self is perceived through direct perception as being none other than the body— as in "I, who am fair-complexioned, know"— [the body is the self].

And thus, since there would be no person capable of connecting with a purpose that arises at a later time, how could a purpose known as dharma and liberation, as well as an object beyond the senses, be accepted? To this, he says:
"From the body... and so forth.
To embodied beings, the self appears through experience as distinct from the body, clearly as "my body," just as one says "my wealth. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.42)
This is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself, whose authority is accepted by the opponent;
for the body is perceived as being related to the self, which is the locus of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃkāra*), in the form "this is my body.
And when there is no perception of identity, the perception of a relationship is not tenable.
Just as in the cognition "this is for my sake," the appearance of a relation is necessarily preceded by the cognition of a distinction;
[one might object: "But in this case, there is no such appearance at all;
rather, it is merely a matter of conventional usage, like saying 'the nature of the jar'. [We reply: No, because there is no basis for such a conceptual construction.
Indeed, such a construction is imagined when there is a misconception;
but it is not so in the present case.
Because for anyone, at any time, there is an absence of the valid cognition "I am the body," this has been stated: "for embodied beings, [the notion of self] exists always."
For this very reason, the objection that even the appearance must be an error is refuted.
If it is argued that there exists the valid cognition "I am fair," we say no;
for it cannot function as a sublater by way of being its opposite. (7.215)
Furthermore, this is not an appearance of the body as the self;
rather, it is an appearance of a property of the body as a property of the self.
And there is no contradiction between two things that reside in different loci.
If it is asked, "In the absence of that [object], how can this [cognition] exist?",
is this an inference (*anumāna*), a postulation (*arthāpatti*), or a mere question?
It is neither the first nor the second.
Because it would result in an abandonment of one's own tenets (apasiddhānta);
and because, even when no difference is perceived between a crystal and a hibiscus flower, the perception of the latter's properties is seen to occur in the former.
As for the third [alternative], it will be explained later.
Let there be cognition; but how can it be said to be "perception"?
For the opponent does not admit any cognition other than perception that possesses an uncontradicted appearance.
Or, even if it were accepted [as manifest], its status as a valid means of knowledge would not be avoided;
furthermore, because it is experienced as being directly present (*aparokṣatayā*), this has been stated: "it is manifest" (*vyaktam*).
Nor is that [existence] unestablished,
because it occurs even in the absence of the consideration of inferential marks and so forth;
otherwise, the manifestation of the body would likewise not occur.
This too has been stated: "always."
Some say that the knowledge of the distinction between the body and the self belongs only to those who possess the full maturation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
that is incorrect.
From the cowherd to the shepherd, the appearance [of the body] as "my body" is undeniable;
for this very reason, he says: "of embodied beings who possess the conceit of a body. (7.218)
Granted that there may be a self distinct from the body, nevertheless, what is the proof for a human goal (puruṣārtha) that transcends wealth and pleasure, as well as for the means to achieve it?
We reply: scripture, such as the Vedas, and inference.
If it is asked, "From where does its authority derive?"
To this, he says: "Of perception alone."
By what means is it determined that perception alone possesses the status of a valid authority?

It must be stated from what source that object and so forth, which has been accepted by another, is established. If you say "by perception," then by what is the validity of perception itself determined?
And thus, if the human goal and its means alone were not established, the world would fall into inactivity.
Direct perception is indeed experienced;
moreover, its validity is apprehended by whatever apprehends the cognition itself.
Therefore, how can the aforementioned fault be maintained?

For even in the theory that the validity [of cognition] is extrinsic (*parataḥ*), the validity of perception is established through the absence of sublation and so forth; thus, he says: "If... (*yadīti*).
If that [reasoning] establishes it, why would it not also establish the authority of the Veda?
If it is argued that for the validity of perceptual knowledge, either the apprehender of the cognition or the absence of sublation and so forth constitutes the proof,
then why should that very same [proof] not be the proof regarding the validity of the Veda?
For it is not the case that knowledge does not arise from the words of the Veda.
And it is not the case that [the Veda] is not perceived;
here, the mention of "Veda" is illustrative.
For this very reason, he will later state generally: "another" (*anyā*). (7.220)
Is it not the case that the general rule (utsarga) is that the grasper of a cognition is also the grasper of its validity?
However, by way of an exception (apavāda),
even invalidity is apprehended.
How, then, is the validity of the Vedas and other scriptures established?
If it is asked, "Even if validity is extrinsic, why is there an absence of sublation?",
this is equally true for perception as well.
If it is argued that the absence of denial and so forth is established by perception because of non-apprehension,
he replies with "And not," stating that this is the same in the case of the Veda and other such texts.
And nowhere is the non-authoritativeness of another [source] ever determined by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
In some respect, inference and scripture lack validity as compared to perception;
or else, one who accepts the validity of perception must be questioned:
Is the validity of only that single perception which is being experienced by you, or rather of every perception? Regarding the first case, he states the fault: "of perception itself," and so forth.
If other perceptions are also produced by a causal complex identical to that [of the first], by what means is it determined that validity belongs to only one perception?
Regarding the second case, he states the fault: "of perception alone," etc.
Regarding the validity of perception itself: by what means is it determined that "all perception is a valid means of knowledge"?
The meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever that can determine either another perception—distinct from the perception currently being experienced—or its validity.
Since the validity of that [cognition] is understood as being perceptual after one has apprehended it through the words of another or through effort as a direct perception, he says: "If... (yadi).

If the statement that establishes the validity of perception and its authority, as well as inference, are accepted as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then why would this not also apply to the authority of the Vedas and so forth? The word "acceptance" (*abhyupagama*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. In this same manner, there is also an alternative consideration regarding the authority of inference and scripture.

The first [position] has already been refuted as before; furthermore, it involves the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). He refutes the second [position] with the words "And not... (*na ca*).

The meaning is that the other two— namely, inference and scripture, which operate with respect to another person and so forth— are non-authoritative; for, in the former case (inference), the locus and other factors are unestablished, and if one were to accept their establishment, there would be a contradiction.

Now, is it that perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is produced by a sense-organ in contact with an object, whereas inference and verbal testimony—since they take as their objects even things such as the past for which such contact is absent—lack validity?

The intention [of the opponent] is this: is validity merely "correspondence with reality" (*yāthārthya*), and is contact the regulator of that [validity], since otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? Or is validity the state of being produced by a sense-organ in contact with its object?
Even regarding the first [alternative], is it any kind of contact whatsoever that is the restrictive factor, or is it conjunction (*saṃyoga*) alone?
He refutes the first [position] with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
If that is so, then the other two means of knowledge—inference and scripture—are not non-authoritative;

the point is that the proximity consisting of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) and so forth exists there as well. He states the fault in the second [alternative] with the words "kvāpi" (nowhere).

In some instances of visual and auditory perception, the fact that [cognition] is produced by a sense-organ in contact with its object is neither determined nor accepted by the opponent, on account of the eyeball and so forth.
Because an additional [entity] such as the eye and so forth is not admitted,
and because there is no contact with an object for that which consists of those [senses],
it follows that even some form of perception would lack validity.
He refutes the second [position] with "And not... (na ca).

One should not assert that validity (*mānatā*)—characterized by being produced by a means of cognition (*karaṇa*) in close proximity to the object—is something other than its correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*).
Why? To this he says: "In some cases" (*kvāpi*).
The meaning is that, as before, there is no over-extension (avyāpti) in the case of visual perception and so forth.
This is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa);
it should also be understood that there is over-extension (ativyāpti) in the case of error (viparyaya) and the like.
If it is argued that this is the definition provided that there is correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*), then let that alone suffice; what is the use of the qualified term?
If it is argued that it is for the purpose of excluding inference (*anumāna*) and so forth, we say no.
He says "and not" because the invalidity of that [cognition] has not yet been established even now.

If it is objected: "But how can the Vedas and so forth possess authority, since their subject matter is sublated by non-perception? We say: no, because they are indeed perceived through the Vedas themselves.
If it is argued: "They are not perceived by anything other than that," [we reply: no.
Is it then the case that validity consists in being corroborated by another means of knowledge? If you say "yes," he replies to that: "And not... (na ca).
The meaning is that validity, characterized by corroboration by another means of knowledge, does not exist [in this case].
To the question "Why not?", he says: "In some cases" (kvāpi).

Because it would lead to an infinite regress, no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is ever established; or rather, one should construe it as follows: in some instance, such as the cognition of one's own pleasure and so forth, even the correspondence (*saṃvāda*) itself is not established. Enough of this. *7,225*
He summarizes the meaning of the sūtra according to his own view:
"A position such as this, which is devoid of meaning according to one's own view, should be disregarded. (MAnu 2.2.44cd)
By its own admission, it is devoid of meaning, being devoid of both subject matter and purpose;
such is its nature, characterized by the non-acceptance of God and other supersensuous entities.
Thus ends the section on "Admission" (*abhyupagama*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*. (7.226)
[======= JNys_2,2.IV: Puruṣāśmādhikaraṇa =======] // Now, the section on the man and the stone in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
If it is argued that it is like a person and a stone, even so:
*Oṃ puruṣāśmavad iti cet tathāpi oṃ*.
Here, the view of a certain school of Nirīśvara Sāṅkhya—who assert that the primary cause (prakṛti), with the Puruṣa as its subordinate, is the agent—is refuted.
[Objection: In that case, this should indeed have been commenced immediately after that [previous section].
[Response: True.
Nevertheless, this statement is made in accordance with a further suspicion;
for it was previously stated that the agency of all things belongs solely to the Supreme Conscious Being, the Blessed One.

The doctrine that [the world] is created by primordial matter (*prakṛti*) alone is directly contradictory [to the Sāṃkhya view] and was therefore refuted first. Therein, the apprehension that "let there be no agency over the world for primordial matter alone, which is insentient; however, it shall possess such agency when favored by God" was refuted in the second section (*adhikaraṇa*).

One might object: "Let there be no agency for that which is insentient; rather, let agency belong to the body itself, which is the locus of sentience. Anticipating this, it was stated in the third [chapter] that since the body cannot be the locus of sentience, the impossibility of its agency remains as before. Now, however, although agency is impossible for an insentient entity in isolation, it might be possible through the proximity of a sentient being; therefore, what is the need for a Lord (Īśvara)?
The doubt expressed by "no" is thus refuted.
Since the method of that [opponent's] doctrine has already been stated in the Sūtra itself, he explains that very point: "Because of proximity. (*7,227*)
Even if the insentient proceeds because of the proximity of the sentient,
nevertheless, since it would lack prior intelligence, the aforementioned fault would remain the same.
Just as indeed the body, though itself insentient, performs tasks such as bringing stones merely through the proximity of the sentient self (ātman),
so too will primordial matter (prakṛti), though insentient, produce effects such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest through the proximity of the person (puruṣa).
And thus is the formal argument (prayoga):
"The Great Principle (mahat) and the rest have as their agent Nature (prakṛti), which is subordinate to the Puruṣa, because they are effects, like the bringing of stones and so forth.
Such is the meaning of the objection: "And if this is so, what is the need for a Lord (Īśvara)?
Even though this further objection has been raised, nevertheless, the fault already stated—namely, that "the formation [of the world] is impossible"—would remain equally applicable.
It would not be avoided.
Why?
Because it is not preceded by conscious intention.
The word "prakṛteḥ" (of nature) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
That which has intellect as its precursor is "buddhipūrvam";
the meaning is knowledge, desire, and effort.
That which does not exist through prior intelligence is called "tathā" (thus); its state is "tattva" (the fact of being thus). Therefore, this is what is meant: [it is not produced intentionally].
For agency consists in possessing knowledge, desire, and effort;
and even when the Puruṣa is present, it is not possible for Prakṛti to possess intelligence.
This is because it would contradict the accepted position that [the self] is insentient.
Furthermore, in the absence of cognition, its two effects—desire and effort—are also impossible.
Thus, the thesis that an insentient entity is an agent is indeed contradicted.
[Objection: But surely, the agency of the body—which has the self as its adjunct—in acts such as bringing stones and so forth has been demonstrated.
[Reply: If you ask how this can be so, it is not so; for, according to the reasoning already stated, agency is not admitted even for the body. *7,229*
And in order to demonstrate another refutation regarding the example, the Sūtra states:
Oṃ. [The self is not the agent] because it is impossible for it to possess limbs. Oṃ.
Thus [it is said].
He explains that: "Because it is the principal factor (aṅgin)."
And because being a constituent part is untenable:
"The status of being the principal (aṅgin) is experienced by everyone as belonging to the Person (puruṣa) alone;
by asserting that he is a constituent part (aṅga), one would be a denier of everything. (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 2.2.46a–d)
The word *ca* (and) has the sense of collecting other refutations.
The word *eva* (indeed) is for the purpose of clarifying the *a fortiori* argument (*kaimutya*) that is about to be stated.
"Being the principal" (*aṅgitva*) means being the primary [element]; the word "the body" (*śarīram*) is to be supplied as the object of the perception.
Because it is stated to be a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of that [sacrifice], it is accepted as being secondary (*upasarjana*);
the ellipsis to be supplied is "it would be Sāṅkhya. But is this not contrary to the present context?
For this undertaking is intended precisely to establish that the Supreme Lord is the agent of all things.

Thus, one might ask: "How is it that establishing the primacy of the individual soul (jīva) in actions such as bringing stones does not contradict the context? If you say this, we reply: when even the refutation of the non-primary agency residing in the individual soul constitutes a contradiction with the authoritative means of knowledge (pramāṇa), then what need is there to mention [the case of primary agency]?

Intending to show that this is precisely for the purpose of refuting the denial of the Lord who is the creator of all—since the author of the Sūtras establishes the soul as the principal agent—he says: "But what [is the reason]? etc.
How much more so from the mere glance of this Lord of All, from whom everything originates?

With the word "hi" (for), he indicates that this [objection]—concerning that which is intended to be established as the creator of all—will become clear in the subsequent sūtra as being a statement of concession (*aṅgīkāravāda*).

To the question, "How is it that the refutation of the Lord by means of an even greater refutation of the primacy of the individual soul (*jīva*) is contrary to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?", he says: "Since... (*yataḥ*).

Because all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—consisting of yogic perception, inference, and scripture—establish the Lord as the creator of all, therefore [the conclusion follows]; this is the connection with what precedes.
Thus ends the section on the "Person and the Stone" (*puruṣāśmādhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
[======= Section on Inference of Difference (anyatānumityadhikaraṇa) =======]
Now begins the section concerning "Inference Otherwise" (*anyathānumiti*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
And in the case of inference otherwise, there would be a lack of the capacity for knowledge.
*Oṃ* and in the case of inference otherwise, there would be a lack of the capacity for knowledge. *Oṃ*.

Here, the view of a certain faction of the atheistic Sāṅkhya— who maintain that the person (*puruṣa*) is the agent while primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is subordinate— is refuted. For it has been stated that, in activities such as bringing a stone or fetching water, the predominance of the person and the subordination of the body are established by experience.
And thus, by that same analogy, the effects such as the Mahat and so forth are also inferred to have the Puruṣa as their agent, with Prakṛti acting as a subordinate factor.
Furthermore, since the Puruṣa is conscious, there is no logical inconsistency in his being an agent;
yet, because agency is not perceived during states such as deep sleep, it must be admitted that Prakṛti functions as a subordinate auxiliary.
And thus, [the objection] "What is the use of God?"—to this it must be said: does the solitary Puruṣa have no independence anywhere at all, or does he have it?
To refute the first position, he explains the Sūtra: "The state of being the principal" (aṅgitva).
If that [Primal Being] alone possesses the status of being the principal agent, then it does not have complete independence;
for since it is incapable of impelling itself, another independent being must be required.
If it were the case that the person alone possesses the status of the principal— the meaning being its preeminence and agency—
whereas primordial matter (prakṛti) possesses only the status of a subordinate, then the previous doctrine would be inferred to be otherwise.
Furthermore, if the position is accepted that the person possesses no absolute independence even in that regard, then another independent Supreme Lord must necessarily be admitted.
Why?
Because the person lacks the power to impel primordial nature (prakṛti).
Granted that there may be no need for dependence on Īśvara for the sake of producing other effects;
nevertheless, he must still be depended upon for the purpose of impelling Prakṛti—this is the meaning of the word "api" (even/also).
This is what is being said:

The subordinate status of the *pradhāna* toward the *puruṣa*, its agent, does not arise merely by virtue of its existence or its mere conjunction; for if it were so, that status would undesirably follow even during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution.
Rather, it arises through [the *pradhāna*] functioning as an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth.

Furthermore, it is never observed that something which is not being employed by an agent can function as an instrument (karaṇa) or the like; nor can that very same thing serve as the instrument for its own impelling,
because that would involve a contradiction of self-referential activity.
And thus, since the *puruṣa* alone, independent of *prakṛti*, lacks the capacity for any activity whatsoever, it must necessarily have another auxiliary cause;
yet that [auxiliary] cannot be of the same nature [as the *puruṣa*],
because if that too were to depend on another auxiliary, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Therefore, this [cause] must be accepted as being independent;
and since that very thing is God, why is He not admitted?
He refutes the second [position] with the words "nor" (*na ca*).
And he does not possess independence in this matter... // Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.48a //

The meaning is that, such being the case, it would follow that [the effect] is independent of its material cause (*prakṛti*), which would result in a contradiction with one's own established doctrine (*svasiddhānta*).
By this, the sūtra "And because of contradiction" (*vipratiṣedhācca*) is explained.
[And because of contradiction, it is inconsistent.
He states another meaning of the sūtra: "perception and so forth."
... because it contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition. (MAnu 2.48b)
For through means of valid cognition such as direct perception, a person's lack of independence is observed at all times (and in all respects).
He explains it in another way: "beneficial," etc.
And because of faults such as performing what is beneficial [only] for oneself, etc. ... // MAnu 2.48c //
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), the performance of what is beneficial is included.
Having thus refuted the five [other] views, he concludes: "It is auspicious" (bhadram).
...is considered auspicious; [that which is] without a Lord is not so regarded.
Since the Lord (Īśvara) as conceived by the Pātañjalas lacks the defining characteristics of a Lord, that system is also considered to be "without a Lord" (anīśvara).

Now, one might ask: there are other systems without a Lord, such as those of the Bhinnaka-saṃsāra-mocakas and others; why are they not refuted? [The author] replies: "Because they have already been rejected by the very faults mentioned above, and because there is no further suspicion [of similar flaws]"—thus he says: "Of the transmigrating beings... (*saṃsāriṇaḥ*). *7,235*

Those who do not accept that this transmigrating world of sentient and insentient beings is distinct from the Lord of All— who is omnipotent, incomparable, and dependent upon Him— are all equal to these [who deny the Veda]. (Manu 2.49)
The term "saṃsārin" (transmigrating being) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for anything other than Īśvara;
"of all [beings]" (*sarveṣām*) is the substantive term (*viśeṣya*).
Therefore, there is no tautology.
*Upama* itself is *aupama*;
the suffix *aṇ* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). One for whom there is no *aupama* (comparison) is *an aupamaḥ*.
Alternatively, this term *aupama* means "pertaining to a simile" (*upamā*); that is to say, it means "possessing a simile. From that, a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is formed.
"Of this phenomenal world"— the ellipsis being "these faults have been stated.
These faults apply not only to one who does not accept the essential nature of all things.
However, even for those who accept darkness (*tamas*) while not accepting its specific attributes such as being distinct from living beings (*jīva*) and so forth—
in that case, as a result, it would follow that it is not God (*anīśvara*). (7.237)
What follows from this, if the doctrine of non-divinity (*anīśvaravāda*) is thus inconsistent? To this he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, by means of the authority of the Vedas and through logical reasoning, it is firmly established that Hari is the Supreme, eternal, and must be accepted as such by everyone.
Since the establishment of one's own position does not occur merely by the refutation of the opposing side, it was stated, "by means of the authority of scripture," and so forth.
"Supreme" (*para*) means excellent, endowed with the aforementioned qualifications.
By implication, "eternal" (*nitya*) is a qualification of [the Self's] acceptance.
The word "always" (*sarvadā*) means up to this point.

Because certainty does not depend on anything other than the establishment of one's own position and the refutation of the opponent's position, and because it is impossible for a certainty based on valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika-niścaya*) to be incorrect, it is said to be "well-ascertained" (*suniścitam*).
The intention is that Brahman, as defined [in the sūtras], is established by means of the refutation of the opponent's position as explained in the first chapter.
If it is argued: "In that case, then the subsequent sections (adhikaraṇas) should not be commenced at all,
because even though they are about to be refuted, God— possessing the aforementioned qualifications— is not accepted [by you]."
True;
nevertheless, the subsequent section of the text is intended to set forth further refutations in order to demonstrate that those doctrines must be utterly rejected.
Thus concludes the section on "Inference Otherwise" (*anyathānumiti*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*. (7.239)
[======= JNys_2,2.VI: The Section on the Vaiśeṣika =======] Now begins the section on the Vaiśeṣika in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
Or, as the large and the long [arise] from the short and the circular;
*oṃ*, as the large and the long [arise] from the short and the circular, *oṃ*.
Others say that Īśvara is endowed with eternal knowledge, effort, and desire, as well as the five qualities beginning with number.

Here, the doctrine of the Vaiśeṣikas and others who maintain that [the world] is composed of atoms is refuted. Now, one might object: "The Vaiśeṣikas and others certainly do accept a Supreme Lord; so why is this section commenced for the purpose of refuting them? Anticipating this doubt, [the author replies]: although they accept the Lord in his essential nature, they nevertheless disagree regarding his attributes, such as pleasure and so forth.

Since they likewise conceive the process of creation, dissolution, and so forth in a contrary manner, the commencement of this section (adhikaraṇa) is justified for the purpose of refuting that view; with this intention, he sets forth their opinion, beginning with the words "nitya" (eternal).
The connection with what follows is: "Others say [it is] Īśa," as will be stated.
He is so described because his knowledge, effort, and desire are eternal.
By "number and so forth" is meant number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction.
And this [statement] is restrictive;

that is, they speak of it as having exactly eight qualities. Unity, individual separateness, and dimension residing in eternal substances are themselves eternal, whereas duality, dual separateness, and so forth [are not].

Since conjunction and disjunction are established as being invariably non-eternal, the distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal regarding [qualities] such as number and so forth, although existing, has not been mentioned.
However, because qualities such as cognition (jñāna) which reside in the individual soul (jīva) are non-eternal, their eternity is proclaimed here [only for those residing in the Lord].
Although some describe the Lord as possessing six qualities, [the author does not do so here].
Nevertheless, because that [knowledge] is not considered supreme, it was presented as possessing only eight qualities.
Likewise, Ātreya’s impermanence of knowledge was not presented;
or rather, the mention of its permanence was made as a logical argument for the absence of other qualities.
For instance:
individual souls are endowed with nine specific qualities—namely, intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression.
Among these, because there is an absence of delusion in eternal and true knowledge, there is an absence of aversion, which arises from that [delusion].
In the absence of that [ignorance], there is the absence of dharma and so forth, which are rooted in it.
Since desire also lacks the nature of passion due to the absence of delusion, it cannot be the cause of dharma and the like.
And in the absence of dharma and so forth, there is likewise the absence of pleasure and pain, which are their effects.
Because knowledge is eternal, memory is impossible, and since there is no agent for such a process, even mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is absent.
Alternatively, by its eternity, it indicates that knowledge and the other qualities are indivisible (*akhaṇḍatva*).
Having thus presented the disagreement regarding the subject of God, he now presents the disagreement regarding the subject of creation: "By His will... (*tadicchā*).
Impelled by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) of that [will],
all atoms of the four classes join together in pairs.

For at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the eternal category to be described hereafter, as well as impermanent factors such as merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), remain.

Then, at the end of a hundred Brahma-years, the desire to create arises in Maheśvara for the sake of providing experience to living beings. Through that desire, the unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) characterized by merit and demerit residing in all souls attain their functional activity.

Then, by His will— that is, by the will of the Lord characterized as the desire to create— and by the unseen forces (adṛṣṭas), meaning by the conjunctions of the selves with those possessing unseen forces; "impelled" means set in motion,
which is to say, they come to possess activity.
Atoms existing in their prior undivided state—those consisting of the four qualities, namely the earthy, the watery, the fiery, and the airy—conjoin in pairs.
Here, if one were to say simply "atoms," there would be the inclusion of the *manas* (minds) as well.
Even though conjunction exists in those [minds], their capacity to initiate a substance—as will be explained later—is untenable because they lack tangibility, just like space (*ākāśa*).
Therefore, to exclude that [possibility], it is stated that they are "groups of four.
Alternatively, by this he indicates that only the conjunction of similar [substances] is the initiator of a substance, and not any other kind.
[The word] "entire" (akhilāḥ) [is used].
Because of the restrictive statement regarding conjunction occurring in pairs:

those atoms which conjoin for the purpose of initiating a substance do so entirely in pairs, that is, only two at a time. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "The atom... (*paramāṇu*).
From two atoms alone, that which is called a dyad (dvyaṇuka) is produced;
from three dyads, a triad (tryaṇuka); and from four of those, that which consists of them [is formed]. (2.52)
Therefore, the production of parts and wholes occurs without any fixed rule;
and consequently, the production of all wholes occurs without any fixed rule.
