By the word "and" (eva), he excludes the doctrine of the heap of atoms (paramāṇupuñjavāda), the doctrine of transformation (pariṇāmavāda), and the doctrine of non-restriction (aniyamavāda).
[The object] consists of exactly two atoms,
and not two atoms produced in immediate proximity.
Nor is it the case that only two atoms, having attained a specific transformation through conjunction, [produce the effect], nor three and so forth;
by stating "it is born," this indicates the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (asatkāryavāda).
The singular number is used in consideration of the genus (*jāti*).

Therefore, the meaning is that from two atoms of the same kind which are conjoined, there arise substances called *dvyaṇukas*—which are entirely distinct from those [atoms], inherent in them, and previously non-existent.
It follows that from three *dvyaṇukas*, a *tryaṇuka* is produced.
And so it is.

Here too, the explanation is as before. Since the dimension of minuteness (aṇutva-parimāṇa) is the same in both the atom (paramāṇu) and the dyad (dvyaṇuka), just as the designation "dyad" is appropriate, the designation "triad" (tryaṇuka) is likewise entirely justified.
From four triads (tryaṇuka) of that same kind which have combined, a substance consisting of those [triads] is produced;
for the designation "atom" (aṇu) is applied metaphorically to the triads.
Some, however, maintain that the production of a tetrad (caturaṇuka) occurs through dyads (dvyaṇuka) alone.
According to their doctrine, it should be explained as being "by those dyads.
Three dyads (the substance) which initiate a body is a triad (*tryaṇuka*).
"A tetrad is commenced by four [atoms]";
in this case, the designation is used in its primary sense.
From that, [it arises] from either triads or tetrads.
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of specification.
He states that very point:
"without restriction" means without a fixed numerical limit such as "only by this many."
The substances that are inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) are the composite bodies (*kāryadravya*), which are the partial wholes (*khaṇḍāvayavin*).

The plural number is used to indicate that among the intermediate stages between the triad (*tryaṇuka*) and the ultimate whole (*antyāvayavin*), it is not only one partial whole that exists, but rather many such wholes arise without restriction.
Consequently, by means of those partial wholes, there occurs—without any fixed numerical limit—the production of all ultimate wholes, namely bodies, sense organs, and objects.
By this, the production of substances has been stated;
the production of qualities and actions within their own substrates, the substances, is to be understood. Every effect, being of the nature of an existent entity, is produced from a triad of causes.
And causes are of three kinds: inherent (samavāyi), non-inherent (asamavāyi), and instrumental (nimitta).
Among these, that in which the effect inheres when it is produced is the inherent cause.
He shows its essential nature by saying: "the cause."
The causal factor known as the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) consists of atoms and so forth; for it is therein [that the effect inheres].
In this context, regarding the production of effects such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, the substance-category of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
Why?
Because, in this regard, all effects arise as inherent in the substance of the atom and so forth; "because" is the implied sense of the argument. (7.254)
The efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) is that cause distinct from the inherent (*samavāyin*) and non-inherent (*asamavāyin*) causes.
He illustrates it with the word "Īśa" (the Lord).
The will of the Lord (Īśa), unseen destiny (adṛṣṭa), and time (kāla) are considered the efficient causes (nimitta-kāraṇa).
The connection [of the words] is "but the cause.
And this has been shown as the cause common to all effects;
in the same way, other [causes] are also to be understood.
For example, the shuttle, the loom, and so forth [are causes] of a cloth, and so on.
An *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause) is that which is proximate to the *samavāyikāraṇa* (inherent cause) and whose capacity has been ascertained.
Proximity to the inherent cause consists in being inherent in either the inherent cause itself or its own inherent cause.

And the determination of causal capacity occurs through the state of being invariably antecedent and not otherwise established; furthermore, this cannot be expressed by a single term— such as "non-inherent cause" or "inherent cause"— because it is distinct for each respective effect.

Therefore, in order to demonstrate that through their distinction, and because the knowledge of those [categories] depends upon the knowledge of the body [of categories], he first states the division between what is to be done and what is not to be done: "The universal, the ultimate particular, and inherence—this triad is eternal; action is non-eternal; but substance and quality are of two kinds. (MDh 1.2.55) The universal (*sāmānya*), the ultimate particular (*antyaviśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*)—these three are eternal. Action (*kriyā*) is non-eternal. However, substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) are of two forms [eternal and non-eternal].

Because of the necessary concomitance between being an effect and being non-eternal, by the statement of the division between the eternal and the non-eternal, the very division between the produced and the unproduced is established.
These six—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—are categories in the form of existence;
non-existence is the seventh.
Existence is of the nature of affirmation;
non-existence is of the nature of negation;
substance is that which is the substratum of qualities.
Or [it is] the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa).
Quality (guṇa) is that which possesses generality (sāmānya), is not an inherent cause, and has a non-moving nature.
Action (karman) has the nature of motion.
A universal (*sāmānya*) is that which is eternal, one, inherent in many, and co-inherent in a substance.
Ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*) are those which exist only in eternal substances and exist only [therein].
Alternatively, they are the causes of absolute distinction.

Inherence (*samavāya*) is the relation between two things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*). Those two are necessarily established as having the relationship of substratum and superstratum; thus they are inseparably established.
Or [the definition] is "an eternal relation.
In that context, this triad—universal (sāmānya), ultimate particularity (antyaviśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya)—is eternal and unproduced.
If one were to say merely "particularity" (viśeṣa), there would be the inclusion of substance, quality, action, and universal as well.
For "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) means that by which something is distinguished.
A substance, such as a staff and so forth, distinguishes Devadatta and others from those who do not possess the staff;
and a quality distinguishes a substance from that which lacks qualities.
Action (*karman*) is also formless and corporeal.
Universals (*sāmānya*) are of two kinds: the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). The higher is existence (*sattā*), because it has the most extensive substratum.
Furthermore, [categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) are "lower" because they have fewer substrata.

In that regard, although the higher universal (*parasāmānya*) is merely a universal because it is the cause of only positive inclusion (*anuvṛtti*), the lower universal (*aparasāmānya*) is also a particular (*viśeṣa*) because it is also the cause of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Those which are exclusors are "ultimate" (*antya*);
that is to say, they are the causes of absolute exclusion (*atyantavyāvṛtti*).
The staff and so forth are not like that,
because they do not differentiate [an object] from other staffs and the like.
Actions— consisting of upward throwing, downward throwing, contraction, expansion, and going— are also impermanent.
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis;
the meaning is that they do not possess both forms like substances and so forth.
Qualities and substances are each of two kinds, distinguished as eternal and non-eternal.
To explain: the substances (dravya) are earth, water, fire, air, space, time, direction, self, and mind.
Among these, the four beginning with earth exist in the form of atoms (paramāṇu).
The five [substances] beginning with space are eternal;
the four [substances] beginning with earth, in their forms such as dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth, are non-eternal.
Furthermore, qualities residing in non-eternal substances are themselves exclusively non-eternal.
In an earth atom (*pārthiva-paramāṇu*), unity, individual separateness, dimension, and gravity are eternal;
color, taste, smell, touch, plurality, multiple separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and momentum are non-eternal.
(And in water: In a watery (*pāthasīya*) [atom], color, taste, touch, unity, individual separateness, dimension, gravity, substantiality, and viscidity are non-eternal.
Multiplicity, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and momentum are impermanent.
In the fiery [substance], color, touch, oneness, individual separateness, and dimension are permanent;
multiplicity, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, substantiality, and momentum are impermanent.
In air, touch, unity, separateness, and dimension are eternal;
multiplicity, manifold separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and momentum are non-eternal.
In space, unity, separateness, and dimension are eternal.
In the case of space, non-plurality, plurality, conjunction, and disjunction are impermanent;
in time and direction, singularity, singular plurality, and dimension are permanent;
while multiplicity, plural plurality, conjunction, and disjunction are impermanent.
In the self (ātman), unity, individual separateness, and dimension are eternal;
multiplicity, manifold separateness, conjunction, disjunction, and the nine qualities beginning with cognition (buddhi) are non-eternal.
A specific distinction regarding the Lord (īśvara) has also been stated.
In the case of the mind (*manas*), unity, individual separateness, and dimension are eternal;
multiplicity, manifold separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and mental impression (*saṃskāra*) are non-eternal. This is the distinction. (7.271)

Having thus explained the distinction between what is to be produced and what is not to be produced, he states what constitutes the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for each respective effect: "The effect," and so forth.
In the case of an effect, the inherent cause of qualities and actions is another cause;
however, qualities and so forth residing in the cause, as well as conjunction, are the causes of substances.

The mention of "cause and effect" is illustrative; therefore, for qualities (*guṇa*) arising in a substance— whether that substance be an effect or a non-effect— the qualities residing in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), as well as the action (*karma*) residing in the inherent cause,
constitute the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), while the inherent cause itself is the other type of cause.
And it should be understood that for action (*karman*), the qualities (*guṇa*) themselves, which occupy the position of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), are the non-inherent cause.
The first particle "tu" (but/however) highlights the distinction from substance (*dravya*).
As for the second [particle], its syntactical connection is with the phrase "the cause of substance" (*dravyakāraṇa*).
Alternatively, both [particles] have the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned;
and this has been stated as follows:
"For instance:"

For those qualities residing in an effect—namely color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, unity, individual separateness, subsequent conjunction, disjunction, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, and momentum—their respective causes, such as color and the rest residing in the cause, are the non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
For color, taste, smell, and touch residing in an earth atom, the non-inherent cause is the fire-conjunction residing in that very substance which resides in the earth and fire atoms.
In all cases, for multiplicity and multiple individual separateness, the non-inherent causes are the unity and individual separateness residing in their respective substrates.
Action residing in the substratum is the cause of conjunction, disjunction, and velocity;
spatial and temporal conjunctions residing in the substrata are the causes of priority and posteriority;
and mental conjunction residing in the self is the cause of the specific qualities of the self.
In the case of sound, the causes are conjunctions, disjunctions, and sounds residing in space;
and in the case of action, they are gravity, fluidity, velocity, and conjunction residing in its substratum.
However, for a substance, the non-inherent cause is the conjunction of its constituent parts, which are the inherent causes. (7.275)
He states an exception to what has been said in certain cases with the word "evam" (thus).
Even though the established doctrine remains thus, a distinction has been postulated therein.

Although it is established as a general principle in the Siddhānta that the dimension residing in the cause is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the dimension residing in the effect, the Vaiśeṣikas nevertheless postulate a specific distinction—a different state—regarding particular dimensions therein.
To the question "How so?", he says: "In the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)."
In the dyad and in the atom, there is shortness and sphericity.
The cause does not [transfer its own] quality to the effect... // MAnu 2.58a //
Dimension is fourfold:
minuteness, largeness, shortness, and length.
Among these, minuteness is of two kinds.
It is both eternal and non-eternal.
It is eternal in the four kinds of atoms and in the mind;
it is also called "sphericality" (pārimāṇḍalya).
The dyad (dvyaṇuka) alone is impermanent.
Greatness (mahattva) is also of two kinds, distinguished as eternal and non-eternal.
The eternal [greatness] is supreme greatness (paramamahattva), which exists in space, time, direction, and the self.
Impermanence exists in effect-substances such as triads;
shortness exists only in dyads;
and length exists only in effect-substances such as triads.
Some maintain that even in an atom there is shortness, and even in space and so forth there is length.
In that context, shortness resides in a dyad;
this is an illustrative indication.
And "minuteness" (aṇutva) resides in the qualities of the effect, namely the dimensions of the dyad (dvyaṇuka) and the triad (tryaṇuka), which are effects;
this is a locative of object (viṣayasaptamī).
It does not serve as the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) for the largeness (mahat) and length (dīrghatva) of the triad.

Similarly, the spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) residing in an atom does not serve as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the two qualities—shortness and minuteness—which are the qualities of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), the product of the atom;
however, the largeness and length residing in a triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth certainly do serve as the non-inherent causes for the dimensions of the tetrad (*caturaṇuka*) and beyond.
To the question "Why is it conceived thus?", he says: "Because of dissimilarity" (*vairūpyam*).
"... deformity is the cause in that case;
so they say. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.58bc)

In this regard, the cause for the absence of causality between the dimensions of dyads and atoms on the one hand and the dimensions of triads and dyads on the other is dissimilarity (*vairūpya*), that is, heterogeneity (*vijātīyatva*).
For it is only observed that there is a causal relationship between dimensions of the same class (*sajātīya*), such as those of threads and cloth.
And thus is the formal argument (*prayoga*):
The dimensions of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and the triad (*tryaṇuka*) do not possess the relationship of cause and effect, because they are dimensions of heterogeneous kinds;
by way of contrast, this is like the dimensions of a thread and a cloth.
The same should be understood for the dimensions of the atom (*paramāṇu*) and the dyad as well.

If it is argued that the atomicity of the atom (*paramāṇu*) may be the cause of the atomicity of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), we say no; for even in that case, there exists a dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) between the eternal dimension (*nityaparimāṇatva*) of the atom and the [non-eternal] atomicity [of the dyad]. If this is so, what then is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the dimensions of the dyad and the triad? To this, he says: "dissimilarity" (*vairūpyam*).
The meaning is "multiplicity.
The number two, which arises in dependence upon the cognition of the Lord, produces minuteness and shortness in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) formed from two atoms.
Furthermore, the number three, which arises in dyads, produces largeness and length in the triad (*tryaṇuka*). *7,278*
In order to refute the view thus presented, he introduces the *adhikaraṇasūtra*: "tān" (them).
Then the Lord himself, the master of knowledge, spoke to them.
The phrase "he said" is to be understood as "as in [the Sūtra] beginning with 'either like the large or the long'.

To the question of how the author of the Sūtras possesses the capacity to refute doctrines fortified by powerful reasoning, it is stated: "He himself is the direct lord of all sciences; therefore, he is the Master.
One should not suspect that the meaning thus stated might be otherwise due to contradictions with the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others.
Because that [position] is contradicted by the evidence;

for instance, as for what was stated— that the dimension of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth is not the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the dimension of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth— [that is untenable].
Demonstrating that this is contrary to logical consistency, he explains the sūtra, "Or like the large and the long from the short and the spherical," with the words: "And largeness... and so forth.
Furthermore, largeness and length are attributed to the triads (tryaṇuka) and other such entities;
from that, a similar effect is produced in their subsequent effects.
Just as it is because of shortness, so too from spherical dimension (pārimāṇḍalya),
a similar effect would indeed arise in the product due to its equality [with the cause].
The word *eva* (only/just) is connected either with "only in the triads and so forth" or with "is merely imagined.
[It refers to] in substances such as the triad (*tryaṇuka*).
Therefore, because of the largeness and length existing in an effect such as the triad—which is distinct from the ultimate composite—[the atoms are inferred].

The word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin the meanings of the sentences. "Kārya" means magnitude. "In those effects" refers to the effects such as triads and so forth, namely the quaternaries and subsequent compounds.
By the word "tathaiva" (in the same way), he dispels any suspicion of a discrepancy between the example and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*).

The statement of the reason is: "because of equality," that is, because of the similarity in being the size of an effect (*kāryaparimāṇatva*) and so forth, in both the triad (*tryaṇuka*) and the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).
The word "hi" indicates pervasion (*vyāpti*). *7,281*
Although words such as *mahat* (the Great) and so forth denote substances, they nevertheless express dimensions because [in this context] the emphasis is on the state (*bhāva*);
it is for this reason that "greatness" (*mahattvam*) and so forth were stated.
The author of the Sūtra’s expression, emphasizing the state, follows the system of Kaṇāda’s Sūtras.
"For [an object] is large due to the multiplicity of its causes, the largeness of its causes, and a particular kind of aggregation"—
this is what that [sūtra] means.
In the expression "like the large and the long," the suffix *vati* is used in the sense of the genitive case.
Either by changing the case-ending or by supplying the word "from" (*sakāśāt*), it is stated as "from that" (*tasmāt*).
In this regard, the following must first be stated:
just as an effect arises from that [cause] among effects, so too would a dimension arise in the effect even from spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) because of their equality. (7.285)
This is what is meant:
the dimension of a dyad arises from the dimension of the inherent cause of its own substratum’s substratum, because it is a dimension of an effect, like the dimension of a tetrad and so forth;
and the dimension of an atom is a producer of dimension, because it is the dimension of the inherent cause of the substance [in which it inheres].
The two dyads (dvyaṇuka) and the triad (tryaṇuka) possess dimensions produced by [other] dimensions, because they are effect-substances, like a tetrad (caturaṇuka) and so forth;

or, the dyad and the atom possess dimensions that are the non-inherent causes of dimension, because they are inherent causes of substance, like a triad. Thus, there is no failure to establish the intended point.
This is because its establishment follows from the principle of "inexplicability otherwise" (anyathānupapatti).

Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in cases where dimension is initiated by mere aggregation (pracaya) alone, for such a case is also equivalent to the subject of the proposition (pakṣa).
And this being the case, there is no contradiction,
because the status of [the atoms] as causes of accumulation is not precluded;
nor is there the fault of excessive complexity (gaurava) in postulating that they possess both types of causality.
Because the causal capacity is established for both:
the dimension of a dyad does not produce the dimension of a triad,
and the dimension of an atom does not produce the dimension of a dyad.
If it is argued that there is a counter-argument (satpratipakṣa) based on the reasoning "because it possesses magnitude, like the magnitude of a cloth" and so forth, we say no;
for the absence of magnitude in the atoms that are its inherent causes serves as the limiting condition (upādhi).

Furthermore, [the argument] that "the dimension of a triad does not produce the dimension of a tetrad because it is a dimension, like the dimension of a cloth," and so forth, is of the same logical status as fallacious arguments;
nor is it the case that "the dimension of an atom does not originate another dimension because it is an eternal dimension, like the dimension of space."
Because the absence of dimension in the inherent cause of a substance (*dravya-samavāyi-kāraṇa-parimāṇatva-abhāva*) serves as a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Furthermore, even the color of an atom (*aparamāṇu-rūpa*) does not initiate [another] color, because it is eternal, like the dimension of space (*gagana-parimāṇa*);
likewise, atoms do not initiate substances, because they are eternal, like space.
And because it is similar to such fallacious arguments as these:

by this, the claim that "the dimension of the dyad and the atom do not originate other dimensions because they possess minuteness (*aṇutva*), like the dimension of the mind" is also refuted. Nor is "non-minuteness" a valid limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Because the intermediate genus of dimension (*parimāṇāvāntarajāti*) has been refuted by the reasoning to be stated hereafter, and because [the property] does not exclude itself from being a subject of the thesis (*pakṣīkṛta*) due to its shortness (*hrasvatva*).

Now, one might object: since the dimension of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) and the dimension of a tetrad (*caturaṇuka*) are of the same genus (*sajātīya*), it is logical that there exists between them the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakaraṇabhāva*).

However, since the dimensions (*parimāṇa*) of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and triads (*tryaṇuka*) belong to different classes (*vijātīyatva*), how can they be analogous? To address this, it is stated that the example and the subject of the illustration are similar. Just as a dimension of the same class arises in a tetrad (*caturaṇuka*) and so forth from the dimension of a triad and so forth, so too, because it is precisely the production of a dimension of the same class from the dimensions of a dyad and an atom (*paramāṇu*) in a triad and so forth that is intended to be established, there is no fault; this is the meaning. (7,294)

But surely, since largeness and length are established by valid means of knowledge in triads and the like, while minuteness and shortness are established in dyads and the like, how could there not be a sublation (bādha) when proving their homogeneity? To this it is said: "And largeness... and so forth.
This is merely a conceptual construction of the Vaiśeṣikas; there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a distinct intermediate genus within the category of dimension (*parimāṇa*).
Rather, the intended meaning is that dimension is of a single genus alone, despite its variations in increase and decrease.
By this, it should be understood that the [opponent's] argument regarding dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) has been shown to be unestablished (*asiddhi*).

Now, one might object: "Since there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against the view that the dimension (*parimāṇa*) of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth is not produced from the dimensions of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth, these inferences are unproven (*aprayojaka*). For it is possible for the dimension of dyads and so forth to arise from number (*saṅkhyā*) alone. Dispelling this doubt, he explains the word "or" (*vā*) with the words "If it were not so... (*na cediti*).
If it were not so because of its greatness, nor even because of its long duration.
The two particles *ca* and *api* signify mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).
The word *eva* is connected [to the preceding] as "it must certainly not be so.
This is what must be stated here.
Does the definition of an *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause) apply to the dimensions (*parimāṇa*) of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, or not?

In the first case, even if the definition of an *asamavāyikāraṇa* is present, if the dimension of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth were produced from the dimension of a dyad and so forth, then the dimension of a tetrad (*caturaṇuka*) and so forth would [arise] from the largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) residing in the triad and so forth; this is the remainder [of the argument].
This is what is meant:

if, despite the presence of proximity to the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and other such conditions, something were not to possess the status of a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), then this definition would be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) and thus not a valid definition.
Consequently, even such qualities as magnitude (*mahattva*) and the like would not have the status of a non-inherent cause.
Regarding the second [alternative], is it that there is no proximity to the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), or is it that its causal efficacy has not been determined?
It cannot be the first,

because it is established by valid cognition that the dimension of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth inheres in the dyad and other such entities, which are themselves the inherent causes of the inherent causes of the dimension of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth.

If it is argued that the dimension of a triad (tryaṇuka) and so forth does not arise from the dimensions of a dyad (dvyaṇuka) and so forth because of the absence of inherence in a common inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), then the dimension of a tetrad (caturaṇuka) and so forth would likewise not arise from the largeness (mahattva) and length (dīrghatva) residing in the triad and so forth, since those too lack inherence in a common inherent cause.
Not the second [alternative];
for capacity must be determined by being invariably antecedent and not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha*),
and that [capacity] exists in the dimension (*parimāṇa*) of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth.
Even so, if the production of the dimension of a triad and so forth does not occur, then the aforementioned undesirable consequence remains.
If it is argued that because it has been determined that only a similar dimension can be a cause, this dissimilar dimension is not a cause and its presence is unavoidable; [we reply: no.
What is this "dissimilarity"?
Is it a difference in genus, or is it merely a difference in characteristic?
The first [alternative] is not tenable,

because it has been established through inference that the dimensions of dyads, triads, and so forth, as well as atoms, belong to the same genus. As for the second, if causality does not arise from mere dissimilarity, then even largeness (*mahattva*) and other such qualities would not possess it.
For the largeness (*mahattva*) of a triad and a tetrad is not non-different;
this is because its superiority is established by experience.
[Objection: If it is argued that since production occurs from number alone, the causality of dimension (*parimāṇa*) need not be postulated.
Nevertheless, the same over-extension (atiprasaṅga) remains;
for it would follow that even the dimension (parimāṇa) of a tetrad (caturaṇuka) and so forth could arise from number alone.
However, where there is a specific determining factor, then dimension should also be taken into account.
Although this is not the path of those who maintain the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavādins*),
according to whom the material causes (*upādāna*), endowed with their own qualities, simply attain the state of such an effect;
nevertheless, relying on the opinion of others, [this is stated] for the sake of others alone.
There is no harm in stating this refutation.

Thus, it has been established by inference that the dimension of a dyad arises from the dimension of an atom, from which the birth of the dimension of a triad occurs, and that these [dimensions] belong to the same genus.
That is incorrect.
Because it is refuted by counter-reasoning (*pratitarka*). To explain:

is it being proved that from the dimension of an atom (*paramāṇu*) a minute dimension (*aṇutva*) of the same genus arises in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), and from the dimension of a dyad a minute dimension arises in a triad (*tryaṇuka*); or rather, does a large dimension (*mahattva*) arise, or a short dimension (*hrasvatva*)? Or what [is the case]?
Regarding length:
he declares that all these positions are flawed—
“For of a similar effect, there is no connection whatsoever” (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.61cd).
"Yoga" means connection.
"In some way" means by any manner among those previously mentioned.
Why? To this, he states the undesirable consequence regarding the first position: "non-perceptibility."
If it is argued that [the atoms] would thus be imperceptible because they are minute in their effects... // MAnu 2.2.62a-c //
If a dimension similar to that of an atom were produced in a dyad by virtue of being minute,
and a dimension were produced in a triad by virtue of the dimension of the dyad,
then, because of the consequence that all effects would be minute, they would simply be imperceptible to people like us; therefore, this is not the case.

The non-perceptibility of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is indeed accepted; therefore, this is an emphatic restriction. For otherwise, all effects whatsoever would be non-perceptible, rather than some being perceptible.
For the perceptibility of a substance by people such as ourselves is pervaded by the possession of manifested color and touch, provided that largeness (*mahattva*) exists.
Consequently, since triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth possess minuteness (*aṇutva*) and thus lack largeness, they would be imperceptible.
By this, the third [position] is also refuted.

For even in the case of triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, if they possessed shortness, it would be difficult to avoid the undesirable consequence that they would not be perceptible due to the absence of largeness (*mahattva*).

In the second case, however, there would be the contingency of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) also being perceptible if they possessed largeness. Nor can it be argued that their non-perception is due to the absence of one or both of manifest color (*rūpa*) and manifest touch (*sparśa*).
For [if it were so], that [absence] would also follow in the case of triads and so forth;
for this very reason, the fourth [position] is also refuted.
As for the argument that "in the case of length, largeness is unavoidable," the refutation of these two positions has not been stated here because it is obvious.

Although this has already been refuted by stating that the sub-classifications of dimension, such as minuteness (*aṇutva*) and so forth, lack any basis in valid cognition (*aprāmāṇika*), it is nevertheless raised again for the sake of clarifying that very point; thus, there is no fault.
Here, among the alternatives considered, he first takes up the position of largeness (*mahattva*): "Nor is it largeness," and so on.
... nor does magnitude exist even in an atom or in an atom-part. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.62cd)
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of including length.
The phrase "how is it not stated?"—which is to be explained later—is connected here as well. "In the atom" means in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).

Regarding what was asked—namely, whether the production of atomicity is being established, and so forth—the meaning is that this position is first adopted: that from the magnitude of the atom, magnitude arises in the dyad; and from the magnitude of the dyad, magnitude arises in the triad.

Although it should be stated here that such an alternative is not even tenable because there is no subordinate genus of dimension (*parimāṇāvāntarajāti*), nevertheless, one should understand that the author has adopted this position with a hidden intention (*gūḍhābhisandhi*) precisely in order to demonstrate that such a genus does not exist.
For this very reason, he also entertains another alternative, asking: "How indeed? (*katham evam iti*).
How can even the state of being minute not be predicated of those things that precede the triad?

The sense is that one might adopt the position that because an atom (*paramāṇu*) is minute, there is minuteness in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*); because of the minuteness of the dyad, there is minuteness in the triad (*tryaṇuka*); and from that, there is minuteness in the tetrad (*caturaṇuka*).
But if this were the case, the faults mentioned for both positions would arise, and furthermore, an additional contradiction would ensue. To explain:
Starting from the atom up to the final composite whole, if everything possessed manifest color and touch and were large, then everything would be perceptible;
whereas if it were minute, it would be imperceptible.
Furthermore, it is not logical that atoms and the like should be perceptible while triads and the like are imperceptible;
for perceptibility and imperceptibility are mutually exclusive.
That which is perceptible, such as a jar, is not imperceptible.

Furthermore, that which is non-perceptible, such as space and so forth, is not perceptible; thus, because these two exist by way of mutual exclusion, how could it be appropriate to admit both largeness (*mahattva*) and minuteness (*aṇutva*)—which are mutually contradictory—in a single [locus]? As the author of the Sūtras said: "And because of the example. (*dṛṣṭāntācca*)

Nor can the contradiction be resolved by means of a difference in time, because dimension (parimāṇa) persists as long as the substance exists; anticipating this objection, the author removes the inconsistency by stating that the two consequences—being perceptible and being non-perceptible—are indeed intended with respect to the person: "Perceptibility and its opposite [apply] to everything in relation to the person. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.63ab).
Since both perceptibility and imperceptibility exist in every substance, even in atoms and the like, these two reductio arguments are not tenable; nor is there any contradiction,
because the established distinction is possible in relation to different persons.
This will become clear later [in verse 7.312].
Now, he dispels the contradiction regarding minuteness and magnitude with the words: "And minuteness... (*aṇutvaṃ ca*).
And minuteness and magnitude [arise] from the relative perspective of the object itself.
The word "in all" (akhile) is understood to carry over.
Both minuteness and magnitude exist in every object; they are not, however, contradictory.
How so?
Because, in relation to the object itself, it is that very same thing which is called both "atomic" and "large"—this is the construction [of the sentence].
This is what is meant:

This contradiction would arise in the acceptance of minuteness and magnitude in all substances, such as atoms and the like, if there were a connection with the universals (jāti) of minuteness, magnitude, and so forth, within dimension (parimāṇa), just as there is a connection with the universals of blueness and yellowness in color (rūpa).
But this is not the case, because there is a lack of valid evidence (pramāṇa).
However, just as the opponent accepts that in triads and so forth, magnitude (*mahattva*) is of a single genus despite possessing degrees of excellence and deficiency,
and just as atomicity (*aṇutva*) exists in atoms and dyads; [so too must the genus of cognition be accepted].

Thus, dimension (*parimāṇa*), devoid of intermediate sub-species, exists in all substances with varying degrees of excellence and deficiency. Accordingly, when a dimension resides in one substance, it is called "atomic" (*aṇutva*) in relation to a larger dimension residing in another substance;
that very same dimension is called "large" (*mahattva*) in relation to a smaller dimension residing in yet another substance.
And thus, how could there be any contradiction?
For indeed, just as a single substance, when described as being both near and far in relation to different substances, does not become a locus of contradiction; so it is here.
For this very reason, even the contradiction between perceptibility and imperceptibility is dispelled;
for that contradiction would exist only if those two were caused solely by magnitude and so forth,
but it is not so.
However, [the perception of atoms] is caused solely by the sharpness of the sense faculties of men;
otherwise, even one with weak vision would perceive a triad (tryaṇuka).
If it is argued that, in that case, space and so forth might also occasionally become objects of direct perception, we say no.

Because of the absence of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*), the non-perception of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) depends on the absence of specific qualities; for it is like the non-perception of a visible substance that is in contact with light and the sense organ due to its [lack of] manifested color. As for arguments such as "like the non-perception of wind," these are established otherwise by means of [the absence of] diminished magnitude (*apakṛṣṭamahattva*) and so forth.
If it is argued that, in that case, mountains and the like would be imperceptible, we say no; for what is intended is a specific degree of diminution.
If it is further argued that such a [diminution] does not exist as a fixed state, we say no.
True;
for this very reason it was stated, "with respect to the person.

Let it be so that there is no intermediate genus within dimension (*parimāṇa*); nevertheless, it is not tenable to accept [the presence of] largeness (*mahattva*) and minuteness (*aṇutva*) everywhere.
For it has been stated that atomicity (*aṇutva*) and magnitude (*mahattva*) are called intermediate dimensions in relation to superior and inferior dimensions;
and these two are possible in the dimension of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth,
but not in the dimension of an atom (*paramāṇu*).
Indeed, there exists no dimension smaller than the dimension of an atom,
relative to which that [atom] could be considered "large.
Therefore, the atom possesses only minuteness.

And thus, since magnitude is not perceived [as a separate quality], it is not non-existent; therefore, he says: "Because all objects of experience exist in a state of relative gradation. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.64ab)
Because all things exist precisely through a gradation of magnitude;
that is, relative to their own magnitude, they possess either superior or inferior magnitudes,
or rather, all substances are endowed with a magnitude that is superior to some [other] magnitude.
Therefore, the connection is that even for an atom, largeness is logical. Herein is the formal argument:
an atom is endowed with a dimension superior to something [else].
Alternatively, [the inference may be stated as]: "It possesses a dimension smaller than its own dimension, because it is a substance, like a thread.
Nor is the subject matter of this [inference] invalidated by the absence of a substance with a smaller dimension in the case of an atom.
Because their parts will be explained later; nor is there any deviation [from the rule] in those very cases, for they too possess parts. *7,321*
Thus, it is established that the inference stated in the Sūtra is valid because there is no difference in kind (*vaijātya*) among the dimensions of atoms, dyads, and so forth.
Even if one were to admit a difference in kind, the causal relationship could still be established;
otherwise, number (*saṅkhyā*) would also result in being a non-cause.
Since the restrictive rule that "it is thus for measurement alone" lacks any foundation, it must nevertheless be stated that this is simply the actual state of things.
Therefore, it should be understood that the inference has been established by demonstrating homogeneity through the exclusion of the sub-class of "measurement-ness. *7,322*
It raises an objection to what was stated—that even an atom is the substratum of the maximum dimension—by means of the word "yathā" (just as).
Just as the cessation of magnitude is accepted, so too is that of minuteness.
If it is argued that [the self] exists because of its having a limited magnitude... // MAnu 2.2.65a //

The construction is as follows: "If it is maintained that just as there is a point of rest for magnitude (*mahattva*), so too there is a point of rest for the reason of dimensionality (*parimāṇatva*) and for minuteness (*aṇutva*).
Here, by the words "magnitude" and "minuteness," the excellence and deficiency of dimension are expressed.
And by means of those two, that gradation is perceived;
"because of their dimensionality."
The meaning is that this is because there is a gradation in their degrees of minuteness (*parimāṇa*).
Thus, once the two [atoms] are established, the establishment of their minuteness follows; and once that [minuteness] is established, those two [atoms] are established.
In this way, the fault of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*) is refuted.

This is the meaning: the gradation of the decrease of magnitude must rest somewhere, because it is a gradation of magnitude, just like the gradation of the increase of magnitude; thus, by means of this inference, once the resting point of the gradation of the decrease of magnitude is established, that wherein it rests is the atom, beyond which no further [smaller] atom exists.
Since that [atom] is established as an atom by virtue of being the ultimate limit of the diminution of magnitude, how could its "largeness"— which is called a superior magnitude— be proven,
either by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*) or by one's own words?
Regarding the phrase "because of contradiction" (*vyāghātāt*),
it must be stated here:
what is this so-called "resting upon something" (*kvacid-viśrānti*)?
What is this limitation?
It is that the dimension is exactly one-sixth part of the dimension of a triad (tryaṇuka), and there is nothing smaller than that.

Alternatively, [the opponent might argue that] the existence [of qualities] in some substance is indeed devoid of any limitation in the degree of its diminution— that is, it possesses infinite parts— yet all of that is nonetheless necessarily dependent upon something.
To this, he says "No," because in the first case of the probandum (sādhya), the example is deficient in the property to be proven (sādhyavikala).

"...there is no rest even for greatness. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.65ab). The meaning of "even" (*api*) is that there is no such resting point (*viśrama*)—as previously described—for greatness when it is taken as an example, nor even for the gradations of excellence in magnitude. It is not only the case for the subject (*pakṣa*).
To the question "Why does it not exist?", he says: "Because it is seen."
"He is seen as infinite," thus indeed... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.65c //

The meaning is that the state of being progressively greater in measure is seen as infinite and boundless, rather than as having a determinate limit of quantity; this is because there exists subverting evidence [to the contrary] and an absence of establishing evidence [for such a limit].
He states that, in this case, the inference is also subject to the fallacy of "missing the proper time" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), by saying: "In the same way."
...so too is infinity present even within an atom.
The word "tathā" (likewise) serves to aggregate the refutation.

The meaning is that not only is infinity observed in the state of the progressive degrees of excellence (*utkarṣa-taratama-bhāva*) of magnitude (*parimāṇa*), but this infinity—that is, limitlessness—is also observed in the progressive degrees of diminution (*apakarṣa-taratamya*) of magnitude in the case of the minute (*aṇu*). *7,326*
The word "only" (eva) in the phrase "it is seen as infinite only" indicates that a limitation of magnitude is not observed in the illustrative example;
he clarifies this with the word "not" (na).
The Lord is not limited by the quality of the principle of Mahat, thinking "He is only this much. ... [He is] not circumscribed. 2.66a-c.
"Mahattvam" is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for this very specific substance;
therefore, the rule "ānmahataḥ" does not apply.
For it is accepted that "in both technical terminology and Vedic usage, a designation follows what is observed [in actual usage]."
As it is said: "The word *bahu* [is used] in the sense of *tanni*. Here, the word *guṇa* is employed twice by way of *tantra*.
Of these, the meaning of the first is a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*) known as dimension (*parimāṇa*).

The second [point] is that "the Lord is the multiplier" (*guṇana*), which serves as an indicator for the substance that is the substratum of supreme magnitude. For if that were the case, a limit to the gradations of excellence in magnitude would be observed;
that is, if the Lord and others were delimited by a calculation of magnitudes such as "this much," being possessed of fivefold or sixfold magnitude.
But it is not so;
for if that were the case, supreme magnitude would be untenable—this is the meaning of the word "hi" (*for*).
Here, by the mention of the principle of magnitude (*mahattattva*), he indicates this.
What has been stated by the Vaiśeṣikas and others— that there are only nine substances, beginning with earth— is incorrect,
because the great principle (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and so forth also exist.
Nor is there a lack of valid means of knowledge regarding them.
This is because there exist means of valid cognition such as scripture;
nor is it the triad of atoms (tryaṇuka) and so forth that is thus described,
since [scripture] speaks of its being unmanifest (avyakta) and so on.
Furthermore, there exists no subverting argument by which one might suppose this is merely a figurative designation.
By the mention of "the Lord" (Īśvara), he indicates that the claim made by others— that even individual souls possess supreme magnitude— is incorrect.
It will indeed be established that the individual soul (jīva) is atomic (*aṇu*).
He states the purpose of establishing the absence of rest in the illustrative example with the word "tathā" (so).
...and likewise, for the atom, there is nowhere such a division into parts.
Since there is no statement that the magnitude of the example is limited to this many qualities and not more than this,

it follows that by such an example, the degree of minuteness— that is, the reduction of magnitude— of the atom cannot be established as having a definite limit, such that its magnitude is reduced by exactly one-sixth from the magnitude of a triad (tryaṇuka) and not more; such a specific measure does not hold for any substance.
For it is not possible to prove that a mountain possesses fire by taking a great lake as the subject of the inference;
and if that [lake] is unestablished, the intended object is not attained.

For, when the meaning that "the measure is restricted to this much alone and not more than this" is established, there is established a substance that serves as the basis for the limit of diminution—a substance that is not exceeded by anything whatsoever.
Alternatively, by this statement he states the counter-argument:

for it has already been established that the gradation of excellence in magnitude does not rest anywhere; because there is no such thing as a limit, one cannot say that magnitude is excellent only up to this many qualities.
Likewise, by means of that illustration, it is established that the atom does not possess such a divisible nature in any respect.
Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*):
The gradation of the decrease in magnitude does not come to rest anywhere, because it is a gradation of magnitude, just like the gradation of the increase in magnitude. (7.330)
He raises a second objection with the words "viśrānta" (rested).
If it is understood that there exists some infinite part [of the self] which has come to rest, [then one is liberated].

The second position is understood— that is, it is accepted— if the meaning of the term "rested" (*viśrānta*) is that there exists some particular substance which, in comparison to triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, possesses infinite parts by way of its dimension;
this is what is being stated.

The gradation of the diminution of magnitude is indeed not limited by any specific quantity; however, even though it consists of infinite parts, it is nonetheless dependent upon something. He refutes this, saying: "No. (7.331)
It cannot be determined with certainty solely because of contradictions.
The word "then" (*tarhi*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The term "anyone" (*kaścit*) continues to apply.
Thus, when proving [this], it is not possible to determine even any specific substance whatsoever.

This [atom] alone possesses the minimum possible magnitude; there is nothing with a smaller magnitude than this. Thus, because it is the ultimate limit of all things, no one is able to conceive of anything further.
Why? Simply because of direct contradiction:
for it is a logical impossibility to claim that there is a reduction in magnitude and yet it is infinite and final.
And there must be an end [to this process];
otherwise, since it would be possible for everything to have both maximum and minimum dimensions, it would be impossible to refute the [alleged] magnitude of the atom.
By the word "eva" (only/precisely), he indicates that the contradiction cannot be avoided.
By this, a departure from one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*) is stated.
For if the meaning of the proposition were merely that, disregarding infinity, there exists some basis for a gradation in the diminution of magnitude,
even so, the desired [conclusion] would not be established.

If it is argued that the intended meaning is that a terminus is obtained [in the sense that] there is no substance with a smaller dimension than an atom— just as there is no substance with a larger dimension than space and so forth—
then that is true.
If it is argued that this [infinite] is not obtained from here,
and that what is intended is the statement: "The gradation of the decrease of magnitude reaches its ultimate limit somewhere, because it is a gradation of magnitude,
just like the gradation of the increase of magnitude," then what indeed is this so-called "ultimate limit"?
Is there an excess, or a deficiency, or is there something common? In the first case, there is sublation (bādha).
In the second case, the example lacks the property to be proven;
the third is not [viable] because of its non-existence.
This is because inference does not proceed on the basis of mere similarity of words.
If it is argued that, just as the dimension of space and so forth lacks both limits,
so too the dimension of the part of the triad (tryaṇuka) must be the probandum, we say no.
Because there is no reason [for such a claim];
because the property of being a magnitude (parimāṇatva) is inconclusive with respect to the magnitudes of jars and the like;
and because the permanence of eternal magnitude is unestablished, since its dependence on an impermanent substratum will be stated later.
And because the state of being the ultimate limit of measurement (*parimāṇakāṣṭhatva*) is what is to be proven;
in this way, other intended meanings (*tātparya*) should also be refuted.
It has been stated that the gradation of the excellence of measurement is seen to be infinite.

Anticipating the question, "By what means of valid cognition [is this known]? [the author] states: "Only" (*kevalam*). For substances such as time, space, and God are held to possess the quality of supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*); among these, the infinitude of the excellence of dimension in the case of time and space is established by direct perception (*sākṣisiddha*). Thus he says: "Only."
By the mere fact of being a witness, neither time nor place has any limit.
By the word "only" (kevala), he asserts the absence of any other means of valid cognition.
By "space," the ether (ākāśa) is meant. "Not limited" (nāntavān) means possessing an unlimited excellence of dimension.
The phrase "it is seen" is connected here as well, as it will be stated later.
For it was established in the first chapter that time and space are established solely through the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).
Therefore, by that very same [reasoning], the fact that the excellence of its magnitude (*parimāṇotkarṣa*) is also unlimited is understood.
It has been stated that the gradation of the diminution of magnitude (*parimāṇāpakarṣatāratamya*) is also seen to be infinite.

Anticipating the question "By what means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is this known?", he says, "And it is unending," indicating that for time (*kāla*) and space (*ākāśa*), it is known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) itself.
And the non-termination of the atom is observed by the witness in both cases.
The meaning is: at two times, in the sky, and in the case of the atom (*aṇu*)—that is, regarding the gradation of the diminution of magnitude (*parimāṇāpakarṣatāratamya*).
"Non-termination" (*aparyavasiti*) means infinity (*ānantya*).
"Now, this is irrelevant;

for while there is a presentation of proof regarding the existence of a dimension smaller than the dimension of an atom, there is no purpose in presenting a proof for the infinite increase of dimension in the case of time and space.
Do not say so.
It was not stated by the opponent that this [limit] exists directly;
rather, it was stated that just as there is a series of increases in magnitude, there is also a series of decreases in magnitude that must reach a terminus.

And so, how could the presentation of the witness-argument (*sākṣipramāṇa*)—concerning the absence of a terminus for the series of increases and decreases in the magnitude of time and space—not be relevant?
Granted that there may be an unlimited excellence of dimension in time and space;
but how can there be an infinity of its diminution?
For that would be contradictory.
Not so;
because it is established by direct perception (*sākṣisiddha*).
For when an object has been cognized, there is no room for contradiction. (7.340)
If it is argued that an infinite diminution of magnitude at the beginning of time is simply not accepted because it is established by perception (*sākṣisiddha*), [we ask]:
is it not apprehended by perception, or is it apprehended but nonetheless unreal?
Alternatively, there is no such means of valid cognition as "witnessing.
He raises the initial doubt with the words "If... (yadi).
If that is not accessible through witnesses...
The word "tat" refers generally to the infinity of the diminution of measurement [resulting] from time and so forth;
he refutes this with the words "mahattvam" (greatness).
...by what is its greatness understood? Mānava 2.2.69b.
The phrase "of time and space" is understood [to carry over].
"Greatness" (mahattva) is the unsurpassed excellence of dimension.
The word "then" (tarhi) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
This is the underlying intention:
for the opponent, having accepted that there is an infinity of increase in magnitude with respect to time and so forth, does not accept an infinity of decrease therein.
To this, it must be said:
By what means of valid cognition is the infinity of excellence understood?
If you say "by a witness," then why is the infinity of deficiency not also accepted on the strength of that same witness?
If it is argued that this is not understood by that [scripture] because of the witness [of perception], then why,
by the force of that same [witness], is the infinite regress of downward displacement (*apakarṣa*) not also accepted?
If it is argued that "it is stated that this is not understood by him," what is the answer to one who says, "this too (or even that) is not understood by him"?
If it is argued that the denial of experience is not tenable,
this applies equally to the case at hand as well;
for just as the unlimited excellence of time and so forth shines forth in experience.
Likewise, there is also an infinity of diminution; so why this partiality toward one side?
Otherwise, if one were denied, the denial of the second would also be difficult to avoid.
It might be argued as follows:
We do not say that the infinite excellence of magnitude in time and so forth is established by direct perception (*sākṣi*);
rather, it is to be known through inference (*anumāna*).
And thus, there is no taking up of a counter-argument (*pratibandī*). To this, he says: "resting" (*viśrānti*).
For rest is observed through inference according to its varying degrees.
The phrase "by a succession of increases in magnitude" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
In the expression "by means of inference" (*anumānataḥ*), the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the instrumental case; that is, it does not mean "by inference.
For by means of inference, there is no establishment of an unlimited increase in magnitude regarding time and so forth.
For indeed, because that [limit] is seen to be reached through inference based on gradation;

that is to say, it is contradicted by a counter-inference (pratyanumāna) such as: "The gradation of excellence in magnitude must have a limit of its own, because it is a gradation of magnitude, just like the gradation of decrease in magnitude.
Nor should it be said that our example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavikala).

Since it is stated that for the opponent—who, while accepting the finitude of the gradation of decrease, infers the infinity of the gradation of increase—such a counter-argument might arise; and thus it must be said that this is a counter-inference contrary to direct perception (*sākṣiviruddha*). How then could he not establish an unlimitedly superior magnitude in respect to time and so forth? (7.343)
Let it be then that the proof of an unlimitedly superior magnitude [of the world] is established through scripture (āgama) and time; anticipating this objection, he says: "If... (yadīti).
If that greatness is understood to be infinite from scripture,
why is its minuteness not likewise determined to be infinite?
This [is known] from scripture, such as "He is infinite" and so forth.
Its "greatness" is the excellence of its measurement in terms of time and other dimensions;
its "subtlety" is the diminution of its measurement.
This is what is meant:
scripture does not itself establish things that are infinite, such as time and so forth.
Because that [object] is already manifested by the witness-consciousness even prior to the operation of that [cognition],
this [cognition] is merely a restatement (anuvāda). Alternatively, if it were a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), our purpose would not be exhausted by it.
Because from that very scripture an unlimited excellence of time and so forth is understood, from that same source the infinity of the assembly is also understood;
for the word "infinite" (ananta) denotes merely the absence of limitation,
and it is explained as referring to an excellence of magnitude.
In the same way, its diminution (*apakarṣa*) can also be explained.

Just as there is an infinity of time and so forth with respect to the increase of magnitude (*parimāṇotkarṣa*), the infinity of its diminution is likewise perceived through direct perception (*sākṣin*) or scripture (*āgama*).
Nevertheless, that [diminution] is not real.
He refutes the second [position]— that truth is not established merely by being perceived— due to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), with the words "mahattve" (in greatness).
No ultimate rest for either magnitude or minuteness is ever found.
No limit or delimitation of magnitude—whether its increase or decrease—is ever apprehended by any authoritative means of knowledge (pramāṇa) as resting upon time and so forth.
Here, the mention of "greatness" (mahattva) is for the sake of illustration. What is meant is this:

Just as the infinity of the excellence of magnitude in time and so forth— established by direct perception and other means— is indeed real because there is no valid cognition to the contrary, so too is the infinity of its diminution.

If the infinity of the diminution of magnitude in time and so forth, established by direct perception and other means, were unreal in the absence of a subverting factor, then the infinity of its excellence [in time and so forth] would likewise be unreal.
It would have to be true,
because there is no distinction;
and consequently, the acceptance of an undetermined magnitude [of the self] would be undermined.
It would perish. However, the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) has been set aside by the absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).
[Objection: But surely there is indeed a subverting argument against the admission of infinity in the case of the reduction of magnitude (*parimāṇāpakarṣa*).
For instance:
diminution means smallness,
while infinity means not being small.
Furthermore, a relationship of qualifier and qualified is not possible between two contradictory things;
for it does not occur that something is both "yellow" and "not yellow.

Therefore, because of the existence of such a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), even that which is perceived—the infinity of the removal (*apakarṣānantya*)—is abandoned. To this, he says: "It is quite another," and so forth.
For infinity is indeed something quite other than both greatness and minuteness, which are equal [to it].
Infinity is not merely the state of being non-little;
rather, it is something else entirely, consisting in the absence of limitation.
Therefore, it is logical that it possesses a common characteristic with both the increase and decrease of magnitude.
In this case as well, the mention of "greatness" (mahattva) serves merely as an illustration;
just as it is a qualification of greatness, so too is it a qualification of minuteness (aṇutva).
If "endlessness" (anantatva) were simply non-littleness, then it could not be a qualification of excellence (utkarṣa) either.
For that very thing cannot be its own qualifier, as we do not observe such usage as "yellow is yellow.

Therefore, in that case, one must accept that what is called "infinity" (anantya) is the absence of delimitation, and on this basis, the relationship between qualifier and qualified is to be established.
The same applies to the case at hand as well.

For just as the excellence of magnitude (*parimāṇotkarṣa*) in space and so forth is unlimited, so too its diminution (*apakarṣa*) is likewise without limit; thus, there is no fault whatsoever in accepting the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.
To demonstrate that what is called "infinity" (*ānantya*) is nothing other than "not being small," he states another example: "in multiplicity," etc. (*bahutve*).
Just as multiplicity and scarcity are perceived in arithmetic, so too is infinity... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.72a-c]
Just as in the case of number, infinity is perceived as a qualifier of both plurality and singularity—
such that plurality is infinite and singularity is infinite—
so it is in the present case as well.
If "infinitude" were simply "not being small," then it could not be a qualifier of "plurality," because it would be impossible for that very [plurality] to qualify itself;
nor could it be a qualifier of "smallness," because of their mutual contradiction.

Therefore, having accepted that infinity (*anantatva*) is simply the absence of limitation (*avacchedābhāva*), one should understand the relationship between qualifier and qualified as follows: "multitude," "fewness," and "infinity" are themselves unlimited; the same applies to the increase and decrease of magnitude (*parimāṇa*).
But is it not the case that there is no infinity of plurality or scarcity within the realm of number?
For plurality terminates at the "highest numeral" (*parārdha*), and scarcity terminates at the "one" (*eka*).
Its limit is as follows:
as it has been said,
"And that [number] extends from unity up to the highest unit (parārdha)."
Therefore, as to how this is an illustration, he says: "One," etc.
...for indeed, only the quantity of single parts is counted. For the science of calculation (*gaṇita-śāstra*) has proceeded with reference to number;
and therein, in the sections concerning fractions, interest, principal, parts, sub-parts, multipliers, divisors, and so forth, it is the single parts that are reckoned.
Since that very limitlessness is understood, it is therefore comprehended that there exists a number even inferior to oneness that is limitless.
The existence of numbers even beyond the *parārdha* (the highest count) is so self-evident that it need not be further established;
for it is indeed possible, through the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) of others, for a number beyond the *parārdha* to arise even in respect to atoms and other such entities.
Beyond that, the application of designations for the enumerators (gaṇakas) is due to a lack of necessity.

To remove this very misconception, the employment of examples of number has been made. Thus, having established through a witness the infinite increase and decrease of the dimensions of time and space, he establishes it with respect to the Lord by means of His scripture: "And [He is] more minute... (*aṇīyān*).
"The Blessed One is declared in scripture to be both subtler than the subtle and greater than the great.
By such scriptural authority as "The Self is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great," the Blessed Lord is declared to be subtler even than the subtle and greater even than the great.
Moreover, in that context, nothing fixed is expressed by the terms "minute" (aṇu) and "large" (mahat),

because there is no qualifying attribute [to establish a limit]. Therefore, it would have to be said that whatever has a diminished dimension is even more diminished than that, and whatever has a superior dimension is even more superior than that.
In this way, it is established that the degrees of increase and decrease in the dimensions of the Lord are indeed limitless.

Now, one might object: since it has been stated regarding the Blessed One, "He is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great," how can there be a limitlessness of those two [dimensions], given that they terminate in Him? To this, he says: "Subtler... [and so on].
"Though it has been stated that [the Self] is 'smaller than the smallest' and 'greater than the greatest,' this is because those terms refer to the domain of speech.
[Objection: "If that is so, does it not follow that one is both inferior and superior even to oneself?
[Reply: Who says "no"? No one.
How this is so will be explained later.
Furthermore, there is another scriptural passage which establishes the infinity of the Lord with respect to the increase and decrease of His dimensions; thus he says: "By infinity... etc.
A word expressing infinity serves as a means of valid cognition even regarding the two kinds of infinity.
... he goes. // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.74a //

In the passage, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," the word *ananta* (infinite), which denotes the infinity of Brahman, expresses its infinitude in terms of space, time, and substance. Among these, spatial infinity (*deśānantya*) means the possession of unlimited magnitude.
Temporal infinity (*kālānantya*) means having an uninterrupted existence.
Infinity of substance (*vastvānantya*) means possessing an unlimited number of qualities, actions, and forms.

In that regard, when it expresses the infinity of dimension (*parimāṇānantya*), it attains the status of a measure even for the two kinds of infinity, despite their being infinite through increase and decrease.
"But it is not [the case] regarding mere infinite excellence, because there is no distinction [between them].
Now, is it not improper for a word to have multiple meanings?
What contradiction with logic is there in this?

Since it is improper to employ a word that is devoid of meaning, one [single] referent must first be accepted. However, if a second were accepted, there would be no basis for it, resulting in the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*).
To this, it is replied:
For this [objection] applies only where, one object being already established, the acceptance of another object is entirely redundant;
but it is not so in the present case.
Indeed, the word "infinite" (ananta) expresses the mere absence of limitation.
For indeed, limitation (pariccheda) occurs only through space, time, and substance;
and in that case, there is no priority for any one of them.
Nor is there any reason for the abandonment of any one [of these].
Thus, it should be understood that even regarding the final limit of magnitude, there is an inclusion of excellence (*utkarṣa*).

[Objection: But if this were so, then for the word "infinite" (*ananta*), which denotes infinity in terms of time and qualities, its meaning would instead be a short duration of time and a small number of qualities.
If it is argued that otherwise even the possession of a small magnitude would not be possible because there is no distinction, [we ask]:
what is this "smallness" to be established in terms of time and quality— is it that only a few qualities exist in Brahman and not many more?
Likewise, existence would be only for a short time and not for an extended period;
or else, that which exists at all times would have to abide even during a short time,
and even a great quality would become a minor quality.
He refutes the first [position] with the words: "Not at all."
... neither the smallness of qualities nor the smallness of time is established by [mere] measurement. MAnu 2.74ab.

The proposition, made with a hidden intention, is that the infinitude of Brahman— which is established by the Śruti as "Brahman is infinite"— would not exist if its qualities were few and its duration were short, as is known from [the evidence of] direct perception. He will state the reason for this later.
Anticipating the second objection, he accepts it with the words: "All," etc.
Even for one who has passed away at all times, there may be a state of persistence even for a short duration.
If it be argued that even a small virtue may belong to one who possesses great virtues, let it be so.
It is brought about;
that is to say, it would come into being.
Here, the mention of "quality" (guṇa) is also an elliptical indication for "action" (kriyā) and so forth.
The intentional inclusion of both quality (*guṇa*) and time (*kāla*) is for the purpose of refuting [the notion of] primacy;
by this, he indicates the avoidance of the aforementioned burden of conceptual construction (*kalpanā-gaurava*).
Now, if a diminution of time and a diminution of quality are indeed accepted...
How, then, is the refutation of the claim that there is "not even a small degree of excellence" to be understood? To this, he reveals the underlying intention: "It is precisely that much."
In that case, you yourself would not even exist... // MAnu 2.75c //
The meaning is that there is indeed only a small amount; "as stated previously" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
If one asks, "Why should this not be so? [the answer follows].
He says, "Even in a location," because there is an absence of a producer.
... even in that country, this is not our opinion. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.75c)
The meaning is: "even in the case of measurement. This much alone is [the extent] of us, that is, of ourselves.
This is what is meant:
having observed our own scriptural exposition regarding the subject of measurement, this [same principle] is applied to both quality and time as well;
for there is no other means of establishing it.
Nor is it our interpretation that regarding measurement,
there exists only an inferior measurement without limit and no superior one;
for it has been stated that there are two kinds of infinity.
Therefore, this argument is groundless.
Now, one might object that this attempt to establish a supreme and infinite magnitude for Īśvara and others is improper,
because it has not been stated anywhere by the author of the Sūtras.

Since the sūtra "as in the case of the large and the long" can be supported either by establishing that there is a causal relationship even between heterogeneous things, or by establishing that there can be an increase or decrease in magnitude even when the substrates are different, [the author] says: "of the large..."
For one who knows the Veda has declared that even the vastness of the great becomes small, like space.

The author of the Sūtras states in the portion of the Sūtra beginning with “and like space” (*vyomavacca*) that even Brahman, which possesses an excellence of infinite magnitude, can possess a small magnitude, using space as an illustration.
Therefore, it is indeed the established tenet [of this system] that both Brahman and space possess the existence of both an excellence and a diminution of infinite magnitude. (7,368)

Furthermore, whatever object is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that allows no room for alternative possibilities, and the negation of which would lead to an undesirable consequence— all such cases constitute a tenet (*siddhānta*). In this regard, it has been stated that the existence of an unlimited degree of increase and decrease in dimension (*parimāṇa*) in time (*kāla*), space (*ākāśa*), and the Lord (*īśvara*) is established both by direct perception (*sākṣin*) and by scripture (*āgama*).
He states the subverting argument for the opposite of that: "If..."
If it were situated in only a small portion [of space], it would not exist everywhere.
The phrase "of time and so forth" continues [from the previous context],
as does the term "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) in all instances.
Furthermore, the omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) of time and the other categories has been accepted even by the opponent.
And omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) consists in being situated in all locations;
likewise, if time and so forth were not situated in increasingly smaller locations, [omnipresence would not be possible].
In that case, there would be no abiding anywhere at all.
Why? To this he says: "For of that which is already abiding..."

For one who remains within limited spaces, omnipresence would certainly be impossible; how much less so for one who does not abide even in a single place? How, then, could there be residence in all things? (2.77)
The word *dhruvam* is used for emphasis,
meaning "only while remaining in a small portion [of the articulatory space].
For indeed, just as when one utters each individual phoneme (*varṇa*), there is simultaneously the utterance of the entire scale of tones (*svara*).
But this is not so for one who does not utter even a single phoneme;
for it is only by being situated in very small and increasingly smaller regions that [the sound] could be considered as existing in all regions.
If it is not established even in each individual region, how indeed could it exist in all regions?

By this, the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) have been shown: that which pervades a whole necessarily pervades its parts as well, and that which does not pervade its parts does not pervade that whole.

It is not only that there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of omnipresence due to the absence of occupying even very small or smaller locations; [there would also be such a consequence regarding the whole].
But [the opponent] says that even existence would not exist, like the horn of a hare and so forth; therefore, [the author] says: "It is indeed emptiness."
That which has no stability even in a single place must be empty indeed.

And thus, when time and the other categories occupy increasingly smaller spaces, it is unavoidable that they also possess increasingly smaller dimensions; therefore, the reduction of dimension to an infinite degree is established.
As for the increase to an infinite degree, however, it is already accepted by the opponent as well, so no refutation has been stated against its opposite.
Or rather, it should be understood that [the argument] applies everywhere: "it would not exist at all."
For omnipresence is not possible in the absence of supreme magnitude. Thus it has been said: "Space is great because of its pervasiveness," and so forth.
That which is restricted to smaller and smaller locations possesses smaller and smaller dimensions.
If it is argued that space and so forth are not like this,
then is space and so forth a composite form, by virtue of which it would attain the status of being both a finite and an infinite object? Or is it rather a single entity?
And if that [space] were to reside in increasingly smaller regions, it would indeed possess those respective dimensions.
If you argue that if it possessed those respective dimensions while residing there, then the same consequence would follow for jars and other objects as well, we say no;
for in their case, that [consequence] is otherwise established due to their being composed of parts.
But is it not the case that being omnipresent means simply being in conjunction with all corporeal substances, rather than being present everywhere?
Because space and so forth are non-dependent,
conjunction would certainly occur even in the absence of those respective dimensions;
for a jar, when conjoined with space, does not thereby become infinitely large, nor does an atom, when conjoined with [another] atom, become an atom.
For what reason?
Because conjunction exists only partially.
This is not so.
