Because all dimensions exist in space, and because a minute particle (paramāṇu) can only conjoin with a portion of a jar;
for it is thus:
by means of a specific power.
Even though space is indivisible, it is endowed with infinite parts;
therein, unlimited excellence and deficiency in dimension exist according to their respective limitations.
Consequently, a jar comes into contact with only that portion of space which has the dimension of a span.
And what is the fault in [the pot] itself being of that same dimension?
Since the conjunction of atoms exists only in a part of the pot and not in the pot as a whole, how can the pot possess the nature of an atom?

If it is argued that, in that case, it is merely the spatial points (ākāśapradeśa) themselves— possessing conjunctions with fewer and fewer points— that would have those respective dimensions, and not space itself, we say no; for even they are of the nature of space.
Otherwise, conjunction could not reside in a specific location due to contradiction.
Having established the infinity of the increase and decrease of dimensions in time and so forth, he concludes with "ataḥ" (therefore).
Therefore, there is no ultimate rest in either atomicity or magnitude anywhere.
In some cases, this refers to the triad beginning with the lapse of time (*kālātīta*);
or rather, this is a summary of the refutation of inference. Consequently, the faults of *kālātīta* and the defect of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) remain unavoidable.
It has been stated that there is an infinity of both the increase and decrease of dimension in Time, Space, and God.
This applies not only to them, but also to other all-pervading, supremely great substances such as Primordial Matter (prakṛti) and so forth; thus he says: "Both... (ubhaya).
Therefore, according to that aforementioned principle, if the "Great" (mahat) were to be primary, it would be characterized by both infinitudes; [in this context],
the primary "Great" is the Supreme Great (paramamahat).

If even time and the like were infinite, then how could it be said that "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," with infinity being stated as a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of Brahman? For a definition cannot be over-extensive (ativyāpta). To this, he says: "And that... (tacceti).
And that Brahman is supreme, directly manifest, and eternally endowed with all-infinity.
The word "supreme" (param) has the sense of "exclusive" (kevala).
Although time and so forth are also infinite, nevertheless, Brahman alone is said to be that infinity.
Why?
Because it is directly infinite, without depending on anything else;
that is to say, because it does not depend on another.
He states another alternative: "All," etc.
... which is always endowed with all-infinity.
In this scriptural passage, it is not merely infinity that is stated as the defining characteristic; rather, [infinity] is stated with respect to space, time, qualities, and so forth.
And since such [a being] is none other than Brahman itself, there is no fault.

As it has been said: "The excellence [of beings] is threefold—by way of place, by way of time, and by way of qualities; that [excellence] belongs entirely to Hari alone, for no others possess perfect, true qualities.
He introduces another alternative view with the word "sadā" (always).
The connection is with what precedes.
Thus, even though there are infinite spatial points (*deśalakṣaṇa*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
It has also been stated that even in the case of an atom (*paramāṇu*), there is no resting point for the gradation of the diminution of dimension (*parimāṇāpakarṣatāratamya*).
That is incorrect,
because dimension must reside in a substance;
for there is no substance that could serve as the substratum of a dimension even smaller than that of an atom.
Not so;
for there exist parts of atoms,
and there is no final rest in them.
Since those [parts] also possess parts, they too have the nature of being composed of parts (*sabhāgatva*).

From where, then, could an uninterrupted succession of parts be established? Therefore, in order to state that there is no witness (*sākṣin*), he first states the refutation of one who claims that there is no such thing as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called a "witness," beginning with the words "If... (*yadīti*). *7,383*
If the witness were self-evident, by what means would it be known? And how could the validity of perception and the other [means of knowledge] be established? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.80a–c)

If it is not accepted that the witness (sākṣin) is a means of valid cognition (māna), then how can the validity of cognitions such as those born of the senses be established? By the word "and" (ca), [the author implies] by what means of valid cognition are external things like time and space, as well as internal things like pleasure, known?
By none at all.
This is because there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could apprehend it;
nor should it be said that "let it not exist," for that would entail the collapse of all conventional practice regarding it.
Granted that this may be a subverting argument for one who does not accept the existence of a witness, but what is the proving argument? To this he says: "Self-luminous" (svayambhāta).

However, one who disputes the self-luminous nature of the witness (sākṣin) should be enlightened by the following reductio-ad-absurdum (prasaṅga)-based inference: "The validity of perception and other means of knowledge possesses a valid basis, because it is a real entity, like a jar.
Furthermore, the negation of what has been proposed will occur according to the logic to be explained later.
Since [the witness] is established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends its substratum (dharmin), no separate proof need be stated for its validity.
For this very reason, it is called "valid cognition" (*māna*).
Even if a witness (*sākṣin*) is not admitted, it does not follow that the validity of sensory and other types of knowledge becomes unproven;

for that [validity] is established through inference based on the efficacy of purposeful action (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*) or by virtue of belonging to the same class [of cognitions]. Therefore, he says: "an infinite regress" (*anavasthā*).
...or else there would be an infinite regress.

Otherwise, if one were to admit that the witness is cognizable by a means of knowledge other than itself, then the validity of that witness would also have to be apprehended by another, leading to an infinite regress. If this is objected, we say no; for that [witness] is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).
This has been stated as "self-luminous" (*svayambhāta*).
What follows from this, if such a thing as a witness (*sākṣin*) exists as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, all objects always possess parts, because they are connected [to others] in all directions... // MAnu 2.81a-c //
The meaning is "it is witnessed.
The meaning is that [this applies] to all things, including atoms and their constituent parts.
The phrase "they indeed exist" implies that they are established as such.
Alternatively, by the phrase "of all things," he also indicates an inference:

"An atom possesses parts (sabhāga), because it is a thing (padārtha), like a jar. Nor is there a lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) or a contradiction with the means of apprehending the subject (*dharmigrāhakavirodha*).
Because it has been stated that the existence of atoms is established by means of a witness,
and because they are established by that very homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*),
there is no futility of inference in this case.

This is because the convergence of multiple means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-samplava*) is accepted, and because [the argument] is purposeful for one who is in disagreement regarding mere homogeneity (*sabhāgatva*).
He states another inference: "at all times," etc.
The meaning is "simultaneously.
Because of the connection—that is, the conjunction—with substances situated in all directions, it is understood that there are parts.
Even though mere possessiveness of conjunction is sufficient as a probans for establishing mere possession of parts;
Since there is no deviation [of the reason] even in the case of space and so forth, provided that they are admitted to have parts,
nevertheless, the inclusion of the qualification is for the purpose of establishing many parts. To explain:
An atom possesses ten parts because it is simultaneously conjoined with ten forms, like a jar. [Objection:
But surely, being a substance (*dravyatva*) alone is sufficient; what is the use of its being conjoined?

We say that this is for the purpose of indicating a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the opposing position (*vipakṣa*), which consists in the eradication of the cause (*hetūcchittirūpa*). To explain:
There is, indeed, a conjunction of one atom with another atom,
for otherwise the commencement of dyads and so forth would be impossible;
nor is there a rule that it must be with only one [atom].

In the process of conjunction arising from the conjunction of causes and non-causes, it is accepted that each individual atom simultaneously enters into conjunction with two atoms—both homogeneous and heterogeneous;
furthermore, it would otherwise be impossible for an atom situated in the midst of a stone or similar object to lack conjunction with the atoms surrounding it on all sides.
Moreover, it is not possible for corporeal entities to occupy the same location simultaneously.
Furthermore, conjunctions occupy only a portion [of their relata],
because this is established by direct perception and because it is observed in the case of jars and the like, and is thereby inferred even for atoms.
And thus, if the atom were not composed of multiple parts, it would not be able to be simultaneously conjoined with many [other atoms].
Now, one might object that the so-called "subsistence in a location" (pradeśavṛttitva) of conjunction is simply its coexistence with the absolute non-existence of itself in the same locus.
But it is not the case that the conjunction with the pot resides in a part of the pot;
so how can there be an impossibility of conjunction in the absence of parts?
Do not say this.
For it is improper to abandon what is established by perception and other means of valid cognition—the property of having parts—and instead accept something unauthentic that contradicts [evidence];
and this will be explained later (*7,399*).
Now, the statement "an atom has parts" is indeed the primary example of self-contradiction.

For that which is most minute in every respect, beyond which no further atom exists, is called an "atom" (paramāṇu). If it were to possess parts, then since the dimensions of the parts of a composite object must necessarily be even more minute than those of the whole, how could there not be a contradiction? To this, he says: "indivisible" (avibhāga).
... indivisibility is supreme minuteness.
This contradiction would exist if this were the basis for the application of the term "atom" (paramāṇu);
but it is not so,
because that [basis] is impossible given that [the atom] is established by direct perception as possessing parts.
However, indivisibility (*avibhāga*) and supreme minuteness (*parāṇutā*) are the grounds for applying the term "atom" (*paramāṇu*). Thus, how could there be a contradiction?
But one might ask: how is it understood that [the atom] is indivisible?
If it is argued that there is an absence of qualities characterized by divisibility in every respect, we say no;
for this would entail the consequence that even qualities and so forth possess the nature of atoms.
If it is argued that there is no such fault because of the qualification "provided they are substances," we say no.
Because it is impossible;
for if the intention were the absence of any division whatsoever, it would follow that even Mount Meru and Mount Mandara are atomic.
If it is argued that what is intended is the absence of division of parts, we say no.
Not so;
for there is this explanation: that which possesses distinct parts, yet for which a further division of those parts can never occur, is an atom (*paramāṇu*).
By this, [the objection regarding] the lack of a finality in the succession of parts is refuted.
The objection that there would be an infinite regress in the absence of effort is also refuted,
because it has been indicated that there is no destruction of the root. Alternatively, "division" (*vibhāga*) means that which is split or separated.
The absence of that [composite] is what constitutes an atom (*paramāṇu*).
That is to say, since there exists no entity that is independent of its own parts, partless in form, and of minimal dimension, that [entity] is an atom. *7,413*
Now, if there is no resting point for this succession of parts, then because both are equally composed of infinite parts, there would be no difference in size between a mustard seed and a mountain.

Nor can it be argued that even when the number of constituent causes is equal, the difference in size between the mustard seed and the mountain arises from a difference in the accumulation (*pracaya*) of those parts; for such an explanation is untenable as long as the infinity of parts remains the same for both.
It is said:
Is this a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga), or is it an inference (anumāna)?
For the meaning in the first case is this:
if the mustard seed and the mountain were such that their parts did not mutually cease [to overlap], then it would follow that they are composed of infinite parts;
and in that case, they would necessarily be of equal magnitude.

In both cases, there is a lack of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*). [The two reasons given are: "Whatever has parts that do not rest within one another is composed of infinite parts," and "Whatever is such [composed of infinite parts] is of equal magnitude."
What indeed have you perceived?
Furthermore, if there were no cessation in the succession of parts, would they all not, taken together, be infinite?
But from where could there be an infinity of those things that originate the earth and its mountains?
For this very reason, the probans of the second undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) is unestablished.

By this, the following argument is also refuted: "In the absence of a final rest in a series of parts, there would be an equal number of constituent parts; consequently, in the absence of any distinction in the dimensions of the parts, there would necessarily be no distinction in the dimension [of the whole].
This is because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished.
Furthermore, it is not established that [the two] are composed of an equal number of constituent parts.
Regarding the second [alternative], this would have been stated:
"A mustard seed and a mountain are not composed of an infinite number of parts, because they possess dissimilar dimensions."
"The two subjects of dispute do not have a series of parts that terminates, because they are composed of infinite parts.
Regarding the first [reason], it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*);
for it is not accepted by us that mustard seeds and the like are composed of infinite parts simply because there is no termination to their series of parts.
However, there is an infinity of things that have come into being; therefore,
in establishing their non-existence against me, there is an absence of an illustrative example,
because there is no proof [of such non-existence] in the case of qualities and so forth.
"But for the second [position], there is no logical necessity (*aprayojakatā*).

It might be argued as follows: "If the succession of parts of a mustard seed were infinite, then since corporeal objects cannot occupy the same location, the world would be pervaded by the parts of the mustard seed; consequently, the mustard seed itself would become all-pervading (*viśvavyāpī*), leaving no room for a mountain."
If it is argued that this is for the purpose of establishing [the existence of space], we say no;
for even though the atoms of earth are infinite, one observes that they provide room for other corporeal objects.
Furthermore, a mustard seed is seen to exist occupying a certain amount of space, and within that very same space, an unlimited succession of its own constituent parts also resides.

For this very reason, even in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, an infinite succession of parts has been accepted, thereby establishing an infinity of the diminution of magnitude (*parimāṇāpakarṣa*).
[Objection: "Granted that the seeds initiating a mustard grain and those initiating a mountain may not have an equal number [of parts] directly;
nevertheless, since there would be an equal number of constituent parts due to the lack of a final term in the series of parts, no difference in magnitude would arise. [Response: This is not so.
Even though they are infinite, a gradation is possible;
for while the atoms of earth are infinite and the ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*) are also infinite,
they are not equal in number.
Even so, since that [state] would result in the absence [of distinction] even among non-atomic entities;
likewise, although transmigrating beings are infinite across all kalpas,
nevertheless, by virtue of liberation, a gradation must indeed be admitted.
Thus, there are many such examples.
This refutation stated by the author of the Sūtra regarding the non-inherent cause of dimension (*parimāṇa*) is merely illustrative.

Intending that one should likewise infer the refutations against other non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for oneself, he dispels a misconception regarding the conjunction that serves as a non-inherent cause for substances: "From their conjunction...
[Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.82ab]: "From their conjunction, which is not restricted, the production of entities would occur."

Even the Vaiśeṣikas and others, who maintain that the conjunction of parts (*avayava-saṃyoga*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) of a substance, assert that in the production of the effect of an atom, the causality belongs specifically to the conjunction of two atoms, and specifically to those of the same genus, and so forth. This is not to be trusted; for how indeed could the birth of entities—that is, substances—arise from a conjunction of causes that is indefinite and devoid of the aforementioned restriction?
A certain effect arises from the conjunction of two atoms;
that is called a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).
Sometimes, from three [atoms] it arises as a triad (*tryaṇuka*), and when it is commenced by four atoms, it is a tetrad (*caturaṇuka*).
The same applies to other cases as well:
likewise, some [conjunction] arises from the conjunction of two atoms of the same class, while some arises from those of different classes;
similarly, some arises from the conjunction of two atoms alone, while some arises from an atom and a dyad (dvyaṇuka), and so forth.
In this way, one should also observe that there is no fixed rule regarding the production of the effect consisting of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).

If one asks why, he says: "Because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) for the stated rule," namely, that [the dyad] arises from exactly two [atoms]. (*7,422*) Thus he states: "From only two."
But by what is it determined that conjunction occurs only between two things?
The word "tu" (but) serves to specify;
by it, the restriction that [conjunction occurs] between two atoms of the same class is obtained.
The remainder of the sense is that conjunction is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the initial effect.
"By what means of valid cognition?"—this is a rhetorical objection. This is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood as "by means of exactly three dyads."

[Objection: But surely multiple conjunctions are possible for that which has parts; however, since an atom is partless, the restriction that [conjunction] occurs only between two [atoms] is established. [Reply: This has already been answered:
even in the case of two [atoms], conjunction is not possible if they are both partless.
Because conjunction resides in parts.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the rule—that only a conjunction of like kinds is productive—is without proof?
For there is indeed proof for this in the production of odor and so forth in the effect of atoms.
For instance,
if a single effect were produced from both an earth atom and a water atom, then that [effect] would become odorless and ununctuous.
If it were produced from an earth atom and a fire atom, it would be produced as being odorless and colorless.

Because a single [quality] such as odor does not initiate [a new substance], it follows that the initiation of conjunction with its own kind is established precisely by the production of odor and so forth; therefore, he says: "of the cause."
Therefore, the qualities of the cause would also exist in the effect.
"By that."
The meaning is: "due to the absence of a restrictive rule that [the production] occurs only from two.
This might be a refutation of the theory that heterogeneous substances can originate [from others]:
if there were a valid means of knowledge for the restrictive rule that the conjunction of only two atoms is the originator of an effect.

But this is not the case; and thus, when many heterogeneous atoms originate an effect through their conjunction, the qualities such as odor residing in the causes— being homogeneous— are present in the effect.
They might also be the initiators of smell and so forth in the effect; what is the fault?
[Objection: Surely, for one who maintains the absence of restriction, the conjunction of two [atoms] is accepted as the initiator.
In that case, if atoms of different classes were the initiators, it would follow that smell and so forth would not be produced in the effect. [Response: This is not so.

Since there is no subverting argument against each individual [quality] such as odor being a producer [of the effect], one might object: "The undesirable consequence that [the effect] would arise continuously follows because there is nothing else to be depended upon. If this is said, we reply: No, because the production of the resultant substance itself must depend [on other factors].
Because an effect does not arise in the absence of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
Otherwise, even if one were to accept multiple odors and so forth, the same fault would apply.
And this has been stated according to the system of another school.
In reality, however, since causes themselves arise in the form of effects, the qualities of the cause alone would reside in the effect.
Therefore, what fault is there in [the theory of] the production of a heterogeneous [effect]?
If it is argued that, in that case, there would be a confusion of universals such as "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth;
What follows from that?

If it is argued that there would be a collapse of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*), we say no; for [the scripture states]: "But because of its distinctness, there is a designation of that. (*Vaiśeṣyāt tu tadvādaḥ*)
This is because [the objection] will be refuted later.

Even so, if it is argued that—by means of the example of an effect produced from causes of the same class as those already accepted—one may infer that even for those who disagree, the effect is likewise produced from causes of the same class, we say: no.
This is because the notion that [atoms] originate something of a different genus is sublated by the evidence of perception and other means of valid cognition.
It might be argued:
"If it were the case that the conjunction of many atoms possesses the capacity for origination..."
But this is not the case;

for the gradation of the decrease in the number of constituent parts must rest upon something somewhere, because it is a gradation—just like the gradation of magnitude. Once the resting point of the decrease in the number of constituents is established through this inference, it follows that a single entity acts as the constituent.

Because it would entail the undesirable consequence of continuous production and so forth, and because it is more parsimonious (lāghava) to postulate three or more [atoms], the rule that the conjunction of exactly two atoms is the initiator of a substance is established; therefore, he says: "due to the gradation... (tāratamya).
For all things, whether great or minute, exist according to a gradation of degrees.

Since all objects, from the greatest to the smallest, are established through a gradation of degree, the example "like that which possesses a gradation of dimension" is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). Furthermore, by what means is it determined that conjunction occurs only between two [atoms]?
Moreover, by this very same logic, why is the capacity to initiate [a larger whole] not also accepted for the conjunction of two dyads?

If it is argued that "because in the absence of plurality, the magnitude of the effect would result in an impossibility," we say no; for all things, whether large or minute, are established through degrees of intensity. Thus, since the magnitude of the dyad (dvyaṇuka) exists, its production is logically possible.
As for the objection that "there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in every inference by using the example of an effect produced from two atoms," [we reply: no.
If it is asked: "Granted that there is a lack of evidence for the aforementioned restrictive rules, what then is the proof for the creation of things without such restriction?"—the answer is:
first, direct perception;
and second, inference based on the observation that effects such as clods of earth and the like are produced by causes that are indefinite in number, heterogeneous, and dissimilar.
Furthermore, there are many scriptural traditions (āgama) on this point.
If it is argued that the perception of those [traditions] is erroneous,
is this stated solely because of a contradiction with the valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehends the restrictive rule?
Furthermore, [it is not so] because of contradiction with the conceptualizations of the Vaiśeṣikas and others taken alone.
He refutes the first [position] with the words "And not" (*na ca*).
And there is no authority for the creation proclaimed by him [in that context].

However, there is no evidence for that creation described by him— which is subject to restrictive rules such as "only from two atoms," "only from those of the same genus," and so forth— and it would therefore constitute a sublation of our own accepted mode of creation, which is established by witnesses and other means;
as was stated previously.
He refutes the second [position] with the words "kevala" (only).
...is merely a fabrication;
how could it ever possibly prevent that which has been directly perceived? (2.84b–d)
The meaning is "to root out.
The term "witness" (*sākṣin*) is an elliptical expression for this undertaking of an unrestricted [practice].
The sense is that if mere conceptual construction were to exclude what is established by valid means of cognition (*prāmāṇika*), it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
By stating "in the creation proclaimed by him" in a general sense here, it is indicated that whatever else has been imagined by him is likewise devoid of validity.

For instance, having set aside this process well-known from the Śruti and other sources—namely, "From Prakṛti comes Mahat; from Mahat comes Ahaṅkāra; and from Ahaṅkāra, in sequence, the great elements beginning with Ākāśa"—the creation of the four [elements] beginning with Vāyu is described as being mutually independent and even in a reversed order, without any subverting evidence, as in:
"From Ākāśa comes Vāyu; from Vāyu comes Agni."
Thus, the ablative case in such instances is accepted as figurative;
furthermore, the arising of that which is absolutely non-existent is admitted,
and it is maintained that every creation depends upon the three types of causes, beginning with the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*).
In this regard, the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) is untenable because it will be stated later that inherence (samavāya) lacks any means of valid cognition (apramāṇika).
For the same reason, the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) is also untenable;
for its definition depends upon [the definition of] that [inherent cause].
Furthermore, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) with respect to both the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
For instance, in the case of two-ness (*dvitva*) produced in a thread and a cloth, the cloth is the inherent cause of that [two-ness].
And that [number two], because it inheres in the thread which is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the dyad, is proximate to the inherent cause;
furthermore, its capacity has been determined through its status as an inherent cause.
As for the dyad produced in the body and the self, the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is the efficient cause (*nimitta*).
And that [number] possesses the aforementioned definition because it is inherent in its inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), namely duality, and because it is a non-inherent cause (nimitta).
It is intended that the determination of causal capacity is based on proximity to the inherent cause.
If it is argued that this is not the case for the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), [we reply:]...

Nevertheless, this would result in the absurdity that the cognition of the pervaded (*vyāpyabuddhi*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the cognition of the pervader (*vyāpakabuddhi*), and that merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are the non-inherent causes of pleasure and pain;
for a cognition of the pervaded residing in one locus cannot be the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of a cognition of the pervader residing in another locus.
If it is argued that this is not so because of the distinct spatial locations (*pradeśabheda*) within the self (*ātman*), we say no.
For it would follow that words such as "first" (*ādya*) could not be the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of words such as "second" (*dvitīya*).
If that [causality] were possible because they reside in the same space (*ekākāśagatatva*), then the same applies to the case at hand.
In this way, over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in other cases is also to be inferred.
If it is argued that this is merely the teacher’s convention and therefore one should not insist too much on this point,
then it follows that this entire grammatical system is indeed rootless; thus it is established.
Furthermore, they accept a theory of maturation (*pākaja*) that lacks scriptural authority;
this will be discussed later, so let it suffice here.
Now, since even the existence of atoms and dyads is not established by direct perception, how can there be any process of their origination?
How then can it be said that [the object] is "measured by direct perception"?
To this, he says: "If... (yadi).
If this is not proven by witnesses...
"This" refers to this very thing.
[The phrase] "beginning with atoms" [is used].
In that case, the implication is that such [atoms] would consequently become entirely lacking in any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This might be so.
Although atoms and the like are not objects of the visual sense and other faculties due to their lack of magnitude, nor is the mind [an object] because it lacks external independence,
scripture and so forth do not differ from inference.
Since it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention for a difference that is beyond the senses, it is not an object of scripture;
nevertheless, inference will serve as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard.

To the question, "How then does the absence of being known by the witness (sākṣivedyatva) lead to the consequence that atoms and so forth lack a means of valid cognition (aprāmāṇikatva)? he says: "No."
...inference does not apply there. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.85b)
If it is asked, "How so?"—
is this being proved by taking the atom and so forth themselves as the subject (*pakṣa*),
or something else? *7,451*
Regarding the first [alternative], is that established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not?
He states the fault in both positions with the words: "to make it the subject" (*pakṣīkartum*).
Since it is impossible to make [the subject] into a formal side (pakṣa), how indeed could there be an inference?

If [the atom] were established, it would lack the characteristics of a subject (*pakṣa*); if it were unestablished, it would not be an object of reasoning (*nyāya*). Since it is impossible to take the atom as the subject, an inference based on taking it as the subject is dismissed from afar. Now, one might ask: "Even if taking it as the subject is impossible, why is inference untenable? To this, he says: "Where... (*yatra*).
Where there is no footprint, who can reach that domain?
The words "in such a way" (yathā tathā) are to be supplied;
"where" (yatra) refers to whatever object (viṣaya),
and "object" (viṣaya) refers to a location (deśa).
For just as the placement of the foot is the cause for reaching an object— since the conjunction with a post or a non-post has as its cause the action of that which is not a post—
therefore, in the absence of the placement of the foot, there is no reaching of the object either.
Likewise, the act of taking [the mountain and so forth] as the subject (pakṣīkaraṇa) is the cause for the arising of inference.
For neither the mountain and such, nor the fire and such, is the object of inference;
rather, it is their relationship.
Furthermore, the knowledge of a relation is not possible without the knowledge of the related entities;

therefore, in the absence of making [the subject] the locus of the thesis (*pakṣīkaraṇa*), the arising of inference is not possible. He refutes the second [position] as well with the words: "to make the locus of the thesis" (*pakṣīkartum*).
For, having taken the dyad as the subject of the proposition, the atom must be inferred;
since it has been stated that the effect itself is the means of proof here,
and since that [dyad] is even now unestablished and thus impossible to take as the subject, how indeed could there be an inference of the atoms which are its cause?

If it is argued that, having taken the dyad (dvyaṇuka) as the subject of inference, the atom will be inferred, we say no; for if that too is established by taking the atom itself as the subject, then the same fault already mentioned applies. Thus he says: "to take [the atom] as the subject."

Since even today the atom (*paramāṇu*) remains unestablished, it is impossible to make it the subject (*pakṣa*) of an inference; how, then, could there be an inference of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) as its effect?

If it is argued that the atom will be established by the following inference—"The gradation of atomic dimensions must terminate somewhere, because it is a gradation of dimension, like the gradation of large dimensions"—we say no, because the conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) do not hold.
By the term "atomic dimension" (aṇuparimāṇa), is the diminution of dimension intended, or rather the dimension of an atom (paramāṇu),
or else the dimension of a dyad (dvyaṇuka)?
Or if it were of both dimensions:
not the first [alternative],
because it has already been refuted.
He refutes the three counter-arguments with the words: "to make [them] the subject."

The meaning is that since the atom (*paramāṇu*) and the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) are not established, their dimensions are likewise not established; furthermore, there is an absence of gradation within each of them.
That which is perceived as the most subtle dust particle everywhere, situated in the rays of the sun passing through a lattice window, is called a triad (*tryaṇuka*).
This [object] is large,
because it is a substance visible to the eye, like a jar;
and it is an effect, because while being large it is visible to the eye, or because while being large it possesses action.
And it possesses parts because it is a product-substance;
its parts are those called dyads (dvyaṇuka),
and they too are products and possess parts.
"Because it is the originator of a large substance, like a thread;
and that which is its part is itself the atom, since there is a lack of evidence for postulating further parts and because there is a subverting argument [against such a postulation].
Therefore, the proof of the atom and the dyad is established by inference alone"—to this he says: "in order to make it the subject of the proposition."

Since the triad (tryaṇuka), which is directly perceived, could itself be a paramāṇu, it is impossible to make it the subject (pakṣa) for proving that it is an effect or possesses parts; how then could there be an inference regarding the dyad (dvyaṇuka) and the paramāṇu?
If it is argued, "How can this be a paramāṇu given its magnitude?"—no, because its magnitude is unestablished.
If it is argued that its existence is established because it is a substance visible to the eye, we say no;
for there is no subverting evidence against the visibility of some things even if they are not large.
And if it is argued that largeness (*mahattva*) is the cause for the visibility of a substance, [we respond as follows].
True;
in some cases, another cause might also be postulated.
If it is argued that this would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), we say no.
Because the conceptualization of a mere property is simpler than the conceptualization of a substratum possessing that property; or even if it were [conceptually] more complex,
what contradiction would there be in its being contained within something minute?
Furthermore, the proof based on being an effect is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*),
because even a self of great magnitude can be established as visible like a perceptible object,
and because action is possible even in the absence of supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*).
If it is argued that the cause of magnitude is a plurality of causes, we say no,
because [magnitude] is established as being eternal.
If it is argued that this is not so because of the magnitude perceived by the eye, we say no.
Because there is no subverting evidence [to the contrary], for this very reason the status of being an effect-substance (*kāryadravyatva*) is unestablished.
Or, even if those parts exist, they themselves would be atoms; since it is impossible to take them as the subject (*pakṣa*) for further proof of having parts, how could there be an inference at all?
If it is argued that they too must necessarily possess parts because they originate a large substance, we say no;
for there is no subverting evidence against a partless entity originating a large substance.
Since the commencement of magnitude is possible through multiplicity alone,
and since being composed of parts (sāvayavatva) is useless for the commencement of a substance;
or even if there were parts of the dyad (dvyaṇuka), from what would those [parts] themselves be atoms?
Because they too must possess parts, as inferred from their being the originators of large substances.
If it is argued that an infinite regress (anavasthā) serves as a subverting argument, we say no;
for that regress terminates at those parts or the parts of those parts, which are themselves partless.
And how is this infinite regress a fault?
It has already been refuted that it leads to the absurdity of Mount Meru and a mustard seed having equal dimensions.
If it is argued that it results in the non-production of effects such as jars, we say no.
Because it is only that which possesses parts for which permanence is logically possible;
as it has been said:
"The indivisible [atom]..."
Regarding the phrase "ramāṇute" (*7,460):

having thus refuted the proof of the atom and the dyad through inference, he elaborates upon what was stated incidentally—that it is not tenable for the infinite increase of the magnitude of space and so forth to be established by inference—starting with the words "deśāntara... (in another location).
And words such as "another country" and so forth are like words such as "the horn of a hare."

This region, which is commonly recognized as being delimited by measures such as a *yojana*, is indeed established as infinite through the excellence of the dimensions of space and so forth by means of such inferences as: "This [region] is conjoined with another region that is inherently gross, because it is a region, like the region of the hand," and so on.
These are the terms "another region" (*deśāntara*) and so forth.

The applications of inference that establish [the existence of] things such as other lands function in the same manner as the applications of inference that establish things such as a rabbit's horn— just like the words "rabbit's horn" and so forth.
The point is that, by this very method, even a rabbit's horn and the like can be inferred.
The word "words" (śabdāḥ) is used to indicate that this is merely a verbal assertion and not a valid inference.
Furthermore, the inference of the infinite increase of the magnitude of space and so forth is refuted by counter-arguments.
Rather, [the argument] is that all currently perceived horns possess internal sub-horns because they are horns, like a cow's horn;

and that all sons under dispute are accompanied by other sons because they are sons, like Devadatta’s son—and thus it shares the same logical status as fallacious inferences that establish things such as a hare's horn.
We do not, however, infer an infinity in this manner through the excellence of the dimensions of space and so forth.
This would lead to an over-extension [of the argument].
Rather, a disputed location is composed of another substance that is itself coarse and either similar or of the same class, because it is a location, like the location of a hand or other such parts;
and that [substance] is likewise [composed], and that too is likewise.
In the same way, time is also to be inferred;
however, an inference of a rabbit's horn is not possible in this manner.
This is because that which is absolutely non-existent and unperceived lacks both similarity and commonality with the horns of cows and other animals.

Nor is it the case that there is an absence of similarity and so forth even in the case of space and other such entities because each is a single unit; for that [absence] is established through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Therefore, he says: "And what indeed is similar... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.87ab): "And what indeed is similar, that is, of the same genus, on our side? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.87ab)

Is it not the case that for those who do not accept the infinite excellence of the magnitude of space and so forth in our own position— [a magnitude] which is similar to and of the same class as the admitted [magnitude] of space and so forth— it does indeed occur?
Indeed, it certainly does occur.

Furthermore, since it is already established that the currently perceived location is possessed by something coarser than itself, or by something similar to it, or by something of the same class, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhanatā*).

Moreover, because the infinitude resulting from the excellence of the dimensions of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth is not established, there would be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratā*).
If it is argued that the existence of God (*Īśvara*) and others in the currently perceived location is sublated because of the absence of a connection, we say no.
Because there is no connection even with another location;
by this, the objection regarding sublation (*bādha*) in the case of an inference establishing [the existence of] a rabbit's horn and so forth is also refuted,
since the same principle applies to the inference of another location as well.

Thus, it has been stated that it is untenable to accept that the two types of atoms (paramāṇu) and dyads (dvyaṇuka), as well as the ultimate limit of the increase in magnitude such as space (ākāśa), are known solely through inference, while disregarding their establishment by direct perception (sākṣisiddhatā). Following this, he states—by way of a consequential argument—that even the inference of God (Īśvara), dharma, and so forth, is improper if one disregards scripture (āgama): "yenaiva... [By that very same...].
And by the very same method through which an extremely unestablished thing is inferred,
it would likewise be possible to conceive of the existence of things such as a hare's horn.
By the phrase "extremely unestablished" (*atyasiddha*), he demonstrates a disregard for scripture (*āgama*).

The expression "of a rabbit’s horn, etc. (*śaśaśṛṅgādi*) is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of that which lacks any basis in valid cognition (*aprāmāṇika*). This has been shown in brief here and there. (7.471)
Nor is it logical to claim that these inferences are invalid merely because they are undermined by the counter-example (*pratibandī*) of the inference of a rabbit's horn;
for if that were the case, it would follow that even the inference of fire from smoke would be invalid.
For in that case as well, one could say: "If a mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke, then a rabbit should also possess horns because it possesses the nature of an animal (*paśutva*)."
Now, it might be argued:
"For a counter-argument (pratibandī) is valid only when the two cases share an identical status of success and failure;
otherwise, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)."
Nor is there an equivalence here with the inference from smoke, because that is accompanied by the capacity of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth,
whereas the inference of a rabbit's horn and the like lacks it;
this is equally the case in the present instance as well.
Since even the inferences under discussion possess pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other such characteristics, he says: "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).

Only that which is determined by either direct perception or authoritative scripture constitutes valid pervasion (vyāpti); no other [pervasion] is a means of knowledge, because its foundation is doubtful.
The word "vā" (or) signifies a conjunction; the particle "api" (also) has the sense of adding inference [to perception];
"niyāmaka" means that which apprehends.
Pride is that which is useful for the validity of inference;
it is other than what is grasped by perception and so forth,
and it is doubtful because its root is doubtful.
Because of the possibility of deviation;
for non-deviation is the very root of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the case of coexistence.
In that regard, pervasion grasped through perception is, for example, that of smoke with fire.
That which is apprehended through scripture is, for example:
"A Brahmin must not be killed.
That which is apprehended through inference is, for example:
In the formulation of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*),
this is what is meant:
for it is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, as ascertained by perception and other means of knowledge, that constitutes the basis for the validity of inference.
It is not established by itself alone,
because it is doubtful and subject to deviation.

Furthermore, because the foundations of [your] doctrines are doubtful, and because in the case of inferences such as that from smoke [to fire], the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other factors are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), their refutation cannot be achieved merely by seizing upon a parallel case (*pratibandī*). However, this is not the case for inferences concerning atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth; therefore, due to being caught in the trap of the parallel case, they lack validity altogether.
[Objection: But if there is an absence of pervasion (vyāpti) and so forth, what is the point of employing a counter-example (pratibandī)?
For the lack of validity (aprāmāṇya) is established from that very [absence] alone.
[Reply: True.

If validity were granted even to [cognitions] whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth have not been ascertained by perception and other means, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); or, if they lack validity, the example is illustrated by the taking up of a counter-example (*pratibandī*). Thus, there is no fault.

This is true: pervasion ascertained precisely by perception and other means is what is useful for the validity of inference. And that [pervasion] certainly exists in inferences of atoms and so forth, just as in the inference from smoke.

Since smoke is observed to coexist with fire, and likewise since the properties of being a great whole, having parts, and so forth are observed to coexist [in the case of atoms], he says: "together" (saha).
Pervasion is not determined by mere observation alone.
Pervasion is not determined merely by the observation of smoke and the like together with fire and the like;
for if it were so, then [the property of] being composed of parts and the like would also be determined from [the property of] being the originator of large-scale effects and so forth.
If that were the case, there would follow the undesirable consequence that fire and the like would also be ascertained as pervaded by smoke and the like.
Because even in that case, [the property] exists merely upon being seen.
If it is argued that when no deviation is perceived, the observation of coexistence is the cause for determining pervasion (*vyāpti*),
then is this non-perception restricted to all places and times?
Or is it based on its specific particulars?
Not the first,
because that is impossible for people such as ourselves.

Not the second [alternative], because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). How, then, could there be a determination of pervasion (*vyāpti*)? To this he says: "At the very moment... (*yadaiva*).

For when there is either sense-perception or scripture regarding non-separation, that very [perception or scripture] which establishes the logical connection is the pervasion; it is not something else.
Regarding "non-exclusion" (*avyatireka*), which means the absence [of the probans] where the property intended as the probandum is absent:

if this property intended as the probans were established through a logical argument (*yukti*) as the cause for determining pervasion (*vyāpti*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because that pervasion too would have to be determined by another logical argument, and so on. Therefore, it was said:
"Thus determined."
The word "pervasion" (vyāpti) is to be supplied [from the context].
By this, the meaning is that it is one whose pervasion has been ascertained through either perception or scripture; it is not the other kind, which is based merely on the observation of concomitance.
This is the meaning:
pervasion (vyāpti) is indeed a necessary relation, not merely any relation;
and necessity is the absence of deviation.

Therefore, just as in the case of literary aesthetics (*sāhitya*), even in the absence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) functions;
nor is this impossible.
For, since the failure of inference would entail the collapse of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), that [pervasion] is established simply by the observation of the effect (*kārya*).
The specific mode [of inference], however, is now considered.
In that regard, the connection between smoke and fire is first apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
and no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is apprehended within familiar places and times.
However, when [the subject] has gone to another country or the like, doubt regarding deviation remains; and that [doubt] is not produced by the observation of a sign of deviation.
Rather, even properties observed as frequently concomitant and whose deviation has not been seen have been observed to be deviant.
And this [notion] "this is dharma" arises in such a way.
In that case, if this were of a nature that exists simultaneously with that, then it would exist simultaneously even elsewhere,
because its nature does not depart.
If its nature is to not coexist, then it would not coexist even in this case.
If it were argued that even for that which has a nature of non-coexistence, coexistence occurs in dependence on other causes, then it might be observed here;
however, the groundless suspicion that even for that which has a nature of coexistence there will be deviation due to other causes simply does not arise.
Because it would follow that all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) would cease to exist.

Thus, perception (*pratyakṣa*), when assisted by investigation (*mīmāṃsā*), grasps the connection of smoke with fire and also encompasses the absence of deviation; it therefore certainly determines pervasion (*vyāpti*).
However, the manner of grasping pervasion through inference (*anumāna*) and scripture (*āgama*) is [more] easily understood.
"Only a grasper," etc.

(*7,479*). If it is objected: "By this very same logic, since it is possible to determine pervasion (vyāpti) for [properties] such as being the initiator of the great [substances], how is it that inference does not function regarding atoms and the like?

We say: no, because there is no certainty regarding the absence of deviation (vyabhicāra), since it is possible for the state of being "other than the subject" (pakṣetaratva) to constitute a limiting condition (upādhi).
Now, if it were argued that it does not possess the status of being a limiting adjunct (upādhi), he states the subverting argument (bādhaka) with the words "otherwise" (anyathā).
Otherwise, even the existence of a seventh taste would follow by means of inference; for inference, acting according to its own whims, would lead to all undesirable conclusions.

The meaning is that, disregarding the status of "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) as a limiting condition (*upādhi*), one accepts the establishment of atoms and so forth through inference alone, unaided by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Otherwise,] by such inferences as "taste is sweet, because it possesses the mutual absence of tastes other than the five [tastes] beginning with salty, since it is a taste," all things— such as the coldness of fire and so forth— which are not desired [by the opponent], would follow as logical consequences.
Why?
Because such an inference acts according to one's own whim.

If it is argued that inferences are flawed by the presence of the "otherness of the subject" (pakṣetaratva) as a limiting condition (*upādhi*), since they are sublated by the non-perception of a seventh taste and so forth, then the same applies to the case at hand as well.
Since even [entities] such as atoms are sublated by non-perception,
if you argue that they are unfit [to be perceived],
then the same applies to the seventh taste and so forth.

If it is argued that, regarding the validity of inference, one must assume the incapacity [of inference] to establish things such as a seventh taste, and that once that is assumed, the validity of inference is established— thus resulting in a circular dependency (anyonyāśraya)—
this too is exactly the same.

If it is argued that there is complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a seventh taste and so forth that cannot be experienced, [we reply] that the solution is the same. That "complexity is not a fault when something is established by valid cognition" (*pramite na gauravaṃ doṣaḥ*) is likewise the same for both sides.

Therefore, since you have accepted that atoms and so forth are cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi*), how can you not accept that [the relation] is also cognizable by the witness-consciousness? For, because of the acceptance of inherence (*samavāya*) and because of the resulting parity, there would be an infinite regress. *Oṃ, and because of the acceptance of inherence, due to parity, there is an infinite regress.* Oṃ. *7.482* Because of the acceptance of inherence and because of the resulting parity, there is an infinite regress.
Oṃ. And because of the acceptance of inherence and because of the resulting parity, there is an infinite regress. Oṃ.
Oṃ. In either case, there is no karma; therefore, it does not exist. Oṃ.
Thus is the Sūtra.

Thinking that this will be explained by the very commentary on the forthcoming Sūtra, "And because [the Self] exists eternally," he sets that aside and refutes the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others by means of another reason.
He explains this sūtra—"And because of the acceptance of inherence, there would be an infinite regress due to [its] equality"—with the words "kārya... and so forth.
And indeed, between cause and effect... // MAnu 2.91a //
The phrase "inherence is observed" is connected here as well, as it will be stated later.
By this, he restates in substance the opponents' sūtra establishing inherence: "That from which [the cognition] 'here' arises with respect to cause and effect is inherence."
In this context, the words "effect" (*kārya*) and "cause" (*kāraṇa*) denote the part and the whole, respectively;
the word "and" (*ca*) is intended to indicate that these two terms are used figuratively (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The word "only" (*eva*) indicates that the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) is not established by the cognition of "here" (*ihapratyaya*). (7.484)
He explains this himself [in the following verse]: "Of qualities, etc. (guṇādeḥ).
And [the relationship] of the fivefold group beginning with quality (guṇa) is held to be inherence (samavāya), which is a distinct relation from the others.

"Of the pentad beginning with quality" means of quality, substance, action, universal, and particular. By the word "and" (ca), he conjoins [the pentad] beginning with the possessor of quality (guṇin). Now, one might ask: since the quality, the possessor of quality, and so forth are either non-different or both different and non-different, what is the need for inherence? To this it is said: "of that which is indeed different."
The word "tu" (but) serves to specify:

it is not the case that inherence (*samavāya*) occurs between just any two things, such as a quality and its possessor; rather, it occurs only between those things that are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*).

If inherence were of the very same nature as the quality, the possessor of the quality, and so forth, then no distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*) would be established; therefore, it is said to be "other" (*anya*).
It is indeed asserted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others; therefore, for this reason as well, that system is untenable—this is the remainder of the sense.
This is the meaning:

The Vaiśeṣikas and others, having accepted an absolute difference between part and whole, quality and possessor of quality, action and agent of action, genus and individual, and particularity and eternal substance, further accept a relation called inherence (*samavāya*) that is itself absolutely distinct. Therefore, they too speak what is untenable. *7,486*

But is it not the case that the absolute difference between qualities, the possessor of qualities, and so forth, is established by means of valid cognition, such as the difference in their designations?
Otherwise, there would be no absolute difference even between pillars and jars. And yet, here [we have the expression]: "the cloth is in these threads."

In this cloth there is color; here, in this embodied thing, there is action; here, in the cow, there is "cowness"; here, in the eternal substance, there is a particularity—such is the uncontradicted cognition.
And a cognition of the form "here [is] this" is not possible without a distinct relation, since the cognition "the jujube fruits are in the bowl" is seen to be preceded by conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
And this relation, being between two things that are not established separately, differs from conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
For conjunction is the relation between two things that are established separately,
and it subsists only in substances.

Thus, since inherence (*samavāya*) has been established by valid cognition in this manner, how can the Vaiśeṣikas and others be considered proponents of an untenable position? To this, he says: "If there were difference... (*bhinnatve...*).
Because it shares the quality of being distinct [from them], its connection with those two is certain.
The phrase "due to the similarity of being distinct" is an elliptical expression;
it should also be understood as "due to the similarity of the cognition of 'here'.
[This refers] to that inherence (*samavāya*).
Conjunction (*yoga*) is the relation (*sambandha*) with those two related entities, such as the part and the whole;
this is what is meant.

In this context, one who infers *inherence* (samavāya) on the grounds that the cognition "the cloth is in these threads" and so forth is preceded by a relation— because it is an uncontradicted cognition of "being here," like the cognition "the jujube fruits are in the bowl"— must necessarily accept the following pervasion (*vyāpti*): whatever is an uncontradicted cognition of "being here" is preceded by a relation.
Furthermore, the uncontradicted cognition "it is here" exists in this case regarding the yarns and the cloth;
therefore, one would necessarily have to admit that there is also an inherence of that inherence with both the yarns and the cloth,
yet such is not admitted.
Therefore, in that case, the inference is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Now, is the inherence (samavāya) of the threads and the cloth established or not?
If it is established, what is the use of an inconclusiveness that arises at a later time?

If it is argued that there is no lack of invariable concomitance, do not say so; for what is intended is the necessity of turning back upon seeing an instance of deviation in a relationship that was initially perceived at first sight. *7,487*
But why has the similarity of being distinct been introduced here? For distinctness has not been made the reason [for the argument].
True.
The mention of "distinctness" (*bhinnatva*) is for the purpose of indicating that [the cognition] is not sublated (*abādhitatva*).
Indeed, in the absence of distinct entities, the cognition here would be sublated.

If it is argued: "The cognition that 'herein is the inherence (*samavāya*) of the threads and the cloth' is also necessarily preceded by a relation, because the inherence of the threads and the cloth has this [relation] as its cause," we say: no.
This is because the opponent intends to establish the relationship between the two things perceived as the locus and the located;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) could not be established in the case of "the conjunction of a post and a hawk," and there would also result the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by means such as the contact of the sense organ with its object. *7,489*
How then is the sūtra "on account of non-abiding" (nanv-anavasthiteḥ) to be understood?
It is as follows: if, in order to avoid the charge of deviation, one were to postulate yet another inherence for inherence itself.
Regarding the phrase "then there is no finality":
here, some who declare inherence (*samavāya*) to be perceptible,
explaining the word *yataḥ* as a locative of object (*viṣaya-saptamī*), cite inference for the sake of establishing its stability.
For them, the fact that a cognition here is preceded by a relation means nothing other than being preceded by the cognition of that [relation].
In their view, an infinite regress is manifest.
As for those who do not accept [the relations] as being perceptible, [the regress remains].
They [the opponents] maintain that the relation, by its mere existence, is the cause of the cognition "here" (*ihapratyaya*), just as they hold that the inherence (*samavāya*) is.

Their established position (*siddhānta*) is this; "lack of finality" (*anavasthiti*) is the contradiction of that, and thus the word *anavasthiti* is explained as denoting a "failed conclusion" (*apasiddhānta*).

Alternatively, since the relation is the cause of the cognition "here"—just as in the case of "the jujube fruits here in the bowl"—one must likewise posit a cognition [of the relation], and thus one must speak of a regress (*anavasthā*) in this case as well.

If it is argued: "Since the conjunction between a pit and a jujube fruit is unavoidable due to its inherent fitness (*yogyatā*), its cognition cannot be the cause of the notion of 'here' (*ihapratyaya*);
for while its status as the cause of the notion of 'here' is established by its mere existence, there is no reason to postulate that its cognition is also a cause," we say: no.
Even when a conjunction exists, the cognition of "here" does not arise if it is not perceived due to some obstruction.
Furthermore, it occurs even when there is no conjunction, due to the opposite of that; thus, there is no basis for postulating positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
For even relations such as "owner and owned" are observed to be the causes for linguistic usage based on a connection only when they are known, not otherwise.
If it is argued that these are not true relations because they do not reside in both [relata], we say no.
Furthermore, since it will be stated later that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) also does not reside in two things,
in that case, even inherence (*samavāya*) would not be a relation,
because it is admitted to be non-dependent (*anāśrita*).

[Objection: "If that is so, then [the reason] is not inconclusive; rather, there is simply an infinite regress (anavasthā), because the property of being a non-sublated 'this'-cognition does not apply to that [infinite series], since it is itself sublated. [Reply: This is not so.
For an infinite regress functions as a sublation of the *sādhya* (the probandum), and not as a sublation of the *sādhana* (the probans).
This is because the acceptance of the sublation of the probans occurs only after the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been ascertained through the very sublation of the probandum.
The cognition that "there is inherence between the threads and the cloth" is likewise preceded by a relation; however,
if it is argued that this relation is merely superimposed, we say no, because that would lead to an infinite regress.

For "being preceded by the superimposition of a relation" is simply "being preceded by the superimposition of a relation"; and since this infinite regress has already been stated regarding cognition, how can there be an escape from it?
Furthermore, by speaking in this way, you would be abandoning the view that the relation functions as a cause through its very existence (*sattā*) alone. *7,490*

Furthermore, if this cognition were to occur even without being contradicted merely through the superimposition of a relation, then why would it not occur in the case of threads and cloth as well? Thus, inherence (*samavāya*) remains unestablished.
If you argue that there is a superimposition of what is established in some cases [but not others], and that it is unestablished where it is entirely absent, we say no;
for a relation exists between a post and a hawk.
Otherwise, even in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), there could be no superimposition of another inherence, because another inherence is impossible anywhere.
If it is argued that "it is only difference (*bheda*) that is superimposed upon inherence, not another inherence," we say no;
for the cognition of "here" (*ihapratyaya*) cannot arise by that much alone.

If it is argued that the state of being related through a relation is also superimposed [upon the objects], we say no; for if that were so, then even in the case of threads and cloth, since the cognition "here" (*ihapratyaya*) would be accounted for by mere superimposition, what would be the use of inherence (*samavāya*)?
Now, one might object: even in the case of inherence, the cognition "this is here" is indeed dependent upon inherence itself.
Nor is there a contradiction with one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*) or an infinite regress (*anavasthā*),
because that very inherence (*samavāya*) is self-establishing;
for it is that same inherence which constitutes the relation of the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth to its parts (*avayava*) and so forth.
He raises the following objection—“That [is it]”—suggesting that this very thing is the relationship between the parts and the whole, etc., by way of its own nature.
If he were to be self-sustaining... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.92c //

That [inherence] is the inherence of parts, wholes, and so forth. To this, he offers a rebuttal: "What is the use of inherence? since it is possible for the substance itself to be its own own-establisher; thus he says: "The substance alone..."
Why is it that wealth alone does not likewise [attain such status]? Mānava 2.2.92d.
The word "then" (*tarhi*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis;
for it functions to establish itself.
Why? From what [reason]?
This is the intended meaning:
the cognition that "this is here" does not necessarily depend upon a relation with something distinct from itself,
because in some cases it is self-sustaining.
In that case, one should not accept that even the cognition "this is here" regarding substances, qualities, and so forth, is dependent upon an additional relation;
for that [cognition] is accounted for by the substance itself acting as its own establisher.
Since inherence (samavāya) consists of the nature of a relation, it is self-establishing.
If it is argued that [the relation] is not a substance, we say no; for if that is unestablished, the nature of being a relation is also unestablished,
and it would follow that even conjunction (saṃyoga) must be self-sustaining.
If it is argued that this is not so because that [inherence] is impermanent, we say no;
for the permanence of inherence is unestablished.
Thus, even if qualities and the like were absolutely distinct from substance, no further relation characterized as inherence would be established between them.
It has been stated that it is logical for a substance itself to be its own unifier (svanirvāhaka), as this results in parsimony of hypothesis (*kalpanālāghava*).

Now, with the intention that inherence (*samavāya*) is not established because qualities and so forth do not possess absolute difference from substance, [the author] first states an introductory argument (*upodghāta*) to refute the reasons adduced by the opponent regarding their absolute difference:
Regarding the term "distinction" (*viśeṣa*):

If a distinction—such as its being contained within that [object] and so forth—is determined to exist even in what is non-different, then for what reason would there be a negation of forms such as qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and the like? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.93)
"In the case of non-difference, inherence [is the relation]" is the ellipsis; "is determined" means "is accepted.
"Of the particular characterized by qualities, actions, and so forth" is the ellipsis.
For what reason? For none at all.
This is what is meant:
first of all, in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), its existence as residing in parts and wholes and so forth has already been admitted.
This is because of the statement: "And [inherence] exists elsewhere than in eternal substances.

Furthermore, it is not possible for inherence to have a mode of existence characterized by inherence (samavāya-lakṣaṇa-vṛtti) such that it resides within those [eternal substances], as is the case with non-eternal substances, qualities, actions, universals, and particulars.
Because that [inherence] is non-different,
it must be admitted that what is called "residing in that" is simply the very nature of inherence itself.

If it is argued that being perceived as dependent constitutes its being a property of that [substratum], we say no, because it is untenable for that [perception] to possess the nature of inherence (*samavāya*).
If it is argued that it is a property of that [substratum] because it has that as its object, we say no.
Because even the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*) does not differ from the very nature of inherence (*samavāya*);

likewise, existence (*astitva*), nameability (*abhidheyatva*), knowability (*jñeyatva*), relatedness (*sambandhatva*), and so forth, which are also admitted in the case of inherence, do not differ from the nature of inherence itself.
For their distinction must be explained by means of inherence (*samavāya*);
otherwise, how could these [qualities] exist therein?
And yet, such a relation is not tenable.
Since conjunction, being a quality, subsists only in substances, and since inherence is non-different [from its relata],
we ask this: [what is the nature of their relation]?
If inherence and its properties such as "residing therein" were non-different, how could they be denoted by non-synonymous terms, nor could there be the relation of property and property-possessor,
nor the use of the genitive case?
It is logical that [the object] possesses both knownness and unknownness, as well as unity and multiplicity, and so forth;
for in this case, it is not appropriate to assume [these properties] through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) or other such conceptual constructions.
Since the primary application and so forth are not observed,
[the relation] is not merely inherence (samavāya) as residing in that [substratum], by which it would be untenable.
However, even though it is non-different from the inherence [of the universal], it consists of the nature of that particular;
therefore, distinctions such as different designations are appropriate.
Since the particular serves as the representative of difference, this must be stated as the resolution in that case, as there is no other way out.

And thus, if even though inherence (*samavāya*) is non-different [from its substratum], a distinction such as "belonging to that" is admitted, then qualities, actions, and so forth should likewise be the very nature of the substance itself, existing as specific forms (*viśeṣa*), rather than being merely [entities] possessing the properties of inherence;
for there is no reason to distinguish them by saying that qualities and the like are not specific forms of the substance.
If this is so, what follows? To this he says: "It is indeed a substance."
Therefore, substance itself, by virtue of its nature as possessing infinite particularities, is always the cause for various worldly transactions... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.94a-c]
The meaning is that qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth possess the nature of inherence (*samavāya*) because they are specific types of substances (*dravyaviśeṣa*).
The word "infinite" (*ananta*) indicates as many linguistic usages (*vyavahāra*) as exist in any given case;
the meaning is that these consist of various usages such as differences in designation (*vyapadeśabheda*) and the like.
This is what is meant:
for inherence (samavāya) as their relation is established only if a complete difference between quality and the possessor of quality and so forth is established;
however, such absolute difference between quality and the possessor of quality is not supported by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
For instance, perception is not a means of valid cognition in this case, because [the two] are not perceived together, as is the case with a cow and a horse. Therefore,
the quality and the possessor of the quality are absolutely distinct, because they are denoted by non-synonymous terms.
One must state the inference as "like a jar and a cloth" and so forth; however, that [inference] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to inherence (*samavāya*) and its properties.
Furthermore, [the property of] being denotable by non-synonymous terms is established otherwise even in the absence of difference;

for example, in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), although there is no difference among its attributes such as "residing therein" (*tadgatatva*) and so forth, [its] being denotable by non-synonymous terms and the like must be explained solely through a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) which is another name for "particularity" (*viśeṣa*),
because there is no other possible way.
Likewise, even though there is absolute non-difference between qualities, the possessor of qualities, and so forth, because qualities and the like are particularities of substance,
that [quality] is indeed that very substance.
The specific power (viśeṣaśakti) itself will serve as the cause for linguistic usage such as being denotable by non-synonymous words;
thus, since there is no subverting argument against the contrary position, the logical reasons [adduced] are inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).

Alternatively, by the very statement that "the specific [property] consists in its residing therein" and so forth, the inconclusiveness and lack of probative force of those reasons intended to prove the absolute difference between quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of quality (*guṇin*) have been described.

If, in the case of inherence— which is non-different from properties such as "residing in that"— one accepts specific distinctions such as "residing in that," and if all linguistic conventions are carried out by means of those very distinctions,

then since the reasons for [the opponent's] arguments— such as the difference in designation— are fallacious due to being inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) or otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*), by what reason could one negate that a substance, in its form of qualities and actions, possesses the very nature of those qualities and actions?
(He will do so; it is being done.
That is to say, by what reason will the absolute difference between quality and the possessor of quality and so forth be established?
Revealing precisely this [reason of] being established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*), he concludes: "It is only substance (*dravyam eva*)."
The phrase "like inherence" (*samavāyavat*) connects here as well with what is to be stated later.

Just as inherence serves as the cause for the conventional usage of different designations and so forth by virtue of its nature as specific attributes such as being "located therein," so too the substance itself—such as a jar and the like—becomes the cause for various conventional usages by virtue of its nature as infinite specific attributes such as qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and so on. (7.507)
Now, one might argue that it is possible to refute the logical reasons by accepting that worldly conventions are either metaphorical or rooted in error;
so what is the point of accepting this specific distinction?
It is not possible to do so.
For in cases where [a term] is used figuratively, there might occasionally be conventional usage regarding liberation;
however, it is not the case that the conventional usage of "Ganges" and so forth always applies to a riverbank and the like.
And this is not so in the present case, because qualities such as being expressible by non-synonymous terms exist eternally [in liberation].

Even when "form alone" (*rūpam eva*) is conventionally used for the sake of understanding non-difference— such as in the cases of "the pot" or "Brahman is consciousness"— even then these do not become synonyms,
because they are not experienced as such.
Therefore, the underlying reason for this must indeed be stated here.
