This is what was stated: "always" (*sadā*). If it is argued that it is contradictory for a single substance to consist of infinite particularities (*viśeṣa*), is this a direct contradiction, like saying "the mother is barren"?
Or is it by way of pervasion, as in the case of [the argument] "what is produced is eternal"? Not the first,
because infinity is a specific number.
And oneness is non-difference.
It is not the second [alternative],
for that would only apply if there were the pervasion (vyāpti) that wherever there is multiplicity, there must necessarily be difference.
But this is not the case;
for the number "many" is established precisely by means of a particular (viśeṣa) that serves as a substitute for difference. Thus he says: "infinitude" (anantatva).
... its infinity in particular. // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.94d //
It should be understood that while the substance called Īśvara possesses infinity (*anantatva*), other [substances] possess multiplicity (*anekatva*).
Here too, the phrase "like inherence" (*samavāyavat*) is to be connected; for it is accepted that inherence is indeed one, yet consists of multiple attributes. *7,509*

Now, if this particularity (*viśeṣa*), which is the cause for the maintenance of various linguistic conventions, were of the very nature of the substance itself, how then could it be a "particularity of that substance"?
For being "belonging to that" is pervaded by difference.
Not so;
for even without a further distinction acting as its substitute, it is possible for a particular (viśeṣa) to belong to that [ultimate particular] by means of a qualifier alone.

If this were the case, then another distinction would have to be admitted to establish the "particularity" of that very particular, leading to an infinite regress; therefore, he says: "And the particular... [and so forth].
And that which possesses the distinction is itself [the substratum], just like inherence.
Just as inherence (samavāya) is accepted by the opponent to be inherent in itself without requiring another relation— thereby avoiding an infinite regress—

in the same way, that particularity (viśeṣa), which is the cause for establishing the linguistic usage of "many" in a substance, is itself the qualifier of itself and not through another particularity.
Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. The phrase "like inherence" (samavāyavat) is an illustration; it should also be understood as "like existence and ultimate particulars" (sattāntyaviśeṣavat).
Just as existence (*sattā*) is accepted as being existent by its very nature, serving as the cause for the conventional usage of "existent" with respect to substances, qualities, and actions;

and just as the ultimate particular (*antyaviśeṣa*) is likewise [accepted] as being ultimately distinct by its very nature, serving as the cause for the cognition of absolute distinction among eternal substances—
so too it may be argued.

By me, who accepts the distinction between quality and the possessor of quality and so forth, inherence (*samavāya*) is admitted here for the sake of establishing the conventional usage of "this is here";
and its self-establishing nature is accepted in order to avoid an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
[Regarding] non-difference...
Furthermore, since you yourself accept a particularity (*viśeṣa*) in order to establish that [the universal] is denotable by synonymous terms and so forth,

and since it must possess the quality of being self-sustaining (*svanirvāhakatva*) in order to avoid an infinite regress— given that these two positions are equal, what distinction is there in the position of non-difference (*abheda*) such that it alone should be accepted?
If it is argued that inherence (samavāya) lacks any basis in valid cognition,
this applies equally to the particularity (viśeṣa) as well.
If it is argued that the latter is established through non-synonymous linguistic usage and the like, [the same could be said for the former].

If it is argued that "then inherence (samavāya) is also established by such [perceptions] as 'this is here,' so the case is equal," and if it is further argued that "that [inherence] has been stated to be inconclusive (anaikāntika)," then it is equally the case that non-synonymous usage and so forth are also inconclusive with respect to a pot and a cloth.

In that case, it would follow that even the difference between quality and the possessor of quality (guṇa-guṇin) is inconclusive with respect to everyday linguistic usage and so forth, just as in the case of jars and cloths; thus, the situation remains the same.

If you argue that the distinction lies in the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the difference between quality and the possessor of quality, we say no, because there is likewise an absence of any means of valid cognition for their non-difference.

If it is argued that non-perception through distinction—like [the case of] a cow and a horse—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for non-difference, then the response is that the symmetry of the solution remains: for there exists the means of valid cognition for difference, namely the difference in designation and so forth.
If it is argued that this is refuted by the fact that [the former] is deviant and [the latter] is established otherwise, [we reply:]...
The means of valid cognition for non-difference is likewise of that same nature;
for it too is subject to deviation in cases such as milk and water,
and because its establishment is otherwise accounted for by way of inseparability (*ayutasiddhatva*).
Therefore, since this partiality toward non-difference is not based on a [valid] cause, he says: "It is a conceptual construction."
Because of the fault of conceptual complexity, it is not indeed a separate category of entity.
The phrase "distinct entities" refers to the qualities, the possessors of qualities, and so forth; this is the ellipsis.

Although there is parity between the positions of difference and non-difference due to the acceptance of a specific inherence (*samavāya*) that serves as its own establisher, nevertheless, because of the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanāgurutā*) in the position of difference, the status of qualities, their possessors, and so forth as distinct categories (*padārthāntara*) is not accepted.
"It is accepted that there is indeed non-difference because of the parsimony of conceptual construction.
To the question, "How is there a heaviness of conceptual construction in the theory of difference? he says: "Having postulated..."
Having merely conceptualized the six categories along with their absences,
if that distinction resides in a single [entity], why was it forgotten previously?
The word "only" (kevalam) is connected with both "six" (ṣaḍ) and "in one" (ekasmin).
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "if that [inherence] is accepted as the cause of the various conventional usages in a single inherence."
Why? From what? The meaning is: previously, as a substance.
Of that particularity. *7,513*
This is the underlying intention:

relying on the force of such means of valid cognition as the distinction in designations and so forth, the Vaiśeṣikas and others have postulated that there are exactly six categories of existence (bhāva), such as substance and the rest,
and that non-existence (abhāva) is a seventh.
Furthermore, the properties such as "residing in that" (tadgatatva) which are perceived in inherence (*samavāya*) are not distinct from inherence itself;
rather, it is precisely through the *viśeṣa*—which has another name, namely "essential difference" (*svabhāvabheda*)—that the production of distinctions in designation and so forth occurs therein.

Consequently, since one must ultimately admit a *viśeṣa* that serves as the basis for the resolution of distinctions in designation and the like, it must be stated that the resolution of those [distinctions] regarding substance (*dravya*) is also effected by that very same *viśeṣa*.
The determination of the seven categories (saptapadārthī) need not be undertaken;
or else, just as in the case of substance, even for inherence (samavāya), one must accept a distinction regarding its being located therein and so forth.
And if it is impossible to include these within substance and the other categories, the restriction to seven categories must be abandoned.
If one were to admit difference in some cases and distinction in others without a specific cause, how could there not be conceptual complexity?
Or, in the absence of such a cause, how could there not be conceptual simplicity in the doctrine of non-difference?
As for the argument that there is a distinction based on whether or not a difference is perceived, that will be refuted later.

Here, by the very purpose of demonstrating the two-fold conceptualization in the first half-verse, it should be understood that the necessity of accepting a "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) in inherence (*samavāya*) is also established.
For this reason alone, there is a connection with the word "only" (*kevala*).
For there are only seven categories;

and since it is not possible for those possessing the property of inherence (*samavāya*) to be included within them, they must therefore admit these very [inherence-possessing entities] as particularities (*viśeṣa*).

It is not only because the distinction between quality and qualified and so forth can be accounted for by the particular (*viśeṣa*) alone—without having to accept a difference in substance (*dravyabheda*)—that one abandons the view of difference and adopts the position of non-difference upon accepting a single particular within [the substance], on the grounds that it would involve the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanāgaurava*);
rather, it is also because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*) for the existence of inherence (*samavāya*). *7,517*
For instance,
perception is not a means of valid cognition in that case,
because there is no such apprehension as "the inherence of the cloth in the threads," in the same way as one perceives "the conjunction of the curd in the bowl."
If it is argued that the cognition of the relation itself is the cognition of that [relation], we say no; for such a cognition is not admitted.

By this same reasoning, this cognition of the relation between the threads and the cloth is produced by the eye, because it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance of the [visual organ] and is not otherwise established, just like the cognition of the cloth.

The proof for the perceptibility of inherence (*samavāya*), namely: "This relation between the thread and the cloth is the object of a direct perception not produced by yoga-born dharma, because it is a relation between a thread and a cloth, like the conjunction between this thread and another cloth," is also refuted;
for since the relation between the thread and the cloth and the cognition thereof are unestablished, there is a fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
If the relation were not perceived, there would be no cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "the white cloth."

If it is argued that [inherence is established] because we observe that in cases such as "the one with a staff" (daṇḍī) or "the one with earrings" (kuṇḍalī), [the designation of the possessor] is preceded by that [possession], we say no,
because there is a deviation in cases such as "inherence exists" (samavāyo 'sti).
Nor is it established by inference.
Because the cognition "this is here" has already been refuted,
and because there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the cognition "the absence of a jar on this ground.
If it is argued that there is no fault because [the definition] is qualified by having "mere existence" as its object, we say no.
For even if existence were established as being like non-existence, it would be otherwise-established;
furthermore, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) has not been avoided in the cognition "there is knowledge in this jar.
If it is argued that this [cognition] is sublated (*bādhita*), we say no.
Because no other [corresponding] cognition is perceived.

By this, the following argument is refuted: "The qualified discourse concerning universals (*jāti*) and so forth is restricted to their relata, because it is a qualified discourse that is uncontradicted and has as its object mere existence, like the discourse 'the ground with a jar'";
for [in such cases], one says "the jar is known."

This is because there is a deviation [from the rule] in cases such as "there is inherence" (*samavāya*). Furthermore, the following arguments are also invalid: "These threads are connected to this cloth because they have it as their substratum, like the ground";
and "This cloth is connected to these threads because it is dependent upon them, like grass and other things dependent upon that same ground."
This is because the relationship of substrate and superstrate between the threads and the cloth is not established.
If it is argued that this relationship is established because the conventional usage "this cloth is here in these threads" is established, we say no;
for there is a deviation [from the rule] in cases such as "existence exists here in inherence."

The argument that "the color and other qualities of the ground are connected to the ground because they are qualifiers of the ground, like a jar" is also incorrect, because it suffers from the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the cognition that qualifies the ground.

Furthermore, the cognition "the cloth is here in these threads" is produced by a relation that lacks the nature of conjunction— which is the cause of such a cognition— because it is a cognition of the form "it is here," just like the cognition "the jujube fruits are here in the bowl."

Nor is it correct to claim that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the cognition "there is no jar on this ground," because even in that case, the quality of being produced by the contact of the eye with the ground and so forth exists;

for [that argument] shares the same logical fate as the fallacious inference: "this cloth is produced from a material cause devoid of the threads that produce it, because it is a cloth, like another cloth."

The argument that "form and the other [qualities] possess a relation because they are objects of cognition, like a jar" is also untenable, because it is subject to deviation in the cases of inherence (*samavāya*) and absence (*abhāva*).
If it is argued that this is not so because even in those cases a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is admitted, we say no.

This is because it is not accepted that there is a relationship with something beyond that [object]; or, if it were accepted, it would result in the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (arthāntara) by means of that very [relationship]. Furthermore, the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*) would be absent, and the subject matter would be contradicted.
The claim that "inherence is related to itself" (and so forth) is thus refuted. Furthermore,

this eye is a producer of a cognition of a relation devoid of the quality of being a cognition of conjunction produced by it, because it possesses the nature of an eye (*cakṣuṣṭva*), like any other eye.
"I possess knowledge of a relation devoid of the property of being a cognition of a conjunction with one who is devoted to me, because I am a self, like another self";
"this time possesses knowledge of a relation devoid of the property of being a cognition of a present conjunction, because it is time, like other times"— such arguments [are invalid],
because they share the same logical status as fallacious appearances (*ābhāsa*).
Furthermore, these [alternatives] are rejected because they result in a different meaning (*arthāntara*) due to the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṙyabhāva*), and so forth.

As for the argument that "conjunction-ness (*saṃyogatva*) is excluded from other relations because it is a universal (*jāti*), like cowness (*gotva*)," this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). This is because, as will be stated later, a universal is restricted to each individual instance; thus, a single conjunction-ness is necessarily excluded from other conjunctions.
[The inference] fails because of the exclusion [of the reason] from the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), and so forth.

Furthermore, in the argument "the earth under dispute is connected with this jar, because it is a substance, like space," there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*) due to its connection with other jars.
Even if one specifies "connected with *this* jar," the reason remains inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it applies to a destroyed substance that never attained connection with *this* jar.
If it is argued that even in that case there exists a mediated relationship, then it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*),
because the ground joined with clay is [already] joined with the jar. *7,523*
The argument that "the yarns and the cloth are eternally connected because they are substances, like space" is rejected because the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*).

In the argument "conjunction is distinct from a relation other than itself because it is an object of knowledge, like a jar," if by the term "other than itself" one intends its own mutual non-existence (*svānyonyābhāva*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
Because one conjunction is distinct from another conjunction;
if one intends to express that it is devoid of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyogatva*), then there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).

If this is resolved by means of the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) and so forth, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by that very same [relation].

Furthermore, arguments such as "this conjunction is distinct from any relation that lacks the nature of being a conjunction with something other than itself, because it is an object of cognition, like a jar," and so forth, are to be disregarded, as they share the same logical vulnerability as fallacious appearances (*ābhāsa*).
Thus, since there is a lack of valid evidence for inherence (*samavāya*), the position that [universals and particulars] are distinct is not accepted. (7.531)

Now, it was indeed argued here that even the position of non-difference should not be accepted, because there is a lack of evidence for any distinction; to this, he replies with the words "by which" (yena).
Since by means of this which is established through direct perception all worldly transaction occurs—
through the distinction between existence and non-existence, and without which it could not happen in any way—
what aversion could there be among disputants toward this particular object of observation?

By the phrase "by that which is established through perception," it is understood as "that which is established through perception. By demonstrating, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) exists by means of this and would not exist without it, [the author] shows that worldly transaction has this specific thing as its cause.

It is stated that the impossibility of accounting for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) otherwise is the proof for the existence of particularity (*viśeṣa*), and that if this were not admitted, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of all worldly transactions.
This is the explanation of the term "entire" (*akhila*): [it means] "by way of the division of existence and non-existence, and by way of the distinction between affirmation and negation.
The phrase "is indeed twofold" is the ellipsis to be supplied. *7,532*
[Objection: "But surely, even in the view that [the universal and the particular] are distinct, all worldly practice can be accounted for by the admission of inherence (*samavāya*);

and it can be accounted for even in the case of absolute non-difference by the acceptance of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Furthermore, it would be all the more so in the case of both difference and non-difference.
So why is there a need for *viśeṣa*? To this, it is said: "in some way or other" (*kathañcana*).
What hatred can there be toward such a thing, which is the cause for the maintenance of all worldly transactions? And what is the reason for its non-appropriation?
For the absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed the reason for its non-appropriation;
the meaning is that when valid cognition exists, there is no reason for its non-appropriation.
Lest there be no conventional usage, it was therefore stated: "of the disputants."
This is also an elliptical indication; it should be understood that "and of those who know" is also to be included.
For it is the conventional usage characterized by the expression of higher knowledge regarding specific objects that is under discussion here. *7,534*
Furthermore, since there is a lack of evidence for the distinction between parts and the whole and so forth, one should abandon that [view] and accept the position of non-difference.
Now, it was argued that even regarding non-difference there is no evidence;
to this he replies: "By way of non-difference."
And the cognition of non-difference regarding this category of entities, which begins with cause and effect and ends with non-existence, is determined as being accompanied by distinctions.
Here too, by the mention of "cause and effect," the whole and its parts are intended;
by the word "prior," the quality, the possessor of the quality, and so forth are meant;
and by the word "non-existence," mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is grasped.
Because that very [entity] is non-different from its properties;
or rather, by this [means], both the absence and its properties are indicated and ascertained by the witness.
For instance:

is the cognition whose objects are threads, cloth, and so forth, subsequently determined (*anu-avasīyate*) as being distinct from the cognition whose objects are entirely different things such as jars and cloths, or as being non-distinct?
It cannot be the second case.
Because the denial of dependent origination is untenable;
in the first case, how can it be said that there is no cognition of non-difference?
[This is] by means of the relation...
If it is argued that [the whole] is taught [as distinct], we say no;
for even from the cognition of a jujube fruit in a bowl, there is an experience of a difference [between them].
If it is argued that this is so because the two related entities are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*), we say no.
Because it would be ineffective at the time when [the two] exist in the relation of container and contained,

there would be no perceived distinction between the threads and the cloth, or the bowl and the jujube fruit, even though their difference and their connection are identical; for there would be no utility for the perception of the destruction of the connection occurring at a later time, or for the separation of the connected entities.

Furthermore, the cognition of a thread and a cloth is experienced as being distinct from the cognition of a bowl and a jujube fruit; thus, it is understood that this [cognition of the cloth] has non-difference as its object.
Moreover, prior to the production of the cloth, the threads occupy as much space as they do, and the cloth occupies exactly that same amount of space.
And it is not logical for two corporeal entities to occupy the same location.
By this it is known that the cloth is non-different from the threads.

Furthermore, since a duality— such as [the distinction between] form and taste— is not experienced between the part and the whole, the proofs for non-difference, beginning with this, should be inferred by oneself.
Now, if non-difference is indeed perceived by direct perception itself,
then how can there be linguistic usage such as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions like "the white cloth moves" (*śuklaḥ paṭaś calati*)?
Because that [cognition] has difference as its object, just like the cognitions "he has a staff" (*daṇḍī*) or "he has earrings" (*kuṇḍalī*).
For there can be no linguistic usage that contradicts actual experience; therefore it was said: "as possessing distinctions" (*saviśeṣa*).
It is endowed with a specific object;
this is the meaning: where only non-difference is perceived, there the linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not occur.

Just as in the case of "jar" and "pot," here too, the non-difference that is perceived is perceived only as accompanied by a distinction; and this distinction, acting as a substitute for difference, gives rise to the linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). (7.541)
Now, one might object: how can the cognition of difference, having overcome the cognition of non-difference, produce its own effect?
And if it does so, why should the cognition of non-difference not likewise overcome the cognition of difference and produce its own effect?
This is not so.
It is not the case that linguistic usage occurs merely because there is cognition; rather, it occurs when there is also a purpose.
And the purpose [of such usage] is largely through the practice of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in both worldly and Vedic contexts.
However, when the practice of non-difference is purposeful, that too is indeed observed, as in "Brahman is consciousness, bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam brahma*), and so forth.
Alternatively, it has been stated that the particular (viśeṣa) is established through perception and presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
To the question "How so?", he first establishes its establishment through perception with the words: "by non-difference" (abhedena).
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
The singular number in the term *padārtha* refers to the universal (*jāti*), because it exists; therefore, the construction is: "therefore, that [universal] is apprehended as possessing particulars.
And from this, the following is the meaning:
There is, indeed, a cognition of identity regarding the collection of categories such as parts and wholes;
for this cognition is determined to be distinct from the cognition of a bowl and jujube fruits,
and there can be no cause for such distinction without identity.

Therefore, since there is no other basis for cognition, this [cognition]—arising from the perception of another entity distinct from the differentiated object—rests precisely upon non-difference (*abheda*).
And yet, the linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth still exists.
In that regard, if this [cognition] had non-difference alone as its object, it would not produce the linguistic usage of coreferentiality and the like.

Because we do not observe such linguistic usage as "the jar is the pot," it is known that this [cognition] possesses an additional object as well. Nor should it be said that this [additional object] is a difference (*bheda*).
Even in the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*), a limit must be accepted for the particularity (*viśeṣa*).
Thus, this perception of non-difference, being born of the senses, is determined as possessing a particularity.
As was stated previously regarding inherence (*samavāya*), a particularity must be admitted.
"It is performed"—that is not all;

rather, showing that it applies to all categories (padārtha), he establishes that the particular (viśeṣa) is proven by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for linguistic usage, stating: "The universal, etc. (sāmānyādi).

How can all properties such as residing in that [substratum] be excluded by disputants from categories like universals, even though the underlying entity is one and the same? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.99)
"Residing in that" and so forth mean "residing in the individual" and so forth.
Regarding the objection "How so?",
it is because even though the substance is one and the property is one.
To the question "Why is it not prevented?", it is said: "by the proponents."
That is to say, because it is established through non-contradictory worldly practice.
He elaborates on this very point with the words: "of the effect."

How could there be no distinction between the fact that an effect resides in its respective causes and the qualities (guṇas) and so forth being all-pervasive? There is indeed none. ... MAnu 2.2.100a-c.
There exists, first of all, the property of the whole (avayavin) known as its subsistence in its parts (avayavaniṣṭhatva).

Among qualities, some, such as color (rūpa) and the like, possess pervasion of their substratum (āśrayavyāpitva), while others, such as conjunction (saṃyoga) and the like, have localized occurrence (pradeśavṛttitva);
furthermore, there is the manifestness (udbhūtatva) of color and other such qualities.
All [categories] possess twenty-four types; action (karman) has pervasion of its substratum, non-eternality, fivefoldness, and residence in corporeal things;
generality (sāmānya) also has residence in substance, quality, and action, as well as eternality and concomitance.
This collection of properties of categories is extremely vast, consisting of two kinds.
Nor is it logical to claim that this [collection] is entirely distinct from its substratum;
for there exists the conventional usage of "property," "property-possessor," and so forth.
A cloth does not exist in its threads, nor does a pot exist in a cloth, and so forth.

Since this [distinction] would be untenable if there were absolute non-difference, it leads one to understand a particularity that accounts for itself; thus, how could there be no particularity whatsoever among all entities? (7.546)
True;
indeed, those various properties exist within all seven categories, such as substance and the rest. But are they not distinct from their substrata?

And thus, with the intention that a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) which is established solely by way of being based on that relation is not capable of implying any further distinction among all categories of objects, he raises an objection: "And if that [property] is another... (*sa cet... yadi*). 7.547 ... "And if that property is another... (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.100d).

The meaning is that not only are qualities and so forth distinct from substances and so forth, but that other property— such as "residing in this or that"— is also distinct from its own substratum, provided that it is accepted [as such]. He refutes this with the word "six."
It would result in something exceeding the six categories of existence... // MAnu 2.2.101a //
In that case, there would be an excess of dharmas beyond the six categories (padārtha).
And thus, the restriction that "there are only six categories" would be violated.
[Objection: But surely, even though dharmas are distinct from their own substrates, they are not [distinct from the six categories].
They do not exceed the six categories;
rather, those very same [factors], when serving as mutual qualifiers, are called *dharmas*.
As it has been said: "Even though *dharmas* do not differ from the six categories..."

However, those very same things become both properties (*dharma*) and property-bearers (*dharmin*) in relation to one another; as it is said elsewhere: "Those very same [entities] are their properties when they function as mutual qualifiers.
Therefore, how can there be a violation of the rule?
Not so;
for properties such as "having that as its object" (tanniṣṭhatva) cannot be subsumed within the six categories [of Vaiśeṣika]. To explain:
And it is accepted [in your system] that "the state of being dependent (āśritatva) exists in all things except for eternal substances";
thus, the effect-substance, quality, action, universal, particular, and inherence are admitted to reside in parts and so forth, yet they are not [themselves] substances and the like.
For it is logically impossible for qualities and the rest to subsist [in those categories].
Nor is it inherence (*samavāya*), because its subsistence in itself is untenable. Furthermore, inherence is held to be the relation between that which is supported and that which supports;
how then could that very same [inherence] be both the supported and the support?
Likewise, the pervasiveness of form and the other [qualities] across their substrates is not included among [the categories such as] substance and so forth,
because it is impossible for them to function as qualities.
Furthermore, inherence has already been refuted by the method previously stated.
Furthermore, inherence (*samavāya*) is merely the state of being present;
however, "pervasive presence" (*vyāpyavṛttitva*) must be defined as something distinct [from it].
If it is argued that this [pervasive presence] is inherence in its entire locus, we say no.
Because a substance, by virtue of not being a composite, lacks the possibility of being "entire" (kṛtsna) and so forth;
and if it is argued that non-coexistence with an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) constitutes pervading occurrence (vyāpyavṛttitva), we say no,
because that too must be included within [the aforementioned categories].
If it is argued that this [conjunction] is a non-entity (*abhāva*), we say no; for that will be refuted later.
Thus, the view that conjunction and the like reside in a specific location (*pradeśavṛttitva*) has been rejected.
Furthermore, "manifestness" (udbhūtatva) is not a specific universal (jāti),
because the relationship of higher and lower [universals] is untenable with respect to "color-ness" (rūpatva) and so forth.
For if color-ness were the higher universal, then the manifestness of touch would not exist.
If, moreover, "manifestness" (*udbhūtatva*) were something distinct, then since all color-form (*rūpa*) would be manifest, there would be perception even of the eye and other [faculties].
Furthermore, the number twenty-four is not a numerical category, because it is accepted that qualities (*guṇa*) are themselves devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).
If it is argued that this is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), we say no;
because there is no basis for such a designation.
To begin with, inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*) cannot be the basis.
Because there is no restriction to twenty-four [qualities] regarding substance (*dravya*),
and because it would follow that each individual [quality], such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, would possess that [number].
If it is argued that [the number twenty-four] refers to being denotable by the word "twenty-four" non-synonymously (*aparyāya*), we say no.
Furthermore, this is because the number twenty-four does not exist even in the word itself.

If it is argued that [the universal] consists in being denotable by synonymous words uttered by twenty-four persons, we say no; for this would entail the absurd consequence that the deaf and others could have no linguistic usage regarding numbers in relation to forms and other objects.
In this same way, the inclusion of other phenomena (*dharma*) should also be refuted.
Someone says:
"The category of phenomena (*dharmapadārtha*) is included within non-existence (*abhāva*)."
That is incorrect;
because it is not cognizable by a cognition of negation,
and because, since non-existence itself is not admitted [as a category], its properties cannot logically possess the nature of non-existence.

If it is argued that "non-existence" (abhāvatva) consists in the absence of being devoid of at least one of the six characteristics, such as substance (dravya) and so forth— and not in being cognizable by a negative cognition— that is not so; for if one disregards worldly consensus and relies on one's own arbitrary construction, there would follow the absurd consequence of constructing that substance itself is existence, and that which lacks its characteristics is non-existence.
Therefore, properties such as being established in this or that [particular] must be accepted as being identical in essence (*tadātmaka*) with the substance itself and so forth.

Thus it has been said: "The very nature of an entity (*bhāva*) is called 'existence,' 'knowability,' and 'nameability' according to its different states (*avasthābheda*). Furthermore, a difference in state cannot be defined apart from the particular (*viśeṣa*). (7.557)
But surely, the properties (dharmas) are indeed distinct from the substratum (dharmin),
and thus the aforementioned fault does not apply;
for the Naiyāyikas and others, who maintain the theory of the composition of atoms, do not accept the restrictive rule that there are only six categories (padārthas).

Furthermore, because the category of "dharma" (property) is accepted as distinct [from substance], and since all worldly transactions are possible through the connection with distinct properties, the particular (viśeṣa) is not established by the argument of its otherwise inexplicability; therefore, he says: "padārtha... [and so on].
For even if there were no fixed rule regarding the objects [of dharma],
it would lead to an infinite regress for dharma because of the succession of dharmas.

For even in the position that there is no restriction that categories (*padārtha*) are exactly six, since this [position] would be a source for the non-termination (*anavasthā*) of a property (*dharma*) from the continuum of properties, therefore—given that the non-difference of the substratum (*āśraya*) of the property and the property-bearer must necessarily be accepted—one must accept a "particular" (*viśeṣa*) therein, because otherwise the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of property, property-bearer, and so forth would be inexplicable; this is how it should be construed.
"Mine" (*khani*) means a source (*ākara*). (7.558)
This is what is meant: one who asserts that the category of "dharma" is distinct from substance and so forth must be asked:
does existence and so on also possess existence and so forth, or not?
In the case of the position "no," there is a contradiction with experience;
furthermore, there is a contradiction with one's own action in asserting that existence is neither knowable nor expressible.
Otherwise, it would follow that even substances and so forth lack existence.

In the first case, is that [existence] different from or non-different from its substratum? In the first case, there would be another existence and so forth even therein, leading to an infinite regress.
In the second case, however, the conventional usage of "property" (*dharma*) and "substratum" (*dharmin*) still persists even there.
And since that [distinction] is untenable, it indicates a specific difference.
Furthermore, if the properties belonging to a dharma are non-different from its substratum, then what fault have the properties such as existence belonging to substance and so forth committed,
by which they would be distinguished from substance and the rest?
Because of the equality of acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*).

Therefore, since there is no difference in substance and so forth among those [entities], the establishment of a particularity (*viśeṣa*) occurs precisely within substance and the rest, because otherwise linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) would be impossible.
[Objection: But surely, even within the properties (*dharma*) such as existence (*astitva*) belonging to substance and the rest, there exists further existence and so forth?
And that [non-conceptualization] is indeed distinct by virtue of its basis;
yet, in this way, there is no fault of infinite regress for a dharma because it arises from an unlimited continuum of dharmas,
since there is an absence of any obstruction to its arising or its manifestation.
As they have said: "For they declare that an infinite regress (anavasthā) is a defect because it destroys the root.
That for the sake of which one pursues a series of successive [justifications] is the "root," whether it be production (utpatti) or cognition (jñapti).
Therefore, a conventional usage (vyavahāra) that is established through a distinct cause is not capable of implying a further distinction; hence he says: "Of the universal (sāmānya) as well..."
For this reason, a universal of a universal and a quality of a quality have not been admitted... // MDh 2.2.102ac //
Of the universal, such as "cowness" (gotva) and so forth,
there is the universal characterized by existence (sattā);
and of the quality, such as color (rūpa) and so forth, [there is likewise a universal].
The qualities such as number and separateness have not been accepted [as real entities] precisely for fear of infinite regress;
this is the intention.
For even a universal has not been accepted by the opponent as possessing another universal.
Likewise, a quality (guṇa) of a quality has not been admitted [by you].
It must be explained why this is so;
it cannot be because of a lack of perception.
The existence of "cowness" (*gotva*) and the twenty-four qualities [are established], because the appearance that "taste is distinct from color" is difficult to deny.
Nor is there any subverting proof (*bādhaka*) such as "there is no existence of cowness," by which even what is perceived would have to be abandoned.
[Objection: Cowness is not an existence [in the same sense as substance], because it lacks other lower universals (*aparasāmānya*), just like a particular (*viśeṣa*).
If it is argued that there is a subverting proof (bādhaka), such as "qualities do not possess qualities because they are not substances, like action," we say no;
for [that argument] is non-conclusive (aprayojaka) due to the absence of a subverting proof against the counter-example (vipakṣa).
Furthermore, [the argument fails] regarding the two examples.
And because it lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*).

If existence (*sattā*) were present in "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, then it would also have to be present in existence itself; and if that were the case, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatva*). If this is argued, we say no.
Because it is established that [the self] is a distinct entity.
Furthermore, what will the fact that cognition has the self as its substrate accomplish?
Otherwise, properties such as being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) would not be purely positive (*kevalānvayi*).

Because the exclusion of [properties] such as "knowability" from that very [subject] is due to the fear of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), since that itself constitutes the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
And it has been said: "If it is asked how its own occurrence (*svavṛtti*) is desired, let it be understood as it is elsewhere;
in the case of occurrence, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the refuge, not the state of being different or non-different."

If it is argued that if qualities (guṇas) were themselves possessed of qualities, they would incur the status of substance (dravyatva) due to their connection with the definition of substance, we say no; for another definition must be formulated in accordance with actual cognition. Therefore, one must simply state that a universal (sāmānya) is not admitted in a universal, nor a quality in a quality, precisely out of fear of infinite regress (anavasthā).
As it has been said: "Non-difference, identity, confusion, infinite regress, loss of form, and lack of relation—this is the summary of the subverters of a universal (*jāti*).
Furthermore, an unbounded series of universals and a series of qualities is not the cause for an obstruction to their production or cognition.
And thus, just as that [other instance] is a refutation, so too is this present case a refutation;
for if it were not, then that [present case] would also not be one, and consequently, even universals and the like would have to be accepted as possessing further universals and so forth.
If, however, in some way, the state of being an obstacle to cognition (*jñapti-pratibandhakatva*) were established in that case, [then it would be a refutation here as well].
"In that case, we too shall explain it here.
If someone, out of impudence, were to say:
"There certainly exists a universal even for a universal, and a quality even for a quality, because they are established by unimpeded cognition."

Since an infinite regress (anavasthā) is not a fault when it serves as a cause for the non-obstruction of origination and manifestation, this [infinite regress] is not to be prevented by that logic out of fear of an infinite succession of dharmas.
To this, he says: "And that... (sa ca).
And if that [infinite regress] were not to occur anywhere, then there would be no such thing as an infinite regress.
And that [universal] is also a universal of a quality;
by the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that if one accepts that it is also a universal of a universal, then we say that there would be no infinite regress (*anavasthā*) anywhere.
This is the intended meaning.
It must be stated whether one who speaks thus accepts the refutation of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) or not; for if one does not, one would likewise not accept any other refutation,
as there is no distinction between them.
And thus, one would not be qualified for the discussion.
It cannot be the first [alternative],
because if the non-termination of common properties and qualities is not a defect, it is impossible for even a disputed [non-termination] to be a defect.
Because there is no specific reason [to distinguish between them].
[Objection: Even if there is a similarity consisting merely in an endless succession, that which acts as an obstacle to production and so forth constitutes a fault;
whereas that in whose absence something occurs is not a fault. If this is your argument:
For what purpose should one follow the sequence of "obstructing origination" and so forth?
For *anavasthā* (infinite regress) is a specific type of *tarka* (logical reasoning),
and *tarka* is the adducing of an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasañjana*).
Furthermore, the obstruction of origination and so forth is untenable,
because it would entail the abandonment of what is established by valid cognition;
for origination and the rest are indeed established by valid cognition.
Therefore, since it would not constitute a *tarka* if there were no such obstruction, how could it be a further refutation?
If you argue that being a refutation in this very way leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), we ask:
is it only the abandonment of what is established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*) that is undesirable, or is the acceptance of what is not so established (*aprāmāṇika*) also undesirable?
Not the first,
because there is no regulating factor.
In the second case, how is it that the fault of infinite regress regarding the subject under discussion does not arise?
Because even a succession of entirely distinct properties lacks any basis in valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*).
Now, if the acceptance of what lacks a basis in valid cognition is not a fault,
then the abandonment of what possesses a basis in valid cognition would likewise not be a fault.
If it is argued that "it may be so," and thus infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would not be a fault in any case;
or if it is argued that the fault of infinite regress is a cause for the non-attainment of a result, but not for the non-attainment of a form—[we reply: No.
An infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is a defect only when it is undesirable in form;
however, since it could also be argued that it is not a cause for the non-establishment [of a proof], an infinite regress—even if accepted in some cases—would not constitute a defect.

Therefore, it must be stated that an infinite regress consists either in the abandonment of what is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), the acceptance of what is not so established (*aprāmāṇika*), or an uninterrupted succession [of causes].
For this very reason, there is no over-extension [of the argument].
Thus, since even the succession of dharmas would be non-terminating, one must admit that they are indeed non-different.
And so, by the aforementioned reasoning, because worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would otherwise be impossible, the existence of the particular (*viśeṣa*) is established. *7,570*

Furthermore, he who accepts the difference and inherence between a property and its substratum, while disregarding their non-difference and particularity, must—fearing an infinite regress—either deny the very perception of qualities and universals, or assert that it is an error even in the absence of any subverting evidence.
Or else, fearing the denial of what is perceived, he would face an infinite regress; thus, in trying to join one thing together, he falls away from another.

However, for those who accept both non-difference and distinction, these two objections do not apply; therefore, with the intention that one should thus take their side, he says: "In our own position..."
In our view, the qualities and so forth are indeed possessed by those [substances] specifically;
because they are non-different [from them], there is no infinite regress.

The meaning is: the position of those who maintain a qualified non-difference between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmī). "Qualities and so forth" refers to qualities (guṇas) and universals (sāmānyas); "possessing them" means possessing qualities.
And [the categories] possess universals.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with such cognitions as "the twenty-four qualities" or "the existence of the category of substance," because—
[as the remainder of the argument implies]— there is no difference between the property (dharma) and the property-possessor (dharmin).
For this [succession] consists of an unauthoritative and endless series.

If there were no difference [between the cause and the effect], how could that [succession] occur? Thus, the contradiction with experience remains as before; therefore, it is said: "for they possess it specifically."
"For a particular (viśeṣa) is that which effects both difference and relation.
Thus, the non-difference of parts and wholes and so forth has been established here.
Now, he states the exception—that in some cases both difference and non-difference exist—with the words "difference" (*bheda*).
...so too would there be a distinction [between them] at the time of destruction. // MĀnuv 2.2.103d //

Alternatively, if the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth were non-different from the parts (*avayava*) and so forth, then how could they perish while the parts themselves still exist? To this, he says: "Difference" (*bheda*).
The word "tathā" (likewise) signifies conjunction.
The meaning is that even while the parts and so forth exist, there would be both difference and non-difference upon the destruction of the whole and so forth.
Here, the term "destruction" is used as an illustration.

Where there is the non-existence of the whole while its parts still exist, and where there is the non-existence of the quality while the possessor of the quality exists—in those cases, difference and non-difference [are to be understood], and so forth should be observed.
Otherwise, in a case where the parts, the whole, and so on perish simultaneously, difference and non-difference would not have been stated. This is what is meant.

Even if that [whole] exists, by means of this reason—“because it is non-existent”—is it merely the difference of the whole and so forth from its parts and so forth that is being proved, or is it absolute difference?
In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) and the fallacy of the reason being unestablished in part (*bhāgāsiddhi*). For instance:
Even though there is an appropriator, the appropriated object may sometimes be non-existent,
as in the case of a cloth.
Even though a substance exists in this way, some qualities are non-existent, such as those produced by heating (*pākaja*) and so forth;
likewise, even though a substratum exists, some actions are non-existent, such as the movement of a cloth (*paṭacalana*) and so forth.
Furthermore, there is a certain kind of genus (*jāti*) which exists while the possessor of the genus (*jātimat*) does not exist, such as [the genus] "Brāhmaṇa.
In that case, because both difference and non-difference are accepted, the proof of difference has an already established object as its domain.

"The reason is partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*) because of the absence [of the property to be proven] in the ether (*ākāśa*), in its parts, and in the qualities, actions, and universals such as knowledge that reside in God (*Īśvara*) and others.
This is not the second case either,
because the reason is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
This is because non-difference has already been established and will be further established.
It might be argued:
"Just as it was stated that the arguments for difference, such as the difference in designations and so forth, are otherwise accounted for by depending solely on particularity (viśeṣa)."
If that were so, even while it exists, let its non-existence be established by the qualification itself;
what is the use of accepting both difference and non-difference?
Do not say so.
Because a particular (viśeṣa) merely effects the maintenance of the conventional usage of differentiation, it does not effect its destruction;
for if it were to perform all the functions of differentiation, the particular would itself be differentiation and could not be its substitute.

Furthermore, if there were absolute non-difference between the whole (avayavin) and its substrata, or between duality and so forth and their substrata, it would follow that the substrata themselves would be mutually non-distinct.
To avoid this consequence, a distinction must necessarily be admitted therein.

Moreover, since the domain of both difference and non-difference cannot be subsumed without a delimiting factor (avacchedaka), one must accept that [the quality] exists as long as its substratum exists.

The argument that even in that case, a specific distinction itself will prevent confusion is refuted. Furthermore, the systematic arrangement follows the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not one's own whim;
it will be explained later that the means of valid cognition apprehends both difference and non-difference.

[Objection: But are not qualities such as unity (*ekatva*) and so forth, which reside in impermanent substances, themselves possessed of difference? For they too, being effects of the substance, exist in the moment subsequent to it. [Reply: Not so; for this has already been answered.
For this has been stated:
"The substance of the material cause transforms into the effect by way of possessing qualities.
[Objection: But surely difference and non-difference are contradictory in a single locus?

How then can there be an admission of both difference and non-difference between the parts and so forth, and the whole, its qualities, actions, and universals—which are understood to exist as long as their substratum exists? To this he says: "Only a particular [difference]."
Relying precisely upon the specific distinction...
The connection is that difference and non-difference exist in one and the same thing.

The restriction is for the purpose of excluding distinctions such as those of time and so forth. To the question, "How is the contradiction resolved by resorting to specific distinctions? he says: "Contradiction... [verse 7.577].
...for a specific [rule] is more powerful. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.104b)
The phrase "the powerful cause of differentiation" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Therefore, the logical connection (*anvaya*) is that difference and non-difference exist in one place by relying upon a particularity (*viśeṣa*).
This is the meaning.
For distinction is the cause for the pacification of contradiction;
for instance,
in some cases there is a distinction of locus, such as Devadatta’s presence in Mathurā and his absence in Srughna.
In some cases there is no difference in time, as in the case of Devadatta’s presence and absence at Mathurā itself.
In some cases there is a difference in the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), as when it is said that a gavaya is both similar and dissimilar to a cow and a jar.
And it has been stated that "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) is a substitute for difference.
Therefore, why would it not establish both difference and non-difference simultaneously in one and the same place?
If that were so, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), since contradiction could be eliminated everywhere by resorting to some distinction; to this he says: "dṛṣṭi" [and so forth].
And also by the measure of what is seen... // MAnu 2.104c //
"View and its means of valid cognition"—
the meaning is that the view has become a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabhūtā dṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, the connection is that difference and non-difference are not contradictory.
The word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin [the absence of contradiction] with the particularity (*viśeṣa*).
By accepting that difference and non-difference do not exist by mere whim, the absence of contradiction through the particularity is stated;
the word "eva" (only/just) is used so that there may be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It has already been stated that there exists a perception grasping the non-difference between parts and the whole,
because it is determined through a subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) as being distinct from the cognition of related objects.
Furthermore, there exists a perception grasping difference, produced by a logical reason, which arises even when that [non-difference] is present, because [the former] does not exist [in the latter].
Nor are these two related as the sublated and the sublator, because that would entail the non-occurrence of one or the other; nor are they related as opposites.
Otherwise, there would result an indifference toward both [distinction and non-distinction] on the part of those who practice;
but this is not the case.
Therefore, since both distinction and non-distinction are understood through their respective validity, there is no contradiction between the two.
This is what was stated: "by means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇataḥ*).

Now, one might object: "Granted that difference and non-difference could both exist in one and the same thing at one and the same time through valid cognition; nevertheless, how is the contradiction resolved? To this, he says: "contradiction" (*virodha*).
...how can there be contradiction in the philosophical systems? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.104d)
When there is simultaneous perception, how can contradiction be asserted?
The point is that it is a self-contradiction to say that two things are perceived together and yet are contradictory.
He explains this very point with the words: "For contradiction... and so forth.
Since both contradiction and non-contradiction reside within the scope of perception,
how can wise men attribute contradiction to that which is actually perceived?
Everywhere, the observation of existence through mutual exclusion is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for contradiction characterized by non-coexistence;
whereas the observation of coexistence in some cases indicates non-contradiction,
because no other [mode] is discerned.
Therefore, when two entities characterized by difference and non-difference are perceived simultaneously, how can a contradiction be asserted?
For if they are perceived together, there would be no contradiction;
moreover, if one continues to speak of a contradiction, the resulting logical inconsistency (vyāghāta) remains unavoidable.
By the word *hi*, he demonstrates that the sole means of proof for [observing] contradiction and non-contradiction is seen in cases such as cold and heat, or color and taste.
The word *tu* is to be construed with "but when it is seen" (*dṛṣṭe tu*). The phrase "by the good, by the wise" (*sadbhir vidvadbhiḥ*) is intended as a derisive remark.

For the Vaiśeṣikas and others, having accepted that the specific qualities of conjunction, disjunction, sound, and the self possess both existence and non-existence at that very same place and at that very same time, claim that there is no contradiction because they are observed together; yet, by raising a contradiction despite this very observation,
how can they be considered wise men— speaking in a manner that contradicts themselves, prone to forgetting their own statements, and biased toward their own views?

If someone, out of mere obstinacy, should think that there is coexistence between the two views of being entirely different or identical, it is precisely against such a person that the demonstration of contradiction is made, and not otherwise.

Having stated briefly that difference and non-difference between property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*) exist "in some cases," [the author], in response to the inquiry as to whether this applies to all substances or only to some, says: "non-different."
The Blessed One is non-different from himself; he possesses differentiation only through that which is other than himself.
"Bhagavān" is an indicator for pure consciousness alone.

By means of its own parts, qualities, actions, and so forth, as well as by that which is other than it—the phenomenal world consisting of primordial matter (prakṛti), individual souls (jīva), and insentient objects—difference and non-difference are thus established; the meaning is that they do not, however, have a single identical object.
To the question, "Why should there not be both difference and non-difference with respect to properties that exist as long as the substance exists? he says: "They are eternal."
But all his eternal duties are not at all distinct from us.
The word "tu" (but/then) is used for emphasis;
[it refers to] from this cause,
from this Blessed One.
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "they are distinct from numbers such as duality (*dvitva*) and so forth.
To the question, "Where then do difference (*bheda*) and non-difference (*abheda*) reside?", he says: "in totality" (*sāmastyena*).
Except for those that destroy everything, other phenomena possess both forms;
[this applies] in the case of existence... // MAnuv_2.2.107a-c //
Except for the Supreme Lord— meaning,
in the case of an insentient object—
the properties that undergo total destruction while the substratum itself still exists are of both natures; that is to say, they are both different and non-different.
The term "in its entirety" (*sāmastyena*) is stated for the purpose of excluding [the view of] overcoming [the cause].
Alternatively, it should be explained that even when there is no destruction because the substance is complete and undiminished, those [qualities] are "perishing" (*ucchedinaḥ*).

Why? Because they are non-different at the time of their own existence, yet different at the time of their non-existence; thus, difference and non-difference would occur through a difference in time. To this, it is said: "existence" (*bhāva*).
The meaning is that they possess both forms precisely at the time of their own existence;
for since that which has perished lacks existence, there is no occasion for considering its difference [from what remains],
and because destruction is impossible if there were absolute non-difference from before.
From what [source] are they distinct or non-distinct? To this he says: "They are those very [same ones]."
... precisely because of their annihilation, as well as all others besides them.

By the force of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), those [properties] are indeed of the very nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpa*). Because of their annihilation, while the substratum itself exists, the reason (*hetu*) is non-existent; therefore, they are "other than that" (*tadanye*).
The two words "and" (*ca*) serve the purpose of mutual conjunction (*samuccaya*).
The term "in their entirety" (*samastaśas*) is stated with the intention of referring to that which persists as long as the substance exists (*yāvaddravyabhāvin*). (7.584)

Regarding what was stated—that for a whole which exists as long as its parts exist, there is absolute non-difference from the parts, whereas for that which does not exist as long as its parts exist, there is both difference and non-difference—he says [the following] to show that by this, another objection is also resolved: "Of the part and the whole... (*aṃśāṃśinoḥ*).
For, through the non-difference of the part and the whole, it is indeed the conjunction of the parts [that constitutes the conjunction of the whole].
There is no infinite regress for the possessor of parts, even if there is no final rest in the parts themselves.
For instance,
as for the statement that conjunction occurs partially because there is a connection even in all directions, that is incorrect,
because it would lead to an infinite regress.

For the conjunction of a jar is preceded by the conjunction of its parts, and that [conjunction of the parts] is also preceded by the conjunction of their own parts. Nor should it be said that this series does not find its rest in partless [atoms].

Since it is admitted that the succession of parts is without rest, it follows that if the conjunctions of each preceding part do not arise, the subsequent ones cannot arise; therefore, the rule that "conjunction occurs [only] partially" is untenable. This, however, is inconsistent.

Even if conjunction occurs only partially, and even if there is no final rest in a succession of parts within those parts, nevertheless, because there is no difference between the part and the whole, the conjunction of the parts is indeed the conjunction of the whole;
for this is the intended meaning.

This infinite regress would only occur if our position—that conjunction occurs only partially—were intended to mean that the conjunction of the whole is produced solely by the conjunction of its parts.
But this is not the case;
rather, whatever conjunction belongs to a whole resides in that part.
But where indeed could the conjunction of something partless reside?
Therefore, since atoms possess conjunction, one must admit that they have parts in order for that [conjunction] to reside in them.
For this being the case, there is no infinite regress,
because there is no reliance on an unestablished succession of causes and effects that would lead to such a regress.
This much might be the case:
that there would be a conjunction with the jar;
however, this is also contradicted by valid means of cognition.
Furthermore, the conjunction of a jar would itself be a conjunction residing in the jar;
this is because it contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For [the inference] "the conjunction of a jar resides in the jar, because it is its quality, like its color" [would be contradicted].
"The conjunction that resides in a part of the jar is not the conjunction of the jar, because it resides in something other than that [the jar],
just like the conjunction of a cloth.
This argument, too, is without foundation.
Because the non-difference between the part and the whole has been established,
there would indeed be an over-extension [of the argument] if even a part of a jar were absolutely different from the jar, as a cloth is;
but if there is non-difference, where is the over-extension?
Even for the first inference, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*),
because [the property] exists in the pot precisely by way of existing in its parts.
If one were to prove that it exists in the pot while not existing in its parts, the example would be deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*).
As for the second reason, it is either unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*) or established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*).
If one asks, "If the conjunction with the pot resides in a part of the pot, then where does the conjunction with that part reside?", we reply:
by this very same logic, that [conjunction] resides in its part, and that [part] in its own part, and so on.
And there is no infinite regress in this way, because all conjunctions of parts reside in their respective parts; thus, there is an absence of mutual dependence.
If it is argued that, in that case, a conjunction residing in an atom would also be a "conjunction with a jar," [we reply:]...

Who says "no"? For the conjunction of the parts is indeed the conjunction of the whole; therefore, there is no infinite regress. He explains this resolution of the infinite regress, stating: "In one... and so forth.
If another conjunction were to arise only when one [conjunction] has already arisen, then there would be an infinite regress; but if the conjunction is a single entity, where could that [regress] be?

If we were to accept that there is no resting point in the succession of parts, such that for every conjunction of parts that has arisen, another conjunction of parts arises immediately, then indeed there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). However, if we maintain the position that when the conjunction is one and the same, the conjunction of the whole (*avayavin*) produced by the action resides in its parts, and that there is no other conjunction of the whole apart from the conjunction residing in the parts; then [the fault does not apply].
"Where is that lack of stability?
By this, the following [objection] is also refuted: that which they say—

Conjunction is of three kinds, distinguished as being produced by the action of one, produced by the action of both, and produced by conjunction. Among these, that produced by the action of one is [the conjunction] of that which possesses motion with that which is motionless, such as [the conjunction] of a post with a hawk.
Conjunction produced by the action of both [substances] is the meeting of two things having actions in opposite directions,
as in the case of two wrestlers.
Conjunction produced by conjunction, however, is the conjunction of an effect and a non-effect resulting from the conjunction of a cause and a non-cause.
Just as there is a conjunction of the body-tree [with the ground] resulting from the conjunction of the hand-tree [with the ground],
for there is no conjunction of the body-tree distinct from the conjunction of the hand-tree by which it could be produced by that.
Because there is no evidence for such a thing.
Rather, it is simply the conjunction produced by the action of the hand and residing in the hand that, due to the non-difference between the hand and the body, becomes the conjunction of the body.
For this very reason, practices such as washing the body when the hand has come into contact with something impure are also logically justified. *7,591*
For this very reason, even disjunction produced by disjunction is refuted;
for they describe that [disjunction] as being of two kinds:
from the disjunction of cause and non-cause, and from the disjunction of causes.
Among these, the first is as follows:
from the disjunction between the hand and the tree, there is the disjunction between the body and the tree.
The second is as follows:
An action produced in the thread, which is a constituent part of a two-threaded dyad, effects its disjunction from the other thread;
through that disjunction, the conjunction between the two threads perishes,
and thereafter the destruction of the two-threaded dyad occurs.

Therefore, [it might be argued that] the disjunction currently occurring in the two threads now produces a disjunction of the active part from a location such as space that was previously conjoined with the two-threaded cloth.
In this regard, the first [alternative] is untenable,
because no disjunction between the body and the tree is perceived that is distinct from the disjunction between the hand and the tree.

For a disjunction produced by manual action (hastakarman) becomes a quality of both the hand and the body because of their non-difference; therefore, the disjunction under dispute does not have action as its non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), because it does not reside in the same substrate as the action, just like sound—this [argument] is refuted on the grounds that it is unestablished (asiddha). *7,592*
The second [alternative], however, is even more untenable;
for since the production of disjunction from another thread and from locations such as space is logically established by the action of the thread itself, the postulation of a sequence is unjustified.
Otherwise, it would follow that by the action of a finger, there is disjunction from another finger alone, whereas there is disjunction from locations such as space only through [prior] disjunction.
Is it not the case that the action of a finger produces both the disjunction from another finger and the disjunction from space and so forth,
because those two disjunctions are not contradictory?
But the action of a thread [produces] the disjunction from another thread and the disjunction from space and so forth...
It cannot be so produced,
because those two divisions are opposed in nature— one being the opposite of the conjunction that initiates a substance, and the other not being so;
for it is impossible for a contradictory effect to arise from a non-contradictory cause.
Not so;
for it is accepted that both conjunction and disjunction are produced from a single action alone,
and because it is admitted that the action of a thread produces the conjunction with another thread— which is a non-producer of the substance— as well as the conjunction with space.

Otherwise, one would have to accept that there is also a conjunction produced solely from the conjunction of causes, just as there is a conjunction produced from the conjunction of a cause and a non-cause.
Now, it may be argued that there is no contradiction in conjunction in its own nature;
for a conjunction that is inherent in substances which do not themselves initiate a substance is itself non-initiating of a substance.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds of substances that do not initiate other substances:

those that have initiated a substance, those that are final parts lacking touch, those in a state of perishing, those in conjunction with something in a state of perishing, those whose initiation is fruitless, and those that are heterogeneous. Therefore, it is established that the production of two conjunctions occurs through action alone.
In that case, what contradiction is there even between the two disjunctions?
This is because the perception of contradiction arises from being conditioned by the initiation or non-initiation of the substance.

The action of the thread that produces the disjunction of the two threads does not produce the disjunction of the thread and space, because it is an action that produces a disjunction which is opposed to the conjunction that initiates the substance.
This is because it shares the same logical vulnerability as the fallacious argument: "It possesses an action that produces a disjunction which opposes the conjunction initiating the substance.

If it is argued that there is a sublation of the evidence in the case where one might employ the following formal argument—"The action in a thread does not produce a disjunction from another thread, because it is an action, like an action that is commonly accepted [to produce such a disjunction]"—then the same applies elsewhere as well.
This is because we experience two disjunctions occurring simultaneously.
Furthermore, there is a counter-argument: "The action in the thread produces a disjunction from space, because it is an action.

If it is argued that this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), on the grounds that it is accepted that action is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) when a disjunction is to be produced by another disjunction from space, we say no.
Because the word "janaka" (producer) has the meaning of "non-inherent cause" (*asamavāyin*).

By this, the following [argument] is refuted: "The subject of dispute (the action under consideration) does not produce a disjunction that is either opposed to or non-opposed to the conjunction that initiates a substance, because it is an action.
[And: "The subject of dispute (the action under consideration) does not initiate a conjunction that initiates a substance nor one that does not initiate a substance, because it is an action."
This is because it is fallacious, being similar to the argument regarding the action of a hawk (*śyenakarmavad*), and because it constitutes a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*).

If it is argued that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that "an action which produces a disjunction from space does not produce a disjunction that opposes the conjunction initiating a substance, as in the case of the action of a finger," and therefore the action of a thread, if it were to produce a disjunction from space, would not produce a disjunction from another thread—[we reply]: no.
If something does not produce a division of space-points, it does not produce a division of the substance situated in those space-points;

because of this pervasion (*vyāpti*), if [the action] did not produce a division from a point of space, it would likewise fail to produce a division from another thread—thus there is the possibility of an undesirable consequence (*pratiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, if the division of the thread from space were born of division (*vibhāgaja*) and not born of action (*karmaja*), then why would it not occur for an inactive [thread] just as it does for one that is active?
Because the status of being a cause is equal in both cases;
if it is argued that this is not so because in the subsequent disjunction action is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), we say no,
because once its function is exhausted by the mere production of the initial disjunction, its status as a cause cannot be determined.

Or rather, because the absence of inherence (*asamavāyitva*) is not precluded by the restriction [of the definition], otherwise that definition would be over-extensive (*ativyāpti*); enough with this elaboration.
Having thus refuted the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā-prasaṅga*) on the grounds of it being a quibble (*chala*), he refutes it in another way, stating: "In part" (*aṃśe*).
The meaning is that there is no fault of infinite regress because it is observed that the conjunction of a whole resides in its parts.
To the question, "Even if it is observed, how is it not a fault?", he says: "Because it is observed."
And because conjunction is observed in a part... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.110a]
When the object possessing parts (āpādaka) is perceived, what kind of infinite regress (anavasthiti) would not be a fault?
This is what is meant:
if conjunction were to occur only partially, then there would be an infinite regress, and consequently, the very absence of conjunction would result.
And that [infinite regress] is not tenable;
therefore, one must conclude that conjunction does not occur partially,
because an infinite regress is a logical fallacy (*tarka*).
And because there is a rule that fallacious reasoning (tarkābhāsa) necessarily results in error; ... "What endless regress is there regarding what is perceived? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.110b).
