In this context, what is the meaning of "it does not occur in partial conjunction"? If it means that there is no rule requiring the conjunction of a whole to be preceded by the conjunction of its parts, then we say: "It is so.
That is, if the conjunction of a whole does not subsist in its parts.
That is not so;
for since the subsistence of the conjunction of a whole, such as a jar, in its parts is directly perceived, any conclusion to the contrary is sublated.
The conjunction with the jar exists in the jar itself.
If it is argued that, however, because it is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), it appears as if it were subsisting in a part [of its locus], we ask:
what is this so-called "non-pervasiveness" other than subsistence in a part? If you say it is "co-occurrence with its own absence" (*svābhāvasamānādhikaraṇatva*), we say no.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction because [existence and non-existence] are observed, we say no;
for there is doubt as to whether existence and non-existence are observed through a distinction of parts, or whether it is the jar itself [that is so observed].
For when there is no contradiction regarding the object, it is not appropriate to admit a contradiction regarding the object.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction because of a difference in limiting conditions (*upādhi*),
then what are those limiting conditions?

If it is argued that they are indeed parts, then let those very [parts] be the substrata for conjunction and disjunction; what is the point of accepting parts (*aṃśin*) as existing, which is contradictory [to their nature]?
Since the over-extension [of the argument] has been rejected by means of the non-difference between the part and the whole, he says "If...
to show that this over-extension is also refuted by counter-reasoning (*pratitarka*).
If conjunction does not reside in parts, how can there be magnitude in effects?
The meaning is this: if the conjunction of causes were to reside only in their parts, then there would be no increase in magnitude in the effects produced by them relative to their causes.
This is the underlying intention:
in all cases, the increase in magnitude in an effect relative to the magnitude of its cause is produced by *pracaya* (aggregation).
For it is observed to be so in the case of two layers of cotton;
furthermore, because that [quality] is not perceived in a rope-substance produced from two pieces of cotton lacking accumulation (*pracaya*),
and accumulation is the loose conjunction of the two causes.
Furthermore, looseness of conjunction consists in its occurrence in some parts and its non-occurrence in others;
it is nothing else, for no other [kind] can be discerned.

Therefore, since conjunction does not subsist in parts, this accumulation would not occur; thus, due to the absence of its cause, the production of a larger dimension (*utkṛṣṭaparimāṇa*) would not take place. [Objection:
Let conjunction belong to other things in whatever way it may;
in the present case of the atom, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because conjunction does not subsist in parts. [Reply: No.

Because it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the dimension of an effect which exceeds the dimension of its cause is produced by a conjunction residing in parts known as *pracaya*, and because of the rule that the absence of an effect necessarily follows from the absence of its cause, there exists this very subverting argument (*bādhaka*): if the conjunction of atoms did not reside in their parts, then in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), which is the effect of those atoms, a dimension exceeding the atomic dimension would not be produced.
Is this not merely an undesirable consequence?
For there is no increase in magnitude from a single atom to a dyad. To this, he says: "From the atom... [and so forth].
"The statement that there is no magnitude in the atom (*aṇu*) beyond the atom (*paramāṇu*) is a marvelous claim.

This means that the claim—that there is no magnitude (*mahattā*), which is an excellence of dimension, in the dyad (*dvayaṇuka*) which is subtler than the dimension of an atom—is marvelous, self-contradictory, and contrary to valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Just as one says "this man is wealthy" and "this man is supremely wealthy," the dimensions of subtlety are understood through the very words "atom" (*aṇu*) and "supreme atom" (*paramāṇu*); therefore, the statement denying such [magnitude] is self-contradictory.

Furthermore, because the magnitude of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is understood through inference to be superior to the magnitude of an atom (*paramāṇu*), by virtue of being the magnitude of a substance produced from aggregated parts—just like the magnitude of a two-threaded cloth (*dvitantuka*).
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that only that superior magnitude which is produced from the magnitude of the cause is also produced from accumulation (*pracaya*)?"
Just as the dimension of a triad (tryaṇuka) is not produced by the dimensions of its causes, the dimension of a dyad (dvyaṇuka) likewise is not produced by the dimensions of its causes;

rather, it is produced solely by the number of its causes. Therefore, how can it be argued that in the absence of the aggregation (pracaya) of atoms, there would be no production of an increase in dimension in the dyad? To this, he says: "of the atoms" (aṇūnām).

How can this statement be justified: "Even in a triad (tryaṇuka), that [largeness] occurs without regard for the largeness of atoms, and even in an atom, there is largeness without [the accumulation of parts]"? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.111c–f)
The meaning is as follows: how can this statement be consistent—that the excellence of dimension in a triad arises from mere number alone, without depending on the excellence of dimension in dyads;
and likewise, that the excellence of dimension in a dyad arises from number alone, without the excellence of dimension in an atom?
This is because [the example] "like the large and the long" has already been refuted.
The two words "ca" and "api" signify mutual conjunction (*itaretara-samuccaya*).

Here, although it would have been sufficient to mention merely "dimension" (*parimāṇa*), the use of the terms "breadth" (*prathimā*) and "greatness" (*mahattva*) is intended to remind us of the refutation of the cause for disregarding dissimilar dimensions. He clarifies what was stated—that there is absolute non-difference between part and whole, as well as difference-and-non-difference—by saying: "of the whole" (*aṃśinaḥ*).
This non-difference [of the whole] from its parts is real; however, there is difference and non-difference with respect to each individual part.

Just as there is absolute non-difference between the parts and the whole—such as the sky and so forth—which exists in all its constituent parts, so too there is absolute non-difference between the whole, such as a cloth, and all its parts; however, with respect to each individual part, there is both difference and non-difference.
This is connected to the subsequent sentence beginning with "this.
But [an objection may be raised]: is this not improper?
Even when all the threads are present, there are times when the cloth is absent;
furthermore, since both difference and non-difference are admitted when it is torn apart,
therefore, by means of each individual [thread], both the difference and non-difference of the cloth are accumulated by all of them as well.
And so it has been said in the *Brahmatarka*:
"To whom has a cloth ever appeared directly as something other than its threads?
If it were non-different [from them], then in the absence of the threads, how could there be an absence of the cloth?"
It is said:
for it is understood that the threads are distinguished by their interconnection;
and as long as they exist, there is never an absence of the cloth.

Therefore, since the cloth is absolutely non-different from all the threads characterized by a specific interlacing (*vyatiṣaṅga*), there is no contradiction whatsoever in saying that when the interlacing is not intended to be expressed, the cloth is both different and non-different from all the threads.
[Objection: But if that is so, then since the cloth does not exist apart from the interlaced threads, would this not result in the doctrine of a mere heap of atoms (*paramāṇupuñjavāda*)?
Not so;
for just as qualities do not exist apart from a substance,
yet a substance is not devoid of qualities.

And just as others maintain that there is no non-existence [of a cloth] even though existence (*sattā*) does not exist as something distinct from the commonality (*sāmānya*) and so forth, so too it is the very threads interwoven that are the cloth; nevertheless, there is no absence of the cloth.
Rather, when the threads are interwoven, both the threads and the cloth exist.
And that [universal] is not distinct from them.
If it is asked how this is so, we reply: it is by virtue of its specific capacity (*viśeṣa-śakti*). *7,616*
But surely, even though the cloth is distinct from all the interlaced threads, its difference [from them] must be admitted, because the cloth arises only after the interlacing of the threads.
And how can there be non-difference with each individual thread, given that the cognition of "cloth" does not occur in relation to each one? To this, he says: "All... (sarva...).
For how indeed can that which is the object of everyone's direct perception be set aside?
This point has already been stated, since it is an object of direct perception for everyone; therefore, how can it be set aside?
This is what is meant:
there is indeed a direct perception of the non-difference between the cloth and the threads that are interwoven.
This is because the difference between the cognition of that [non-duality] and the cognition of two related entities is established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*);
furthermore, there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for difference,
by which it too might be accepted.
Granted that a cloth is said to arise from the interlacing of threads;
however, it is a specific form of the threads that exists when they are so interlaced. Furthermore, upon the removal of each individual thread, there is no such thing as "all the threads" remaining.
Therefore, even in that case, there is indeed the cognition of non-difference;
however, the absence of the cognition of a "cloth" in each individual [thread] implies difference, but it does not subvert the non-difference established by perception. *7,621*
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"The non-difference of the whole (avayavin) and so forth from their parts (avayava) and so forth is not tenable;
for the whole is one, whereas the parts are many."
If there were no difference [between the whole and its parts], it would follow that either the parts themselves are non-different or the whole is differentiated.
Likewise, some qualities reside in many;
for instance, a single instance of conjunction exists between each pair of two things.
Likewise, manifestation through division is also [of two kinds]. And number is twofold, due to the distinction between oneness and manifoldness.
In that regard, although oneness resides in a single substance, duality and so forth reside in many;
likewise, separateness is also of two kinds:
separateness from one and separateness from many.
In that regard, although singularity-of-separateness (ekapṛthaktva) resides in a single substance, duality-of-separateness (dvipṛthaktva) and so forth reside only in multiple substances.

And thus, if the qualities were identical with the possessor of the quality (guṇin), it would follow that there is either no distinction between the multiple substances that serve as the substrata for conjunction and so forth, or else there would be a distinction between the conjunctions themselves.
A universal (*sāmānya*) is one and resides in many;

if there were no distinction between its manifestations (*vyakti*), it would follow that either the manifestations themselves are not distinct, or else the universal itself must be divided. Therefore, since conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), and individuality (*pṛthaktva*) do not reside in many [simultaneously], he says:
"And conjunction, as well as disjunction and individuality, are each distinct. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.113ab)
"Differentiation" (bheda) means distinctness (pṛthaktva). The word "and" (ca) indicates mutual conjunction (itaretarayoga).
The meaning is that they are each individually dependent upon their respective substances.

Furthermore, if there were non-difference [of qualities] due to a single quality, there would also be non-difference between the two substances; thus, the reason that brings about this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*).

It has been stated that the objection—that if a quality were non-different from multiple substances, the quality itself would have to be divided—is a consequence of what is already accepted (*iṣṭāpatti*).
Now, one might object: "The differences between the conjunctions and disjunctions of a jar and a cloth are experienced as being related to the jar and the cloth."
In that case, how can they each depend on one another?

And if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence that the cognition of conjunction and so forth would occur with respect to each individual [atom] alone. To this, he says: "mutually" (*anyonya*).
For it is observed that both [the father and the son] stand in a relationship of mutual opposition.
*Pratiyoga* means the state of being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*).
*Anyonyapratiyoga* is the counter-correlation of one with another.
That conjunction or other relation which is observed in both [entities] occurs precisely by way of the causal condition of mutual counter-correlation.
In this context, the phrase "of both" is an illustration for many [cases],
because difference is also perceived as being related to many things.
This is what is meant:
Conjunction and the like, having the jar as their counter-correlative, exist in the cloth;
likewise, [conjunction] having the cloth as its counter-correlative exists in the jar.
Therefore, it is logical that there is a manifestation through the relation of both, and that no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) occurs. *7,625*
This might be so if there were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of conjunction and the others as subsisting in each individual [locus];
but that very thing does not exist. Therefore, he says: "mutually," etc.
The phrase "separately, indeed" (pṛthak pṛthageva) is understood to carry over.
For, by reason of their mutual opposition, conjunction and so forth are seen to belong to both [entities] separately indeed.
This is the meaning.

When it is perceived that "the cloth is conjoined with the pot," "separated from the pot," or "different from the pot," the property of the cloth—namely conjunction and so forth—is perceived as having the pot as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
And that which has something as its counter-correlate is not a property of that thing;
for example, posteriority (*aparatva*) having an elder as its counter-correlate is not a property of the elder.
Therefore, this conjunction and so forth is not a property of the jar.
Likewise, conjunction and so forth, being perceived as having the cloth as its counter-correlate when it is a property of the jar, cannot be a property of the cloth.
Thus, conjunction and so forth are understood to be distinct properties belonging to each [individual] object in various ways. *7,626*
Granted, let this be the case regarding conjunction and disjunction;
but it is not so for separateness (*pṛthaktva*).

For that which is perceived as being mutually correlative—such as "the cloth is separate from the jar" and "the jar is separate from the cloth"—that single separateness is admitted to be distinct in each instance.

As for the cognition that "these two are distinct" or "these are distinct," that [cognition] refers to a plurality of separateness (*aneka-pṛthaktva*) residing in multiple substrates; for there is no evidence that it resides in a single substrate when it is not defined by a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Therefore, he says: "distinct."
For a collection of distinct things is indeed perceived as "divided," just as [the distinction] among objects is perceived... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.114a-c //
In the cognition "these are distinct" and so forth, plurality—the collection of distinctions—is indeed observed.
How?
Just as it is with respect to objects.
This is what is meant:
just as in the cognition "these cloths are white" and so forth, many cloths and many instances of the quality whiteness appear as qualifiers,
so too in the cognition "these are distinct" and so forth, it must be admitted that many objects and many distinctions manifest.
Furthermore, there is no specific authority by which another rule might apply here;
by this, the cognition that "these two are conjoined" and so forth should also be understood as explained. *7,628*
Now, if it is argued that the distinction between these two is perceived as "the distinctness of these," whereby a distinctness (pṛthaktva) residing in multiple substrates is apprehended—
how can this be so?
Do you take as your authority the appearance of the multiple as the locus (dharmin) in this case?
Or [is it] the appearance of the oneness of dharma, or the appearance of both?
To all three positions, he states the reply: "Of these two..."
...and also [the distinction] between these two. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.114d)
From this [state] to that, and from that to this, a distinction characterized by two properties is observed. (2.115ab)
In this perception as well, a difference characterized by two relata is observed, such that "the difference of this cloth from that jar" or "the difference of that jar from this cloth.

Thus, even though there are multiple relata (*dharmin*), since it is not admitted that the property (*dharma*) appears as a single entity, it is stated that the intended object is not established by this [perception].
By this very [argument], the perception "this is the conjunction of these two," and so forth, should also be understood as explained.
Indeed, words and grammatical markers reflect the intention of the speaker;
and here, the singular number is employed in the word "difference" (*bheda*).
By this, it is inferred that in this cognition, only a single difference characterized by two properties is perceived.
Therefore, it cannot be said that the cognition has as its object multiple differences residing in multiple substrates that are mutual counter-correlatives; hence he says: "In that case" (tatra).

In that context, the singular number is used just as in the expression "the feeding of Brahmins. This refers either to the phrase beginning with "there is a distinction between these two," or to the two types of distinctions.
The singular number in "food" (*bhojanam*) means "in whatever manner [it may be].

By this singular number, it is stated that the inference—that because the cognition [of the word] has a single object as its domain—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and that it is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*) by virtue of having a composite whole (*samudāya*) as its domain;
for there is no fault even if the possessor of parts (*avayavin*) is a single entity.
Just as space is non-different from its own parts, the non-difference of the parts themselves is also accepted;
and that very same collection of threads by which the cloth is said to be absolutely non-different is indeed one,
for it is the specific form of those interwoven threads.
Furthermore, because it is adventitious (*āgantuka*), it is both distinct and non-distinct from the threads.

Although it is non-different from each individual thread as well as from all of them together, since distinction also exists [between them], there is no consequence of their being mutually non-different; this should be inferred by oneself, so it has not been explicitly stated.
[Objection: If that is the case, then one should not say that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like are dependent on each individual [substance].
"Because the objection and its resolution were stated precisely through the distinction and non-distinction [of the quality] by virtue of its persisting as long as the substance exists.
True;
nevertheless, there is no fault, for this is merely a statement of the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*).
Furthermore, this meditative absorption (samādhi) is not possible in the absence of conjunction (saṃyoga).
If it is argued that such conjunction does not exist because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for it, we say no;
for the conjunction of an atom with space and so forth is accepted [in our system].
If it is argued that this [sound] is also produced by the action of atoms, no;
for that would entail the consequence of its prior non-existence [as a composite].
If it is argued that this is not so because of the distinction between parts, no.
Because an intrinsic [connection] is not admitted,
and because a connection based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*) will be refuted later;
furthermore, space is conjoined with the Lord because it is a substance, like a jar.
Nor is "corporeality" (mūrtatva) a valid limiting adjunct (upādhi), because the qualification would be redundant;
it is sufficient simply by virtue of possessing a limited dimension (paricchinnaparimāṇavattva).
Indeed, the qualification "limited" (paricchinna) is entirely superfluous.
If it is argued that "space is not conjoined with Īśvara because it is formless, like color," we say no;
for "not being a substance" is the limiting condition (*upādhi*). Now, he states that generality resides in each individual: "non-existence and so forth."
In this same way, the state of being human and so forth [is attained]. // MĀnuv 2.116a //
The meaning is that [the universal] resides in each individual, just like conjunction and so forth.

Although it could have been stated simply as "the universal also," the term "humanity and so forth" was used to indicate that a solution is also possible there by virtue of [universals] such as Brahminhood not persisting for the duration of the substance. Furthermore, since the demonstration is not of a single kind, there is a division of the yoga (compound).
From where [is it known] that human-hood and so forth differ with respect to each individual? To this he says: "tattad" (that respective...).
...is understood as such by virtue of its respective nature.

For just as when humans are perceived, their specific form and so forth are perceived as restricted [to them], so too humanity and the like are understood and seen precisely as restricted properties belonging to each respective [individual]; thus it is called "perception" (*pratyakṣa*). Alternatively, a property that depends on many [instances] is not perceived in the cognition of each single [instance].

Just as duality and so forth [are not perceived in each individual instance], human-ness (*naratva*) and the like are likewise perceived in each single perception; therefore, he indicates by this that they are not inclusive (*anugata*).
Furthermore, human-ness and the like do not persist across multiple instances, because they are properties (*dharma*), just like color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
He provides a refutation of this view: "No."
There is not a single dharma that exists... // MĀnuv 2.116c //
All phenomena possess the property of having multiple modes of occurrence;

therefore, the nature of being a phenomenon (*dharmatva*) does not have its pervasion violated—this is the remainder [of the argument]. Furthermore, the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is indeed manifest.

Indeed, the number "plurality" (anekatva-saṃkhyā) must reside in many [entities], because it is impossible even to suspect its existence in each individual [entity], such as in the case of duality and so forth.
For duality and so forth are not perceived in the cognition of each individual [object],
nor are they defined by their counter-correlates (*pratiyogi*),
since multiple objects are experienced precisely as subjects (*dharmin*).
Therefore, because of this reason of being a property (*dharmatva*), there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) in that case; hence he says: "But the aggregate... (*samudāyas tu*).
But the aggregate consists of distinct elements.
A collection (*samudāya*) is plurality (*anekatva*); it is distinct [from its parts] and resides in many [substrata].
True plurality as a numerical category (*saṃkhyā*) likewise resides in many;
nevertheless, there is no fault because the reason is qualified by being other than that [collection], such is the intended meaning.

And since that [cognition] is produced by a comparative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), it does not persist as long as the substance itself; being both distinct and non-distinct, there is no consequence of the identity of the two substrates.
The Prābhākaras, however, say:
"Similarity (*sādṛśya*), moreover, is a single entity that inheres in many."

In that case, there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the reason of "being a property" (*dharmatva*). Nor should it be argued that similarity is simply a universal (*sāmānya*), and therefore this objection regarding deviation in the subject (*pakṣa*) is untenable;
for that would entail the undesirable consequence of a confusion of universals (*jātisaṅkara*).
For indeed, there exists a similarity between certain horses and donkeys.
In that regard, if similarity were something other than the nature of being a horse (*aśvatva*), then all horses would possess similarity with donkeys;
and if it were something else [distinct from both], then the nature of being a horse would also exist in the individual donkey.
The same should be said regarding the nature of being a donkey.
We do not say that similarity resides in horses and donkeys; rather, we say it resides in their parts.

For we accept that similarity—residing in substances, qualities, parts, and actions—is indeed nothing other than a universal (sāmānya); therefore, there is no fault of confusion between universals (jāti-saṅkara). If this is argued, we reply: no.

Because common usages such as "the cow is similar to the gavaya" would otherwise result in being non-primary (amukhya), and because a universal (*sāmānya*) is not defined by its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), whereas similarity (*sādṛśya*) is so defined, the distinction between these two is clear; therefore, he says: "And such [as this]... (*etādṛśaṃ ca*).
And such similarity exists individually among various objects.

Let it be granted that similarity (*sādṛśya*) is distinct from the universal (*sāmānya*); nevertheless, it exists separately in each of those objects, and thus there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason "being a property" (*dharmatva*).
The phrase "of such a kind" refers by extension to the reason stated therein.

For there is no proof for the existence of similarity as residing in multiple things, since its occurrence is established in this way: "this is similar to that," or "these two are white," and so forth.

Furthermore, [the expression] "the similarity of these two" and so forth is justified by the understanding that "this has similarity with that" and "that has similarity with this. Moreover, the use of the singular number is appropriate— as in the case of "the feeding of the Brahmins"— and because it is impossible for the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) to function as the locus (*dharmin*).

And because, even though [the universal] resides in a single [individual], it is defined by its counter-correlate (pratiyogin), it is possible for it not to be perceived even when each individual is perceived.
Regarding the view that the universal such as "humanity" (naratva) differs with each individual, he states another inference: "In one... (*ekasmin*).
For even when one [instance] has perished, it is perceived elsewhere.
When one person has perished, the "human-ness" (naratva) dependent upon him is indeed destroyed;
nevertheless, that dharma characterized as human-ness is still observed in another person. Therefore, it is connected with what was stated [in the verse]: "human-ness and so forth.
Alternatively, "savināṣṭam" means that which exists together with destruction (*vināśa*); that is to say, in that which possesses destruction.
Alternatively, the construction is: "that which has perished along with its substratum is 'perished-in-that'.
The formal argument here is as follows:
human-ness, when residing in a substrate that is both destroyed and not destroyed, possesses differentiation because it is the locus of contradictory properties, like shadow and sunlight.
Nor is the reason unestablished; for while humanity, whose basis has perished, is destroyed,
that which is other [than it] is not destroyed, since it is observed to exist.

This [argument] would hold true if the nature of being human (*naratva*) were to perish even when it is based on a perished person— just as a pot [differs from its material cause] because it is not destroyed—
or if that nature of being human were to differ from the non-perished state of being human because it is destroyed, like a pot.
(*8,12*) This would be so if the nature of being human, even when residing in a perished person, were itself to perish.
This is not the case because that [nature] is eternal; therefore, he asks: "Why? (kutaḥ).
How can one who has attained the state of ashes be expected to regain human form again?
The continued existence of humanity (naratva), even when residing in a person who has perished, is not without proof, because it is established by direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Humanity, as residing in both persons who have perished and those who have not, is indeed one;
and that [humanity] is perceived again in a person who has not perished.

For this very reason, even inference has its object sublated; therefore, he says: "In the case of oneness... (*ekatve*) // MAnu 2.2.118c // "And there is no means of knowledge for oneness... (*nāsti mānaṃ ca*).
It might be so if there were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the identity of these two;
however, such does not exist—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not a valid means of cognition.
Because its nature as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is itself doubtful;
and by the word "and" (*ca*), he combines [this] with the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*).
For if there were oneness, then again—of that—
"The establishment of the substance [sattva] follows from the establishment of that [the universal], and from the establishment of that, the establishment of oneness [of the substance] follows.
Having thus stated the perception and inference regarding the difference of universals and so forth in each respective substratum, he also cites scripture, saying: "Scripture also..."
...the Śruti also says with reverence: [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.118d]
All things, though distinct and possessing distinct properties,
are nonetheless non-different from their own respective properties and from their own essential natures in every respect.
But phenomena whose destruction has not yet ceased possess both forms;
therefore, the Blessed One is not distinct from his own qualities.
Thus... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.121a]
He says: the ellipsis is "the distinction of universals (sāmānya) and so forth with respect to each substratum.
They are distinct, meaning they possess mutual difference.
Those things whose properties (dharma) are mutually distinct are called "distinct in their properties" (bhinnadharma).
To dispel the doubt that by the phrase "having distinct properties" a distinction based on their substrata (*āśraya*) is also implied, it was stated: "by their own [properties]."

Just as the Blessed One [appears] through his own forms such as the Fish and others, they are non-different from their respective attributes; this is the exception to the rule that [the substrate] does not cease. Those whose destruction occurs even while the substrate has not ceased are described as such.
Just as the blackness of an unbaked jar and so forth are both distinct and non-distinct from it;
[the scripture] concludes its own subject matter with the words, "not by anything."
In this context, respect [for the teaching] is understood from such statements as "in every way" (*sarvaśas*) and from the aforementioned explanation.
Now, when a substance such as a jar, which has water as its constituent, is connected with fire, then—
either through the impact of the fire or through its impulsion— [the qualities] arise in the atoms that constitute it.
Actions arise;
from them come disjunctions, and from disjunctions come the destructions of conjunctions.
A product-substance perishes due to the destruction of its conjunctions.
When that [substance] has vanished, through the conjunction of fire with the atoms, there occurs the destruction of qualities such as blackness, depending upon heat.
Then, from another conjunction with fire, depending upon heat, qualities produced by cooking (*pākaja*) arise.

Immediately thereafter, when actions arise in atoms due to the production of qualities born of heating (*pākaja*) resulting from the conjunction of the self and the atoms—dependent upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) of sentient beings—a causal substance is produced through their mutual conjunction in the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth;
and therein, the production of color and other qualities occurs through the process of the qualities of the causes.
How, then, can it be said that the blackness of an unbaked jar and such qualities persist as long as the substance itself exists?
Not so;
for there is no evidence for this. The production of action upon the occurrence of impulsion and so forth is the evidence [for this].
There are divisions during actions;
in those [divisions], there is the cessation of the prior conjunction;
therein, there is the destruction of the effect-substance.
And in that case, the transformation of the prior form and so forth,
as well as the subsequent arising of another form and so forth, is the proof for the production of a gross substance;
it [occurs] within the series of its constituent parts.
That [conjunction] occurs in the dyad; its production is due to the conjunction of atoms, and that [conjunction] arises from their action.
That [existence] resides in that series of parts; that [series of parts] resides in that [series of parts];
that [existence] resides in the dyad.
If it is argued that their production occurs through the conjunction of atoms, and that conjunction occurs through the action of those atoms,
which in turn arises from the conjunction of the self with one who possesses unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), we say no.
For it is possible that, just as in the case of atoms, in effect-substances there occurs the cessation of the previous color and so forth and the arising of new color and so forth.

[Objection: The color and other qualities of an earthy composite substance perish solely due to the destruction of their own substratum, because they are the color and other qualities of a composite substance, like the color of a burnt cloth;
and they arise from the qualities of the causes alone, for exactly the same reason and in exactly the same way. [Response: This is not so.
In some cases, even when there is a real substratum, there is no contradiction between the destruction of [qualities] such as color and their being produced by contact with fire;
otherwise, one could also argue that "an effect-substance perishes solely from the destruction of its conjunction, because it is an effect-substance, like a dyad (dvyaṇuka)," and so forth.
Now, does the contact with fire exist in all parts or not?
If it does not, then the destruction and production of color and other qualities would be impossible therein;
and thus, there would be a difference in the color and other qualities between the part and the whole.
If it is argued that in the first case, the destruction of the whole (avayavin) is unavoidable because the particles of fire enter everywhere,
[we reply] that this is possible because composite substances have pores through which entry occurs;
furthermore, since there is no loss of the configuration (saṃsthāna), the destruction of the whole is untenable.
"Because it is precisely such [a case] that has been cited; enough [of this].
Thus, the existence of a universal residing in multiple instances has been refuted by means of proofs.
That is incorrect.
Because there exists a subverting argument against its existing as multiple occurrences.

For instance: if a single, pervasive universal of "cowness" (*gotvasāmānya*) did not exist in all individual cows, then there could be no linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*), characterized by the grasping of the connection between the word "cow" and its referent, with respect to them.
For linguistic proficiency arises through the instruction of the usage of elders and the like; yet such usage does not exist for every individual object, because,
due to their infinity, it would follow that a person's entire lifespan would be exhausted merely in the process of acquiring proficiency.
Therefore, linguistic proficiency and usage would occur only where there is instruction and so forth.
Alternatively, one might grasp the convention— that is, the application of the word "cow"— to another individual cow even without a single cause, despite the absence of instruction and the like.
In that case, why would it not also apply to a lump of horse-flesh?
There is no distinction [between the two].
However, this fault does not arise once the universal "cowness" (gotva) has been understood through instruction and other means as the basis for the application of the word "cow" (gośabda).
Therefore, since it is otherwise impossible to grasp the connection of a single word to multiple [individuals], one must necessarily admit a single, recurring [universal].
[Objection: But how, then, is the connection of words such as "element" (*bhūta*) or "corporeal" (*mūrta*) grasped with respect to earth and so forth, which are devoid of a [single] universal?
It is said in reply:

Even in that case, the linguistic usage [of the term "substance"] is based solely on limiting conditions (*upādhi*), such as being the locus of qualities perceivable by a single external sense-organ, or having a magnitude delimited by a specific quantity.
For although these limiting conditions are mutually exclusive, there is no fault [in using a common term], because they serve as the locus for a recurring universal (*sāmānya*).
Furthermore, in the absence of recurring universals such as "threadness" (*tantutva*) or "clothness" (*paṭatva*), it would be impossible to determine the relationship between cause and effect.
Consequently, those seeking an effect would not engage with its cause.
For when there is a causal relationship, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists either in positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) or in instruction (*upadeśa*).
However, the apprehension of positive and negative concomitance is not possible among entities that are mutually exclusive.
Because it is difficult to ascertain both the rule and its deviation; furthermore, it has already been stated that instruction is simply impossible regarding infinite particulars.
Moreover, even the cognition of pervasion would be untenable in the absence of a recurring universal.
Because it is impossible to comprehend positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) among entities that are mutually exclusive;
furthermore, the principle of the general rule and its exception (*sāmānyāpavādanyāya*) would not exist in the absence of a persisting universal (*anugatasāmānya*),
for [it applies only when] two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have a single nature as their object.
Otherwise, one of the two would necessarily lack validity.
If they had different objects, there would be no scope for sublation;
yet, there certainly exists the inclusive cognition in the form "this is a cow."
And this [cognition] does not occur with respect to excluded things,
because it would follow that it is erroneous;
nor is this based on the exclusion of all other things (*anyāpoha*).
For that [exclusion] also is distinct with respect to each individual object;
or, if it were pervasive, what would the universal have done wrong?
And in that case, even the cognition in a positive form would be established. (8.40)

And since the universal "cowness" (gotva) and so forth must be accepted as following [the individuals] in this way, its eternality is likewise unavoidable; therefore, he says: "The derivation [of the word] also..."
For even proficiency is understood through similarity alone.
The particle *api* serves to include the determination of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth.
The word *hi* has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
[The verb] *gamyate* means "is accepted," "is admitted," or "is understood."
There exists, indeed, a distinct category called similarity (*sādṛśya*),
because it is established by perception in such cases as "the *gavaya* is similar to a cow," and it is by means of that very [similarity] that [cognition] is accounted for.
[This concerns] the acquisition of linguistic proficiency and so forth.
Therefore, one need not postulate that "cowness" (*gotva*) and other such universals possess a quality of persistence (*anugatatva*) for that purpose.
Now, he begins to demonstrate the manner in which the acquisition of words occurs through similarity, starting with the verse: "In all... (*sarveṣu*).
The word "all" is applied simultaneously to things that are similar.
For there are indeed many means for grasping the connection between words and their referents.
Among these, when one acquires proficiency through instruction, then the instructional sentence "This is a cow" serves as the means for grasping the pervasion (vyāpti).
How so?
Through the imposition of similarity, the word "this" and so forth is applied simultaneously to all individual cows at one and the same time.

The meaning intended by the speaker—that "this is a cow" implies that all these [others] similar to this are also denotable by the word "cow"—is likewise apprehended by the listener. This is the sense.

The point is that, since both [the proponent and the opponent] desire universal linguistic proficiency (*sārvatrikavyutpatti*), it is untenable to assume that a sentence has as its object only a single individual entity (*ekapiṇḍa*).
This is because the sentence "This is a cow" and so forth does not have only a single individual as its object.

However, if that [relation] were intended as a universal pervasion (vyāpti)—namely, that "this and all things similar to it are denotable by the word 'cow'"—then, after the relation has been grasped, upon being told "bring a cow," there would be a cognition of every cow from the word "cow. Yet, only the specific cow intended is actually perceived; how is this so? He dispels the objection of the bystander with the words "tathāpi" ("nevertheless").

Nevertheless, because of its attainment, because it is expressed in the singular number, and because of its specific nature, there would be a comprehension [of the whole] through the desire for it... // MAnu 2.2.122a-c //

Although an instruction does not have a single specific individual as its object, nevertheless, when it is said, "Bring the cow," there will indeed be an understanding of a particular cow that is intended.
How so?
Because of its attainment through fitness.
The meaning is that, having observed the absence of the capacity for being brought in the case of cows that are past, future, or situated in an extremely remote location, they are excluded.
If it is asked, "In that case, why does there not occur a cognition of all cows present [nearby]? the answer is no, because of the singular number in the word *gām*.
Even so, it might be argued that the cognition would belong to any single cow-individual whatsoever, and not exclusively to Abhīṣya; if this is said, we reply:
no, because of specific qualifiers such as "the brindled one," "the black-spotted one," or "the dark-eyed one."

This is what is meant: from the word "cow," the cognition of all cows indeed arises; however, by the force of indicators (*liṅga*), context (*prakaraṇa*), and so forth, the cognition of a specific action occurs with respect to a particular individual. *8,45*
Let this sentence, "This is a cow," and so forth, be intended to convey pervasion (vyāpti).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "The capacity" (śakti).
... for power resides in similarity. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.122d)
And this word "that" clearly indicates that it is of such a nature.
For the denotative power of a word resides in similarity— that is, it is related to similarity and pervades similarity;
this is understood from the following statement, as is implied by the ellipsis.
Therefore, it clearly makes known that power (śakti) as a similarity (sādṛśya) with respect to this or that object.
To the question "How so?", he shows the method of application [of the term] by saying: "tādṛśa" (such).
The word *yat* is used in the sense of "because.
This [object] being perceived is similar to the lump present at the time of instruction;
therefore, that which has the word *tat* as its designator is so described.
The word *iti* expresses a manner or mode.
This is the collective meaning here:
for the sake of etymological derivation, one need not accept any underlying commonality whatsoever.
For that [cognition] is established by similarity alone.
Nor should it be argued: "If similarity too is a recurring entity, what has the universal (sāmānya) done wrong?
And if it is excluded [from others], how can it be a factor for universal linguistic convention?"

For similarity is not accepted as being either the object of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśakti*) or as the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*); rather, it is [accepted] as a logical mark (*liṅga*). Just as, for example, the possession of odor (*gandhavattva*) is not what is denoted by the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*).

Nor is that [the exclusion] the cause for the application [of the word]; rather, it is merely an indicator (*liṅga*) regarding the fact that an individual possessing earthness is denotable by the word "earth.
Likewise, although those [exclusions] are mutually distinct, they are employed as indicators for the cognition of that [earthness].
For instance, when there is an acquisition of meaning preceded by the instruction "this is a cow," then that sentence is the grasper of pervasion (*vyāpti*),
because its purpose is precisely this: that all things similar to this conscious [animal] are denotable by the word "cow."

However, when linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) is preceded by linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) and the like, then upon observing repeated usage and so forth, there arises an understanding of similarity and pervasion (*vyāpyatā*).

Consequently, it is inferred from this sentence and so on that the pervasion has been understood: "This [animal] ought to be denotable by the word 'cow' because it is similar to that; whatever is similar to that is denotable by the word 'cow', and this is similar to that; therefore, it is denotable by the word 'cow'. (8.49)

Now, what is the illustrative example here? If it is argued that it is the cow-individual present at the time of instruction, we say no; because that [cow] lacks similarity with [the cow one perceives later].
Not so;
for the restriction regarding the example has already been refuted.
Nor should it be argued that the possession of a dewlap and so forth alone should be the logical mark (liṅga), rather than similarity.
Because that [cowness] is excluded from each individual instance like the property of being a cow (*gotva*),
whereas similarity, despite being excluded, is experienced as establishing a unified result by virtue of being defined in relation to its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Therefore,
we accept that even the possession of a dewlap and so forth functions as a logical mark (*liṅga*) when it is qualified by similarity.
Nor should it be argued that since similarity to a cow exists even in a horse, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) would follow that the word "cow" could also denote a horse through inference;
for this same consequence applies equally if the cause [of denotation] were a genus (jāti).
If it is argued that a specific genus is accepted as the cause, provided that it is non-deviant (avyabhicārī), [we reply:]...
In that case, we say that it is precisely a specific similarity (*sādṛśyaviśeṣa*) that serves as the mark (*liṅga*), which constitutes the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
By this, it should be understood that the determination of the relationship between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth is also resolved,
since those are established through similarity alone.
For in the case of ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*), there is nothing that is common to it, nor is there any qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) that serves as a common substratum;
for if such a thing existed, it would follow that its essential nature— as that which is absolutely exclusive, like substance, quality, or action— would be lost.

Nevertheless, there is therein the derivation of specific terms, such as the determination that [the universal] is the cause for the cognition of absolute exclusion (*atyantavyāvṛtti*), and so forth. In this regard, even by the opponent, similarity in the form of a definition must be accepted. *8,54*
Thus, the derivation [of word-meanings] and so forth have been established precisely by not accepting a recurring universal (*anugatasāmānya*).

However, for one who thinks that derivation and so forth occur only through a recurring universal and not otherwise, he states the following refutation: "If [it were] by way of a genus (*jāti*)," and so on.
If it is by birth, how [could they be so] among them...?

If the determination of linguistic usage and the ascertainment of causal relations and so forth were everywhere based solely on the cause that is the universal (jāti), then how could there be the linguistic usage of words such as "universal" with respect to those very universals, the ascertainment of their being the cause of a recurring cognition, or the knowledge of pervasion such as "cowness is eternal because it is a universal," and so on?
The meaning is that because there would be an absence of "genus" (*jāti*) within the various genera, the process of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) and so forth would not occur there.

If, out of audacity, someone were to say: "Even within the various genera, there exists a genus called 'genus-ness' (*jātitva*), and by virtue of that, the application of the suffix [denoting genus] is possible there," he says in response: "And if in that case... (*tatra cet*).
... if there is no finality in that case. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.123d)

If, in that case, a universal called "universality" (*jātitva*) is admitted even among universals such as "cowness," then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*). To explain: the universal called "universality," which serves as the ground for applying the word "universal" to universals such as cowness, does not reside in its own form, because its self-residence is unproven.
Therefore, it must be stated that [the universal] resides only in universals distinct from itself.
And thus, this [other universal] would be the cause for the application of the word "universal" to universals distinct from itself, but not to its own nature as well.
Consequently, for the application of a single word "universal" to that [particular universal] and to universals distinct from it, another universal must be admitted as the cause.
In that case as well, it would be exactly the same, leading to an infinite regress.
Now, one might argue that the word "jāti" (universal) applied to universals such as "cowness" is prompted by the property of being a universal (*jātitva*);
however, let the application of the term to *jātitva* itself depend upon instruction.
"Because it is a single entity"—
do not say so; for we do not regard the universal (*jāti*) as being like similarity (*sādṛśya*), as you do.
In the application of a word, it is accepted as being a signifier; however, it is not by being inserted through some specific instruction, but rather by way of being a causal condition (nimitta).
In that case, what is the use of presenting an instruction?
He states a refutation even in another context with the words "in the same way."
In the same way, the cognition of an individual is vitiated by the absence of individuality.

Just as the cognition of genus is refuted by the absence of the nature of genus (*jātitva*), so too is the cognition of individuals— the cognition that individuals are denotable by the word "individual"— refuted by the absence of the universal "individuality" (*vyaktitva*) which would serve as its cause.
For substances, qualities, and actions are indeed called "individuals," yet there exists no such generality as "individuality" therein.
Because existence (*sattā*) lacks the state of being either prior or posterior [to individuals],
there could not be a cognition of it as being denotable by the word "individual" (*vyakti*).
If it is argued that even if "individuality" (*vyaktitva*) were not distinct [from existence], existence itself would be the cause for the application of the word "individual," we say no.

Because the universal serves as the cause for the application of synonymous terms; otherwise, since the words "existent" and "individual" would not be non-synonymous, words such as "conjoined" and so forth would also become synonyms for words such as "substance. (8.58)

[Objection: Since a word is based on a universal (jāti), individuality (vyaktitva) indeed exists in substances, qualities, and actions—even though they are devoid of the relationship of higher and lower [universals]—and therefore the aforementioned fault does not apply; to this, he says: "If... (yadīti).
If that [universal] exists, there would likewise be an infinite regress regarding its particular instances.

In that case, that individuality (vyaktitva) would also have to enter into the particulars (viśeṣa), which are themselves individuals; and thus there would be an infinite regress (anavasthiti)—this is the construction [of the argument]. To explain:

If it is accepted that every word denoting multiple things has "genus" (*jāti*) as its cause, and if one were to admit that there is a genus called "individuality" (*vyaktitva*) residing in substances, qualities, and actions, then—
in order for words denoting genus to apply to that [genus] and to other genera— one would have to admit a "genus-ness" (*jātitva*) as a further genus.
If you say, "Yes," [then the following applies].
In that case, the universal "individuality" (*vyaktitva-jāti*) would also be an individual (*vyakti*) with respect to the universal "universality" (*jātitva*).

And since it does not reside in its own form, another "individuality" must be admitted for the sake of applying the term "individual" to the triad beginning with substance (*dravya*) and to that [universal "individuality"] as well.

Furthermore, for the application of the term "universal" to that [second individuality], "universality" (*jātitva*) must be accepted; thus, that too would be an individual by virtue of being the locus of that [universality].
Furthermore, if there were another individuality within that [individuality], there would be an infinite regress.
In another context, he states the refutation: "How so?"
If it is argued that the commonality of intrinsic nature is also known through a recurring [cognition],
then this would be undermined by defects such as infinite regress, extending as far as the derivation of a single [conventional] understanding.
In this context, the word "intrinsic nature" (*svarūpa*) is to be supplied.
Consequently, the meaning is as follows:

if linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) everywhere were based solely on a recurring universal (*sāmānya*), then how could the intrinsic nature of all things be known as being denotable by the word "intrinsic nature"?

Because there is no such thing as a universal "self-natureness" (*svarūpatva*) that persists across [all] individual self-natures, the derivation of the word "self-nature" (*svarūpa*) with respect to those individual self-natures would be impossible. [Objection:

But surely, I do admit a "self-natureness" that is common to all individual self-natures; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. [Response: To this it is said: "If even 'self-natureness' is admitted to be a persisting [universal], then it is vitiated by the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and so forth."
It is so;
for indeed, in all individual essences (svarūpa), there is accepted a universal (sāmānya) called "essenceness" (svarūpatva), which is the ground for the application of the word "individual essence."
Furthermore, that [existence] exists by its own nature;
yet it does not reside in itself,
because self-dependence (ātmāśrayatva) is contrary to worldly experience.
Therefore, for the term "own-nature" (svarūpa) to apply to that [particular] and other own-natures, another universal called "own-nature-ness" (svarūpatva) must be admitted.
But since that too would be a mere own-nature, there would be an infinite regress.
By the word "etcetera," it is implied that a universal of "own-nature-ness" must likewise be admitted for the own-natures of ultimate particulars (antyaviśeṣa).

That [particular] would also be nothing but its own essential nature (svarūpa), leading to an infinite regress. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), it should be understood that if the universal "being an essential nature" (svarūpatva-sāmānya) were admitted in the case of the essential natures of ultimate particulars (antyaviśeṣa), they would not serve as the cause for the cognition of absolute exclusion (atyantavyāvṛtti). Furthermore, in the case of inherence (samavāya) and non-existence (abhāva), there would be an absence of any relation (sambandha).
This indicates that the undesirable consequence of infinite regress and so forth culminates in its opposite: "up to the limit of the derivation of a single [word]."

"One" means exclusively that which is devoid of a commonality (sāmānya) that follows [through multiple instances]. "Mastery" (vyutpatti) regarding that is "mastery of the one"; up to that limit, this objection indeed persists. The meaning is: as long as one does not abandon the position that mastery in all cases is necessarily based on a commonality that follows [multiple instances], and instead accepts mastery even with respect to that which is devoid of such a commonality.

The point is that, in order to avoid an infinite regress and similar faults, one must accept that linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) occurs even without a recurring universal (*anugatasāmānya*). [Objection: But all of this is inconsistent; for instance:
As for what was stated— "it was said that [the word 'universal'] applies to them by virtue of being a universal"— that is incorrect;

for even though there is no further universal within universals, the derivation of the word "universal" (jāti) is justified by the limiting condition (upādhi) of being eternal and residing in many [individuals].
Or let there be a genus called "genus-ness" (jātitva) among the genera;
yet there is no infinite regress,
because it is logical that the word "genus" (jāti) with respect to "genus-ness" is based on its own essential form (svarūpa).
"The same applies to the cognition of an individual (*vyaktivijñāna*);
this too is incorrect.

For even in the absence of an actual individuality (*vyaktitva*), the application of the word ‘individual’ to substances and so forth is logically possible through the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being a manifester of a genus (*jāti*)."

Even if one accepts both individuality (*vyaktitva*) and genus (*jāti*), there is no infinite regress; for in the case of individuality, it is possible for the word "individual" to have its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) as its basis.
As for what was asked: "How?"...
Such [objections] as these are incorrect;
for the etymological derivation of the word "intrinsic nature" (svarūpa) is established precisely by the limiting condition (upādhi) of being cognizable through valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Even if intrinsic nature is accepted, there is no infinite regress.

In this regard, since the word "essential nature" (*svarūpa*) is based solely on the essential nature itself, while in the case of ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*) it is based solely on an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*), there is no loss of its formal character.

Anticipating the objection that in the case of inherence (*samavāya*) and so forth, the essential nature itself constitutes the relation and thus there is no fault, he concludes the refutation of the inclusive universal (*anugata-sāmānya*) with the words: "It is a conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*).
Therefore, because it would involve a conceptual complexity, the assumption of a subordinate [action] is not tenable.
The meaning is as follows: in every case, that which is excluded [from others] alone is the denotable object (*vācya*) and the basis for the application of a word (*nimitta*).

However, while the conventional derivation (*vyutpatti*) is based on similarity, it is sufficient to assume a single uniform nature to achieve consistency across all instances. If one were instead to assume multiple factors—such as a recurring universal (*sāmānya*) as the basis in some cases, an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*) in others, and the essential nature itself (*svarūpa*) in yet others—there would be the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*).
Because of that presence of sublation and absence of proof, [it is argued]:
"But if there is no commonality (*anugatatva*), how can 'cowness' and the like be a universal (*sāmānya*)?
Even if there is no commonality, a subordinate distinction must be postulated, just as in the case of qualities and actions. (8.64)

Having thus refuted inherence (*samavāya*) by way of its essential nature, [the author] now addresses its unity and eternality throughout all things, which was stated in the aphorism “*tattvaṃ bhāvena*”;
that is, its true nature (*tattva*).
The oneness and eternality of inherence (samavāya) everywhere are explained by its being [treated] like existence (bhāva), that is, like the property of being (sattā).
Desiring to refute that as well, he first prepares the foundation to refute oneness, beginning with the words "aupādhika" (conditioned).

Is that entity, even when qualified by adventitious attributes such as being a cook or a priest, or distinguished by qualities such as being blue or fiery, anything other than that [entity] itself? No, it is not. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.126a-c) *Adventitious* (*aupādhika*) refers to those who are defined by their functions, such as cooks or priests; *distinguished* (*viśiṣṭa*) refers to things characterized by attributes, such as being blue or possessing fire.
By the inclusion of the word "first" (ādi), there is an indication of [the remaining categories].
The word "also" (api) serves to aggregate further refutations.
That refers to the triad beginning with the entity (vastu), the adjunct (upādhi), and so forth.

The word "what" (kiṃ) is connected to both sides. Therefore, from among the three beginning with "limiting adjunct" (upādhi), the term "entity" (vastu) is also connected with the phrase "that which is qualified by limiting adjuncts and so forth."
This is the meaning:
since you assert that inherence (*samavāya*) is one and the same everywhere, this must first be examined.
Just as a single person is designated by such terms as "cook" or "sacrificer" through limiting adjuncts—namely, properties such as cooking or sacrificing—so too [must it be for inherence].
Is that contingent object, such as a "cook" or a "sacrificer," non-different from the adjuncts—such as the act of cooking—the person, and their relationship, or is it different?
Likewise, a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is that which is co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) and serves to differentiate;
for example, the blue color of a lotus, or fire on a mountain.
But an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) that is in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) is that which distinguishes;
for example, the blueness residing in the color blue [distinguishes] the lotus.
Others, however, explain the difference between a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and an indicator based on whether they enter into the body [of the object] or not.
For example: "Let Lambakarṇa be brought," or "Let Citragu be brought.
Others, however, [cite examples] by means of verbal co-referentiality (*śābda-sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such as: "Devadatta is a staff-bearer" or "The ascetic is [known] by his matted locks."
Furthermore, some [hold that] at the time of exclusion, it is by way of existence and non-existence.
In that regard, is the specific [object], such as "blue" or "possessing fire," non-different from the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation, or is it different?
And is the indicated [object] non-different from the indicator, the indicated, and their relation, or is it different?
In this regard, the position of difference is simply impossible, as it contradicts experience, accepted doctrine, and logical reasoning.
For a cook or the like is not experienced as something distinct from the three factors of cooking and so forth;
nor is the existence of a thing established when that which is perceptible is not perceived.

Nor is fire-possessingness (agnimattva) and so forth experienced as something distinct from the mountain and the like; for if it were distinct, then since a qualified entity (viśiṣṭa) characterized by adventitious properties (aupādhika) could not possibly be included within the categories of substance (dravya) and so on,
there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of exceeding the six categories of existence, which would contradict one's own accepted doctrine.

Furthermore, if that which is qualified by an adjunct (*aupādhika-viśiṣṭa*) and so forth were something distinct [from the substrate], then there would be a contradiction with established reasoning, such as the fact that when one says "bring the cook," one does not bring a person who is merely a man.

If it is argued: "But surely being delimited (*avacchittir aupādhikatvam*) is the case here; and this delimitation (*vyavacchitti*), as well as the state of being qualified (*vaiśiṣṭya*), is indeed distinct from the triad [of substrate, adjunct, and relation]," we say no.
Because limitation cannot be established;
for is that [limitation] a connection with an adjunct (*upādhi*), or the unity of the person, or an internal difference?
In the first case, there is no exclusion of the triad.
In the second case, however, there is no distinction from that which is without limiting adjuncts (*anaupādhika*). In the third case, there is the consequence of non-existence (*asattva*).
Furthermore, it is incorrect to say that "exclusion" (*vyavacchitti*) is "qualification" (*vaiśiṣṭya*).
This is because it lacks the status of being an object such as "blue" and so forth;
rather, it is experienced as the objective domain of the result, which is the cognition of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*).

Some maintain that a single, uninterrupted cognition—one that apprehends the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation—is itself the "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*), or else there are multiple such cognitions.
As it has been said: "The qualifier and the qualified, which bestow the fruit of their mutual relation,
are known as 'the qualified' because they are of the nature of cognition through their own inherent capacity."
That is not so,
because the qualified [subject] is experienced as having an external object;
otherwise, the thesis would be the subject as qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
Thus, it would be incorrect to say that "he is to be made known through inference" and so forth.
Therefore, the position of [the self] being something additional is simply untenable.

To the objection, "Let it be then that the first three—[the body, senses, and cognition]—are non-different from the self as qualified by adventitious attributes," he replies: "That very same [self]. (*8,74*)
If that very state of possessing fire is [already established], what more is there to be said in that regard?
For the sake of making the response easy, the question was formulated using the suffix *matup* as "possessing fire" (*agnimattva*),
meaning that which is to be established by the inference from smoke and so forth is qualified.
This also serves as an illustration for cases involving adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*) and the like.
This is the meaning:
even if that which is qualified by fire, fuel, and so forth is admitted to be non-different from the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation,
it must still be stated [as follows].
Is that triad each individually qualified, or is it any one of them?
Even in the second case, is fire itself— the qualifier— the meaning of the word "fire-possessor," or is it the mountain— the qualified object?
Now, as for the relation, it is characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Even regarding the position that it is conjunction, is it conjunction without qualification, or is it conjunction with fire?
And even in the latter case, is it merely conjunction with fire?
Or, as in the case of the mountain’s conjunction with fire;
in this same way, a similar dilemma should be seen regarding the cook and so forth, even if they are not distinct from the three [factors] such as the act of cooking.
He refutes all positions other than the final one [the third option] with the words: "Fire... (*agnīti*).
If it were merely contact with fire, that would be proving what is already established.

The phrase "merely the conjunction with fire" is an illustration that encompasses all positions; the remainder of the sense is "if [the object] is the referent of the word 'fire-possessing'. In that case, the inference from the presence of smoke and so forth—whether it concerns the conjunctions of fire with the mountain collectively or individually, or the conjunction with fire itself—is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), provided that these are qualified by being the denotable objects of the word "fire-possessing."

It may be so, because it is the specific [nature] that is to be established by inference; for the specific nature of fire and so forth is established precisely through another means of valid cognition (*mānāntara*). (8.77)

Let it be, then, that the final position is this: the meaning of the word "fire-possessing" (agnimat) is a specific form of conjunction between the mountain and fire, which is to be established by inference.
This is because the aforementioned defects do not apply here.

One might object: although the conjunctions of the mountain with all fires taken collectively, with each individually, and with fire in general are already established, the specific conjunction of the mountain with [that particular] fire is not established prior to the inference. Thus he raises the objection:
"Of Bhūdhara," so it is said.
If the contact with fire of the mountain is indeed the meaning of the genitive case, then what [is the meaning of the sixth case]?
The meaning of the word "agnimat" is a qualified [object] to be established by inference; this is the remainder [of the sentence].
He asks in order to refute [this]: "What is the meaning of the genitive case?"
Even though the mountain and the conjunction with fire are established, the conjunction with fire that belongs to the mountain is not [independently] established; therefore,

by one who asserts that this very qualified object denoted by the word "fire-possessor" (agnimat) is what is known through inference, it is stated— by specifying "of the mountain" (parvatasya) with the genitive case—
that the relation itself, as the qualified object denoted by the word "fire-possessor," is what is known through inference.
Since everything else is already established,
and since grammarians have enumerated numerous types of relations for the meaning of the genitive case,
the meaning of the question is: "Which relation is intended here?"

The word "eva" (only/just) is for the purpose of highlighting its very primacy. [The author] raises an objection regarding the subsequent [point]: "If it is indeed inherence (*samavāya*)... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.128a).

The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that it is well known that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is a quality (*guṇa*), the mountain is the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), and the relation between the quality and its possessor is inherence (*samavāya*).
The phrase "the meaning of the genitive case" (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. He refutes this with the words "asya ca" (and of this).
And because this [self] is one, it is a case of proving what is already established.

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "because this inherence (samavāya) is established just like a mountain and so forth. The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "inference from smoke and so forth would be proving what is already established" (siddhasādhana).
To the question, "How is inherence established?", it is said: "Because of its oneness" (ekatvāt).
For that very same inherence which exists between the thread and the cloth is accepted by the opponent as the inherence between the mountain and the fire;
and the inherence between the thread and the cloth is established either through perception or through inference.
This is the collective meaning here.

If inherence (*samavāya*) were one and the same everywhere, then all inferences would suffer from the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*). Even though validity consists precisely in accordance with reality (*yāthārthya*), nevertheless, because inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) proceeds in dependence upon another—just like verbal testimony—the fault of *siddhasādhanatā* remains indeed present. To explain:
Furthermore, no inference whatsoever has as its ultimate object the mere nature of a real entity;

for if that [nature] is unestablished, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), and if it is established, it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*).
However, it must be stated whether [the object] is qualified by something, or distinguished by something, or characterized by something;
and it is logical that this "qualified-ness" and so forth is not distinct from the triad of qualifiers and the rest,
because there would otherwise be sublation by non-perception and other such means of invalidation.
Even though [the subject] is not distinct from the triad, it is not merely a qualifier;
for that [qualifier] would have to be established prior to the inference,
and if it were unestablished, it would result in the fallacy of having an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
Furthermore, if "fire" were the meaning of the word [agni], the suffix *matup* would be rendered meaningless;
nor can it be the mere nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpa*),
because of the aforementioned fault.
Furthermore, this would result in the propositions "the mountain possesses fire" and [the inference] having the same meaning.
Nor is it merely a relation; for conjunction (*saṃyoga*) might be the relation in some cases, as in that between fire and the mountain.
In some cases, there is inherence (*samavāya*), as for example in the inference of color from taste.
Since both [the reason and the property to be proven] are established by their own nature, this is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Furthermore, one should not say that even though mere conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is established, the conjunction with fire and so forth is what is to be proven.
Because that [conjunction] is also established in the kitchen and so forth.
Now, if it is argued that the conjunction of fire and so on with the mountain and so forth is what is to be proven,
here too it must be distinguished.
Whose [property] is it that, being unestablished here, is to be proven? Since nothing else is possible,
it must be stated that it is the property of the sixth case-meaning, namely, inherence (*samavāya*).
If that [inherence] were indeed one and the same everywhere, then there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
Therefore, because it would follow that all inference (*anumāna*) is abolished, it is illogical for inherence to be a single entity in all cases.

Now, although the inherence of a cloth and so forth in its threads, and the inherence of fire in a mountain through conjunction, are identical in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), [they are distinct in their relational aspects].
Nevertheless, there is indeed a distinction in inherence (samavāya) caused by limiting conditions (upādhi), such as threads and cloth or fire and its contact with a mountain;
therefore, even though [inherence] is established, its status as a probandum (sādhyatva) is justified. To this he says: "If... (yadīti).
If its difference is merely adventitious, how can unity be maintained?
If an adventitious distinction is admitted for this inherence in order to establish its status as something to be proven, then from where is its oneness derived?
For the oneness of inherence is certainly not a specific number,
because it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatvāt*).
However, there is non-difference;
moreover, neither difference nor non-difference has been accepted by the opponent anywhere.
Therefore, since difference is accepted in the case of inherence (samavāya), it is not appropriate to accept its contradictory, non-difference.
Now, it may be objected that inherent unity is contradicted only by inherent difference, and not by adventitious difference;

for even in the case of space and the like, which are inherently undivided, adventitious difference is observed. Furthermore, in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), only adventitious difference is admitted.
To the question, "How then is the acceptance of an intrinsic oneness improper? he says: "No."

For it is not desired that [the two] be indescribable; therefore, since both are real due to their being adventitious, what distinction could there be? ... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.129a-c) *8,81* For the non-contradiction of two things considered to be contradictory occurs through a difference in time.
Just as in that very same spot on the ground there is the existence and non-existence of that very same jar,
either by way of a difference in location;
or just as at that very same time there is the existence and non-existence of that very same jar.
Or by way of a difference in individuals;
for example, in that very same spot on the ground, when there is the presence of one jar, at that very time there is the absence of another jar.
Or [the distinction may be made] by way of ultimate reality and non-ultimate reality.
Just as in the case of form and its absence in space,
