it is admitted even by the opponent that, regarding inherence (*samavāya*), the first three modes— namely non-difference and difference—
are not possible; nor is the fourth mode possible.
The non-ultimate reality of the distinction of inherence (samavāya-bheda) consists in its non-existence or its being indeterminable (anirvācyatva).
In the first case, the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatva) remains exactly as it was. In the second case, however, the following [objection] presents itself:

For since that Vaiśeṣika and others do not accept an indefinable entity, there would be no distinction [between them and us], because of the absence of both non-existence and indefinability; and since both the adventitious (*aupādhika*) and the intrinsic (*svābhāvika*) would possess reality, what difference could there be? The sense is that, because even the adventitious would possess reality just like the intrinsic, the argument for adventitiousness—intended as a means to pacify the contradiction characterized by ultimate versus non-ultimate reality—would accomplish nothing at all.

If it is argued, "What fault is there if I maintain that the difference of inherence (samavāya-bheda) is inexpressible (anirvācya)? [the author] replies, "It would be a deviation from established tenets (apasiddhānta)," stating: "Illusion (māyā)."
... otherwise, he would be a proponent of illusionism. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.129d)
The meaning is that if one accepts an inexpressible entity (*anirvācyavastu*), even a Vaiśeṣika or other [proponent] would become a proponent of Māyā (*māyāvādī*).
Now, it may be argued that the contradiction will be resolved even through a difference in mode (*prakāra*),
just as in that very same place at that very same time, although there is the existence of a blue cloth, there is the absence of a yellow cloth.
Likewise, even in the case of inherence (samavāya), a difference based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi) does not contradict an inherent non-difference; therefore, he says: "upādhi... [and so forth].
If that which is produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) were cognizable through them, it would be merely conditional (aupādhika).
When the suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "produced" (*janya*) or "understood" (*gamya*) following the word *upādhi* in the third case (instrumental), the form *aupādhika* arises.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "In both cases."
In both cases, there would be infinite instances of inherence here and there.

This being the case, the so-called "conditioned nature" (aupādhikatva) of the distinction between inherence (samavāya) must be stated as either being produced by conditions (upādhi-janyatva) or being made known by conditions (upādhi-gamyatva).
Consequently, under both these views, there would be infinite instances of inherence.
To the question "How so?", he says: "hither and thither" (itastataḥ).
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "because the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as parts (avayava) and wholes (avayavin), existing in all places and times, are infinite.
Even though the adjuncts are infinite, why is inherence (samavāya) also infinite? To this he says: "Because of their distinctness."
And there is indeed a state of division among them... // Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.130e //
The word "co" (ca) has the sense of "because" (yasmāt).
For a distinction that is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*) is not, in fact, the distinction of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) themselves;
if it were so, the phrase "of inherence" (*samavāyasya*) would not be possible.
Furthermore, the aforementioned fault would not be avoided;
rather, in those very inherences (samavāyas), there exists a distinctness produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) or cognizable through them.
And since the limiting adjuncts that cause this distinction are infinite, how could inherence not be infinite as well?

Nevertheless, since it has been stated that this infinity is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), one might ask: what follows from this? To this he says: "Who? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.130f): "What distinction is there in that which resides in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)?"
"Acquired through limiting adjuncts" (*aupādhika*) means that which belongs to those adjuncts; that is to say, it is adventitious.
The meaning is: what specific distinction exists in an adventitious difference such that it does not contradict non-difference?
This is what is being said.

For in the case of the statement, "Even though there is the existence of a blue cloth, there is the absence of a yellow cloth," if the affirmation and negation have distinct objects, then there is no contradiction because their objects are different;
this is due to the difference between the blue cloth and the yellow cloth.
But it is not so in the present case;
for even in the absence of a specific difference, it would entail the admission of another difference. And thus, the assertion of oneness is indeed untenable.

It is not the case that because the color and other qualities in an earth atom are produced by contact with fire, whereas those in a water atom are inherent, the former must therefore be devoid of color and other qualities.
Furthermore, if [inherence] has qualifiers as its objects, then difference certainly exists in inherence;
however, it would have to be said that this difference is produced by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) which are the related entities, and is not uncreated (akṛtrima).
And thus, since it is equal to the difference between a jar and other objects, the statement regarding non-difference is empty.
Furthermore, because limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) never depart, it is not logical for difference to be adventitious.
Accepting the position that "that which is understood through an adjunct is adventitious," he raises an objection to avoid the aforementioned fault: "Even though it does not exist... and so forth.
Another inherence, though non-existent,
is nevertheless apprehended through a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Since it is accessible through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the distinction of inherence (*samavāya*) is adventitious (*aupādhika*); and its apprehension is not valid cognition (*pramā*), whereby that distinction could be ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). Rather, it is merely an error (*vibhrama*).

Nor should it be argued that this results in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) because the existence of difference is thereby admitted; for we maintain that it is precisely an otherwise non-existent inherence (*samavāya*) that is apprehended through various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Just as a second moon, though non-existent, is perceived due to the limiting adjunct of the eye being pressed by a finger, so too are multiple instances of inherence—though non-existent—perceived through those various limiting adjuncts characterized by their respective relations.
These very inherences are said to be non-different from the distinctions produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
They alone are denoted by words such as "fire-possessor" and are established by inference as having qualified forms.
Thus, there is no loss of the unity of inherence.
For even though there is multiplicity in those things superimposed as being like the moon, this does not contradict the unity of that which is not so superimposed;
nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) regarding inferences,
because such instances of inherence (*samavāya*) were previously unestablished.
"...he avoids that which indicates it;
[otherwise], that inference which indicates it would not be [valid]. (MAnu 2.131cd)
Even if, under this view, the inference from smoke and so forth does not involve proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*),

nevertheless, that collection of inferences which purports to establish the existence of an inherence (*samavāya*) that is not actually present would— like the inference of the coldness of fire— not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because its object is sublated.
Furthermore, this is merely an illustration.
It should also be observed that since there is nowhere any appearance of inherence (samavāya) without limiting adjuncts (upādhi), it would follow that inherence is non-existent everywhere.

Thus, because all inferences— such as those based on smoke and so forth— would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatva) and other such faults, the unity of inherence is not tenable.
This is also an illustration:
there would also be a denial of scripture if inherence were a single entity, because the categories and their relations would be established as being as disjointed as grains of sand. (8.88)
Now he refutes the eternality of inherence (samavāya) with the words: "In this very same way."
In this very same way, the manifestation of existence from non-existence is considered to be birth.

Just as it was stated that if inherence (*samavāya*) is accepted as being one and the same everywhere, all inferences would be flawed by the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*),

exactly so, if its eternity is admitted, then "origination"— defined as the inherence of existence (*sattā*) in that which previously did not exist— would be rendered impossible. The meaning is that if inherence were eternal, there could be no origination for anything whatsoever.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Even there..."
For even there, there is nothing at all that can prevent the aforementioned defects.
Regarding the aforementioned faults, such as proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) and so forth; for instance,
the opponent has stated the definition of origination (*janman*) as "the inherence (*samavāya*) of existence (*sattā*) in that which previously did not exist."

In that regard, if inherence (*samavāya*) were eternal, then the production of a jar, characterized by that [inherence], would exist even prior to the activity of the potter and so forth; thus, for that purpose, it would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
For in the case of making known (*jñapti*), the establishment of what is already established is possible;
however, in some cases, there is simply a lack of dependence [on causes].
But in the case of production (*kṛti*), it would be impossible for that which is already established to be produced; thus, the activity of the potter and others would be rendered fruitless.

If it is argued that even though inherence (*samavāya*) is eternal, its connection with existence (*sattā-samavāya*)—which was previously non-existent—is what is to be accomplished, and therefore there is no fault, we say no. For this would contradict the unity of inherence.
If it is argued that the difference in inherence (*samavāya*) is merely conditional (*aupādhika*),
then everything previously stated should be considered as applicable as far as possible; for an operation whose object does not already exist is not possible.
Because for that [effect], there is no duty to be performed beyond its existing cause;
and because the existence of the existing cause is not distinct from its inherence in being.
If it is argued that the acquisition of its own nature is accomplished by the operation of the potter and others—
If that is so, then what is the use of another "inherence" (*sattā-samavāya*)? Thus, since the unity and eternality of inherence are in every way untenable,

or rather, as an occasion for refuting inherence, the nature of "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) and so forth as well as the production of the Lord (*janeśa*) as asserted by others has been refuted by the passage beginning with "conditioned" (*aupādhika*), in order to demonstrate the inconsistency of their doctrine.
This must be understood:
is this not entirely contradictory?
For even you, while maintaining the conventions of the world and the Vedas, must necessarily accept [the existence of] a distinct creator and so forth.

Since the aforementioned defects would also follow there, he demonstrates the absence of such defects in his own system regarding the determination of the "distinguished" (viśiṣṭa) and so forth, beginning with the words *asmad* etc.
In our position, since a particularity (*viśeṣa*) is admitted everywhere, there is no fault whatsoever... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.133a-c]
The qualified form is neither the qualifier nor the relation; rather,
it is the qualified object itself,
yet not merely that alone.
For there are two kinds of distinguished forms (*viśiṣṭākāra*):
that which exists as long as the qualified object exists (*yāvadviśeṣyabhāvī*) and that which exists as long as the qualified object exists [only in a specific state].
Of these, the first is absolutely non-different from the qualified object.
Just as Īśvara is omniscient by his very nature, so too,

wherever there is a connection with a qualifier that extends as far as the existence of the qualified object, there the mode of being qualified must likewise be seen as absolutely non-different from the qualified object.

Nevertheless, since a "particularity" (*viśeṣa*)— which serves as a substitute for difference— is accepted in all categories of entities, there is no fault such as the impossibility of the application of non-synonymous terms like "Īśvara" and "omniscient."
First, the non-difference [of the Lord] is established by the cognition that "the Lord alone is omniscient.
As for difference, however, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that leaves no room for it.
But the second [type of omniscience] is both different and non-different from the qualified object (*viśeṣya*).
Just as [one infers] fire by means of smoke;
for just as threads, assisted by a particular conjunction, transform into the form of a cloth,
so too the nature of the qualified object transforms into a qualified form through its connection with adventitious qualifiers.

In this regard, although difference and non-difference are the very nature of a thing, there is no fault of confusion (*saṅkara*) in our position because a particularity (*viśeṣa*) is admitted everywhere;
this is what was stated by the words "in some cases."
The meaning is: in cases of absolute non-difference and in cases of difference-cum-non-difference;
or alternatively, "in some cases" refers to the three types beginning with that which is adventitious (*aupādhika*), because those also fall under the aforementioned categories.
By this, the argument that "even in space and the like, which are devoid of internal difference, a difference based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is observed" is also refuted;
for it is only the parts of space and so forth, which are themselves grounded in specific distinctions, that are made manifest by limiting adjuncts such as jars and the like.
He demonstrates the absence of defects regarding the definition of origination in his own system with the words "asmad... (our...).
The construction is as follows: since the production of a specific transformation (*pariṇāma*) is accepted [as the cause], there is no fault whatsoever.
The meaning is that for clay and other materials, the very assumption of the form of a jar and so forth is the production of the jar and so forth, and not an inherence (*samavāya*).
It might be argued as follows:
In some cases, a positive entity (*bhāva*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), while the qualified form (*viśiṣṭākāra*) is perceived as a negation (*abhāva*);
for example, "a jar does not know" or "primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is not an agent.
In other cases, a negation is the qualificand, and the qualified form is understood as a positive entity.
Non-existence exists;
non-existence is an object of cognition.
Furthermore, it is not logical that there be no distinction between existence and non-existence, which consist respectively of affirmation and negation.
To the question, "How then can that which is non-different from the qualificand be called qualified?", he says: "For existence... and so forth.
For existence is indeed non-existence, and that very same thing is both.
The word "somewhere" (kvacit) is understood to carry over [from the previous verse].

The meaning is that it is well-established that whatever is an entity (bhāva) is itself an absence (abhāva) in some respect, and whatever is an absence is itself an entity in some respect; thus both of these are indeed established.
The two occurrences of the word "hi" (for/indeed) are intended to indicate the well-known status of both [the preceding] sentence meanings.
To the question "How so?", he says: "And of non-existence... and so forth.
And the properties of non-existence would be existents, and all those [existents] would belong to them.
There is indeed this [point]: that even for non-existence (abhāva), there may be existent factors (bhāva-dharma), and likewise for those existents, there may be non-existent factors (abhāva-dharma).
The term "entire" (akhila) is an indication of plurality. Since I do not accept even this, he says: "perceptible" (pratyakṣa), etc.
All this cannot be prevented by means of direct perception alone.
The mention of "perception" (pratyakṣa) is for the purpose of illustration;

for it is established by means of valid cognition such as perception that non-existents also possess positive attributes and existents also possess negative attributes—all of which cannot be denied. (8, 97)
Let it be granted that existence and non-existence possess the properties of being existent and non-existent respectively;
nevertheless, what follows from the claim that "existence has the nature of non-existence and non-existence has the nature of existence" in some respect? To this he says: "All...
"All existents and non-existents, as categories, are always [of such a nature] by that [reason]. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.134ef)
Since it is established that both existence and non-existence possess the properties of existence and non-existence,

and since it is established that all entities (bhāvas) and non-entities (abhāvas) exist as causes through the non-difference of property and its substratum (dharma-dharmin), the statement that all entities and non-entities are mutually one another is logically justified; such is the meaning.

If this is so—that an entity (bhāva) possesses non-existence (abhāvatva) and non-existence possesses existence (bhāvatva)—then how is it that the well-established distinction between existence and non-existence, such as "substance and the rest are indeed existents" while "prior non-existence and the rest are indeed non-existents," remains valid? To this he says: "Nevertheless" (tathāpi).
Nevertheless, that which is first the object of a cognition of negation is non-existence;
but that which is first the object of an affirmative cognition is the other [existence].
The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is between "negation" and "cognition.
It is "another state of being" (*paro bhāvaḥ*).
Although this point has already been stated previously, there is no fault in reminding the reader of it again here due to the context. *8,99*
It has been stated that the possession of the properties of existence and non-existence by both non-existence and existence is established through perception and other means of valid cognition.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Therefore... (tasmāt).
Therefore, that which has its distinctions and so forth destroyed is understood simply as "existent."
*Pradhvasta* means destruction; *pradhvaṃsa* means difference or distinctness.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), properties such as being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) are included, because non-existence possesses the characteristics of existence.

For this very reason, it is understood that non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) and the like indeed possess a collection of positive properties (*bhāvadharmajāta*), such as distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) and cognizability (*prameyatva*).
This is to be construed with "by means of perception and so forth" (*pratyakṣādinā*):
it is understood that destruction is distinct from prior non-existence or from a jar, and is both cognizable and denotable.
We maintain that if one does not admit that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a property (*dharma*), there would be a contradiction with that [very fact].

For instance, in the statement "a jar is not a cloth," it is evident that existence (*bhāva*) possesses the property of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*); thus, this has not been explicitly demonstrated.
Having thus established in general that non-existents consist of both existence and non-existence, he applies this to the present context: "It exists," and so forth.
There is non-existence and there is destruction; the absence of the body is its reduction to ashes.
All this and more is appropriate... // MAnu 2.137a //
The word "therefore" (tasmāt) is understood from the context.
Since it has been established in this way that non-existence possesses the nature of existence and existence possesses the nature of non-existence, therefore non-existence exists; destruction exists.

The meaning is that it is logical to say that "the absence of the body" (*dehābhāva*) is the substantive (*viśeṣya*) and "ashes-ness" (*bhasmatā*) is the qualifier (*viśiṣṭa*), and that there is non-difference (*abheda*) between the two; likewise, in the case of "the jar does not know," the positive entity (*bhāva*) is the substantive and the negative state (*abhāva*) is the qualified form, and there is non-difference between the two—this is what has been stated. [Objection:
If the identity of existence and non-existence is not contradictory, then why would the jar itself not be of the nature of its own non-existence? To this, he says: "from perception" (*pratyakṣāt*).
... by means of direct perception and other valid instruments of knowledge.
The word "siddham" (established) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

The identity of existence and non-existence when they are qualified by their respective qualificanda is established by means of valid cognition such as perception, but this is not the case for a jar and its absence.
Therefore, there is no over-extension [of the argument]; this is the meaning.

Alternatively, is the fact that existence and non-existence stand in the relation of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmin*), and that there is no difference between the attribute and the substrate, established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*)—is this a proof for the identity of existence and non-existence as qualified by their respective qualifiers, or is it a ground for its possibility?
In the first case, the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) applies.
In the second case, a proving factor must be stated; with reference to this, the following was said:
By this, what was stated as "in some cases" is explained.
Alternatively, the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) is elaborated upon by the passage beginning with "for existence," and so forth. To explain:

Some proponents of the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavādins) claim that origination is the manifestation of that which already exists; in order to refute this, he says: "For existence... and so forth.
In this context, the words "existence" (bhāva) and "non-existence" (abhāva) refer to being and non-being.
That lump of clay which is considered the cause is the non-existence of the effect in the form of the jar, yet it is also the existence of that very thing in its own nature.
Alternatively, that jar, prior to its production, is an existing entity (bhāva).
That very non-existence is itself the absence [of being];

or rather, that lump of clay which, prior to the activity of the potter and others, was non-existent in the form of a jar, becomes that same thing immediately thereafter an existence in the form of a jar.
This is what is meant.
The effect is both different and non-different from its cause;
for that very reason, it is both existent and non-existent prior to its production.
Therefore, the cause—which previously lacked the nature of the effect before the operation of the causal factors—attains the form of the effect, and that [attainment] is what is called "production."

Now, since it is contradictory for a single thing to possess both difference and non-difference, as well as existence and non-existence, [the author] first presents a possibility by showing that just as for a single entity being both existent and non-existent is not contradictory, so too is this case; he establishes the existence and non-existence of each individual [entity] with two and a half verses beginning with "of the non-entity" (*abhāvasya*).
The explanation is exactly as before.
Let this be a mere possibility;

but what is the definitive proof? To this, [the author] establishes the existence of non-difference by means of a valid cognition (pramāṇa), since even the opponent accepts the non-existence of difference—therefore [he says]: "Therefore..."
The "distinction of the destroyed" refers to the distinction of things such as a jar that have been destroyed.
By the word "etcetera," the agency of things that have not yet arisen is included.
[As it is said: "Even for things that have perished, their distinction does not perish at all."

Thus, that existence which is perceived when difference has been destroyed, and that agency or objecthood— expressed in such statements as "the jar is born" or "he produces the jar"— which belongs even to what is not yet produced,
is indeed logical only because the effect exists prior to its production and after its destruction due to its non-difference from the cause.
For it is not logical that a thing which has attained absolute non-existence should possess a distinct intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) that is existent.
Nor can that which is absolutely non-existent possess causal agency; furthermore, the effect does not have an existence separate [from the cause],
because it is not perceived as such.
Therefore, one must accept that existence and the non-difference of the cause [are real];
moreover, it is not logical to assume a metaphorical status without a subverting argument,
for that would lead to over-extension.
This which has been stated is indeed understood;
the meaning is that it is not merely a matter of conventional usage.

Furthermore, the properties (dharmas) of non-existence would be existent things, and since they are established by means of valid cognition such as perception and so forth, they are indeed appropriate [to exist] and are not subject to refutation—this is what was stated.
He clarifies this with the words: "It exists."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), the fact that an entity such as a jar possesses the property of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) with respect to a cloth is included.
It might be argued:
even if mutual non-existence is a property of an entity, since it is distinct from that entity, how can it be said that the entity itself is non-existence?

If it is argued that this is not so because mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is a form of difference (*bheda*), and difference is accepted as being the very nature (*svarūpa*) of things, we say no;
for the difference of essential nature (*svarūpabheda*) is distinct from mutual non-existence.
Furthermore, what was stated—that even in the case of non-existence there exists separateness (*pṛthaktva*)—is incorrect.
Because there is a lack of evidence [for such a category];
because non-confusion is established by the very difference in essential nature (svarūpa-bheda);
and because separateness (pṛthaktva) is not something over and above the difference in essential nature—for these reasons, he says: "mutually... (anyonya).
Mutual non-existence, differentiation, and separateness are each distinct [qualities].
"And whatever they conceptualize has already passed away due to the weight of conceptualization.
The meaning is that [the elements] are distinct and separate from one another.
The word "and" (ca) serves to accumulate further refutations.
That which has already passed has been refuted previously;
by this, the fault of redundancy is avoided.
To the question "How [is there] the heaviness of conceptual construction (kalpanā-gaurava) and so forth?", he says: "By way of being synonyms."
For all those words are indeed understood as being synonymous.
The meaning is "by virtue of being employed in succession.
This refers to all [mantras], both worldly and Vedic.
Here, the proponents of Māyā (Māyāvādins) raise an objection.

As for the claim that the nature of all categories is established as consisting of both existence and non-existence— based on the observation that mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) and separateness (*pṛthaktva*), which are not distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of things], possess the properties of existence and non-existence— that is incorrect,
because it is untenable for difference (*bheda*) to be the very essence of a real entity (*vastu*). To explain:
First of all, division (*bheda*) is by nature a tearing apart;

for the word "division" has the form of the verbal root *bhid*, which means "to tear apart. If that [division], being of the nature of a state (*bhāva*), were to have an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then it too would undergo tearing apart.

Likewise, since difference is the very nature of even those parts, there would be a splitting apart therein as well; by this sequence, there would be universal emptiness. Furthermore, if difference were the essential nature of a thing, unity could not coexist within it, because unity—which inheres in a single undivided object—is in contradiction with difference.
In the absence of unity, multiplicity would also not exist,
because the latter is either of the nature of an aggregation of the former or is its effect;
and that which is devoid of both unity and multiplicity results in nothing but emptiness.
Furthermore, if difference were the very nature of an entity, it would follow that it is independent of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*),
because the nature of a thing is independent [of anything else].
For there is no such cognition as "the cloth from the pot," in the way that one has the cognition "the difference of the cloth from the pot."

If difference were the very nature of the thing itself, then even the appearance of a relationship between qualifier and qualified—such as "the jar is different" or "the difference of the jar"—would be difficult to maintain;
for a thing cannot be its own qualifier or its own related correlate.
Furthermore, in this case, doubt and error would be utterly eliminated.
For those two [cognitions] arise with the non-apprehension of difference as their cause.
In that case, if they occur by apprehending the substratum (dharmin), then since the difference—which is of the very nature of that [substratum]—is also apprehended, what room is there for those two?
If not, then all the more so, because they would be devoid of an object.

Furthermore, if difference—which is perceived as being constituted by its counter-correlate (pratiyogin) in the form "this is different from us"—were the very nature of the object, then, because that difference along with its adjuncts would be included within the object's own nature, even the counter-correlate would be submerged into that nature, and the result would be the very doctrine of non-duality (advaita). He refutes this [view] with the words: "Of difference... (*bhedasya*).

But those who claim that difference is the very nature of things and that they are empty are truly marvelous, because it is accepted that for one thing there must be a counter-correlative which is other than itself.

The word "tu" (but) connects with "however" (*tu*), excluding [the view] from the Vaiśeṣika and other systems under discussion. "In its own nature" (*svarūpatve*) means in the nature of the object to be distinguished;
"emptiness of everything" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the previously mentioned refutations. "Adbhutāḥ" means marvelous;
that is to say, such things are not seen among worldly people, nor even among those who investigate.
To address the question "How so?", he first refutes the attainment of emptiness with the words "Since... (yataḥ).

The connection is as follows: whatever difference is held to be the very nature (*svarūpa*) of a thing, with respect to that difference, the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is held to be a different entity altogether; therefore, they are "wonderful" (i.e., marvelous).
To the question, "Even if there is a different counter-correlate, how is the aforementioned fault avoided? he says: "For [with respect to] the counter-correlate... (*pratiyogino hi*).
For this distinction belongs to the counter-correlate; it does not exist in any way with respect to itself.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the reason, as before;
the word "this" (ayam) points to the fact that such a state is established by perception and other means of valid cognition;
and "from itself" means from the essential nature of the subject (*dharmin*).
This is what is meant:
for division, whose nature is tearing asunder, should tear apart that [object] from which it [originates];
but it does not [arise] from anything whatsoever with respect to any [object whatsoever].
For the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the difference that constitutes the very nature of a jar is not the jar itself— which would entail its own disintegration—
but rather other things such as jars.
Therefore, disintegration is not undesirable [in this case].
Because it does not bring about emptiness for that [object].
Furthermore, if the word *bheda* (difference) were derived from the instrumental sense—as in "that by which one is divided"—then difference would have to tear something asunder;
however, this is not the case, because we accept that it is derived from the sense of the action itself (*bhāva-sādhana*).

Therefore, with the intention that this resolution was stated only by way of concession—accepting for the sake of argument that [the suffix] functions as an instrument (karaṇa)—he says: "in any way whatsoever" (kathañcana).
This is what has been stated; the word "this" is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence.
Furthermore, even a cutting tool such as a sickle cuts that with which it is connected, but it does not cut itself.
Therefore, this must be stated in some way within the theory of the difference of properties (*dharmabheda*);
but what room is there for it in the theory of the difference of essential natures (*svarūpabheda*)?
By this very [argument], the claim that "if difference were the essential nature of the thing, unity could not coexist therein" is also refuted.
Unity and plurality are not contradictory in their intrinsic nature, for we observe that even a single jar possesses plurality in relation to something else.
Rather, they are contradictory in this sense: that which is plural in relation to a certain thing must be singular in relation to that very same thing.
In that case, the difference of a jar from another is simply its counter-correlative;
therefore, what contradiction is there in its being manifold in relation to that [other] while being one in relation to itself?
Furthermore, is it the coexistence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of oneness and manifoldness that is contradictory, or rather their relationship as property and property-possessor (dharmadharmibhāva)?
In the first case, there is no contradiction between unity and difference,
because difference, being the very nature [of the entity], lacks co-referentiality with unity. It is not the second case either.
Because one perceives "one" and "two," how can there be emptiness even in the absence of oneness and multiplicity?
For it is possible for that which lacks qualities to exist—just as qualities and so forth exist for the Vaiśeṣikas and others, or as Brahman exists for the proponents of Māyā. *8,114*
But surely, if difference were the very nature of the thing itself, it could not be defined by its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*),
because that [counter-correlate] would be absent from the nature of the thing;
therefore, this solution is not tenable.
If it is argued that, in such a case, by tearing asunder its own self, there is once again only emptiness (*śūnyatā*), we say no;
for neither from itself nor from another is such pervasion established.

For instance, even though the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman and its nature as the essence of Brahman are described by others (the Māyāvādins), they are accepted by us as well; and likewise, properties such as "otherness" (*paratva*) and so forth are accepted by us as being the very nature of substance (*dravya*).
Likewise, what contradiction is there in difference—which is defined by its counter-correlate—being the very nature of the thing?
Furthermore, one who asserts that difference is the nature of the thing must explain how he can accept that the nature of a thing is dependent on another for its definition.
At most, this much could be said:
How can there be a cognition of one and the same object both depending upon and not depending upon the cognition of its counter-positive?
Even in that case, it is not the very same cognition that undergoes both modes;
rather, these are two distinct cognitions.

And since that [distinction] will be consistent even with respect to a single entity by relying on the power of its specific attributes (*viśeṣa*), because difference is established as having another thing as its counter-correlate (*parapratiyogin*), how can there be the consequence of self-division?

Or, let there be division of the essential nature (*svarūpa*); nevertheless, it is improper to conclude that this results in emptiness (*śūnyatā*). With this intention, he says: "By way of division" (*vibhāgena*).
Through such division, there would be only a small portion; how, then, could there be emptiness?
Indeed, when a clod of earth or the like is destroyed through the division of its parts, what is perceived is the remainder of parts of small dimension, and not total emptiness.
Likewise, in every case, through division, there would merely be the remainder of fewer and fewer parts; how then could there be emptiness?

But surely, even if through the tearing apart of five or six locations there remains only a very small, smaller, or smallest amount of substance, and finally some kind of collection of parts reaches a state of emptiness, would that not result in the emptiness of everything? To this he says: "No."
For it is not accepted that an entity arises from the conjunction of things that are empty.

For when a thing is produced through a conjunction, if that [thing] is disintegrated, then following the destruction of the thing due to the cessation of the conjunction, only that [conjunction] remains.
For example, when a jar produced by the conjunction of threads is destroyed through the sequence of the disintegration of the threads and the cessation of the conjunction, the threads remain.

And so, if the production of certain extremely subtle things were to occur from a conjunction with emptiness (*śūnya*), then upon disintegration, through the cessation of the conjunction and the consequent destruction of the effect, only emptiness would remain.
And this is not accepted by those who follow authoritative means of knowledge;
therefore, the establishment of universal emptiness is untenable.
Here, "bhāva" means birth.
Now, it might be argued that "emptiness" (śūnyatva) is not intended here as an absolute non-existence to be established, but rather as the state of being most subtle;
and since that [subtlety] is not undesirable [as an end], he says: "because of its tearing apart" (vidāraṇa).
The verbal root *dhā* signifies the sense of splitting, and it denotes the quality of division.
This might be so if difference were of the nature of division; but it is not so,
because there is a lack of valid evidence [for such a claim].
However, the former resolution was stated precisely by way of concession.
But has it not been said here that the nature of difference as being of the essence of separation is understood from the word "bheda" itself? For that is indeed a form of the verbal root *bhid*.

And since that [root] has been explained as having the meaning of "tearing apart," the response here is as follows: when the root *bhid* is intended to mean "tearing apart," then the word *bheda* denotes the quality known as "disjunction" (*vibhāga*), and not the "difference" characterized as mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
This is what is meant:
"Each individual meaning has been presented merely to indicate that [the root] expresses an action;
for verbal roots possess multiple meanings, which are to be understood through actual usage."
According to this statement, the word *bhid* (to split) denotes both division and difference.
When it is said, "the jar is split," it is understood that it has burst open;
when it is said, "the sky is split from the jar," it is recognized as being different [from it].
In this context, "division" (*vibhāga*) consists of the nature of splitting apart (*vidāraṇā*), not mere otherness (*anyatva*).

Since it is precisely that [splitting] which is under discussion here, and not division, it is entirely inconsistent to suggest that even the reduction of difference— which is characterized by otherness— to the very nature of the entity would result in its extreme attenuation, because such a claim is fallacious (*chala*).

If it is asked, "What is the difference between disjunction (*vibhāga*) and otherness (*anyatva*), such that this is stated?"— it is not so, because the objection has already been refuted by the very mention of "quality" (*guṇa*).
For disjunction is accepted as a quality by the Vaiśeṣikas and others.
"Otherness (*anyatā*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)"— the distinction between these two is clear.
However, for one who, like a proponent of illusion (*māyāvādī*), does not accept the process [of categories] beginning with qualities (*guṇa*),
he says "even in the absence of division" (*avidāraṇe 'pi*) in order to instruct him.
For even though his mouth is not split apart, his two lips are nevertheless parted.
The term "of the mouth" refers to the two lips belonging to the mouth;
and this applies specifically to the proponent of illusion (māyāvādin).

For when the proponent of illusion remains silent due to being unable to provide an answer, even though there is no actual separation characterized by the splitting apart of his two lips, the two lips are nonetheless distinct, possessing a difference characterized by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
It is indeed yours [to say]:
"That which exists when another is absent is certainly different from that [other]," and this is well-established.
Therefore, it is understood that difference, by virtue of being a distinction, is simply a distinct entity.
By the phrase "and of that," it is indicated that no further inconsistency regarding a difference in essential nature (svarūpa-bheda) can be conceived.
If one objects: "But why is there no [inconsistency]?
For [objections] such as the impossibility of the relationship between qualifier and qualified have not been resolved," we say: No.
Even though [the two] are of the same nature, the manifestation of the relationship between qualifier and qualified is possible by virtue of a particularity (*viśeṣa*);
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that such expressions as "Brahman is bliss" (*ānandaṃ brahma*) and "bliss of Brahman" (*ānandaṃ brahmaṇaḥ*) would be untenable.
Furthermore, there is no impossibility of doubt or error [in this case].
This is because the states of being known and unknown are logically possible only if there are specific attributes;

otherwise, since the nature of the Self is self-luminous, its very essence—including such qualities as non-duality and bliss—would also be manifest, and thus no doubt or error could ever arise for anyone regarding it.
If it is argued that this occurs due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), [we reply:]...
In this case as well, one should be satisfied with the fact that it is so by virtue of similarity and the like;
and as for what was stated regarding its ultimate conclusion in non-duality.
It must be explained why this is so.

If one should think: "Just as when a long-eared man has arrived, [the command] 'bring the blue [cloth]' and so forth—whatever pertains to the one possessing the accessory (parikara) also pertains to the accessory itself," [that is not the case].

Likewise, if difference—which is constituted by its counter-correlate—were the very nature of the locus (*dharmin*), then the counter-correlate itself would also be submerged therein; is this stated on the basis of a mere possibility, or as a matter of universal pervasion (*vyāpti*)?
It cannot be the first.
The first [alternative] is not tenable because its root is too loose;
nor is the second,
because that [definition] is absent in cases such as "Let the owner of the painting be brought," or "A resident of Kāśī has arrived."

If it is argued that for one who relies on the ultimate perspective (*pāramārthikī dṛṣṭi*), even that [worldly example] is unestablished (*asiddha*), then alas, what partiality this shows! For, while attempting to establish a pervasion (*vyāpti*) by adducing an undesirable consequence for the opponent, he highly values a worldly example; yet, when there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), he remains indifferent toward it.
If it is argued that one should only produce an undesirable consequence for the opponent using what is established for the opponent themselves, [we reply:]...
In that case, the opponent will also admit the laxity of the root [of their own position] by means of what is established for themselves.
If it is asked, "What is the cause of this diversity?", we reply:
"Because the counter-correlates (pratiyogins) are utilized merely as that which serves to differentiate [the object]."
Thus, since the Māyāvāda is exposed as faulty without even considering the perspectives of one's own or other schools, it is appropriate to simply disregard it as the speech of a madman;
with the thought, "What is the use of refuting it? he concludes with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).
Therefore, because it consists of the words of a madman, the doctrine of illusion (māyāvāda) is to be disregarded.
Now, it may be asked: "Since such a view contradicts the established doctrine (siddhānta), why was it not refuted by the author of the Sūtras?
This is answered by the following: the implication is that it was "neglected" by the author of the Sūtras.

Having thus refuted *samavāya*, he now refutes the disagreement regarding the number of the qualities of God (*īśvara*), since the qualities and so forth—which are related to it—have been brought into the discussion by the context of the relationship itself. He says: "And not... [na ca].
Nor is the Lord— whose ocean of infinite qualities flows with a constant and unceasing bliss—
to be measured by means of the eightfold attributes, because He is beyond being so measured.
Īśvara is not to be known or understood in the form "He possesses exactly eight qualities by virtue of having eight qualities.
Why? Because he is not proven; that is, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding his possession of eight qualities.
However, the object of knowledge is an infinite ocean of excellences, flowing with intense and constant bliss;
like the ocean,
it is an "arṇava," specifically the milk-ocean that overflows with nectar.
And this [state] flows with the nectar of bliss that possesses no small measure of qualities;
it is "possessing infinite qualities" because within it there are infinite auspicious attributes such as the wish-fulfilling gem and others.
This too is "possessing infinite qualities" because within it there are infinite qualities such as bliss and so forth.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which flows with constant and abundant bliss" (*amanda-sadānanda-syandin*), and "that which is infinite in qualities" (*ananta-guṇa*), and "that which is an ocean" (*arṇava*).
Since there is no proof for the Lord’s possession of infinite qualities just as there is for His possession of eight qualities, he says: "In me" (*mayi*).
In me, who am infinite, possessing infinite qualities and infinite forms by virtue of those qualities,
there exists a great ocean of knowledge, power, and majesty consisting of infinite attributes.
"Nārāyaṇa is supreme; he is the highest state beyond all sentient beings"—this and other such infinite Vedic passages establish this very point.
The infinite quality of Viṣṇu... [2.2.146a]
"Anantaguṇaḥ" means one whose qualities are infinite and incalculable.
By the phrase "infinite in qualities," it is intended that each individual quality is limitless and possesses infinite internal distinctions.
The expression "anantavigrahaḥ" concludes the statement of the Blessed One.
The subsequent Vedic statement [is as follows]:
"In the greatness of the qualities" is stated by way of both the general and the particular;
"greatness" (māhātmya) refers to an excellence of magnitude.
Since [the term] "the supreme state" (paraṃ padam) is mentioned with reference to something else, there is no fault of gender discrepancy.
Now, one might ask: why should these statements not be taken as having metaphorical meanings? To this, he says: "How indeed... (kathameva).
... for how indeed can this be set aside? Mānava 2.2.146b.
For a primary meaning is set aside only by the force of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*),
and since no such argument exists here, how could Viṣṇu’s possession of infinite qualities ever be set aside?
Furthermore, that which has been asserted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others— the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of the Lord’s knowledge, will, and effort— is also incorrect.
"‘Infinite in terms of qualities’—this is because it is established by scripture that each of the qualities possesses infinite particularities.
And he states the subverting argument against not accepting this: ‘If...’"
If, moreover, infinite particulars are excluded from that knowledge and so forth, [then...]
How can that specific objectivity be prescribed for the sake of omniscience?
For any distinction based on limiting conditions (aupādhika) has already been refuted previously.

The state of having this or that object—namely, the state of having jars and so forth as objects—is "enjoined," meaning it is accepted as existing. To prevent the objection that there might not be such objective status, it is said: "for the sake of omniscience."
This is an illustration;
it should also be understood as including the sense of being the creator of all things and so forth.
In this context, the phrase "infinite particulars" is a statement established according to the scriptures.
In reality, however, if the knowledge of God and so forth were devoid of distinctions, then it would not possess the status of having those respective objects;
and in that case, His omniscience and other attributes would not exist,
for one is called "omniscient" only by virtue of possessing knowledge of all objects.
Likewise, one who possesses the desire and effort directed toward the production of all effects is the creator of all;
and one who possesses the desire and so forth directed toward the destruction of all effects is the destroyer of all.
Furthermore, omniscience and other such qualities are accepted by the opponent for the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, for that purpose, cognition and so forth must be conceived as having various respective objects;
and if that were the case, how could there be a lack of distinction? By this, the following [objection] is also refuted. *8,127*

As they say: "For knowledge and the like, being impermanent, would require the accompaniment of an object by virtue of their status as the instrument of action; but for that which is eternal, what need is there for an object?"
Furthermore, because objects are infinite, their infinite variety is established.
It might be argued:
"The cognition of the Lord is indeed devoid of distinctions, consisting merely of the nature of consciousness."
That [will], however, is designated as having this or that object by means of various limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as a jar and so forth.
Thus, its will remains indeed undivided and takes the form "let it be so";
nevertheless, through various limiting adjuncts such as creation and so forth, it is called the desire to create (sisṛkṣā), the desire to maintain (saṃjihīrṣā), and so on.
The same applies to effort as well.

Therefore, even though there is no intrinsic distinction [in the self], it is logical that it possesses various objects of cognition and attributes such as omniscience by virtue of adventitious distinctions; hence he says: "adventitious" (aupādhika).
The meaning is as follows: Is there a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*) or not?
If there is, how can there be "absence of distinction" (*nirviśeṣatva*)?
If there is not, then there is again the absence of omniscience and so forth; thus [the objection] is refuted by the very same reasoning stated previously.
Furthermore, does the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), which is connected with cognition and so forth, produce a distinction while being connected, or while being unconnected?
In the first case, since there is no connection other than that of the relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), its status as an object has already been established previously.
In the second case, there is the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, does the creation and so forth occur through a volition and the like having the form "let it be," or through one having the form "let the creation and so forth come to be"? Not the first, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
In the second [case], there is a distinction from itself; such is the general direction [of the argument].

Some, such as the Vaiśeṣikas and others, assert that the knowledge of the Lord (Īśvara) is not self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). He refutes them with the words: "Self-luminosity also... (*svaprakāśatvam api*).
But for those by whom the self-luminosity of knowledge has been denied, how can that [knowledge] possess omniscience? ... MAnu 2.148a-c.

The word "but" (*tu*) is used to indicate that certain [schools], such as the Vaiśeṣikas and others, do indeed accept self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*). [The phrase] "of knowledge" (*jñānasya*) refers to the knowledge of the Lord (*īśvarajñāna*). The connection [of the sentence] is with the words "by which."
The word "of them" refers to their position;
"of him" refers to that Lord.
To the question, "How is it that in the absence of self-luminosity there is an absence of omniscience?", he says: "sva... (*8.130*).
...without the attainment of one's own knowledge. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.148d)
The meaning is: "because there is no apprehension of His own cognition.
For the cognition of the Lord is indeed one and the same, and it takes as its object only that which is distinct from itself, but not its own nature; thus, how could the Lord be omniscient?
He raises the objection regarding the possibility of the Lord's omniscience even in the absence of self-luminous cognition: "Cognition," [he says].
"One knowledge is that which attains the universe, while the other is the supreme object of that knowledge;
by means of these two knowledges alone, the Supreme Lord is omniscient. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.149)
If this is argued... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.150a //

"Omniscient" (*viśvādhiga*) means that whose object is the knowledge of everything other than itself; thus it is so described. This fault would arise if the Lord possessed only a single cognition, but this is not the case.
Indeed, there are two types of God’s knowledge:
therein, one has as its object everything together with a second knowledge distinct from itself;
the second, however, takes that [first] knowledge as its object.
And thus, even though knowledge lacks self-objectification (*svaviṣayatva*), the omniscience of the Lord is established by means of these two kinds of knowledge alone.

Nevertheless, with the intention that otherwise the Lord’s lack of omniscience—or the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of that knowledge—would be difficult to avoid, he states the following reply: "This very [knowledge]... [eṣa eva].
If this very object were determined by that cognition, then it would indeed be self-luminous. MAnu 2.2.150a-c.
Let alone the impossibility of the simultaneous occurrence of specific qualities of the self belonging to the same genus; [one might think],
"I possess two cognitions," or "By means of two cognitions, I am omniscient."
"Is this my knowledge, this is the object of that knowledge, and this is the object of that [other]—is it this very meaning that is known by God, or not?
If the latter position were taken, His omniscience would not exist.
If the former, is it known by one of these two [knowledges], or by another knowledge?"
This is the response to the first [objection]:
if this very object is determined and made an object of experience by one of those two cognitions, then that cognition must indeed possess self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "For cognition... (*jñānaṃ hi*).
For this knowledge is indeed a distinguishing characteristic.
Although this cognition does not, when isolated, become its own object, nevertheless,
it certainly serves as a qualifier for the object of that [other] cognition— namely, the meaning of "I" and so forth, which consists of two cognitions. And thus,
since its object is a qualified thing, its status as the object of itself, being the qualifier, is indeed unavoidable.
For it is not logical to say that the staff does not appear in the direct perception of the "staff-bearer.
Regarding the second [alternative], he states the fault: "by another cognition" (*jñānāntareṇa*).
If it were known by another cognition, there would indeed be an infinite regress.
If this object were to be made an object of a third cognition,
then in this case there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*), and the rule that "the Lord possesses two cognitions" would be absent.
However, one who maintains the restriction that [the Lord] possesses the three types of knowledge should be asked:
does the Lord know such matters as "I am the possessor of the three types of knowledge," or not?
In the second case, however, he would lack omniscience.
Regarding the first [alternative], is it by one of these three, or by the fourth?
It is not the first.
For [otherwise] it would follow that [consciousness] is self-luminous. In the second case, however, there is simply an infinite regress;
thus, the addiction to accepting a succession of further cognitions would be unavoidable. *8,132*
If it is argued, "What fault is there in accepting that the cognitions of the Lord are infinite?",

the author concludes with the words "self-luminosity," intending to show that it is better to accept the self-luminosity of a single cognition than to resort to the conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) of an infinite number of them.
From this, its self-luminosity would unavoidably follow as a consequence.

If it is argued: "Is it not the case that self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) is contradicted by such [inferences] as 'knowledge is not self-luminous because it is an entity' (*vastutvāt*), and therefore how is it appropriate to accept it? [We reply: No.

If the cognition of the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, "whatever is an entity is not self-luminous"—does not take itself as its own object, then the establishment of the pervasion would not be a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāravat*).
Alternatively, this conclusion may be intended by one who holds that if [the Lord] were made an object of cognition, His self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) would be difficult to maintain.
As for what was stated— that the Lord possesses infinite qualities— that is untenable,
because there is no existence of qualities beyond the twenty-four.
Even in that case, [the attributes] are not applicable to some [beings], such as Īśvara.
Therefore, it is established that the Blessed One is endowed with exactly these eight established qualities.
This is not so.
Because qualities such as heroism, magnanimity, and eloquence exist,
and because there is no logical inconsistency even in the case of certain things being accepted by another;
for instance:

If it is argued that the existence of happiness for the Lord (Īśvara) should not be accepted because of the following inference—which establishes a sublation (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position: "The Lord is devoid of happiness, because he is devoid of suffering, like a jar;
if he possessed happiness, it would follow that he must also possess suffering, like Devadatta."
Regarding that, he first states the refutation of the supporting argument (*tarka*):
"He would be possessed of pleasure and possessed of pain; thus, our pervasion (*vyāpti*) would not hold. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.152ab)
To the question "How is there a lack of pervasion? he says: "The state of being free from suffering."
The state of being free from suffering and great bliss is declared by the Lord through the Veda itself.
Although happiness is observed to be concomitant with suffering in cases such as Devadatta, nevertheless,

this objection regarding the subversion of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be raised even at the time of grasping the pervasion prior to its application to the Lord (*Īśvara*), who is indeed devoid of suffering;
for since it can be asserted in this manner in every case, the aforementioned fault cannot be avoided.
Not so;
for this would be the case only if, in a situation where a consequence is drawn based on one's own mere admission, one were to assert a breach of pervasion (vyāpti).
But such is not the case here.
For it is precisely by the authority of scripture that the deviation of happiness and suffering [from the Lord] is established;
thus it has been said: "It is stated by scripture itself."
The singular number is used because each [term] is individually connected.
To the question "What is that scriptural passage? he cites it by way of its meaning: "yaḥ" (he who).

And that [knowledge] is expressed in such passages as: "He who transcends hunger and thirst, as well as sorrow and the rest, knowing the bliss of Brahman, is free from evil," and so forth. (Manu 2.2.153)
By this [phrase], he cites the Śruti passage: "He who transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death";
and by the term *vipāpma* ("free from evil"), he cites: "The Self which is free from evil."
"...such scriptural passages as these," which declare [the Self] to be free from suffering and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Since it is plausible that the scripture concerning bliss (*ānanda*) has as its object merely the absence of suffering, it cannot be said—on the basis of scripture—that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) underlying the reductio (*prasaṅga*) is broken. To this, [the author] says, while for the moment conceding that [the reason] is "conditioned" (*sopādhika*):

Regarding the phrase "of the Lord" (*īśvarasya*): even if it is argued that the Lord’s being thus desired [as the cause] is conditioned by suffering (*duḥkhitvopādhi*), what answer could one who is intent on disregarding the sacred revelation (*śruti*) possibly give? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.154)
Likewise, "being desired" means the state of being desired [with the thought], "May he be miserable.
"The limiting adjunct of misery" (duḥkhitvopādhi) is that which causes misery. By the word "also" (api), the possession of demerit and so forth is included.
Disregard is the abandonment of an established meaning in the absence of a subverting factor.
Let it be that for now there is no breach of pervasion by relying on scripture;
however, it will occur due to the presence of an adventitious condition (*upādhi*).

Because a relationship that possesses an *upādhi* (limiting condition) is necessarily subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). [Objection: Since there is a rule that "whoever is happy must also be miserable" is precisely the object of God’s will (*īśvarecchā*), this [suffering] cannot be an *upādhi*. To this, he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
Nor should there be a desire for one's own suffering; therefore, this is prohibited.
For even though the Lord possesses happiness— according to such scriptural passages as "Knowing the bliss of Brahman"— He does not possess limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Since no one has a desire for their own suffering, the claim that this adjunct is a pervader of what is intended to be pervaded is thereby refuted.
Although this rule is not established by mere observation—
since that would lead to over-extension—
it can nevertheless be said that there is no restrictive factor [to account for it].

Nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated in order to establish a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) for the purpose of preventing the abandonment of the literal meaning of the scripture.
This might be so if the scriptural passage concerning bliss were a statement about [ordinary] pleasure; but this is not the case.
If it is argued that this is because the passage has as its purport the absence of suffering (duḥkhābhāva), [we reply:]...
Is this scripture sublated by some contradicting factor so that it is displaced from its own meaning, or does it remain exactly as it is?
It cannot be the second [alternative],
because since even the scripture concerning the absence of suffering could be interpreted otherwise, it would follow that reasoning (tarka) would become a source of valid knowledge (pramāṇa).
Regarding the first [position], there is neither perception nor scripture that acts as a sublater (*bādhaka*).

Therefore, it must be stated whether the undesirable consequence of suffering (*duḥkhitva-prasaṅga*) in the case of happiness, or the inference of being free from suffering (*nirduḥkhatva-anumāna*), acts as the sublater.
Furthermore, both of these must proceed either by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*) or by the force of mere co-observation (*sahadarśana-mātra*).
Not the first, because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

For only when the scripture's deviation from its own meaning is established can the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of inference based on reasoning be established; and only when that [pervasion] is established can the scripture's deviation from its own meaning be established. (8.138)
But surely this is equally true for you as well:
if the scripture is intent upon its own primary meaning, there is a breakdown of the pervasion (vyāpti) between reasoning and inference;
yet, if that pervasion exists, the scripture must be intent upon its own primary meaning.
Not so;
for it is only the abandonment of a well-known meaning that requires a subverting factor (bādhaka),
not the state of being intent upon its own literal meaning.
[He states] "the absence of sublation," because that [absence] is established simply through cognition.
Regarding the second [alternative], however, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga); thus he says: "together" (saha).
Merely upon seeing him, one becomes a denier of the Vedas.
For how could one not infer that even sacrifices and the like are causes of sin, since they are joined with violence? 2.156a-c.

The term "sahadarśanam" (simultaneous perception) refers to the observation of that which is to be established (the *sādhya*) together with the means of establishment (*sādhana*), or the probans (*āpādaka*) together with the consequence (*āpādya*).
One who denies the scriptures (*śrutis*) that proclaim the bliss of the Lord is one who causes them to deviate from their own meaning.
By the phrase "of sacrifice and so forth," the giving of barley-grass to cows is included by the word "etcetera."
"From conjunction" (*yuteḥ*) means from association.

The point is this: if the scriptural meaning of "bliss" were to be discarded on the mere basis of seeing [the deity] together with it, then one might as well discard the scriptural meaning of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices by seeing them together with violence—since there is no distinction between the two cases—as the principle that "whatever involves violence is a cause of sin" would apply equally.
But surely, the lack of distinction between "being violence" and "being a means to sin" is unestablished; for the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of "being prohibited" exists in their concomitance.

Nor is there any limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the connection between being happy and being miserable. One might object—anticipating the argument that "the Lord's will to act in such a way" is the limiting condition—that this objection will be refuted later; thus he says: "In that case... (*tatra*).
...in that case, if the qualification is prohibited. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.156cd)
The phrase "it is said to exist" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
What indeed is this so-called "prohibitedness"?
If it is argued that it is being stated by the Veda as something not to be performed;
Non-duty (akartavyatā) consists either in the unfitness for performance or in being a cause for the agent's non-desire [to act].
It is not the first [alternative],
because even the killing of a Brahmin is sometimes performed.
Regarding the second [alternative] as well, is it the state of being a means to accomplish what is undesirable directly or indirectly?
Not the first,
because suffering is not observed to arise immediately after the act of violence.

But in the second case, it would be said that being a means to evil is the limiting adjunct (upādhi). And thus, since the presence of this adjunct exists here as well, there is no distinction at all; so he refutes [the objection] with the words: "by not being subject to suffering" (aduḥkhitvena).
And how would the non-mention [of the self] by virtue of its being free from suffering not constitute a limiting condition (upādhi)?

Regarding the phrase "it is not stated as being non-suffering," the meaning is that it is stated as being suffering. To the question, "What is this scriptural statement of Devadatta and others as being subject to suffering? he says: "It is 'without suffering' (aduḥkham)."
Everything else is not suffering; rather, it is living beings alone who suffer.
It is for the sake of removing their suffering that this revealed scripture (śruti) proceeds.
For such is the supreme Vedic revelation... Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.158a.
The meaning is that [the scripture] proceeds to establish the Supreme Self as the means for the abandonment of suffering.

Having thus refuted the reasoning (*tarka*) that supports inference, he now also refutes the inference: "The Lord is not happy, because He is free from suffering, like a jar"—this is what is meant by the phrase "the statement of the Śruti."
If the Vedic injunction is the authority, what need is there for inference, which is like a nipple on a goat's neck? (Manu 2.158b–d)
Regarding the cause of valid knowledge (*pramā*):
is the scriptural passage beginning with "Knowing Brahman as bliss" (*ānandaṃ brahmaṇo vidvān*) a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), or not?
If the latter position is taken, there is an abandonment of one's own established tenet (*apasiddhānta*).

Regarding the first [position], the meaning is that the inference must be disregarded because it is sublated and thus fails to establish the intended object, like the fleshy protuberance on a goat's neck (*ajāgalastana*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "The scripture is indeed a valid means of knowledge; however, because it contradicts inference, its apparent meaning should be set aside and it should be interpreted as referring to the absence of suffering. Anticipating this doubt:
This is not so, because inference is never seen to sublate scriptural revelation; rather,
in some cases, it sublates it only by virtue of being its very basis of existence (*upajīvya*).
In the same way, he states that "by means of inference" there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if one were to accept [the cognition] as being sublated.

If an object perceived through revelation were to be set aside by inference in the manner previously described, then neither God nor Dharma would exist, nor would their fruit... [Mānava-dharma-śāstra 2.159]
By the previously mentioned [reasoning] stated in the *Śāstrayoni* Sūtra;
the sense is that even if God (*īśvara*) were seen in the Vedas (*śruti*), He would have to be rejected due to the contradiction with inference.
And the same intended meaning applies here as well: that dharma would not exist, nor would its fruit exist.
Sacrificial performance is not a cause for an unseen result (adṛṣṭa), because it is an action, like the act of spitting;
or, dharma is not a means to happiness, because it is unseen, like adharma—since such inferences are possible.
He states that the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) is resolved by its opposite with the words "by that" (tena).
Therefore, in this matter, scripture alone must be the authority.

Because an undesirable consequence would follow if one were to accept that the scriptural passage concerning bliss is sublated by an inference devoid of the quality of being a source of subsistence (*upajīvyatva*) and so forth, for that reason this scripture is authoritative (*pramāṇa*) here precisely regarding the Lord’s possession of bliss, and not otherwise;
let it not be the case that the scripture is non-authoritative.
And let it not be that [the scripture] is set aside by a different meaning due to sublation by inference; even so, why would it be a sublater of inference?
It might rather be a counter-inference (pratirodhikā). To this, he says: "Of the Lord" (īśasya).
Since the existence of the Lord is established through inference, the Veda must be a means of valid cognition regarding its nature;
for it is by that [Veda] that the Lord is described as being complete with all auspicious qualities.
An inference of his lack of bliss would not be a valid means of knowledge, because it contradicts the cognition that apprehends the subject itself. ... MAnu 2.161a-c.
The term "inference" (*anumā*) is an indicator for means of valid cognition other than scripture.
"Cognition of the subject" (*dharmipramā*) refers to the means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*).
For inference operates only when the subject has been established by another means of valid cognition, and not otherwise.
In this regard, it has already been established that God is the subject (dharmin) and that He is not established by means of inference;
furthermore, the fact that He is not an object of perception and so forth is agreed upon even by the opponent.
Therefore, by the method of elimination (pariśeṣa), it must be accepted that only scripture (śruti) is the apprehender of the subject, the Supreme Lord.
Thus, by this inference, the authority of the Śruti is accepted;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of its own non-arising.
And that Śruti, which is to be relied upon, declares the Lord to be possessed of bliss.
Therefore, because it contradicts that [perception], inference is indeed not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*),
just like the inference of coldness which contradicts the perception that apprehends the actual nature of fire.
Nor should it be argued that the statement "He who is omniscient," and so forth, is what inference depends upon, rather than the teaching of bliss.
Since the entire Veda forms a single coherent statement, it is impossible for it to function as a partial authority;
otherwise, only that which apprehends fire would be dependent upon it.
But it might also be argued that [the inference] does not grasp the heat at that time.

With this very same reasoning, the author concludes—intending to show that all inferences regarding the Lord’s lack of a physical body and so forth are indeed invalid because they contradict the Śruti—by saying "therefore" (tasmāt).
Therefore, it is not useful even in the slightest degree.

In this statement regarding the Lord (*īśvara*), for this very reason it is said that He is "full of all qualities" (*sarvaguṇaiḥ pūrṇaḥ*); otherwise, he would have simply said "possessing bliss" (*ānandavān*).
Demonstrating another logical inconsistency in the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, [the author] says: "And because [it] exists eternally. (*nityameva ca bhāvāt*) [8.145]
Thus he explains the Sūtra: "Because of the desire for what is eternal."
Because the Supreme Lord possesses eternal desire, because atoms exist eternally,
and because the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and time also exist, the effect would necessarily be produced at all times.

For the Vaiśeṣikas and others indeed accept the creation of the great elements through the process of dyads and so forth at a specific time; however, upon close examination of their respective systems, this is not tenable, for according to their position, the effect would have to exist eternally.
If it were so, then it would have to exist even prior to that [desired time].
Why?
Because the determination of the time of the arising of an effect is dependent upon the completeness of the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*).
In that regard, at the initial creation, atoms—which serve as the inherent causes (samavāyikāraṇa)—exist eternally;
likewise, the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa), which is the will of God (īśvara), is eternal; and so too are time and space.
Even though the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), designated as merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), is not eternal, it is nevertheless accepted that it exists during the dissolution (*pralaya*).
If it is argued that its functional manifestation (*vṛttilābha*) does not exist then, we say no;
for since that [manifestation] is caused by the will of the Lord (*īśvara*) and other factors, its absence when those causes are present would be logically untenable.
For this very reason, the objection that there can be no constant creation of gross objects and the like due to the absence of the non-inherent cause, namely the conjunction of atoms, is refuted.
If it is argued that the non-arising of conjunction is also untenable because of the absence of action as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*),
we say no; for the non-arising of that [action] is likewise impossible.
Furthermore, there is no other cause for the dyad (vyaṇuka) and so forth than this [set of causes];

for if there were such a deficiency, the effect would be absent prior to the desired time. And if the effect were not to arise even after the desired collection of conditions has been present, it would never arise at all.
"Because there is no regulator" means that it possesses the nature of being eternal; "because of its existence" implies [its existence] even during dissolution.
The word "eva" (only/always) is connected with "sadaiva" (always).
Furthermore, the statement "it would be an effect" was said as a concession;
however, in reality, according to that position, the production of dyads and so forth is never possible.
Because the cause of destruction, such as the will of God (īśvarecchā) and so forth, is eternal, it constitutes a counter-argument (satpratipakṣa).

Even if one were to accept that the cause of destruction is the will of God and the like conjoined with the production of the effect, it would follow that destruction occurs immediately after production.
