For this very reason, he will state later: "At the beginning of creation" (*sṛṣṭyādi*). (8.147)
This would indeed be the case if time alone were the cause of either creation or dissolution;
but it is not so.

Rather, it is a specific state of time [that acts as the cause]; therefore, the regulation of creation and dissolution is logically established through the presence and absence of that specific state.

If it is argued that the mere will of God is not the cause of creation and so forth, but rather a specific aspect of it, and that the regulation of creation and so forth is therefore dependent on the presence or absence of that [specific aspect], we say no. Is the distinction of time, place, and so forth, adventitious (*aupādhika*), or is it inherent (*svābhāvika*)?
Not the first, because it has already been refuted;
as for the second, however, it would constitute an abandonment of one's own tenets (apasiddhānta), as he says: "For not..."
For in that view, there is no distinction of time... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.163ab //
By the word "hi" (for/indeed), he recalls that statement [of his own]: "Because space, time, and direction are each singular," and so forth.
The mention of "time" (*kāla*) is also an elliptical indication for the will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*). *8,148*
Is this objection not equally applicable to you as well?
For instance, primordial matter (*prakṛti*), which is the material cause of the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest, is indeed eternal.
Likewise, the instrumental causes such as the will of God (Īśvara), time, and so forth, are also the very same causes of dissolution.
Therefore, the regulation of the timing of creation and dissolution would be difficult to establish even for you; hence he says: "In our view... [asmanmate].
...In our view, this desire of Hari for creation and so forth occurs only at a specific time, yet it is eternal. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.163b–d)
Although in our view Hari’s will is eternal—
and this [mention of] *prakṛti* and so forth is merely illustrative—
nevertheless, the construction is that the creation and so forth of this [universe], beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), occurs only at a specific time.
We accept that difference [between creation and dissolution] exists by its very nature at the appropriate time.

Thus, since it is specifically a particular time that serves as the cause for both creation and dissolution, it is logical that there is a restriction regarding the timing of creation and so forth based on the presence or absence of that [time], even when other causes are present. This is the intended meaning.
[Objection: Should it not rather be stated as "a particular time"?
Not so;
for "viśeṣa" means that which is distinguished (*viśiṣṭa*), and by adopting the analysis of the compound as "that [distinguished thing] which is time."
Is it not the case that it ought to be *sadātani*?
Not so;
this suffix is not one of the two, namely *ṭyu* or *ṭyul*.
However, this suffix *-tan* is used in the sense of "becoming" (*bhāva*);
or else, *tana* is a form derived from the root *tan*. (8.149)
If those temporal distinctions are eternal, then that same undesirable consequence remains as before;
furthermore, the admission of temporal distinctions would be useless.
If it is argued that they are non-eternal, then their cause must be stated.
True;
however, the material cause (*upādāna*) is indeed primordial matter (*prakṛti*).
He states the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) as well: "and the specific qualities" (*viśeṣāśca*). (8.150)
And the specific divisions of time are always subject to the will of Hari.

Not only the Mahat and the other principles, but also the specific divisions of time such as moments (kṣaṇa), instants (lava), and so forth [are produced by Hari alone]. The word "eva" (alone) is to be connected with "of Hari alone. By the term "always" (sadā), it is meant that there is no simultaneous creation of all moments, which would otherwise imply that even those [moments] are momentary.
However, what is meant is that [the creation] occurs as a continuous flow.
Now, from what source of valid cognition is it established that the specific divisions of time are born from the Supreme Lord? To this, he says: "All... (*sarve*).
For the Śruti itself declares with reverence: "All [the moments called] nimeṣas... (Manu 2.2.164cd).

The meaning is that the Śruti itself declares the birth of specific divisions of time from the Lord: "All moments (nimeṣas) were born from the Puruṣa who is beyond the lightning. Here, "lightning" (vidyut) signifies that which shines with distinction; from that Supreme Person, all moments—the various divisions of time—were born, meaning they arose according to their respective natures.
But surely this scripture states that the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of time are born from the Lord,
and not time itself;
for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of redundancy with the subsequent statement, "the *kāṣṭhās*, *kalās*, and *muhūrtas*."
For there exists no unit of time such as a *kāṣṭhā* or a *kalā* that exceeds the *nimeṣa*;
rather, the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the *nimeṣa* and so forth are entirely distinct. Thus, since there is no fault of redundancy therein, it is said: "with reverence."

Since [the text] first mentions that which is produced by a *nimeṣa* (twinkling) and then again mentions that which is produced by *kāṣṭhā* (a unit of time) and so forth for the sake of showing respect, there is no fault of tautology.
As for the objection that a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is not tenable, this has already been stated.
Now, one might object: words such as *nimeṣa* and the like denote the conjunction of the eyelashes and so forth, and do not directly denote time.

Therefore, this scriptural passage is not clearly capable of establishing that time itself is born from the Lord; for this reason, he cites a clear scriptural statement on the matter: "He brings forth... (udīrayati).
Even his speech arouses that power known as Time.

The meaning of the verse, “Thus, having placed the subtle elements within his body, he brings forth the power whose nature is time,” is that even the speech of this Lord declares the origin of time from the Lord.
The phrase “bringing forth the power whose nature is time” means generating the auxiliary power known as time (*kālātmikā*).
In this context, because the word "time" (kāla) denotes that Īśvara possesses the power (śakti) for the creation of the world, there is no room for the postulation of any other meaning.
It might be argued:
"Time, at any rate, is the instrumental cause (nimitta) of all things that have an origin."
Furthermore, there is no other time during the arising of time;
how, then, can its arising occur? If it is argued that prior time is the cause for subsequent time, we say no.

Because time is determined to be a cause by virtue of its being a locus—as in "born now" and "born then"—and because it is certain that a locus is simultaneous with the production of the effect, as seen in cases such as "born in the house" and "born in the cow-pen," he says: "of time."
There is no contradiction whatsoever between time and its having passed away.
The construction is as follows: if the production of time is accepted, not only does the existence of the proof remain intact, but there is also no contradiction whatsoever;
this will be elaborated upon later.
Thus, it has been established that, according to our own view, the temporal restriction of creation and so forth is caused by the presence or absence of specific times.
He establishes that same point in another way with the verse beginning "asaṅkhyātā" (innumerable).
Because desire also lacks a determinable limit, it is likewise [unbounded] at all times.
The phrase "of that which exists at all times" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

The meaning is as follows: although the will of the Lord exists at all times, because it possesses innumerable specific attributes—such as the state of being a desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*) existing in the form of both potentiality (*śakti*) and manifestation (*vyakti*)—it is logical that the regularity of creation and so forth is governed by the manifestation or non-manifestation of those [specifics].
Although this has been resolved merely by means of a difference in time—
since the Lord’s will does not become futile because it takes the form, "I shall create at a specific time"—
nevertheless, this actual state of affairs should be understood as it has been shown here. *8,157*
It has been stated that [this occurs] "by means of time's having reached its end" (*kālagatatvena*);
in that regard, is time inherent to itself, or is it inherent to another time? It cannot be the first [option].
The first [alternative] is not tenable because it is contradictory, like [the impossibility of] mounting one's own shoulders.
Nor is the second,
because that [subject] does not exist.

Alternatively, if [the Lord] were an existent being, the creation at another time would be purposeless; furthermore, if that [creation] were also to arise, it would entail the consequence of having to accept yet another interval of time. Therefore, he explains what was stated along with its proof: "The Lord" (īśa).
The lord, the place, and the time are always inherent within oneself.

"Space" (deśa) is a designation for the indeterminate ether (avyākṛtākāśa). By the expression "inherent within themselves" (svagatā), he wards off the suspicion that space and time might possess independence; [he states] they are "dependent on the Lord" (īśādhīnau). And those two are eternally dependent on Him and reside within Him.
Thus the Śruti also declares that [the funeral rite] must be performed at the very time prescribed for oneself.
Therefore, the Lord always desires only that which is created at that specific time;
for that time exists only then, since time is inherent within itself.
It is stated that the cognition and activity regarding existence depend solely upon the qualification [of the object] and are contingent upon the Supreme Lord.
The phrase "the scripture also" adds the witness as corroborative evidence;
for the scripture declares that time is inherent within itself, and this is established by the witness.
Therefore, because time is inherent within Himself,
that Lord (Īśa) exists at that very time; thus, always directing His attention toward His own time, He desires the creation of each respective period— this is the logical connection.
This is what is meant:
time is the cause as a locus (adhikaraṇa) only for those effects that occur subsequent to time, but not for time itself.
Only for the Supreme Lord—who, like one thinking "I shall create a jar tomorrow," desires the creation of time—remains the question: "What is this time that is intended as the locus?"
To this, the reply is: "It is precisely that which is to be created.
For the thing to be created has no prior existence; therefore, its status as the intended object does not depend upon [prior] existence.

Furthermore, the relationship between the locus and that which is to be located belongs to the One alone, as established by direct revelation (*śruti*) and other means of knowledge, and it is also logically consistent due to the power of specific distinctions.
Therefore, there is no inconsistency whatsoever regarding the production of time.
As for what was stated—that when the Lord’s will takes the form of a desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*), the creation of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest occurs—[that is so].
But when it becomes characterized by the desire to withdraw [the world], then dissolution occurs.
In this regard, it must be stated what the cause of this diversity is;
nor is it logical to say that a specific time is the cause.
Because that [result] would depend upon the will of a Lord, nor would it depend upon human effort, as that would entail a state of dependence; therefore, he says: "from its own nature alone."
For this desire arises from one's very own nature...
This [variety] is manifold;
therefore, since the specific times are dependent upon Īśvara, there is no occurrence of the fault of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya)—this is the meaning of the word "hi" (for).
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Of the God... (devasya).
... because of the Vedic revelation: "It belongs to the god alone. (Manu 2.169b)
"This is understood"—this is the ellipsis.
Another says:
"What is the use of this conceptualization of the diversity of time and so forth?"
Since the restriction of time for both causes and effects is established by their very nature (svabhāva),
one must ultimately accept the doctrine of intrinsic nature; therefore, it is better to accept the doctrine of intrinsic nature from the very beginning.
Therefore, he says: "Even intrinsic nature."
It was stated previously that even intrinsic nature is subject to the will of the Supreme Lord.

In passages such as "the distinction among sentient beings which existed from of old," even one who accepts the doctrine of inherent nature (*svabhāvavāda*) must admit the existence of God (*īśvara*) as its regulator.

Therefore, since the adherence to inherent nature in any single instance must depend upon valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), what is the point of accepting it in multiple instances? This is the intended meaning.
One should not remember only the aforementioned proof;
rather, he says "they are eternal" to indicate that there is yet another proof as well.
"Both eternal and non-eternal, for they are dependent upon that," so says the Śruti.
The referent of the word "tataḥ" (from that) should be understood as the very object of the Vedic revelation;
the remainder of the sense is that the Śruti declares everything to be dependent upon the Lord.
Thus, demonstrating another logical inconsistency in the Vaiśeṣika and other systems:
Oṃ. And because it possesses form and other qualities, there is a reversal [of its nature], as is seen from observation. Oṃ.
Oṃ. And because there is a fault in both cases, Oṃ.
Thus, he explains the two sūtras beginning with "rūpa" (form).
And because it possesses form and so forth, there is the opposite [of permanence], as seen from experience;
and because there are faults in both cases.
Due to causes such as form and touch, the atom is impermanent.
...are to be inferred. // MAnu 2.171a //
The singular number in "of the atom" (paramāṇoḥ) is used with reference to the genus.
The Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that the four kinds of atoms—earthly and so forth—are eternal;
however, that is untenable.
The atoms of earth, those of water, and those of fire are impermanent because they possess color, like a cloth;
or rather, all four types are impermanent because they possess tangibility, like a cloth.
Likewise, the atoms of earth and water are impermanent because they possess taste, like a cloth.
This is because it contradicts such inferences as "earthly substances are impermanent because they possess odor, just like that [earthen pot]," and so forth.
Furthermore, "having parts" (*sāvayavatva*) is not a valid limiting condition (*upādhi*),
because it does not pervade the probandum (*sādhyavyāpti*) in the case of qualities (*guṇa*) and the like.
Nor does this qualify as an *upādhi* when "substancehood" (*dravyatva*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*),
because it pervades the probans (*sādhana*)— insofar as whatever possesses color and so forth is composed of parts—
and there is no contradiction with the cognition that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*).
This is because it has already been stated that the existence of atoms is established by perception alone;
furthermore, if atoms were impermanent, their status as the fundamental cause could not be established.

Moreover, if atoms—even those possessing form and other qualities—were not impermanent, then jars and other such things would likewise not be impermanent, as there would be no distinction between them.
Nevertheless, atoms do not possess the status of being the fundamental cause; nor is there any deviation in the causal principle regarding the Lord (Īśvara),
because [the definition] is qualified by the property of being material.
And so he will say:
"In our view, it is only derivative matter, such as form and so forth, that is pervaded by destruction" (8.164).
"Now, surely we accept the eternity of the subtle elements;
so how can it be inferred in this way?
Do not say so.
For atoms are not subtle elements; rather,
they are merely accumulations of the [four] bases of self-identity (ahaṃkāra).
And because they are of deformed appearance, they are indeed impermanent;
and because they are not grasped, there is absolute indifference toward them.
*Oṃ, because they are not grasped, there is absolute indifference. Oṃ.*
Thus he explains the Sūtra: "And of the three [types of] faith."
...and because it contradicts the Vedas, that doctrine is not to be accepted; therefore, this consistent synthesis is free from contradiction. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.171)
The genitive case is used here merely to express a relationship;
otherwise, the instrumental case would have been required. Furthermore, the scriptural passages state: "From the Self, space [arose]."
Passages such as these, cited here and there, are to be understood.
To the question, "Once it is established that the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others are not to be accepted, what is gained? he says: "And therefore... (ataśca).

The meaning is that this [scriptural statement] has as its object the Supreme Brahman, who is complete with all attributes; therefore, it should not be considered inconsistent due to a contradiction with the tenets established by the Vaiśeṣikas. Thus ends the section on the Vaiśeṣikas in the venerable Nyāyasudhā. (8.1.66)
[======= JNys_2,2.VII: Samudāyādhikaraṇa =======] // Now, the section on the aggregate (*samudāyādhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
Even if the collection were caused by both, that [result] would not be attained.
*Oṃ*, even if the collection were caused by both, that [result] would not be attained. *Oṃ*.
Now, the doctrine of the Sugata is refuted;
they are of four kinds:
the Vaibhāṣikas, the Sautrāntikas, the Mādhyamikas, and the Yogācāras.

In this context, as a preliminary to the refutation of the Vaiśeṣikas and others who assert that the world is truly composed of atoms, the views of the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas—which are not significantly different from one another—are first set aside.
To demonstrate their disagreement, he presents their position, beginning with the words: "The Vaibhāṣikas... and so forth.
Both the Vaibhāṣikas and the Sautrāntikas [hold that] the world is momentary by its own nature.
The phrase "they say" (āhuḥ) is connected with what is to be stated hereafter.
[An object] is momentary, meaning it persists for only a single moment.

Since causes of destruction, such as the blow of a hammer and so forth, are not perceived at every moment, how can there be momentary disintegration? To this, it is said: "by its own nature" (svarasataḥ).
By its very nature it is momentary; this perishability is itself the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the thing. In that case, what need is there for dependence on a cause?
Even hammers and the like are not the causes of the destruction of the thing.
Is it not the case that [factors] such as a pot are indeed the causes for the production of a dissimilar effect, such as shards?

Now, when there is conjunction with the activity of causes, the effect must arise either by being inherent (*samaveta*) in them or by being their transformation (*pariṇāma*). Since the same would apply to that effect as well, how can the world be momentary? To this he says: "Of atoms" (*aṇūnām*).
And the collection of atoms... // MAnu 2.172c //
The world says:
it is only aggregates of atoms that are the objects of cognition in the awareness of things such as cows and jars;
there exists no so-called "whole" (avayavin) distinct from them.
[Otherwise] it would contradict momentariness.

While one should have said "even a minute atom" (*aṇumātra*), the use of the term "aggregate" (*samudāya*)—as in "one large [object]"—is for the purpose of avoiding contradiction with perceptual cognition.
The point is that although individual atoms are imperceptible, and even if they are manifold and not large, it is logical that their aggregate possesses perceptibility and so forth.
For a collection comes into being through some person who brings about its assembly;
since we and others are not such [persons], God must be accepted as existing.
Likewise, if the whole (avayavin) were not admitted, there would be no distinct form such as that of a cow or a jar; therefore, he says: "kāla" (time/form).
... and by reason of the act of death. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.172d)
"For those who are joined at the time of origination...
[Mānava 2.2.173a] ...time and action are their two causes;
therefore, 'at the time of origination' means at the initial creation."
The sense is that on other occasions there is another cause.
The connection is that it is a "collection" (*samudāya*) of atoms (*aṇu*) that have arisen in close proximity to one another.
By the power of karma and so forth, atoms arise in such and such a manner of close proximity.
Since there is the manifestation of various forms such as cows, jars, and so forth, what need is there for a Lord (īśvara) in that case,
or for a composite whole (avayavin)?
For even the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) must admit that karma and so forth are the efficient causes;
and conjunction is conducive to the production of a composite whole. With just this much, everything is logically accounted for. (8.171)
Is it only the proliferation of the non-self that is momentary? No; he says: "the self."
...and that the self exists for only a moment. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.173b)
The meaning is that because the reason of momentariness—existence—is uniform in all cases.
To the objection that there is a contradiction with recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) regarding momentariness, he says: "eternally" (*nityam*).
The continuity of these is eternal... // MAnu 2.173c //
The meaning is that recognition has as its object the continuum (*santāna*) of these atoms (*aṇu*).
And it is not so, because [the reason] "existence" (*sattva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Because there is no existence of a continuum (*santāna*).
Having thus examined it in general, he states the classification: "five."
...it exists as the self consisting of the five aggregates. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.173d)
They say that the world-tree exists by way of the five aggregates;
he states the five aggregates as "formations" (saṃskāra).
The persistence [of the self] consists of the nature of volitional formations, form, consciousness, and perception, which are of the nature of suffering.
The phrase "the abiding of the aggregates" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya).
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) consists of atoms (paramāṇu) having the nature of visible form, taste, odor, tangibility, and sound.
Non-conceptual cognition is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*);
conceptual cognition is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*);
and suffering, which is another synonym for feeling (*vedanā*), constitutes one aggregate.
The connection here is that they say the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is external, while the other four are internal.
To the question, "Since pleasure (*sukha*) and the others exist as distinct entities, how can there be only five aggregates? he replies: "Because of the absence of suffering" (*duḥkhābhāvāt*).
"They say that the absence of suffering is happiness...

By the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that some include happiness within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*). Alternatively, the word "and" has the sense of a collective inclusion (*samuccaya*) of what has not been explicitly mentioned.
Just as space is merely the absence of material form,
and earth and the other elements are merely color and other qualities, so too numbers and other such attributes do not exist at all, because they are not perceived separately [from their substrates].
The arising in another location is precisely what is conditioned by and takes as its object karma;
for that which is momentary cannot be associated with actual karma.
It is precisely this arising, through being proximate or remote, that falls within the scope of conventional designations such as "conjunction" and so forth.
"The exclusion of what is not that (atadvyāvṛtti) alone is what is cognized by the conceptual cognition of universals such as 'cowness,' and so forth.
... "The continuum of formless cognition" (MAnu 2.2.174d).
...liberation. // MAnu 2.175a //
Regarding "formless" (*arūpa*):
consciousness itself, as it continues in a stream, is the self; its affliction by objects is saṃsāra.

They say that liberation is precisely that stream of consciousness which is formless—that is, devoid of objects—and nothing else. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the system of the five aggregates. *8,175*

Having thus presented the view common to both the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas, and intending to address their internal differences at the very outset of the refutation, [the author] explains the sūtra—"In a collection based on either [of two causes], that [collection] is not attained"—in order to refute the claim that the manifold world of cows, jars, and so forth is merely a collection of atoms and that no "whole" (avayavin) exists whatsoever. He says: "That... (sa).
For that collection is not logically possible from any single factor alone.
Is this aggregate, which is accepted as the object of cognitions such as "cow" or "jar," caused by a single atom,
or is it caused by multiple atoms?
Not the first.
Because it is logically impossible for a collection to arise from a single atom;
for no one has the cognition of a "collection of trees" with respect to each individual tree,
or else the conceptualization of a collection would be rendered purposeless.
Because largeness and being composed of sense-faculties have not been established;
by this, the meaning obtained from the word "api" (also/even) has been shown.
He refutes the second [position] with "no."
Nor [should one eat] when both [the giver and the recipient] are impure. // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.175c //
The mention of "both" (*ubhaya*) is an elliptical indication of "more than one" (*aneka*).
The word "from" (*sakāśāt*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. By the word "and" (*ca*), the connection with the "collection" (*samudāya*) is drawn forward.
If it is asked why this is not tenable:
even if there were multiple causes, one must state whether they are multiple causes that have not come together, or multiple causes that have come together.
In the first case, [it would apply] everywhere.
There would be the undesirable consequence of cognitions such as "cow" or "jar," because unaggregated atoms exist everywhere,
and a composite whole is caused by those [atoms] alone.
And there would be the consequence of the futility of accepting a composite whole.
He states the reason for the impossibility of the second [alternative] with the words: "the state of being both."
...and duality [of gender] exists with respect to the aggregate as a whole.
Because duality—which is the state of being combined as a plurality—is dependent upon a collection;
for it is only when a collection has arisen that the state of being combined among many things is possible.
Therefore, the connection is "it is not [the case]. *8,177*

He concludes the meaning of the sūtra—thereby dispelling the doubt as to why the arising of a collection from that which consists of many conjoined things is not tenable even though it depends upon a collection—with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ).
Therefore, because of this mutual dependence, the collection is not tenable.

The meaning is that a "collection" (*samudāya*) consists of many things arisen in mutual dependence. Furthermore, since atoms could not otherwise become the object of a perceptual cognition as "one large thing" if a collection were not produced, one must necessarily admit the existence of a composite whole (*avayavin*).
Furthermore, what is this aggregate? Is it the conjunction of atoms, or is it the number "many," or is it a distinct substance?
It cannot be the first or the second.
Because [the opponent] does not accept [such a relation];
even if they were accepted, it would be impossible for those two, which reside in supersensible [atoms], to be themselves perceptible.
In the third case, that very thing is the composite whole (avayavin).
If it is argued that this [self] is merely conventional (*saṃvṛta*),
then the impossibility of the proofs such as "it is great" and so forth remains exactly as it was before.
If it is argued that this is an illusion (*bhrānti*), [we say] no.
Because error must be preceded by non-error, it would follow that in some cases qualities such as "largeness" would possess actual reality.
If it is argued that this error is beginningless precisely because it arises through the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), we say no;
for then it would follow that even the cognition of blue and so forth would likewise be [mere error]. (8.179)
Is this not an inconsistent statement?
For there exists a subverting argument against the existence of a whole (*avayavin*). To explain:
Does the whole exist in its parts in its entirety, or does it exist by way of partial presence?
In the first case, there follows the consequence of its being multiple.
Not the second [alternative], because a part cannot exist apart from its constituent members;
or, if it did exist, the same dilemma regarding its mode of subsistence would follow here as well.
Furthermore, when some of its constituent parts (tattus) are moving, does the whole (avayavin) residing therein move or not?
If you say "no," it follows that there would be separate establishment (yutasiddhi).

In the first case, however, since it rests upon non-moving parts, it does not move; thus, there is the superimposition of contradictory properties (viruddhadharmādhyāsa), characterized by being both moving and non-moving.
In this way, the superimpositions of contradictory properties characterized by being covered or uncovered, and being colored or uncolored, are also to be understood.
It is replied:
we do not apprehend the whole as something absolutely distinct from its parts.
But that is merely a specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) of it;

in that case, what room is there for an alternative regarding its mode of existence? As for the contradiction regarding mobility and immobility, and so forth, it pertains to [the relationship of] difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*).

Since [the objection] is removed as if it were a contradiction, there is no subverting proof against the composite whole (*avayavin*). Nor should it be said that a collection (*samudāya*) has indeed been accepted by you; for...
Regarding the equality of the objection and the response:

since a collection (*samudāya*) is accepted as the conjoining of many things through the delimitation of a single time, place, action, and so forth, and that [conjoining] occurs only from those things that were previously unjoined.

And he will state that since those [entities] are stable, their arising does not conform to the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*). Having raised an objection against the point already stated, the Sūtra provides the resolution: "If it be argued that [there is no causal relation] because of mutual conditionality, we say no, because [the conditions] are merely the causes for the arising [of the effect]. (Oṃ. Itaretarapratyayatvād iti cet, na, utpattimātranimittatvāt. Oṃ.)
Thus [it is said].
Therein, he first explains the portion concerning the objection: "Mutually," etc.

If it is argued that [the self exists] because of mutual conditionality, we say no, because [the elements] are merely the causes for the arising [of perception]. Through mutual dependence, there arises in a person the cognition of a composite whole. (Manu 2.2.176cd) *Bodhisattvabhūmi* 2.2.19: "If it is argued that [the self exists] because of mutual conditionality, we say no, because [the elements] are merely the causes for the arising [of perception]. (BBs 2,2.19) *Madhyamakāvatāra* 2.2.176cd: Through mutual dependence, there arises in a person the cognition of a composite whole. (MAnuv 2,2.176cd)
If it be argued: "Even though that [impurity] is constant, it is caused by proximity... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.177a-c //
This mutual dependence would exist if this collection were occasional; but it is not so. Rather, we accept that this is eternal.
If it is argued that, in that case, there would be no established order of creation and dissolution, we say no;
for although that collection is eternal, the individual soul may at some time [kadācit] come to perceive it as a collection.
"At some time" is the understood remainder of the sentence.
The sense is that, in view of that [fact], the existence of stages such as creation and so forth is logically established.
Since the aggregate is eternal, one might ask why its perception is only occasional; to this it is said: "And that... (tacceti).
The perception of that [object] as a composite is caused by proximity to the atoms;
and since proximity does not exist at all times, the perception is occasional.
From what [source] is it known that the perception of a composite is caused by proximity? To this, it is said:
He said: "Mutually."
For that [perception] occurs in dependence upon the mutual cognition of atoms;
and mutual cognition does not occur without proximity.
But do not the followers of the Sugata (Buddhists) maintain that feeling itself is the person?
How, then, is there cognition for a person?
It is said: knowledge is indeed of two kinds.
There are two types of cognition: evolving cognition (*pravṛttijñāna*) and storehouse cognition (*ālayajñāna*).
Among these, the storehouse cognition, which is the locus of the suffering of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of evolving cognition, is called the "person" (*puruṣa*).
Evolving cognition, however, is the experience of the collection [of aggregates]; thus, there is no contradiction.
This is what is meant:
a collection is simply a plurality of atoms;
and that very plurality constitutes the state of being a collection.
It exists even when [atoms] are sparse, as if they were joined together;
however, the cognition of a collection does not always occur.
For the cognition of a collection arises only when there is the cognition of one atom accompanied by another atom, and that [other] atom accompanied by yet another atom.
Because relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) manifests multiplicity;
for when there is a cognition of individual atoms, a cognition of a collection (*samudāyatva*) arises,
since relative cognition manifests multiplicity.
For the cognition of a collection does not occur when there is only the cognition of individual atoms.
A mutual cognition between two trees situated in Mathurā and Pāṭaliputra is observed.

Furthermore, there are four causes of cognition: the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), the co-operative condition (*sahakāripratyaya*), the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
The sense-faculty (*indriya*) is the dominant factor (*adhipati*).

It is not the case that sparse atoms arise as the objects of the sense-faculty from among the sparse atoms that constitute its objective field; rather, atoms arise in such and such a manner as to be closely contiguous so as to serve as its object. Furthermore, from non-dominant sense-faculties, dominant sense-faculties arise.
Now, by the power of the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), the cognition "one great [entity]" arises;
therefore, there is no mutual dependence (anyonyāśrayatva),
nor is there any impossibility regarding creation and so forth.
By this, another position is also indicated:
atoms arise in close proximity to sparse atoms;
that itself constitutes their state as an aggregate.
Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. He explains the part concerning the resolution: "kārya... (the effect, etc.).
...the cause is that which is occupied solely with the production of the effect.
But a cause cannot be simultaneously engaged in specific effects.

That cause whose activity consists merely in the production of the effect is called "kāryasambhūtimātravyāpṛti"; because it is such, [the word] "not" is to be supplied [in the verse]. Since this [explanation] as previously stated is not capable of being a refutation, he states the intended meaning: "But not... and so forth.
They are called "particulars" (*viśeṣa*) because they distinguish;
the effects themselves are the particulars, thus "particular effects" (*kāryaviśeṣa*).
The word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is used in the singular to denote the class.

The meaning is that causes indeed possess an activity consisting in the production of effects similar to themselves, but they do not possess an activity consisting in the production of dissimilar effects.
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

Therefore, because the self lacks the nature of being a conjoined entity— which is the causal factor for the conjunction of the object and the sense organ— it cannot indeed possess the status of being a knower.
The meaning is: because of the rule that [a cause] produces an effect similar [to itself].

The "causality of the nature of being in conjunction" refers to the causality of the object and the sense-faculty—which exist in the form of the apprehended and the apprehender—toward those two effects;
that is, the causality of the object and the sense-faculty in their capacity as things in conjunction (*arthendriyasaṃyogirūpakāraṇatā*).
That is not at all tenable.
Why?
Because, for the reason that the self, which is the cause, does not possess that nature of being knowledge; such is the construction of the sentence.
This is what is meant:
for a cause must have either the nature of producing an effect similar [to itself] or the nature of producing an effect dissimilar [to itself].
Or it has the nature of both, or it has the nature of neither.

In that regard, where the first alternative is accepted, then from atoms that are not objects of the sense faculties and are sparsely distributed, atoms of exactly that same nature would be produced; they would never, however, be produced as aggregated atoms that have become objects of the sense faculties.
Furthermore, from sense faculties that do not exercise sovereignty over their objects, sense faculties of that very same kind would be produced.
The sense faculties do not ever have objects as their dominant condition;
and because the self does not possess knowledge of the aggregate, such a self would arise [in isolation],
never possessing knowledge of that [aggregate].
Otherwise, one would have to admit that even causal atoms and the like possess such qualities as being objects of the sense faculties;
for otherwise, there would result the collapse of the inherent nature [of atoms] to produce similar effects.
In either case, the occasional nature of the perception of a composite whole would not be tenable. (8.188)
He raises a second objection with the words: "viśeṣa" etc.
If a cause is held to be that which produces a specific effect, [then it must be momentary].

The sense of this is that, in this way, the production of atoms and so forth that are conjoined with their respective objects from atoms and so forth that are not the objects of the senses and are disjoined from them is logically established.
He refutes this by asking: "Why? (kutaḥ).
How could there be uniformity in all effects whatsoever?
The word "then" (*tarhi*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis; it is connected with the phrase "even in all cases of effects.
Here, the mention of "effects" (*kārya*) is in accordance with the views of others (*paramata*).

If the cause possessed the inherent nature of producing a body dissimilar to itself, then because of the existence of shards [as its material], the form of a jar would not exist in any of the moments of the jar;

rather, from the moment of the jar, the moment of an elephant would arise, and from that, the moment of a donkey. Likewise, from the moment of blue, the moment of yellow would arise, and from that, the moment of a pigeon.
"But there would be no persistence of the blue [color]," it is argued.

"In that case, let the cause possess the nature of both; this shall be the third position," if this is said, we reply: No, because due to contradiction, there is the undesirable consequence that not even one [of the two] could be produced.
But regarding the absence of contradiction, he says: "Therefore."
Therefore, because there is no fixed rule, anything whatsoever may be the cause of anything else.
Having combined the two positions under discussion, he refers to them with the word "ataḥ" (therefore).
Without *niyati*— that is, without the restriction that "a jar belongs only to a jar" or "blue belongs only to blue"—
any arbitrary thing, such as a jar or something blue, [would arise].
It would be the cause of anything whatsoever— be it a jar or the non-jar, blue or the non-blue.
If the momentary jar possessed a nature capable of producing both kinds of effects, it would produce both of them.
And thus it would be perceived; such is the meaning. Some explain this sentence as a supplement to the preceding statement:
"In every respect, there would not be a similarity of form among effects."
But [one might argue] that because it has the nature of producing dissimilar effects, a jar or the like could be the cause of an elephant and so forth.
This is not the fourth [alternative],
because that which is devoid of causal efficacy (arthakriyā) would necessarily follow as being non-existent.
The Buddhists maintain that existence (*sattva*) consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).

Now, one might object: "We do not accept any of the positions mentioned above, but rather that the very nature of a thing is simply the production of an effect. To this, he says: "Therefore... (*ataḥ*).
He refers to this [text] as "the Buddhist Kalpa" (*buddhistham imaṃ kalpam*).
However, the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is not hidden.
It might be argued as follows:

Just as in your own view, although the sense organs and other factors have the nature of producing valid cognition (*pramā*), they produce invalid cognition (*apramā*) due to the influence of auxiliary defects;
so too, even though a cause has the nature of producing a similar effect, it may occasionally produce a dissimilar effect through the power of auxiliaries such as unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Or else, just as for the Sāṅkhyas, the sense organs and other factors possess the nature of producing both valid and invalid cognition.

In that regard, when qualities that are counteragents to error (apramā) are present, they produce only valid cognition (pramā); however, when defects that are counteragents to valid cognition (pramā) are present, they produce invalid cognition (apramā).
Thus, even though the cause possesses both natures, the production of one or the other will occur by virtue of unseen factors (adṛṣṭa) and so forth.

Alternatively, just as for the Naiyāyikas and others the sense faculties and so forth have the inherent nature of producing mere cognition, yet the arising of valid knowledge occurs through the advent of auxiliary factors such as qualities,
so too the cause has precisely the inherent nature of producing the effect.

But [one might argue] that it will produce something similar or dissimilar due to the convergence of auxiliary causes such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); therefore, he says: "The unseen force also..."
How could even that which is unseen (adṛṣṭa) bring about a distinction for him? (2.180cd)
In this context, the mention of the "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*) is an elliptical indication for all auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*).
Even regarding the "unseen," there is [an absence] of the capacity to produce a dissimilar effect in the first case, and of the obstruction of either one in the second case.
Regarding the third [alternative], there is one sentence: "But why does the state of being a producer of both not follow?
For instance:
are the moments of past unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—whether preceding, preceding that, and so forth—non-producers of those [subsequent moments], or are they producers?
However, in the first case, it is not established that this unseen moment (adṛṣṭakṣaṇa) brings about a specific distinction,
because of the absence of a cause; for even this [result] is not produced by an unseen moment that does not bring about a specific distinction.
If it is argued that the entity perceived at the present moment will produce a specific quality through the power of auxiliary causes, this is not so;

for its status regarding those auxiliaries is the same [as before]. Furthermore, there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in having to pursue a further series of auxiliary causes even in that case.
The further statement, "From what does that very cause acquire its specific distinction? is as follows:
even an unseen factor (adṛṣṭa) that brings about a specific exclusion—does it bring about a specific distinction for the intended cause alone?
Or [is it] the mere cause? Not the first,
because of the absence of both a regulator and an indicator of the cause.
From those atoms which are sparse because they lack the sense-faculties as their object, the production of atoms that have come together with those objects is expected;
and from the sense-faculty which lacks the predominance of the object, [there arises] the sense-faculty with the predominance of the object;
and from a self devoid of the cognition of a composite, there likewise arises the production of such a self.
This is said to belong to that very [person].
In both cases,
he refutes the second two alternatives with the words "of whom" (*yasya*).
Whatever specific distinction one might establish for anyone at all.
In this regard, one statement is that "whatever unseen [force] might produce a particularity here [in the atoms].

If even an unseen force from the past or further past possesses the capacity to produce a particularity, then it must certainly produce a particularity in the atoms of the past or further past as well;
for it is not admitted that a capable [cause] can be delayed.
And thus, because the cognition of the whole [would arise from any cause], there would be no restriction regarding the convention (*samaya*).
This is the second [point]: that it would bring about the specific quality of just any [cause whatsoever].
If an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is admitted as that which brings about the specific quality of the mere cause, then the specific quality of all causes whatsoever would be brought about.
And thus, if there were a conjunction of the atoms of a jar, there would be a conjunction of all [atoms] everywhere;
however, the desired state of the atoms would not exist anywhere at all,
nor is the entire collection ever perceived simultaneously.
Now, it might be thought:
"All this is self-contradictory;
for instance:"
If the threads possess a nature that produces an effect similar [to themselves], then they would produce only another thread and not a cloth;
and if they possess a nature that produces an effect dissimilar [to themselves], then an earthen cloth could not arise from them,
but rather some aqueous substance would be produced.
However, having both as its nature is contradictory;
if it were of neither nature, there would be no production of the cloth either.
If you accept that the determination [of its nature] depends on auxiliary causes, this applies equally to those auxiliary causes as well.
Now, it might be argued:
let there be, for the time being, a causal relationship between the threads and the cloth,
since what has been established by valid cognition cannot be denied.
And since it will be conceptualized in whatever way it arises, this is equal for both [positions]; therefore, he says: "and the effect."
Whatever effect and whatever cause there may be for anyone whatsoever.
"Because there would be no determining factor... (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.182ab). [The phrase] "the state of being eternally perishable" connects here as well with what is about to be stated:
that whatever blue or other [color] might be the effect of some yellow or other [color].
Whatever yellow or other color might be the cause of some blue or other color—
why so? Because blue would be the effect of blue alone, not of yellow.
The construction is as follows: "Blue alone is the cause of blue, not yellow," because there is no restrictive factor [to the contrary].
The two words "ca" (and) are used for mutual conjunction.
This is what is meant:
this rebuttal is possible within the doctrine of permanence (*sthiravāda*).

For when the causal relationship is determined through the existence of a regulating factor—namely, that whatever is inherent in something or has transformed into a certain form is the cause or the effect of that thing—the postulation of a supporting principle becomes tenable.

According to the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), however, since there is no continuity between the destruction of the preceding moment and the arising of the succeeding moment, there is no means whatsoever to determine a causal relationship.
This is because both inherence (*samavāya*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*) are absent.
And thus, by whose force would one postulate a productive cause? (8.198)

Even in the absence of an inherent relation (*samavāya*) or transformation (*pariṇāma*), since the restriction is logically established that "whatever precedes in relation to something else is its cause," and "whatever follows in relation to something else is its effect," the lack of a regulating factor is unproven; therefore, he first refutes the restriction regarding the effect: "This belongs to this alone" means "this is the cause of this alone."
Thus, by what means of valid cognition is their constant perishability understood?
This is the cause of blue alone, and not of yellow.
Thus, in this way, the state of blue being the effect of blue—
under the position that there is eternal destruction and that destruction and production occur without any continuity— is not established by any means of valid cognition whatsoever.

The meaning is that posteriority, being merely a relative state, exists in relation to yellow just as it does in relation to blue; therefore, neither spatial proximity (*sādeśya*) nor similarity of form (*sārūpya*) can be the determining factor. If this is argued, we say no.
This is because one accepts the production of dense [atoms] from sparse atoms, and the production of sparse [atoms] from those that have become dense;
it also rejects the restriction of causes by stating, "this is not [the cause]."
Even in the case of the statement "this is not produced from that," there is no [inherent] cause.

The point is this: even when it is determined that blue arises from blue alone and not from that yellow—that is, even when the causality of blue is established—there is no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) [to prove it].
This is because, just as with blue, yellow also exists as preceding blue.

Now, one might object: "Just as for you there is the determination of the causal relationship between the weaver and the cloth even in the absence of inherence (samavāya) and transformation (pariṇāma), so it will be for me as well. To this, he says: "This belongs to this."
The phrase "if the self were eternally perishable" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

For us, it is logical to determine the identity between the efficient cause and its effect through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) that are not exhausted elsewhere; but this is not the case for the opponent.
This is because we accept that the self (*ātman*), which investigates positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), is permanent, whereas the opponent accepts its momentariness.
For such a [self]—determined as being otherwise incapable of exhausting itself elsewhere in positive and negative concomitances—is not desired [by the opponent]. This is the intended meaning.
The interpretation, however, is exactly as before (*yojanā tu pūrvavadeva*).

Having thus refuted the [notion of] a composite whole, the subsequent section of the text is now intended to negate the momentariness of everything by means of the absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) and its contradiction [with that absence]. For instance:
Not only is a composite entity untenable; indeed, the momentariness of everything is also [untenable],
because there is a lack of valid evidence for it.
But surely perception makes known the momentariness of objects?

For that [perception] has as its domain only the present; it grasps the existence of an object as related solely to its own present moment, and not even to its relation with preceding or succeeding moments.
How then is it that the momentariness of objects is without authoritative proof?
It is said in reply: what is this so-called "momentariness"?
Does it mean existence connected with a moment?
Or does it mean possessing arising and destruction within that very moment itself? Or rather, does it mean being connected with a single moment while not being connected with any other moment?
The first [position] is indeed [subject to] the same fault,
because even for a persisting object, existence in a single moment must be admitted.
He refutes the second and third [positions] with the words "vināśa" (destruction), etc.
Furthermore, destructions and origins are never seen to be eternal.
The plural number is used because [the object] is related to multiple entities.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of including the third alternative.
The word "eva" (only/just) is to be connected with "naiva" (not at all).
The "ever-present" (sadātana) are those that exist at every moment.
Indeed, direct perception (pratyakṣa) penetrates the existence of objects in the present time, but it does not [penetrate] their arising and destruction which last for only a single moment,
nor their connection with another moment.
And if that is so, how could momentariness be established by it?
Now, does perception grasp an object as existing in both a preceding and a succeeding moment, or not?
It cannot be the first [alternative].
If it is argued that because [perception] grasps only the present,
and because in the second case the non-existence of the preceding and succeeding moments is established through perception and non-perception, momentariness itself is thereby established—
then we shall first accept the second case.
And in this way, momentariness is not established;
for it is only the non-perception of what is perceptible that indicates non-existence,
and [the object] existing at the prior and subsequent times is not perceptible by direct perception.
Since the opponent has already stated that [perception] grasps only the present,
or even if we grant the first position—

that although some perception grasps only the present, it lacks the characteristic of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the form "this is that very same thing"— [the author] says, "it is seen," with this intention.
Stability is perceived through recognition in all things.
The meaning is that it is made an object [of cognition].
The suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārthe*).
Stability (*sthiratvam*) consists in a single entity's connection with multiple moments.

By this, it is indicated that not only does perception not have momentariness as its object, but it also has stability as its object; thus, the contradiction with evidence regarding the opponent's position and the existence of evidence for one's own position are both set forth. (8.203)
By this, it should be understood that the sūtra “and because of recollection” (*anusmṛteśca*) has been explained.
By the phrase “in all things,” he indicates that the Buddhists’ refutation of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) touches only the views of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, and not our own view.
For instance: is stability being established by this recognition (pratyabhijñā) in respect to atoms and so forth, which are accepted as eternal, or rather in respect to jars and so forth?
It is not the first case.
Because those [atoms] are beyond the reach of the senses, it is impossible to accept that they fall within the scope of perceptual recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
for even the opponent must admit that recognition regarding jars and the like is erroneous.

For when even a single atom, such as the tip of a needle, departs from a jar or similar object, then the dyad (dvyaṇuka) composed of them must necessarily perish, because its non-inherent cause—the conjunction—is destroyed by that disjunction. Upon the destruction of the dyad, the triad (tryaṇuka) perishes due to the destruction of its inherent cause; through this sequence, the destruction of the jar is also inevitable.
Furthermore, the atom is not perceptible, such that its departure or non-departure could be ascertained through perception.
Nor should it be argued that stability will be established by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the case of crystals and the like, which possess densely packed parts;
for even there, the absence of the departure of atoms cannot be ascertained by perception.
And "having dense constituent parts" does not mean having constituent parts that are incapable of disjunction,
because disjunction is established by direct perception;
rather, it means requiring a cause superior even to that of a jar and the like.
Nor can we perceive an absence of specific difference therein;
for a decrease in weight is observed even in substances such as crystal over time,
and that [decrease] is not possible unless there is a departure of constituent parts.
Nor is permanence established for qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*),

because some of them are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), while others are equivalent to jars and the like; furthermore, universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth do not exist at all in terms of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).

"Even if it exists, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) has a validity that is suspected to be no different from that of [the cognition of] form and so forth; therefore, it is not appropriate to employ it as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing stability in any case.
To this, it is said:
"This fault would apply to those who maintain the theory of the composition of atoms (*paramāṇu*)."
This is not the case for us who maintain the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāmavādinaḥ*).

For those proponents of transformation hold that it is that very same entity which undergoes change through the increase or decrease of its parts; it does not become something else entirely. Therefore, it is entirely logical to apprehend stability through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) regarding all things that are accessible to direct perception.
But surely, even in your own view, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is nothing but an error;
for in the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), one must admit both difference and non-difference between the preceding and succeeding entities.
And because recognition in the form "this is that very same thing" apprehends absolute non-difference,
it is said:
when, however (if indeed)...

The non-difference between the [entity] existing at the earlier time and that existing at the later time is accepted as the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). In that case, even if the recognition—characterized by the restriction "that very same thing"—is erroneous, the cognition "this is that" is not itself an error;
and it is precisely by means of this [cognition] that permanence is established.
But when the object is a relation between two times and so forth, then even that [cognition] which includes a restriction is not an error.
If it is asked, "Why might this recognition not be erroneous, as in the case of hair or feet that have been cut off and grown back again?"—
[the answer is] no, because there is an absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).
In the same way,
if error were admitted [as the nature of cognition], it would follow that cognitions of blue and so forth would likewise be erroneous;
and it has already been stated that perception does not constitute a sublation [of this view].
He raises the objection that even if perception is not sublated, inference will be the sublater: "phalādīnām" etc.
By means of the fruit and other such signs, it is inferred everywhere, even in specific cases.
If it is argued that space possesses momentariness because of its existence, then [this must apply] without distinction to space as well.
Since everything exists [in the form of atoms], why is it not inferred that there is no distinction at all?
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), the body, a lamp, and so forth are included.
Specifically, by way of a difference in dimension (*parimāṇabheda*),
momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) [is established].
The connection is that "it is inferred.

Therefore, by means of that example, in all cases—even regarding entities distinct from fruits and the like—the inference that "there are five aggregates" based on the reason of existence will serve as a sublater of the recognition whose object is stability; furthermore, the example of fruits and so forth is not deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
Whatever possesses contradictory dimensions is observed to be manifold, as in the case of a jar and a cloth;
and the fruit and so forth possess contradictory dimensions between their preceding and succeeding moments.
Thus, by means of this inference, the momentariness of the fruit and so forth is established.
He refutes [this objection] with the words: "of space."
"Without distinction" means that there is no difference between the preceding and succeeding moments; "non-distinction" is the absence of differentiation between the preceding and succeeding moments.
This refers to everything that is subject to dispute.
What is being stated is this:
whatever exists is momentary, just like space.

Since the inference [that blue and so forth are real] is fallacious because it is contradicted by a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*), it is impossible for it to subvert recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Furthermore, the example of space (*ākāśa*) is not devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), for it is said:
"Space and the two cessations—these three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are eternal."
This is because [the existence of space] has already been accepted by the opponent, and because the differences in dimension and so forth—which would prove momentariness—are absent in space.
This is also stated [in the verse]: "Because it is without distinction, being devoid of differences in dimension and so forth. (8.213)

Alternatively, the construction is as follows: since space is without distinction—that is, devoid of any difference in dimension—why is it not inferred by that same example that for all things, such as fruits and the like, there is no distinction between earlier and later times, given the absence of any difference in dimension due to their existence? This is what is meant: [The argument is: Since space is uniform and lacks any variation in magnitude, why can we not, by way of analogy, infer that all things—including fruits and so forth—are likewise uniform, insofar as they lack any change in magnitude between their prior and subsequent states, simply because they continue to exist? This is the intended meaning.
Inference cannot serve as a sublater of recognition, because inference is weaker than perception and is therefore sublated by it;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of an inference such as: "the fruit and so forth are devoid of difference in size, because they exist, like space."
For in this case, there is no defect whatsoever except for sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*).

Thus, since the proof of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) in that illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the example would be deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
Consequently, the invalidity of this inference arises precisely through contradiction with perception.
Otherwise, one must simply state that there is the consequence of mutual dependence (anyonyāśrayatā);
and that [consequence] applies equally to the present case as well.
By this, the sūtra “And because there is no distinction in the case of space” is explained;
by this, [the nature of] momentariness—

By asserting that the proponent’s inference is subject to a counter-inference (*satpratipakṣatva*) and has its object sublated (*bādhitaviṣayatva*), it is also indicated that there is an instance of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding space (*ākāśa*).
If it is argued that your own inference is likewise inconclusive because of [the existence of] fruits and so forth, we say no.
In that case as well, because the non-existence of momentariness will be stated later (*iti*) [in verse 8.214],
this [argument] would hold if space were existent;
however, this is not the case.
Because space is the absence of corporeality;
for here "existence" (bhāvatva) is intended to mean "being" (sattva), or rather, existence in the sense of possessing its own nature.
Anticipating the objection that "non-existence is admitted to be devoid of intrinsic nature," he says: "If... (yadīti).
If space were not existent, how could it exist within humans and other beings?

If, having accepted that space lacks existence, you argue that the example in the counter-inference and the inference of over-extension suffers from the deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*), and that your own inference is not subject to the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*), then we ask: how is existence established in the body and so forth?
In that case, even the example belonging to the opponent would suffer from the deficiency of the probans.

If it is argued that the body and so forth possess the nature of being an entity (bhāvatva) because they are known through cognition directed toward affirmation, and possess existence (sattva) because they are objects of valid knowledge (pramā), then this is equally applicable to space as well.
Thus, he provides an introductory argument to refute the claim that space is a non-entity (abhāva) by means of another means of valid cognition, stating: "That [space] is the substratum (dharmī)."
The fact that space possesses a counter-correlative (pratiyogin) with the same property (sadharmipratiyogitva) is understood. In this context, that in which there is absence is the locus (dharmin),
and that of which there is absence is the counter-correlative (pratiyogin).
The state of possessing both [the locus and the counter-correlate] is the regulator and pervader of non-existence.
Whatever is non-existence, all of it is necessarily accompanied by a locus and a counter-correlate,
just like the non-existence of a jar and so forth.
For that [non-existence] is indeed accompanied by the locus (dharmin), such as the ground, and by the counter-positive (pratiyogin), such as a jar.
But is this not untenable?
For regarding non-existence, the rule of its concomitance with the locus and the counter-positive—would it be spatial (deśataḥ)?
Or is it by way of time?
In the first case, there is no spatial co-location with the locus (dharmin) at least;
for the ground [is located] in its own substrate.
However, since non-existence resides on the ground,
it is indeed contradictory with its counter-positive;
whereas the second [type of contradiction], although it might somehow exist with respect to the locus (*dharmin*), is not so [with respect to the counter-positive].

Nevertheless, [one might raise] the objection that there is no such thing as a counter-correlate (pratiyogin) [for non-existence], because it is a rule that antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) and destructive non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva) must occur at times distinct from that of their counter-correlates. Dispelling this doubt, he establishes that non-existence is pervaded by its coexistence with both the locus (dharmin) and the counter-correlate: "Without those two, indeed, non-existence is never observed anywhere. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.187ab)
In this context, by the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), the phrase "without those two" (*tau vinā*) is understood from the context; thus, the meaning is "without that knowledge.

The word "and" (*ca*) serves to connect the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), signifying that non-existence is perceived only when the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) are themselves perceived.
By the word "for" (*hi*), he indicates the well-known status of both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Thus, by means of this positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the pervasion (vyāpti) is established on the grounds that the cognition of non-existence is preceded by the cognition of the locus (dharmin) and the counter-correlate (pratiyogin).
Alternatively, by the word "those two" (tāvit),
it is not cognition that is intended to be indicated.

Non-existence, when being cognized, is cognized only as being constituted by a locus (*dharmī*) and a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), in forms such as "this is not here. It is not cognized as something solitary, independent of those two; thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and through their connection within a single cognition, this [nature of non-existence] is established as a relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva*). This is how it should be understood.
As for the cognition of the non-existence of an elephant and so forth in the morning, we shall explain that in another way.

If this is so, and if the coexistence of the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is a pervading condition for the cognition of an absence, then [the author] says: "The state of being a non-locus and a counter-correlate is understood in the case of space. (MAnu 2.187cd)

The property of having a substratum (*sadharmipratiyogitva*) pervades the cognition of non-existence; therefore, this [property] is excluded from space (*ākāśa*), because space is understood simply as "space," and not as "this is not here.

If it is argued that even this cognition actually has the absence of corporeal form (*mūrtābhāva*) as its object, yet—due to its connection with an expression devoid of the negative particle (*nañ*)—it appears as if it were not so, like the state of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*) and the like, we say: no.
Otherwise, it would follow that cognitions such as "blue" and so forth would likewise be [invalid],
since the lack of direct experience is equal in both cases;
and thus, even for the opponent, there would arise the fallacy of unestablished reasons (*asiddhi*) and so on.
Since the cessation of the pervader necessarily entails the cessation of the pervaded, space is not non-existent; thus,
the formal argument is as follows.
Space is not a non-entity, because it is perceived even without a substratum (dharmin) or a counter-correlative (pratiyogin), just like color.
Furthermore, for one who asserts that space is the absence of corporeal matter, whatever is called the substratum is precisely what we call "space"; thus, only a dispute over names remains.
And this will be explained in the section on the ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*).
He summarizes the meaning of the two sūtras with the words: "svīkāra... (acceptance).
Regarding all things, whether unseen or seen, he alone who is not deranged by passion rightly applies himself to their acceptance or rejection;
indeed, he acts with even greater excellence.
Because he accepts the unobserved [nature] of momentariness and so forth, while abandoning the observed [nature] of stability and so forth,
he is a follower of the Sugata (a Buddhist).
The phrase "more than himself" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The meaning is that it makes even a madman appear to possess greater discernment than oneself.
For a madman does not accept what is entirely unmeasured, nor does he reject what is measured.
[Objection: But if blue and so forth did not exist, then existence would not exist;
for existence is indeed the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
And [all things] are pervaded by either succession or simultaneity,
since there is no third possibility; nor is that possible in the case of a stable entity, as demonstrated by the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*).
For instance: would a permanent entity perform its own causal function successively or simultaneously?
Regarding the first [alternative], is it capable now of the causal efficiency that occurs at a later time, or not? In the first case, it would have to produce that very efficiency right now,
because it is impossible for that which is capable to delay.
Even then, one should not act during the second [moment].
If it is argued that although it is currently incapable, it will act at that time because it is capable then, [we reply:
in that case, the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by capability and incapacity would divide the entity.
In the second moment, however, because everything that was to be done has already been accomplished in the very first moment, its non-existence in the second and subsequent moments is unavoidable.

Thus, since the inference of momentariness—whose logical necessity is established by the force of favorable reasoning—is powerful, the counter-inference based on recognition is sublated by it and is therefore not capable of proving stability.
This is not so.
Because these arguments are fallacious due to being refuted by counter-arguments (*pratitarka*) and so forth;
for instance:
if the entire manifold of self and non-self were momentary, then [the cognition] consisting of both valid and invalid knowledge at all times— *8,223* ...would [be impossible].
Furthermore, conventional practice characterized by inference, scripture, and recognition would be subverted;
even this very reasoning (*tarka*) could not arise,
because it depends upon the repeated apprehension of a relationship between that [object] and something of its kind, or between that [kind of object] and something of that kind.

The determination of pervasion occurs when the absence of deviation has been ascertained— either through the ascertainment of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*), or through the ascertainment of the absence of limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
The perception of the subject and the perception of the mark [liṅga] occur once the pervasion has been ascertained;
from that follows the recollection of the experienced pervasion.
Then there arises the mental synthesis: "This mark, which I have known as being pervaded, exists here in this subject."
Now, the process of inference begins with "inference" (anumiti).
Indeed, all of this is not possible for a self that is momentary;
for by whomsoever smoke was seen once, that very person has already perished.
Whose is the repeated observation, and whose is the ascertainment of the pervasion (*vyāpti*)?
Moreover, that very mountain on which smoke was seen has already perished;
where, then, can there be a recollection of the pervasion through the mark (*liṅga*)?
And where is the determination of the object to be proven? Likewise, in the case of scripture as well, there are the hearings of individual phonemes and the synthesis of words.
The grasping of the convention,
the subsequent hearing of the word, and the recollection of the convention.
The cognition of the meaning of a sentence is a synthesis of many cognitions; this is not possible if the self were momentary.
Furthermore, recognition occurs when that very same person who previously knew an object perceives that same object or something similar to it.
How, then, could that belong to a momentary self? By means of inference, reasoning (*tarka*) has also been explained;
for even though there is a difference between the self and the non-self at every moment, [it is established] by inference.
If this were accepted, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For instance, upon the cognition of pervasion regarding any [subject], even an inhabitant of the Coconut Island (*nārikeladvīpa*) would possess valid knowledge (*pramā*) of fire;
or, by observing a mark on a mountain, one might infer fire even in a lake, and so forth.

If it is argued that the conventional usage of inference and so forth is established because there exists a causal relationship between selves existing in preceding and succeeding moments, as well as between mountains and the like—[we reply:
no, because their distinctness (*anyatva*) remains unaltered;
otherwise, the same [causal] consequence would absurdly follow for the cognitions of a teacher and his pupil, and so on. (8.226)
Now, it might be thought:
the causal moments instill latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) upon the resultant moments;
therefore, the conventional usage of inference and so forth with respect to subsequent selves—which are endowed with the latent impressions of preceding selves—is logical.
Even mountains and the like, possessing their prior formative impressions (*saṃskāra*), attain the status of being the subject of inference (*pakṣatva*);
it is for the purpose of refuting this that the following sūtra is stated.
Oṃ, because of the cessation of the preceding upon the arising of the succeeding, oṃ.
Thus [it is said].
He explains that with the words "the subsequent," etc.
And because the former ceases when the latter arises;

since the former entity perishes merely by the arising of the latter, it is not logical for anything anywhere to impart its formative influence (*saṃskāra*) to another. (BBs 2.20; MAnu 2.2.189) [8.227]
Of a certain cause, in a certain effect.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ).
Therefore, since [it is said] "I have known," and so forth, how could there be an inference regarding that which is to be known? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.190ab)
The meaning is that because the self is momentary and because the transference of conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) is impossible, it is "unknowable"—
that is, it cannot be known in such a way that one could think, "That which was known by me as being pervasive exists here," and so forth. It is impossible to know.
And from that, how could there be inference?
This also serves as an elliptical indication for scripture (*āgama*) and so forth.
[Objection: But surely there exists the conventional usage of inference and the like.

Since it is impossible to deny what is established by all the world, one might argue that by the power of that [perception], even something non-worldly—the capacity to impart a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that does not coexist [with the object]—will be postulated; therefore, he says: "unity" (*ekatvam*).
