Having abandoned the sense of oneness that resides in experience, one becomes free from pride; how then could there be any distinction regarding the self and other such things? ... MAnu 2.2.190c-e.
Is something supernatural to be postulated merely because the conventional usage of inference and so forth would otherwise be inexplicable,
or even if the self and other such entities were momentary?
It is not the first case.
For that [cognition] is established precisely by the permanence of the self and so forth;
the second alternative,
however, would hold if the momentariness of the self and so forth were proven.
And that [oneness] does not exist;

the sense is that it is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and lacks any basis in valid means of knowledge. In the phrase "oneness and difference," the words "in the prior and posterior times" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
It is established by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as residing in experience.
How is it to be accepted? By supplying the ellipsis [of the verb], the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛtā*) is established.
But has it not been stated that recognition is erroneous?
To the question, "How then can the identity of the self and so forth be established from that? he says: "It is indeed a creeper."
... because experience is like that of a child. // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.190f //

For when inference is powerful due to the lack of any scope for it to be subverted by the force of reasoning (*tarka*), recognition would indeed be erroneous because of its contradiction with that inference. But when reasoning is fallacious according to the method described above, then how can there be any superiority in the inference of momentariness?
Furthermore, from what source could there be a sublation of that recognition?
For the experience of recognition is unsublated, since it is indeed more powerful.
Therefore, the connection is that the oneness of the self and so forth is established by it.

By this, the objection that how a difference established by inference could be without a basis (*nirnimittakatva*) is also refuted, because the reasoning (*tarka*) upon which it depends has not yet reached a final conclusion.

Now, one might ask: "Let it be granted that the very arising of the subsequent moment is the cessation of the preceding one; nevertheless, why is it that the preceding moment does not deposit any latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) in the subsequent one? To this, he says: "And of cause and effect... (*kāryakāraṇayośca*).
And how could the subsequent [moment] necessarily be connected with the preceding impression without the cause and the effect being simultaneous? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.191)
Since the very arising of the subsequent [moment] occurs through the cessation of the preceding one, it is established that there is no simultaneity between cause and effect.
Furthermore, without simultaneity, it is not logical for the subsequent [moment] to possess the formative impressions (saṃskāra) deposited by the preceding one.
By the phrase "and necessarily," he indicates that since this is not logical even in some cases, how much less so in all cases?

The meaning is that it is observed that only that which exists at the same time can impart a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and not that which is at a different time; this is because of such a pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Now, one might ask: even in the absence of simultaneity, why should there not be the capacity to impart a latent impression? To this, he says: "only those that are connected."
Only that which is connected imparts a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) elsewhere in its entirety;

how could that which is unconnected, whether preceding or following, produce a latent impression? For all things that impart a latent impression, such as *campaka* flowers and the like, do so only when they are connected with oil and the like, thereby depositing the impression in the oil and so forth.
There is no rule that they must not be unrelated;
however, a relationship between two things existing at different times is not tenable.
Therefore, the former [moment] is connected with the subsequent one; thus, it should not produce a latent impression (*vāsanā*) in that subsequent moment.
To bring the stated meaning to the mind, he summarizes it by saying: "by way of being simultaneous."
How can there be [a relationship] through refinement in the absence of a conjunction characterized by simultaneity?
In this context, the connection between cause and effect is not tenable without simultaneity;
without such a connection, the cause’s capacity to impart a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) to the effect is not possible;
and without that impression, how could there be conventional activities such as inference? Thus, the construction [of the argument] is to be understood by supplying these missing links.
Furthermore, the state of being conditioned (*saṃskāra*) is not tenable;
how could there be conventional usage such as inference and so forth without conditioning? This is the construction [of the argument] by supplying the ellipsis.
If this synthesis were not performed, then [the aforementioned reasons would fail].

If each of the past participles were not understood to possess the status of a cause by imparting a refinement (*saṃskāra*) individually, what fault would there be in stating the probandum (*sādhya*) in every instance? [The answer is:
none other than that it would be blunted by the aforementioned expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
In this regard, there are these formal arguments:
the preceding moment does not impart a conditioning influence upon the succeeding moment,
because it is not connected with it.
That which is not connected with something else does not produce an impression (saṃskāra) upon it,
just as is commonly accepted;
or rather, that which produces an impression upon something is observed to be necessarily connected with it, just as is agreed upon.
If even that which is unconnected could impart a refinement (*saṃskāra*), then musk would perfume all clothing without distinction;
yet the preceding [moment] is unconnected with the succeeding one,
because they belong to different times.
Like those who have already attained [the goal],
there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) regarding the relationship between two things existing at different times;
for the earlier [moment] exists at a different time from the later.
Because it perishes at the very moment of its arising,
just like that which is commonly accepted [as momentary];
for there can be no suspicion of simultaneity with something that has already perished.
If it is objected: "Why should this not be like the redness of a citron flower when it is infused with lac juice?
[The answer is: No; for even in that case, one does not admit production and destruction without a substrate (niranvaya).
Furthermore, since we are instructing the opponent by means of a principle established for him, one should not suspect fallacies such as the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). *8,236*
This might be the case if the very production of the effect were the destruction of the cause; but from what is that established? To this he says: "for only a moment."
A duration of merely a single moment is admitted for all things.
First of all, it is necessary that cause and effect be successive, one after the other; for if they were simultaneous, the relationship between cause and effect would be contradicted.

Therefore, if a cause existing in a preceding moment were to persist even in the moment of its effect, then the accepted [principle] that all things endure for only a single moment would be destroyed.
Therefore, it is only by accepting momentariness that the arising of a subsequent [moment] implies the cessation of the preceding one.
This might be argued:

there is no fault whatsoever in accepting that a cause, having acquired its existence in the prior division of a moment, produces an effect in the middle division, and then, having deposited an impression (*saṃskāra*) therein, perishes in the final division.
To this, he says: "The previous... (pūrveti).
A moment (kṣaṇa) is held to be devoid of prior, middle, and subsequent parts.
In this context, only the division [of time] is designated as "kalā.
Since the prior and the posterior do not exist, the middle which is defined by them is also established as non-existent; this is accepted by the Buddhists. (8.237)

Having thus stated the refutation of reasoning by counter-reasoning, the Sūtra now begins with "Oṃ, if [the cause] is non-existent, there is a contradiction of the thesis; otherwise, there is simultaneity, Oṃ," in order to demonstrate that the defect of reasoning called *anukūlatā* (conformity) consists in the fact that just as a permanent entity is untenable, so too is a momentary entity untenable for the same reason.
Thus, explaining that, he first asks about it by means of an alternative: "Was it previously...? etc.
Otherwise, there would be either a contradiction of the thesis or simultaneity.
Is the effect existent prior to its arising, or does it arise from its destruction? (MAnu 2.2.194cd) BBs 2.2.21.
For existence is intended by the opponent to be the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*),
and that is pervaded by the two alternatives to be stated.
Because a third alternative cannot be established,
and because that [causal relation] is not possible in the case of momentary things;
for instance, when an effect arises from a momentary entity, does it arise while the preceding cause exists?
That is to say, its existence is simultaneous with the existence of its cause;
or, does it come into being when that cause has perished?
Regarding the first case, he states the fault: "simultaneity" (*yaugapadyam*).
If it were simultaneous, there would be the production of all things without exception at once.
If the effect exists when the cause is present— this being the implied sense—
then [it follows that] the cause is indeed momentary.
Furthermore, if the effect were to have an existence simultaneous with the existence of its cause, it would mean that the cause and effect arise together.

Since it has already been stated that there is no division [of time] within a single moment, this same principle applies to each of those effects as well; consequently, all effects occurring within that continuum would have to be simultaneous.
And that [position] contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition.
Although here the impossibility of a causal relationship between two things existing simultaneously is also a refutation,
nevertheless, that can be understood by the disciples themselves.
The statement "because there are faults in both cases" was mentioned in the Sūtra, but it was not stated here [in the commentary].
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "If [it exists] at destruction..."
And if it were destroyed, that would not be its effect... // MAnu 2.195c //
The ellipsis is "if the effect were to exist from the cause"; it follows, therefore, that this is not its effect. Otherwise, everything would be the effect of everything.
For the relation of cause and effect does not consist in mere immediate succession;
for if it did, it would follow that destruction is an effect,
since immediate succession exists even in relation to other things.
Because proximity and other such factors have already been refuted, an effect cannot likewise arise from anything else; thus, there would be neither an effect nor a cause.
In either case, since the preceding entity lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it follows that it is non-existent.
The author of the Sūtra, having prioritized the position accepted by the followers of Sugata, stated the refutation.
However, the author of the Bhāṣya [argues] that because non-existence is dependent upon existence, there is no contradiction with the meaning through that sequence.
*8,241* Now, it is indeed the case that there is the production of an effect at every moment.
Furthermore, an effect is not capable of arising without a cause;
for if that were the case, it would follow that it must either exist eternally or never exist at all.
Therefore, the very production of the effect will itself expose the faults inherent in either of those two positions.
Or [it might be argued that he] will cause another position to be accepted; therefore, he says: "And in the production of the effect," etc.
And what is the proof for the arising of an effect? MĀnuv 2.2.195d.
This might be so if the production of an effect at every moment were supported by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*);
but this is not the case.
Nor does a mere assertion of one's own have the power to imply another fact, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the production of effects at every moment— namely, "whatever exists is momentary, like the body and so forth; and the subject of dispute exists"— we say no,
because this very [argument] is being refuted.
Furthermore, because the body and so forth lack momentariness, the example is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).

To this objection—that it has been stated that the proof of momentariness follows from establishing the difference between the body and so forth in its preceding and succeeding moments due to a difference in their dimensions—the author replies: "Even though there is no difference" (*abhede 'pi*).
"In the case of bodies, lamps, fruits, and so forth, it is logical for us to perceive their specific differences despite their lack of essential distinction. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.196)
The phrase "of the preceding and succeeding moments" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"Specifically" means by way of its distinction from the theory of origination (*ārambhavāda*). By the word "etcetera," sprouts and so forth are included.
The perception of distinction is the perception of a difference in magnitude;
this is the meaning according to our view as proponents of transformation (pariṇāmavādins).
For those who maintain the theory of origination (ārambhavādins) accept that dimension (parimāṇa) exists as long as the substance itself exists;
this is because the distinction between dimensions depends on whether there is an increase or decrease in the number of constituent parts (avayava).
For it is unavoidable that when parts are subtracted, the destruction of the substance occurs, and when parts are added, its production occurs.
Therefore, for them, a difference in dimension must necessarily entail a difference in substance.
For us, however, the view is that the substance remains constant while it undergoes transformation through the increase or decrease of its parts, thereby assuming various dimensions.
In that case, a difference in magnitude does not entail a difference in identity.
Furthermore, is it being proved that there is a difference between the preceding and succeeding moments of the fruit and so forth, or rather that there is an absence of non-difference?
In the first case, there is the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*),
because we also accept the existence of difference;
however, that alone does not establish momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
He states the fault in the second [case]: "Because of experience."
... from experience. // Mānava 2.196d //
If the perception of a specific quality is not a valid means of knowledge, how can there be a perception of stability?

The remainder of the argument is that this inference has its object sublated by the recognition "this is that very fruit," which establishes the non-difference between the preceding and succeeding moments.
If it is argued that recognition is erroneous and thus incapable of proving non-difference,
then we reply that the perception of a difference in size is likewise erroneous and thus incapable of proving actual difference.

If it is argued that the observation of a difference in magnitude is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), he says in response: "viśeṣa... [Verse 8.243]. In that case, why is the perception of stability not a valid means of knowledge? For that too is likewise devoid of subverting evidence.
If it is argued that the perception of a specific difference is what sublates [the opponent's position], then why is the perception of stability not likewise a sublater?
Therefore, [this applies] to these two cases where no specific difference is perceived.

Since the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is untenable and because they are not experienced as mutual opposites, one must abandon partiality for either side and establish [the matter] precisely as having both difference and non-difference as its object.
Otherwise, even due to doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) in the example, the opponent's inference would be vitiated.
In this manner, the deficiency of other members of the logical reasoning (*tarka*) should be inferred by oneself. *8,244*
But why have these sūtras been explained here out of their sequential order? It is said in reply:
By way of introduction (*upodghāta*), the author of the Sūtras himself first refuted the opposing arguments and finally presented Pratyabhijñā as being free from all thorns.
The author of the Bhāṣya, however, for the sake of easy understanding, following the sequence of the student's inquiries, first stated Pratyabhijñā and subsequently removed its objections.
Regarding the statement that "the absence of suffering and happiness [are what is meant by liberation]," which was restated [in the Sūtra], he refutes it with the word "dig" (direction).
And if existence were to exist somewhere, it would be like the example of the sky and pleasure. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.197cd)
"By its own example" refers to the extension of the reason: "from that logic which was stated regarding the existence of space.
The meaning is: "because it is perceived in a positive form (vidhirūpeṇa) independently of both a substratum (dharmī) and a counter-correlate (pratiyogī).
The phrase "if its existence were to occur somewhere" implies "by way of that example."

By this, he indicates a subverting argument (*bādhaka*): otherwise, even form and the other [sensory objects] would not possess the nature of being entities (*bhāvatva*), as there is no distinction [between them].
Although the directions are not distinct from space, they are nevertheless mentioned in order to make known the existence of parts within space.
The singular number, however, is intended to refer to the genus (*jāti*).
By this, the Sūtra passage "and because there is no distinction in the case of space" is explained in another way.
By establishing that space and the other [elements] are positive entities (*bhāva*), the view that the universe consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is refuted.
Furthermore, it is not undesirable (contradictory) for us that the self has the nature of cognition,
because momentary destruction has been refuted and because the subjectivity of cognition is also accepted by the opponent.
Liberation, however, will be examined in the fourth [chapter].
It might be argued:
"That established tenet which is common to both the Vaibhāṣika and Sautrāntika and yet contradicts their own respective positions has already been refuted."

As for that specific tenet of the Sautrāntika: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is twofold, because the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) are twofold. Among these, the entire manifold of form and so forth, which is distinct from cognition, is only inferable (*anumeya*) and not perceptible (*pratyakṣa*)."
"But knowledge, having the form of blue and so forth, is to be known through perception. Why has this [position] not been refuted? To this he says: "The universe," etc.
He who, having abandoned the universe as perceived by direct perception, would speak of it as being merely inferred,
should be shunned like a proponent of illusion (māyāvādin) by one desiring prosperity.

Between those two— the Vaibhāṣika and the Sautrāntika— the Sautrāntika, having set aside the view that the entire universe consisting of form and so forth is perceptible, and not accepting the perceptibility of the universe of form and so forth as asserted by the Vaibhāṣikas and others—
meaning, up to this point— he would state what is inferred; that is, he would accept that the universe of form and so forth is cognizable through inference.
"Like a magician" (māyāvādivat) means he behaves like a magician.
This is what is meant:
just as one who dispels all calamities [even while acting as a magician],...
The proponent of illusion (māyāvāda) has not been refuted here in this chapter;
since it has already been utterly demolished, it need only be disregarded.
This is for the purpose of making it known that there is no refutation of it alongside the systems of the Sāṅkhyas and others, which possess some slight degree of validity.

Likewise, the doctrine that external objects are inferable [is also rejected]. Now, one might object: "The doctrine of illusion (māyāvāda) arose after the production of the Sūtras; how, then, can there be occasion for its refutation?"
Not so;
for it has been stated that "they have functioned from beginningless time."
Otherwise, there would be no occasion even to refute the Sāṅkhya and other schools.

[Vyāsa-3 *8,249*] But surely, according to the maxim that "what is not prohibited is accepted," why can it not be assumed that the author of the Sūtras intended the non-perceptibility of the entire universe, including blue and so forth?

[It is] not so, nor is it possible [to maintain that]. The intention of the author of the Sūtras must be conceived as being non-contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and in accordance with valid means of knowledge.
Anticipating the objection that "this meaning is not thus," he says: "All... [and so forth].
How indeed can that which is always established by all means of valid cognition as distinct from the intellect be of the nature of the intellect? ... MAnu 2.199a-c.
This is the sequence of the reply here:
it cannot be maintained that objects such as blue are not perceptible,
because the immediacy of the cognition of blue and so forth is established by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin).
Furthermore, it is established by inference because it is conditioned by the existence of the operation of the sense faculties.
Now, if it is thought:
"Whatever cognition arises with respect to a certain object, that [cognition] takes on the form of that [object],"
And that cognition, by virtue of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatā*), directly perceives even the forms such as blue that reside within itself.
Therefore, since the multitude of forms such as blue—which are apprehended through direct perception—reside within the intellect (*buddhi*), there is no fault whatsoever.
To this, the following [objection] arises:
How indeed can that circle of forms such as blue, which always appears as manifest and is established by all means of valid cognition as distinct from cognition,
be accepted as being cognition itself?
For this form of blue and so forth manifests as manifest through its outward-directedness, characterized by the "this-ness" (idantā) [of the object].
It is never the case that [one thinks] "I am blue" by way of inward-directedness.
Likewise, immediately after the direct cognition of blue, one who desires blue invariably proceeds toward the external;
therefore, it is inferred that by this [cognition], the external object itself has been directly perceived.
For it is not logical that knowledge [should be directed] toward one thing while activity is directed toward another,
as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle; however, the objection regarding an intermediate inference will be refuted later.

Thus, even when asked by a trustworthy person, "Do you see this directly?", one points with a finger and says "this," referring only to the external object; therefore, by all three means of valid cognition, it is determined that the form of blue and so forth, which appears directly, is indeed distinct from the cognition itself.
Nor is all of this an illusion.
Because there is never an alternative perception [of it as otherwise],
and because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to accept it as erroneous in the absence of a subverting factor (bādhaka),
the form of blue and so forth that appears as immediate is indeed external.
But it does not reside in the intellect.
Furthermore, if external objects were not perceptible, they would simply be unestablished,
because there would be no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for them.
And thus, he says "the universe" [in verse 1.10], meaning that the acceptance of external objects would be rendered empty.
... and what else is the measure of the universe? Mānava-dharma-śāstra 2.2.199d.
The word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the compound].
What is its object of valid cognition (*pramā*), such that it is called "having such an object" (*kiṃprama*)?
If it is argued that the external form is the inferable object, [we reply: no.
Because it is impossible to take as the subject (pakṣa) that which is entirely unestablished,
and because the pervasion (vyāpti) cannot be established due to the absence of a logical mark (liṅga).
This might be argued:
The form residing in the intellect appears as something immediate;
since it is occasional, it must depend on some cause, which will lead one to infer an external object such as blue.
This is not so.
Since the form of blue and so forth manifests precisely as something external,
where has this been established— that whatever is occasional must have a cause?
If it is argued that [the cause] is cognition itself, [we say] no;
for in the theory that external objects are not perceived, even in that case the causality [of cognition] is not established.
If it is argued that cognition is observed to have a preceding cognition as its cause, [we reply:]...
In that case, let it be postulated that even the mental aspect (*ākāra*) is produced by a preceding aspect;
what is the use of this obsession with external objects (*bāhyārtha*), given that there is no production of cognitions of blue?

If it is argued that [the object] is not [the cause] because the production of a yellow cognition is observed immediately thereafter, [we reply]: no; for the opponent has never established anywhere the principle that [a cognition] is produced by something similar [to its object]. (8.253)
Furthermore, it must be postulated that [the cause] produces even a dissimilar cognition by making internal factors such as latent impressions (vāsanā) its auxiliary conditions;
not external ones.
Since it is impossible to postulate an unperceived [cause] when an explanation is possible through what is perceived,
the external object (*bāhyārtha*) is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, because this view is not a fit object for suspicion, it was stated that it is not refuted here.
Alternatively, with the intention that [the faults] can be understood as things to be abandoned by the disciples themselves because they are very clear and not minor defects, he says: "All," etc.
Since the entire world is constantly terrified by this direct experience,
why would one who denies it— not being a proponent of a position devoid of valid means of cognition— not be afraid?
Even the Mādhyamikas and others, though they do not deny external objects (or duality), nevertheless accept conventional existence and so forth out of fear of contradicting experience;
therefore, this experience must indeed be followed by everyone.
Even that [external object] which the Sautrāntika denies, because he rejects the externality of the form of blue and so forth, which is established by experience and is directly perceived.
Likewise, he speaks without proof,
because there is no evidence for the presence of forms such as blue within the mind.
Of that [too]...
What refutation could there not be for that Sautrāntika who denies experience and maintains a position devoid of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
Everything would indeed be [a refutation]. [As it is said:
"Unity resides in experience," "from his own example," and "of him who denies that."
Thus, the contradiction with experience has been stated in various places regarding the opposing position.
To show how that is so, he demonstrates it through a dramatic gesture: "So am I.
[Verse 8.255] "I am that; this very same I am happy; I am the eternal sky and the directions."
Experiences such as "it is true" and so forth always proceed toward their respective opposites.

Here, the experience of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) grasping the oneness of the self as "I am that very same one" has been shown; likewise, the experience of the affirmation of pleasure as "I am happy" pertains to what is not the self.
The sky is existent in the form of a real entity,
and the directions are truly existent in the form of real entities; thus, there is the experience of both the sky and the directions as being existent entities.
By the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of [cognitions] such as "this is blue" and "I am not blue.
Those that go against them are those whose objects are contrary to what has been accepted by them;
[this refers to the systems of] the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas.
He concludes the refutation of the convention with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).
Therefore, who indeed—save for a host of demons—would ever embrace such a wicked doctrine, which is devoid of pride and serves as an antidote to all means of valid cognition? (Manu 2.202)
It is opposed to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and has as its object a meaning that contradicts all means of valid cognition;
for this very reason, it is a "bad doctrine" (*durmata*).
To address the objection—"Since it has been accepted by many such as Dignāga and others, who indeed would accept [this view]?"—it is said: "without" (*vinā*).
The intended meaning is that this objection pertains specifically to the subject of the *satpuruṣa* (the virtuous person).
Nor is such a refutation useless;
for it is explained as a consideration of who indeed would grasp the stated meaning upon reflection.
Thus concludes the section on the "Aggregate" (*samudāyādhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
[8.257] Now begins the refutation of the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavādāpākaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*. This is the section concerning the non-existent (*asadadhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. [The effect] does not arise from the non-existent, because such a thing has never been observed. Oṃ.
The Madhyamaka doctrine is refuted here;
in order to demonstrate that it contradicts the meaning already stated, he first sets it forth with the words "another [says]": "apara" (another).
"Not from the non-existent, because it has not been observed.
Furthermore: "The Void is entirely beyond the range of mind and speech;
it is without distinction, self-luminous, untainted, undecaying, and immortal. (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 2.2.203)
It is free from all defects, infinite in terms of space and time, and [infinite] in terms of substance... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.204a-c //
Another Mādhyamika says: "We say thus"; this is to be connected with what is about to be stated.
The remainder of the sense is that emptiness alone is reality, and there is nothing other than that.
But surely there exist the five aggregates beyond that; therefore it was said: "entirely."
The entire world, consisting of the five aggregates, is indeed empty; the meaning is that there is nothing other than that. As to how that emptiness is established, it is said: "self-luminous."
And self-manifestness does not consist in having itself as its own object of illumination; rather, it is simply the state of not being illuminated by another.
With this intention, it is said: "the mind."
This is an illustration of the mere absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Why is emptiness not an object of a means of valid cognition? Because it is devoid of all properties (*nirdharmaka*).
It has been stated that the operation of a means of valid cognition occurs only with respect to that which possesses a common nature—that is, without distinction.

If the Void (śūnya) were the self of the entire world, then its attributes—such as being subject to stain, old age, death, suffering, and limitation—would belong to that very [Void] itself; how then could it possess qualities such as being devoid of distinctions? To this, he says: "stainless" (nirlepa).
Attachment (*lepa*) is the connection with merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).
Faults (*doṣa*) are suffering and so forth.
And in reality, it is infinite, being devoid of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) relative to any other entity.
Alternatively, since that which is pure, omnipresent, eternal, the self of all, and empty is so described,
how is it said to be "without distinction"? To this, the following was stated:
It is called "pure" merely by the absence of defects such as being smeared;
the doctrine of its omnipresence and so forth is based on the absence of spatial and other limitations, and not by relying on any particular attribute. (8.260)
The nature of a treatise (*śāstra*) is the exposition of categories established in the relationship between means (*upāya*) and ends (*upeya*).

Therefore, having shown the conflicting views regarding the subject matter of reality, [the author] demonstrates the means and the end for those who hold such conflicting views: "I am that" (*tadasmīti*).
...that which is constantly perceived through the meditation "I am that," being free from defects such as passion and the like, shall lead the yogin to that very state of being.

The connection is as follows: that emptiness—which has been made directly manifest through constant meditation in the form "I am that emptiness"—being free from defects such as passion and so forth, leads the yogin to liberation, which is the state of being that very emptiness.
As it has been said:
"Like the extinguishing of a lamp is the liberation of that Protector (Tāyin);
[this is] the nature of what is to come.
If the form of liberation is empty, how then is everything said to be empty?
Therefore, he says: "of that very [person]."
Through that very beginningless conventional reality, the world, consisting of various diverse forms, appears as if it were real... // MAnu 2.205a-c //
It belongs to that which is empty alone.
It is called *saṃvṛti* because by means of it things are concealed; this *saṃvṛti* is ignorance (*avidyā*).
If it were real, non-duality would be lost; if it were merely superimposed, it would require another *saṃvṛti*, and thus it is said to be beginningless.
That which consists of various distinctions and is composed of the five aggregates is called "entirely empty" because it is constructed by emptiness and ignorance;
yet it is not the case that it is simply that very thing itself.
In that case, is this [world] simply non-existent?
Or, if it exists in such a manner, how can there be the appearance of it as "existent"? [It is so] because of the superimposition of existence. (8.263)
He states another alternative: "truthfulness."
... its conventional reality is also accepted. MAnu 2.205cd.
Even though that world is superimposed, its conventional reality is accepted; therefore, there is no contradiction with the cognition of existence.
If the world possesses existence, how then can it be non-existent?
Since it was stated that "by which [it] appears as if possessed of day," he says: "ultimately real" (pāramārthika).
But ultimate existence, however, never belongs to anything other than emptiness.
Ultimate existence (*pāramārthika-sattva*) is the state of being entirely uncontradicted; because that [ultimate existence] is absent, this world is proclaimed to be non-existent.

To the question, "In the absence of ultimate existence, how can there be worldly transactions such as causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in the world? he says: "By means of the conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) alone."
All worldly transaction proceeds by means of conventional truth alone.
The entirety [of worldly activity] is characterized by relinquishment, acquisition, indifference, higher knowledge, salutation, and purposeful action;
for even conventional discourse lacks reality,
as in a dream— this is the implied sense.
It is only ultimate existence that is incompatible with conventional discourse, because it is devoid of all activity;
it is not the absence of such [ultimate] existence. With this intention, it was said: "by means of conventional existence alone. (8.265)
He shows the disagreement regarding the subject of creation and dissolution [in the verse beginning] with "From the void" (śūnyāt).
"From emptiness, through the conjunction with conventional reality, this entire universe proceeds;
then again, at the time of creation and at its end, it becomes still and returns to emptiness.
Thus he says... [MAnu 2.207a-e] *8,266*
"At the time of creation" means it proceeds or arises.
Since that which is empty is devoid of activity, how can it be the creator of the universe? To this it is said: "by way of conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti-yogena*).
"In the end" refers to the time of dissolution (*pralaya-kāla*).
"Stimite" means motionless.
By this, the process of dissolution (*pralaya*)—according to the logic of the division of actions and so forth—of those who assert the reality of the universe is refuted;
the remainder of the sense is "like an elephant in a dream."
He introduces the present section for the purpose of refuting the view thus presented, with the words: "With reference to that."
...with reference to that, the Teacher of the Worlds spoke.

Regarding what was stated—that this world arises from nothingness alone—in order to refute that according to its literal sense, the Sūtra says: "Oṃ, not from the non-existent, because it is not observed; Oṃ.
He explains that as follows: "Not from the non-existent, because it is not observed.
(8.267) Not from the non-existent, because it is not observed.
[Second time:
There is no coming into being of a non-existent world... MĀnuv 2.208a.
The arising—that is, the birth—of the world from a non-existent void, which is devoid of all particularities and equal to a flower in the sky, is not tenable.
Why is this so? To this he says: "For indeed... (na hi).
... for the birth of a non-existent thing is never seen, nor that of an existent thing anywhere... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.208bc //
That is to say, for you who maintain that the effect exists [prior to its production],
the birth of something non-existent is not observed anywhere, because it has never been seen.
In all these cases, it should be understood that the critique is stated by establishing the non-existence of the void (*śūnya*).
This might be so.
The absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) establishes the absence of an object of cognition (*prameyābhāva*),

but not the absence of a particular means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaviśeṣābhāva*). For [otherwise], the non-existence of *dharma* and so forth would be established simply by the exclusion of the perception of people like us.
Therefore, in this case as well, the reason must be stated as "because there is an absence of valid cognition.
But how can it be said that [the object] is "not seen," which is merely a statement of the absence of perception?
Because [the reason] is inconclusive, he says: "And it is a means of valid cognition."
And authoritative perception is indeed better than all [other means of knowledge].
"Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone is the most excellent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), superior to all inference (*anumāna*) and scripture (*āgama*).
This is the underlying intention:

having proposed the thesis that "the world does not exist as a non-existent entity," when the question "Why? arises, one provides the reason: "Because there is an absence of a means of valid cognition for it."

Having kept this in mind, when the inquiry arises as to why there is a lack of proof regarding that [Pradhāna], it is shown that since inference and scripture are rooted in perception, perception alone is the superior means of knowledge; thus,
its absence is demonstrated here on the grounds that it was not perceived at the outset, and not as a reason for the primary thesis.

[If it were so,] the aforementioned fault would occur. Therefore, one must also state that there is an absence of inference and the other [means of knowledge]; to this, he says: "And [it is] a means of valid cognition."
This is the intended meaning:

the validity of the Vedas and so forth is not accepted by the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin), whereas it is accepted by us regarding his own scripture; therefore, students themselves can understand that there is no scripture here upon which both parties agree.
The non-existence of inference is indeed established by the non-existence of perception,
because perception is that upon which inference depends;
for it is only that which has been perceived somewhere by perception that [is inferred] by inference.
This must be established.
Therefore, even though non-existence was not explicitly mentioned [in the definition], it is obtained through inference; thus, the author of the Sūtra stated simply "because it is not perceived."
For this very reason, it was stated previously: "in some cases.
Let there be no direct perception as a means of valid cognition for the arising of the world from emptiness, nor let there be scripture.
Nevertheless, there will be inference [for the opponent].

Even though, in the case of the arising of the existent from the non-existent, perception is absent and thus neither perceived nor inferred [instances] are possible, the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) is still tenable.

For, once the existence of a cause has been negated, one might suspect that birth would result from the non-existent alone; it is with the intent of stating the sublation of such inferences by means of reasoning (*tarka*) that the Sūtra says: "Oṃ, and in this way, even for those who are indifferent, [the effect] would be established, Oṃ."
Thus it is said.
He explains that as follows: "If it is thus..."
And in this way, success would belong even to those who are indifferent.
(BBs 2.2.27) If it were so, then from the seventh taste, sweetness and the like, there would arise corpulence for people, just as the horn of a cat is a killer of a cow. (MAnu 2.2.209)
If any effect whatsoever were to arise from that which is non-existent, then, just as from the sweet [taste] and so forth, there would be the production of the seventh taste, añjana;

or, just as a cow's horn, a cat's horn would also be a killer of people because there is no distinction. By this, the aphorism is explained as follows: if this were the case, it would follow that effects such as corpulence could be established even from the seventh taste and so forth, which are objects of indifference for those who are neutral—that is, things that fall outside the scope of the notions of what is to be abandoned, what is to be adopted, or what is to be disregarded. *8,273*
He explains by way of another method: "one who seeks an effect," and so forth.
One who seeks an effect should never, under any circumstances, accept even a real cause [if it is defective].
If an effect were to arise from that which is non-existent, then a weaver or similar craftsman seeking an effect such as a cloth would never at all take up existent causes such as threads,
since the cloth and so forth would arise from what is non-existent. He states another over-extension [of this argument] with the word "no."
It would not proceed toward an object of desire, because an object of desire cannot exist if [the self] is empty.
Not only is the adoption of an existent cause untenable for the production of an effect that is non-existent,
but [the agent] would neither engage nor exert effort toward the production of a cloth or the like.
Why?
Because it is impossible for [the effect] to arise from that which is empty.
By this, [it is shown that there is no production] from material causes such as threads, etc.
The sūtra is thus explained as meaning that the accomplishment of cloth and other such things would occur for female slaves and for men who lack the desire to act and so forth.
It explains it by another method: "deśa... etc.
In this world, the restriction of place, time, and so forth would arise from that which is empty yet existent.
If an effect arises from a non-existent void, there would be no restriction regarding its place, time, or state.
For instance,
if the world were to arise from a mere void, then wheat would grow in black soil and not in white soil.
In spring, the *kiṃśuka* trees come into flower,
not in the rainy season.
A cow gives birth to a calf only when she is three years old, and not otherwise.

Rice grains possessing husks alone produce sprouts and not otherwise; such a restriction regarding place, time, and other factors would not exist for the production of effects [if they were empty], because emptiness is undifferentiated everywhere.

By this, the aphorism is explained to mean that the accomplishment—that is, the production—of effects would occur even for those things that are indifferent and independent of restrictions of place, time, and so forth.
The collective meaning is that if an effect were to arise from emptiness alone, there would be no dependence upon an agent, material cause, or efficient cause.
[Objection: But surely we maintain that the production of an effect from emptiness occurs only at the time of the initial creation, and not at all times;
however, at other times, it arises precisely from the collection of causes such as the agent and so forth.
Therefore, there is no over-extension; hence he says: "puruṣa... etc.
If anything whatsoever were produced in accordance with the will of a person, [there would be no such thing as destiny].
Why is it not inferred that everything likewise arises from the Puruṣa, because of its being a real entity? ... MAnu 2.2.212a-c.
"Something" refers to a present effect;
this is because it is a real entity and because it is an effect.
"Of everything" means of every such thing.
The meaning is "even of an effect belonging to the beginningless time. By this, a person— the agent of an existing effect belonging to the beginningless time— is to be inferred.
Why?
Because it is observed; since the fact that contemporary effects have a person as their agent is certain, the first sutra is thus explained by another method.
Furthermore, the mention of "person" (*puruṣa*) in both the sutra and the commentary is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth. (8.276)
But is not all of this self-contradictory?
For instance, as it has been said: "Because that which is non-existent is never observed."
That being so, the same applies to the case of [the cause] being existent;
for even the causality of an existent entity is not accepted by either of us anywhere.
But surely, by such examples as "like honey" and "like a cow's horn," the capacity of an existent entity to effect creation and dissolution has been demonstrated.
Not so;
for since the entire world is non-existent, even honey and the like, which fall within it, lack existence.
And as for this over-extension [of the argument]: "If that which is non-existent were a cause, then the seventh taste and so forth would also [be causes] just like honey and the like."
[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence [of the cause] performing its function [at all times].

That [consequence] is also equivalent to the undesirable consequence that, if an existent thing were a cause, threads and the like would perform the function of producing effects such as clay-products.
Even if it is argued that "an existent thing possesses causality in general," [that is not the case].
Because that [existence] has already been stated to be untenable;
for it is impossible to conceive of causality in that which transcends all modification.

This is because there is a distinction based on the presence or absence of the cognition of existence, despite the lack of difference regarding the non-existence of things such as the sweet taste and the seventh taste.
As for the passage beginning with "one who seeks an effect" and so forth:
if God were the sole cause of everything, then since cloth and other such things would arise from Him alone, there would be no need for the appropriation of materials such as threads;
likewise, the will and other factors of the weaver and so forth would be rendered useless—this point is the same [in both cases].
By this, it should be understood that the consequential argument (*prasaṅga*) regarding place, time, and so forth is also refuted.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that [the world] follows the will of a person—that too shares the same logical status as the proof that the effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest are produced by a potter and similar agents. *8,278*
In this regard, in order to refute the claim that the universe is non-existent, the Sūtra states: "Om. It is not non-existent, because it is perceived. Om.
Thus [it is said]. He explains that with the words "And not... (na ca).
"Not non-existence, because it is perceived" (BBs 2.2.28);
"...and the universe is not understood to be non-existent, for it exists" (MAnu 2.2.212cd).
Since... [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.213a]
That which comes into being is an entity (*bhāva*); that which is not an entity is a non-entity (*abhāva*), meaning,
in short, that which is non-existent (*asat*).

By the phrase "since it is understood as 'existent' (sat)," it should be understood that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is stated as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the reality of the universe.
To the objection—"What fault is there if the universe, though experienced as 'existent' through perception, were actually non-existent?"—he says: "anubhava... [and so forth].
But when experience itself is obstructed, from where could there be a statement by the proponent?
The phrase "if [the opponent] were to attempt to obstruct experience" is the ellipsis to be supplied.

In that regard, if even that which is perceived as existent were non-existent, then you would have stated [in response] that it is the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*); since you did not say so, the proponent of emptiness says to the opponent who claims "you are speechless": [this is your defeat].
Due to the absence of any means of refutation, one would inevitably incur defeat.

Furthermore, if [the opponent] were to say, "How can my statement not exist when it has been understood by the judges and others? then the validity of perception would have been admitted; thus, what could possibly be non-existent among the universe perceived as existing?
He raises an objection to avoid the aforementioned fault: "In a dream... and so forth.
Just like a dream or an illusion, this [world] is perceived only through conventional reality.
If [he kills] a living being... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.214a //
"Sleep and delusion"— like sleep and delusion (*svapnabhrāntivat*).
Although for the opponent even sleep is merely a delusion,
nevertheless, it is mentioned separately in accordance with the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), with reference to worldly convention.

Just as in a dream or an illusion, that which is non-existent— such as an elephant and so forth— is perceived as existent and possessing feet, so too this entire universe, though non-existent, is perceived as being real.
This alone is what is called the emptiness of the cause of the universe.
There is nothing further.
In that regard, how can the reality of the universe be established by the perception of it as "existent"?
Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the existence of the substratum— the seer— as well as the sense organs and their defects must be admitted,
lest the diversity of error and so forth be untenable;
for since everything is accounted for through the power of manifesting the non-existent by means of mere conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), such admission would be redundant.
And thus, there is no lack of proof for the statement;
for a statement that exists conventionally (*sāṃvṛta*) is established by direct perception itself.
Since the accomplishment of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is possible through that alone, there is no utility in [proving] ultimate existence (*pāramārthikasattva*). *8,282*
To avoid this [objection], [the Sūtra states]: "Oṃ, and because of dissimilarity, it is not like a dream and so forth; Oṃ."
Such is the sutra.
He explains it as follows: "Furthermore," and so on.
And because of the difference in nature, it is not like a dream and so forth;
furthermore, in this case, delusion does not cease at all.
This might be so if the cognition of existence regarding the phenomenal world were an error, like that of a snake in a rope;
but it is not so.
For if that were the case, why would this error of existence in the phenomenal world not be dispelled?
For the determination that cognitions are erroneous depends upon the cognition of a sublation (*bādhajñāna*),
as is observed in well-established cases.

If it were dependent merely on the status of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*), then even before the arising of the cognition of a sublation, common people and investigators would have to determine that cognitions such as "a snake in a rope" are erroneous.
Moreover, this is not observed anywhere;
nor do we perceive any sublater of the cognition of the existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Therefore, it is not reasonable to determine that [this cognition] is an error.

The absence of error in dreams, the necessity for an illusion to depend upon a substratum and so forth, and the absence of conventional existence's capacity to sustain worldly transaction— these points, established elsewhere, should be considered here as well. (8.284)
This might be asked:
is it being said that there is no sublation of the cognition of conceptual proliferation at this time,
or even at a later time?
In the first case, your determination of the reality of the world does not follow from that alone, because such a determination is impossible in the case of shell-silver and the like.
As for the second case, it does not exist.
"The cognition of conceptual proliferation (prapañca) will be sublated because it is a cognition, like that which is currently accepted"—
since the sublation of future [cognitions] is thus established, he says "of that which is beginningless" (anādeḥ).
If the cessation of this beginningless universe is desired,
then that cessation itself would have to cease, because it is possible for it to be an illusion.
The meaning is: of that which has persisted since beginningless time;
"of the universe" means of that which is based upon it;
"cessation" means sublation.
It would be sublated;
for if the sublation of the cognition of phenomenal proliferation is inferred because it is a cognition,
then there must necessarily also be a sublation of that very cognition of sublation.
Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the reason "being a cognition" (*pratyayatva*) in that case.

If the sublating cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) were itself sublated, the truthfulness (*yāthārthya*) of the cognition of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*) would be established. Let the investigation into ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) rest for now.
In common worldly practice, however, it is indeed observed as such.
This is not merely a logical consequence, but is also probable;
for the reality of the cognition of phenomenal diversity is sublated by the cognition of non-existence.
Because it is possible for that which has continued from beginningless time to possess correspondence (*yāthārthya*) through its concurrence with numerous similar and dissimilar instances,
whereas that which is occasional is precluded by the absence of such correspondence.
Because, by its very nature, there is the possibility of it being an error.
Now, one might object: "The cessation of the manifold world (prapañcanivṛtti) is indeed emptiness (śūnya).
And that, being of the nature of ultimate reality, is not imagined, because it has never been perceived."
How, then, could its cognition be sublated?
Rather, since the world of manifold diversity (*prapañca*) is seen to be possible as a mere conceptual construction, its cognition alone is what is sublatable.
Furthermore, the reason [for this] should be understood as being the cognition of the manifold diversity; therefore, he says: "of that which is seen."
If that which is seen were an illusion, how could there be no delusion regarding that which is unseen?
By the two words "error" (*bhrānti*) and "delusion" (*abhrama*), the state of being imagined (*kalpitatva*) is expressed.
This is what is meant:

it is stated in a contrary sense to take the state of being imagined as the basis for accepting the sublated nature of the cognition of the existence of that manifold world (*prapañca*) which is perceived by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Having apprehended the non-conceptual nature of the void—which is not perceived by any means of valid cognition—one takes up the fact that the cognition of its existence is non-sublatable;
for it is universally agreed that what is established by a means of valid cognition is non-conceptual, whereas what is accepted without such a basis is conceptual.
He demonstrates this very point by means of an example: "of cows," and so forth.
For the state of having horns does not belong to a hare simply because it exists in cows.
The phrase "accompanied by the state of being hornless" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Someone says that cows possess the quality of having horns; another says it is the case for a rabbit.
In that regard, according to the opponent's method, the hornedness of cows is postulated because it is observed.
It might be argued that "the state of being a rabbit's horn" [is a valid example] because it is imagined and has never been perceived;

however, such is not the common understanding in the world (*loka*). Furthermore, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) must be understood precisely in accordance with the world, and not otherwise, because the worldly convention itself is the means for understanding that [ultimate truth].
Thus, the reality of the universe has been established by the force of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and the suspicion of its sublation has been refuted.

To the question, "What is thereby established?", he says that the objection raised by the opponent—that there is a lack of evidence for existence even if it were a cause—is refuted; and in doing so, he also refutes another [objection] regarding parity: "For us..."
Thus it is said.

But for us, everything is consistent because of our authoritative means of knowledge, through the grace of the Lord, and by virtue of the validity of the scriptures as expressed in the manner already stated.
For those who maintain that there is a real cause, everything challenged by the opponent is logically consistent.
How so?

Because when the reality of the world is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is free from sublation, the existence of causes such as flowers for honey and the like is thereby established.

Furthermore, since threads and other such materials are established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as having diverse intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), there is no undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that they would produce effects such as clay.
For there is no difference in intrinsic nature between what exists and what does not exist, because that would contradict their non-existence.
Since causality is perceived only through valid cognition, any argument against it is merely fallacious.

It is entirely improper to postulate a distinction based on the mere cognition of existence for things like sweet flavors that have already been cognized as existing by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, even from a seventh taste—which is understood through the cognition of existence—corpulence would follow as being existent.

Furthermore, although God is the cause of all things, it is indeed logical that there is dependence upon threads and other materials, dependence upon human effort and so forth, and the restriction of place, time, and other factors.
"Let the effect arise only in dependence upon the threads and so forth"—this [is possible] through the grace of, that is, by the volition of, Īśvara.
Nor is such a volition tenable for a featureless void;
nor is this [claim] without authoritative evidence.
This is because, according to the method stated in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*, scripture (*āgama*), inference (*anumāna*), and so forth possess the status of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*).
Nor is the authority of the Vedas and other scriptures unestablished,
since the authority of scripture is established by the method set forth in the first aphorism (*sūtra*).
The charge of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding inference is also dispelled by the very authority of scripture (*āgamaprāmāṇya*).

The word "through grace" (*prasādāt*) is stated to indicate that at the beginning of creation, the Lord looks upon Brahmā and the others out of compassion, so that by their performance of the commands of the Supreme Lord, they may attain the supreme goal of man (*paramapuruṣārtha*).
[This was] previously [stated regarding] the universe.

Having raised the objection that the perception adduced to prove reality might be established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*), the sūtra "And because of dissimilarity, it is not like dreams and so forth" was explained as a refutation of that.

Now, in order to refute by means of a counter-argument the inference stated by the opponent regarding the falsity of the universe, he first entertains the inference for falsity: "Because of being perceptible" (*dṛśyatvāt*).
If it is argued that [the world] is false because it is perceptible, like a dream... // MAnu 2.217ab //

If it were stated that "everything is false," there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) in cases such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell where falsity is already admitted,
and there would also be a contradiction (*bādha*) regarding the void (*śūnya*).
Therefore, it is stated that "the subject under dispute [is qualified] by both reality and falsity."

The meaning is: since the falsity of the entire universe is established by the inference, "The subject under dispute, such as the ether and so forth, is false because it is visible, like a dream," how can its reality be accepted?
[The opponent] asks this in order to refute [the position], saying: "And this... (*iyaṃ ca*).
And this [woman] is my mother. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.217b)
Let the universe be set aside for now;
and as for this inference based on the fact of being perceived (*dṛśyatva*),
the remainder [of the argument] is whether it is false or true.
He refutes the first [position] with the words "it is false."
If it were false, there would be no establishment of the point to be proven... MAnu 2.217c.
The point is that the impermanence of sound is not established by its visual nature (*cākṣuṣatva*), which does not exist in sound.
Regarding the second [alternative], visibility (*dṛśyatva*) is either visible or invisible.
He refutes the first [possibility] with the words "there is deviation" (*vyabhicāra*).
... provided that there is no deviation. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.217d)
If being an object of perception were not false and yet it is an object of perception,
then there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the very nature of being an object of perception.
The meaning is that in the second case, however, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished due to ignorance (*ajñāna*).
This might be argued: we say that the state of being visible (*dṛśyatva*) is indeed false.
Nor does it follow that such [evidence] fails to prove the probandum;
for it is established for both parties that even false things, such as the length of phonemes and so forth, possess proving power,
whereas visuality and the like lack such superimposition.
Even if [the object] is superimposed, it lacks probative force because it is not conventionally real, and not because it is false; therefore, he says: "probative force."
The fact that the unreal can be a means of proof is the thesis to be established, because there is disagreement on this point.

In an example where falsity is admitted, that [falsity] is the probans; and where probative capacity is accepted, there is disagreement regarding its falsity. Therefore, it is precisely the probative capacity of the unreal that remains to be proven, and not something already established for us. *8,293*

If you say, "I shall prove either the validity or the falsity [of my opponent's position] when there is a disagreement," is it by means of a true instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or by means of one that is false?
Regarding the first case, the answer has already been stated.
He states the fault in the second [case]: "And of that... and so forth.
And for him—... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.218c //

For nowhere do we accept that what is false can be a means of proof; therefore, its status as a means of proof remains indeed to be established. Thinking, "I shall establish its status as a means of proof," he says: "Thus... (iti).
... thus there would be an infinite regress ... // MAnu 2.218c //
The meaning is: "in the manner previously stated.

For there is no single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such that everything which is unreal is a prover. Nor would a proponent of existence ever accept the establishment of a probandum by means of a cognition that is indifferent to both existence and non-existence.
"So that there may be the cessation of an infinite regress.

Having thus refuted inference by means of [the fallacies of] unestablished reason and inconclusiveness, he states the sublation by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇabādha*) with the words "And existence" (*sattvaṃ ca*).
And its existence [is established] through experience.
This [world] of manifold diversity is established through experience; therefore, the inference [of its unreality] has a sublated object—this is the remainder [of the sense].
It is not only that the inference based on "visibility" is fallacious due to this defect.

However, he states that this also applies to whatever other inference regarding the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca) is asserted by others—whether it be its insentience (jaḍatva) or its finitude (paricchinnatva)—in the verse beginning with "anubhūti... (perception...).
If [the world] were false due to contradiction with experience, let there be no [such thing as] anything at all.
This is an illustration; it should also be understood that this includes the previously mentioned [fallacies of] deviation (vyabhicāra) and lack of proof (asiddhi). For instance:
Is insentience and so forth real or false? In the first case, does it possess insentience and so forth or not?
In the first sub-case, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra).
In the second case, there is a deviation from the established tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
If [the reason] were false, there would be no establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*).
Non-existence of inferences would occur only if there were a contradiction with direct experience (*anubhava*).
And that [sublation] does not exist,
for sublation— which is a synonym for falsity— is what is to be established by inference;
nor is its absence cognizable through perception.

Since that [cognition] has as its object only the present, even if it somehow has as its object the absence of sublation existing in the present time, it cannot have as its object the absence of sublation occurring at another time; therefore, he says: "The past and future times also are within the range of our witness. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.219cd)
Here, the mention of the "past" is incidental;
the meaning of the particle *api* is that it is not only the present [that is perceived], but also the past.
The word "us" (*naḥ*) means "for all of us."
The meaning is that otherwise, the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) characterized by that [time] would be untenable.
What follows from this if time, even though not present, is an object of direct perception? To this he says: "That... (*tad*).
...existence also [is established] by virtue of its connection with that.
Existence as non-sublation consists in being connected with a subsequent time;
the meaning is that it is not merely the absence of sublation at the present time that is known through experience, but rather its absence throughout all times.
To the question "How is that so?", it is said: "of what is seen."
... [the testimony] of what was seen is that which reaches the witness. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.219f)
The meaning is that the validity of cognitions such as perception is apprehended by the Witness (sākṣin) of that which is the object of those perceptions and other means of knowledge.
For it is not possible to apprehend the validity of a cognition without including within it the fact that its object is unsublated throughout the three periods of time.

If the witness, while apprehending a cognition, were to establish the non-sublation of its object throughout the three periods of time because its very nature is to apprehend that cognition’s validity, then the same witness would also be the grasper of the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; thus, he would have to apprehend the validity of that [erroneous] cognition as well.

Consequently, the non-sublation of its object—such as the silver—throughout the three periods of time would also be established. Therefore, he explains the word "dṛṣṭa" (seen/apprehended) with the term "firm" (*dṛḍha*).
That which is seen with firm conviction is [true] perception; anything other than that is a semblance of perception.
That which is made an object by a cognition determined as being non-erroneous is said to be "seen.
Why?
Because that which is seen in a confused manner by the other [person] is a pseudo-perception (dṛṣṭābhāsa),
and because, between the primary and the secondary, it is logical to accept the primary.
This has already been explained previously (*8.299*).
Intending to show that the inferences such as "because of being visible" possess counter-arguments (*satpratipakṣa*), he says: "Because of error. (*bhrānteḥ*)
The distinction of conventional truth from error is that which is non-deviant;
since that too has been correctly accepted [by him], it is indeed true for us.
The meaning is: "from such things as mother-of-pearl appearing as silver, which are agreed upon as objects of error.

The distinction (*viśeṣa*) or difference of the entire universe—which is accepted as being conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*)—is characterized by non-deviation; that is, it never exists within anything that is agreed upon as false at any time or place.
Therefore, even by the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), [this must be admitted].
"Correctly" means without doubt.
That very distinction, in our view, will establish the reality of the universe; this is the ellipsis.
Therefore, the inferences such as "because of visibility" (dṛśyatva) are countered by valid counter-arguments.
Here, by the phrase "even by him [the opponent] correctly admitted," the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) is established;
however, by the phrase "possessing non-deviation" (avyabhicāravān), pervasion (vyāpti) is established.
The formal argument here is as follows:
The universe is not sublated by the three times,
because it is of a different nature from that which is merely apparent.
"By way of exclusion, like the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell," etc. (*8,300*).

Now, one might object: "In the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like, cessation occurs through the very cognition of the mother-of-pearl and so forth prior to the knowledge of the reality of emptiness;

however, it is only through the knowledge of emptiness that the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) will eventually occur. It is precisely in this manner that I have accepted the distinction between the apparent (*prātītika*) and the conventional (*sāṃvṛta*).
If you cannot establish this as a reason for the reality of the universe because of contradiction, he says: "Because of consciousness" (vijñānāt).
There is no instance observed where this [knowledge] might ever deviate from consciousness; therefore, it is valid cognition (*pramā*). 2.221a–c.
Inconstancy is the cessation [of the reason].
This distinction cannot be accepted, because it lacks authoritative evidence.

For a horse is never seen to be distinguished from others by means of a horn that lacks epistemic validity. [Objection: But surely this will be sublated at some point, since there exists the inference: "This is subject to sublation because it is perceptible, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and so forth. Therefore, how can there be an absence of valid cognition here? To this [the author replies]: *tasyo*... [text fragment]
He recalls the fault stated by himself with the words: "pramā" (valid cognition).
... that would not be valid cognition, because it contradicts itself.
The meaning is that it is that which is suspected [to be invalid].
"On account of its own contradiction" means because it entails the sublation of both its own object and itself.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*); for that [cognition] whose object is non-existent (*asan*) and which is itself sublated, [is not valid].
How could that [distinction] be authoritative?

Therefore, since this particular distinction cannot be accepted because it lacks a basis in valid cognition, another distinction must be accepted—one that is established by valid cognition and not contradicted by valid cognition;
that will serve as the reason for our [position on its] reality.
And its core meaning is that [an entity] is both accessible through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
[Objection: Why, then, is it not stated exactly in this way? [Response:

If it were stated in that manner, much would have to be established, such as the fact that valid cognitions reveal reality, that causal efficiency constitutes existence, and that in the absence of such efficiency there is no existence, and so forth.
This was stated thus for the sake of brevity, and that too has already been established at the appropriate occasion;
or rather, by this [verse], the reductio ad absurdum (pariśeṣa-pramāṇa) regarding the non-sublation of the phenomenal world (prapañca) has been stated.
For it follows that the world must be either sublatable or non-sublatable,
since there is no third possibility.
And sublation occurs either by means of knowledge of the true nature of well-known categories or by something else.
Of these, the first is not accepted by either the proponent or the opponent;
as for the second, it is refuted by the absence of any valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By process of elimination, it is precisely its non-sublatability that is established.
Alternatively, by these two verses, an inference based on the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) as its logical mark (*liṅga*) has been stated.
For subvertibility (*bādhyatva*) is pervaded by being the state of having its reality negated by the knowledge of the true nature of either a well-known object or something other than it.

And that pervader, being excluded from the world due to both non-acceptance [by the opponent] and the absence of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), excludes its own pervaded, namely subvertibility.
Having thus refuted the inferences for the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*), [the author now proceeds] to support them...
And in order to refute even the reasoning (tarka) imagined by others as being contrary to the direct perception of reality, he raises an objection with the words: "As for difference..."
If difference depends upon the apprehension of the qualified object, its substratum, and so forth, then because of the reason of mutual dependence, it would be difficult to grasp... [MĀnUV 2.222a–d]
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) are included;
the ellipsis (*śeṣa*) is "if they are grasped.
And [the word] "then" (*tarhi*).
This is the meaning:
if the manifold of phenomena (*prapañca*) were not conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), then it would not even be perceptible.
For instance:
For the manifold (prapañca) is held to be divided into many distinct parts; and if that distinction were not perceptible, the manifold itself would likewise be imperceptible,
because the cognition of it without its distinctions would result in the cognition of a non-dual void.
Furthermore, the cognition of difference is not logically tenable.

For when difference is perceived, it must be perceived either as a qualifier of the jar and cloth— as in "the jar and cloth are different"— or as the substantive characterized by them— as in "the difference between the jar and cloth."
For there is no cognition of "difference" as such;

rather, one must admit that difference is apprehended either as "the cloth is different from the jar" or as "the difference of the cloth from the jar," where it is grasped with the jar as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the cloth as the locus (*dharmin*).
In both cases, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*):
for difference must be known as a qualifier only when the two qualificands—the jar and the cloth—are already known;
indeed, it is not possible to perceive a staff as a qualifier when Devadatta himself is not seen.
Furthermore, the cognition of a qualificandum depends upon difference;
for without the perception of difference, it is not possible to have a cognition of an object qualified by duality, such as "a jar and a cloth.
The same should be understood regarding the perception of difference when [the object] functions as the qualificandum.
Likewise, when there is knowledge of the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), there is knowledge of difference, because [difference] is defined by them;
and when knowledge of difference exists, there is knowledge of the locus and the counter-correlate.
For when difference is not apprehended, the relationship between the locus (*dharmī*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) cannot be understood;
if it were otherwise, there would arise the cognition that "the difference of a pot from a pot."
Furthermore, mutually dependent effects cannot exist.

Therefore, if difference were real, its perception would be impossible; since that same consequence would apply to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as well, one must accept that this is merely the conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), which is charming only so long as it is not investigated.
[The author] refutes this with: "No."
"... not that. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.222).
The meaning is that what was stated—that difference is difficult to grasp—is not the case.
To the question "How so?", he says: "the essential nature" (*svarūpa*).
The intrinsic nature of a thing is its distinction... // MAnu 2.223a //
