Since difference (*bheda*) is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the thing (*vastu*), when that thing is apprehended, there is no subsequent apprehension of its difference;
rather, the apprehension of the thing itself is the apprehension of its difference.

And thus, where is there mutual dependence by which difference would be difficult to grasp? [It is] that in the apprehension of which there is no apprehension of that [other]. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.223b)
Since there is no non-apprehension of that difference when the object is apprehended, the connection is that difference is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the object.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows:
the disputed difference must be the nature of the jar, because it is not the case that it is not apprehended when the jar is apprehended, just like the nature of the jar itself.

If, in this context, one were to state simply that "it is because [the object] is being apprehended when that [cognition] is apprehended," then there would be an inconclusive argument (*anaikāntikatva*) due to the cloth in the cognition "the jar and the cloth," since the cloth is being known by the cognition of the jar.
To preclude this, it was stated: "When that [cognition] is apprehended, [the object] is not apprehended.
For there is no rule that when a jar is apprehended, the cloth—which is also being apprehended—is necessarily apprehended in every respect within that apprehension of the jar.

If the universal rule (*vyāpti*) were stated as "whatever is perceived in every respect within a cognition of X is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of that X," then in the cognition of a man with a staff (*daṇḍin*), the staff would necessarily also manifest; yet the staff is not the nature of the man with the staff. Therefore, the universal rule must be stated as being restricted to specific instances (*viśeṣaniṣṭha*).

Furthermore, what is called "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) is merely a particular form (*ākārabheda*) of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) caused by its connection with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); even so, there is no manifestation of the qualifier within the cognition of the qualified.
What indeed is this "cognition of the qualifier" that serves as the cause for the "cognition of the qualified"?
Furthermore, because [the process] occurs so rapidly, no sequential order is perceived.

Alternatively, taking the jar and its destruction as the subject (*pakṣa*), their non-difference from one another is to be proven by the fact that when one is necessarily cognized, the other invariably manifests.

For even when there is the cognition of "the man with a staff," the staff does not manifest [as a distinct object]; whereas in the cognition of the staff itself, the man with the staff is never [cognized as such].
"It exists as a throbbing.
This might be so if difference were grasped precisely as the apprehension of a real entity;
but it is not so.
Is it not the case that [the object] exists only at a time subsequent to its dependence upon a thing?
For in non-conceptual cognition, only the mere thing appears.

Difference manifests at a time subsequent to the perception of the object itself, provided there is recollection of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), just as similarity and non-existence do; therefore, he says: "Otherwise... (*anyathā*).
Otherwise, it would not be appropriate to say that there is a distinction between this [scripture] and that [Veda].

If difference were not perceived at the time of the cognition of an object, then even subsequent conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*) in the form "this is different from that" would not arise;
and in that case, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) accordingly would also not occur.
For, by means of the expression "in this [there is] that," difference is known after two entities have been indicated as the locus (*dharmī*) and its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*);
and it is not possible to indicate them in such a way without first apprehending their difference.
Because that [error] would follow even in the case of a single object.
If it is argued that this is possible by the mere existence of difference, [we say] no;
for it would follow that there is no cognition of non-difference between two trees standing at a distance.
If it is argued that this is so because of a defect [in perception], we say no;
for since the manifestation of difference (*bheda*) is effective through its own intrinsic existence (*svarūpasattā*) alone, a defect is incapable of affecting it.

Not only is the subsequent conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*)—such as "this is different from that"—and the corresponding linguistic usage untenable for one who does not accept the manifestation of difference at the time of perceiving the object itself; [it would also be untenable].
To the question "What then?", he says: "ungrasped."
When difference is not apprehended, then there would be the apprehension [of the object] as being from itself... // MAnu 2.224a-c //

If, even when a jar is perceived, its difference [from another object] is not seen, then the counter-correlate (pratiyogin)— the cloth— whether being remembered or being perceived immediately thereafter, must likewise be apprehended without a perception of difference.
And in the absence of a perception of difference, there would necessarily be a cognition of non-difference.
And likewise, at a later time, there would be a conceptual apprehension of difference, [thinking] "it is different from itself";
since this is not the case, he says: "In cognition... (pratītau).
...and because it contradicts common experience... // MAnu 2.224c //

The word "ca" (and) is connected with what follows. For indeed, the conceptual cognition experienced is precisely that "the jar is different from the cloth," and never that "it is different from itself."

Therefore, due to contradiction with experience (*pratīti-virodha*), it is not appropriate to accept such a conceptual apprehension (*savikalpaka-graha*); this is the remainder [of the sense]. Furthermore, if there were a conceptual apprehension of difference in the form "it is different from itself," then at some point there would also be such verbal usage (*vāgvyavahāra*).
And it is not so; thus he says: "For not..."
"...for no one would speak in such a manner. (Manu 2.224d).
By this, is there a contradiction with the cognition of a single person, or a contradiction with the cognition of everyone?
It is not the first, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
The second [alternative] is also refuted by the argument that it is unestablished (*asiddhi*);
for since no one ever engages in such usage at any time, and because there is instead a contrary usage, this is established by universal consensus (*sarvapratīti*).
Therefore, since difference manifests only upon the cognition of the entity itself, it is of the very nature of that entity.

Now, if difference is thus the nature of the entity, then because there is no distinction in its cognition and because its mutual dependence is entirely absent, it has been stated that there is no circular reasoning (*anyonyāśrayatva*).
In that case, is difference the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*)?
Or [is it] even from the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)?
Not the second [option],
because if a single difference were to possess the nature of both, it would entail the consequence of non-duality (*advaita*).
In the first case, although there is no mutual dependence between the cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) and the cognition of the difference (*bhedajñāna*),
how can the mutual dependence [of the cognition of difference] upon the cognition of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogijñāna*) be avoided?
Do not say so.
For when difference is known in its own nature, there is no dependence on the knowledge of the specific counter-positive;
and when the nature of the counter-positive is known, there is no dependence on the knowledge of this difference.
Let it be, then, that there is mutual dependence regarding the knowledge of the particulars.
For that [cognition] arises in the form, "The cloth is different from the jar.
In that case, the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) belongs either to the substratum (*dharmin*) as perceived through its difference, or otherwise;
it cannot be the latter.
For [otherwise] there would be the consequence of the cognition of difference even from itself.
In the first case, when the difference consisting of the very nature of the counter-positive is cognized, the same logic applies to the subject's status as a counter-positive.
And thus, in the cognition of the difference of the jar from the cloth, there is the cognition of the difference of the cloth from the jar; this results in mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*).
Not so;

for when the cognitions of the essential natures of a jar and a cloth—which are in fact mutually correlative—exist, and provided there is no obstacle such as similarity, there is no sublation to the cognition of a qualified difference characterized by mutual correlativity. *8,321*

Having thus refuted the charge of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) regarding the cognition of difference according to his own view, he states the rebuttal of those who maintain that differences are distinct [from one another]: "dharmitve... and so forth.
If the state of being the subject, the state of being the counter-correlate, and their mutual difference are apprehended simultaneously,
then the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation are likewise grasped.
And this is an elliptical indication;
it should be understood that the substratum (*dharmī*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) are also included.
The state of being that [relation] consists in being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) and being a qualificand (*viśe�syatva*).
In this context, because difference is one or the other of the qualifier and the qualificand, it is not mentioned separately.
This is the meaning.
Is it being asserted that there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-pratīti*), or in conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-pratīti*)?
Not the first;

for in that case, the substratum (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), their respective natures (*svarūpa*), their existence (*tadbhāva*), their difference (*bhedas*), or the two differences themselves, are all [apprehended] simultaneously.
Because of the manifestation of the forest,
there is likewise the state of being the qualifier and the qualified.
Furthermore, because the difference between the jar and the cloth, as well as their respective existences, are perceived simultaneously,
since everything is in contact with the sense faculty at one and the same time.
And because it is perceptible.

Now, it may be objected that those who maintain the doctrine of distinct difference do not accept that there is another [entity] called "the state of being" (tadbhāva) between the locus and the counter-correlate, or between the qualifier and the qualified.
How can this be?
It is not so,
because that [position] has been accepted by the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa* and others.
And this is the rebuttal to those very [objections]:

"Is it not the case that where the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is perceived later, there is no simultaneous manifestation? Therefore, by that example, it is inferred that the same applies everywhere? If you say this, we reply: No, because to establish the non-cognition of even a proximate object—just like one that is remote—is contrary to experience.
Even where the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is not present, the simultaneous cognition of the locus (*dharmin*), its properties (*dharmas*), and their distinctions is not untenable.
This is what was stated: "What contradiction is there?"
What contradiction is there? ... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.226a //
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "by its own nature."
... but it is precisely difference that is apprehended in its own form;
furthermore, it is apprehended specifically as "this from that."
The phrase "from this [to] that" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*);
it should also be understood to include "the difference between these two" and "these two are distinct.

Since in determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) there appears only the mutual distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) among objects already perceived by indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), and nothing further, even in that case there is no circular dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
Thus have those who maintain the theory of distinct difference (bhedabheda-vādinaḥ) said:

"When both difference and the things that differ appear simultaneously within a single non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-saṃvit*), then, by taking one of those differing things as a reference point (*avadhi*), a conceptual cognition arises in the form 'this is different from that. How [could this not occur]?"
Nor is there mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) in the view that difference is non-distinct [from the object]. Now, for what purpose is this presentation of the opponent's view?
[The answer is: because even for us, the cognition of a particular (*viśeṣa*) occurs without the separate existence of difference.
This is for the purpose of making it known that this very [previous] response is the solution.
"In that case, let this very statement be explained in that way.
[Reply: It is not possible to do so.

And because there is a contradiction in perceiving a separate distinction [between them] by the phrase "and its distinction," it was stated in the *Vaiśeṣika-parīkṣā* that even perception by way of the relation between qualifier and qualified does not differ from the modes (*prakāra*) of the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); therefore, no further exposition has been made here. *8,327*
Having thus refuted the consequence of mutual dependence by not accepting [the existence of] producers (*āpādaka*), he now announces another objection with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*).
And furthermore... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.227a //
The meaning is "something else.
If it is asked, "How so?"—[the answer is:
if here difference were perceived in dependence upon the cognition of the locus (*dharmin*) and so forth, then there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*).
Is it thus being established, or rather, that if difference were perceived, there would then be the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*)?
Regarding the first case, he states the defect: "Difference... [and so forth].
To him who asks, "How can difference be apprehended?",
it is replied that he has stated a circular argument, because the apprehension of difference depends upon the apprehension of the substratum and so forth.
"How?"— this is an objection;
"he asks" is a mild expression,
meaning as much as "he objects."

"Because of the apprehension of distinctions such as the substratum (dharmin) and so forth," means because of the apprehension of distinctions that depends upon the apprehension of the substratum and so forth.
How is this obtained?
Because the term "substratum and so forth" (dharmyādi) serves as an indicator for the apprehension of those [distinctions].

And because the word "beginning" (ādi), which has the sense of "cause," does not recur [in the subsequent terms], this [position] is mutually contradictory; such is the remainder [of the argument]. To explain:
Having asserted the proposition that "difference is difficult to apprehend," this is stated in order to establish it.
By this, if difference were to be apprehended in dependence upon the cognition of the locus (*dharmin*) and so forth, then there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*).

Thus, by means of the reductio ad absurdum (*āpādana*) that it would not be apprehended [in that case], it is established that it *is* indeed apprehended; therefore, it follows that its apprehension does not depend upon the apprehension of the locus and so forth.
And so, how is there no contradiction between the preceding and following statements, namely, "difference is difficult to grasp" and "it is nevertheless perceived"?
We ask this regarding the second [position].
Is it that no difference has ever been apprehended by anyone else, or is it that it has been apprehended somewhere?
He refutes the first alternative with the words "anyatve" (in the case of otherness).
If difference is not perceived, how can there be mutual dependence? Thus it has been stated.
If otherness is not apprehended anywhere, then it is impossible to even raise the charge of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*),
because there would be no basis for it.
For that [charge] occurs only when one relies upon a causal relationship between two things already perceived as distinct.

Finally, if there is no apprehension of the distinction between the proponent and the opponent, or between the object of refutation and the refuter, or between that which is to be entailed and the entailment, then the act of entailing simply does not arise.
He refutes the second [position] with the words "anyatvam" (distinctness).
If otherness were established, how could there be mutual dependence?
"Established" means well-known.
For if there were mutual dependence, the very cognition of difference would not occur;
indeed, effects that are mutually dependent are never observed or postulated anywhere.
And so, if there is indeed the cognition of difference, then this mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) is certainly merely an appearance, because it lacks the capacity to obstruct [the cognition].

If you argue that while the cognition of difference exists, its purport is simply that "it is not valid," we ask: do you hold that mutual dependence obstructs the *arising* of one from the other, or does it obstruct a property (*dharma*) thereof?
In the first case, how could even an invalid cognition of difference arise?
Nor is the second [case] possible;
for it is illogical that two distinct things should be mutually dependent while yet another thing is lost.
If you say it is conventional cognition (*saṃvṛti-pratīti*),
then what of that cloth?
Regarding the term "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*), [the opponent might argue that] it will be the cause of those very threads from which [the cloth] was produced.
To the question, "But what refutation of this reasoning has been stated by this [author]? he says: "Of such a kind... (*etādṛśasya*).
Both the speaker of such [words] and those who produce fallacious rejoinders—the illusionist and the Mādhyamika—are likewise [to be avoided]. 2.229abc.
This is not merely a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*), but whatever else that person has said is also [futile].
For instance: "If difference itself were to be differentiated by another difference, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)."

Likewise, if the imposition of difference occurs upon that which is already different, then there is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatva*) because the state of being different would be established by that very same difference.
If, however, another difference is admitted, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If the imposition of difference occurs upon that which is non-different, then it follows that even a cloth would possess difference inherently (*svataḥ*).

Likewise, difference is not perceived by direct perception (pratyakṣa) as such; for there is no experience of a cognition that apprehends "difference" alone. Even when a real entity (vastu) is cognized, the cognition of the entity does not occur preceded by the cognition of its difference.
Because of the fault already stated,
the cognition of difference is not preceded by the cognition of the thing-in-itself;
for if the cognition of difference were to occur when [the thing] is cognized as non-different, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Nor can they be simultaneous,
because the cognition of a thing is the cause of the cognition of its difference, and thus simultaneity is impossible;
nor is there any other alternative.
Likewise, either existence resides in the cause, or the cause exists within existence.
In the first case, the cause would be non-existent;
in the second, that which is non-existent would itself possess causality, and so forth.
The phrase "of such a kind" is stated in order to indicate that all of this is a *jātyuttara* (futile rejoinder),

because everything [so asserted] involves self-contradiction; for it is untenable for either difference (*bheda*) or existence (*sattā*) to have a nature distinct from their own essential form (*svarūpa*).
And because it is accepted that [the state of being] conditioned is indeed untenable.
If it is asked, "What is this 'jāti'?", [the answer is] no; for if the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) exists, this insistence is pointless,
and because it would be included within the fallacies of the "uncaused" (*ahetuprasaṅga*) and the "perpetual" (*nityasama*).
Because the word *māyā* belongs to the *vrīhy-ādi* group [of nominal stems], the form *māyī* is grammatically correct.

It is stated that "and the *māyī*" in order to indicate the extension (*atideśa*) of the principle that by the very refutation of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), the doctrine of illusion (*māyāvāda*) is also to be understood as refuted.

The word "eva" (only/just) is connected with what follows. [Objection: Why was this issue of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) and so forth not refuted by the author of the Sūtras himself? To this, he says: "That... (*tad*).
... those two should be disregarded by those desiring prosperity.
Therefore, because they are mines of futile rejoinders (*jātyuttara*), they should simply be disregarded;
the opponent should not be made to provide a refutation.
This is what is meant.
Only a statement that possesses a valid basis (*sadalama*) must be refuted, not one that lacks a basis;
otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
And this [fallacy] has been disregarded by the author of the Sūtras because it is a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) and thus lacks a valid basis.
However, we have refuted this for the sake of instructing our disciples.
It might be argued:
the proponent of emptiness considers emptiness to be the cause of the world.
But [the opponent objects]: "The Māyāvādin [holds that] Brahman [is the cause];
so how can there be an extension (atideśa) of the refutation of the Śūnyavāda—beginning with the words 'Because it is not seen [to arise] from the non-existent'—to the Māyāvāda?
For an extension is impossible when there is a difference in philosophical systems. To this, he says: "If... (yadi).
That which is the void for the proponents of emptiness is precisely Brahman for the proponents of illusion.
Therefore, the ellipsis is that "extension [of the rule] is logical.
To the question "How so?", he says: "For not..."

For there is no difference in defining characteristic between those two, because they are devoid of distinction. Indeed, a difference that is subject to dispute must be made known through a difference in defining characteristic; and such a [defining characteristic] is not possible for emptiness and Brahman.
This is because both [positions] are accepted as being without distinction. Now,

it may be argued that although there is no difference in external characteristics due to their lack of distinction, the proponent of Māyā (the Māyāvādin) accepts "being of the nature of reality, consciousness, infinity, and bliss" (*satyajñānānantānandātmakatva*) as the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of Brahman,
whereas the proponent of Śūnya (the Śūnyavādin) does not accept this for the Void (*śūnya*).
Thinking that there might therefore be a distinction between Brahman and emptiness, he says: "Because of falsehood, etc."
And the characteristic of both is their opposition to falsehood and the like.

For the proponent of Māyā, Brahman’s nature as consisting of truth, knowledge, and so forth is intended precisely as its opposition to falsehood, insentience, and the like, since no other meaning is possible;
this is also evident from his commentary [on the *Vedāntasāra*]: "The threefold end is a form opposed to falsehood and insentience, and is contrary to bondage, suffering, and the state of non-bliss."
Furthermore, the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādī) considers even emptiness to be the opposite of falsehood and so forth,
because of the statement: "That which is the opposite of dullness, conventional reality, suffering, the end, and prior faults."
Therefore, since even this [distinction] does not constitute a differentiator, the extended application (*atideśa*) is indeed appropriate.
It might be argued:

"The Sūtra states, 'And because of dissimilarity, it is not like a dream and so forth,' for the purpose of refuting the inference regarding the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*)."
In that regard, the refutation stated as "of error,
[which is] conventional truth" is understood in the Sūtra as being due to dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

As for what was further stated—that because the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) would arise if the state of being visible (*dṛśyatva*) were real, its falsity must be asserted, and thus it would be non-probative—this is not seen in that very sūtra. To the question, "How then is this [sūtra] to be explained? he says: "In one's own statement... (*svavākyeti*).
Because it accords with the absence of his own statement, there is no need for the opponent's response.
The unborn [Lord] refuted that position by means of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), stating "not like a dream and so forth," because [the world] does not arise from effort. MAnu 2.232a–c.
Here, by the word "sentence" (*vākya*), the meaning of the probans-sentence—namely, "visibility"—is indicated. In the phrase "in that subject" (*tatpakṣe*), the locative case denotes the object;
that is to say, it refers to the object of the proof of its falsity.
The word "iti" indicates the reason: because it is without effort— that is, without applying effort—
and because of the difference in nature, [the dream example] is not like that of dreams and so forth.
The connection is that [the author] has refuted [this] by means of this [argument].
This is what is meant:
the falsity of the property of being perceptible (*dṛśyatva*) is admitted precisely by the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*).
It is well-established that what is false has no probative power;
therefore, for this very reason, there is nothing at all to be done by proponents of existence (sadvādins) regarding this matter.
Because if one were to explicitly elaborate upon this refutation, it would contradict the nature of a *sūtra*.
Therefore, the author of the *sūtra* did not exert effort in elaborating this refutation;
however, we have made his intention clear. *8,342*

Nevertheless, as for what was stated regarding the contradiction with perception concerning the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*)— namely, "And its existence has been experienced"—
and also [the statement], "If it were false, there would be no [experience at all]"—
Thus, there is a lack of authoritative proof;
since neither of those two is seen in the Sūtra, he says "and" (ca).
...and thus [the Creator] indicated its contradiction with established views as well as its lack of authoritative proof. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.232d–f)
Regarding this falsity:

[an objection is raised] that these two refutations are indicated by the word "and" (ca), which has the sense of an unexpressed conjunction; therefore, it is explained accordingly. If that is so, then let that [objection] also be explained as being the meaning of the word "and."
What is the point of accepting [the opponent's position] on the grounds that it was not stated?
It is not so, because it has been said: "There is no duty for the respondent."
Let it be granted that the absence of proof [for the opponent's position] is indicated by the fact that no specific reason is mentioned in the Sūtra.
Furthermore, why [accept] the interpretation that the word "and" (ca) indicates both meanings? It is not so;
for when the word is present, it is improper to resort to an interpretive indicator (*jñāpaka*) that allows for an alternative possibility.
The sūtra "like a dream and so forth" has been explained as "like a dream.
What is the intended meaning here?
It is said:

The author of the Sūtras employed the word "etc. (ādi) to indicate the opponent's conceit that this pervasion (vyāpti), having been grasped in many instances, cannot possibly be subject to deviation (vyabhicāra).
Nevertheless, at the time of formal application (prayoga), only a single example (dṛṣṭānta) should be adduced; otherwise, redundancy (adhikya) would result.
As he has said:

The reason why [the author] stated "like a dream" (*svapnavat*) alone, rather than providing the full logical structure including the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), and so forth, was to indicate that these [additional elements] are superfluous; thus, everything is well-established.
Thus ends the section on the non-existent (*asad-adhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā. *8,344*
[======= JNys_2,2.IX: The Section on Non-Apprehension =======] // Now begins the Section on Non-Apprehension in the Illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
Oṃ, there is no existence, because it is unperceived. Oṃ.
Here, the view of the Yogācāras is refuted.
To that end, he presents it as follows: "Cognition alone..."
There is no [external] entity, because it is not perceived;
only consciousness alone shines forth, bearing the forms of all objects of knowledge. (BBs 2.2.30; MAnu 2.2.233ab)
The meaning is that the Yogācāras maintain that consciousness alone is reality, and not the four aggregates beginning with form.
Even while accepting consciousness as a factor [of existence], he states a distinction: "one."
The meaning is "without a second.

Now, an objection is raised: since objects of knowledge such as form and so forth are established by perception and other means of valid cognition, how can consciousness alone be the reality? To this, he says: "In its entirety," and so on.
Knowledge itself takes the form of the object of knowledge;
the meaning is that there is no such thing as an object of knowledge that exists separately from knowledge.
To the question, "On what basis does the object of knowledge have the nature of knowledge? he says: "It appears."
For knowledge indeed shines forth.

Thus, once it is established that the state of shining forth is pervaded by being knowledge, it follows that even blue and other such objects, insofar as they shine forth, are established as being knowledge; this is the meaning.
Alternatively, the ellipsis is "it shines forth together with blue and so on."
By this, it is stated that "because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension, there is no difference between the blue object and the cognition thereof.
Now, one might object: is it not illogical for there to be non-difference between the cognition and the cognized?
Because difference is perceived,
it is incorrect to say that [consciousness] is one;
for there exists a difference among the streams of consciousness, and within each individual stream, there is also a differentiation of cognitions.
Furthermore, let alone any other distinction;
for the absence of distinction is indeed admitted.
Since by that very [absence] consciousness would not attain the state of having a second, its oneness is not established; therefore, he says: "In that case... (tatra).
In that regard, the differentiation of the continuum, its own differentiation, and indeed differentiation itself—
these are conceptualized and appear across various levels of conventional reality.
In this context, the connection is that there is a distinction between cognition and the object of cognition.
"Distinction of continua" refers to the mutual distinction between various continua.
"Internal distinction" refers to the distinction between preceding and succeeding cognitions within even a single continuum.
The connection is that they are "merely imagined" (kalpitā eva).
[This occurs] in various conventional grounds, in internal organs which are locations of manifold ignorance;
or else, it is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), meaning "in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) which have various conventionalities as their cause."
As it has been said: "But difference is perceived only by a deluded cognition, just as the moon is seen as two when it is actually non-dual" (8.347).
He refutes this restated position with the words: "This too... (*ityetadapi*).
This [position] of ours is also not tenable...
The word "api" (also/even) serves to aggregate the previous opinion.
By this [statement], [it is shown that] "not in the case of existence... [is also not tenable].
Thus the portion of the sūtra has been explained.
The meaning is that the existence of the world is not cognition,
because the root *bhū* signifies "to experience" (or "to undergo").
For prefixes are merely manifesters of the meaning already inherent in the verbal root.
If it is asked, "Why is this not logical? [the answer is:
How could that which is non-existent in its own nature as an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) be superimposed upon consciousness and thus become of the nature of consciousness?

Is it that [the world] is liberated [from its nature], or rather that the knowable world, which exists in the ultimate sense, is of the very nature of consciousness, while its mere differentiation is non-existent? The first alternative has been refuted according to the method of the previous section.
It is not the second either.
Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the non-difference of the world from cognition, he states— beginning with "for not"— that perception does not exist in that regard.
For the world does not appear as having the nature of cognition... // MAnu 2.234bc //
By this, the statement "because of non-apprehension" has been explained.
Let it be that the identity of cognition and its object is not established through direct perception;
however, [it may be established] through inference, such as from the fact of being manifest.
But [if it is argued] that it will arise from this [memory], he says: "Of experience alone."
... because it contradicts experience itself, [this view] is untenable. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.234cd)
That is his opinion... // MAnu 2.235a //
The genitive case is used here in the sense of mere relationship.
By the word "eva" (only/itself), he indicates that direct experience possesses greater force than inference.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "that [inference] which is his [the opponent's] view, i.e., the inference he favors."
Or [the view] that "there is identity between knowledge and the object of knowledge" (ca).

The meaning is that because the clear distinction between knowledge and its object is established by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), the inference is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (vitiated by the lapse of time).
By this, the arguments "because of non-perception" (*anupalabdheḥ*) and "because of contradiction with perception" (*upalabdhivirodhāt*) have been explained.
If it is objected that perception apprehending difference is erroneous, we say no;
for there is no sublation (bādhaka). Nor should it be said that inference is the sublater.
Because direct perception is stronger than inference;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the abolition of the "mistimed" (kālātīta) fallacy,
since direct perception [is not subject to] error.

Furthermore, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) because the validity of inference depends upon the non-existence of the object, and the erroneous nature of perception depends upon that [validity of inference].
And in order to demonstrate the contradiction of inference by means of inference, the Sūtra states: "Oṃ, and because of momentariness, Oṃ. (*kṣaṇikatvācca*). *8,353*
Thus [it is said].
He explains that: "And because of momentariness."
And because of momentariness:
"And because cognition is momentary, [it cannot have] a stable form; therefore, the object of knowledge [is established] in the manner already stated. (MAnu 2.2.235a–c)
The meaning is: "because of its extremely rapid perishability.
Furthermore, the momentariness of cognition is not erroneous, as it is an uncontradicted perception (*abādhitapratīti*).
Because it is established by reasoning;
because it possesses a stable nature (due to being devoid of extremely rapid destruction);
and because of recollection, and so forth, according to the manner stated above.

In this context, by stating that the imposition of contradictory properties characterized as momentariness and non-momentariness is the cause of difference, it should be understood that various other associations of contradictory properties—such as being internal or external—are also implied.

Thus, having refuted each of the Buddhist doctrines individually, the following Sūtra is presented to refute them through a common defect: *Oṃ, and because the production of all things is untenable, Oṃ*.
Thus it is said;
he explains that [with the words] "all," etc.
"And because [the self] is impossible in every way; ...
because of contradiction with all the scriptures, and also because of contradiction with direct experience, these positions are inauspicious. (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 2.2.32, 235d–f)
Since the authority of the Śruti has been established, it is indeed appropriate to state its contradiction even with respect to one who is non-Vedic;
or else, it may be directed toward a disciple who has accepted the authority of the Śruti.
By this, it is made known that those positions are inauspicious.
[Objection: But surely the contradiction with experience has already been stated; why is it stated again? [Response: There is no fault, as it is for the purpose of a summary (upasaṃhāra).
Or rather, it is because [the same applies] even to other objects of knowledge belonging to that [system].
Thus concludes the section on Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*. [8, 355] Now begins the section on "Not in One" (*naikasmin*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
// Oṃ, [the doctrine of a personal soul] is not [tenable], because it is impossible for [contradictory attributes] to exist in one [substratum]. Oṃ.//
The Jaina doctrine is refuted here;
he introduces it with the words "He says" (āha) in order to make known the portion that is to be refuted.
"Because it is impossible for [contradictory attributes] to exist in one [thing]. (BBs 2.2.33) The Jaina says: "The universe is both existent and non-existent, dual and non-dual;
all this is both dual and non-dual, eternally characterized by the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī). (MAnu 2.2.236)
The universe is twofold,
consisting of the sentient (jīva) and the insentient (ajīva), and is without a Lord;
furthermore, it consists of six substances (ṣaḍdravya).
And those substances are named soul (*jīva*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), matter (*pudgala*), time (*kāla*), and space (*ākāśa*).
Among them, souls are of three kinds:
bound (*baddha*), perfected through yoga (*yogasiddha*), and liberated (*mukta*).
Dharma is the cause of motion and pervades the world; adharma is the cause of stability and is likewise all-pervasive. The person (pudgala) is a substance, like color, taste, smell, and touch.
That is twofold:
atomic form (*paramāṇurūpa*) and composite form (*saṅghātarūpa*). Time, which is the cause for the conventional usage of "was," "is," and "will be," is also atomic form.
Space is one and possesses infinite divisions;
it is of two kinds: space of the world (*lokākāśa*) and space beyond the world (*alokākāśa*).
Among these, the terms "substance" (*astikāya*) refer to those [categories] other than the atom (*aṇu*).
The term *astikāya* (existential body) is applied to a substance that exists in multiple locations.

These are fivefold: the *jīvāstikāya* (existential body of souls), the *dharmāstikāya* (existential body of the medium of motion), the *adharmāstikāya* (existential body of the medium of rest), the *pudgalāstikāya* (existential body of matter), and the *ākāśāstikāya* (existential body of space).

Furthermore, there are seven categories (*padārtha*) relevant here for the sake of liberation: soul (*jīva*), non-soul (*ajīva*), influx (*āsrava*), bondage (*bandha*), shedding (*nirjarā*), restraint (*saṃvara*), and liberation (*mokṣa*).
The *jīva* possesses the qualities of knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy.
The *ajīva* is the entire collection of things that are objects of enjoyment for the *jīva*.
*Āsrava* refers to the instruments of such enjoyment, such as the sense organs and so forth.
Bondage is of two kinds, distinguished by the fourfold division of destructive (ghātika) and non-destructive (aghātika) karmas.
The former [obscures] the qualities of the soul, such as knowledge and bliss.
The first is an obstacle to [spiritual] progress;
the second consists of the bodily configuration, the identification with it, its maintenance, and that which causes the pleasure and pain resulting therefrom.
Nirjarā is austerity (tapas), the means for achieving liberation.
Restraint (*saṃvara*) is the cessation and subduing of the sense faculties.
Liberation (*mokṣa*) is the manifestation of the essential nature of the self.
By the very mention of liberation, the path to liberation is also included.
And that [path] consists of the three jewels known as right knowledge, right vision, and right conduct.
Regarding this entire universe, the Kṣapaṇaka says that each thing is sevenfold, characterized by the seven modes (saptabhaṅgī).
How so? "Existent" is the first mode; "non-existent" is the second.
The third [position] is that the two are of the nature of both existent and non-existent;
the fourth is that they are non-dual and inexpressible;
the fifth and sixth are that they are both dual and non-dual.
In that regard, "both existent and inexpressible" is the fifth; "both non-existent and inexpressible" is the sixth;
and "neither all of those nor that" is the seventh.
"Everything" consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
"not that" refers to the inexpressible (*avaktavya*).
Here, in order to refute the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*), he explains the sūtra "because it is impossible in one [thing]" with the words "this is not so."
This [sevenfold nature] is not tenable for a single category of object, because it contradicts perception.
From what [source] does this sevenfold nature arise? From impossibility.
How is that [possible]?
Because it contradicts perception;
for everything exists in its own substrate, but does not exist in the substrate of another.
An entity is non-existent in its nature as something else, and so forth;
it is eternal in its substantial form and non-eternal through its various states.
It is perceived as non-different from its own nature and so on, yet as both different and non-different from its own qualities and so forth.
Not by any other manner;

therefore, because it is impossible due to the contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition that apprehend restrictive rules according to this established order, the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) is indeed untenable.
[Objection: Since the absolutist view (ekāntadarśana) is a false perspective, its contradiction does not bring about impossibility; to this, he says: "bhāva... (existence...).
By whatever form the universe is measured as being existent or non-existent,
who can prevent the rule that it is indeed of that very form?
The phrase "by way of existence and non-existence" is a further explanation of the very expression "by which form.
This should be understood as an illustration of established existence, non-existence, and so forth;
or else, [it refers to] by way of existence and non-existence, and by whatever other [quality], such as existence and so on.
The construction is with "by means of form" (*rūpeṇa*).
Alternatively, it should be construed in grammatical apposition as "by means of that form which consists of existence and non-existence.
Or else, this is an adjective qualifying the term "existence and non-existence."
"By which established form"—
this is the question of by what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). It might be argued that this [position] results in the view of restriction being a false view (mithyādṛṣṭi).
If there were a powerful means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could refute the observed rule and establish its non-exceptional nature, then it would be so;
but such a thing does not exist.
Furthermore, it is not logical to assume the falsity of cognitions without a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
He raises an objection that subverts the rule with the words "tattad" (that and that).
If [the Veda] has been accepted in various forms for the purpose of removing those respective defects...

For the proponents of existence (sadvādins) have established the existence of the universe through means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and have described the faults that arise if it is not accepted. Likewise, the proponents of non-existence (asadvādins) have also demonstrated the establishment of non-existence and the refutation that follows if it is not accepted.
Similarly, others as well have provided proofs for their own positions and formulated objections against the failure to accept them.
And likewise, if reality (*satyatva*) were not admitted, then the proof (*pramāṇa*) put forward by him would be subverted and a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) would follow;
the same applies if non-existence (*asattva*) and so forth are not admitted.

Therefore, for the sake of avoiding those defects and for the sake of following the respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), I have accepted the nature of each [object] as being that very thing in the universe. Thus, since there exists powerful evidence for non-absolutism (*anekānta*), how could there be an absence of sublation regarding the rule? He provides the rebuttal with the words: "By them" (*taih*). (8.365)
...by all those defects, one of fickle vision is defiled. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.238cd)
The word "then" (*tarhi*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
This must be stated here:
at the time of following the doctrine of the proponents of existence (*sadvādin*), do you accept the formulation of non-existence and so forth, or not?
Thus, at the time of entering the refuge of the feet of one who speaks what is unreal, do you accept the various modes such as existence and so forth, or not?

A similar dilemma applies to other positions as well. If it were the first case, then that person, possessing unshakable views and always accepting all positions, would be tainted by all those faults.
For instance,
proponents of existence have not merely established the means of valid cognition regarding existence and the refutation [of its opposite] upon its non-acceptance and then desisted;
rather, they have also demonstrated the faults in positions such as non-existence.

Thus, even those who maintain the doctrine of non-existence have ceased after merely stating that there is no proof for non-existence and that there is no sublation [of existence] if it is not accepted; indeed, they have also demonstrated the faults in positions such as existence and so forth.
So too have others.
And likewise, if all positions were accepted, how could there not be the taint of the defects found in the various positions asserted by those respective opponents?
Now, you might think:
These are not faults, but rather fallacious appearances (ābhāsa);
and since they do not invalidate the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda),
how then can those [reasons] be considered valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa)?
Furthermore, the faults [adduced] when [the sevenfold predication] is not accepted are not fallacious;
they are not such that one need only follow [the arguments] of others.

Therefore, by one who accepts the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) in accordance with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and other principles expounded by various disputants, there must also be a rejection of those positions based on the faults of the opposing views as stated by them.
Thus, being pulled from both sides by acceptance and rejection, this [position] would fall into a miserable state.
Now, is not the "one-sided" (ekānta) twofold,
through the distinction between succession and simultaneity?
In that regard, first, in the case of non-absolutism regarding succession (*kramānekānta*), acceptance and rejection are not contradictory.

Even in the case of non-absolutism regarding non-succession (*akramānekānta*), there is no contradiction because there is no acceptance [of such a claim] as that "by the very same form through which there is permanence, by that same form there is impermanence," and so forth.
Thus, since I, who accept the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*), have established those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and refutations (*dūṣaṇa*), the aforementioned fault does not apply.
Not so;
for those respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth are worthy of being established. Indeed, not [that]... [pramāṇavā...]
Since those various means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth have been presented by [opponents] such as the Dvaitins as being subject to objections,
therefore, among all disputants (*vādin*), the course of action for one who is supremely devoted to the truth has indeed been stated. *8,366*
Moreover, even in this way, the acceptance of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) is entirely groundless;
for proponents who speak in such a manner are not well-known. And if it were accepted merely on the basis of possibility, there would be no definitive limit to the number seven.
Because the scope of possibility is limitless;
furthermore, in the position that accepts all [alternatives], the two positions— "it both exists and does not exist" and "it may exist and may not exist"— are not distinct from one another.
In the second case, however, the very fault is that [the doctrine] possesses a shifting view;
thus, one would be a proponent of a non-established tenet (*apasiddhāntin*).

Therefore, it has been stated that the acceptance of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and is devoid of epistemic authority (*aprāmāṇika*).
By the statement "it is tainted by all defects," it is also indicated that there is a mutual contradiction [inherent in the position].
Furthermore, he points out the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that would result from accepting such a sevenfold modal logic (*saptabhaṅginaya*), stating: "exceeding... (*atihāya*).
Having disregarded the rule established by authoritative means regarding existence and non-existence—
[a rule that is] entirely consistent and always free from pride— it is indeed contradicted.

For one who speaks in every possible way, there indeed arise all the faults such as the abandonment of what has been seen, the failure to grasp [the truth], and self-contradiction. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.240)

The justification for the statement "speak without remainder and without contradiction" is that one does not overstep the limits established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and authoritative tradition (*āpta*), through a fixed existence and non-existence.
That which has all modes of the universe belongs to such [a description],
or alternatively, it is both that [universe] and its mode.

Now, it might be argued that in the case of non-exclusive succession (*anekānta*), there is no contradiction because of the difference in time; and in the case of non-exclusive simultaneity (*akrama-anekānta*) as well, there is no contradiction because of the difference in form. To this, it was said: "They speak always and in every way."
The word "sadā" (always) is also an elliptical indication of the non-difference of form (*rūpābheda*).
This is the underlying intention:
if there were multiplicity either through succession or through a difference in form, then this doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) could not be established.
This is because it is accepted by all disputants;
for there is no disputant whatsoever who does not accept the diversity of the states of things in terms of both time and form,
such that the introduction of the doctrine of manifoldness (anekāntavāda) would be applicable against them.

Either momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) alone, or the doctrine of the absolute pre-existence of the effect (*atyantasatkāryavāda*), or the absolute difference between the states and that which possesses the states (*avasthāvat*) must be rejected.

Therefore, by one who introduces the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*), it must be stated that [the entity] possesses all modes precisely through the non-difference of its form at all times.
And thus, there is no escape from contradiction.

For one who asserts that everything is always and in every way non-contradictory, there would be a loss of what is observed [in experience]. Furthermore, for one who asserts that everything is always and in every way devoid of pride, there would be an overestimation, which is the acceptance of what lacks valid authority.
The construction is as follows: for one who speaks in every way always contradicted, there would be self-contradiction.
The phrase "and so forth" is stated in order to include other attendant faults, such as the abandonment of what is perceived (*dṛṣṭahāni*).
The word *hi* (for/indeed) everywhere serves to indicate the reason for the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*).
This is the meaning:

if the manifoldness of the universe were accepted even though it contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then one would have to accept such things as the coldness of fire, or that the immolation of cows and the like are means for achieving dharma.
Furthermore, there would be no refutation of opposing views by means of contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Rather, one would have to accept momentariness and the like, even though they contradict recognition and other such [cognitions],
because there is no distinction [between them].

If even that which lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were to be accepted in every respect, then one would have to accept such things as the horn of a donkey or the fact that eating beef and so forth is a means for attaining *dharma*.
Furthermore, the refutation of the positions of others could not be carried out due to the absence of valid cognition;
even that [refutation] would have to be accepted, since there would be no distinction.

And thus, for one who is devoid of both the refutable and the adoptable, even the composition of a treatise would be impossible. Furthermore, if one were to accept that [the Buddha] possesses omniscience in every respect despite it being contradictory, then it would follow that even a barren woman is a mother,
and that the teaching of the Jina— which is accepted as a valid authority— is actually invalid.
The state of being liberated even for one who is bound,
the state of being bound even for one who is liberated, and the state of possessing passion even for one who has attained perfection.
One would have to accept everything, including the fact that even a dog-cooker (śvapaca) could achieve spiritual perfection;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the collapse of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda).
And thus, the effort of composing this treatise would not be necessary, since it has already been composed by those who are intoxicated, insane, and so forth.

Having thus refuted the "all-encompassing nature" (*sarvaprakāratva*) of the universe as asserted by the Jainas (*kṣapaṇaka*), he repeats their other stated position in order to refute it as well: "He speaks," etc.
He speaks of himself as his own light, [identifying] the body as the measure of the Self... // MAnu 2.241ab //
The term "ascetic" (kṣapaṇaka) continues [from the previous context].
It has its own radiance, meaning it is self-luminous; it is so described because its measure—its dimension—is like that of the body.
In this context, the point of contention is precisely the measurement of the body;
however, its self-luminosity is indeed agreed upon by us. Alternatively, "self-luminous" (*svaprabha*) may be understood as an adverbial modifier of the action.
[The opponent] speaks merely by conjecture, without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), based on his own radiance;
or else, by this [statement], he restates the absence of proof for the Jaina claim that [the soul] has the size of the body.
In that context, by the word "own" (*sva*), one's own body is meant.
In that context, he who possesses such radiance is described as "tathoktaḥ" (so-called).
And thus is the formal argument (*prayoga*): the self of Devadatta, [is...]
It exists in that very body and indeed everywhere;
for it is perceived precisely there and everywhere as the substratum of its own unique qualities.
Whatever is perceived as the substratum of its own unique qualities in a particular place,
exists in that very place.
And it exists everywhere therein;
just as a lamp, whose specific qualities such as luminosity are perceived both in Devadatta’s house and everywhere else,
so too is this [case], and therefore it is so.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that one would never experience one's own pleasure, which is the source of joy everywhere, through the embrace of a beloved daughter.
And thus, there would be no arising of effects such as horripilation extending over the entire body.
Alternatively, "self-luminous" (*svaprabha*) refers to that which possesses a radiance inseparable from itself, like that of a lamp.
This sūtra is intended to refute the view that the self has the same dimensions as the body.
Oṃ, and thus there is no totality of the self; Oṃ.
Thus [it is said].
He states its intended meaning: "That too," etc.
And thus, the self would be non-omnipresent.
(BBs 2.2.34) Nor is there a lack of contradiction even through sequential states, because of [the resulting] transformation and so forth.
(BBs 2.2.35) ... That too is sufficient [to refute the position].
He is called *duṣya* because he enters into various bodies and undergoes transformation.
Why?
Because it would entail the consequence of being incomplete and so forth—this is the remainder of the argument.

For if the self, which has the same size as the body of an ant or similar creature, were to obtain the body of an elephant, a gavaya, or the like due to the ripening of karma, it would be incomplete therein.

Furthermore, since the size [of the self] residing in a body such as that of an elephant would exceed [the capacity of] a body such as that of an ant, the theory of the self's size being equal to the body is untenable in either case.
It is with this very purpose that the phrase "in various bodies" (*nānāśarīreṣu*) should be construed.
In this context, "because of becoming otherwise" means that it would follow that the [self] lacks a fixed bodily dimension.
One might object:

"The self assumes whatever body it enters and becomes the size of that very body; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. To refute this doubt, the Sūtra states: "Oṃ, and there is no non-contradiction even through succession, because of transformation and so forth. Oṃ."
Thus [it is said].
He states its intended meaning: "That too is sufficient."
He refers by that word to the sequence of measurements residing in the mind:
"because of entering various bodies and because of becoming otherwise," meaning that through entering gross and subtle bodies, there arises [the perception of] gross and subtle measurements.

The meaning is that this is not the case, because since we do not admit an absolute difference between the measure and that which possesses the measure, it would follow that the self itself undergoes change.
To the objection, "Let the self indeed undergo change; what fault is there in that? he says: "If otherwise... (*anyathā*).
It is an established principle that whatever entity is subject to change is impermanent;
according to that view... [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.242a-c]
Persistence is pervasion;
this is accepted in the Jaina system—
that is the ellipsis to be supplied.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "That" (tad).
... that impermanence ... // MAnu 2.242c //
Since such pervasion [of change] exists, and since its being otherwise is admitted, therefore it follows that the self is impermanent; this is the remainder of the argument.
Herein is the example: "the person" (pudgala).
"...is unobstructed for the person.
The word "iva" (as if) is to be supplied;
[it means] "as if for the person's body."

Alternatively, since the word *pudgala* has been accepted by the old Jainas as denoting the self (*ātman*), it here denotes the self; or else, according to his own view, this term is employed in the sense of the self,
as they have said:
Regarding the statement, "The person goes to hell," is it not the case that the impermanence of the self is indeed admitted, even if only in the form of a change of states?
To address the question of how the impermanence of the person (*pudgala*) is established, it was stated that it is "like the body.
Just as the body possesses impermanence characterized by its reduction to ashes without abandoning its bodily form and name, such impermanence is likewise established for the self (*ātman*).
[Objection: But there is no such pervasion (*vyāpti*) between change-of-state and this kind of impermanence, because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) found in atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth.
How, then, can this be established?
It is not so;

for since change characterized by the alteration of dimensions is invariably concomitant with such impermanence as has been observed in the body and other such things, it is impossible to deny that the self, which possesses those [dimensions], is likewise subject to such impermanence.
This is what was stated: "unobstructed.
Now, one might object: "Just as in our own view, in your view as well there is indeed a transformation of the self (*ātman*), since you admit its being high or low through pleasure and pain;
and it is observed that whatever undergoes transformation, such as the body and so forth, is impermanent."
Therefore, even in your own view, the impermanence of the self is difficult to avoid; thus he says: "No."

In our position, however, impermanence does not apply to consciousness and other such qualifiers; for if that defining characteristic were to cease, then consciousness itself would no longer exist anywhere.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "it would follow that even the self possesses change.
To the question "How so? he says: "of consciousness and so forth."
The phrase "in our view" (asmanmate) is understood [from the previous context],
as is the term "impermanence" (anityatā).
The word "but" (tu) serves to emphasize.
In our view, impermanence would belong to the object characterized by the definition—namely, the qualified entity—only upon the cessation of that very definition such as consciousness;
it is not, as the Jains maintain, through mere alteration (anyathābhāva).
This is what is meant.
The basis for the impermanence of a given entity is not merely any change, but rather a change consisting in the cessation of that entity’s specific characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

If this were the case, then since space (*ākāśa*) and so forth lack the characteristics of sound and the like, they would undergo destruction at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); likewise, because the body lacks its support (the vital breath), it would dissolve during states such as deep sleep. Therefore, it is said: “of the qualifying characteristic.”
The meaning is that it is the definition of that which possesses specific qualities, and not the definition of the mere definition itself.
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "No."
The word "that" (tat) refers generally to the meaning of the sentence.
If the exclusion of the specific characteristic, which was stated as the cause for impermanence, were not to occur in anything conscious,
then its impermanence would likewise not exist.
The phrase "whatever that may be" refers back to the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

The ellipsis is: "that which exists in a conscious entity does not cease anywhere. It has been stated that if the defining characteristic (*viśeṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*) were to cease, the defined object (*lakṣya*) would become non-eternal.
He clarifies that with the word "otā" (woven).

However, impermanence would only occur upon the cessation of such characteristics as the state of being woven lengthwise and crosswise in a cloth, or the arrangement of limbs in the body. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.244)

The term "the state of being woven lengthwise and crosswise" refers to a specific kind of conjunction among threads; the remainder of the sentence implies that this is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) in the case of a cloth.
"The configuration of the limbs" refers to a specific arrangement of the limbs, such as the hands and feet. The word "etc. (*ādi*) expresses a variety of types.
The remainder [of the sentence] is "impermanence belongs to the characterized object" (*lakṣya*).
The cessation of those characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) that persist as long as the characterized object exists is precisely the cause for the impermanence of the characterized object.
And such is the consciousness (*caitanya*) of the self (*ātman*).
Furthermore, since that [nature] never ceases, how can there be the possibility of its destruction?
As for the claim that "the self is self-luminous," that too is incorrect;
for by virtue of being self-luminous, it would follow—just as in the case of a lamp—that it possesses both visible form and tangibility.
Furthermore, because it would entail perishability due to possessing form and so forth;
for the opponent himself has accepted the pervasion that "whatever possesses form and so forth is impermanent.
[Objection: But even in your own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the possession of form and so forth by the self (*ātman*) is indeed admitted.

And there is the pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever possesses form and so forth is impermanent," because it has been stated: "And because of possessing form and so forth, the opposite [of permanence] is observed."
To the question, "How then is the objection regarding impermanence avoided?", he says: "But that which is derived from the elements... (bhautikaṃ tu).
"In our view, however, it is only material form and so forth that is pervaded by destruction.
The word "however" (*tu*) is for the purpose of distinction;
it is explained as "only material" (*bhautikam eva*).
The meaning is not that it consists merely of form and so forth;
nor does the material form and so forth exist within the self.
Therefore, the implication of impermanence does not follow—this is the intended sense.
Just as you specify "alteration" (*anyathābhāva*) [as follows]:

alteration, which consists in the exclusion of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇavyāvṛtti*), exists as long as the characterized object (*lakṣya*) exists, and is thus pervaded by impermanence (*anityatva*).

And the possession of form and so forth follows from being composed of the elements; likewise, even in our view, the aforementioned fault does not arise when the qualification is added. Therefore, he says: "Not so."
It is not so for him... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.245c //

In the view of that Kṣapaṇaka, neither "being otherwise" (*anyathābhāva*) nor "possessing form and so forth" (*rūpādimattva*) is qualified; rather, it is accepted that the universal (*sāmānya*) alone is pervaded by impermanence. Therefore, the aforementioned fault is not avoided—this is the meaning.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Otherwise... (*anyathā*).
...the alteration of which is declared to be its impermanence.
Likewise, for the sake of establishing that the world is perishable, [the proof is given] for that which is endowed with form and so forth.
The Jaina (Kṣapaṇaka) has stated that whatever undergoes change, such as the earth, mountains, and so forth, possesses impermanence in order to establish their perishability;
the word "tathā" is used in the sense of conjunction,
meaning that even that which is endowed with form and other qualities is stated to be impermanent.

Alternatively, the construction is as follows: "Whatever is endowed with form and so forth, that is likewise declared to be impermanent. The word "tasya" (of that) is to be construed with the word "yasya" (of which).
Otherwise, however, upon hearing the word "yat" (which), there is the ellipsis of the word "tat" (that);
or, the word "tasya" (of that) is carried over from the preceding sentence.
This will be demonstrated later. *8,383*
He concludes what has been stated with the words: "By pervasion."
By that pervasion, because of its being otherwise, the self would be impermanent.

"Whatever is subject to change is impermanent, and whatever possesses form and so forth is impermanent"—this is by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*). "Because it is subject to change" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*);
it should also be understood as "because it possesses form and so forth."
It might be argued: "The superimposition (or attribution) of the pervaded, whose pervasion is already established, results in the superimposition (or attribution) of the unestablished pervader."
"Paṇa" means reasoning (*tarka*).
Now, if pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not accepted here, how then can it be considered reasoning?
Do not say so.
Even though the pervasion of the pervaded (*vyāpyavat-vyāpti*) is also accepted by the opponent, there is no contradiction with its being a form of *tarka*.

In the same way, there is no fault even when the locus (*āśraya*) is not agreed upon by both parties; and this will be stated later: "Refutation, however, is by means of the logic of the other" (*paranyāyaiḥ*). (8.385)

In order to refute another object of cognition asserted by the Jainas (Kṣapaṇakas), the Sūtra states: "Om. And because of the permanence of the final state, and because of the lack of distinction due to the eternity of both. Om.
Thus [it is said].
Regarding that, he first explains the portion "and because of the persistence of the final state" as follows: "eternal."
And because of the final state and the eternity of both, there is no distinction. [Objection:
This upward motion, which is said to be liberation, is also eternal;
how then could it not be a modification for one who has reached the *alokākāśa*? (2.2.36) [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.247] *8,386*
The word *api* (also/even) serves to include the exclusion of other objects of cognition (*prameya*).
The word *ca* (and) serves to include [liberation] together with its synonyms, such as "dimension" (*parimāṇa*).
How could this liberation—which the Jainas describe as the eternal upward movement of the self—not be a transformation (*vikṛti*) of the self?
It would indeed be so.
How so? For one who has reached the space of light (ālokākāśa).
For this self, situated initially in the world-space (*lokākāśa*), reaches the space beyond the world (*alokākāśa*) by means of an uninterrupted upward motion;
thus, because it undergoes such a change of state, the implication is that the self would fall into impermanence (*anityatva*).
By this [it is shown that] the final...
"Abiding" is characterized by a continuous upward movement;
therefore, the meaning of this fragment of the Sūtra is stated to be that it would follow that the self is impermanent.
Now, it was argued that mere change of state is the defining factor of impermanence, and thus your position is not tenable.

Nor is it my own position. Therefore, how can the consequence of impermanence for the liberated self (*muktātman*) be established merely through a change consisting in conjunction with a particular location? To support the claim that this is actually the Jaina position, he asks: "Of what kind?"—that is, of what kind is this "alteration" (*anyathābhāva*) intended to be the cause of destruction? (2.248ab)

For the Kṣapaṇaka, while establishing the non-absolute nature (anekānta) of everything such as earth and so forth through its eternity and other qualities, has stated that there is both eternity and non-eternity by way of substance (dravya) and modification (paryāya).
Eternity exists because the form of the substance never departs;
modification is the state of becoming otherwise, and from that comes non-eternity.
In this regard, it must be stated:
what kind of alteration (*anyathābhāva*) is here intended as the cause for destruction?
Is it of the nature of the departure from characteristics such as shape (*saṃsthāna*), or...
The sense is that it might be common [to both]. He raises the first objection with the words "saṃsthāna" (configuration).
If it is the departure from its shape... // MAnu 2.248c //
The mention of "grasping the configuration" (saṃsthānagrahaṇa) is an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa).
The connection [of the sentence] is that it is intended as the cause of destruction.
He negates this with the words: "That is not so."
... for it does not exist in the earth, oceans, and so forth. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.248d)
The word "can be said" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
To the question "Why not?", he says: "For that is not... [sa na hi].

The meaning is as follows: as long as the transformation characterized by the disappearance of the characteristics that will exist until the end of the object (*lakṣyabhāvin*)—as seen in cases such as the earth or the ocean, which constitute a single part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśa*)—has not been cognized, the reason would therefore be "unestablished due to doubt" (*sandigdhāsiddha*).
However, if it were indeed cognized, there would be no doubt even regarding its impermanence, and thus the inference would become redundant.
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, let the second [type of transformation] be the one," he says: "whatever [transformation]" (*yaḥ kaścit*).
Whatever alteration of state there may be, if... // MAnu 2.249ab //
The connection is exactly as before;
the meaning is that the specific qualification is not intended to be expressed.
With the thought that, "In that case, the consequence of impermanence would also apply to the liberated self," he says: "And liberation..."
...and liberation is likewise of that same nature.
Such is its nature as being subject to change. Even so, if the self were eternal, then the earth, mountains, and so forth would also have to be eternal;
otherwise, the reason [adduced for the self's eternity] would be inconclusive.
This has been stated by the author of the Sūtra:
"Because both are eternal.
If it is argued that change, characterized by the increase and decrease of parts, is the cause for impermanence, [we reply: no.
Because [the property] is doubtful in one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśa*), such as crystal and the like.
If it is argued that there is no fault in employing "possessing color and so forth" as a qualified [reason], we say no;
for it would result in the opponent's [argument] being rendered purposeless (*vaiyarthyaprasaṅga*).
For no one else accepts that anything possessing form and so forth is eternal;
rather, the possession of form and so forth has been attributed to the self by its own radiance,
or else the possession of form and so forth by the self is simply [the consequence of] its own established doctrine.

If one accepts the pervasion that "that which possesses form and so forth is impermanent," the previously mentioned undesirable consequence regarding impermanence must be explained. He restates the "different point" (*arthāntara*) asserted by the Jainas (*kṣapaṇaka*) in order to refute it, beginning with the words "deha... (the body).
Thinking that there might be a transformation [of the self] within the measure of the body, one regards those who are stationary as non-self.
He said: ... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.250a //

"In the measurement of the body" means when the measurement of the body has been determined; "there would be a modification" refers to the Self, because it is accepted that stationary beings possess a self— this is the ellipsis.
This is for the purpose of [the thought] "may it not be so";
[he refers to] stationary things such as trees,
which are non-self, meaning they are not presided over by a self.
The Kṣapaṇaka says:

Here, when it should have been stated simply that "the Kṣapaṇaka asserts that stationary things are not the Self," he instead says this because the size of the Self has been established as being equal to the body; [he argues] that if trees and such were also possessed of a Self, they would necessarily possess that same size, and thus [the Self] would be merely atomic in its sprout stage.
Furthermore, in the state of being a great tree, there would follow the consequence of being subject to great transformation, and from transformation, impermanence;
lest this [consequence] should occur, he states the reason in this way: "it does not follow."
This is for the purpose of strengthening the aforementioned thesis.
If the Jaina were not to accept that mere mutability is the determinant for impermanence,
then his own previously accepted position— that immobile beings lack a self because he feared the consequence of their being impermanent due to their mutability— would be untenable.
For in the case of stationary beings (*sthāvara*), there is no disappearance of the characteristics of the self (*ātman*) when they possess a self;
rather, there is merely a change of state.
Alternatively, this restatement of the reason (*hetu*) is for the sake of making the refutation easier. *8,393*
Therefore, this acceptance of the non-selfhood of stationary beings out of fear of falling into the state of being subject to modification is incorrect;
for if that were the case, it would follow that one must likewise accept the non-selfhood of the bodies of elephants and so forth as well.
To the question "How so?", he says: "hastyādi... [the body of an elephant, etc.].
For even in the bodies of elephants and other such creatures, there may indeed be a change of state.
"Because there would be a change [in its nature] when those [beings] of that same size residing in bodies such as ants reach bodies such as elephants.
Alternatively, having established that the body alone is not the self, this demonstration is now being made.
In all bodies, such as those of elephants and others, there would be a transformation of the self; for at the time of their birth,
the bodies [possess dimensions] such as the length of the trunk or the span of the arms.
Because [the body] has the measure of a mere embryo at birth, whereas in youth it has a superior measure;
by this, the meaning of the fragment of the Sūtra "because there is no distinction" is explained.
But is this not an unequal comparison?
For the modification of the self (*ātman*) in the bodies of elephants and the like is indeed slight,
whereas in trees and the like it is great;
therefore, if trees and the like lack selfhood, elephants and the like must likewise [lack it].
Since it might be argued that causing [the body] to fall is improper, he says: "of one whose body is atomic" (aṇudehasya).

For the soul, whose body is minute, there is indeed a modification when it assumes the state of an elephant to pervade that body; but what distinction is there for it in the body of an immobile being?
