When a living being with a minute body, such as that of an ant, attains the state of an elephant;
or alternatively, at the time of birth, when a being with a minute body— measured by a cubit, a span, or the like—
attains the state of a massive elephant, [there occurs] the pervasion of the body.

To whatever extent there is transformation, and to whatever extent there is transformation in the stationary body and in the human being— what distinction is there between each of those respective transformations?
No one [would say so].
This is the meaning:
why should a great transformation of the self not be accepted as a consequence of its being caused by impermanence?
Or is it merely a transformation?
Not the first [option], because magnitude is not established; for even if one were to postulate its establishment, it would be absent in certain trees and other such things.
If, in order to conform to that [argument], one accepts [the presence of a self] as an established fact, then since that [self] exists in elephants and so forth as well, [the fault remains].

In the second case, however, because there is no distinction between the two in terms of being subject to transformation, one must accept the absence of a self in elephants and so forth just as in trees and so forth;
likewise, one must not abandon the view that trees and so forth possess a self, just as elephants and so forth do.
By this, it should be understood that another meaning for the [reason] "because there is no distinction" has been stated.
It might be argued:
"We do not assert that trees and so forth lack a self out of fear of falling into the state of being subject to transformation."
However, because there is an absence of evidence for their possessing a self (*sātmakatva*) and because there exists evidence that contradicts it,
trees and the like cannot be bodies; for if they were bodies, they would necessarily possess sense organs, which is their pervader (*vyāpaka*), yet such organs do not exist in them.
Because its effects, such as hearing and so forth, are absent;
and that [absence] too is due to the absence of anything that indicates it.
Furthermore, since there is no possession of a self when there is no body—as in the case of stones and the like—it is said: "because of singing," etc.
From its song comes the acquisition of flowers and fruit; from touch, emaciation; and from its sap, stability.
Since these effects are seen even in a tree, it must possess a manifold nature.
From song, even a tree is seen to obtain flowers and fruit;
by that, its hearing is inferred.
The subject under dispute possesses the faculty of hearing, because when in the presence of song it undergoes transformation, just like a king or similar beings.
Nor is this [existence] merely an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), for that consequence would apply even to kings and others;
rather, the existence of the auditory faculty is inferred by means of hearing.
Thus, emaciation is observed due to specific sensations of cold and heat;
by this, the cognition of touch is inferred, as in the case of one with a delicate body,
and by that, the existence of the tactile faculty (*tvagindriya*) is established.
Likewise, the persistence—that is, the continued existence—of that which is not drying up is observed due to the presence of the essence of water and so forth.
Therefore, just as in the case of the accepted body, the cognition of taste leads to the inference of the existence of the gustatory faculty (*rasanendriya*).
Similarly, by beholding a beautiful woman, the swelling of a sesame tree is perceived.
Because of that, there is a desire to see;
from that, the eye and the mind are established.

Furthermore, since the sense of smell is established through the perception of excellence resulting from the application of incense, the lack of selfhood (*anātmatā*) in stationary beings (*sthāvara*) would not be established, as their bodies are no different from those whose existence is well-known.
Some, inferring a connection with the internal wind from the upward movement of water poured at the root of a tree, infer that it possesses a soul;
that is incorrect, because of the fallacy of deviation in the case of lumps of ash and the like.

By this, the statement "because there is no distinction" (*aviśeṣāt*) is explained by way of another method. To dispel the doubt of the dull-witted— who might ask why such things as "it speaks its own light" (*vakti svaprabham*) and so forth were described outside of the Sūtra— he establishes them as being grounded in the Sūtra with the words "And thus" (*evañca*).
And thus, regarding the "incompleteness of the self," the knower of the Veda says for that very reason:
"the three-stranded [cord]"—this is the ellipsis;
"for that very reason" means for the sake of that very purpose.
This has been stated precisely for the purpose of establishing the meaning already expressed.
Furthermore, it is said in order to indicate that even when there is an explanation elsewhere without the citation of a Sūtra, one should not entertain such a doubt.
Thus ends the section "Not in One" (*naikasmin*) in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, [verse] 8.399.
[======= JNys_2,2.XI: The Section on the Husband =======] Thus concludes the section on the husband (*paty-adhikaraṇa*) in the venerable Nyāyasudhā.
// Oṃ. Because the Lordship [of Brahman] is inconsistent, Oṃ.//
Here, the view of those who proceed by placing Mahādeva at their forefront is refuted.
They are of four kinds: Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Kālāmukhas, and Mahāvratas.

Although there are internal differences among them, their common object of knowledge (prameya) is restated for the purpose of refuting it, as it is utterly opposed to the Vedic doctrine—beginning with [the claim of] omniscience and so forth.
Because of the inconsistency of [the Lord] as a husband:
"Sadāśiva, who is endowed with all qualities such as omniscience and the like, who is the creator of the manifold arrangement of the world, and who is free from defects. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 12.252)

The Pāśupatas say... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.253a]. Those who belong to Paśupati are called Pāśupatas; thus, all four types are included. They declare Sadāśiva to be the creator of the world’s diverse arrangement.
Then, regarding the statement "from which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]," some might say it is "unreal.
To address how they could call the Creator of the world one possessed of defects such as ignorance, it was stated: "devoid of defects."

Since the abandonment of ignorance and other defects is not possible for a conscious being in the absence of omniscience and the like, it is therefore stated that [the Lord] is endowed with all qualities such as omniscience.
Alternatively, the statement that he is "endowed with all qualities such as omniscience and free from defects" is an introduction of a meaning contrary to the definition of *pradhāna*.
It should be understood that the phrase "the creator of the world's diverse arrangement" expresses a meaning contrary to the definition of Brahman according to the Śruti.
To refute this, he states the purport of the Sūtra "On account of the lack of consistency in [the doctrine of] the Lord" (Brahmasūtra 2.2.37) with the words: "And that... (tacceti).
...and because it contradicts the teachings of those who have heard much, that doctrine should not be accepted. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.253a–c)
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction with the views of the former [masters].
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates a reason.
That doctrine of Paśupati, which holds that he causes all the world to be blind and so forth, is not to be accepted.
Why?
Because [it contradicts] the Lord, Paśupati.
The construction is as follows: "Because of inconsistency" means because of being faulty;
and "if that [position] is not accepted, there is contradiction with many scriptural passages.
To the question "Which are those scriptural passages?", he cites them with the words "of this [self]."
... praise this god who has mounted his chariot-seat. Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.253cd.
I praise the Lord of the virtuous who crushed his head;
for when I drew forth Rudra to slay him, he [Viṣṇu] occupied the highest step of Viṣṇu.
"O gods of the phallus, let him whom I desire, even if he be fierce, not [be deprived of his virility];
O gods of the phallus, may this one alone remain unharmed—he who is the supreme Nārāyaṇa. (Manu 2.255)
Therefore, Rudra and Samprasāda both attended the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice;
they worshipped with sacrifice and bound the Puruṣa as the victim.
He who is Rudra, the lord of beings, the bull who moves within the fibers.
By this [verse], he cites the Śruti: "Through oblations, we [attain] the power of this bountiful god Viṣṇu, the impeller;
for Rudra knows his own Rudrian greatness, and I shall go toward the wondrous, food-bestowing path" (Ṛgveda 7.40.5).

With the words "Praise him who dwells in the pit," [one praises] according to the verse: "Praise the famous one, who sits upon the chariot-seat, the youthful, fierce, and deadly like a terrifying wild beast;
O Rudra, being praised, be gracious to the singer; let your missiles strike down someone other than us" (Ṛgveda 2.33.11).
By the word "utpipeṣa," [the text refers to] "The tip of Rudra’s bow indeed snapped. By the word "gṛṇīṣe," [it refers to] "Even a young boy did not bow back to his father as he approached in homage;
I praise you, the giver of abundance, the true lord; being praised, grant us remedies" (Ṛgveda 2.33.12).

By the phrase “the footprint,” [it refers to]: “For your glory, O Maruts, they groom themselves; O Rudra, that birth of yours which is beautiful and wonderful—that supreme footprint of Viṣṇu which was established, by means of that you guard the secret name of the cows” (Ṛgveda 5.3.3).
By the phrase “whomsoever I desire,” [it refers to]: “Whomever I desire, him I make fierce; him I make a Brahman, him a seer, him wise” (Ṛgveda 10.125.5).

By the word "mā" (do not), [it refers to]: "O Śiśnadevas, do not even speak the truth. By the word "ghnan" (slaying), [it refers to]: "May the slaying of the Śiśnadevas be through superior splendor. By the word "ekaḥ asau" (he alone is), [it refers to]: "Nārāyaṇa alone existed; there was neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara."

By the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*), [it is meant]: "He was the one who became wrathful, he was the one who became gracious; therefore Rudra and Prasāda came into being. By the word "Vaiṣṇava," [it is meant]: "The glory of their sacrifice reached Vaiṣṇava.
Regarding the words "by means of sacrifice" (*yajñena*) and "they bound" (*abadhnan*): [these refer to the sacrificial acts].
The phrase "of beings" is well known.
To address how the status of Paśupati as the Lord (*īśvara*) is not contradicted by these scriptural passages, he states their intended meaning (*tātparya*) with the words beginning "ityādi."
From the force of such scriptural passages as these, [it follows that] birth and death consist in dependence on another.
Dependence on others, failure to attain what belongs to others, ignorance, and non-existence at the time of dissolution—these are perceived... // MAnu 2.258a-c //
Non-existence is absence;
the ellipsis is that these are perceived by Paśupati.
"Of this god... (*asya devasya*).
By this, the attainment of a state dependent on another is indicated:
[the state] of the bountiful one (*mīḷhuṣaḥ*), who is a showerer (*secaka*), and of the impeller (*eṣasya*), whose nature is desire (*icchā*).
When the oblations have been offered to this god Viṣṇu— meaning, during his "pramṛtha," that is, his slaughter or worship— the binding Rudra, vaya, [acts].
The majesty of Rudra, the station of Rudra— he has found, discovered, and obtained it;
for in that manner, O Aśvins, you two as well are possessed of *irā*, that is, food.
*Varti* means turning;
by saying "you two have arrived" (*yāsiṣyaṃ ayāsiṣya prāptavantau sthaḥ*), [the dependence is shown].
By the word "Praise! (*stuhi*), dependence is indicated through the act of praising.
O Rudra, you are the famous and well-known one,
dwelling in the cave of the heart (gartasat),
the youthful one.
Like a terrifying deer, like a fearsome lion,
he is fierce among the fierce Daityas,
the destroyer of destroyers.
Praise Nṛhari; you praise him. Being thus praised, you who are praising him—
To the singer,
to me who praises you— be gracious; have mercy and grant me happiness.
"May these armies strike down and kill someone other than us.
By the word "of Rudra," ignorance, dependence, and death are indicated.
[This refers to] the head of Rudra—who stands grasping the bow that has been placed [upon his shoulder]—[which was struck] by the bowstring.

When the bowstring was severed by Indra in his form as Kāmarūpa, it was drawn up and crushed; thus [the text] says "it cut. By the word "Kumāra," both dependence and birth are indicated. O Rudra, you are the son Kumāra who went to Kailāsa for the purpose of deluding the world.
Bowing to you, he prostrated toward his father Kṛṣṇa.
Praised by him, you—whom we praise as the Lord of the virtuous and the bestower of abundant human goals—sing, laud, and have praised [him].
Being such as you are, praised by us, grant (rāsi), that is, bestow upon us (asme), the medicines (bheṣajā)—that is, the wisdoms that eliminate the disease of saṃsāra. Grant them! Thus [he prays].
By the phrase "for your glory," [it is meant that] birth is the attainment of a state dependent on another, as well as subjection to another.
O Rudra, those Maruts from whom your birth— your origin— arose are, for your glory, Brahmās who have passed away or are present.
That which is excellent, beautiful, wonderful, marvelous, and comparable to the highest splendor— such that the Goddess Lakṣmī herself acts as its bearer—
that very foot of Viṣṇu, which they cleansed, purified, and washed,
has been placed by you within your heart.
For that reason, among cows—that is, among words—you protect the secret name beginning with Nārāyaṇa; you guard it through means such as recitation and instruction.
By the word "I," death is indicated.

"I stretch out—that is, I extend—the bow at the time of universal dissolution (pralaya) in order to slay Rudra, the destroyer, for the sake of the arrow of the Daityas who hate the Veda, [namely] for the sake of one who hates the Veda.
By the word "yam" (whom), the attainment of a state dependent on another is indicated:
"Whichever Rudra I desire to make, that fierce Rudra I indeed make; likewise, him I make into Brahmā, him into a Ṛṣi, and him into Sumedhas, the wise one."
By the word "mā" (do not), ignorance is indicated;

[it means] that even the gods and Rudras, who possess pride regarding the secrets of the past, future, and present, have not known (*mā aguḥ*) our object of worship—the immortal Brahman whose nature is knowledge.
By the word "ghnan" (striking), death is indicated.
"Destroying the gods who possess secret pride, the Lord, by means of his form and power, has surpassed and overcome everything.
By the word "one," both non-existence and birth at the time of dissolution are indicated;
by the word "therefore," birth is indicated.
The meaning is that Rudra is born from the wrath of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara),
while Samprasāda is Brahmā.
Their state of dependence [on the Lord] is expressed by such statements as "of them" (*teṣām*).
The glory of those gods reached Rudra, who had been appointed as the sacrificial animal in the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice at the Viṣṇu-sacrifice; that is,
"by means of the sacrifice, with Rudra as the animal, the gods sacrificed to Viṣṇu."
"The gods bound the person, Rudra, as a sacrificial animal.
This means that Rudra, who is the sovereign lord of all beings, moves along the "rope" (tanti) which is the form of Viṣṇu’s command, like a bull [moving] along a well-known rope.
The demonstration that these scriptural passages have this meaning should be understood from the other statements cited by the Teacher himself and from his commentary (*ṭīkā*).
For this very reason, it was stated "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*).
He summarizes the meaning of the sūtra with the words: "because of being faulty" (*sadoṣatvāt*).
... because he possesses passion (doṣa), therefore Paśupati is not the Lord (īśa).
Therefore, by the force of scripture, because he possesses defects, Paśupati—the Lord—is not the creator of the world;
for it is impossible for one who has defects, such as Yajñadatta, to be the creator of the world.
With another argument to refute Śiva’s status as the creator of the world, the Sūtra states: "Oṃ, and because a connection [with the world] is impossible, Oṃ."
Thus [it is said].
He states its meaning: "because of being bodiless" (aśarīratvataḥ).
And because a relationship is untenable:
"Since he is bodiless, a connection with the world in any way as an agent is not logical... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.259a–c).
Regarding that Śiva:
since one observes a connection between the bodiless [Śiva] and the world, such as the ether and so forth, [the author] explains the nature of that very connection:
"in some effect."
"By way of being an agent" means that a relationship characterized by the body being the agent is not tenable.
By the word "in some cases," he indicates the question: from what [source] does there arise the status of being the agent of all things?
The formal argument here is as follows: Śiva is not an agent because he is bodiless, like one who is asleep or dissolved [in deep sleep].
Now, is Śiva established [as a subject] or not?
Not the second [alternative],
because the substratum is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
But in the first case, since it is established precisely as an agent, there is a contradiction with the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇavirodha*).
Furthermore, even in your own view,
the agency and embodiedness of Śiva are indeed accepted;
thus, there would be both the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*) and the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the reason (*anyatarāsiddhi*).
It is said:
the underlying intention here is this. One who asserts that Paśupati is the cause of the world should be questioned as follows:
Is this stated on the basis of scriptures such as the Pāśupata and others, or on the basis of inference, or rather on the basis of Śruti and so forth?
Regarding the first [alternative], this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is stated:
if this is asserted on the basis of the Pāśupatas and others, then its bodilessness (*aśarīratva*) would also be established from that source, and thus that too would have to be accepted;
and in that case, there would be an impossibility of agency (*kartṛtva*).
For this very reason, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used in the phrase "it is not tenable.
Regarding the second [alternative], however, it will be explained later;
and thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

Since our own nature as Śiva is established through the Vedas and other sources, there is no lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Furthermore, because we establish the absence of agency based on the opponent's own admission of bodilessness (*aśarīratva*), there is no contradiction with the means of knowledge that apprehend the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇavirodha*).
By this, the claim that the Vedas must be interpreted otherwise due to conflict with the Pāśupatas and other schools is refuted. *8,412*

[Objection: Surely, even for one who is bodiless, there is no subverting factor against agency; therefore, this reductio argument is devoid of pervasion (*vyāpti*), since agency consists in being the instigator of causal factors (*kāraka*) and not in possessing a body. To this, he says: "of the embodied" (*dehinaḥ*).
... for the embodied soul, from the perspective of the vision of knowledge.
It is true that agency (*kartṛtva*) consists precisely in being the instigator of an agent, and not in possessing a body;
and that [agency] is not possible without effort (*prayatna*),
nor is effort possible without desire (*icchā*).
Nor is there desire without knowledge,
nor is there knowledge apart from a body,
since knowledge is observed only in embodied beings who are awake.
Because [the self] is not perceived when embodied beings are asleep or in a state of deep absorption,
the body— which is the pervader of agency— excludes that [agency] as well by its own exclusion from Śiva, who is non-dual. But surely,
the body's utility lies only in the production of knowledge?
Since knowledge is produced by the sense organs,
and since the sense organs are necessarily conjoined with a body,
what use has the Lord Śiva for a body, given that he possesses eternal knowledge?
In that case, since desire is useful only for that which is produced by effort, there would be no desire for one whose effort is eternal.
Likewise, since knowledge is useful only for the arising of desire, there would be no knowledge for one whose desire is eternal.
Now, if it is argued that agency does not consist in mere effort, [the response follows].
Furthermore, [one might argue] that knowledge and desire are also [required],
for the elders say that agency consists in being the instigator of causal factors whose efficacy has been observed. Even so, there is no subverting argument against the abandonment of desire.
And from what [reason] should it be conceived in this way?
If you say, "Because it is observed to be so in the case of a potter and others," then has the body not been seen there as well?
If it is argued that even what is seen is useless, is this accepted because of a lack of necessity,
or because it is subsumed elsewhere?
Not the first,
because there is no deviation [in the concomitance].
If it is argued that there is no other body for the impelling of a body, we say no.
Not the first, because [the self] would then possess a body;
not the second,
because it has already been refuted.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even knowledge and the other qualities would be useless.
Furthermore, on what basis is its possession of eternal knowledge established?
If you say "from scripture," it is not so.

Because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*). For if the authority of the scripture were established, then the existence of an eternal knowledge-possessing Lord would be established; and if His existence were established, then the authority of the scripture would be established by virtue of its being composed by Him. Anticipating an objection that might avoid the aforementioned fault, the Sūtra is stated for its refutation: "Oṃ. If it is argued that [the Lord is like] an instrument, [we say] no, because of [His] experience and so forth. (Oṃ. *karaṇavaccenna bhogādibhyaḥ* Oṃ).
Thus [it is said].
He first explains the portion ending with "not that" (tanna), beginning with "and not" (na ca).
If it is argued that [the Lord] is an instrument, it is not so, because of [the necessity of] experience and the like;
nor would the universe belong to Him in the same manner as the body and so forth.
As for the claim that because Śiva is bodiless, his status as an agent is untenable—
that is incorrect.

For potters and other such agents, being unable to directly control the staff and other tools through their own immediate effort, would require those tools to be directly controllable by immediate effort in order to be controlled.
Therefore, what need is there for another body?
For this very reason, the Blessed One is celebrated as the "Universal Form" (Viśvamūrti).
Nor is there an absence of causal agents prior to the initial creation.
Because illusion (*māyā*) and so forth have existed from beginningless time;
otherwise, creation would be impossible.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of the sense organs and the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) which will be discussed later.
The meaning is that this is not tenable.
To the question "Why not?", he explains the reason given in the Sūtra: "Because of enjoyment," and so forth.

...because of the occurrence of experience (*bhoga*). (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.260b) *8,417* If the collection of causal instruments (*kārakagrāma*) were directly governed by the effort of Śiva, then it would be the cause of his experience characterized by the perception of pleasure and pain;
for such is observed in the case of bodies like ours, which are directly governed by effort.

If it is argued that such a state belongs only to what is acquired through karma, we say no; for since [the world] would then be subject to direct effort, it would follow that even the state of being so [subject to effort] would apply [to the Lord]. Furthermore, one who possesses experience and the like cannot be the Lord.
Therefore, because this [view] entails the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that Śiva would possess experience and so forth, this conception is not tenable.
Refuting Śiva’s status as the creator of the universe by means of another reason: "And because of the impossibility of [his] presiding, om."
Thus he explains the sūtra: "In the basis."
And because a substratum is untenable:
"A creator residing in a substratum is perceived as performing an action. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.260cd)
Any agent, such as a potter and the like, is perceived to produce an effect such as a jar only while remaining situated upon a substrate, such as the clay;
indeed, no one whatsoever is ever seen performing any action without a substrate.
By this negative concomitance (*vyatirekāvinābhāva*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "lack of a substrate" by "non-agency" is established.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"He has no power over the presiding [of elements] at the dissolution of beings then. (Manu 2.260ef)
Of this Śiva;
then, at the time of the original creation;
from what [cause] would it not exist?
Since the great elements, such as earth and the rest, which arose previously, undergo dissolution, it follows—this is the remainder of the argument—that his status as an agent is also untenable.
[Objection: But surely the instruments themselves will serve as the locus of superintendence.
Not so;
for it has already been stated that there would follow the consequence of experience and so forth for a conscious being (cetanā) that possesses a substratum.

Now, one might object: this reason (*hetu*) of "being without a substratum" is *asādhāraṇa* (inconclusive), because it is excluded not only from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), such as the potter who is a conscious agent, but also from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as the jar which is a non-agent.
Not so; for it exists in the similar instances (sapakṣa), such as space and the like. [Objection:
Why have these two sūtras been explained in reverse order?

This is for the purpose of making it known that the refutation of both— the impossibility of a relationship and the impossibility of a substratum— is accomplished by the phrase "as in the case of the instruments" (*karaṇavat cet*).
For if [the sūtra] were explained strictly according to the sequence [of the objections],
then this would be understood as refuting only the rejection of the impossibility of a substratum which was immediately preceding.
However, when both [terms] are explained in reverse order, it is understood that they relate to both;
for this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya that "it has the form of a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth," whereas here it is said to be "like the body and so forth.
Now, it is indeed appropriate that a potter requires a substratum and possesses a body.
For a body, due to its weight, is subject to falling and thus requires a tangible substratum for its support;
since one whose body is not stable cannot function as an agent,
what indeed could serve as a substratum for the Lord, who is devoid of a body?
Since the worldly convention "this was born here" can be established by relying on space and so forth, he says: "If [the self] were bodiless... etc.
If he were bodiless, he would be eternally non-omniscient, like stone or wood.
By the word "always" (sadaiva), he establishes pervasion (vyāpti).
For this very reason, there is the employment of multiple examples such as stone, wood, and so forth.
And thus, from where [could] omniscience arise?
And from what [source] does his status as the creator of all arise? This is the sense.
It might be argued:
Sadāśiva is not entirely bodiless.
However, he assumes bodies even as a mere sport;
therefore, this is not a fault,
nor is there any attainment of enjoyment and the like.
Because a body assumed through divine play (līlā) cannot be the cause of that [bondage], he says: "If the embodied one... and so forth.
If the embodied soul were finite, it would be subject to death, as illustrated by the example of Yajñadatta;
this [statement] is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa).
It should also be observed that [the self] would possess suffering and so forth. Now, it was argued that this analysis (vigraha) is not the cause of that [suffering];
but this is not so.
Because it is contradictory [to claim] that the body is not the locus of experience,
and because it is inferred as such precisely by virtue of being a body;
this is what he expresses with the word "evam" (thus).
By this, the Sūtra stating, "The self would either be finite or omniscient," is explained.
Since the sequence of meaning is more important than the sequence of recitation, the explanation is given out of order. *8,421*
Now, what is the intention of those who thus refute Śiva’s status as the cause of the world? Is it that this universe is indeed without a creator,
or rather that its creator is Viṣṇu?
Not the first [alternative],
because it is contradictory for an effect to be without an agent,
and because it would entail the fallacy of abandoning one's own tenets (apasiddhānta).
Not the second [alternative],
because even if Viṣṇu were accepted as the agent, these same defects would apply equally, resulting in self-contradiction.
For instance, that inconsistency which was alleged regarding Śiva applies equally to Viṣṇu as well,
because defects such as birth are heard of in passages such as, "He was born from Viṣṇu."
Since the impossibility of a relationship and so forth is indeed clear, he says: "And not... (na ca).
And all this [is not applicable] to Viṣṇu...
It should not be said that "this entire collection of defects is the same even if Viṣṇu is accepted as the creator of the universe.
Why?
Because the fact that Viṣṇu is the cause of the universe has been established by the Śruti itself through the removal of all objections.
Now, one might object: "But the status of Paśupati as the cause of the world has likewise been established by the Āgamas and by inferences;
therefore, what is the distinction? To this, he says: "By the Śruti... and so forth.
... because of the weight of the authority of the revealed scripture (śruti). MAnu 2.262b.
This is because the authority of the Vedas is more weighty than even that of the Pāśupata and other such systems.
What is meant is this:
for the Pāśupata and other systems would only be determined to be authoritative on the grounds of being composed by Śiva, once he is established as the omniscient creator of the world.

And if its authority is established, then the proof that Śiva is of such a nature follows; thus, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatā*), and its authority remains difficult to ascertain.
If the nature of Śiva as such were established by some other means, this [scripture] would be superfluous.
Yet, there is no other such means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Because inferences have been refuted,
the authority of the Veda is not established in that same way;
for, being of non-human origin, in the absence of defects in its causes and in the absence of any subverting cognition, it is itself inherently and unshakably certain.
Therefore, by means of the Śruti, whose status as a valid authority is certain, Viṣṇu’s causality of the world—freed from even the scent of defect—is indeed established.
To the question "Which are those Śrutis?", he cites them: "The mind... and so forth.
We perceive that very Viṣṇu himself as the constituent part of the mind and the intellect.
That very body is consciousness, sovereignty, and exalted power;
O Viṣṇu, that body of yours, O Viṣṇu, was not Vāsudeva who stood before you.
In the beginning, there was only one Nārāyaṇa; there was neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara. From the navel of the Unborn, there arose one [lotus], placed by him as a measure of his supreme power.
He whose body is truth, whose fragrance is happiness, whose light is knowledge, and whose supreme effort is for the good;
he who is the knowledge of knowledge and the bliss of bliss—he is Viṣṇu, the supreme imperishable.
In the beginning, O Ānanda, there was only one Lord, Nārāyaṇa;
Priya was the head of that Hari, and Modas and Pramodas were his two arms.
Ānanda was from the middle; Brahmā was the tail, and nothing else existed anywhere.
From his mind Brahmā was born, and from his forehead Śaṅkara.
On his two sides were Garuḍa and Śeṣa; from his mouth issued Sarasvatī.

The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet. (Manu 2.268) By this [verse], he indicates that the Blessed One possesses intelligence (*buddhi*) and mind (*manas*), as well as major and minor limbs.
He cites the scripture: "Possessing intellect, mind, speech, limbs, and minor limbs.

By the phrase "who indeed," he means: "Of whatever nature the Blessed Lord is, of that same nature is the manifest individual; of what nature is the Blessed Lord? He is of the nature of knowledge, of the nature of sovereignty, and of the nature of power."
"Exalted" means powerful;
it is unimpeded everywhere.
The Blessed One has this as his essence, and therefore his body also has this as its essence—this is the meaning obtained from the scripture.

By the phrase "not [reached] by you, O Viṣṇu," [it refers to]: "O Viṣṇu, neither one being born nor already born has reached the furthest limit of your divine majesty. By the phrase "Vāsudeva," [it refers to]: "Vāsudeva indeed was this in the beginning."
Regarding the phrase "by measure" (*mātrayā*), [the author] cites: "O you who have grown beyond measure with your body, they do not reach the limit of your greatness.
To the question of how the intended meaning is established by these scriptural passages, he states their purport: "beginning with 'these' (*ityādīti*)."
On the strength of such collections of scriptural passages, it is understood that the entire universe manifested from the body of Viṣṇu, whose nature consists of eternal qualities.
And because it is eternal and consists of the qualities (guṇas), it is described as such;
therefore,
in that context, [the term] "intellect" (buddhi) [is used].
Thus, by this scriptural passage, Viṣṇu’s possession of a body is understood;
"aṅga" means the body,
and "pratyaṅgāni" refers to the limbs such as the hands and so forth.
We perceive; we make known.
How so?
"The Blessed One is of such a nature," and so forth.
Thus, because the body of the Blessed One consists of qualities such as knowledge and so forth, "manifestation" (vyakti) refers to the body. [As it is said: "Not in Viṣṇu."
Thus, O Blessed One, the body consists of qualities such as knowledge and is beginningless and eternal;
for its greatness—which cannot be attained through birth and the like—would otherwise be inexplicable.
Furthermore, by the two scriptural citations [beginning with] "Vāsudeva," its state of having a beginningless and eternal body is established.
By the phrase "of the unborn," his state of being unborn despite possessing a body is indicated;
by the phrase "beyond measure," the fact that his form is unlimited by space, time, and qualities is shown.
By the two scriptural passages beginning with “saddehaḥ” (having an excellent body), it is shown that [the Lord] possesses a body whose nature consists of qualities free from defects such as birth.
A "saddeha" is a body devoid of defects such as birth.
"Sukhagandha" means having a pleasant fragrance.

The term *jñānabhā* does not mean "having the nature of light" (*taijasabhā*), but rather means "possessing superior knowledge" (*atiśayitajñāna*) and so forth, as indicated by the phrase "knowledge of knowledge" (*jñānajñāna*). Words such as *priya* and others denote specific types of pleasure (*sukha*).
The other [portion] consists of the *prākṛta* and so forth.

By the two scriptural passages beginning with "of the mind," [it is shown that] the world possesses a body and its birth from that [mind]. [And by the passage] "the Brāhmaṇa is this... [it is shown that the world has a head, etc.]
This is because of such supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*).
"On the two sides" means on the two flanks.
In this regard, in certain *śrutis*, the intended meaning is not clearly perceived.
However, with the intention that this is to be established through logical proof (upapatti), it was said: "by force" (balāt).
By the phrase "it became manifest" (āvirāsīt), he indicates the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
It is "gone to" (*īyate*), meaning it is known.
In this regard, since the fact that [Brahman] alone is the cause of the entire universe is established by scripture (*śruti*), the avoidance of all defects is indeed accomplished.
For that [liberation] is not possible while defects exist;
nevertheless, objections based on the absence of a body have been raised.
And since that body consists of qualities such as knowledge and bliss, the avoidance of defects such as birth is also established.
However, the passage beginning with "janitota" must be explained otherwise, as it is contradicted by many scriptural statements that are otherwise without scope (*niravakāśa*).
This very point has been stated: "by the force of the context.
One might object as follows:

To claim that "the body consists of qualities such as knowledge and bliss, and is beginningless and eternal" is contradictory, like saying "a rabbit has horns. This is because we observe the rule that whatever is a body is composed of the elements (*bhautika*) and possesses birth and other such characteristics. Therefore, if one accepts Viṣṇu’s body and yet accepts its non-material nature (*abhautikatva*), one would have to accept that even a rabbit has horns. For this reason, he first dispels the contradiction regarding the body's non-material nature with the words: "because it exists [only] mentally" (*mānasattvāt*).
What contradiction is there because of being human? ... // Mānava 2.270a //
The word "ka" is used in the sense of an objection;
the meaning is that there is no contradiction.
Now, he releases the counter-argument regarding the horn of a hare by saying "no."
...is not desired for anyone at all. // MAnu 2.270b //
We would even accept the existence of a rabbit's horn if the fact that the body of the Supreme Lord consists of bliss and so forth were established by valid means of knowledge;
but it is not so.
For that which lacks authoritative basis can never be established by anyone, anywhere, or at any time.
Now, one might ask: even if it possesses authoritative basis, how is there an absence of contradiction? To this, he says: "Non-contradiction."
For both non-contradiction and contradiction are understood by means of valid cognition alone.

Non-contradiction exists between two things that are observed together in some instances; however, contradiction exists between those two things which are necessarily observed as having different loci. Thus, the non-contradiction and contradiction of entities are to be understood through the means of cognition characterized by their being observed together or not being observed together.

Because there is no other [means of knowledge] that could restrict it, how could there be a contradiction with an object perceived along with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since that would involve a self-contradiction?
He concludes: "Therefore... (*ataḥ*).
Therefore it has been said: "And all this is appropriate for Vāsudeva. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.271ab)
Since contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be suspected regarding an object perceived through them,
it has been stated by the cited scriptural passages that the state of being the cause of the world belongs in its entirety to Him whose stainless form consists of consciousness, bliss, and so forth.

It should be understood that this, which will be explained later starting with the words "and like that which is formless," was stated here by the Teacher out of his desire for the welfare of his disciples.
[Objection: But is this not the same for us as well?
For instance:

Although the Pāśupata and other such systems have a status as authoritative means of knowledge that is impossible to definitively establish, nevertheless: "Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace"; and "Rudra is one; he has no second."
"By his lordships, he rules over these worlds"; such scriptural passages declare that Śiva is the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe,
because he possesses names such as Śiva and others.
Furthermore, since it is impossible for such a [scriptural] passage to be inconsistent, the cited Śruti texts must be interpreted otherwise.

Therefore, the Śruti itself will either cast doubt upon the impossibility of the relationship and so forth, or it will postulate some other factor to resolve it; thus he says: "Śivādi... (beginning with Śiva).
And Vedic passages associated with names such as Śiva and others are also designations for Viṣṇu.
This would indeed be so if these scriptural passages were devoted to Śiva;
but they are not.
Rather, although they employ names such as Śiva and others, they refer exclusively to Viṣṇu.
But from where does this [certainty] come? This being the case, we too are certainly able to say that even such scriptural passages as "Nārāyaṇa is one" are in fact devoted to Śiva.
Not so;
for names such as Śiva possess denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to Viṣṇu,
whereas names such as Nārāyaṇa lack denotative power with respect to Śiva.
To the question "What is the proof for this as well?", he says: "All names...
(Manu 2.2.272): "He who alone bears all names is the one who holds the names of the gods;

"The names of Nārāyaṇa do not apply to others besides Hari"—such scriptural passages are the authority in this matter, and thus the systematic reconciliation has been stated. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.273)
By this [word "one"], he cites the Vedic scripture beginning with: "In the world there are no names for all things.
By the word "one," [he indicates this].
"He who alone is the name-giver of the gods. He is called "name-giver" (nāmadhā) because he bestows names; these names are not the designators of anything else.
Other words such as "Śiva" and so forth do not apply to those others; and the connection is that it has been stated that the concordance (samanvaya) therein is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
By the inclusion of the term "concordance" (samanvaya), this point is also resolved:
namely, that I shall explain these very scriptural passages as having Śiva and the other [deities] as their subject matter.
This is because [the text] has been determined to have the Blessed Lord as its ultimate purport through internal indications such as the introductory passages and so forth.
*8,431* Let it be that the determination of Śiva’s status as the cause of the universe does not occur through the Śrutis; however, it will occur through the Śaiva Purāṇas.
Nor are those [Purāṇas] devoted to Viṣṇu.

Because it has been determined to have Śiva as its subject matter through the force of its introductory passages and other criteria, [the author] says: "The Purāṇas... [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.274ab]:
"The Purāṇas are not authoritative on that point because they are contradicted by the Purāṇas and other [scriptures]."

Because they are contradicted by Vaiṣṇava texts such as the Purāṇas; for prior to considering their relative strength, there is a conflict of opposing arguments (satpratipakṣa), and subsequently, they are sublated (bādhitatva).
In that regard, concerning Śiva’s being the cause of the world:
the Śaiva Purāṇa is not only unauthoritative because it contradicts the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas and others;
rather, [it is so] because of the Śaiva authority (Purāṇa).
He says "that" because it is also contradictory:
"We have no authority regarding those things that are contradictory, due to the conflict between what precedes and what follows. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.274cd)

Regarding those things contradictory to that [Veda], such as the Śiva being the cause of the world and so forth which are contradicted by the Śaiva Purāṇas and other texts, they are not authoritative;
the word "Śaiva Purāṇa" is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
To the question, "How can there be a contradiction of the Śaiva Purāṇa by a Śaiva Purāṇa?", he says: "By the former," etc.
And this has been demonstrated elsewhere.

Furthermore, because it contradicts the Brāhma Purāṇa—which is devoid of partiality toward either the Śaiva or Vaiṣṇava positions—the Śaiva Purāṇa is not an authoritative source regarding the matter under dispute; thus he says: "It is equal," etc.
And because it would contradict the equality with Brahman... MĀn 2.275b.
This has also been shown elsewhere:

"In that case, the Purāṇas and other texts of the Vaiṣṇavas would also lack authority, because they too contradict the Śaiva and Brāhma Purāṇas and because of internal inconsistencies. To this, he says: "Because of the rule" (*niyamāt*). (8.432)
... by rule, even among the Vaiṣṇavas. // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.275b //
Because it is of a single nature;
because there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows;
and because the *Śaiva* and other Purāṇas lack the capacity to oppose this—such is the meaning of the word "api" (also/even).
The ellipsis is "their [scriptures] are not invalid.

Now, one might object: even in the *Purāṇas* and other texts belonging to the Vaiṣṇavas, the fact that Śiva and others are the cause of the world, as well as the reason for Viṣṇu’s praise of them and so forth, is indeed perceived.
Therefore, how can such a restriction be asserted? To this, he says: "For the purpose of delusion."
And also for the sake of delusion and liberation... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.275c //
The statement that Śiva and others are the cause of the world and so forth is intended solely for the purpose of deluding those who are unfit;

and because of the word "and" (ca), it is also due to the restatement of what was done by Viṣṇu—such as the praise of Śiva—for the sake of delusion, that the restriction [of the Vedas] is not contradicted.
To the question, "How is it that the Śaiva Purāṇas and others lack the capacity to oppose [the Vedas]? he says: "For the sake of delusion."
This is because the Śaiva Purāṇas and other such texts were composed through mere verbal assertion solely for the purpose of deluding people;
and by the word "and" (ca), it is implied that the Vaiṣṇava works were likewise composed solely for the purpose of [attaining] knowledge of reality.
Regarding this point, authorities from other sources have been cited elsewhere. *8,433*
He concludes the subject matter with the words: "Viṣṇu."
... Viṣṇu alone is the ocean of qualities.
"Therefore" means that "it is established" is the ellipsis.
Now, one might object: since there are also views held by the Skandhas and others that contradict the meaning already stated, why are they not refuted here? To this, he says: "The Skandhas... etc.
The doctrines concerning Skanda, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, and others have been refuted from this [work] onwards by means of logic.
"From that [work] by way of logic"—that is, by way of the logic for refuting the Pāśupata doctrine;
"therefore they are not refuted" is the ellipsis.
To the question, "How is their refutation accomplished by this logic?", he says: "in its entirety."
...without exception, according to the established doctrine without distinction.
In its entirety, there is no distinction between his doctrines and the Pāśupata doctrine;
the difference in doctrine consists solely in the adoption of a different deity,
while the methodological procedure (*prakriyā*) is identical everywhere.
Therefore, the sense is that its refutation is indeed appropriate by the very same logic used for the previous refutation.
Thus ends the section on the Lord (*pati*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
[======= JNys_2,2.XI: Non-capability of origination (utpatty-aśakti) =======]
[The Section on the Origin (or Incapacity)] // Now begins the section on the origin (or incapacity) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
Oṃ, because origination is impossible, Oṃ.
The Śākta doctrine is here refuted.
It should not be considered something that ought not to be refuted,
because it has already been rejected by the same logic applied previously to the doctrines of Skanda and others.
For instance,
having read "of Skanda" and so forth in place of "of the husband," when an inconsistency arises, Vedic passages concordant with that [reading] are cited,
and the impossibility of a [logical] relationship and other such arguments are applied to that subject.
Likewise, it can certainly be said even regarding the *śakti* (potency):
otherwise, even the *skandhas* and so forth would have to be refuted separately.
Now, it might be argued:

It may be argued that because differences in practice (*ācāra*) and so forth exist between the Śākta system and the Pāśupata, there is no difference in their established tenets (*siddhānta*). This is not so; for such differences are found even within the Saura and other systems.

Now, what is the point of that? You might say: "Apart from the acceptance of a specific deity, the refutation of an argument that contradicts the stated meaning is exactly the same in all cases. [We reply: That is equally true for this [position] as well; therefore, this too does not require a separate refutation. To this, he says: "In the refutation... (nirākṛtau).
Because origination is impossible;
since the particular has been refuted, that which possesses power is separately criticized... [MAnu 2.2.277a-c].
True;
for even the doctrine of Śakti, like that of the *skandhas* and so forth, does not differ from the Pāśupata system,
and for this very reason, it too is subject to the entire range of faults already mentioned.
Nevertheless, because a unique refutation exists therein, the Sūtrakāra refutes the Śakti doctrine separately by means of a distinct method, with the intention of addressing that [specific point].
For the impossibility of origination (*utpatty-asambhava*) is indeed the unique defect of the Śakti doctrine alone, and not of those who hold Puruṣa as their deity.

"And we shall explain this," [he says]. Having thus established the commencement of the section (*adhikaraṇa*), he now sets forth the position of the Śākta school with the words "The Great One" (*mahatī*).
The great goddess Hrīṅkarī, the cause of all, is designated by such names as Tripurābhairavī and others. (Mānavadharmaśāstra 2.277c–f)
The term "the doctrine of Śakti" (śaktimata) is understood to carry over. It is connected with every subsequent word "iti.
According to the doctrine of Śakti, the Goddess is the Great One, the most excellent of all. Thus [ends] the doctrine of Śakti.
To explain how it is "great," it is said: "the cause of all."

Because she is the cause of the creation and other functions of the entire world, the Blessed Lady (Bhagavatī) possesses all qualities such as omniscience and is far removed from all defects; therefore, she is the most excellent of all.
[Objection: But how can this treatise be authoritative if it contains internal contradictions?
For in the Bhuvaneśvarī-tantra, she alone is called the Great One, the cause of all;
in the Tripurā-tantra, however, it is Tripurā;
likewise, in the Bhairavī-tantra, it is Bhairavī.
In this way, various [forms] appear in the Kubjikā and other Tantras;
however, since it is not logical for many [deities] to possess the status of being supreme among all, it is therefore stated:
that one Bhagavatī alone is designated by such names as Hrīṅkārī, Tripurā, and Bhairavī.
Therefore, there is no mutual contradiction.
Furthermore, the powers are of three kinds.
[They are] Mahāvāmā, Madhyavāmā, and Aṇuvāmā.
These very [three] are sometimes referred to by the terms Śākta, Śāmbhava, and Āṇava.
Among them, he shows the specific doctrine of the first [group] with the words "tasyā" (of her).
From her are born the gods, humans, Sadāśiva, and others; this entire world of beings and their material elements [arises from her]. (Manu 2.278)
This refers to that very power alone.
By the mention of Sadāśiva, the distinction from other philosophical systems is shown;
for in those systems, the birth of Sadāśiva from Power is not admitted.
Having thus presented the Mahāvāma doctrine, he states that it is indeed untenable: "That," etc.
"...that is not tenable.
[The word] "that" refers back to the doctrine of Mahāvīra, which has been presented immediately prior.
When there is an expectation as to why this is so, the Sūtra provides the reason: "because of the impossibility of its origination."
To explain that, he first establishes the pervasion (vyāpti), beginning with the words "dṛṣṭa" (perceived).
Creation is always observed from males, or more specifically from both male and female;
it is never from females alone, because birth [from them] is impossible.
"The Mahāvāma doctrine is not to be honored... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.280a).
Here, by the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*), the birth of offspring is intended, not creation in general;
for the latter is seen even from women alone.
The word "sadā" (always) indicates the absence of deviation;
the word "vā" has the sense of the word "tu" (but/rather);
and "viśeṣataḥ" means "preeminently" or "in abundance."
For the production of certain individuals, such as Droṇa and others, is observed to come from males alone.
But surely, by the rule *acatur-ādi*, it ought to be *strīpuṃsebhyaḥ*;
how then can it be *strīpuṃbhyaḥ*?
"The rule regarding the application of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) is not mandatory";
thus it will be [understood].
Or rather, this suffix is prescribed as being applied after a *dvandva* compound.
But here, since it is "men together with women" (*strīmumāṃsaste*), and not a *dvandva* compound, [the suffix] will not occur;
[it would apply] only from those [women] who are devoid of the favor of men (*puruṣānugrahahīnābhyaḥ*).
[They arise] from those [seeds] which have been assisted.
To the question "What follows from that?", he explains the Sūtra with the word "tataḥ" (from that).

Because the pervasion is thus established, and because the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) alone is the source from which Śiva and the others are born—this being the reason why the birth of offspring from that power (*śakti*) is impossible; such is the meaning. *8,439*
The formal argument here is as follows:
the production of offspring at the beginning of time was not performed by women alone, because it is an instance of the production of offspring.
The arising of that offense is not committed by women alone,
as is commonly accepted;
for it is sometimes seen to arise from a mere man, and at other times from women who have been assisted by men.

Furthermore, it has never been observed anywhere that [a woman] produces offspring from women alone, such that there would be a deviation from the stated pervasion. Alternatively: "The capacity [to produce offspring] does not belong to one who does not give birth, because she is a woman alone, like a woman universally accepted as being a woman alone."

In this context, it should be understood that the statement of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—"not indeed from women alone"—is intended to avoid the charge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) and so forth. Alternatively, if one were to raise the objection: "If the power [to produce offspring] did not belong to a woman solely by virtue of her femininity, then even Puruṣottama would likewise not possess it solely by virtue of his masculinity," the phrase "seen" and so forth was stated beforehand precisely to refute such an objection.
And with the intention that its state of being "exclusive" (kevalatva) is unestablished for the Lord of Lakṣmī, [the author] said "from women and men" (strīpuṃbhyaḥ).
However, the form "from exclusive ones" (kevalābhyaḥ) serves to establish pervasion (vyāpti).
Alternatively, there is the principle: "Because when a specific [qualification] is excluded, [the general property] exists."
By this, the unique nature (*asādhāraṇatva*) of this fault has been stated; the citation beginning with "dṛṣṭā" is presented in order to establish that.
Now, raising another view based on a further doubt, he says: "vāmaiḥ" (by the left).
... another [type] is proclaimed by the left-handed ones. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.280b)
The meaning is "with the middle and left [hands]";
the rest is according to the Mahāvāma-siddhānta.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "Śiva," etc.
Śakti, with Śiva as her subordinate, created this universe on all sides.
Thus... [Manu 2.281a]
That which has Śiva as its subordinate element is "śivopasarjanā.
This is an explanation of the word "this" (idam), meaning that which exists in all directions and at all times as an object.
This is what is being said.
In our view, there is no impossibility of origination,
because we accept that the power (śakti), when conjoined with Śiva, is the source of the manifestation of the entire universe.
Nor does this entail a contradiction regarding the supreme excellence of those two,
because it is accepted that Śiva’s power is subordinate to the Lord.
He refutes this with the words "And that... (tacceti).
... and that is not tenable. // MAnu 2.281ab //
The sense here is that even in this case, the impossibility of origination has not been avoided.
Nor is there an instrument for an agent,
because Śiva is devoid of instruments.
Because he is bodiless... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.281bc //
The phrase "because of being without instruments" (*akaraṇatvataḥ*) is an explanation of that very term [of the root verse], namely "because of being bodiless" (*adehatvāt*).
Alternatively, the meaning is "because of being without instruments," that is, because of the absence of causes such as cognition (*jñāna*).
To the question "How is that so?", it is stated: "because of being without instruments, that is, because of being devoid of sense faculties" (*nirindriyatvāt*).
To the question "Why even that?", it is said: "Because he is bodiless" (*adehatvāt*).
This is what is meant:
for Śiva, being possessed of a body, must exercise his assistance through his power (*śakti*) in the production of offspring.
Not by means of a bodiless [self],
because for such a self— whose faculties, consciousness, and so forth have dissolved and which is devoid of them— that [agency] is impossible.
Furthermore, there is no power belonging solely to Śakti for the production of Śiva’s body,
because of the fault previously mentioned;
otherwise, if such a production were possible here as well, it would result in the redundancy of accepting Śiva at all.
Nor [is it possible] with Śiva included,
because it is logically impossible for one who is bodiless (videha) to provide assistance.
Therefore, even though Śiva is accepted [as a cause], he is like the fleshy protuberance on the neck of a goat (ajāgalastana), and thus the production [of the world] is impossible here as well.
He raises another opinion with the words: "Moreover" (api hi).
For others might even say that the Lord is omniscient.
"Aṇuvāmā... (*Mānava Dharma Śāstra* 2.2.282a).
The word "others" (*anye*) is the syntactic connection (*anvaya*).
He states those very [women] by their specific names: "Aṇuvāmā."
The word "hi" (indeed) is used to indicate the prevalence of this view in the world. "Omniscient" (*sarvajña*) is an elliptical expression;
it means one who is endowed with all the causes necessary for the creation and so forth of the universe.
This is what is meant:
for me, who maintains that Śakti accompanied by Śiva is the mother of the universe, the aforementioned fault does not apply;
because Śiva possesses innate omniscience and other such qualities, he has no dependence upon a body or sense organs.
"Because even the enjoyment [of the fruits of action] is possible through the assumption of a body for sport (līlāvigraha), by means of which power (śakti) provides assistance"—
this he refutes with: "Not that."
... that is not appropriate ... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.282a //
To the question "Why?", there is this sūtra: "Oṃ, or rather, if consciousness and the rest exist, there is no negation of that [Brahman]; Oṃ."
Thus,
its meaning is as follows:
if the state of Śiva possessing consciousness and so forth is accepted, then no refutation is made of that doctrine.
Now, is this view [of yours] an inference or not?
It cannot be the first,
because it contradicts the meaning already stated.

Since the statement "that is not tenable" is itself untenable, and since it was asked how there could be no refutation of that in the second case, and furthermore how this [statement] could serve as a reason for the claim "that is not tenable," he first provides a reason outside the sūtra in order to establish that there is no such refutation: "Īśa... (The Lord...).
Or, if consciousness and so forth exist, there is no negation of them;
for [otherwise] one would be entering into the doctrine of a creator god.
The meaning is that it would result in the consequence of entering the Śaiva doctrine. [Objection:

But surely the Śaivas accept only a single Śiva endowed with qualities such as omniscience, whereas the Śāktas accept both Śiva and Śakti; thus, there is a great difference in their fundamental tenets.
How, then, can there be an entry of the Śāktas into the Śaiva doctrine? Anticipating the objection that this would result in the aforementioned fault, he says: "Omniscience, etc. (sārvajñādīti).
The two [the Buddha and the Veda] are endowed with qualities such as omniscience through the conceptualization of them as teachers.
It is not appropriate... // MĀnuv 2.283a //
It is true that the Śākta school accepts a duality known as Śiva and Śakti, endowed with qualities such as omniscience and so forth;
however, that is not tenable,
because it involves the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*).
For instance, an omniscient being endowed with such qualities is not established by direct perception;
this is because the mental states of another person are beyond the senses of that other person.
Nor can it be established by scripture,
because there is doubt regarding the authority of a scripture whose capacity [to convey truth] is [itself] dependent on another,
and because an authorless scripture (apauruṣeya-āgama) is not accepted as authoritative by the opponent.
Or, if one were to accept [that position], it would follow from that very fact that one's own doctrine is abandoned.
Therefore, precisely because the construction of such elaborate conceptualizations is untenable, an entity of that kind must be postulated;
for everything is indeed accomplished by a single being endowed with omniscience and other such qualities.
And thus, the postulation of two such entities would be a mere waste, resulting only in the burden of conceptual proliferation (kalpanā-gaurava).
Therefore, one should accept only a single such entity.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "From that...
... "Therefore, however, the Lord alone is the sole instigator. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.283b)

Since it has been stated that one alone must be accepted as possessing omniscience and other such qualities, if one accepts mere power (*śakti*) alone, the consequence would be the impossibility of creation; therefore, the Śāktas themselves would have to accept that the Lord (*Īśa*) alone, endowed with omniscience and the rest, is the agent of the construction of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
And if this were so, how could the Śākta doctrine not be a form of the Śaiva doctrine?
What follows from this if it is so?
If you say that the proponent of the Śākta position would suffer defeat due to a deviation from their own tenet, that is true;
nevertheless, it remains the case that the Blessed One’s tenet is not thereby undermined.

Since the Śaiva doctrine must also be refuted because it contradicts your own established tenets, he introduces the portion of the sūtra "tadapratiṣedhaḥ" (the non-refutation of that) along with its supporting reasoning, beginning with the words "uktā" (as stated).
And since that position has already been refuted by the previously mentioned defects, it is not further criticized here.

Since the Śaiva position has already been stated as subject to the aforementioned defects within the context of the immediately preceding section, it is not refuted here again for fear of the fault of tautology.
Thus, having individually refuted the three views, the following Sūtra is intended to reject them all by means of a common refutation:
"Oṃ, and because of contradiction, Oṃ."
He explains that [verse] as follows: "Śruti... etc.
And because of contradiction:
"Due to the total conflict between the Śruti, Smṛti, and Itihāsa, and because it is loathed by the virtuous, that doctrine must certainly not be accepted. (Manu 2.2.284)
Because it is censured among the virtuous and because it is desired to be protected;
or else, since the genitive case is used for the agent with a *kṛt* suffix according to the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti," the meaning is that it is condemned by the virtuous.
By the word "hi" (for/indeed), he indicates the well-known status of the Śruti and other authorities.
Some explain this group of four sūtras as being intended for the refutation of the Bhāgavata doctrine; for instance:

The followers of the Pāñcarātra teach the following process: from Vāsudeva, the individual soul named Saṅkarṣaṇa is born; from Saṅkarṣaṇa, the mind known as Pradyumna is born; and from Pradyumna, the ego-sense named Aniruddha is born.
Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "Because of the impossibility of origination."
To say that a living being named Saṅkarṣaṇa is born from Vāsudeva is improper,
because it is impossible for a living being to arise [from another].
For if the living being were subject to origination, defects such as impermanence would necessarily follow.

Consequently, for him there would be neither attainment of the Blessed One nor liberation; furthermore, this would contradict such scriptural and traditional texts as "He is not born, he does not die," and so forth.
Furthermore, an instrument does not arise from its agent;
thus, the birth of the mind—designated as Pradyumna—from the individual soul—designated as Saṅkarṣaṇa—as described in the Pañcarātra is untenable.
For in the world, an instrument [does not arise] from an agent such as Devadatta.
An instrument such as an axe is seen to be produced;
and when it is produced, it is indeed an object (karman), not an instrument (karaṇa).
For the living being (jīva), the agent is the mind (manas) and the instrument is [the axe].
Therefore, that [ego] cannot have originated from that [mind].
From this very [Brahman], the vital breath, the mind, all the senses, and consciousness are born; for there is scriptural testimony regarding the birth of the mind from the Supreme Lord alone.
By this, the claim that the ego known as Aniruddha is born from Pradyumna is also refuted.
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"These [beings] such as Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others are not intended to exist in the form of individual souls (jīva) and so forth;
rather, all of them are accepted as being none other than Īśvaras, endowed with divine attributes such as knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor."
"Therefore, this is not a fault.
To this, he states the rebuttal: "Or, even if [the qualities] such as consciousness exist, there is no refutation of that;

for even if it is admitted that Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others, like the Supreme Self Vāsudeva, possess the sixfold qualities beginning with consciousness and are consequently regarded as Lords (Īśvara), the fault of the impossibility of their origination remains unrefuted."
In another way, this fault of the impossibility of origination indeed follows.
For instance, these four are not distinct from one another.
For if one were to postulate multiple lords, defects such as unnecessary complexity (gaurava) would arise;
however, if they are non-different, how could the production of oneself from oneself be possible,
given that there is no distinction [between cause and effect]?
Furthermore, these manifestations of the Blessed One would not be restricted to a number of only four,
because it is admitted that His manifestations are infinite,
and because there is a contradiction [otherwise].
Furthermore, there is a mutual contradiction within the Pañcarātra:

in some places it is said that knowledge, sovereignty, strength, heroism, power, and splendor are the qualities (*guṇa*) of the Blessed One; [in others], these are said to be the very selves (*ātman*) of the Blessed One.
In some places, it is stated that [Vāsudeva] is the very nature of the Blessed One (*bhagavatsvarūpa*), and so forth;
furthermore, there is here a rejection of the Vedas.

The venerable Śāṇḍilya, having studied the Veda with its six auxiliary limbs, yet not attaining final perfection in that great traditional corpus, became possessed of a powerful discriminative inquiry, thinking: "How may I know that dharma which is supreme among all and beyond which nothing higher exists?

In this regard, it is observed that there would be a censure of the Veda [if one were to claim] that the scripture was proclaimed to the venerable Śāṇḍilya by the venerable Saṅkarṣaṇa as something manifest, like sound.
And likewise elsewhere:
"O Blessed One, the Vedas have been studied by me along with their limbs, sub-limbs, and in full detail; and the auxiliary sciences, as well as the Vākovākya texts, have been heard by me."
“Moreover, among all these [systems], I do not see anywhere a path to the highest good that is free from doubt, by which success might be achieved. Therefore,
the Pañcarātra scripture is untenable.
He rejects this misinterpretation with the words: "The Pañcarātra."
If they declare these [sūtras] for the purpose of prohibiting the Pañcarātra,
that is highly contradictory to the sūtras themselves...
They declare and explain;
the word "yadi" (if) is used in the sense of "yat" (that which); that is the explanation. *Ati* [is used] excessively.
The meaning is that it is contradictory to common sense (*śayena viruddham*), self-contradictory (*svavyāhatam*), and sublated by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntarapratihatam*).
To the question "How so?", he first demonstrates the self-contradiction with the words "Since... (*yataḥ*).
... for as it says in that *Bhārata*: [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.285d]
The meaning is that since the author of the Sūtras himself has stated the authority of the Pañcarātra in the Mahābhārata, there would be a contradiction of his own words for him to refute it here.
He cites that statement from the Mahābhārata: "Of the Pañcarātra... and so forth.
Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the entire Pañcarātra;
O Indra among kings, this [system] is superior to all these other systems of knowledge.
But those who know the Pañcarātra, O King, who are devoted to its proper sequence and have attained single-minded devotion, they enter Vāsudeva.
"... thus: 'Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāśupata, and likewise the Veda and Āraṇyaka—these systems of knowledge are distinct; or rather, are they not? Let it be told. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 12.94) *8,450*

Regarding the question of whether the Sāṅkhya and other systems—designated by the term "knowledge" because they are causes of knowledge—are mutually contradictory or not, the following resolution has been stated: "Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pāśupata, and the Vedic Āraṇyaka—these knowledges are distinct; no deliberation should be made on this point."

Furthermore, since conceptual constructions regarding objects are untenable and because all mutually contradictory systems cannot simultaneously possess validity, when the inquiry arises as to which among these is authoritative, [the author]—

having stated that Sāṅkhya and other systems were composed by non-reliable authors through such statements as “Kapila is the speaker of Sāṅkhya”— establishes the validity of the Pañcarātra (indicated here by the term *vedāraṇyaka*) on the grounds that it was composed by Nārāyaṇa, who is the supremely reliable authority.
It is stated by way of a formal argument.
However, because the Vedas are of non-human origin, their authority is established by its very nature; thus, it was not explicitly stated [for them].
Furthermore, the Pañcarātra is authoritative because it generates purposeful activity that yields results.
This is stated by the phrase "those who know the Pañcarātra":
those who are devoted to the sequence [of the scriptures], devoted to the gradations of the deities,
and who have attained unswerving devotion by entering into a state of single-minded dedication (*ekāntabhāva*).
He states another way in which [the position] contradicts itself: "And [the statement] 'the Gītā... etc.
And the Gītā is declared to be a compendium of that scripture.

The summary of that scripture is known as the *Pañcarātra-saṅkṣepa*. "That knowledge consisting of the *Pañcarātra*, which was formerly given by Viṣṇu to Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and Sūrya— Vyāsa imparted it to the Pāṇḍavas."
During their very descents, and specifically for Arjuna in the midst of the army,
[the Lord] bestowed [this teaching], which is designated as the Gītā.
The word "famous" (*vikhyātam*) is to be understood as being supplied from the Purāṇic passage beginning with "briefly [it was told] to Ayuyutsu" (*saṅkṣepeṇāyuyutsave*).

Therefore, since Bādarāyaṇa—who composed the Gītā as a summary of the Pañcarātra—has already accepted the authority of the Pañcarātra, how could there not be a self-contradiction in attempting to refute it here once again? He demonstrates this self-contradiction by another means with the words: "By the Veda... (vedena).
Indeed, by means of Vedic knowledge, by the five-night rite, and through devotion as well as sacrifice.
"I am visible [only] in this way, not otherwise, even in hundreds of millions of years"—
such is the statement of the Varāha [Purāṇa].

Thus, since the authority of the Pañcarātra is accepted here as being equal to the Veda as a means for the vision of the Blessed One in the Varāha Purāṇa, to subsequently refute it would indeed constitute a contradiction.

Having thus established the internal contradiction [of his own position], he demonstrates the contradiction with other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) by means of the verse beginning with "ślokāḥ."
... "these are the verses," such is the word heard in the ear. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.289d)
The word "speech" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
"The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvāṅgirasa, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the sciences, the Upaniṣads, the verses, the aphorisms, the explanatory treatises, and the commentaries."

In this scriptural passage, within the context of enumerating the authoritative sources such as the *Ṛgveda* and others, the *Pañcarātra* is included by the term "ślokas. Furthermore, in the statement, "The foremost knowers of the *Pañcarātra*," which refers specifically to the *Pañcarātra* under discussion, [it says]: "The invisible Puruṣottama spoke to all those sages."
For the word "śloka" is used in the *Mahābhārata* in the passage: "A hundred thousand most beneficial verses have indeed been composed.
Furthermore, in the *Chandoga Śruti*, beginning with "The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda," and so forth, the *Pañcarātra* is called "Ekāyana."
By that designation, it is understood—that is, known—that the entire term "śloka" refers to the Pañcarātra.
Therefore, the authority of the Pañcarātra is established by the Veda; thus, any doctrine asserting its lack of authority contradicts the Veda.
Furthermore, he demonstrates the clear contradiction with the Veda [in the verse] beginning with "vedaiśca. (8.453)
And through the Vedas and the Pañcarātras, the supreme Nārāyaṇa is to be meditated upon.
The meaning is: "in the manner taught in the Vedas and the Pañcarātras.
The plural form "by the Pañcarātras" (*pañcarātraiḥ*) is used because there are various divisions of the *saṃhitās*.
To address the question of how meditation can be performed according to two mutually contradictory scriptures, it is stated: "and the Pañcarātra."
The implication is that stating the lack of authority of the Pañcarātra based on such Vedic statements is contradictory.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "The Pañcarātra... [etc.].
The Pañcarātra and the Vedas are but a single knowledge, though it is established in two ways.
By such Vedic declarations as these, the Pañcarātra is set aside.
How indeed... [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.291a-c]
Since the refutation of the Pañcarātra in this manner is both self-contradictory and contradicted by other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
how can it be possible to say that "the author of the Sūtras here sets aside and refutes the Pañcarātra"?
For the Blessed One does not speak contradictory words.
It might be thought:
"This contradiction does not exist."
“That Supreme Self, who is celebrated as Nārāyaṇa beyond the Unmanifest, remains having manifested Himself in manifold forms by means of His own self.

Having worshipped that Blessed One— who possesses the embodiment of the six attributes— for a long time through the fivefold observances consisting of approaching, taking up materials, sacrifice, study, and yoga, one whose afflictions are destroyed attains the Blessed One alone.”
Because the meaning set forth in the *Pañcarātra* and other such texts has been accepted [by you],
it follows that the statements in the *Mahābhārata* and other works must be understood as having that very [Pāñcarātra] as their ultimate purport.
This is not so.
This being the case, since there exists a portion to be accepted even in the treatises of the Sāṅkhyas and others, it would be untenable to specifically assert the authority of the Pañcarātra;
furthermore, the qualification "of the whole" would be untenable. [As it is said:
"The Ṛgveda and the rest, the Mahābhārata, and the entire Pañcarātra..."
"Since the entire Pañcarātra is to be known as that which fulfills the meaning of the Vedas"—because this contradicts the word "entire" (*akhila*), [the opponent's objection fails].
For this reason as well, he states that the refutation of the Pañcarātra is not tenable: "In this regard... (*atrety*) [verse 8.455].
... what fault is there in this? ... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.291c //

In this regard, what fault is there in the *Pañcarātra* such that it would be rejected? The meaning is: none at all. Now, one might ask: "How can there be no fault, given that the impossible birth of a living being (*jīva*) is taught therein? To this, he replies by way of a concessive argument: "Birth... [and so forth].
...and thus it is said that "the origin [of the world] is known from this. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.291d)
It has been stated right here... [Manu 2.292a]
