Is it merely the mention of the soul's origination that is adduced as the reason for the lack of authority of the Pañcarātra? Or is it the mention of the soul's origination in the sense of coming into being from what did not previously exist?
In the first case, [the soul's] mere origination occurs right here [in this world].
In the Mīmāṃsā treatise, which is accepted as authoritative,
it is stated by the sūtra "jño 'ta eva" (he is a knower for this very reason); by the word "api," [it is implied that] "all indeed..."
He brings together [the arguments] by noting that it is stated in the Śruti: "Those selves emerge.
Consequently, there would also be a lack of authority for the Veda and its Mīmāṃsā.
The sense is that otherwise, the reason would fall into the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntya*).
Against one who is mistaken regarding the meaning of the aphorism "He is the knower for this very reason," scripture itself must be cited as an example.
This might be so.
Only the second reason is adopted; however, that [reason] does not apply to the Śruti and the Sūtra, for in those texts,
it is stated that the birth of the individual soul (jīva), which already exists prior to it, is spoken of only with reference to limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body.
Because it does not have the characteristic of being a non-existent entity, he says: "And not..."
"And even there, the coming into being of what was previously non-existent is not asserted.
Even in that case— referring to the five nights—

the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*), although it is perceived in both the Śruti and the Sūtras, is explained as pertaining to its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), setting aside the notion of the production of something from nothing.
In that case, let even what is stated in the *Pañcarātra* be explained accordingly;
thus, the meaning is that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*). [Objection:
But this presentation is unequal.

Indeed, in both the Śruti and the Sūtra, [it is stated] by such passages as "asleep through beginningless Māyā" and "because of being beginningless," that [the soul is bound] by beginningless karma and so forth.
The relationship is being stated;
for this [relationship] is not possible for a living being (*jīva*) that possesses existence after having been non-existent.
Therefore, in accordance with that [scriptural authority], even the birth of the individual soul (jīva) understood there must be interpreted otherwise;
for there is no such subverting evidence here by which we might abandon the primary sense and resort to a secondary one.
Therefore, since the reason would not be unestablished (*asiddhi*) if the primary meaning were to be accepted, he says: "beginningless" (*anādi*).
Bound by beginningless karma, the individual soul wanders within the circle of transmigration.
For such is his statement: "He wanders eternally by the will of Vāsudeva."
Those words refer to the statements of the Pañcarātra.

Since the Pañcarātra, like the Śruti and the Sūtras, declares that the individual soul (jīva) has a connection with beginningless karma, the birth of the soul mentioned therein must likewise be explained otherwise, in accordance with that [scriptural authority];
for there is no reason to show partiality [to one text over another].
The meaning is that, in this way, the reason remains unestablished (*asiddhi*).
Furthermore, it might be argued:

nowhere in the Vedas or other such texts is it clearly stated that the transmigratory existence of living beings has a beginning, nor is there any clear statement indicating that they come into being after not having existed.
If it is argued that this [objection] leaves room for another interpretation, [the author] says "no" with the intention that this same point applies here as well:
"For the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is nowhere stated in the Pañcarātra. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.293cd)
By this very same reasoning, the statement "the instrument does not belong to the agent" must also be refuted;
for it is as follows:

Is the pervasion (vyāpti) that "an instrument is not produced from its agent," or is it that "in whatever action a certain instrument is employed, that instrument is not produced from the agent of that action"?
It is not the first,
because of the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra).
Otherwise, it would follow that the instruments [of cognition] could not arise at all.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
because even in the case under discussion, such a state of affairs is not established.

Regarding the contradiction with the Śruti statement "from this [Self] it is born": would this apply to the mere admission that the mind is produced from the individual soul (jīva), or to the admission of a specific mode of production?
It is not the first case.
Because of the Vedic scripture beginning with, "Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts," the mind arises daily from the individual soul (jīva); thus,
the second [alternative] is not tenable.
Since even in the present context, suchness (*tathātva*) is not accepted [as the cause],
the same objection regarding the mind’s production of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) must likewise be avoided.
Thus, by accepting the literal meanings of terms such as "living being" (*jīva*), the refutation of the faults imputed to the two sūtras has been stated.

Now, he states a different meaning from the meaning imagined by others regarding the statement, "From Vāsudeva, the individual soul (jīva) named Saṅkarṣaṇa is born," and so forth: "The individual soul," etc.
The birth of Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is the presiding deity of the individual soul (jīva), is said to be from Vāsudeva;
and likewise, the birth of Pradyumna is from him.
Thus, for one who is conceited in mind, desire alone... // MAnu 2.295ab //
In order to establish the ground for the application of the term "jīva," it was stated that he is the "one who identifies with the individual soul" (jīvābhimānin).
To exclude Saṅkarṣaṇa, the Blessed Lord, from this definition—since there is no birth for him—it was stated by name that "of Śeṣa, [who is] Saṅkarṣaṇa.
This was expressed by the sentence beginning with "Vāsudeva, etc. (proktā vāsudevāditi).
Then, from Saṅkarṣaṇa;
the word "tathā" (likewise) is used in the sense of conjunction;
the meaning is that his birth has been described.
The purpose of the phrase "of Kāma, who possesses the conceit of mind" is the same as previously stated.
By the word "thus" (*evam*), he extends the method of explanation already mentioned to the statement that from Pradyumna arises the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) named Aniruddha;
thus, the birth of Aniruddha, the son of Kāma and the possessor of the conceit of the ego-sense, has been declared. (8.461)
[Objection: Even so, the defect of the impossibility of origination remains in the same state, because Śeṣa and the others are also living beings.
[Reply: Not so;
for here the origination of Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others is not being asserted.
However, it is called "birth" (*janir*) because it is born (*jāyate*);
and birth is manifestation (*prādurbhāva*).
They read [in the lexicon]: "the root *janī* means manifestation."
Furthermore, the manifestation of the living being (*jīva*) upon the arising of a body is well-established;
this is what was meant by the statement that "birth" has been explained.
For this very reason, the previous position was merely a provisional assertion (*abhyupagamavāda*).
He states another point as well: "directly," etc.
...in some places, the manifestation (vyūha) of Hari is spoken of directly by names such as Saṅkarṣaṇa and others, due to his eternal, inconceivable, and vast power. ... // MAnuv_2.2.295b-e //
For Śeṣa and others are also called "Dhara" because they are portions of the Blessed One; therefore,
the word "directly" was stated in order to exclude them.
The grammatical connection is that the manifestation (vyūha) has been described as belonging directly to Hari himself under names such as Saṅkarṣaṇa and so forth.

Now, an objection is raised: "But was it not stated here that there is no negation of that [manifestation] because of Hari's lack of birth? To this it is replied: "The manifestation is said to be merely a division (vibhāga), not an origination. Furthermore, it was asked: "Are these [forms] distinct from one another, or not?"
The answer to that is: "Of Hari alone. Now, if this is so, then since He is unsurpassed (niratiśaya), how can there be a division of Himself from Himself? To this it is said: "Eternal" (nitya).

The meaning is: what indeed is difficult to conceive regarding the Blessed One that could be measured? As for what was also said—that these manifestations of the Blessed One are not fixed at a number of only four because they are infinite—the answer to that is "in some cases."
The meaning is: "at a specific time and for a specific purpose.
[The opponent] is ignorant of the Bhāgavata tradition.

In the beginning, indeed, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa manifested as the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) consisting of Vāsudeva and the others, for the purpose of bestowing his own state of liberation and so forth.
Subsequently, at another time, for the sake of other purposes, he became the tenfold or twelvefold manifestation (daśadvādaśavyūha).
This is what is called "pure creation" (śuddhasṛṣṭi) by the followers of the Pāñcarātra.
In view of that, how could the description of the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*) possibly be untenable?
Thus, this statement is entirely appropriate for the purpose of propitiating specific types of qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*).
As it has been said: "He is one-formed, four-formed, or even five-formed."
"Or Hari, distinguished by twelve [forms] and so forth, is worshipped by the virtuous.
He states the purpose of explaining another meaning with the words "otherwise": *anyathā*.
...how can it be declared defective by restating it otherwise? // Manu 2.295ef //
How can one state a refutation by providing a misrepresentation of a sentence uttered with the intention of expressing one meaning as if it were something else?
[This would result] in the fallacy of equivocation (*chala*).
Furthermore, there is no logical inconsistency regarding words such as "living being" (*jīva*) and so forth.

As for the claim that the Pañcarātra contains mutual contradictions— based on the interpretation of the Sūtra "and because of contradiction"— which asserts that the Lord alone is primarily endowed with the maintenance of life and so forth,
that too is refuted by the very statement "by His eternal and inconceivable great power.
For it is through the power of the Lord alone that the conventional usage of qualities, the possessor of qualities, and so forth, is established.
And the *viśeṣa* (ultimate particularity), which has been established and consecrated as the term for difference, is the cause that accounts for all objects of valid cognition.
As for what was said—that in the account of the story of Śāṇḍilya, the Pañcarātra appears to harbor hostility toward the Vedas—he refutes that with the words "If... (*yadīti*).
Just as one would say, "If he should know the four Vedas," there is a completion of the Veda [by the Pañcarātra]; so why this hatred toward the practice of Śāṇḍilya?

In this statement— “If a twice-born man should know the four Vedas along with the auxiliary sciences and the Upaniṣads, but does not know the Purāṇa, he would not truly be a learned man”— it is intended that the completion of the Veda is achieved through the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth.

Likewise, in this case as well, when the explanation is that the *Pañcarātra* intends precisely the fulfillment of the Veda, how could it be perceived that there is an aversion to the Veda in the *Śāṇḍilyavartana*?
The meaning is that it is not so perceived.

Alternatively, since these two statements are identical, why do you harbor such animosity toward the statement alone that describes Śāṇḍilya’s conduct, by which [you claim] that the phrase "if one should know" is intended to show that the Itihāsas and Purāṇas supplement the Vedas, while the passage beginning with "the Blessed One" is explained as being intended to show that the Pañcarātra contradicts the Vedas? The following is the sequence of the response to this:

If, on the strength of this statement, the non-contradiction of the Pañcarātra is postulated, then, on the strength of the statement "if one should know," the same should be postulated for the Itihāsas and Purāṇas as well, since there is no distinction [between them].
Or, if in that case the intention is that the Itihāsas and so forth serve to supplement the Veda; [then the same applies here].
In this case as well, let that very same [principle] be postulated, since there is no distinction; for it is said:
"One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas."
If it is argued that such an interpretation is appropriate because it conforms to the contradiction with the subsequent statement,
then here too [it must be understood that] "the Pañcarātra is to be known as that which fulfills the meaning of the Veda."

Because of such statements as these, one should make such an interpretation; thus, there is no difference [between our view and others], except for [mere] malice. The statement from the *Paramasaṃhitā* should also be explained in exactly this way.
He concludes the refutation of the false interpretation with the words: "Therefore, beyond this..."
Therefore, the censure of the Pañcarātra raised by the Asuras out of hatred for the Supreme Teacher is not even worthy of consideration; that is,
it is not fit to be examined at all, as it is logically inconsistent.
If so, why was it said "arisen"? To this it is replied: "Supreme" (paramā).
The *Pañcarātra* is the supreme scripture.
To the question "What is the basis for this very aversion?", it is said: "By the Asuras."
For in the Bhāgavata-śāstra, the enmity of the asuras is indeed innate;
it is not caused by the perception of faults.
And these commentators are connected with the asuras and possess their very nature.
By stating that this was spoken by the Asuras and not by the author of the Sūtra, it is implied that this is not the meaning of the Sūtra, but rather a refutation of the Śākta doctrine;
by this, the following point is also answered.
Some explain that this section is intended to refute the objection that the Pañcarātra, like the Sāṅkhya and other systems, lacks authority;
for instance, according to the reasoning already stated: "Because of the impossibility of origination" (Brahma-sūtra 2.2.42) and "Nor can an instrument belong to an agent" (Brahma-sūtra 2.2.43).

Thus, having raised the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the lack of authority of the *Pañcarātra* by means of these two sūtras, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) was reached with the statement: "Or, if there is the state of being consciousness and so forth, there is no negation of that.
By the word "or" (*vā*), the position is reversed.
"Consciousness and so forth" (*vijñānādi*) refers to the Supreme Brahman, who is consciousness and the rest.
Even though Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha possess the nature of the Supreme Brahman, the authority of this scripture which expounds them is not negated; moreover,
because of contradiction, for the birth of the individual soul (jīva) is indeed prohibited even in this system.
As it is said in the *Paramasaṃhitā*:
"Inert, for the sake of another, eternal, and constantly changing;
composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and the field of actions—such is the nature of *prakṛti*."
"The connection between that [attainment] and the person exists in the form of attainment;
for it is determined to be, in the ultimate sense, beginningless and endless.
Indeed, only when a doubt regarding the lack of authority of the Pañcarātra has arisen would an effort to refute it be purposeful.
Furthermore, objections based on a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) are not capable of inducing such a suspicion;
for these are merely quibbles (*chala*) and do not necessitate such a shift in locus,
as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, this is inconsistent with the context;
for here the refutation of the opponent's position is the subject at hand, not the establishment of one's own position,
and that has already been accomplished by the passage beginning with "Because of the difference in characteristics" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*).
Furthermore, this interpretation does not conform to the literal words of the Sūtra;
for nowhere in this context is a term such as "consciousness" (vijñāna) employed to denote Brahman.
Moreover, the phrase "the non-denial thereof" would be redundant.
It should not be said that this is because of wisdom;
for in this way, the sutra would be both concise and clear.
Therefore, it is established that the meaning of the sutra is exactly as stated. *8,467*
He concludes the meaning of the verse with the words: "Therefore, without remainder..."
Therefore, Nārāyaṇa— the sustainer of the entire world without exception, a vast ocean of faultless virtues— is determined through the intended meaning of the collection of Śruti texts.

The meaning is that since those doctrines opposed to Sāṅkhya and others have been refuted in the first chapter, the two-fold definition of the Lord established through the harmonization of all the Vedas is indeed determined.
This might be so;
however, one should not engage in debate by means of suppression.
This refutation of others, which is prohibited by such Smṛti passages, must certainly not be performed.
If it is asked why, then, a refutation of the Sāṅkhyas and others was carried out, the answer is:
because this prohibition concerns [the refutation of] what is real (sat).
If it is asked, "Whence this restriction?
[the answer is: because the Śruti is more authoritative than both Śruti and Smṛti;

and because in the Śruti, the rejection of the other [Smṛti] is understood as something that must be performed. With this intention, [the text says]: "Into blinding darkness they enter who worship ignorance."
"Then, as it were, even greater darkness falls upon those who delight in knowledge alone.
But he who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—
having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality through knowledge."
Thus he restates the meaning of the two mantras with the verse beginning "blind":
"Into blind darkness enter those who worship ignorance; into a darkness even greater than that, as it were, they enter who do not even condemn it. (Manu 2.9)
Then, he who understands both knowledge and ignorance together,
having transcended these through the knowledge of their defects, attains immortality by means of knowledge.
They go toward ignorance— that which is imagined by ignorance and whose object does not exist— just as [one goes] toward darkness; the word "iva" has the sense of "to some extent."
The word *u* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
It expresses the meaning already obtained by the statement "those who are devoted solely to knowledge," namely,
that they are certainly not revilers of that [knowledge].
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement, "By means of knowledge, one attains immortality.
This is because, in the absence of the removal of ignorance, defects would still persist.
The word "together" (saha) indicates a rule of conjunction.

By the phrase "having transcended this through the knowledge of its defects," the meaning is understood to be that one has transcended— that is, crossed over— death, which is that very ignorance (*avidyā*) along with its effects such as suffering, by means of knowing it as being corrupted by ignorance.
Although the knowledge of reality does not arise merely through the instruments of valid cognition belonging to one's own school, [it arises through other means].
As long as the evidence of the opposing position has not been refuted, a counter-balanced argument (*satpratipakṣa*) cannot serve as a factor for reaching a definitive conclusion.

Therefore, by one who desires the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the refutation of the opposing position must necessarily be undertaken just like the establishment of one's own position; this point is established by logical necessity.

Nevertheless, with the intention that one who persists in opposition by relying upon scripture must be enlightened in that very same manner, two mantras have been cited; thus, everything is beyond reproach.

Thus ends this section on the Samaya [tradition] in the second chapter of the commentary (*Ṭīkā*) on the *Anuvyākhyāna*—the work of the venerable Pūrṇaprajña Bhagavatpāda—composed by the ascetic named Praguṇajayatīrtha, which explains the meaning of difficult words and sentences.
Adhyāya 2, Pāda 3 [JNYS_2,3...: ...the section on the locus...
// Now begins the third quarter of the second chapter.
Now begins the section on the ether (*viyadadhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
He shows the subject matter of the section beginning with "na vyomāśruteḥ" (not space, because of the lack of scriptural mention), along with its logical connection, by saying "atha" (now).

Then the Lord, intending to dispel all contradictions with the entirety of the sacred tradition (samāmnāya) regarding the deities, the elements, the individual soul, and the Supreme Self, [proceeded].
The Lord, the author of the Sūtras,

by means of this third chapter— which is present to the intellect because it is intended to be explained— demonstrates the mutual non-contradiction, that is, the absence of contradiction, among Vedic statements; such is the statement of the subject matter to be expounded.
In order to demonstrate the connection characterized by inclusion within this [work], it was stated: "without remainder" (*aśeṣa*).
The analysis of the compound is: "and all those contradictions with the *samāmnāya*.
The word "kariṣyan" (intending to do) is used with reference to the time of commencing this chapter.
Indeed, the author of the Sūtras has begun this second chapter in order to resolve all contradictions with the Vedas.

Since even the mutual contradictions among Vedic statements are included within that [category of contradiction], their refutation here is indeed appropriate. The word "atha" (now) is used to indicate the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) as the connection (*saṅgati*). Since the occasion has arrived, and because the removal of the contradiction with reasoning is primary, it is treated first; and since [the following] consists of its detailed exposition, [the text proceeds].

Since the resolution of contradictions regarding the *samaya* (traditional doctrine) occurs immediately prior to that, this is the occasion for the resolution of mutual contradictions among the *śrutis*.

[Objection: If that were so, there would be no distinction between this quarter (*pāda*) and the fourth quarter, because in the latter as well, the mutual contradictions of Vedic statements are being set aside. To this, it is said: "with regard to the divine" (*adhidaiva*).

The *adhidaiva* are the deities presiding over the unmanifest and so forth; the *adhibhūta* are the elements beginning with space, together with their effects and causes. This is what is being stated.
Although in the first two quarters only the mutual contradictions among Vedic statements are being resolved,
nevertheless there will be a distinction due to the difference in subject matter:

here [in the first two quarters], the subject matter consists of statements concerning the divine and so forth, whereas in the fourth [quarter], it consists of those concerning the internal self (adhyātma).
Nor does this quarter [of the verse] become manifold because it has multiple objects;
for its unity is established by virtue of its having both internal and external objects.
Regarding the determination of the sequence here as well, the Teacher himself will state the reason. *8,475*
But one might object: for what purpose is the resolution of mutual contradictions among Vedic statements?
If it is argued that this is for the sake of ascertaining their authority—since the authority of mutually contradictory statements cannot be determined otherwise—we say no;
for if that were the case, it would follow that this is a treatise on logic (*tarka-śāstra*), which would contradict its status as Mīmāṃsā.
It is said:

Indeed, the ascertainment that Brahman is the cause of the entire universe can only occur when there is a determination of the nature of the entire universe and a determination of its being an effect and so forth; it cannot occur otherwise.
Furthermore, if the scriptural passages concerning that subject are mutually contradictory, no such determination of its nature can take place.
Therefore, this resolution of mutual contradictions is solely for the purpose of determining the true nature of the objects concerning the deities and so forth.
This has also been stated: "Precisely for the sake of ascertaining the essential nature."
With this chapter, the one of immeasurable luster demonstrates the lack of contradiction among the various statements for the purpose of determining their true nature.
Now, is the mutual contradiction of only a few statements being resolved, or that of all of them?
It cannot be the first,
because it would be pointless.

In that very case, because there remains an irresolvable state of uncertainty due to the existence of contradictions with other scriptural statements, the second [alternative] is not tenable; furthermore, since the Vedic sentences are infinite, they cannot be fully known. Therefore, it is said: "of immeasurable splendor" (*amitadyuti*).
The meaning is "the Omniscient One.

Having summarized the arguments for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding this section on the [first] quarter, he says: "In experience," and so forth.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with experience, reasoning, and many scriptural statements;
moreover, all this would result in the equality of the existent and the futility of the means [to liberation]. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.3)
It follows established views and reasoning, does not contradict other meanings, accepts well-known names, and conforms to many scriptural statements. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.3.4)
Conformity with worldly views, equality with living beings, beginninglessness,
thorough knowledge in each respective case, and likewise the scriptural teachings on the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas).

The state of having an origin, the non-experience of one's own qualities, the assumption of [the world] being small, the existence of various Vedic texts, and diversity— these are the arguments belonging to the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
The impossibility of fixed rules, independence, conformity, primacy, possession of power, diversity, and universal inclusion. (Manu 2.3.7)

The movement [of the soul] and so forth, the power of the Lord, the non-contradiction with all authorities, the clear establishment of the fulfillment of desires, the reversal of what is established by scripture,
and the specific cause— these are the proofs for the very tenet.
Oṃ. Space does not exist, because it is not heard [in scripture]. Oṃ.

In this section, the production of the ether (*viyat*) has been established by taking as figurative those scriptural passages such as "This ether is indeed beginningless," and as primary those such as "From the Self, the ether was produced. In that context, one should understand that the word *viyat* does not refer merely to the ether, but rather serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the self (*ātman*), time (*kāla*), and so forth—all of which, other than the Supreme Self, are subjects of conflicting scriptural statements such as "The Person, primordial matter, the self, and time are indeed eternal. With this intention, he says:
"Nature."
[The ether does not exist] because it is not heard [in scripture].
Primordial Matter (prakṛti), the Person (puruṣa), Time (kāla), the gods who preside over them, and the principles beginning with the Great One (mahat) are born... [Manu 2.3.9a-c].

*Prakṛti* is insentient; *puruṣa* is the individual soul (*jīva*), who possesses the conceit of being that [principle]. "Those possessing the conceit of *prakṛti* and so forth" refers to those who identify with *prakṛti* and the rest. "The Great One and the others" (*mahadādyāḥ*) refers to what are called the Great Principle (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), the sense organs, and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
He states the meaning obtained by the negation "no" regarding the impossibility of the production of the aforementioned [principles]: "they are born."
This is the underlying intention:
it is not reasonable to first maintain that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the other [principles] are indeed devoid of birth.

"‘The abandonment of the proposition [results] from the non-difference of words’; since the [faults] such as the abandonment of the proposition mentioned in the statement ‘But as far as there is modification, there is division, as in the world’ apply here as well,
otherwise those [faults] would fall into the error of being inconclusive."
Nor are they of undisputed origin,
since a conflict with the Śruti has already been demonstrated;
furthermore, there is no other section (adhikaraṇa) intended for that purpose.
Therefore, it is appropriate that they are indicated here by the term "ether" (*viyat*).
However, another section (*adhikaraṇa*) is commenced to dispel further doubts regarding wind (*mātariśvan*) and the subsequent elements.
Here, some maintain that the birth of ether, as previously described, is characterized by coming into being after not having existed, just like a jar or similar objects.
Intending to refute that [position], he first states his own view: "Dependent on another," etc.
...characterized by dependence on another; "he created all this" here expresses the state of being subject to birth. MAnu 2.3.9d-f.

Relying on such scriptural passages as "From the Self, space was produced" and "He created all this," as well as logical arguments such as its being divided, that which has been stated here in this section regarding the origin of space (viyat) must be understood as characterized by the attainment of an excellence dependent upon another.

For when a specific excellence (*apūrvaviśeṣa*) arises, the arising of a specific form is necessarily concomitant; and since that specific form is non-different from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the entity, it is the arising of that very [nature] which occurs.

Indeed, we observe the conventional usage of "birth" (*janana*) applied even to an entity whose essential nature remains stable, merely through the acquisition of a particular state—as in "Devadatta has become embodied," "he has become learned," or "the jar has become conjoined," "it has become disjoined."

Now, in the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda), even for things such as a jar, this very process constitutes their production: namely, that clay and the like, whose essential nature remains constant, merely attain another form or reach a different state.
Furthermore, even by our opponents, only the theory of transformation is accepted, not the theory of new origination (ārambhavāda).
Therefore, since there is no dispute, this undertaking is purposeless;
however, the Teacher himself will clarify the subject of the dispute so that it is not purposeless.
In this regard, [it is said]: "He created all this."
This citation from scripture (*śruti*) and so forth is intended to indicate that birth (*janman*) should be explained in exactly the same way even in other scriptural passages;

furthermore, it is intended to suggest the logical justification for the view that the term "ether" (*viyat*) is meant to be indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*) of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the like, according to the method already stated. *8,481*

If it is asked, "Why could the origination of space not be intended by the Śruti and Sūtra to be characterized by 'coming into being after not having been,' just as in the case of a jar and other things according to the view of others?"—to this we ask:
what is intended by the word "space" for the opponents?
Is it mere vacuity, as held by the Vaiśeṣikas and others, or is it the absence of material form, as held by the outsiders (Bāhyas)?
He refutes the first [position] with the words: "merely a space."
Space is merely the absence of obstruction; otherwise, how could it arise?

Otherwise, if one does not accept that birth (*janman*) is the acquisition of a specific state dependent on another, but instead accepts that birth is the coming-into-being of what did not previously exist, and if one further accepts that space (*ākāśa*) is merely an absence of obstruction, how could it arise?
The meaning is that its arising is not logically possible;
for all [entities] indeed possess a material cause (*sopādāna*).
Emission is observed [to require a material cause], yet there is no material cause for the production of space;
furthermore, it will be pointed out in the *Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa* that Brahman’s status as a material cause is not tenable.
Moreover, whatever has an origin must be preceded by its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
Furthermore, the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of space is not possible,
because such a cognition is untenable;
for when non-existence is perceived, it is perceived as belonging to something— namely, "its [non-existence] is here"— and never without a substratum.
Furthermore, the perception of a substratum for the absence of space is not tenable;
for that very thing which is pointed out as "this" is itself space.
Even in the theory that an absence resides in its material cause (*upādāna*), since that [cause] is absent, the perception of the absence is not possible.
And so says the Śruti:
"For there is no absence of space, since even here [in Brahman] it is not the case that there is an absence.

Furthermore, the claim that Brahman itself—being of the nature of non-space—is called the prior state of space (its *prāgabhāva*) is also refuted by the fact that Brahman is not an *upādāna* (material cause).
The locus of absence is precisely the locus of its counter-positive.
If it is argued that since space has no locus, its absence must likewise be without a locus, we say no;
for if it were without a locus, its status as an effect would be untenable.
Furthermore, since space is perceived as its own substratum, its absence would also have to be perceived as having space as its substratum; thus, a contradiction arises.
Some hold that primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is the cause of space;
according to that view, it follows that primordial matter itself would be subject to birth.
Now, if it is admitted that there is the attainment of a specific quality dependent on another in that case [of space],

then this same must be admitted even for ether and so forth, whose production is impossible. Regarding the second [alternative] as well, is this stated by admitting space to have the nature of parts, or without admitting it?
In the first case, is the production of the absence of some particular material substance intended, or that of all [material substances]? Not the first,
because since that [production] is established by perception and other means of valid cognition, it does not provide a reason for undertaking this inquiry.
He refutes the second [position] with the words "yadi" (if).
If there was previously no space, what was this world composed of dense material form?
If one accepts that all absence of material form arises during creation, then its absence must necessarily be admitted at the time of dissolution;
for it is impossible for that which is absolutely non-existent to be born.
And if it is admitted that prior to creation, at the time of dissolution, there is no absence of space— that is, the absence of all material substance—
then is it admitted that the world is then densely packed with material things?
He clarifies this very point with the verse beginning "mūrta" (material).
And there would indeed be a state of being filled with urine if there were no space.
If the absence of space characterized as previously described were to exist at the time of dissolution, then there would necessarily be a complete filling by material forms;
for the absence of an absence does not exceed existence,
or because [material form] is pervaded by that [space].
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned;
thus, after the time of creation, nothing that possesses form would exist either.
And in this way, there would be a reversal of creation and dissolution.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that space would be entirely filled with material objects during the dissolution of the universe.
To refute the second position—that space is merely the absence of material substances and nothing more than that—the author states: "Material substances... [and so forth].
For corporeal substances indeed always remain situated within space.
And the meaning of "ca" (and) is "the absence thereof.
One who accepts corporeal substances and their absences must necessarily accept space as something distinct from them;
for the construction is that they [the substances] always abide in space.
This is what is being said:
when one bird has flown away, it must be stated where the second bird should fly.
If you say, "Where that [first bird] is not," then one must accept a distinct entity (arthāntara) as that locus by which the absence of the first bird and the presence of the other are distinguished.
Since that very region is space, how can it not be accepted?
Furthermore, in the perception "here is a bird, here is no bird," the region is established by direct experience as the locus for corporeal objects and their absence; how can this be denied?

Moreover, is space the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a corporeal substance, its posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsa*), its absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), or its mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)?
It is neither the first nor the second [alternative],
because it would follow that there is no space after the time of creation;

for since antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) reside in their material causes (*upādāna*), it would result in the cognition of space being restricted to those [causes] while its absence would occur elsewhere.
Not the third,
because it is impossible for there to be an absolute absence of a material entity wherever and whenever that entity exists.
Nor the fourth.
For if the mutual absence of a jar were simply the cloth or that which resides in it, then the conceptualization of "space" would apply to those as well.

If you argue that space is merely the absence of contact with corporeal substances, then for a bird in flight, with what could it have contact such that the absence of that contact would constitute space? Therefore, one must necessarily admit a locus [of that absence].

Thus, it is established that the arising of space in the form of coming into being after not having been is logical. Let this be the case; however, let the aforementioned misinterpretation by others stand as it is. What, then, is the meaning of the word "space," and what is its acquisition of particularities dependent upon another? To this, he says: "Therefore... (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, the deity of that [space], Vināyaka, who is designated by the word "ether" (ākāśa),
is declared by the Śruti to have been produced together with the production of the body.

The meaning is that the interpretation offered by others is untenable. Thus, the statement "that deity [is] the presiding principle of the elemental ether" establishes that Vināyaka is denotable by the word "ether," as found in the scriptural passage beginning with "the ether of the Self."
"By the arising of a body" is an elaboration of the attainment of specific qualities dependent on another;
since this consists of two statements, it is appropriate [to say] "here" and "by means of scripture."
And he states another object of scripture: "even what has occurred."
Even though it has come into being, it remains unseen; it arises only within the range of divine vision.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: even the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), which is denoted by the word "ether," is declared by the Śruti to be produced, just like a jar or other such objects.
To the question, "On what basis does the elemental ether possess the quality of being produced? it is said: "It is dark" (asitam).
The meaning is "because it possesses form.
And thus says the Śruti: "Blueness arises in space."
Since that being the case, there would follow the undesirable consequence [of the self] being visible, it is therefore stated: "by means of the divine [eye]."
By the word "tu" (but), he indicates the qualification of being unmanifest.
This is what is meant:
is it mere visibility that is to be established as a consequence, or visibility for people such as ourselves?
In the first case, however, there is the production of a supernatural power,
because it is admitted that [the self] falls within the range of divine vision.
In the second case, however, there is a breakdown of the pervasion regarding bodies composed of the elements and so forth.
"In that regard, the assumption of [the ether] being unmanifested (*anudbhūta*) and so forth is equally applicable here as well, on account of the authority of scripture.

[Objection: Having just now refuted the production of space (*ākāśa*) characterized by coming into being after not having existed, how can there not be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows if it is accepted again here? To this he says: "The unmanifested... ... "For the unmanifested sky is within the range of the witness (*sākṣin*). (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.13cd)
Since it has been stated that space is indeed indeterminate and does not arise, and not because it is a primary element (*bhūta*), there is no contradiction.
He also states another reason for its non-arising: "for it is eternal."
And this is not unestablished,
because there is no cause for destruction;
for the will of the Lord is never observed to be the cause of destruction without depending on some other cause.
If it is argued that even this [creation] must be postulated because of scriptural statements regarding its origination, we say no;
for such statements have scope as they refer to the elements and the prideful beings who identify with them.
And this must necessarily be so.
Because the passage beginning with "From the Self, space was produced" occurs within a context concerning the elements (bhūtas).

Now, if it is argued that there is no proof whatsoever for unevolved space (avyākṛtākāśa), and thus it must be stated of what its non-production is said, it is therefore replied: "The Witness" (sākṣī).
To the question "How so?", he says: "In a particular location."
It should be understood as a mere designation, for it is never produced.
If it is argued that this very thing is the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), we say no;
for there exist scriptural statements regarding its having form and being formless, its being unmanifest and unmanifest, and its being limited and unlimited.
Furthermore, the contradiction between the scriptural passages concerning its origin and its non-origination also indicates a duality of ether.
Since the absence of contradiction is established through this systematic arrangement, it is impossible to assume that the scriptural statements regarding non-origination are merely figurative;

furthermore, as was stated previously, the origination of a mere portion [of Brahman] is not tenable. But was it not said by the author of the Sūtras himself that "figurative interpretation is impossible"?
This has been explained by the author of the commentary and elucidated by us.
[Verse 8.491] Now, one might object: "Since there is no arising of unconditioned space (*avyākṛtākāśa*), let there be no contradiction regarding the statement that 'space was produced'."
If it is argued that there will be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "He created all this," we say no;

for although there is no possibility of production characterized by coming into being after not having existed (*abhūtvābhavana*), there does exist a kind of production consisting in the attainment of a particular state dependent on another. Thus he says: "Even so... (*tathāpi*).
Nevertheless, it is space itself— endowed with particularities dependent upon prior relations—
that is intended by the word "originating" when used in scripture.
The analysis of the compound is: "this is a formal relation (*mūrta-sambandha*) and it is a particularity dependent on another (*paratantra-viśeṣa*).
The meaning is that what has been described as being without beginning is itself the "own" (*sva*).
The word "scripture" (*śruti*) refers to the scriptural statement: "He created all this. *8,492*

Having thus explained the arising of space as taught in the Sūtras, he now explains the arising of the primary cause (prakṛti) and the rest, which are characterized by those [elements]: "The primary cause," and so forth.
Primordial nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), and time (kāla)—
all these are proclaimed to be produced by the specific power dependent upon the Lord.

when the intermixture of the qualities has occurred, he is born as before.

The meaning of the statement from the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, "by the vision of duality," is as follows: "He who is the first among all moving and stationary beings, who contains the Vedas within himself, together with the ṛṣis,
the lords of yoga such as Kumāra and others, and the perfected ones (*siddhas*) who promote yoga..."

Through the knowledge of the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord, through self-respect, through great reverence for the Lord, and through the cessation of ritual action, he becomes liberated upon attaining union with the Supreme Brahman— known as the Supreme Person— who is endowed with qualities such as omniscience and is the creator of the universe.

Having entered [that state], when the time for creation arrives, he is born once again in the world of Viṣṇu— which is distinct from the [guṇa] *sattva* and free from the transformations of the *sattva* and other qualities— as the sovereign of all liberated souls, just as before, by means of the form of the Supreme Lord known as Time (*kāla*).
But here, the distinction is indeed clear.
Because it is the liberation of Hiraṇyagarbha, its status as the supreme liberation is established.
"One sits nourishing the Ṛg-verses, always impelled by the Supreme. (Manu 2.3.36ab)
"One nurtures the abundance of the Ṛg-verses, having caused them to flourish; another sings the Gāyatra upon the Śakvarī verses;
another, as a Brahman, speaks the knowledge of all that has been born; and yet another measures out the proportions of the sacrifice.
This is the meaning of the mantra.
In the place of liberation, one Brahman sits nourishing the growth of the *ṛcs*, remaining there while performing the nourishment of the *ṛcs*;
another Brahman sings the *gāyatra* sāman mounted upon the *śakvarī* verses;
another Brahman speaks the knowledge of birth (*jātavidyā*), the knowledge concerning man (*pauruṣeyavidyā*).
"Your Brahmā measures out the very measure and portion of Viṣṇu’s sacrifice while meditating.
Here too, a distinction is clearly manifest;
for the abundance of Brahmas is heard of, as is their state of supreme liberation.
Nor can this refer to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*),
because it is not well-known that the *brahman* priest possesses knowledge of all the sciences (*jāti-vidyā*).
Furthermore, if all four quarters were to have a different subject matter from the *hotṛ* and other priests, then the phrase "in the third quarter" (*tṛtīye tu pāde*) would be rendered meaningless.
The word "ca" (and) serves to include the remainder of the statement.

By the phrase "impelled by another, always," [the author] refers to such scriptural passages as: "That very person established in Brahman, having cast off this mortal body and attained Brahman, beholds [all] through Brahman."

He also cites such Smṛti passages as: "They revolve according to their desire, sustained by His very grace," and "Whatever he desires, that he truly creates; he creates it even through his own self. (Manu 12.36cd) *8,516*
By the phrase "whatever he desires," the scriptural passage—"Indeed, his action is not exhausted; for from this very Self, whatever he desires, that he creates"—is cited.
Whatever the liberated one desires, he creates that very object as his action.
How so?
That which it emits is from this very Self, solely through the grace of the Supreme Lord; such is the meaning.
For the word *addhā* (certainly) indeed conveys the sense of *eva* (exclusively).
In this regard, the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is indeed clear;
moreover, because of the statement regarding the non-exhaustion of karma, there is the state of supreme liberation:
"Having transcended those qualities, he enjoys his desires together with Brahman. (Manu 2.3.37ab)
By the word "together" (*sahaiva*), he cites the scriptural passage: "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman.

However, the interpretation that "he enjoys all desires simultaneously (*yaugapadyena*) by virtue of having Brahman as his self" is inconsistent with the literal words of the scripture and inconsistent with its established tenets.
By the word "nistīrṇa" (one who has crossed over), the Śruti passage, "For then he becomes one who has crossed over all sorrows of the heart," is understood.
The meaning is that at that time, having crossed over all sorrows, he is liberated and becomes a remnant of the Brahman of the heart.
Because it is the abode of the heart, Brahman is the "Heart" (hṛdaya).
Its qualities are the "qualities of the heart" (hṛdguṇāḥ), such as suffering and so forth.
Here, by means of crossing over all sorrow, the state of supreme liberation is understood.
And having abandoned suffering and the rest... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.3.37c //

By the phrase "having abandoned suffering and the rest," the following statement from the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa* is intended: "Those who liberate the universe by their own will enter bodies composed of light; they experience only supreme bliss and never suffering or the like."

Here, by means of the plural number, both difference and the state of supreme liberation—due to the absence of suffering and so forth—are determined and manifest. ... "Devoid of activity toward the world. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.3.37d)
...he enjoys exalted pleasures together with them. ... // MAnu 2.38a //

By the phrase "in the activity of the world," the statement from the *Vārāha Purāṇa* is intended: "Upon attaining their own supreme bliss, liberated souls have no desire even for the activities of creation and so forth; they enjoy only other [worldly] desires."
And here, a distinction is understood by way of the limits of sovereignty;
he concludes the proof of his own position with the words "and so forth."
...according to such scriptural authority, how indeed can there be non-difference for one who has attained liberation, given that difference is perceived? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.38b–d)
...of the individual soul and the Lord.
The phrase "of the liberated supreme Brahman" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Now, intending to refute the opposing view, he begins to refute that which was stated—namely, the inference supported by the authority of the scriptures and the strength of reasoning—with the words: "And it is not inference. (8.519) This refers to the inference that was previously presented in conjunction with the testimony of the Vedas; he now proceeds to set that aside.
Nor can inference establish its non-difference from that.
The word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin the establishment of one's own position with the refutation of the opposing position.
"Pramāpayet" means one should make it known or establish it as cognized.
Alternatively, this is a proposition intended to refute all the proofs adduced by the opponent regarding the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara).
And thus, the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "both Śruti and Smṛti" has that meaning.
To the question "How so?", he first restates the inference: "It is indeed false," and so forth.
If it is argued: "The difference that is under dispute is indeed false, because it is a difference, like the difference in the appearance of the moon... MAnu 2.3.39c-e.

If it were merely stated that "difference is false," one would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of the difference between [two] moons and so forth; therefore, the term "disputed" (*vimata*) is used.
This means "the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.

Alternatively, it is intended to indicate that since the difference between a pillar, a pot, and so on, is equivalent to the subject under discussion (*pakṣatulyatva*), one should not suspect a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason "being a difference" with respect to those cases.
"Whatever difference there may be that is subject to dispute, all of it is [of this nature].
The mention of "difference" is for the sake of clarity.
By the restriction of the probandum (*sādhyāvadhāraṇena*), he indicates the exclusion of fallacies such as the unestablished (*asiddha*).
The underlying sense is that once the falsity of difference is established, non-difference alone is established as real. He asks "the probandum" (*sādhyeti*) in order to refute this.
...this property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is either existent, non-existent, or neither. MAnu 2.3.39ef.
This [distinction] between the individual soul and Brahman is characterized by falsity;
it is "existent" according to our own philosophical system.
Now, if falsity is existent, then that to which it belongs must also be existent.
For it is not possible that there be no substratum (dharmin) while the property (dharma) exists;
and thus, [your claim] would be the exact opposite.
Do not say so.

Falsehood (*mithyātva*), indeed, is the state of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), and that [non-existence] is apprehended solely through the medium of cognition.
Even for that which is absolutely non-existent, a cognitive appearance is admitted.
Thus, the meaning of the statement "falsehood exists" is that the absolute non-existence having that [falsehood] as its counter-correlative exists.
And there is no contradiction here;
"non-existent" is stated in accordance with the Madhyamaka view,
for there is no confidence [in the existence of things] on the part of the opponent.
We conclude that he would not speak by overstepping his own position;
whether both [positions] are new or not depends on following the opponent's view.
We say this because of the equality [of the faults] in the refutation of the positions beginning with "existent" and so forth;
or else, the third position is that it is "both."
"No" is the fourth [position];
it means that one does not know both.
He refutes the first [position] with the words "If... (*yadīti*).
If [the opponent] exists, it would be a departure from one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*). ... MAnu 2.3.40a.
If this property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is said to be "existent," then there would be a deviation from the established tenet (*apasiddhānta*) for the proponent of Māyā.
For the falsity of the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is not Brahman itself;
if it were, then even if that difference were existent, there would be no deviation from the tenet for the proponent of the reality of non-duality (*sadadvaitavādin*).
Because Brahman is free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpaka).
Regarding the second [alternative], he states the fault: "That very [same thing]" and so forth.
... that very thing is called "present" (āsann). // MAnuv_2.3.40b //
This is indeed a contradiction of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
Even if falsity (*mithyātva*) were non-existent,
there would still be existence (*sattva*) of the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.
Furthermore, it is their position that what is non-existent is not an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By this, one should understand that the position of both existence and non-existence is also refuted.
He refutes the final [position] with the words: "If neither."
If it is neither, then that is not established... // MAnu 2.3.40c //

Furthermore, this state of being distinct from both [the individual soul and Brahman] is not established anywhere else—neither in the falsity of the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, nor in any other instance.
If it is argued: "What is meant by this? It is that the qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatvam*)," we say no.
This is because the distinction from both the existent and the non-existent is not intended as a qualification of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*).

Rather, it is falsity (*mithyātva*) alone that is presented as the qualification of the subject, and the distinction from the existent and the non-existent is simply a property (*dharma*) of that [falsity].
Nor should it be argued that, as in the case of the argument "the subject of dispute is preceded by an intelligent agent," there must necessarily be a well-known qualification.

Because of the disparity. For that which falls within the scope of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and is also the subject of dispute (*vivādapada*) must necessarily be established; otherwise, it would not constitute the basis for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Because [the latter] is impossible;
for while the property of being intelligent is included within the extension of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), the property of being distinct from both existence and non-existence is not.
It is said:
for whatever object is to be established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must be found to possess one or another of the possible modes [of existence].

However, this falsity of the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman cannot be accepted as having a mode such as "existence" (sat) and so forth, because the three possible modes are refuted by our own established tenets (apasiddhānta).
Because the fourth alternative lacks any authoritative basis (*aprāmāṇika*), nothing possessing attributes can exist through an unauthoritative mode.

Therefore, the intended collective meaning is that the falsity of the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman cannot be established, as it is sublated by the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*); thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
With this very intention, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) should also be understood.
He states another refutation: "thus [the phrase] 'of the mental' (*mānasya*)."
... thus is the refutation of pride. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.3.40d)
"Māna" means that which is measured (*mīyate*);
this is according to the rule "the *kṛtya* suffixes and *luṭ* are used diversely.
The meaning is that even after analyzing the sense of the word "mithyā," the refutation should be stated in this very manner.
For instance:
what is meant by "false"? Is it non-existence, or is it ineffability?
In the first case, there is a deviation from an accepted tenet (*apasiddhānta*);
in the second, the subject (*pakṣa*) has an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*).
If it is argued that "the absence of existence is the referent of the term *mithyā*," we say no.
Because there is no escape from the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*) by treating that very non-existence as the referent of the word and the meaning of the term;
thus he states another fault with the word "iti."
Regarding the mark of pride (*māna*),

if one analyzes whether the reason for its differentiation exists, does not exist, both exists and does not exist, or is inexpressible (*anirvācya*): in the first case, it is unestablished (*asiddhi*) for the proponent of non-duality (*advaitavādin*),
and the example is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*).
The meaning is that the refutation should be stated for both the second and third [positions], as well as for the proponents of dualism (dvaitavādins) regarding the fourth. Furthermore,
there is no universal property of "difference-ness" (bhedatva-sāmānya) in existence, non-existence, and so forth.
By which [reasoning] this logical mark (*hetu*) would be like the "possessing smoke" [inference].

In other inferences as well—such as "the individual soul (*jīva*) is not different from Brahman, because it possesses selfhood (*ātmatva*), like Brahman"—one should likewise formulate the alternatives and state further refutations. Thus he says: "Thus, of the means of knowledge... (*iti mānasya*).

Alternatively, he extends this [critique] by stating "iti" (*8,531*), indicating that one must state the defect by thus analyzing both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*) in all those inferences employed by the proponents of non-duality (*advaitavādin*) regarding contradictory subjects.

The claim that "it is not established" is incorrect; for it is possible to establish—inconceivability (*anirvacanīyatva*)—by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) either in the difference (*bheda*) made the subject (*pakṣa*), or in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), or in ignorance (*avidyā*), or in the case of the shell-silver (*śukti-rajata*) and so forth. To this, he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
And this cannot be established anywhere by means of any other source of knowledge.
When the refutation of the falsity of difference is stated through the conceptualization of existence and so forth, then the word "internal" (*antara*) expresses a specific distinction; however,
when the meaning of the word "false" (*mithyā*) is being analyzed...
The statement of a refutation by means of a small [argument] is then another measure, distinct from other measures;
this is "inexpressibility" (*anirvācyatva*).
"In some cases" refers to the instances previously mentioned. *8,532*
If it is asked how that is so, it is as follows:

having set forth in the mind the alternatives—whether perception, inference, scripture, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), comparison, or non-existence (*abhāva*)—is said to be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the inexpressibility of some entity, [the author] first refutes inference in accordance with the abundance of the opponent’s own admissions, stating: "If [it is claimed] by inference... (*anumānena cet*).
If it were by means of inference, then that same infinite regress would indeed occur.

If the indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*) of shell-silver and the like is established by such an inference as "it is indeterminable because it is sublatable," then there will be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
How so?
For that very same series of inferences, intended to avoid the fallacy of having an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), would itself have to be established; this is the meaning.
What ought to be said on this matter has already been stated by us in the very first sūtra. He rejects the scriptural authority [of the opponent] with the words: "And not... (na ca).
And there is no scriptural authority for that meaning...
The meaning of that is "having an indefinable object";
the intention is that it is because [such an object] is not perceived.
Now, how could it not exist?
Since the scripture exists stating, "There was neither non-existence nor existence at that time," he says: "He would not say 'there was no non-existence'...
The word "thus" implies the phrase "so says the scripture.
That is the inexpressible reality.
This is the intended meaning.
For the meaning of a sentence is indeed the relation between word-meanings understood through the power of the syntactical connection of words, and nothing else;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and other means of knowledge would be included within verbal testimony (*āgama*).
And in this context, from the sentence, only the mere absence of Being (*sat*) and so forth at the time of dissolution is understood, and not an indefinable entity (*anirvācya-vastu*).
Therefore, this scripture does not have an inexpressible meaning.
Let it be that this scripture does not have an inexpressible meaning;
nevertheless, by the force of this very statement, an inexpressible meaning will be established.
For instance, here first the non-existence of both the existent and the non-existent at the time of dissolution is established.

By the force of that [negation], when the existence and non-existence of the object present at that time are both negated, its indeterminability (anirvācyatva) is understood through the method of elimination (pariśeṣa).
Furthermore, it is not the case that there is an absence of the mere entity (vastumātra) at that time,
for otherwise, subsequent creation would be impossible.
And because non-existence must be accepted,
one raises the objection— “by way of elimination” (*pariśeṣāt*)— suggesting that it is either presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or inference (*anumāna*).
If, by process of elimination, it were established as being inexpressible...
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "If it is argued that, by way of elimination, an inexpressible entity would be established.
To this we reply:
This might be so if, in this context, the words "existent" (*sat*) and "non-existent" (*asat*) were to have their commonly understood meanings.
But this is not so, because it consists of the five great elements, some of which are perceptible and some imperceptible; thus it is said: "It is neither existent nor non-existent."
Because [the term] is employed in such passages as these.

If one asks, "Why is this so?", the author, intending to show that there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of the meaning being unintelligible, says: "of the supreme Self" (*parātmanaḥ*).
... than one's own self. // Manu 2.3.42d //
It would simply be inexpressible... // MAnu 2.3.43a //
The meaning is that, in that case, the very Supreme Self accepted by the Sāṃkhya would have to be inexpressible.
Why? To this he says: "For [the Self] remains as the only alternative."
For at that time, he remains as what is left over.
By the force of the negation of both existence and non-existence, it must indeed be admitted that that which remains at the dissolution of all effects is precisely indefinable (anirvācya).
Since that Supreme Self remains at the time of dissolution in an unmerged state, it follows that He is indefinable.

Nor should it be argued that although the Supreme Self (paramātman) indeed exists at the time of dissolution, nevertheless, because of the proximate statement "darkness existed" (*tama āsīt*) and so forth, "darkness"—meaning ignorance—is present in the intellect; thus, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), even the means of valid cognition will establish the indeterminability (*anirvācyatā*) of that very darkness as residing in the intellect affected by it. For by the statement "breath existed, unbreathed" (*ānīdavātam*), Brahman also is present in the intellect.
If it is argued that there is no denial [of the world] because its reality is understood from the statement "truth and knowledge," we say no;
for since darkness is also understood to have existed [in the past], there would likewise be a denial [of its reality].
If it is argued that its existence is merely conventional (*sāṃvyāvahārika*), [we reply: so too is the existence of the world.
Why should it not be the same for Brahman as well?
Furthermore, in this interpretation, the word "then" (*tadānīm*) would be redundant, because darkness is always inexpressible. If you argue that the sentence has another purpose, [we reply: no.
Nevertheless, the statement "it was not non-existent" is indeed futile, because there is no possibility of its attainment. [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.18]:
"You do not know him who generated these; something else has come between you."
"Enveloped by mist, prattling, and satisfied with what is not life-sustaining, the reciters of hymns wander;
these desires of theirs are real, but covered by the unreal"—such scriptural passages are the authority for the inexpressibility of ignorance; therefore, he says: "And not... [na ceti].
And there is no other traditional authority (āgama) regarding that matter... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.43c]
In this context, the ellipsis is "the means of knowledge regarding an indefinable object.

Since the terms "other" (anya) and "unreal" (anṛta) denote indefinable ignorance (anirvacanīyājñāna), one might ask how it is not so; therefore, he explains its indefinability [by stating]: "neither existent nor non-existent" (sadasat).
... [it is] the counter-correlative of both existence and non-existence.
That which has "existent and non-existent" as its counter-correlates is described as such;
that which is neither existent nor non-existent is "indescribable" (anirvācya). Furthermore, there is no word here that expresses that [indescribable].
"But because the word 'untruth' (*anṛta*) and so forth is explained otherwise" (*8,539*), he rejects [the claim that it is] perception (*pratyakṣa*) with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
And there is no such thing as mere perception... // MAnu 2.3.44a //
Neither any common person nor any investigator perceives with the eyes or other senses that "this is inexpressible.
If it is argued that they do perceive it because of the subsequent recollection—"silver appeared as false after the sublation"—we say no;
for the word "false" (mithyā) has the meaning of "non-existent" (asat).
He refutes presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) with the words: "And not... (na ca).
... nor is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) accepted [as a means of proof]. MAnu 2.3.44b.
The phrase "separate from inference" implies "by those who accept valid means of knowledge.
The intended meaning is that inference has already been refuted on the grounds that its qualifier is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*).
Furthermore, there exists no such untenable object by virtue of which the inexpressibility (*anirvācyatā*) of any object would follow. *8,542*
Now, it might be thought:
if the universe, such as space and so forth, or [an illusion] such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell were real, then it would not be sublated;
for there is no possibility of sublation for that which is real.
For the existent Self is not sublated;
if it were non-existent, it would not be perceived.

Because that which is non-existent cannot be perceived dependently—for a horn does not appear in a man as it does in a cow—it is understood from the impossibility of both sublation and perception [of such a thing] that it is indefinable (anirvācya). Therefore, he says: "Sublation... and so forth.
Because it is impossible for that which exists to be sublated... // MAnu 2.3.44c //
The phrase "implication (arthāpatti) is not accepted" carries over [from the previous context].

It should be understood that by the mention of a single part, everything stated is included. The meaning is that the implication already explained—beginning with "because sublation of an existent thing is impossible"—is not sufficient to establish ineffability (anirvācyatva).
The point is that there is no logical inconsistency in the existence of ether and so forth, nor in the non-existence of the silver in the mother-of-pearl shell and so forth.
Now, it might be argued: "If ether and the like were real, then there would be no sublation (bādha)"; to this he replies: "Because of the absence of sublation."
... for it is precisely because there is no contradiction that the desired conclusion is accepted. ... // MAnu 2.3.44d-e //
This is an undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpādana) based on the fact that there is no sublation of the universe beginning with space; for if it were real, there would be no sublation.
If it is argued that there is indeed sublation in the form of the scriptural negation, "There is no diversity here," we say no.
Because that [objection] has already been refuted previously;
he expresses this very point by means of the word "hi" (for/indeed).
By this, the proof of non-instantaneousness (*akṣepaka*) is also stated:
"The subject of dispute is sublatable because it is perceptible, like an illusion"; since sublation is thus established in the case of space and so forth, he says: "Not... (*na hi*).
For even in the case of an error, no sublation is perceived.
Therefore, the meaning is that the example is deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*).
If one asks, "How so?", it must be stated: (hi ka) [the following].
In that case, when there is sublation, of what is it?
Of the cognition or of the object?
Not the first.

This is because sublation (*bādha*), as defined by the opponent as being "destroyed by the knowledge of the substrate" (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna-nāśyatva*), is absent in that case [of a dream], which is fragile by nature;

otherwise, it would follow that even valid cognition (*pramiti*) would be subject to such sublation. Furthermore, according to the opponent's own doctrine, since consciousness (*jñāna*) acts as the witness (*sākṣin*), its destruction is impossible.
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "of the object."
How could there be sublation of an object? For it is that which exists which is subject to sublation.
The meaning is "not from anywhere. If one asks why not, [the reply is:
what is intended as the object—is it the mother-of-pearl and so forth, or is it the silver and so forth?
He states the reason for the first [point]: "For that which exists... and so forth.
For the son of a barren woman cannot be executed; indeed, it is Yajñadatta who is executed.
“Indeed, not in the case of error”; therefore, by the rule of *maṇḍūkapluti* (leaping over), the word “not” (*na*) is carried over [from the previous verse].
That which exists and continues even after the arising of knowledge corresponding to reality is certainly not sublated.
The sense is that, if that were so, it would follow that the self itself would be sublated.
Regarding the second [position], he states the reason (the logical argument): "For that which exists... and so forth.
Only that which previously existed can be destroyed by something else, but not that which does not exist.
Since illusory silver and the like are non-existent, it is impossible for them to be destroyed; therefore, sublation (*bādha*) directed toward them is all the more untenable.
Regarding the point that non-existence cannot be destroyed, but only that which exists can be, he provides two examples, beginning with "nahi" (for not).
The formal argument here is as follows:
silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is not subject to destruction because it is non-existent;
whatever is non-existent is not subject to destruction, just like the son of a barren woman.
Alternatively, that which is sublatable is not non-existent, just as, for example, Yajñadatta.
This might be argued:

if sublation is not admitted, there would be a contradiction with worldly and Vedic conventions and a fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (apasiddhānta). Therefore, since sublation must be accepted in every respect, it follows—by the analogy of that [Yajñadatta]—that space and so forth cannot be established as existent, because their sublation is impossible. Thus...
He said: "It afflicts."
Where is this pervasion—that what exists is subject to sublation—ever observed?
The word "where" (*kva*) expresses an objection;
this is what is being said: "It is true that we indeed admit sublation (*bādha*)."
However, for that which has been cognized otherwise, there exists the characteristic of being the object of correct cognition;
this indeed exists even in the case of space and so forth, as if in an error,
because that which was cognized in the form of momentariness or the transformation of Brahman is subsequently understood in the form of permanence and so forth.
Since it has already been refuted earlier that [the world] can be destroyed by the knowledge of the true nature of its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-yāthātmya-jñāna*),

proving that would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*). Furthermore, it is not possible for that [knowledge] to negate the existence (*sattva*) of space and the other elements.
This is because the pervasion—that "whatever exists is not sublated"—is not established;
for it is admitted by both parties that even the Self, when known through a form other than its own, falls within the scope of correct cognition.
Nor should it be argued that if presumption (*arthāpatti*) were a separate means of valid knowledge, what need would there be for pervasion?
We do not challenge the absence of pervasion by means of a supporting reason for that which is impossible;
rather, we do so by means of the absence of sublation in the case of existence, or the absence of existence in the case of sublation.
For it is not the case that sublation itself is the impossible object.
However, sublation (bādha) occurs when there is [initial] cognition;

and for one who demonstrates the impossibility of that [cognition] otherwise, it must be stated that either a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga)—to the effect that there would be no sublation if it were non-existent in every respect—or an inference (anumāna)—to the effect that it does not exist because of sublation—must be invoked.
And both of these necessarily depend upon pervasion (vyāpti).

But when there is a contradiction between two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) [is invoked], then the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is clearly a fault.
Now, for what purpose is the ablative case in the phrase "because of the impossibility of sublation" (*bādhāyogāt*)?
It is said: [it serves to indicate the reason].
It is explained as follows: "Where is this pervasion (vyāpti) seen, such that in the inference ‘this which is being sublated is not real because of the impossibility of sublation for what is real’?

Alternatively, if one accepts the sublation favored by us, then [the opponent's claim] that "because of the impossibility of sublation for what is real" and so forth is untenable; thus, the explanation proceeds by the recurrence of the negative particle (nañ).
To the question "Why?", the passage beginning with "pervasion" (vyāpti) should be explained.

Thus, having taken for granted the sublation characterized by destruction, it was stated that sublation is unestablished in the case of nacre-silver and so forth, as well as in the case of ether and so forth.
Now, in order to explain that very point, he asks further regarding the nature of sublation: "What is it? (kaśca).
And what is this "sublation" (bādha) that has been mentioned? ... MAnu 2.3.46c.

Regarding this sublation (*bādha*) which has been pointed out for the purpose of establishing the non-existence of reality in the case of space and so forth, as well as in the case of mother-of-pearl-silver and so forth—what is it?
