Is it destruction by cognition, or is it cessation, or is it the negation of existence across the three times, such that [the object] "was not, is not, and will not be"? This is the sense.
Now, what is the difference between destruction and cessation?
It is said:
some indeed, the proponents of illusion (māyāvādins),
maintain that ignorance together with its manifestations perishes through the knowledge of the true nature of the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna).
"There are as many instances of ignorance as there are cognitions"—
according to this view, it is said that [ignorance] is destroyed.

Others, however, considering that each individual instance of ignorance is merely a specific state of that [consciousness] and serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for silver and so forth, [hold that it is removed] by the knowledge of the reality of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-tattva-jñāna*).
Ignorance, along with its effects, is concealed;
according to that principle, there is cessation.
Alternatively, the destruction of ignorance occurs through knowledge.
The view of others is that the effect, such as silver and so forth, dissolves by itself upon the destruction of its material cause;
this [text] presents two alternatives in accordance with those two views.
Alternatively, it may be according to the view of those who maintain the production of an extraordinary (alaukika) silver, [wherein the effect] perishes.
However, according to the view of the Māyāvādins, it is "cessation" (*nivṛtti*).

Alternatively, "destruction" (*vināśa*) is the view of the Māyāvādins; whereas the view of the Prābhākaras is that for one who has engaged in activity due to the non-apprehension of discrimination, there is "cessation" upon the apprehension of discrimination. *8,550*
He refutes the first [position] with: "No."
...for there can be no destruction of that which is non-existent. MĀn 2.3.46d.
The term "of the non-existent" (*asataḥ*) is an elliptical expression.
By the force of the subsequent experience that "silver appeared as something non-existent," shell-silver is indeed non-existent.
Furthermore, destruction is not possible for that which is non-existent, such as a hare's horn.
For destruction is the cessation of one's own nature;
and that which is non-existent has no nature of its own, because that would involve a contradiction.
Nor is the destruction of ether and so forth possible, because they are eternal.

The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used here to remind us of what was stated previously: that even the destruction of a jar and the like occurs only through the blow of a hammer or similar causes, and not through knowledge of the underlying reality (*adhiṣṭhāna-tattva-jñāna*).
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "and cessation."
And how can the cessation of that which has not yet begun to proceed even be possible?
Indeed, cessation (nivṛtti), which consists of concealment and so forth, must belong to that which possesses activity (pravṛtti) consisting of manifestation and so forth;
and it has been stated that true reality is manifestation,
whereas [things such as] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell are unreal.
Therefore, how could the cessation of that which has never arisen be logically possible?
Alternatively, the cessation by means of knowledge (*vidyā*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects—which have arisen from it—is established in the manner described;
however, illusory silver and the like do not have ignorance as their material cause (*upādāna*).
Because of non-existence;
therefore, how can the cessation of that which has not arisen even be possible?
By this, it should be understood that the lack of proof for sublation (bādhāsiddhi) regarding space and so forth has also been stated.

It should be explained that this is not the definition of sublation (*bādha*), because it lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a person who, having set out toward a shell-silver due to the absence of a desire for silver according to the Prābhākara view, subsequently desists;
thus, [the opponent] restates the third [definition] in order to refute it: "nāsīt" (it was not).
If there were sublation [of that cognition], then the status of being an object of knowledge would not exist for that which "was," "is," or "will be."

The meaning is that "sublation" (*bādha*) consists in being the object of a cognition whose nature is the negation of existence across the three times— namely, the cognition that "that which appeared for such a long time was not, is not, and will not be.

Although it should be stated that such a cognition is sublation, nevertheless, it is described as "the state of being the object of cognition" (*jñānameyatā*) in order to indicate its connection with [the appearance of] silver and so forth.
He refutes this with the words "tadā" (*then*).
... At that time, non-existence was accepted by him for that very reason. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.3.47cd)

If, in this way, you accept that the sublation of space and so forth, as well as of the silver in the mother-of-pearl and so forth, consists in the negation of their existence throughout the three periods of time,
then by that very act of accepting their distinction from the non-existent,
you would have accepted their non-existence once again; for apart from the absence of existence, the non-existence of things such as a rabbit’s horn cannot be defined.
The intention is that, for fear of contradicting one's own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*), this sublation (*bādha*) cannot be accepted by the opponent;
furthermore, it has already been stated that this sublation is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of the ether (*viyat*) and so forth.
[Now, as for] what was said—that because nacre-silver and the like are non-existent, a sublation characterized by destruction and so forth is not possible—[that is incorrect].
Thus, [the following] is established:
that which is under dispute is not non-existent, because it is being perceived;
whatever is perceived is not non-existent, just like a cloth.
Furthermore, that which is non-existent is not perceived, as in the case of a hare’s horn, because its lack of existence has been ascertained by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For this very reason, the objection that—since there is no impossibility regarding non-existence—presumption (*arthāpatti*) must be explained otherwise, is also refuted; for it is precisely the perception itself that is impossible.
As for what was said—that in the negation of existence across the three times, there is the consequence of accepting non-existence—that too is incorrect;
for since non-existence is untenable given that [the object] is perceived, the negation logically results merely in the removal of existence.
Furthermore, as for what was stated here—that "non-existence" is difficult to define apart from the absence of existence—[that is also refuted].
And that is incorrect;
for if it is argued that non-existence consists in being indefinable (*nirupākhyatva*), we say no,
because if there were no cognition of the non-existent, all of this [subsequent discussion] would be impossible.
But this is not the case;
for you, who are refuting the cognition of a non-existent thing, must yourself accept that such cognition exists. With this intention, he says: "Cognition... (pratītiḥ).
By stating that there is no cognition of what is non-existent, he does not admit it [as a real object].
The term "speaking" (*vadan*) is an elliptical expression;
it should also be understood as "knowing" (*jānan*).

To the question, "Since you are negating that there is no cognition of a non-existent thing, on what basis is the cognition of a non-existent thing to be admitted?", he says: "For the negation... (*niṣedho hi*).
For the negation of that which is not perceived is in no way possible.

Regarding the statement "there is no cognition of the non-existent," is it being denied that there is a cognition of the non-existent, or is it the status of the non-existent as an object of cognition that is denied? In the first case, the non-existent must necessarily be admitted as the object of the negation; in the second case, it must necessarily be admitted as the object of the cognition being negated. Thus, in either case, the cognition of the non-existent must be accepted.
Therefore, the negation of a relation belonging to something that has not been cognized in either of the two aforementioned ways is not tenable;
for a negation such as "there is no jar on the ground" is never observed when neither the ground nor the jar is cognized.

By this, the following proof is indicated: the subject under dispute possesses the cognition of a non-existent thing, because he is an agent who negates its relation [to a locus] or because he engages in its conventional usage, just like a consensus case.
Furthermore, that which is authoritative must necessarily be accepted by the investigator.
By stating "acceptance in the mind but denial in speech," this [author] has indicated a contradiction between one's own actions (*svakriyāvirodha*).
Having thus refuted presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), he now refutes comparison (*upamāna*) with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
And there can be no analogy for this... // MAnu 2.3.49a //
In this context, the word "pramāṇam" (the means of valid cognition) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence], meaning:
because that [perception] has a restricted object such as similarity and so forth. This is the intended sense.
"It refutes non-existence by means of perception... and from perception, existence itself [is established]. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.3.49b)

It must be stated that the establishment of an indefinable object follows from the proof of the absence of both existence and non-existence regarding space and so forth, or regarding the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, by means of perception or non-perception;
however, that is not tenable,
because through perception, existence alone is ascertained in the case of space and so forth.
By the word "and" (ca), it is understood that non-existence in cases such as shell-silver is also determined;
the meaning is that perception is contrary [to the claim] and non-apprehension is unestablished.
Having thus stated the refutation of each [means of knowledge] beginning with inference, he states the common refutation: "pratyakṣāt" (from perception).
By means of direct perception, existence alone is determined in the case of space and so forth, whereas non-existence alone is determined in the case of shell-silver and the like;
[thus one knows] "space exists" and "ignorance exists in me."

Since it is impossible to deny the direct perceptual experience (*sākṣātkāri-pratyakṣa*) witnessed by all the world—that "silver appeared as something truly non-existent"—therefore, the inferences and other means of knowledge suspected [of proving] its indeterminability (*anirvācyatā*) have their objects already seized by perception; thus, it is correct to say: "If neither [of the two] exists, then that [silver] is not established.

Alternatively, he states another refutation of the inference such as "the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is false because it is a difference": "[It is countered by] perception," and so forth.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is determined.

Therefore, the meaning is that the inference establishing the falsity of the difference between the individual soul and the Lord and so forth is "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), because it contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
One might object as follows:
First of all, Īśvara is not established by direct perception, because it is accepted that he has scripture as his source. Nor are all individual souls [established by perception].

Because it is not admitted that the self of another is directly perceived by oneself, and because the distinction between objects that are not directly perceived cannot be established through perception—let alone their reality—it says: "By scripture" (śāstra).
A distinction between one's own self and the Supreme Lord, who is accessible through the scriptures, is perceived.
"It is perceived by direct perception"—this is the ellipsis.
It has already been stated that a single difference does not subsist by being distributed across multiple loci, but rather has one thing as its counter-positive and another property as its locus.
And for the perception of that [difference], the perceptibility of the locus itself is required.
However, there is merely the cognition of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*),
as is observed in the world.

In that regard, although it is impossible to know through perception the difference whose locus is the Self because the Lord and other Selves are not perceptible, the difference whose locus is one's own Self has the Supreme Lord as its counter-correlate.
It can indeed be known through direct perception,
because one's own self is perceptible and the Supreme Lord is understood through scripture.

However, one who does not know the Lord through scripture should not be deluded by that [objection], namely, that there is a difference of his own self from Him as its counter-correlative. For it is only for one who has known the Lord through scripture that perception is stated to be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the difference of his own self from Him. Nevertheless, how can the inference be considered "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), given that the superiority of the perception apprehending difference has not been established? To this, he says: "anubhūti... (*8.559*).

Even so, how can the inference be said to be "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), given that the superiority of the perception apprehending difference has not been established? To this, he says: "anubhūti... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.3.50ab]: "How can unity be asserted in contradiction to direct experience?"
Here, by the word "experience" (anubhūti), the witness (sākṣin) is understood.
It is said that [the object] is inferred;
for since the application of inference for the sake of others consists of speech, it is stated that "[it] is spoken."
Alternatively, the word "by inference" (*anumānena*) is to be supplied [to the text].
What is meant is this:
it is indeed accepted that the direct perception of the witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*) grasps the distinction between the individual self (*svātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).
And that [scriptural testimony] is indeed more powerful than inference,

because it is the basis upon which inference depends, as it apprehends both the nature and the validity of that [scripture], as well as the individual soul (*jīva*) who is the subject of the proposition.
Therefore, due to this contradiction, the identity of the individual soul and Brahman cannot be inferred.

Granted that direct perception by a witness is stronger than inference; however, how is it certain that this [perception] grasps a difference between the Lord and one's own self, such that inference would have its object sublated? To this, he says: "Something...":
"And everyone experiences that there is a doer of some [action] who is subject to suffering. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.50cd)
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is heard of as being omniscient and possessed of all powers.
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); "possessing little knowledge" and "possessing little power" are also to be understood from the first half [of the verse].
Likewise, "the creator of all" and "free from suffering" are to be understood from the second half.
The ellipsis is "is experienced as one's own self.
It has been heard [in scripture]: "He who is omniscient," and "His power is supreme."
The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: [he is mentioned] in such passages as "for he is the creator of all" and "without organs."

This is the underlying intention: for it is a matter witnessed by all that whoever, having apprehended a certain object, perceives through direct perception (pratyakṣa) something possessing a property contradictory to it, necessarily sees the difference of that [latter] from the former through direct perception.
Although difference is established by perception, there is no fault in this, because the observation of the counter-positive’s dissimilarity (vaidharmya) acts as an auxiliary to that perception.
For it is observed that the knowledge of scriptural definitions serves as an auxiliary in the direct realization of the true nature of a gem.

Likewise here, a person who has understood through scripture that the Lord possesses attributes such as omniscience, while experiencing himself—by means of the witness-consciousness (sākṣin)—as possessing contrary attributes such as limited knowledge, how could he [fail to realize] his difference from Him?
Regarding the phrase "one should not perceive [it directly]":
let it be granted that for a single individual soul (*jīva*), its difference from the Lord (*īśvara*) is established by direct perception (*sākṣisiddha*).
Nevertheless, when one infers the non-difference of the Lord elsewhere while setting that aside, there is no sublation by perception; therefore, it is said: "by all indeed."
The sense is that even in the absence of contradiction by one specific perception, contradiction by this or that particular perception is difficult to avoid.

Now, it might be argued: "This contradiction with perception would occur if one were to take the individual soul (*jīva*) as the subject (*pakṣa*) and attempt to prove its non-difference from the Lord (*īśvara*);
however, it is not in this manner that the inference is formulated."
However, since [the opponent] takes God as the subject and asserts non-difference from the individual soul (jīva), he says: "Because of the [scriptural statement] 'from the experienced... etc.
For this Vedic revelation speaks of him as distinct from that which has been experienced.

For one who makes Īśvara the subject of proof, his existence must necessarily be stated; and since he is not established by perception or other means of knowledge, scripture alone must be accepted as the apprehender of him. And this [scripture], being the means of valid cognition for the substratum (*dharmin*), states: "He who is omniscient."
The Vedic scripture beginning with "Truth" (satya) declares that the Lord is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), which is perceived as having limited knowledge and other such attributes.

Therefore, even in the absence of a contradiction by perception, the fallacy of *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (proving what has already been refuted) remains unavoidable due to the contradiction with the foundational scripture.

Since the scripture establishes the nature of the Lord as possessing omniscience and other such qualities against the nature of the individual soul—which is always understood to possess limited knowledge and so forth—it thereby establishes that the two are indeed distinct.
Because experience cannot be denied,

this very point also refutes the inclusion of both positions [as being equally valid], since they are sublated by the direct perception and scriptural authority upon which [the other] depends. *8,561*
Having thus refuted inference, he now refutes such scriptural passages as "He who I am... and so forth, with the words: "upajīvya" (being dependent).
But how could the Śruti teach identity, which is contrary to what must be relied upon for subsistence?
The word "tu" (but/however) serves to indicate a distinction;
for a faulty inference indeed becomes nothing other than a mere semblance of an argument (*apramāṇa*).
Regarding the scripture, however, there is merely a displacement of the literal meaning [to a figurative one],
namely, the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara).

For if the scripture, having referred back to the individual soul, were to teach its identity with the Lord, then it would have to depend upon the witness-consciousness (sākṣipratyakṣa), which perceives the individual soul.
And since that [scriptural passage] has been stated to apprehend difference, there is a contradiction with what is presupposed (*upajīvyavirodha*).

If, by way of restating the Lord (*īśvara*), His non-difference from the individual soul (*jīva*) were being enjoined, then another scriptural passage such as "He who is omniscient" would itself have to be presupposed;
and since that too has been stated to apprehend difference, there is indeed a contradiction with what is presupposed.

Furthermore, if non-difference alone were to be understood by way of a reference to both [the individual and the universal], then both would have to be depended upon; thus, a contradiction with the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that is depended upon is quite evident.
Although all of this was already stated in the very first sūtra, there is no fault in beginning it again for the sake of further elaboration.

Now, what is the determining factor in the principle that "the dependent is sublated by that which it depends upon," by virtue of which it was stated that inference and scripture lack authority due to their contradiction with perception and scripture?
It is said in reply:
For in this case, regarding both [cognitions] concerning difference and non-difference—which stand in the relation of the dependent and the basis—either both are valid or both are invalid;
or one is valid while the other is invalid.
Even in that latter case, either the dependent is valid and the basis is invalid, or vice versa.
The following positions are possible: that the dependent [cognition] possesses validity while the dependent-upon [the source] lacks validity.
Among these, the first is not tenable, because it is impossible for two contradictory [cognitions] to possess validity simultaneously.
Alternatively, [the object] cannot be established, because it would result in the object having two natures;
furthermore, it would entail the impossibility of establishing the distinction between error and sublation. Nor can its establishment occur through both difference and non-difference.
Because it is about to be refuted,
and because it is not universal;
nor can one find deliverance through the doctrine of non-ascertainment.
This is because a restrictive qualification is impossible for both [positions].

Nor is the second [position] tenable, as it would entail that the entity lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). Furthermore, one cannot achieve a resolution by accepting its ineffability (*anirvācyatā*).

Without refuting the two positions—that [the Veda] could originate from Brahmā as well—because they are too obvious in their defects, he refutes the third [position] with the words: "aprāmāṇyam" (lack of authority).
When the word denoting difference shall become invalid, [then there will be non-duality].
Since that very [cognition] is the grasper of the substratum, how could there be non-difference from it?
The phrase "of the scripture that expresses difference" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*);
it should also be understood as referring to "the perception that grasps difference.
This is because [this point] has already been explained in the commentary on the verse "in that case, it is that very same [thing]."
[This refers to] the subjects (dharmiṇaḥ), namely the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara).
The word "iti" is to be supplied [at the end]. The ellipsis is: "how are they to be understood? (kathaṃ bodhyaḥ).
This is what is meant:

if the perception or the scriptural statement that apprehends the individual soul (jīva) as characterized by ignorance and so forth, or the Supreme Self (paramātman) as characterized by omniscience and so forth, were to lack authority, then,

since the individual soul and the Lord would remain unestablished, there could be no communication of their non-difference through such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (tattvam asi) or through inferences.
Because it lacks an object;
and thus, due to the contradiction of what [object], would there be invalidity of perception and the other means of knowledge?
Furthermore, this matter is informative (jñāpaka), not productive (kāraka).

Even the communication of an indivisible meaning (akhaṇḍārtha) has been accepted by the opponent as occurring through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) after following the logic of ordinary worldly sentences;
it is not established in this manner [directly],
because a non-worldly mode of operation is not a constituent factor for cognition.

Therefore, since it is impossible for that which is depended upon (the upajīvya) to be invalid due to a contradiction with that which depends on it (the upajīvaka), it follows by process of elimination that only the fourth type [of contradiction] is established. It would indeed be the case that the depended-upon is stronger than that which depends on it, and in the event of a contradiction between them, the dependent is invalid. What, then, is the specific distinction in this case?
For the relationship between the supported and the supporter is of many kinds:
in some cases it is by way of being the grasper of the locus (*dharmin*),
and in other cases by way of being the grasper of the probandum (*sādhya*).
In some cases by virtue of being employed for the apprehension of that [object], in others by the apprehension of its own nature,
and in some instances by the establishment of its validity.
In some cases, it is by way of establishing a constituent member such as pervasion (*vyāpti*).

In all such instances, that which depends [on another] (*upajīvaka*) is necessarily sublated by that upon which it depends (*upajīvya*), because that which lacks a locus (*āśraya*) and so forth would result in the impossibility of its arising.
Furthermore, where that which is to be depended upon (the upajīvya) by the negator (the pratiṣedhaka) is itself the provider of the object to be negated (the pratiṣedhya),
then this principle does not apply;
nor can the thing depended upon be sublated by that which depends upon it.
Since that [inference] depends upon those two [perception and scripture], it serves only for the purpose of negation;
for it is observed that the cognition "this is silver" is sublated by the cognition "this is not silver.

Therefore, in this case as well, what was said—that the inference and scripture regarding non-difference lack authority because they are contradicted by perception and scripture which they depend upon—is incorrect.

Since perception and scripture are the bases upon which inference and scripture depend for their capacity to provide the objects to be negated, a negation of difference cannot possibly occur without them. Therefore, it is appropriate that the invalidity belongs precisely to those bases—perception and scripture—which contradict the dependent [inference and scripture]. Consequently, he first refutes the invalidity of the scripture beginning with "He who is omniscient" by stating: "Invalidity..."
[This refers to] the scripture that expresses distinctions and establishes the Supreme Self as qualified by attributes such as omniscience.
What is meant is this:
indeed, the lack of authority of a scripture stating "He who is omniscient," etc., must be accepted only when contradicted by an inference or scripture that possesses a [valid] basis of origin.
If this [scripture] were not authoritative, the very emergence of inference and other means of knowledge would be difficult to achieve;
let alone their sublation,
for the subject (dharmin) characterized as the supreme self is cognizable solely through that [scripture].
[Objection: Since inference and the like lack a basis, their operation is untenable.
[Response: But in that case, would not the invalidity of the cognition "this is silver" fail to occur due to its contradiction by the cognition "this is not silver"?
[Reply: It would not fail to occur.

For the cognition "this is not silver" does not arise by taking an object qualified as silver as its substratum (dharmin), but rather [it arises] with respect to the mere thing-in-itself (svarūpamātra).
For indeed, everything...

"Knowledge is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the substratum (*dharmin*), but it is erroneous regarding the specific mode (*prakāra*). [This is] the statement from the *Vārtikasāra* in Sāyaṇa’s commentary on the *Śikṣā*: "Proponents maintain that all knowledge is non-erroneous with respect to the substratum; however, they declare it to be erroneous with respect to the mode, such as [the appearance of] silver and so forth."

In this regard also, in the third chapter, fourth section [of the *Ślokavārttika*], it is said: “Likewise others have stated that all cognition is valid with respect to the substratum (*dharmin*), but there is error regarding the qualifier (*prakāra*). Thus, even here, the cognition “this is silver” is valid with respect to the “this-portion” (*idamaṃśa*). Consequently, since the sublating cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*) operates by relying on this very form of the “this,” its contradiction with the silver-portion renders the invalidity of the prior cognition entirely appropriate.

Indeed, by this very reasoning, one might argue that the scripture stating "He who is omniscient," etc., can be shown to lack authority due to its contradiction with the inference of non-difference and other scriptures.

This scripture also serves as a means of valid knowledge regarding the mere nature of Brahman; therefore, depending solely upon that [nature], the inference and other scriptures will be rendered non-authoritative regarding the aspect of being qualified by distinct attributes such as omniscience.
And thus, there is no contradiction of the inference and so forth by that which apprehends the subject (*dharmī*).
And since that which is contradictory is not a means of valid cognition regarding that subject (dharmin), he says: "That which... [yad iti].
That which is the means of valid cognition for grasping the essential nature [of a thing], how could it not also apply to its properties?
If that verbal testimony is accepted as a means of valid cognition for the purpose of apprehending the nature of Brahman,
how could it not be a means of valid cognition regarding its attributes, such as its specific qualities like omniscience?
This is the underlying intention.

It is indeed logical that the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is valid with respect to the "this" aspect (idamaṃśa), but invalid with respect to the aspect of its qualification as silver (rajatavaiśiṣṭyāṃśa);
for the latter aspect is contradicted by a subverting cognition (bādhakapramāṇa),
whereas the form of "this" persists even subsequently.
The subverting cognition that arises is "This is not silver," and not "This is not silver, and [it is] not [silver]";
nor is this the correct principle here,
because there is no subversion regarding the qualified aspect either, just as there is none regarding the essential nature itself.

Nor do inference of non-difference and scripture constitute sublaters [of the distinction between the individual soul and Brahman], because they involve mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). For, inference and the like can be sublaters only when scripture lacks authority due to being sublated; yet scripture, which contradicts that inference, lacks authority only when the inference and the like—being free from contradiction with their own basis—are established as sublaters. Thus, there is a circularity.
And how could inference and the like subvert the Veda?
Not merely by virtue of being contradictory, for it would be equally easy to argue the reverse.
Nor can it be [sublated] by being a subsequent cognition that contradicts it, because we observe the cognition "this is silver" following immediately after the cognition "this is a shell-silver.
Nor can it be argued that a contradictory cognition which is not itself followed by another is sublatory, while this one is followed by another;
for sometimes even a cognition of silver may occur without being followed by any subsequent cognition.
However, an answer that has been examined to the best of one's ability sublates a preceding one that has not been examined, provided it is contradictory;
but this is not the case here.
Not only is this distinction unjustified due to the equality of the absence of a sublater, but why else? To this he says: "Of one... (*eketi*).
Through the cognition and representation of a single [object], duality will become non-measurement;
if that one is not non-measurement, then even that duality would not exist here.
This cognition—generated by such scriptural revelation as "He who is omniscient," and so forth—is indeed of a single nature;
it is not manifold like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, which is a valid means of knowledge regarding the thing's own nature alone but invalid regarding its specific form.
Thus, through the manifestation of direct perception aided by investigation, this pair of cognitions, containing both the attribute and the substratum, [is established] in their specific forms.
Cognition indeed occurs even with respect to [the object] itself;
and this point will be explained in detail later.
Alternatively, it should be applied thus: "the two" refers to the two cognitions, which exist in the property (dharma) just as they do in its own nature (svarūpa).

Alternatively, what is the intention of one who asserts that the scriptural passage beginning with "He who is omniscient" has authority only regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman, while its lack of authority concerns the qualified form such as omniscience?
Does he mean that this is a single cognition which, like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, is both valid and invalid depending on the difference in its objects?
Or does he mean that there are two cognitions here, one of which is valid and the other invalid?
He refutes the first [position] with the words "yad" (that which).
The intention is indeed the same as before.

He refutes the second [position] with the word "one" (*eka*); the remainder of the sense is that since this consciousness is only one, as established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣivijñapti*), its manifoldness should not be imagined.
Otherwise, even in cases such as "this is a pillar," there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate two distinct cognitions;
and if that were so, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) could not be known by anyone.
Or, let us grant that these are indeed two cognitions, yet it cannot be maintained that one of them is invalid.
He says "the two" because, just as the knowledge of the essential nature [of things], the knowledge of their properties is also uncontradicted.
The meaning is that both types of knowledge [are included].
Although one could have said "the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) as well," the use of the word "both" is intended to indicate the equality of the underlying principle.

Thus, even though there is a similarity in being examined for the absence of sublation, he states an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) against one who, while accepting two cognitions—one based on scripture and the other otherwise—asserts partial validity and invalidity; this is expressed in the words "If not... (na cet).

If that scriptural knowledge were not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its specific dual aspect, then it would likewise not be a valid means of cognition even with respect to the aspect of its own nature (*svarūpa-aṃśa*) in this context,
because there is no distinction between them.
And thus, inference and scripture, being without a basis, would simply fail to arise.
Alternatively, if that cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to one specific aspect regarding this object, then it would not be so with respect to both;
it would likewise not be a valid means of knowledge even with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*), just like the specific aspect,
because there is no distinction between them— this is the sense.

In the doctrine that accepts two cognitions (*jñānadvayāṅgīkāravāda*), if the cognition whose object is qualified by that [object] is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within those two cognitions, then even the two cognitions themselves would not be means of valid cognition.
For, like the cognition of the qualified object, the cognition of its own nature (*svarūpajñāna*) would also be invalid, as there is no distinction between them.

Thus, it has been refuted that the scriptural testimony "he who is omniscient" serves as a basis for the inference of non-difference (*abheda*) and for the scriptures, acting as the provider of the object to be negated.
Nevertheless, there is no contradiction with the foundational means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for inference (*anumāna*) and scripture (*āgama*),
because [inference] proceeds by relying solely on the nature of Brahman established by such scriptural texts as "He who is omniscient.
For there is no restrictive rule that one must proceed by means of inference and so forth by taking hold of a specific form qualified by omniscience and the like.

Then, [the author] offers a conclusion while dispelling the following doubt: "Since a contradictory form is useless and cannot be relied upon, and since the mere nature of that which is relied upon is not contradictory, there is no contradiction with the evidence (pramāṇa) that is relied upon;
however, there might still be some contradiction with the evidence for inference and so forth. He concludes with the words: "The subject (dharmī)..."
Therefore, the contradiction with the apprehension of the subject is a refutation of that means of knowledge.
The word "tu" (but) serves to specify;
it excludes [the objection] on the grounds of contradiction with the mere means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). There is a contradiction with the scripture that apprehends the subject (dharmin).
"Of the non-difference-cognition" refers to that which takes the form of inference and scripture.
This is the intended meaning:
it must be explained how there is a contradiction with the foundational [evidence] for such inferences as "atoms possess parts" and for such scriptural statements.
It might be argued that it is possible to say that what is not depended upon is not the uselessness of atomhood (*paramāṇutva*), but rather its mere essential nature (*svarūpamātra*).
However, this is not tenable;
for without [the properties] such as partlessness (*niravayavatva*) and so forth, it is impossible to establish the atom as the subject (*dharmin*) of a proposition.
If it is argued that making [the subject] a locus characterized solely by its own essential nature (svarūpa) would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhārthatā),
this applies equally to the present case as well;
for even Brahman cannot be made a locus without [attributes] such as omniscience.
If one takes as the subject (dharmin) that which possesses only its own essential nature (svarūpa), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).
What fault is there in taking as the subject that which is distinguished by superimposed [qualities] such as omniscience?
If you say, "It would be like saying, 'This post is a person,'" we say no.
If it is argued that because [the subject] is excluded by the superimposed [property] such as partlessness, it is possible to take that very thing as the subject even there,
and thus the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which apprehends partlessness and so forth is determined to be [valid],
whereas the superimposed [property] is not; [we reply:]...
The same applies here as well,
because the authority of scripture is also established through certainty.
Thus, just as the subject is qualified by properties such as partlessness which are established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so it is here too.

Since the subject (*dharmin*) itself is being qualified by ultimate non-duality and so forth, the contradiction with the means of cognition that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇavirodha*) is difficult to avoid.
It might be argued:

"Just as inference and scripture—which are two means of valid knowledge for non-difference—cannot establish non-difference due to a contradiction with their own basis (*upajīvyavirodha*), so too the cited scriptural passage on difference, such as 'He is different and inconceivable,' cannot [establish difference] because of a contradiction with its own basis."
The capacity to establish difference is possible;
for what is called "difference" is indeed a negation whose counter-correlate is identity (*tādātmya*).

Now, it is not logical to communicate the negation of identity when that identity has not been established. Therefore, how can the scriptural text on difference—which functions by depending upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes non-difference—not be in contradiction with that which it depends upon?
Furthermore, based on its undifferentiated essential nature (*svarūpa*), its differentiation must be made known; and if that is so, how is there no contradiction with that which is to be relied upon?
As it has been said: "A cognition that does not delineate non-difference is incapable of delineating difference."
"Thus, in the first case there would be valid cognition, but not in the latter, because of the contradiction with its own dependence";
to this he says: "No.
For here, non-difference is not that which must be relied upon, because in some instances there is the force of scriptural statements regarding difference. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.3.55cd)
The word "hi" indicates the underlying reasoning;
"non-difference" refers to that which apprehends it;
and "herein" (atra) refers to in some cases.
The meaning is "in the case of being the subject (dharmin), etc. This is the sense:
for the scripture concerning difference does not, first of all, depend upon the cognition of non-difference by way of presenting the subject.
This is because only the nature of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) possesses the status of being the subject (dharmin);
nor is it established by the apprehension of the validity of its own nature,
since that is already established by perception alone.
Therefore, it must be stated that [the injunction] functions solely as the means for establishing what is to be prohibited.
Furthermore, its contradiction with that [prohibition] does not entail a loss of authority,
for that would lead to the undesirable consequence of rejecting the prohibitory scriptures themselves.

Furthermore, this is not a negation of that which is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); rather, it is a negation of that which is [erroneously] established through a failure to understand the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

As for the claim that difference is to be understood by taking the undivided essential nature (*svarūpa*) as the basis, even there, one cannot resort to the non-difference of those two things whose difference is to be made known.
However, taking as the subject (*dharmin*) an entity that possesses internal difference, its ultimate difference is understood.

Therefore, since the scriptural texts concerning the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) do not depend upon that [non-dual] non-difference, they possess authority characterized by independence; thus, their capacity to establish difference is established—this is the remainder of the argument.
Furthermore, let alone the dependence of scriptural passages such as "He who is omniscient" [on other means of knowledge].
Nevertheless, it would indeed constitute a sublation of the inference of non-difference and of scripture;
for this Śruti, while establishing the Lord as qualified by omniscience and other attributes, requires nothing else,
whereas inference and scripture are dependent [on other factors].
And because that which is independent is stronger than that which is dependent, he says—with this intention—"For [the latter] is not to be depended upon."
In this context, between the two means of knowledge regarding difference and non-difference:
"from the scripture of difference" refers to the scripture concerning a substratum qualified by a differentiating attribute;
"non-difference" refers to the means of knowledge for non-difference.
This is an indication of independence;
therefore, the implication is that it possesses the power to invalidate the means of valid cognition for non-difference.
This might be so.

The scriptural passage beginning with "He who is omniscient" and so forth does not establish Brahman as qualified by attributes that differentiate it from the individual soul (jīva); rather, it merely restates what is already known.
Therefore, there is no sublation of that [Brahman] by inference and other means; to this, he says: "And not... (na ca).
And Brahman is never, at any time, an object to be attained through other means of knowledge.
The goal (*upeya*) is that which is to be known.
The word "that" (*tat*) indicates that it is endowed with omniscience and other such qualities;
by saying "in some cases," it suggests that [the goal] is not even something apprehended through error.
To begin with, Brahman, characterized by omniscience and other such attributes, is not accessible through any means of valid cognition other than scripture (*śruti*),
because it has been established that its sole source is the scripture.
Nor is it apprehended through error (*bhrānti*).
Because in some cases there is a superimposition of that which has already been cognized elsewhere,
and because it is impossible for there to be a restatement of what has not been attained through either a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or through error (*bhrānti*),
this scriptural passage is not merely reiterative (*anuvādinī*).
What indeed does it establish as being of the aforementioned nature, namely Brahman?

But even so, there is no contradiction with the means of valid cognition upon which [inference] depends, such as inference and the like; for that contradiction would arise only if [inference] were dependent upon Śruti.
But this is not the case, because [the cognition] depends upon a means of valid cognition distinct from that [object]; therefore, he says: "And not... (na ca).

Fire, though separated by its object and unperceivable through perception and other means in a place where there is no smoke, is nevertheless apprehended in some location through either perception or inference.
Likewise, gravity, though inaccessible prior to the occurrence of a fall, is apprehended at a certain time through inference.
But Brahman is not in this way to be attained by any other means of knowledge in any instance.
By means of which there could be the operation of inference and other means of knowledge dependent upon it. Or, let Brahman be cognizable through another means of valid cognition;
even so, the contradiction with the foundational means of cognition for the inference of non-difference and the like is difficult to avoid.
Intending to show that this [scripture] also possesses the capacity to convey difference, just like the Veda, he says: "By which..."
By that very pride through which this bow is broken, it is understood.
The remainder [of the sentence] is "Brahman is the goal to be attained.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Omniscient," etc.
If the Lord is somehow to be understood as consisting of all-knowledge,
then his distinction [from others] is perceived precisely through that quality of omniscience.
Dharma and so forth are perceived by someone because they are objects of cognition (*prameya*), like a jar; this is an inference that establishes an omniscient being.
Furthermore, this serves as an illustration for other inferences, such as [the one establishing] the existence of an omnipotent creator.
The word "thus" (eva) excludes direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The phrase "in any way whatsoever" (*kathañcana*) indicates that this is a statement of formal admission (*abhyupagamavāda*).
The term "omniscience" (*sarvajñatva*) is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The syntactical connection is "by that very [means].
First of all, perception cannot even be suspected to apply to the Lord;
therefore, only inference must be stated.
For even that [object] which has been refuted by a counter-argument and the like remains in some way subject to doubt;
moreover, inference establishes only something qualified by a particular attribute,
but not the thing in its abstracted essence.
Furthermore, the Lord (Īśvara) is not established merely by the establishment of an object qualified by attributes common to living beings and the like;
therefore, its establishment must proceed precisely through the qualification by distinguishing attributes.
And thus, the contradiction with the foundational basis of inference and other means of knowledge becomes as indelible as "vajralepa" (adamantine cement).

Although inference is inherently weaker than scripture (*śruti*), it nonetheless functions as a sublater (*bādhaka*) by virtue of being its very basis (*upajīvyatayā*). Thus, by this [argument], the validity of scripture—which apprehends the Lord (*īśvara*)—with respect to Him as characterized by distinguishing attributes has been established.
Now, [the author proceeds] to [address] the perception (*pratyakṣa*) which apprehends the individual soul (*jīva*) as distinct from the Lord...
Validity is established with respect to the subject, the living being (*jīva*). For instance:
let the scripture be a means of valid cognition regarding God (*īśvara*) as possessing the qualities of being free from suffering, omniscience, and so forth.
Nevertheless, there is no invalidation of the inference and scripture regarding non-difference by contradiction with a foundational means of knowledge (*upajīvyapramāṇa*).
For that would be the case only if the suffering and so forth of the individual soul were real;
but this is not so, because the experience "I am suffering" and the like is a false experience.

For an evil such as suffering, which resides within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is false by its very nature; it merely shines forth in consciousness (*caitanya*) like the redness of a hibiscus flower in a crystal.
And a real entity is not divided by a differentiator apprehended through error; therefore, he says: "No."
Nowhere does the experience of suffering ever become a false experience.
"Anywhere" (kvāpi) means "in every way" (sarvathā). This might be so if the experience "I am suffering," and so forth, were a false experience; but it is not so.
Rather, it is indeed a valid means of knowledge;
for although suffering and so forth reside within the internal organ,
they nevertheless exist as real by their very nature.
And because the individual self (jīvātman) is the enjoyer of that [result], its possession of those qualities is indeed real.
The intention is that attributes such as limited power and dependence belong to its very nature.
To the question "Why?", he says: "For not... (*na hi*).
For no sublation is ever observed in the case of the experience of suffering and so forth.
The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis, and is to be connected with the phrase "not at all.
The term "in some cases" (*kvacit*) is stated to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding those instances where delusion has not yet been sublated.

Indeed, no one ever says, "I am not suffering," [thinking] that the self is not suffering, but rather that it considers itself to be suffering solely due to a false suffering residing in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
The meaning is that [the self] is seen to possess a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*).

Now, one might object: since scriptural passages such as “He who is already liberated is being liberated” and “That thou art” serve as subverters of this experience, how is it that the experience of suffering is not an illusion?
For here it is established that the true nature of this self is indeed free from afflictions such as suffering; therefore, he says: "If..."
If it is determined that the experience of suffering is an illusion,
by what means is it understood that the scriptural teaching on being free from suffering is not an illusion?
"It is determined by relying on scripture"—this is the ellipsis.
For what reason?
Because error exists both in terms of its own nature and in terms of its object.
"It is understood" means it is accepted;
the phrase "relying upon experience" is to be supplied as the remainder.
This is what is being stated:
This scripture would be a sublater of this experience if it were established as having the status of a valid means of knowledge;
but it is not so.

This is because we establish its lack of authority on the grounds that it contradicts the experience that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*), and because the opponent remains even now occupied with attempting to avoid that [contradiction].

Such being the case, there would follow the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*): the certainty of the authority of scripture would depend upon the illusory nature of the experience, and that [certainty] would depend upon the certainty of the authority of scripture.
[Objection: But surely this is the same even when one asserts the lack of authority of the Śruti on the grounds of contradiction with experience.
[Reply: It is not the same;
for experience is independent, whereas the Śruti is dependent upon it.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the contradiction with the grasper of the subject (*dharmigrāhakavirodha*) would be eliminated in all cases.
[Objection: In that case, it would be improper for the cognition "this is not silver" to be a sublater (*bādhaka*) of the cognition "this is silver. [Response: It would not be improper.
This is because the validity of the cognition "this is not silver" has been ascertained through the examination of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*),
whereas that is absent for the cognition "this is silver.
For it is accepted that a dependent [cognition] whose validity has been examined sublates its basis when that basis is not of such a nature.
For the principle of the dependent and the dependant applies to cases other than that;
indeed, it is when there is doubt regarding validity that one resorts to reasoning— once validity is ascertained, what is the use of this?
And the Teacher will say this:

"In that case, since the validity of the Śruti is also ascertained by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) aided by investigation, its status as a sublater of [ordinary] experience is established. With this intention, he raises the objection with the words "śrutī" (*8,588*). "In that case, since the validity of the Śruti is also ascertained by the witness-consciousness aided by investigation, its status as a sublater of [ordinary] experience is established"—with this intention, he raises the objection with the words "śrutī" (*8,589*).
The nature of the Veda and its meaning are determined by means of valid cognition alone.
Validity (*prāmāṇya*) itself has been stated through a distinction in intended meaning as being both the nature of the text (*svarūpa*) and its object (*artha*).

This is because, for this scripture which establishes the soul’s identity with Brahman who is free from suffering, there is no difference in the result between the nature of the scripture and its object;
indeed, this very [identity] constitutes its validity as well.
He refutes this by means of the witness "pride" (māna), stating: "If that... and so forth.
If that pride has been grasped by you, why this delusion regarding the experience of suffering?
The indeclinable *ta* is used in the sense of the instrumental case;
or, one may supply the words "they are thought" (*mata*).
What? For what reason?
"The delusion regarding the experience of suffering" means that the experience of suffering itself is a delusion;
"is accepted" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Or rather, why is it accepted that there is an error regarding the experience of suffering, even though that witness is a means of valid cognition?
This is what is meant:
it cannot be maintained by an opponent that the authority of the Śruti has been ascertained by the witness.

If that were the case, it would follow that its validity must be admitted. If you say, "That is indeed accepted," then since that very [cognition] would also have suffering and so forth as its object— such as "I am suffering"— its validity alone would have to be accepted there as well, and not its status as an error.
"If it is argued that there would be no error even in the apprehension of the authority of the Veda [the author replies]:
But surely, if there is authority in one instance, there must be authority in other objects as well; and if there is non-authority there, there must be non-authority elsewhere too—how can this be so?
Let it not be that such a rule applies only to a single sense organ like the eye. To this he says: "And not... (na cet).
And there is no specific sublation such that only that which is unsublated [is authoritative].
Even for a single [scripture], there may be validity in some instances and invalidity in others due to a specific cause;
and that [cause] consists of a defect in its production or a sublation in its cognition.
Even a defect (doṣa) is to be inferred solely from sublation (bādha),
as it has been said:
"Defects are to be known through a stronger means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and not otherwise."
Therefore, sublation (*bādha*) alone is the distinguishing factor.
And there is no such distinguishing feature in the form of sublation regarding the direct experience of the witness (*sākṣin*) concerning objects such as suffering;
by virtue of which that [experience], though being a means of valid knowledge regarding the authority of scripture, would constitute an error with respect to suffering and so forth.

Since it is so, therefore, just like the authority of the Vedas (*śrutiprāmāṇya*), that suffering and so forth of the self must also be accepted as true and indeed uncontradicted. Or rather, since it is so, why [should one say] that the experience of suffering is an illusion? [This is what was stated] by the previous [argument].
There is no connection. [Objection:

But surely this authority of the scripture and [the existence of] suffering and so forth are both apprehended by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) itself. [Response: And it is not logical for the witness-consciousness to possess authority with respect to both.
Because they are mutually contradictory,
since it is necessary that one of them lacks authority, it must be understood that this lack of authority resides in [the Smṛti] regarding suffering and so forth;
for the authority of Śruti has been grasped through an investigation of its non-human origin and other such qualities.
If it is argued that, for this reason, suffering and so forth are merely false, we say no;
because even regarding suffering and the like, there exists an examination in the form of corroboration by similar and dissimilar instances.

If that is the case, then since there is doubt, it is not logical for you to claim a certainty regarding the reality of suffering and so on; thus, it cannot be said that the Śruti is sublated by experience. To this, he says: "It is indeed uncontradicted."
This is the intended meaning for one who determines that "that suffering is indeed real":
it is true;
the authority of the scripture and the existence of suffering and so forth are indeed apprehended by direct perception.
And since there is no sublation even in the case of one [of these two], both are valid means of knowledge, with the Witness as their witness;
nor is there any contradiction,
because the validity of the Śruti is possible even without the existence of non-duality.

For arguments such as the lack of human authorship do not assist in determining the certainty of validity restricted to a specific object; rather, they assist in the determination of validity in general.
Objections and the like have indeed been addressed here and there;
however, without the existence of suffering, the validity [of the scripture] in that regard would be impossible.
Nor is there any contradiction with the mere validity of the Śruti by the existence of suffering.
Since that [cognition] can occur even with respect to other objects,
it follows that suffering and so forth are indeed real; thus,
scripture does not subvert direct experience.

However, it has been stated that [the cognition of the Veda] is sublated by experience alone, which is powerful because it apprehends the subject (*dharmin*). The intention is that the power of this experience does not consist solely in its apprehending the subject, but also in its apprehending the validity of the very nature of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*); with this in mind, he says: "The Veda... (*śruti*...).
"Artha" means "possessing a purpose," which is to say, "validity.
For a sacred text (*śruti*), having been ascertained both in its own form and in its validity, must be employed for the accomplishment of the intended goal, and not otherwise.
The form of the sacred text and its validity are ascertained by the very means of knowledge characterized as the witness (*sākṣin*), and not by any other.

Although the nature of the Veda is perceivable by the sense of hearing, nevertheless, as long as its validity—produced by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) arising from that hearing—is not grasped by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), it is not established; therefore, even the determination of the nature of the Veda depends solely upon the witness-consciousness.
Or rather, by the word "Veda" (*śruti*)...
The cognition produced by that [means] is not what is being discussed here. Regarding this, we ask:
do you also accept the validity of that witness or not?

In the case of the position "no," since the very nature of the scripture and so forth would be unestablished, it is not proper to claim that the experience of suffering and the like is an error on account of its contradiction with that [scripture].
He refutes the first [position] with the words: "If that... (tacced iti).
If that very nature of the witness has been grasped by you as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then how could the experience of suffering not be an illusion?
It is in no way otherwise.
Indeed, that is said in contradiction to scripture;
however, since that [scripture] is sublated by experience—which is its basis because it apprehends the validity of its own nature—how could it possibly have the power to sublate that [experience]?
This might be so.
The validity of the Witness (sākṣin) is accepted with respect to both the nature of the Veda and its authority;
however, regarding other objects such as suffering, its lack of authority is maintained due to contradiction with the Veda.
To the question, "How then does the aforementioned defect arise?", he says: "And not... (na ca).
There is no distinction in the scripture—which is intended as the sublater—over and above the witness who is intended as the object of sublation;
rather, there is a distinction belonging to the witness itself, according to the manner already stated and to be stated hereafter.
This is clear to the disciple. *8,595*
Furthermore, one who asserts that the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) of "I am suffering" and so forth is erroneous should be asked:
is the erroneous nature of the witness-consciousness accepted in all cases, or is there some instances where it possesses validity as well?
He states the fault in the first case: "The nature of the Veda," etc.
The meaning is that [the existence of the object] is established by the witness-consciousness itself;
thus, if that [consciousness] were erroneous, the object would not be established.
Furthermore, one should not say, "Let it not be established in the ultimate sense."
Because it has been accepted that [the Veda] makes known reality (*tattvāvedakatva*).

Now, having restated the second position—that its status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) is accepted regarding the nature and so forth of the Śruti itself—he states the reply: "If that... (*tacced iti*).
Since validity must be admitted in one case, it must also be admitted in the other; why is this so? To this he says, "Because there is no distinction," namely: "And not... (na ca).
The explanation is as before.

Thus, having accepted that the witness (sākṣin) possesses a nature common to other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), it has been stated that the erroneous nature of such [cognitions] as "I am suffering" cannot be established due to the absence of any sublation (bādhaka).
Now, because the witness (sākṣin) is necessarily restricted to truth, the suspicion of error regarding objects such as suffering and the like is not possible.

With the intention that there is no need for searching for a sublater (bādhaka), he supports the witness’s restriction to truth by means of a sublater in the case of the opposite view, [stating]: "If there were a sublation" (*bādha*).
This means: if a sublation were to occur regarding an object experienced and cognized by the witness, then the witness would be non-veridical in some respect.
This was stated because the sublation (*bādha*) of that which is not in accordance with reality is what leads to such a conclusion.
At that time, how can the determination of objects—such as "this is a pillar" or "this is a jar"—be maintained or accepted?
He elaborates on this very point with the words "ko 'pi" (anyone).
For no matter what the subject may be, it cannot be determined with certainty by one who speaks out of delusion.
The meaning is that if a witness who speaks erroneously— that is, one who asserts error in some instance— were to be incorrect in any matter, then there would be no determination of the facts;
as others have also said:
“If knowledge were fallible, what would be the basis for confidence?
[Objection: But surely, both *nirṇaya* (ascertainment) and *niścaya* (certainty) are said to be forms of knowledge characterized by determination (*avadhāraṇātmaka*).
And that arises with respect to objects such as pillars and jars solely through the power of their respective causal complexes (*kāraṇasāmagrī*).

For, by the perception of common characteristics (*sāmānyadharma*) and so forth, conjoined with the absence of a decisive factor (*nirṇāyakābhāva*), a cognition consisting of non-determination (*anavadhāraṇātmaka*) is produced, which is what is designated by the term "doubt" (*saṃśaya*).
And by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) distinct from that, a determinate cognition (*avadhāraṇajñāna*) is produced.
In this regard, what is the utility of the witness's rule of truthfulness (*yāthārthyaniyama*)?
Furthermore, what will be removed by its absence?
It is said:
for here, there is indeed a cognition restricted to a single form, namely, "this is not a pillar."
It is designated by terms such as "ascertainment" (nirṇaya) and so forth;
rather, it is the confidence regarding the actual state of things that arises immediately after that.
For instance:
People say: "It is perceived as a pillar," or "This is indeed a pillar," or else, "But we do not know the true nature of this thing."
For what reason?

Because even among cognitions restricted to a single form, we frequently observe that some are erroneous while others are non-erroneous; therefore, even when a cognition restricted to a single form arises now, it is impossible to have confidence in the actual state of the object.
Let it be granted that the assurance regarding the true nature of an object is a determinative judgment (*nirṇaya*) arising subsequent to the perception of that object.
Even that [judgment] depends precisely upon the determination of whether that perception was erroneous or non-erroneous.
For if the cognition were erroneous, it would be concluded that the object is not as it appears.

If, however, it is an error, then it is of such a nature [as being sublated]. Thus, what is established by the witness through the rule of its being in accordance with reality, and what is removed from it by virtue of its being an error? To this, he says: "Error-ness."
When both error and non-error are admitted as being based on experience, then if one of them is erroneous, how can the other be non-erroneous? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.3.62c–f)
It is true that the determination of a real object depends upon the determination of whether cognitions are erroneous or non-erroneous.

But how, in that case, is it to be determined which among those cognitions regarding a single pillar or similar object is erroneous—such as the cognition of a person—and which is non-erroneous—such as the cognition of the pillar? It cannot be determined from anything at all. Why? Because [there is no basis].
The erroneousness or non-erroneousness of cognitions must be determined by the Witness (sākṣin) alone, based on experience.
It might be argued that the erroneousness or non-erroneousness of cognitions will depend upon defects in the instruments of knowledge, subverting cognitions, or correspondence.
Anticipating the objection as to how there can be such non-determination [of truth], he clarifies the stated point:
"Error and non-error—indeed, everything that is knowable is witnessed by the Witness.
If that Witness were to be corrupted in any respect, how could a definitive conclusion be reached? (Manu 2.3.63)

The erroneousness or non-erroneousness of cognitions, as well as everything required for their ascertainment—such as defects in the instruments of knowledge and so forth—must be determined by the Witness (sākṣin).
This is because there would be the undesirable consequence that what is not determined by the Witness could not be ascertained as erroneous and so on.

If that Witness were defective in some respect and thus unreal, then how could the determination of the defect in the instrument, the erroneousness of the cognition, or the actual nature of the object be established?
This is what is meant:

although the determination that cognitions are erroneous depends upon defects in the causes and so forth, nevertheless, this would not be established if there were no rule regarding the witness-consciousness being in accordance with reality.
For that [object] is not useful in its own essential form,
because that would lead to an over-extension;

rather, it is precisely the ascertainment [of the object], and that ascertainment depends upon the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), either through a direct perception or through a succession of perceptions.
For he ascertains its erroneous nature either by himself determining defects in the causes [of cognition] and so forth, or by apprehending the invalidity of that which grasps it;
and consequently, because it would result in being untrustworthy due to its lack of correspondence with reality in some instances, there would be no certain determination.
However, the ascertainment of non-erroneousness does not depend upon corroboration;
for if it did, defects such as infinite regress would arise, as has already been stated.
Rather, it depends solely upon the witness-consciousness.
However, the inclusion of corroboration occurs only when there is a removal of the suspicion of error;
moreover, even corroboration is not a factor unless it is itself certain,
and that certainty depends precisely upon witnesses.
And if that [testimony] were in some cases non-correspondent with reality, then there would be no determination of either of those two [truth and falsity].
Now, even if there is a restriction on the witnesses being correspondent with reality, it is argued that the determination of whether cognitions are erroneous or non-erroneous is not established;
for correspondence with reality is not functional by its own nature alone.
Because it would lead to an over-extension;
rather, it must indeed be certain,
yet there is no means for its ascertainment.

Therefore, because that [the pillar] is not ascertained, there is indeed no ascertainment of its pillar-ness and so forth, due to the error arising from defects in the causes and the like; thus he says: "The particulars."
All these distinctions indeed fall within the scope of the evidence of witnesses.
They are called "distinguishing factors" (*viśeṣa*) because things are distinguished by them; these are the defects of the cause and so forth.
The connection [of the sentence] is that they are exclusively within the range of the witness's direct perception (*sākṣipratyakṣagocara*).
The meaning is that the determination of the truthfulness of a witness is possible through the witness himself,
and because this matter is established by the fact that the legal proceedings to be described hereafter would otherwise be impossible.
*8,603* If a witness should ever deviate [from the truth], then by that unreliable person— what [could be done]?
There would be no certainty regarding the defects of perception and so forth;
and in the absence of that, the erroneous nature of cognitions could not be determined;
and thus, there would be no ascertainment of the reality of things.
It has been stated that in the absence of a cause, the arising of an effect is impossible;
if it is argued that "let none of this be so," we say no.
If that were the case, it would follow that all worldly conventions, such as rejection and acquisition, would be abolished.
How so?
Because all worldly conventions would not have that [reality] as their causal basis; thus he says: "and having accepted... (ūrīkṛtya ca).
And having accepted all of them, legal procedure proceeds.
The meaning is "having ascertained.
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis.
All of them... [kā]...
Since the legal proceeding proceeds by not accepting the faults of the battle and so forth, the identity of the agent is figurative (*gauṇa*).
Alternatively, it should be explained as "having accepted," "having taken up as a cause," or "having made into a cause."
For instance,
one who has acted out of the delusion "this is silver" [seeks] a defect in the cause and a subverting cognition.

Having ascertained that cognition—that is, having determined its erroneous nature—and having established the reality of the object by concluding "this is not silver, but only mother-of-pearl," one abandons it. Similarly, having perceived "this is water" and suspecting that this cognition might be otherwise even at first sight, one resorts to corroboration;
and having grasped the validity of its own nature and determined its non-erroneousness, one concludes "this is indeed water" and takes hold of it.

Now, it might be argued that there is no such rule that worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) must necessarily be preceded by a determination of the reality of an object in the manner described; for we observe that transactions occur even through doubt and the like. To this, he says: "The witness."
But when witnesses have reached a conclusion, it is called a legal proceeding.

A judicial proceeding (*vyavahāra*) that is undertaken with resolve, free from doubt, and non-contradictory is said by us—according to the method described—to require witnesses; however, this does not apply to every kind of transaction. Furthermore, no specific type of transaction ever deviates from being preceded by a determination of the actual state of the matter.

Anticipating the objection, "Let there be the abolition of worldly convention; what is lost or destroyed?", he states the conclusion of the aforementioned undesirable consequences by way of their contrapositive: "Therefore... (tasmāt).
Therefore, for the sake of establishing universally recognized worldly transactions,
we must always accept only one witness who is entirely free from defects.

Because, if a witness were sometimes unreliable, there would arise the contingency of not ascertaining defects in the cause [of cognition] and so forth; this would lead to the impossibility of determining whether cognitions are erroneous or non-erroneous, which in turn would result in the absence of any determination regarding the true nature of objects, thereby destroying unhesitating and non-contradictory worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
Nor can its elision be admitted,
because it is well-known throughout all the worlds;
and of such a [thing]...
Because it is impossible for worldly investigators to disregard [conventional reality],
and because the consequence of madness would follow if one did not accept objects as they are cognized;

therefore, for the sake of establishing the unhesitating and non-contradictory conventional discourse that is renowned to all the world, the determination of whether a thing is as it truly is or otherwise is the cause (or must be performed).
An actual [error] must be accepted;
for its establishment, one must accept that witnesses determine whether cognitions are erroneous or non-erroneous by means of ascertaining defects in the causes and so forth.

For the sake of establishing that [truth], the witness must be trustworthy; and for the sake of establishing that, it is not accepted by investigators that a witness is always faultless and necessarily true. Now, one might object: "In that case, let there be a rule of necessity that all cognitions are true, according to the direction of the Prābhākaras and others. To this, he says: "Only one... [eka eveti].

The sense is this: since everything is established by the rule that a single [cognition] is in accordance with reality (*yāthārthya*), what is the use of an unproven and scripturally contradicted rule that all cognitions are invariably in accordance with reality?
What follows if it is thus that the witness (*sākṣin*) is invariably non-deviant from the object? To this he says: "Pure" (*śuddha*).
When a witness is established as pure, how can his state of suffering be averted?
By that [reasoning], the state of suffering is understood to belong to the *jīva*; this is the ellipsis.
To the question "And what follows from that?", he says: "upajīvya" (having depended upon).
For that very means of valid cognition which is to be relied upon is indeed what apprehends difference.
Scripture and inference have that [perception] as their foundational means of valid cognition (*upajīvya-pramāṇa*); therefore, it is the grasper of difference and the prover of difference.
Thus, the sense is that because it contradicts its own foundation, the scripture teaching non-difference and so forth lacks authority.
To the question "What follows from that?", he concludes the meaning of the Sūtra with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord is firmly established by the power of the Śruti.
The scripture [states], "He is distinct and inconceivable," and so forth.
Capability consists in being without opposition. *Om. But because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated as such, like the Intelligent One (the Self). Om.*

If, in this way, the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) alone were established as ultimately real, then what would be the status of non-dualistic Śruti texts such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi), and Smṛti texts such as "I am Hari" (ahaṃ hariḥ)?

For it is not reasonable to claim that these are entirely devoid of authority like inference, since their causes—namely, being authorless (apauruṣeya) and being spoken by a trustworthy person (āptokta)—are present. To resolve this doubt, the Sūtra [is presented].
