"But because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated as such, just like the Wise One (the individual soul).
He explains this with the words: "Nevertheless," and so forth.
However, because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated by that name, as in the case of the Supreme Intellect (prājña).
Nevertheless, qualities such as consciousness and bliss, which resemble Him, remain as its essential nature even in liberation. (Māṇḍūkya Anuvyākhyāna 2.3.67)
Therefore, these scriptural passages indeed proclaim [the Self] as being non-different,
and the Puranic statements do so by relying on the non-difference that exists through similarity.
Although there is indeed a difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, the connection [of the word "non-different"] is nevertheless "as if non-different."
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of specification,
and we shall explain that later.
"Similar to that" means similar to the qualities of the Supreme Self.
The term "essence" (*sāra*) is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*), and its meaning is explained as "essential nature.
Of what? Of this living being (*jīva*). Why?

Since it remains even in liberation (mukti) and even in absolute isolation (kaivalya), it is like non-difference; that is, "as if non-different. This [usage] is to be added as an extension to the rule "tatra tasyeva" (Pāṇini 5.1.116).
This is due to the application [of the term] by the student;
or rather, "non-difference" (abheda) refers to that which indicates it.
The connection is therefore with the words "for this very reason" (ata eva).
These have been cited by others.
The word "hi" (for) indicates an obstacle to the primary [meaning].
The phrase "sādṛśyena" (by similarity) is an explanation of "ata eva" (for this very reason).

The meaning of the sentence is that non-difference is simply similarity; thus, "similarity-non-difference" refers to this figurative designation, as in the case of "Devadatta is a lion. Indeed, by the proponents of non-duality (advaitavādins), the primary grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the terms *tat* and *tvam* is accepted through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a single part [of their meanings], by abandoning the mutually contradictory portions of their respective referents.
Therefore, it is better to accept that both terms have their primary meanings and to accept that the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) alone is figurative;
furthermore, the indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparya-liṅga*) have been interpreted differently in various places.

Intending to show that this explanation of the non-difference taught in the Sūtra is merely illustrative, he states another point by repeating what was already said: "And because of similarity. (*sādṛśyācca*)

"And because of similarity, because of being the primary [cause], and also because of independence, they speak of the identity of the individual soul with the Lord... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 12.3.69a–c).
The grammatical connection is: "also because of being the primary [cause]."
The sacred revelations (śruti) say so;
and the same applies to the statements from the Purāṇas.
The restatement of what has already been said is for the sake of facilitating comprehension.
Its preeminence constitutes its distinction.
It has been stated that designations such as "That thou art" are figurative on account of similarity.

The teaching beginning with "There is no other seer than this" is figurative (lākṣaṇika) by virtue of [the self's] independence and preeminence. In that context, by the word "seer," both the superimposed distinction and independence are indicated.
Thus, the meaning that results is: "There is no other seer who is distinct or independent."
Alternatively, even the instruction "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and so forth is explained as being figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) by virtue of [the latter term] denoting sovereignty and preeminence.
For instance,
by the word "that" (*tat*), its sovereignty and preeminence are indicated.
Furthermore, by those two [terms], its status as an object is indicated;
consequently, the meaning of the sentence becomes that it has that as its primary focus and is dependent upon that.
This, too, is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Another interpretation of [the passage] beginning with "Not this, you are" (neti neti) should also be seen here.
It might be argued:
the word *tu* in the Sūtra has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), and by it, any meaning other than similarity is excluded.
To the question, "How then can this be described as a different meaning?", he explains otherwise with the word "not."
... nor anywhere does it abandon its own essential nature.
"In some instances" means that they do not state the identity of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), which is the sense of the word "but" (*tu*);
it does not mean, however, the cessation of [the mention of] predominance (*prādhānya*) and so forth.

"Let it be so that the individual soul (jīva) is one with Brahman; however, how is that [oneness] of the liberated soul (mukta) to be explained? Nor is it correct to say that even that is according to the logic already stated, for if that were the case, specific statements such as 'But when for him... would be untenable. To this, he says: "Identity of state."
Residing in the same place and being of one mind, however, is the distinction for one who is liberated.
The word "by Īśa" (īśena) continues [from the previous context].
It is not only the three previously mentioned causes that are intended; rather, these two causes are distinguished.
Therefore, the statement regarding their non-difference as qualifiers is logically justified.
In that case, the designation of identity based on the identity of location is figurative (lākṣaṇika),
because that which is one in its location is applied to the occupants of that location.
However, when the application is based on the cause of unanimity (aikamatya), it is a case of figurative indication of the indicated (lakṣitalakṣaṇā).
"Because the object is one, the cognition is one; and therefore, for those possessed of intelligence... (*8,616*).

Furthermore, with the intention that the similarity which was stated to be common to all living beings is unmanifest in the transmigrating soul but manifest in the liberated one, he says "And the similarity," meaning that it is also logical to speak of non-difference specifically with that in mind.
And similarity [is determined] specifically by... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.70c //
The phrase "by the Lord" (īśena) continues [from the previous context].
Now, an objection is raised: "But similarity and so forth are found even in insentient things;
how then can it be said of them that 'all this, indeed, is Brahman'?"

In passages such as "Viṣṇu is the beings, Viṣṇu is the worlds, Viṣṇu is the forests, the mountains, and the directions," the designation of identity with the Supreme Self occurs only in certain instances, and not generally with respect to the individual soul (jīva). Therefore, he says: "Of the insentient [entities]," etc.
But for the dull-witted, there are only two [options].
That which has that as its primary factor is precisely its dependence on it;
this is the connection with the word "of insentient things.
To the question, "Since a third [factor], namely similarity, also exists, how can there be only two? he says: "It may be..."
There may be a very slight similarity with the Supreme Self as the third [category].

The term "of the insentient" (jaḍānām) continues [to apply here]. It is true that there is similarity, but it exists only through [the qualities of] existence and so forth, and not through bliss and so forth as in the case of the living soul (jīva).
Therefore, since only two [categories] exist, the statement regarding their abundance is logical.
If it is argued that similarity with Ānanda and the others does not even exist among the individual souls (*jīva*),
because some individual souls are admitted to be of a different nature, let it be so.
The statement "That thou art" is not addressed to every living being,
because such beings lack the qualification for the Vedas;
rather, it is addressed to one who is fit to be an enjoyer [of the fruits of knowledge], and thus there is no fault.

In this context, the identity of location is stated with reference to the forms of the Lord residing in the Ocean of Milk and so forth; therefore, it is not common to both sentient beings and insentient matter.
By explaining it as non-difference from the insentient, the illustrative example "like the Prājña" is also explained;
for it is said in the Sūtra, "like the Prājña."
This is its meaning:
just as the designation of non-difference regarding the Wise One (prājña) is not primary, so it is here.

Since no specific counter-correlative is mentioned therein, the entire designation of non-difference—such as "Consciousness, Bliss, Brahman"—should be understood as non-primary by virtue of similarity with [the attributes of] eternity and so forth.
Intending that this [misconception] not arise, he says: "Īśa" (Lord).
"And in every respect, there is a primary identity of form between the Lord and his forms, actions, qualities, and likewise his limbs. (Manu 2.3.71)
Forms are fish and so forth;
actions are creation and so forth;
qualities are knowledge and so forth.
The term "of the same class" (savarṇa) is connected with each [member of the compound].
The word "tathā" (likewise) is used in the sense of conjunction.
The word "eva" (only/precisely) is construed with the word "mukhyataḥ" (primarily).
The "parts" are the hands and so forth;
their "identity of nature" (svarūpaikya) means identity with the nature of the Lord (īśvara), or rather, the statement that establishes that [identity]. This is the sense.
The remainder [of the sentence] is that it must be explained primarily [in this way].
The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of excluding insentient things (jaḍa).
Thus, the intended meaning is that this example is indeed a specific instance of an insentient thing.
Nor is there the fault of the reason being equivalent to the probandum (sādhyasama), because this inquiry has been undertaken against one who maintains the non-difference of all living beings.
If it is asked, "Why is this so? [the answer is: No.
In that regard, because it has been stated that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in perceiving difference, he says: "Just as... (*yathā*).
"Just as water rained upon a mountain peak flows away in different directions,
so too one who perceives phenomena as distinct runs after them alone"—
according to this Vedic scripture... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.72a-e]

Just as water that falls upon a mountain peak in a difficult place flows downward, so too one who perceives the attributes of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-dharma*) as distinct from Him rushes toward hell immediately following that perception; this is the meaning.
[Objection: But surely, for you, there is both difference and non-difference regarding the attributes of the Lord?
In this way, the scriptural example—that the statement of absolute non-difference is not primary—will have its application unrestricted.
And let this scripture be intended for the purpose of censuring the perception of absolute difference; therefore, he says: "Nor both."
...nor is both [of them]—that which is called difference and non-difference—accepted.
The word "it is accepted" (*iṣyate*) is understood as referring to the author of the Sūtra.

While one might have said "difference and non-difference are not accepted," the expression "both, called difference and non-difference" should be understood as being in accordance with the explanation of the scriptural passage (*śruti*) that is about to be cited.
To the question "Why are they not accepted?", he says: "Because [Brahman] is indeed one alone. (*ekameva*)
"Only one, without a second; there is no diversity whatsoever here. He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity."
Thus, from the phrase "as it is heard," there is the rejection of both difference and non-difference.
It is one and undivided;
for this very reason it is said that even a single object, such as a jar, is perceived as possessing a division of parts.
It is "without a second," meaning it is devoid of any equal or superior.
In this Brahman, there exists nothing whatsoever that is manifold, such as qualities and so forth. Yet,
whoever perceives the qualities and so forth existing here in Brahman as if they were manifold and distinct— and by the force of the word "as if" (iva), as non-different from it— [sees falsely].
"He attains death after death, [and] hell"—
this is because of the word "iti" as it occurs in the Śruti;
and this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
From the word *eva*, it is understood that the refutation of difference and non-difference has been accomplished;
thus, the construction is "therefore it is not accepted.
To the question, "How is this obtained from the use of the word *iva*? he says: "The word *iva*..."
And "both" refers to similarity; thus it is stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*.
The meaning is that what was stated regarding both [entities] by means of the first term applies to the second, which is its counterpart.
And here,
the word *iva* is employed as if [the two were] not non-identical (*anānā*).

By the statement "it grasps," the primary [view] known as difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) is refuted; the word "speech exists" is the remainder [of the sentence]. *Śabdanirṇaya* is the name of a specific treatise.
Thus concludes the section on "Teaching as Separate" (*pṛthagupadeśādhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
Now begins the section on "Parts" (*aṃśādhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.

Oṃ. [The soul] is a part [of Brahman], because of the designation of difference, and also because otherwise the state of being taught as a speaker of doubt would result; moreover, some [scriptural passages] record it thus. Oṃ.
Some explain it as follows:
the individual soul (jīva) is a part (aṃśa) of the Supreme Self (paramātman),
and this state of being a part does not consist in being a constituent cause (ārambhakatva).
Because the Supreme Self is unoriginated, it possesses no fragmentation; because it is indivisible, it possesses no divisibility.
Nor is it a mere spatial part, for that would entail the consequence of impermanence, as in the case of a jar or similar objects.
Rather, what is it? It is the state of being both different and non-different.

In this regard, some maintain that difference is adventitious while non-difference is innate; and they hold that the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is beginningless, indeterminable ignorance (*anirvācyā-avidyā*).
Others, however, maintain that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth are indeed real.
Why is this so?
Because of various designations such as "Two birds" and "The eternal among the non-eternal," and so forth.
Furthermore, this is so because of scriptural designations of non-difference such as "That thou art" and "I am Brahman.
Moreover, it is not that there is both difference and non-difference between the single individual soul (jīva) and Brahman; rather, this applies to all souls.
As for the statement that some read "the *brahmadāśas* and *brahmakitavas*" as "the *brahmararas* and *dāśakitava-ādityas*," and so forth—
that is incorrect.
For instance:
What is this non-difference? Is it primary, or is it secondary,
characterized by similarity and so forth?
He refutes the first [position]—namely, that of difference—with the words "of difference":
"Because of the designation of manifoldness, and also otherwise; for some record that he possesses the nature of a fisherman, a kitava, and so forth.
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.43) "Because of the statement regarding difference even in liberation, that position is also refuted. (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 2.3.75ab)
The connection is "even in liberation.
That position is the position of primary non-difference:
that the difference of the individual soul (jīva) from the Supreme Self (paramātman) is merely adventitious (aupādhika).
However, by one who asserts that non-difference is innate, the absence of difference in liberation must be stated;
for in that state, ignorance, the internal organ, and so forth do not exist. And that [assertion] is not tenable.
Because even in the state of liberation, the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is declared by the previously cited scriptures and traditional texts (smṛtis),
this position must be rejected precisely because it contradicts authoritative means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "because of being conscious, etc. (cetana-tvāt).

If it is maintained that similarity, such as sentience and so forth, constitutes non-difference, then this has already been accepted by us; however, we never accept an identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekatā*) anywhere.
"Similarity" is an illustration; it should be understood that "having that as the primary [object]" and so forth are also included.
If non-difference is accepted, how can there be a refutation of that position? To this, he says: "No."
"In some cases" means in saṃsāra or in liberation.

He states that the acceptance of both difference and non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is not only contrary to reason, but also contrary to scripture—thus he says: "Not by anyone... [8.625]
There is no non-difference whatsoever, nor even difference-and-non-difference anywhere,
for Viṣṇu, except in relation to a collection [of attributes] or apart from his own qualities and so forth.
Thus, according to the sacred revelation, there is no distinction or non-distinction of that [Self] by anything whatsoever.
Non-difference accompanied by difference is "difference-and-non-difference" (*bhedābheda*).
It is to be connected with the phrase "even in some cases.
The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction.
In the case of the *ṛte*-construction, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) must also be added by way of supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyātavyā*),
because of its usage in Vedic scripture (*śrauta-prayoga*).
The word "also" (*api*) is used for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaye*).
The word "vā" has the sense of an alternative; and that is a fixed alternative [applied] except in the case of a collective whole (samudāya).
Difference-and-non-difference exists with respect to something;
non-difference does not exist without its own qualities and so forth.
"With respect to anything whatsoever" is the logical connection (*anvaya*).
By this, Yadavaprakāśa— who asserts that both difference and non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman are innate,
and that difference is not based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as ignorance (avidyā),

and therefore there is no contradiction with our own statements regarding the difference of the liberated— has also been refuted. This is because [our position maintains] that even in liberation, difference exists [only as a conventional reality].

"Because it contradicts specific scriptural statements such as 'in some cases by someone' (*kvacit kenacit*). [Objection: If this is so, and there is neither difference nor non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, then how can there be an illustration of scriptural passages concerning difference and non-difference in the Sūtras? To this, he states the intended meaning of the Sūtra according to his own view: "Non-difference... (*abhedeti*).
The scriptural texts concerning non-difference [are applicable] because of being a part... // Mānava-Dharmaśāstra 2.3.77c //
This is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood that "and the scriptural texts concerning difference" is implied.
For the remainder of the sense is that these [texts] are indeed consistent because [the individual souls] are parts [of Brahman].

Having stated the grounds for the designation of various kinds of relationships [between the individual soul and Brahman], the author now states an argument based on presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) with the words "and otherwise, too" (*anyathā cāpi*), and so forth.
For instance, there certainly exist scriptural passages that speak of both difference and non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.
And these [distinctions] are possible only because the individual soul (jīva) is a part of Brahman, and not otherwise.
For if the jīva were absolutely different from Brahman—like a jar from a cloth—then the scriptural texts concerning non-difference would be contradicted.
Alternatively, if it were non-different from Brahman, then the scriptural texts concerning difference would be sublated.
Nor should it be said that the consistency of the two scriptural passages is achieved by resorting to both difference and non-difference;
for that would contradict the cited scripture stating, "not by anything.
Therefore, because the scriptures regarding difference and non-difference cannot otherwise be explained, the individual soul [is] Brahman...
The meaning of the sūtra is simply that this [objection] must be accepted;
and for this purpose, it should be construed as a single syntactical unit with the passage beginning "not by anyone," and so forth,
as has been stated.
"Since this [individual soul] is described both as distinct from and non-distinct from Him, its status as a part (aṃśatva) is intended; difference and non-difference are not primary.
If it is accepted that the individual soul is a part of the Supreme Self, how then is there no admission of both difference and non-difference?

Because it is impossible to define "being a part" (aṃśatva) in any other way, and because non-difference is admitted in the case of the Fish and other incarnations who are parts of the Supreme Lord, he says: "And similarity... (sādṛśyaṃ ca).
...and its similarity consists in being a part of it.
The individual soul's status as a portion of the Supreme Lord, however, consists in its similarity to Him;
by the word "and" (ca), it is meant that it also possesses existence and so forth dependent upon Him.
By this, the objection that this section is already covered by the previous argument regarding [the soul's nature being] like masculinity and so forth is also refuted.
Alternatively, the word "ca" (and) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
It is true that the word "part" (*aṃśa*) is used in the case of the fish and so forth based on non-difference.

Nevertheless, since there is a similarity with respect to the primary part, the very existence of that [Brahman] constitutes the "part-nature" (*aṃśatva*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), characterized by its own existence; thus, this word "part" is used in a secondary sense. Regarding the multivalence of the word "part," in order to dispel the doubt as to why the Fish-incarnation and others are parts consisting of His very nature (*svarūpāṃśa*) while the individual souls are parts that are distinct (*bhinnāṃśa*)—and specifically, why the former are parts of His nature while the latter are not—the following is stated:
He recites the scriptural statement: "But the portion... (Manu 2.3.78):
"But the portion is to be known as twofold: the portion consisting of its own nature and that which is other.
The distinct portion shall have diminished power, being endowed with only a slight degree of similarity."
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the Lord] is indeed twofold and not merely of one kind.
Furthermore, the phrase "possessing some degree of similarity" should be explained in both ways as before.
"Power" (*sāmarthya*) is characterized by being the creator of the world and so forth.
The essential nature (*svarūpa*) consists of [attributes] such as perfect bliss (*pūrṇānanda*);

its state (*sthiti*) consists of dimensions such as omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*). If that very [Self] is endowed with those capacities and so forth, it is the "this-portion" (*idaṃśa*); in that case, it should be understood as the "portion of the essential nature" (*tatsvarūpāṃśa*).
"Manifestations" is an illustration of that very [point].
Likewise, "as living beings," and so forth, should also be understood as an illustration of this.
By this, the intended meaning of the statement "the Supreme is not thus, like light and so on" has been expressed. *8,633*

Although there is equality in the sense that both the fish and other [manifestations] and the individual souls (*jīva*) are portions of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), they are not of the same kind;

rather, the fish and others are portions of His very nature (*svarūpāṃśa*), whereas the souls are distinct portions (*vibhinnāṃśa*). To dispel any doubt regarding this point, the author of the Sūtras has provided the analogy "like light" (*prakāśavat*).
However, these [analogies] appear somewhat inappropriate, because in both cases there exists an equality in the coexistence of difference and non-difference.
In order to dispel the doubt that [the statement] might refer to the presiding deities (*abhimānidevatā*), the Commentary states: “This is with reference to the presiding deities.
Since that is not entirely clear, he clarifies the examples from the Sūtras, beginning with the word “sūrya” (the sun).
One [deity] presides over the solar orb with the conceit of its light;
then there is Sūrya, and the lord of the waters of the outer ocean beyond the seven seas.
By virtue of its solidity, the deity of the earth— even of Mount Meru and the like—
is the goddess Dhara.
The sun is the possessor of the solar orb, and its portion is that which possesses the conceit of being its light; and that portion is one and the same.
The word "yathā" (as) is to be construed with every instance.
The word "atha" (now/then) is used in the sense of conjunction.
The presiding deity of the outer ocean is the presiding deity of the seventh sea, and her constituent part is one and the same.
The goddess Dharā, who is the presiding deity of the earth extending fifty crores [of yojanas] and is its constitutive whole, [resides on] Meru and so forth.
Even the deity presiding over the earth is one and the same in its essential nature as a partial manifestation (*aṃśa*).
Since it is well known in the Purāṇas that there are presiding deities (*abhimāninaḥ*) for Mount Meru, the Himavat, and so forth, it is therefore said: "by way of hardness."
According to the Vedic revelation, "That which is hard is earth," Dharādevī alone is the presiding deity (abhimāninī) over the entire earth,
while others are the presiding deities over its intermediate parts.
By this, the aspect of its own nature (svarūpāṃśa) has been illustrated.
He shows the application to the case in question (dārṣṭāntika) with the words "in this very same way."
In this very same way, the one Lord Viṣṇu, the imperishable,
whose qualities are ever complete, remains present through various forms of incarnation.
The construction is as follows: the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is the whole (aṃśin), existing in various forms of incarnations (avatāra), while the parts (aṃśa) are one and the same.
The demonstration of non-difference is established in accordance with the forthcoming sūtra: "He is imperishable, always full of attributes.
Having first explained the illustration of the distinct parts, he explains the subject of the analogy (dārṣṭāntika) with the words: "feces, urine... and so on.
Just as those who pride themselves on excrement, urine, eyes,
and so forth are distinct from the deities such as the Sun, even so this transmigrating soul is separate from the Supreme Self.

Deities whose names have become corrupted are partial manifestations (aṃśa-rūpa) that are distinct from their source-deities— the Sun, Varuṇa, and Earth— just as [the parts] are distinct from the wholes.

In order to logically establish the distinctness of the individual souls (jīvāṃśas) from their source (aṃśin), the Supreme Lord, the Sūtra states: "Permission and prohibition [apply] due to connection with a body, as in the case of light and so forth. Here too, suspecting that the examples might be inconsistent, he explains them as referring to the presiding deities (abhimānin): "Due to connection with a body," etc.

Permission and prohibition apply [to the soul] due to its connection with the body, as in the case of light and other such things. Furthermore, because they are corrupted by the defects of the body, those deities known as *apabhraṣṭa* are distinct from the gods such as the Sun and are always subject to their favor.
In this very way, transmigrating beings are considered distinct from Viṣṇu;
they are to be favored by Him alone, and through His grace, they attain liberation.
But it is not intended that those in the form of fish and so forth are to be favored.

The state of being a deity consists in the possession of powers such as invisibility and so forth, [attained] through the defects residing in another body. The word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin the two reasons.

For it should also be understood that those [beings] are indeed recipients of favor from the sun and other [luminaries], because the cessation of obstacles depends upon their grace. In the phrase "and recipient of favor" (*anugrāhyaś ca*), the word *yataḥ* (because) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
Furthermore, the phrase "due to being smeared with bodily defects" (*dehadoṣaliptatvāt*) is also to be understood.

Now, one might object that the three reasons—such as permission and so forth—exist even in the portions consisting of the Fish incarnation and others; thus, they are inconclusive (anaikāntika) and are not sufficient to prove a difference between the individual souls (jīvāṃśas) and the Supreme Lord. To this, he says: "But not... and so on.

The phrase "being worthy of favor" is an elliptical expression; the remainder of the sense is that [the soul] is not so favored by the force of such scriptural passages as, "They are not born at all. *8,637*

In this very context, the Sūtra states: "And because there is no continuity, there is no confusion. This is understood as establishing only the difference of those portions of the individual soul (jīva) from the Supreme Lord, and not their non-difference, as in the case of the fish and other [examples].
Therefore, he explains it as an illustration: "by means of qualities."
And because there is no continuity [of a single entity], there is no confusion [between different moments];
furthermore, because he is filled with all qualities without exception, there is no primary non-difference from others. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.3.85cd)

The phrase "of those having the forms of fish and so forth" continues [from the previous context]. There is non-difference of the Lord with other individual souls (jīvas) due to the non-difference from the primary [form], and yet there is no [non-difference] because of their incomplete qualities.
The [sūtra] "permission and avoidance" (anujñāparihārau) should also be explained as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of this same point;
or rather, the sentence should be construed as: "for that purpose, but not for those having the form of fish and so forth. *8,638* // Oṃ, and it is merely an appearance, Oṃ. //
Thus, the difference of the individual soul (*jīva*), who is a part (*aṃśa*), from the Lord (*īśvara*) has been established by means of valid proofs (*pramāṇa*).

As for the one who would seek to prove non-difference on the grounds of being a part, if his reason is merely the fact of being denoted by the word "part," then its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) has already been stated.

If, however, the reason is actual primary part-hood, then it is unestablished (*asiddhi*). Thus he explains the aphorism *cet syād ābhāsa eva* (if [it were so], it would be a mere fallacy) with the words beginning *aṃśa*.
And it is merely a manifestation;
all partial manifestations are not, in the primary sense, parts of the Supreme.
All beings are indeed living souls (*jīvas*).
He confirms that the living souls are partial manifestations (*aṃśābhāsa*) by means of another scriptural passage, beginning with "Just as... (*yathā*).
Just as this shadow exists in a man, so is this [world] spread out upon him.
Likewise, within this Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), this entire multitude of living beings is spread out; this very fact constitutes His being their part (aṃśatva)—this is the intended meaning.

Now, one might object: is this not contradicted by the Śruti? For in the mantra, "A foot of Him are all beings, three feet of Him are the immortal in heaven," the word *dyu* refers to Anantāsana, Śvetadvīpa, and Vaikuṇṭha, and therein reside three forms [of the Lord]. As for those denoted by the word *bhūta* (beings) [in the verse],...

Anticipating the objection that living beings (*jīvas*) are also designated as "feet" of the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), the author—intending to show that it is logical to assume multiple meanings for the word "foot" based on the force of specific scriptural statements—says: "But not... (*na tv iti*).
"But these living beings are not like the feet of a man;
rather, they are the very qualities of that Supreme Self, existing as His manifestations.
Thus did the supreme Śruti speak concerning Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme.
Like the three immortal feet of Puruṣa, as in the case of the man's feet;
why?
Because they are full.
He spoke of Nārāyaṇa, who exists in the form of manifestations,
who is superior to and distinct from the portions of individual souls.
It was stated that this chapter was commenced for the purpose of determining the true nature of the deities and so forth.
To what conclusion has this determination arrived? Therefore, in order to facilitate its comprehension, he states it in summary form: "It is imperishable."
The Blessed Viṣṇu is imperishable; he is the abode of Lakṣmī and remains established in dissolution.
He remains even during the dissolution (pralaya) entirely free from the decay of the body and other such elements.

By this [the Sūtras] state: "But the existence of the existent is impossible, because of the impossibility [of its destruction]," and "The Self is not [destroyed], because of the eternity [implied] by scripture, and on account of those [scriptural passages]."
Thus, the purport of the section is stated.
Regarding the phrase "the abode of Lakṣmī":
by stating that even the Goddess remains during the dissolution [of the universe], [it is indicated] by the term *viyat* (space).
Because she is characterized by defects, her birth is not like that of the individual soul (jīva).

By the inclusion of the terms "ether" (viyat) and so forth, it is indicated that the production of bodies and so on for Brahmā and the others occurs only during the state of identifying with those [elements], and not in liberation.
This it indicates by the words "by the liberated ones" (muktaiḥ).
He is constantly meditated upon by the liberated ones, beginning with Brahmā, who abide in various degrees of excellence.
Nevertheless, with the intention that the gradation indicated by the establishment of the sequence of creation and dissolution does not disappear even there, it is said: "The gradation [is] heavy."
"But the sequence here is by way of reversal" means that the sequence for dissolution is stated as the reverse of the sequence of creation.
To show what that sequence in creation is, he states the purport of the section concerning ether (*ākāśa*) with the words: "The primordial nature (*prakṛti*)."

The fourfold set consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), time (kāla), and the Vedas is eternal by its very nature; however, it is said that their "origination" occurs merely through the attainment of specific manifestations from Viṣṇu, while Lakṣmī is the presiding deity over them.
Then, from this [Prakṛti], Vāsudeva produced the male named Brahmā, who is the Sūtrātman and is also called Prāṇa; and the two goddesses are those who regard themselves as Prakṛti.
From him was born Rūpa, the great egoity (ahaṅkṛti) of Brahmā; from him came Śiva, known as the intellect (buddhi) of Brahmā; from him Indra, called the mind (manas);
and from him Skanda and all the other gods were born.
And Lakṣmī, who identifies with that [nature], is likewise; such is the meaning.

Then, since one might ask what the sequence of creation is, he states the purport of the section concerning ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*) while demonstrating that sequence: "Nature (*prakṛti*)," and so forth.
And Lakṣmī, who identifies with that [state], is likewise; such is the meaning.
"Then" means immediately after that.
From Saṅkarṣaṇa comes he whose name is Prāṇa.
The two goddesses Sarasvatī and Bhāratī [arise] from the principle of Mahat, which considers itself primordial matter;
from that, from the ego (ahaṅkāra).
From that very [text], Indra and Skanda [are mentioned];
others are those who take pride in the [lower] principles (*tattva*).

There is no fault here, for even though these [deities] are merely indicated, a definitive determination will be made by means of the passage beginning with "likewise, the vital breath" (*tathā prāṇaḥ*) in order to dispel any further suspicion regarding their eligibility (*adhikāra*).
He states the intended meaning for establishing the sequence and reversal of creation and dissolution with the words "Therein."
In that case, the earlier one is superior by virtue of all qualities in their entirety.
"In all respects" means "in all [the elements].
He states the intended meaning of such passages as "From that, fire [arose]" and "Through meditation upon that": "And from them," etc.
And from them, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.92c]
The word "superior" (śreyān) continues [from the previous context].
Here, the word "in its entirety" (samastaśas) is either connected with the fifth case ending.
It has been stated that the birth and dissolution of everything depend upon the Supreme Lord.
And [the scripture] provides the impetus for activity through such passages as "But that [is known] from another" (*parāttu tacchūteḥ*).
He states its purport: "dependent upon that."
... these are always dependent upon him. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.92d)
Birth, subsistence, dissolution, ignorance, destiny, knowledge, transmigration, and liberation... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.93a-c //
These entities begin with birth and end with liberation.
The word "of these" (eteṣām), which will be mentioned later, is also connected here.
Although it is a dual compound treated as a singular, the absence of the neuter gender is a Vedic anomaly (chāndasa).
Just as in the rule *yuvoranākau*,

[the author] says "subordination to Him" (*tadadhīnatvam*) to show that even though there is an absence of birth for one who is liberated, there is indeed subordination to the Blessed One regarding [their] continued existence and so forth.
...their dependence upon him is by no means lost. // MAnu 2.3.93cd //
"Even in liberation... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.94a). Regarding these [beings] beginning with Brahmā, he states the supreme object of knowledge: "He alone," and so forth.
He alone is independent and possesses perfect, auspicious qualities.
He summarizes: "Thus."
Thus has the Lord declared in this chapter, based on both scriptural authority and logical reasoning.

Thus ends the fourth section (Gaganacaraṇa) in this second chapter of the commentary on the *Anuvyākhyāna*— the work of the venerable Pūrṇaprajña Bhagavatpāda— composed by the ascetic named Praguṇajayatīrtha, as a clarification of the meaning of difficult passages.
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter.
*8,647* Now begins the fourth quarter of the second chapter.

Although in the fourth quarter (*pāda*) as well, only the mutual contradictions among the scriptural statements are resolved, it was already indicated previously that the distinction [of the quarters] is established by virtue of their having the internal self (*adhyātma*) as their subject matter.
To show the division of the quarters in another manner, he says: "The meaning of the scripture" (*śrutyartha*).

Where the meaning of the Veda appears to be contradicted by either the Vedic texts themselves or by reason, the Lord establishes its determination through most excellent arguments; this is what is expressed by this quarter-verse... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.4.1a-e].

Although the intended meaning is established even by saying merely "the Śruti," since the contradiction among sentences exists only through their meanings, the commencement of this section (pāda) is nevertheless for the sake of determining the meaning and not for the sake of determining its authority; thus, the word "meaning" (artha) was stated to show that there is no loss of its status as Mīmāṃsā.

Although there are also logical arguments (*yukti*) in the previous section (*pāda*), nevertheless, the distinction here is that these [arguments] are more powerful because they possess a pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth established by scripture (*āgama*).
It was stated "as if" (*iva*) because a definitive resolution is difficult when there is a contradiction regarding ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*).
This refers to cases concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other such subjects.
The meaning of the scripture, beginning with "origination and so forth," appears as if it were contradicted by the scriptural texts when accompanied by reasoning.
The construction is: "that is the final determination.

To the objection—"When the prima facie view has been established by means of scriptural texts accompanied by reasoning, how can there be a determination of the opposite meaning by scripture alone?"—it is said: "by that which is most distinguished."
By this [word], which is present in the intellect;

likewise, since the meaning of the sūtras beginning with "prāṇāḥ" (the vital breaths) is already clear in the Bhāṣya itself, he summarizes the arguments of the preceding and following positions and says: "In that regard... (tatra).
In this regard, the Vedic revelation is of clear meaning.
Discrepancy with specific scriptural statements, greatness, manifest excellent qualities, perceived irrationality, equality, the capacity of the agent, and intermixture. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.4.2)
In the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*), such well-determined logical reasons (*yukti*) are presented;
however, it is the Lord himself who has declared these very same logical reasons for the sake of the final determination (*nirṇaya*).
In that regard, [this occurs] in the fourth quarter (*pāda*).
"Such as these" means those denoted by the word "that.

Regarding the conclusion (*nirṇaya*), which is the established tenet (*siddhānta*): if they are such [as previously described], how could they reach a conclusion? To this it is said: "But when well-concluded."
The ellipsis is "such objects.
To the question "Why is this so?", it is said: "by itself" (svayam).
The connection is with the word "by himself" (svayameva).

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in this commentary on the *Anuvyākhyāna*— the work of the venerable Pūrṇaprajña Bhagavatpāda— composed by the ascetic named Praguṇajayatīrtha, which explains the meaning of difficult words and sentences.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
